units.tr: To the most illustrious, most reverend and heroic princes, bearers of heroic and unique virtue, Lord Frederick the Younger, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Upper and Lower Bavaria, etc., and also Lord Otto, Landgrave of Hesse, etc., administrator-elect of Hirschfeld: to their Lordships and most gracious patrons, Rudolph Goclenius, Doctor of Medicine, offers, dedicates and consecrates this treatise on prolonging life well and healthfully, with due reverence, in humble submission and obedience, with a humble hand.

units.la: SAnitatem, Principes Illustrissimi, summum & maximum mum esse bonum & donum, vixq; habere se vllum in hac vita praestantius, nemo, nisi cyclopica in barbarie natus, inficias ibit. Vnde sequitur, eam medicinę partem longe caeteris esse praestantiorem, quae docet rationem & modum sanitatis conseruandae, & ex consequenti vitae prorogandae, absque enim illa haec prorogari non poterit. Sanitas illa potissimum consistit in opportuna & idonea qualitate, quantitate, vtendi ratione & occasione sumendorum, vt sunt esculenta ac potulenta, itemq; aer proximē mènos ambiens. His tribus illegitimè intemperantiusq; adhibitis, malaq; qualitate vitiatis, magnę ac pernitiosę mortalib. struuntur insidiæ, vnde sæpe perit homo funeris ante diem. Quapropter cum horis successiuis, legitimisq; officiis perfunctus meditari cœperim, seu potius efformandum suscepérim vniuersæ hygieinæ, hoc est, sanitatis prorogandæ corpus, proplasmaq; effingere vniuersum, ad quod angustius opus aliquādo dedolari possit, ægre tamen ac difficulter omnia pro animi sententia perperficere potui, ob varia quæ ex parte mea mihi obiecta sunt domi forisq; obstacula. Parte tantū, quantū per ingenii imbecillitatē licuit mihi esse industrio & otioso, in lucem emitto, malo enim in eo periculum facere, in quo errare foret leuius, & me in parte operis potius quàm in ipso toto censoriis hominū iudiciis exponere. Erunt, qui hunc meum conatum & laborem improba contradicendi cupiditate sunt improbaturi, quod post eximios viros, qui de hac materia scripserunt, ego inter hos obscurissimi rissimus idem argumentum tracto, inque medium proferre audeo. Non defuerunt, qui peculiares tractatus de hoc scripserunt erudite eruditi viri, nec forsan defuturi sunt, qui omnis doctrinae & laborum conficientissimi praestituri sunt id acrius & ingeniosius. In quos ego incidi, ii vel breuiter & stricte nimis, vel accurate & methodice minus materia illam pertractarunt. Quapropter non gloriae cupiditate, quae praestantibus fere ingeniis omnibus est insita, adductus in tam trito a praeclaris viris
units.tr: Health, most illustrious princes, is the highest and greatest good and gift, and no one, unless born among the Cyclopean barbarians, will deny that there is nothing more excellent in this life. From this it follows that that part of medicine which teaches the reasoning and method of preserving health, and consequently of prolonging life, is far more excellent than the rest, for without it life cannot be prolonged. That health consists chiefly in the right and suitable quality, quantity, manner and occasion of using the things we take in, such as food and drink, and likewise the air which immediately surrounds us. When these three are used unlawfully and intemperately, or are corrupted by bad quality, great and deadly snares are laid for mortals, and so man often perishes before his day. Therefore, since I began to meditate in the hours left over from my lawful duties, or rather undertook to shape the whole of hygiene, that is, to set out the body of prolonging health and to sketch the whole outline of it, from which a narrower work might at some time be hewn out, I have nevertheless with difficulty and labour been unable to bring everything to completion as I wished, because of the various obstacles raised against me at home and abroad. I publish only that part which the weakness of my talent allowed me to be diligent and at leisure about, for I prefer to make trial of a subject in which error would be less serious, and to expose to the judgement of critics a part of the work rather than the whole. There will be those who, from an unfair desire to contradict, will disapprove of my effort and labour, because I, the most obscure of men, treat the same subject after distinguished men who have written on it, and dare to bring it before the public. There have not been wanting learned men who have written special treatises on this, and perhaps there will be others, most skilled in all learning and labour, who will handle it more keenly and ingeniously. Those whom I have met have treated the matter either too briefly and narrowly, or with accuracy but with less method. Therefore I am not moved by a desire for glory, which is almost innate in all excellent minds, to seek a reputation for talent in a subject so worn by distinguished men,

units.la: argumento, Ingenii quæro famam, qui ante me tanta ar-te & diligentia huic materi-am elaborarunt, elabora-tam illustrarunt, vt de eo-dem argumento agendi nullum sibi neque posteris locum reliquum fecisse vi-deantur. Verum, quemad-modum Aristotelem à scri-bendo non deterruit ampli-tudo Platonis, neq; Cicero-nem M. Crassus, Antonius vel Hortensius Oratores à Romano foro prohibuerút, In magnis enim conatibus pulcrum est in mediis consi-stere: sic & mihi vitio non vertevertetur, in tam fertili medi-cinę agro, à diligentissimis illis, qui me præcesserunt, messoribus, relicta spicilegia, non mediocrem prouentus accessionem rei medicæ fa-ctura, postremus ego & infi-mus messor, ficilirem. Publi-ca igitur vtilitas, cupiditas voluntati meæ satisfaciendi, & auctores viri graues, qui-bus hoc scriptum meum pla-cere & probari intellexi, me ad hunc fœtum excluden-dum compulerunt, cuius ca-put ac pectus, vobis, Serenis-simi Principes offero atque commendo, humiliter rogi-tans, tans, vt clementi benignaq; manu præcipuas istas fœtus mei partes fouere, versare ac tractare, ad diuinę maiestatis amplificationem & gloriam, Ecclefiæq; ac Reipublicę vestræ salutem & emolumentum, deniq; totum vitę vestræ curriculum salubriter, hoc est, temperanter, prorogandum, mentemq; sanam in corpore fano retinendam, non grauemini.
units.tr: who before me have worked this material with such skill and diligence, and have so illuminated what they laboured over, that they seem to have left no room for anyone, either themselves or posterity, to treat the same subject again. Yet, just as the greatness of Plato did not deter Aristotle from writing, nor did M. Crassus, Antonius or Hortensius, orators, keep Cicero from the Roman forum, for in great undertakings it is noble simply to stand among them, so I too should not be blamed, in so fertile a field of medicine, for gleaning the leavings of those most diligent reapers who went before me, and, as the last and humblest reaper, for adding no small increase to the harvest of medical science. Public usefulness, the wish to satisfy my own inclination, and serious authors whom I have understood to approve and commend my writing, have therefore compelled me to bring forth this offspring, whose head and heart I offer and commend to you, most serene princes, humbly asking that you would with a gracious and kindly hand cherish, consider and handle these principal parts of my offspring, for the enlargement and glory of the divine majesty, for the safety and advantage of your Church and commonwealth, and finally that you would not be reluctant to have the whole course of your life prolonged in a healthful way, that is, temperately, and a sound mind kept in a sound body.

units.tr: Hence the divine power of herbs serves you, and hence the race and order of poets rises for you. Clearly, from you and from the nymph Coronis your son, they have set up a shrine as to a god. Am I mistaken, or is the Greek fable ambiguous? Or is credit rather owed to our own times? Behold the father of poets, that Goclenius Rodolphus; behold likewise that Rodolphus, the son of his father,

Nulla Chelys tā docta fuit, nulla arsq; medendi, Quale opus est medicum docte RODOL- PHE tuum, Quale parentis opus, quo conciliauit amicè Dissimiles inter se, similesq; Sophos. Dicite Pierides lauro hic, an dignior ille? Et lauro hic dignus, dignus & ille fuit. Non bene conueniunt discrimina dissona voci, Nec nisi concordi pectine grata lyra est: Sic nisi conueniant sapientum linguaq;, mensq;, Gratia quanta fuit, gratia tanta perit. Talis inest Patri sapientia, visq; docendi, Per quem iam coeunt, quæ coitura negès. Qualis inest Gnato prudentia, visq; medendi, Per quem sanantur, quæ moritura putes. Et quia non tantum laudatur acumine Pallas, Quantum laudata est Vtilitate Dea, Vnde oleæ inuentrix celebratur dia Minerua, Vsibus humanis commoda multa ferens:
units.tr: Apollo too is mine, the son of the nymph Coronis, and for them I think shrines should rather be set up. No lyre was ever so skilled, no art of healing; what a work is yours, learned Rodolphus, what a work of your father, by which he has amicably reconciled men unlike and yet alike, wise men. Tell me, Pierian Muses, is this one worthier of the laurel, or that one? Each is worthy of the laurel, and each was worthy. Discordant notes do not agree well with the voice, nor is the lyre pleasing unless the strings are in harmony. So unless the tongues and minds of the wise agree, how great the grace, so great it perishes. Such wisdom and power of teaching is in the father, through whom things that were about to part now come together, things you would deny could meet. Such prudence and power of healing is in the son, through whom things are healed that you would think were about to die. And because Pallas is not praised so much for her cleverness as the goddess is praised for her usefulness, whence the divine Minerva, inventress of the olive, is celebrated, bringing many benefits for human uses:

units.la: Hoc quod opus nostris ysibus ille dedit, Nestoreos vitae vsura qui extendat ad annos, Differat atq; tuum curua senecta pedem. Qua non ars melior, qua non magis indiga vita est, Qua meritae laudis non magis vlla ferax. Suauius hanc tractas, iucundaq; pocla propinas, Et Medicina tuo grata fit eloquio. Qualis quae rutilo circundata fulgurat auro, Gemma nitens reficit lumina grata magis: Sic tibi Romanae facundia cognita linguae, Nobilitat tua quod Musa peregit opus. Salue o Phoebe mihi: salue o Epidauria proles; Tu Phoebus, Phoebi filius, esq; Nepos.
units.tr: He who gave this work to our use, so that a lifetime of Nestorean years is extended, and crooked old age delays its step for you. What art is better, what life has greater need of it, what is more fertile of deserved praise? You handle it more sweetly and pour out pleasant cups, and medicine becomes pleasing through your eloquence. As a gem set in gleaming red gold shines and refreshes the eyes more pleasantly, so for you the known eloquence of the Roman tongue ennobles the work your Muse has accomplished. Hail, O Phoebus, to me; hail, O offspring of Epidaurus. You are Phoebus, the son of Phoebus, and his grandson.

units.tr: As nothing sweeter than the breath of life can come to the human race, so nothing is to be extolled with greater praise in life than what prolongs the day of living by its art. Since this book of yours, distinguished and outstanding Doctor, does this, the world has nothing more learned. Nor is it a lesser virtue to keep what has been won than to seek it, as the rounded words of the Sulmonian (Ovid) sound: nature gives the soul, then art preserves the same. Who would deny that this is also a great work of art? If anyone asks what this book promises, and what that boast in its title means, I answer: what wonder is it? Look into the author's mind, and you will see that nothing absurd lies in the matter. Whoever sets the end also appoints the means by which a thing reaches its goal. Each person's day is fixed, and fate is inevitable, ordained by God, who is the fountain and origin of life. Yet the first cause of things does not remove secondary causes, but bids them each keep their own course. Thus the threads of life are indeed fixed by decree, and fate allows no living beyond them. Yet lest this life stop short of those appointed times, a failing life comes to be helped by art.

units.la: DE VITA PROROGANDA TRACTATUS.
units.tr: ON PROLONGING LIFE: A TREATISE

units.la: Vitæ prorogandæ sanitatisq; custodiendæ rationem Philosophi ac Medici præstantes sex rerum generibus sunt complexi, quorum justa debitaq; mensura atq; observatio diæta, conseruatio sanitatis, modus tuendæ valetudinis, vel regimen sanitatis dicitur. Sunt q; aer, cibus, potus, somnus, vigilia, excretio, & retentio, animiq; affectus, hæc legitimè & moderatè adhibita vitam prolongant, & incorruptam valetudinem conseruant, unde & conseruatrices appellantur causæ & salutares: immoderatè vero adhibita, insalubria evadunt & morborum causæ: indeq; res non naturales dicuntur, quod videlicet extrinsecus accedant, & nobiscum non nascantur, sinistreq; se habentia (ut cum aer est male affectus vel venenatus) corpus humanum alterant & ladunt, ut experientia id testatur quotidie.
units.tr: The philosophers and physicians of note have grouped the means of prolonging life and preserving health under six classes of things, whose just and due measure and observance is called diet, the preservation of health, the method of guarding well-being, or the regimen of health. These are air, food, drink, sleep, waking, excretion and retention, and the emotions of the mind. When they are used lawfully and moderately, they prolong life and preserve sound health, and for this reason they are called preserving and healthful causes. But when they are used immoderately, they become unwholesome and causes of disease. Hence they are called non-natural things, because they come from outside and are not born with us; and when they are badly disposed (as when the air is tainted or poisonous), they alter and harm the human body, as experience daily bears witness.

units.la: Proœmii autem loco sequentes quæstiones scitu discussuq; dignas, (de quibus etiam inter doctissimos non convenit) & ab instituto nostro minime alienas, præmittere placuit.
units.tr: By way of a preface, I have thought fit to set out the following questions, worth knowing and discussing, which are not at all foreign to our purpose, although even the most learned do not agree about them.

units.la: A QVÆ-
units.tr: THE QUESTIONS.

units.la: QVAESTIO I. Circa operis hujus titulum:
units.tr: QUESTION I. Concerning the title of this work.

units.la: An praefixi huic operi tituli & inscriptionis sit aliqua necessitas, cum cuiq; vitae suae terminus praefinitus sit, ut illa neq; prorogari, neq; ante tempus abrumpi possit?
units.tr: Is there any need for the title and inscription prefixed to this work, since each person's span of life is fixed in advance, so that it can be neither prolonged nor cut short before its time?

units.la: NON abs re discutiendam in operis hujus vestibulo quaestionem hanc propono, quod sciam, aliquibus eam otiosam & inutilem videri, si scilicet praefiniti sint sui cuiq; dies, ut nec temporius, nec serius vitam praecidere alicui quid possit. Sed vehementer mirari subit, inueniri quosdam posse & potuisse, qui hac de re dubitarent, cum non tam vtilis, quàm necessaria quaestio sit, arduaq;: id quod sequentib. probatur rationibus, quae, si forsan primo intuitu alicui appareant non satis firmae, vel accuratius expendantur, (quod prudentis est) vel inconcussae relinquantur, (quod verecundi & modesti est.) Constat autem rem nullam corrumpi naturaliter, quantisper calor ejus congenitus durat. Hic enim autor est, & conseruator tem peraturae, qua incolumi permanente, nulla res interire potest. Manet vero calor ille infi-tus tantisper, dum alimentum ei conueniens superest, habet enim se instar flammae in El-lych. lychnio, vel funiculo candelæ accensæ: alimentum vero ejus, seu pabulum est humidū illud primigenium, seu radicale à primordio generationis insitum & innatum, rationem habens lucernarum olei, vel sebi in candelis, in his enim flamma tàm diu pascitur & viuit, quàm diu cera, sebum, vel oleum superest, quo absumto, ipsam quoq; flammam (deficiente scnutrimento) interiri & extingui necesse est. Hoc igitur humidum in re aliqua, Vita longa quo copiosius est & viscosius, eò difficilius gloria dissipatur & absumitur, quò verò tenuius & breviora aquosius est, eò facilius diffluit, reiq; cujusq; causa vitam seu durationem efficit breviorem. His ita positis, quis vitam arte produci ad illum Hocteme terminum posse, quo rei cujusq; calor insitus propriam humidum depopulat naturaliter, tum Penegabit? Dum enim damus operam, vt calor ripatetici ille præter naturæ modum non augeatur (vt nominat in febribus fit) & humidum è contrario non fatum minuatur vel dissipetur, rem certè ab interitu celeriori præseruamus.
units.tr: I put forward this question for discussion at the threshold of this work, not without reason. As far as I know, some think it idle and useless, on the ground that each person's days are predetermined, so that nothing can cut a life short either earlier or later. But it is astonishing that there are, and have been, people who doubt this, since the question is not so much useful as necessary and difficult. This the following arguments prove. If they seem at first glance not sufficiently firm to someone, he should either weigh them more carefully, which is the mark of a prudent man, or leave them unshaken, which is the mark of a modest and humble one. It is agreed that nothing is naturally destroyed for as long as its inborn heat lasts. For this heat is the author and preserver of the temperament, and while that temperament remains intact, nothing can perish. That innate heat remains for as long as a suitable nourishment is still present. It is like the flame in a lamp or the wick of a lit candle. Its nourishment or fuel is that primordial, or radical, moisture implanted and innate from the beginning of generation, and it corresponds to the oil of lamps or the tallow of candles. For the flame is fed and lives only as long as the wax, tallow or oil remains, and when that is used up, the flame itself must, with its nourishment failing, die out and be extinguished. Therefore the more abundant and viscous this moisture is in any thing, long life the more difficult it is for it to be dissipated and used up; but the thinner and more watery it is, the more easily it runs off, and so it makes the life or duration of each thing shorter. Given this, who could bring life by art to that end at which the innate heat of any thing naturally consumes its own moisture, then? For while we take pains that the so-called peripatetic heat is not increased beyond the measure of nature, as happens in fevers, and that the moisture, on the contrary, is not wholly diminished or dissipated, we certainly preserve the thing from a swifter death.

units.la: Videmus plantas, quæ frigoris alioqui aut hiemis asperitate interiissent, in cella, calido-ve aliquo loco positas, ad vet vsq;, vel etiam intectas, multis annis conseruari. Fructus nonnullos arte, qui vix mensem integri mansissent, per totum fere annum recentes seruati experientia satis testatur. Ob contrarias quoque causas à nonnullis arboribus & plantis tardius produci fructus & femina experimur. Ex quibus evidentissime probatur, calorem natiuum arte augeri conseruari minuiq; posse, vt eius operationes maturentur vel impediantur: precaueri item posse, ne pabulum ejus justo celerius absumat: quod autem hoc praestat, υγιεινή est, h. e. Sanitatis tuendae ratio. Cum enim sanitas sit dispositio seu affectio naturalis corporis, a qua operationes sunt proueniunt, & plaerraq; animae potentiae organis vtantur corporeis, ipsequre homo propter animam sit homo, & organa quoq; ipsa aut no agant, aut male agant, nisi sint sana, facile videre est, quantum sit situm in organorum omnium justa temperie & sanitate, ipsiq; animae interesse, vt corpus sit sanum. Unde prudenter dixit Poeta:
units.tr: We see plants which would otherwise have perished from cold or the harshness of winter kept for many years, when they are placed in a cellar or some warm place, or even left uncovered. Experience amply confirms that some fruits, which would hardly have stayed whole for a month, are kept fresh through almost the whole year by art. We also find by experience that some trees and plants bear fruit and seed later, from the opposite causes. From these things it is most clearly proved that the innate heat can be increased, preserved or diminished by art, so that its operations are hastened or hindered; and likewise that care can be taken that it does not use up its fuel too quickly. What achieves this is hygieine, that is, the art of preserving health. For since health is the natural disposition or condition of the body, from which the operations proceed, and since the powers of the soul mostly use bodily organs, and man himself is man on account of the soul, and the organs themselves do not act, or act badly, unless they are sound, it is easy to see how much depends on the due temperament and health of all the organs, and how much it matters to the soul itself that the body be sound. Hence the poet wisely said:

units.la: Orandum est, ut sit mens sana in corpore sano.
units.tr: One must pray that there be a sound mind in a sound body.

units.la: Itaq; etsi nobis omnibus moriendum semel, nec mors curari aut medicina vlla auerti potest, differri ea tamen saepe posse non infinitum est. Non enim, quia meta nobis posita est & viuendi terminus, consiliuq; Deinde vitae termino ignoramus, officium nostrum deserere debemus, sed sedulo nobis faciendum est, quod ordinauit & mandauit, quicquid tandem Deo facere sit visum. An quia mortis horam praefiniuit nobis Deus, necesse etiam non habemus edere & bibere? An non deliraret, quod de alto se loco praecipitem dare mallet, quam per scalas descendere? An non tentaret Deus, qui, cū ex aquâ poflet enatare, enatare nolit, quia Deus etiā in aquis, quos vult, conferuare potest? Jubet Deus ne follicit sim°, qd edamus, quid bibamus, q& & passerum & liliorū agri curam gerat, preterq; eius voluntatem ne capillus capitis nostri defluere possit.
units.tr: Although we must all die once, and death cannot be cured or averted by any medicine, it is not unlimited that it can often be put off. Because a goal and a limit to living have been set for us, we should not on that account abandon our duty while we are ignorant of the end of our life. Rather, we must diligently do what God has ordained and commanded, whatever it may finally please him to do. Or, because God has fixed the hour of our death, do we therefore have no need to eat and drink? Would not a man be mad who preferred to throw himself headlong from a high place rather than go down by the stairs? Would not someone tempt God who, though he could swim out of the water, refused to swim, on the ground that God can keep him safe even in the waters, wherever he wishes? God bids us not to be anxious about what we shall eat or drink, and he cares for the sparrows and the lilies of the field, yet not apart from his will is a hair of our head able to fall.

units.la: Idem interim Deus arare terram, metere, occare, triturare, vites colere, vuas colligere, fructus reponere pcipit & vt vno dicam verbo, Deus miraculose vitam nostram nunc nō sustentat, sed per media & inftrumeta ab ipso ordinata, vt ita successus à Deo expectandus fit, noftrū interim, quod est non negligendum. Dū enim facientes juuant, auxilioq; esse solent industriis & pro virili sua conantib. Qui igitur propterea juxta præscriptum Dei agere nolunt, fiduciaq; opis diuinæ industriâ remittunt, quòd sciunt, Deum ab æterno providisse, quæ profutura sint nec ne, non fine culpa sua moriuntur, nec possunt non graviter ob neglecta media vulnerare conscientiā, per quæ nihilominus suam nobis potentiam clementiamque liquidissimè Deus ostentat. Quocirca non vtilis tantum est, verum etiā necessaria proposita quæstio, nisi quis inscitè ac superciliosa quadam fatuitate affirmare ausit, profligationem morborum, qui humidum congenitum dissipare ac depascere fe-ftinanter possunt, (vt sunt febres ardentes,) necessariam non esse. A Non enim tollit artis exercitium Dei præscientia. Quin & ipse Christus ægrotos medicis indigere affirmat, inque Dei populo semper fuisse medicos, manifeste patet ex Gen. 50. Exod. 21. 2. Par. 16. & Eccl. 38. qui expresse habet, (quòd inprimis notandum) medicum à Deo creatum, propterq; necessitatem honorandum esse, stipendiumq; ei dari præcipit, additq; Deum ex artis medicæ miraculis & sanationibus laudari velle & prædicari, ipse namq; inquit, per medicamina sanat, doloribus-que hominēs liberat. Qui igitur Dei ordinationi sic paret, ac moritur nihilominus, bona conscientia coram Deo consistet, dum nulla sua culpa se mortuum intelligat.
units.tr: Likewise, God commands us to plough the land, reap, sow, thresh, tend the vines, gather the grapes and store the fruits. To put it in one word, God does not now sustain our life miraculously, but through means and instruments ordained by himself. Thus success is to be expected from God, while our own effort, which must not be neglected, is also required. For those means help those who act, and are wont to be of aid to those who strive with their industry and to the best of their ability. Therefore, those who for this reason are unwilling to act according to God's prescription, and who give up their diligence and their trust in divine help because they know that God has foreseen from eternity what will or will not be profitable, do not die without fault of their own. They cannot but gravely wound their conscience by neglecting the means through which God nonetheless most clearly shows us his power and mercy. Wherefore the question proposed is not only useful but even necessary, unless someone should rashly and with a certain arrogant foolishness dare to affirm that the checking of diseases, which can swiftly consume and devour the innate moisture (such as burning fevers), is not necessary. For God's foreknowledge does not abolish the practice of the art. Indeed, Christ himself affirms that the sick need physicians, and that there have always been physicians among God's people is plain from Gen. 50. Exod. 21. 2. Par. 16. & Eccl. 38. which expressly says (and this is especially to be noted) that the physician was created by God, and commands that he be honoured on account of his necessity and that a fee be given him. It adds that God wishes to be praised and proclaimed for the wonders and healings of the medical art: "For he, it says, heals with medicines, and frees men from their pains." Therefore, whoever thus obeys God's ordinance and yet dies will nonetheless stand before God with a good conscience, since he knows that he dies through no fault of his own.

units.la: QVAESTIO II.
units.tr: QUESTION II.

units.la: An subiectum morbi & sanitatis sit ipsius partis essentia, hoc est, an febris constitutat in partium cordis constitutione essentiali? N.
units.tr: Is the subject of disease and health the very essence of the part itself? That is, does fever consist in the essential constitution of the parts of the heart? No.

units.la: BONa Pseudomedicorum pars in hac opinione consenuit, principium morbi materiale & formale in ipsius partis esse fixum substantia, cujus sententiæ falsitatem, tot quotidie monstrant errores in praxi. Morbus enim & sanitas non consistunt in essentiali partium constitutione, sed accidentali duntaxat. Non enim, quicquid partem comcomponere, vel constituere dicitur, sanitatis & morbi subiectum est, essentialis enim forma vna cum materia non sanitatem, sed partium constituit essentiam: Sed est alia quaedam compositio, κατασκευή, quasi apparatus quidam, praeparatio, vel apta conformatio, quae accidens est, non substantia, quale in instrumentis contemplamur praeter materiam & formam, vt in gladio duritiem, acicm, nitorem, quib praeditus optime potest incidere: ejusmodi est in simili parte ipsa temperies, in organicis accidentalis forma, quae structura dicitur: accidentalis igitur partium constitutio, est apparatus quidam ad formae actiones exercendas, materiaq; & forma tanquam substantiae nunquam citra subjecti corruptionem abesse possunt, neque magis & minus recipere, temperies vero & structura multis modis immutantur, praeterid, quod separabilia sunt accidentia non minus quam sanitas & morbus: materiae item & formae nihil vt contrarium aduersatur, sed ipsa tantum priuatio omnis transmutationis est autor, temperies vero & structura contrariorum expertia non sunt, quamobrem solius temperamenti integritas sanitatis nucupationem meretur, seruato enim temperamento seruantur actiones & sanitas.
units.tr: The false physicians have long grown old in this opinion, that the material and formal principle of disease is fixed in the very substance of the part; the falsity of this view is shown every day by so many errors in practice. For disease and health do not consist in the essential constitution of the parts, but only in an accidental one. For not everything that is said to compose or constitute a part is the subject of health and disease: the essential form, together with the matter, constitutes not health but the essence of the part. There is another kind of composition, a kataskeuē, as it were a certain apparatus, preparation, or fitting arrangement, which is an accident and not a substance. We observe something of this kind in instruments, beyond matter and form: in a sword, for instance, the hardness, the edge and the polish, by which it can cut very well. Of this kind, in a similar part, is the temperament itself; in organic bodies it is an accidental form, which is called structure. The accidental constitution of the parts is therefore a certain apparatus for carrying out the actions of the form. Matter and form, as substances, can never be absent without the corruption of the subject, nor can they admit more or less; but temperament and structure are changed in many ways. Besides, accidents are separable, no less than health and disease. Nothing opposes matter and form as a contrary; mere privation is the author of every change. Temperament and structure, however, are not free of contraries. For this reason the integrity of the temperament alone deserves the name of health, since by preserving the temperament the actions and health are preserved.

units.la: QVAESTIO III. An humores sint subiectum morbi & sanitatis? N.
units.tr: QUESTION III. Whether the humours are the subject of disease and health? No.

units.la: NOn defuerunt, nec etiam nunc desunt, qui affirmatiuam defendendam suscepepunt. Non ita pridem, cum negotiorum quorundam meorum causâ Budingâ irem Lichamincidi, certa tamen arrepta occasione in Parochianû quendam, non quidem leuiter literis imbutum, sed saltem scelerata loquentia & impostoria deblaterati one de vrinaria inspectione infamem; Is adeo obstinate & pertinaciter affirmanti sententiae patrocinabatur, vt scirrhum quis quauis durissimum, citius concoxerit, quàm hac ei opinionem ex animo eripuerit: Nulla autem ratione alia negatiuam peruertere, suam vero prauam affirmatiuam tueri conabatur, quam quod sibi persuasum habebat, vna cum humoribus corruptis ac depravatis, siue per sudorem, siue per vrinam, siue per aluum exturbentur, etiam morbum expelli. Non absimile est, quod putidus quidam hyperbolicusq; Paradoxorum defensor se vidisse scribit vna cum vomitu reiectam febrim. Nam ei morbus in numero causarum est, causa vero morbi radix & seminarium immutabile, quod suo loco excludi non possit Sed hæc extra rem. Veritatis studiosi pro demonstrato habeant, quòd nulla sanitas vel ægritudo possit esse in parte aliquâ corporis, in quâ non exercentur operationes corporis, operationes enim sunt in compositis non constituentibus, virtus enim vitalis in substantiâ cordis est, non humoribus & spiritibus, qui instrumentum sunt tantum, & vehiculum, vel principia & nutrimenta.
units.tr: There were not lacking, nor are there even now lacking, those who have undertaken to defend the affirmative. Not long ago, when I was going to Büdingen on some business of mine, I came to Lich, and there, seizing an opportune occasion, I met a certain parishioner, not lightly educated in letters but at least notorious for wicked and impostor-like babbling about urine-inspection. He defended the affirmative opinion so obstinately and stubbornly that one would sooner digest the hardest scirrhus than tear this opinion from his mind. He tried in no other way to overturn the negative, but to defend his own perverse affirmative, which he was persuaded of, namely that when corrupt and depraved humours are expelled, whether through sweat, urine, or the bowels, the disease is expelled along with them. Not unlike this is what a foul and hyperbolic defender of paradoxes writes that he saw a fever thrown out together with vomit. For the disease is among the causes, but the cause of disease is the root and the unchangeable seed, which cannot be removed in its place. But this is beside the point. Let those who study the truth hold as demonstrated that there can be no health or sickness in any part of the body in which the actions of the body are not carried out. For actions belong to composites, not to constituents; the vital power is in the substance of the heart, not in the humours and spirits, which are only instruments and vehicles, or principles and nourishments.

units.la: Sic febris colerica dicitur, non quod in colera fit tanquam subiecto, sed quòd à colerâ eiusq; putredine dependeat, vt ita putredinis subiectum fit humor, febris verò ipsum cor, in quo humor flammam vel intermittentem vel continuâ primum concipit, nisi ea fit symtomatodes, h. e. aliunde cordi impetiatur.
units.tr: Thus a fever is called bilious, not because it exists in the bile as its subject, but because it depends on the bile and its putrefaction. So the humour is the subject of the putrefaction, while the heart itself is the subject of the fever, in which the humour first kindles a flame, either intermittent or continuous, unless it is symptomatic, that is, assailed on the heart from elsewhere.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: DE AERE EIVSQVE CONDITIONIBUS, ESSENTIA, QUALITATE, REGIONUM, POPULORUM & LOCORUM VARIETATE, DEQUE VTENDI MODO, & PESTE AERIS SEU VENENO AEREO.
units.tr: ON THE AIR AND ITS CONDITIONS, ITS ESSENCE, QUALITY, AND THE VARIETY OF REGIONS, PEOPLES AND PLACES, AND ON THE MANNER OF USING IT, AND ON THE PLAGUE OF THE AIR OR AERIAL POISON.

units.la: Inter sanitatis tuendæ decreta & capita primum sibi & principem locum vendicat aer, in omne corpus promte penetrans, caloris nativi pabulum & refrigerium, quo sine nec sanitas conseruari integrè, nec morbus tutò profligari, imò ne quidem vitam agere homo potest.
units.tr: Among the rules and heads of preserving health, the air claims the first and chief place for itself. It penetrates readily into every body, and it is the food and cooling of the native heat. Without it health cannot be kept whole, nor disease safely overcome; indeed, a person cannot even live.

units.la: Vnde grauiff. & sapientiff. autores posteri-tati reliquerūt, pro vario cœlo multifariā ho-minum naturam, mores, & morbos, numero-sam plantarū, animaliumq; prolem, simulq; sterilitatem & fertilitatem immutari: siquidem aer ambiens, etiam nobis inuitis ad corporis tutelam hauriendus, corpus nostrū vel conseruat, & tuetur, si temperatus est & bonę qualitatis, vel id labefactat & immutat. si substantia vitiatus est, & immoderatæ qualitatis.
units.tr: Hence the most serious and wise authors have left it to posterity that, according to the different climate, the nature, customs and diseases of human beings, the number of plants and the offspring of animals, and likewise their barrenness and fertility, are changed in many ways. For the surrounding air, which we must draw in to protect the body even against our will, either preserves and guards our body if it is temperate and of good quality, or weakens and alters it if its substance is corrupted and its quality immoderate.

units.la: Itaq; danda est opera, vt summa animi contentione aeris essentia & qualitas accuratè obseruetur, vt sanitatem iucundius conseruare, & morbos tutius præcauere liceat. Et primo quidem aeris essentia perpendenda est, pro vario cœlo, vrbium, locorumq; situ, proque diuerso solis accessu & recessu, ex quibus celerem sæpè mutationem subit.
units.tr: Therefore care must be taken, with the greatest attention of mind, to observe accurately the essence and quality of the air, so that we may preserve health more pleasantly and guard more safely against diseases. And first of all the essence of the air must be weighed, according to the different climate and the situation of cities and places, and according to the different approach and retreat of the sun, from which it often undergoes rapid change.

units.la: Aer enim tenuis, purus, serenus, temperatus, tranquillus, tetroq; stagnorum, paludum, imbrium cadauerumq; habitu non conspurcatus, spiritus collustrat, ingeniumq; acuit, ac corpus in vigore conseruat.
units.tr: For thin, pure, clear, temperate and calm air, not polluted by the foul exhalations of ponds, marshes, rains and carcasses, brightens the spirits, sharpens the mind, and keeps the body in vigour.

units.la: Hæc aeris constitutio ob cœli amœnitatem & puritatem homines facit venustiores, beniiores, maiores, & effœminatiores, quales Hipp. ait esse Asianos: Europęi ob cœli incōstantiam magnitudine corporis varii existūt & differētes, audaces & robusti (quamuis hic nō minor est victus varii & discrepantis vis.)
units.tr: This constitution of the air makes people more graceful, better, larger and more effeminate, because of the pleasantness and purity of the climate; such, Hippocrates says, are the Asians. The Europeans, on account of the inconstancy of the climate, vary and differ in the size of their bodies, being bold and robust (although the variety and diversity of their diet is no less influential).

units.la: Aer
units.tr: The air

units.la: PROPAGANDA.
units.tr: PROPAGANDA.

units.la: Aer Serenus est, qui nubibus & nebulis, seu su-mis caret: huic opponitur inferenus & nebulosus. Tr aquilus, q; veris: huic opponitur tumultuas. Tenuis defœcatus est purus & transparens: crassus contra opacus est & impurus.
units.tr: A serene air is one that lacks clouds and mists, or dark masses (sumis, i.e. summis, "highest" or "heavy" vapours); its opposite is the air that is low-lying and misty. A calm air is one free of storms; its opposite is a tumultuous air. A thin air is clear and pure, and transparent; a thick air, by contrast, is opaque and impure.

units.la: Tenuis itaq;, purufq; aer sordida alicuius causæ externe illuuie nō infectus, omni ætati & temperamento saluberrimus est: impurus, crassusq; pernitiosus. Hanc sententiam confirmat Gal. l. 1. de sanit. tuend. c. 11. Aerem, inquit, optimum in pulmones trahere omnib9 salubre est: optimū aerem censeo, qui profusus sit purus. Eiusmodi vero fuerit, q nec stagni, nec paludis halitus sit perturbatus, nec ex profundo specu pestilenté aurā spirante infectus, nec qui ex cloacis, quæ magnam aliquā vrbem aut numerosum exercitū purgent, vitium contraxit, nec, qui ob flumen vel stagnū vicinum, nebulosus est, nec, qui, editis vndiq; montibus, in cauo loco clausus nullum recipit perflatū. Suffocans enim putrisq; est, simulis ei, qui in domibus quibusdā est inclusus, in quibus ob putredinem & perflatus defectū plurimus coaceruatur situs & corruptio. Huiusmodi ergo aer omni plane ætati est noxius, sicut è diuerso q purus est omninò, nulli nō ætati est vtilis. At vero, quæ ex calore, frigore, siccitate, humiditateue diuersitas aeris contingit, non perinde se ad omnes homines habet: sed corporibus, quæ sunt optimo tem- perāperamento, etiam optimè temperatus aer est saluberrimus: in quibus verò exuperans qualitas dominatur, iis vtilissimus aer est, qui ei qualitati maximè aduersatur, frigidus calidæ, calidus frigidæ, humidiori siccus, siccori quà par est, tantò humidior, quantò siccitas ipsa modum excedit. Hallenus Galenus.
units.tr: Thin, pure air, not tainted by the filth of any external cause, is most wholesome for every age and temperament; impure and thick air is harmful. Galen confirms this opinion in book 1 of On Preserving Health, chapter 11: "To draw the best air into the lungs is healthy for all; I judge the best air to be that which is wholly pure. Such air is not disturbed by the exhalations of a pool or marsh, nor infected by a pestilential breath rising from a deep cave, nor has it contracted corruption from the sewers that cleanse a large city or a numerous army, nor is it clouded by a nearby river or pool, nor does it, shut in a hollow place with mountains on every side, receive any breeze. For such air is suffocating and putrid, like the air of certain houses shut in, where much mould and corruption gather because of putrefaction and lack of airflow. Air of this kind is therefore harmful to every age, just as, conversely, entirely pure air is useful to every age. But the variations of air that arise from heat, cold, dryness or moisture do not affect all people alike. For bodies of the best temperament, even well-tempered air is most wholesome; but in bodies where some excessive quality dominates, the most useful air is that which most opposes that quality: cold air for the hot, hot for the cold, dry for the moist, and moist for the dry, though only as far as is proper, and the moister the air the more the dryness of the body exceeds its due measure." Thus far Galen.

units.la: Vnde sanitati minus consulere videntur, qui circa stagna, paludes, nemora aut valles nullù flatum recipientes, aut flumè vicinù, aut loca auftrù spectantia domicilia construunt. Sed longè peius faciunt Magistratus & proceres quidà, qui caulas, stabula & receptacula canù & equorù in arcib* extruunt vel loca cadaue-rù excoriandorù, sepulturamq; humanorum corporum in ipsis vrbibus, vel prope cœstitu-unt etiam seuero edicto. Quid? quod apud quasdà gentes, cumprimis verò Danos, Suecos & his vicinos, nunc verò etiá Germaniæ proceres plerosq; mos inualuit, in coenacula quosuis canes venaticos veltigiatores, pecuarios, molossos, & villaticos recipere etiá seuerissimo edicto, vt cane exire iubens citius piaculum commisisse dicatur quam hominem.
units.tr: Hence those seem to have less regard for health who build their homes near pools, marshes, groves or valleys that receive no breeze, or near a river, or in places facing south. But far worse do certain magistrates and nobles, who build pens, stables and kennels for dogs and horses within their citadels, or places for flaying carcasses, and who bury human bodies within the cities themselves, or even set these up nearby, despite strict edicts. What of the fact that among some peoples, above all the Danes, Swedes and their neighbours, and now also most of the nobles of Germany, the custom has prevailed of admitting hunting dogs, tracking dogs, herding dogs, mastiffs and house dogs into upper rooms, even under the most severe edict, so that one who bids a dog leave is said to have committed a worse offence than if he had driven out a man?

units.la: Quid quæso sanitati magis obnoxium, quid fœdius & sordidius, quà suauissimos ex cibis variis vaporesque halitusq; exhalantes, tumq; cœnaculum complentes canù sterco-ribus & oletis obsolefieri & inquinari? Tenuem enim & naturâ purum aerem eiusmodi exhala-
units.tr: What, I ask, is more harmful to health, what is more foul and filthy, than that the most pleasant air, exhaling the vapours and breaths of various foods and filling the room, should be spoiled and polluted by the dung and stench of dogs?

units.la: Canes nō sunt admittendi in cœnaculo & gynæcea. exhalationibus facilè vitiari, vitiatum à nobis inspirari, inspiratum ob arteriarum cū venis coadstomosis sanguini permisceri, permixtū spiritus, quorum præcipuum fomentum est, inficere & tenebricosos reddere, non dicam ipsum sanguinem incrassare, plus quam notū est. Quare totus debet esse Sanitatis custodiendæ studiosus in aeris essentia penitus examinanda, & in vario locorū situ circūspectius perlustrando, præsertim vero qui humaniorib9 literis operā dant, in arduis negotiis exhauriendis, officiis publicis administrandis sunt occupati, nec non valetudinarii in hoc vnicè inuigilabunt, vt aerem purum & temperatū habeant, vel industria, arteq;, si opus fuerit, talem præparent. Noster certè hīcaer Budinga non adeo salubris est, quia rarò purus; cū, quia montib9 altis vndiq; fere clausus & interceptus, nō est perflabilis, vnde putris euadit similisq; ei qui in domibus quibusdā, caluisq; habitationū locis inclusus ob perflatus & ventilationis defectū sæpe & facile corrumpitur: tum ob paludosam fossam lacunam mq; mediam vibem transeunte, tetrumq; æstate halitum expirantem, vnde aerem vehementer infici & immutari testes sunt ipsi incolæ & quotidie fere inuadentes morbi. Huc accedunt validiores austrinorum ventorum afflatus, quib. Budinga nostra ex illa parte qua Fracofurtum spectat & meridie, maximè expositā & sub-
units.tr: Dogs are not to be admitted into dining rooms and women's quarters. Exhalations easily spoil the air; the spoiled air we breathe in; breathed in, through the connections of the arteries with the veins, it is mixed with the blood, and the mixed spirits, whose chief fuel is the blood, infect it and make it gloomy, not to mention thickening the blood itself, as is more than well known. Therefore everyone who is anxious to guard his health should examine the nature of the air thoroughly and survey carefully the varying situations of places. This is especially true of those who devote themselves to the humane letters, who are occupied with difficult business and public offices, and likewise of invalids, who should take great care to have pure and temperate air, or to prepare such by diligence and art if need be. Our own air at Budingen is certainly not very healthful, because it is rarely pure. Being almost enclosed and cut off on every side by high mountains, it is not open to breezes, so it becomes putrid, like the air of certain closed houses in hot places, and is often and easily corrupted for want of wind and ventilation. Moreover, a marshy ditch, a pool and a stream run through the middle of the town, and in summer they give off a foul vapour; from this the air is strongly infected and altered, as the inhabitants themselves and the almost daily illnesses bear witness. Add to this the stronger blasts of the south winds, to which our Budingen is most exposed and subject on the side facing Frankfurt and the south.

units.la: {a} Aeris Budingensis essentia. & subiecta cernitur; nam certû est eiusmodi ventos multa sæpe inquinamenta & sparsa morborum semina ex meridionalib9 illis regionibus & locis huc deponere, quæ postea in cauitatibus inclusa, atq; retenta rationem habet causæ efficientis & procreantis morbi, vt extrinsecus accidentia, & in corpore nostro non sponte generata. Ego, vt ab eiusmodi contagione perlte immunis, itinerib9, crebro exercitio, vel subdialibus montanisq; inambulationibus, Septentriones versus vel Orientê corpus soleo ventilare & perspirabile reddere, ex quib. postea me bene habere & valere testantur viri & amici optimi, eundé in finé id mecum ex suasu meo pertentantes. Hactenus de essentia aeris, Sequitur eius qualitas.
units.tr: {a} The essence of the air at Budingen. Such winds are seen to be of this kind; for it is certain that such winds often bring here from those southern regions and places many pollutants and scattered seeds of disease, which afterwards, enclosed and held in the hollows, take on the character of an efficient and generating cause of disease, as things that come from outside and are not spontaneously generated in our body. As for me, to be quite free from such contagion, I am accustomed to air my body and make it open to perspiration by travelling, frequent exercise, or walks in the open air and among the mountains, turning towards the north or east. My good health and strength are afterwards attested by excellent men and friends, who, at my suggestion, try the same for the same end. Thus far on the essence of air; follows its quality.

units.la: Hæc non minus ad sanitatem tuendam, morborumq; præcautionem confert, quam ipsius essentia.
units.tr: This contributes no less to preserving health and guarding against disease than the essence of the air itself.

units.la: Aer enim calidus confert frigido tempe-ramento præditis, affectibusq; frigidis & diuturnis: frigidus calidis, humidus siccis, siccus-que humidis opportune est accommodand*.
units.tr: For warm air suits those of a cold temperament and chronic cold affections; cold air suits the hot; moist air suits the dry; and dry air suits the moist, as each case requires.

units.la: Præterea cömoda & incömoda adnotare coducit, quæ vnaquæq; aeris qualitas secū afferre consueuit. Calidus aer corpora languidiora reddit, breuiorisq; vitæ. Calorem n.innatum & fluentem à centro ad circumferentia educendo citius resoluit, cordiq; incömodat & morbis calidis, sed frigidis congruus est cerebrumq; recreat, & refocillat. Fri-
units.tr: It is also useful to note the advantages and disadvantages that each quality of air usually brings with it. Warm air makes bodies more languid and shortens life. By drawing the innate heat outwards from the centre to the circumference, it dissolves it more quickly; it is harmful to the heart and suits hot diseases, but suits cold ones, and it refreshes and revives the brain.

units.la: Frigidus aer robusta, pertinacia & longa ua facit alitq; corpora, testis Dania, Suecia, & caeteri Septentrionis populi, cerebro praeter ea incommodat, cordi vero refrigerium est.
units.tr: Cold air makes bodies robust, tenacious and long-lived, as Denmark, Sweden and the other peoples of the north attest. Besides this, it harms the brain, but it is a refreshment to the heart.

units.la: Humidus aer pinguia, mollia, glabra, moribusque humanioribus exornata profert corpora, ficcioribusque temperaturis, morbisque calidis & siccis plurimum opitulatur, pedum vero ac crurum vlceribus noxius.
units.tr: Moist air produces bodies that are plump, soft, smooth and endowed with gentler manners, and it greatly helps drier constitutions and hot and dry diseases, but it is harmful to ulcers of the feet and legs.

units.la: Siccus humidis corporibus, affectibusq; pulmonibusq; vlceribus eximie confert, sanitatiq; conseruandae & tuendae prae caeteris auxiliatur. Siccitates n. inquit Hipp. in aphor. imbribus sunt salubriores. Verum hoc tenendum, sicut aer siccus corpora ad morbos reddit minus pcli-uia, sed bretuioris pfert vitae, sic humidus corpora affectib. magis obnoxia reddit, sed vitae logioris.
units.tr: Dry air is excellent for moist bodies, for affections and for ulcers of the lungs, and it helps the preservation and maintenance of health more than other kinds. For Hippocrates says in the Aphorisms that dry seasons are more wholesome than rainy ones. But this must be held: just as dry air makes bodies less prone to disease but gives them shorter life, so moist air makes bodies more liable to affections but gives them longer life.

units.la: Verum hic oriuntur dubia quaedam, quae discutienda sunt. I. Cur Galenus, aerem calidum & humidum vocet peßimum, cum tamen in calore & humido consistat vita animationi?
units.tr: But here some doubts arise, which must be discussed. First: why does Galen call warm and moist air the worst, when life itself consists in heat and moisture, which are the conditions of animation?

units.la: II. Quodnam anni tempus sit salubrius, & an autumnus recte dicatur frigidus & siccus, vel calidum & humidum, ideoq; temperatum? R. ad I. Vitam in caloris innati humorem depascentis, & humoris caloram fouentis legitime conseruere temperatione, ita accipiendum est, vt non excludatur frigidum & siccum, absque frigido n. & sicco nulla esset caloris & humidi terminatio & vnio, sed dissolutio, distinctio & humo-
units.tr: Second: which season of the year is healthiest, and is autumn rightly called cold and dry, or warm and moist, and therefore temperate? Answer to the first: the life which preserves the innate heat and moisture, and which nourishes the moisture by means of heat, is kept by a lawful temperature. This must be understood so that cold and dry are not excluded; for without the cold and dry there would be no limit and union of heat and moisture, but dissolution, separation and outflow of the moisture.

units.la: priorum: quaestionis humoris diffluxus. Haec esse vera ostendunt animalia frigidioris & ficcioris temperamenti, quae omnium longissime viuunt, vt elephanti, cerui, corui, & in hominum tribus melancolici, qui omnium consensu sunt frigidi & sicci, & ratio haec est, quod humor melancolicus in causa est, vt humidum non ita promte & calidi & humidi cito diffluat calorq; dissipet, fedarte vniatur & terminetur. Videbitur hoc multis paradoxon, sed ii li in experimento acquieuerint, re ipsa coperient, me no plane falsum dixisse. Ac huius sententiae veritate confirmant Septentrionis populi, qui aerem spirant frigidum & siccum temparamento eorum familiarissimum, vnde diutissime viuut & innoxie, nisi frequés & crebrior salsamentorum vsus funeris ante diem eos enecaret, peßimo incorporib. ipsorum conducto inquilino Scorbuto. Cur autem Galenus aerem calidum & humidum vocet peßimum, facit ratione habita ad frigidum & siccum, id est, comparate. Verba eius l. de re-per. c. 4. haec sunt. Ego vero, tantum abest, vt aut ver calidum & humidu pronunciem, aut si quid temperatum est, calidum dicam atq; humidum, vt quod plane contrarium est affirmem, omnium aeris ambientis temperamentorum peßimum esse id, quod calidum & humidum est. Et paulo post, variorum affectum, quorum nullum aite esse, putredinis qui soboles non sit, enumerationem subiungit, quippe cum nec à sicco putrefieri quicquam fit aptum, nec à frigido: sic carnes & reliqua, quaecunq; aßeruari ab hominibus solent, haec sale, alia muria, alia aceto, vel alio quopiam, ꝙ ficcar, commodè praeparantur: deprehendes & Borea vento naturâ frigido & sicco omnia quâ diutißime imputria durare, contra putrescere facilime ven o austrino, qui calidus & humidus est. Itaque nos in totum contra quam illi statuunt calidum & humidum esse ver, decernim*, cum neq; tale sit, neq; si esset, vtiq; salubre esset. Hæc Galenus. Cū igitur promtißimè putrescant corpora calida & humida, teste eodem Gal. 1. de diff. febr. c. 3. & quidem celerius in locis calidis & humidis, quam frigidis & siccis, vt demonstratum est, sequitur calidam humidamq; aeris ambientis constitutionem atque temperiem esse caeteris peiorem. Corpora autem calidiora humidioraque putredinis noxam (nisi difflentur & refrigerentur) citius contrahere, quam frigidiora & sicciora, ostendunt febres humorales. Omnis n. humor alienus à natura corporis, in quo continetur, neque aptus ad eius nutritionem necessario putrescit, febremq; accendit, putrescit autem celerrimè, cum locus, in quo fuerit collectus, est calidus: id quod ventriculus manifestat plus iusto calidior, nullus enim cibus immodicè calfactus, sine putredine in eo permanere potest, corrumpi n. cibum ob immoderatam caliditatem, & humidi defectum {·}stum necesse est. Verum de his commodius & explicatius cap. de cibis.
units.tr: Of the former question, the flowing away of moisture: that these things are true is shown by animals of a colder and drier temperament, which live longest of all, such as elephants, stags and ravens, and among human types the melancholic, who by universal agreement are cold and dry. The reason is that the melancholic humour is the cause that the moisture does not so readily flow away; heat and moisture are not quickly dissipated, but are joined and bounded. This will seem a paradox to many, but those who have accepted the experiment will in fact find that I have not spoken falsely. The truth of this opinion is also confirmed by the peoples of the north, who breathe cold and dry air, most familiar to their temperament; hence they live very long and without harm, unless the frequent and constant use of salted meats kills them before their time, scurvy being the worst lodger in their bodies. Why Galen calls warm and moist air the worst is because he judges with reference to cold and dry, that is, comparatively. His words, in the book cited as de re-per., chapter 4, are these: "I, however, am so far from calling spring warm and moist, or from saying that whatever is temperate is warm and moist, that I affirm the very contrary: the worst of all the temperaments of the surrounding air is that which is warm and moist." And a little later he adds a list of various diseases, none of which is free from the offspring of putrefaction; for nothing is apt to putrefy from being dry, nor from being cold. Thus meats and other things that men usually preserve are conveniently prepared with salt, or brine, or vinegar, or some other dry thing. You will find that under the north wind, which is cold and dry by nature, all things last longest without rotting, while they putrefy most easily under the south wind, which is warm and moist. Therefore we decide, contrary to them, that spring is warm and moist, since it is neither such, nor, even if it were, would it be healthful." Thus Galen. Since, therefore, warm and moist bodies putrefy most readily, as the same Galen teaches in book 1 On the Differences of Fevers, chapter 3, and indeed more quickly in warm and moist places than in cold and dry ones, as has been shown, it follows that a warm and moist constitution and temperature of the surrounding air is worse than the others. That warm and moist bodies incur the harm of putrefaction more quickly than colder and drier ones (unless they are dissolved and cooled) is shown by humoral fevers. For every humour foreign to the nature of the body in which it is contained, and not suited to its nourishment, necessarily putrefies and kindles fever; and it putrefies most quickly when the place in which it has gathered is warm, as the stomach shows, which is warmer than it should be. For no food that is immoderately overheated can remain in it without putrefaction, since food must be corrupted by excessive heat and the lack of moisture. But these matters will be discussed more conveniently and explicitly in the chapter on foods.

units.la: DE SECUNDO. An autumnus, recte dicatur frigidus & siccus, hiems frigida & humida &c. acute disputat Galenus l. de temper. cap. 3. & 4. perstringens eos, qui veré esse calidi & humidi temperamenti ideoque temperatum, autumnum frigidum & siccum, ideoque intemperatum & morbiferum exististimarunt, in qua etiam opinione bona physicorum pars permansit, persuasum sibi habens, ver, quia calidum & humidum, esse saluberrimum. Verum ex Galeni iudicio res se longe habet aliter.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE SECOND POINT: whether autumn is rightly called cold and dry, and winter cold and moist, etc. Galen disputes this acutely in De temperamentis, chapters 3 and 4, where he censures those who thought that spring, being of a warm and moist temperament, was therefore temperate, while autumn, being cold and dry, was therefore intemperate and harmful. A good part of the physicians remained in this opinion, persuaded that spring is most healthful because it is warm and moist. But according to Galen's judgement the matter stands quite differently.

units.la: Non enim aduertunt antiquos Atta-lensis Athenaei sectatores temperatam crasin, statumque praetermisisse, eiusque plane non meminisse.
units.tr: For they do not notice that the ancient followers of Athenaeus of Attalia passed over the temperate constitution and state, and did not remember it at all.

units.la: Sanitatis enim tuendae victum inuestigantes, calidiusque iusto corpus iubentes refrigerare, vel frigidius calefacere, vel humidius siccare, ficciusque, humectare, quid aliud intendunt, quam temperatum quendam atque mediocrem statum efficere? Si igitur calidum & humidum excessus nomina sunt, non potest verum esse, quod verum sit in omnibus mediocre. Si autem iccirco humidum est & calidum, quod aestate humidius est, hieme vero calidius, quid obstat, quo minus id frigidum etiam siccumque sit, propterea quod aestate frigidius & hieme calicalidus : hacque ratione erit omnia, calidum, humidum, frigidum & siccum : Sed quia 4. qualitates in vna eademque re præpollere non possunt, neque æstati neque hiemi ver comparare æquum est, sed potius ipsum per se æstimare. Neque enim hiems ipsa ea de causa frigida dicitur & humida, quod reliquis temporibus humidior sit, frigidiorque, sed quod humiditas in ea superet siccitatem, & frigiditas calorem: ad eundem modum & æstas calida & sicca, quod in ea humor vincitur à sicco, & frigidum à calido. Sic & autumnus non recte frigidus dicitur & siccus, absolute, non enim frigidus est, si per se consideretur, vt hiems est, sed vbi cum æstate confertur, quâ frigidior est: & quia inæqualiter temperatus est, vtpote meridie multo calidior quam mane aut vespeti, nec in humido & sicco medium & æqualem statum obtinet, ita vt eodem die modo frigus modo calor vrgeat, propter hanc inquam, inæqualem temperiem morbiferum recte appellatum censendum est: vt ita 4. anni temporum quodlibet ex suapte natura non ex alterius comparatione calidum, humidum, frigidum vel siccum æstimandum fit & nominandum. Quod autem Hippocrates ver vocat saluberrimum, ratio est, quod omnium excessuum medium sit ver, id est, quia æqualitatem quandâ tenet caloris, frigoris, humidi & sicci, obidq; morbis mortiferis minime obnoxius.
units.tr: For those who investigate the diet for preserving health, and who order a body that is too hot to be cooled, or one that is too cold to be warmed, or one that is too moist to be dried, or too dry to be moistened, what else do they aim at than to produce a certain temperate and moderate state? If therefore hot and moist are names of excess, it cannot be true what holds true for all things, that the mean is best. But if something is moist and hot because it is more moist in summer and hotter in winter, what prevents it from also being cold and dry, since it is colder in summer and hotter in winter? In this way everything would be hot, moist, cold and dry. But since four qualities cannot predominate in one and the same thing, it is not fair to compare spring either with summer or with winter, but rather to judge it in itself. For winter is not called cold and moist for this reason, that it is more moist and colder than the other seasons, but because in it moisture exceeds dryness and cold exceeds heat. In the same way summer is called hot and dry, because in it moisture is overcome by dryness and cold by heat. So autumn is not rightly called cold and dry absolutely; for it is not cold when considered in itself, as winter is, but when it is compared with summer, in which it is colder. And because it is unequally tempered, being much hotter at midday than in the morning or evening, and because it does not hold a middle and equal state between moist and dry, so that on the same day now cold and now heat presses, it should be judged rightly called harmful on account of this unequal temperament. Thus each of the four seasons is to be judged and named hot, moist, cold or dry from its own nature, not from comparison with another. As for Hippocrates calling spring the most healthful, the reason is that spring is the mean of all excesses, that is, because it keeps a certain equality of heat, cold, moisture and dryness, and is least liable to deadly diseases.

units.la: B 2 HafleHactenus de quaestionibus propositis ex Galeni-cis fundamentis: Redeo ad ea a quibus parum de-flexi.
units.tr: So far concerning the questions proposed from Galen's foundations. I return to those matters from which I have digressed a little.

units.la: Verum enim vero, quia pro vario acceßu & recessu Solis, vaporum, pluuiarum & im-brium occursione diuersam mutationem subi-tamque alterationem aer subit, facile etiam corpora nostra eum variis afficere modis posse existimandum est. Itaque a temperie multum recedens, impensceq; calidior vel frigidior, eo-dem recessu, quo a temperie declinauit, corri-gendus est. Et quidem plus iusto frigidior igni-bus luculentis cum suffumigiis aromaticis, vt ligno iuniperi, mastiche, thure, baccis iunipe-rinis, heibis etiam & floribus calfacientibus humi sparsis vel accensis & super carbones proiectis, vel, (quod ego saluberrimum exi-stimo, in crebroq; id vsu habeo, licet aliis sit vel ignotum vel extra vsum) herbis leuiter deco-ctis, fumoque in conclaue immisso, vel nares recepto, vel reliquas partes externas, vt manus ac pedes eo imbuendo, vix enim credideris quàm hoc tempore frigidiore commodet: inter herbas praecipuam laudem obtinet lauen-dula, thymus, Satureia, rosmarinus, maiorana, hyssopus, origanum, serpyllum, mentha, cala-mintha, betonica, saluia, & similes. Beatiores nobis longe sunt Sueci & caeteri Septentrionis populi, qui suis focis & caminis apponunt li-gna abiegna aliarumq; resiniferarum, quarum
units.tr: Indeed, because the air undergoes a varied change and sudden alteration, according to the varying approach and recession of the sun, and the encounter of vapours, rains and showers, it must be thought that it can affect our bodies in various ways too. Therefore, when the air departs much from temperance and becomes too hot or too cold, it must be corrected by the same route by which it has departed from temperance. And indeed, when it is too cold, one should use bright fires with aromatic fumigations, such as juniper wood, mastic, frankincense and juniper berries, and also herbs and flowers that warm, scattered on the ground or set alight and thrown on coals, or (which I consider most healthful, and which I often use, though it may be unknown or out of use to others) herbs lightly boiled, with the smoke let into the room, and either received into the nostrils or applied to the other external parts, such as the hands and feet, to be soaked in it. For you would hardly believe how much this helps in colder weather. Among herbs, lavender, thyme, savory, rosemary, marjoram, hyssop, oregano, wild thyme, mint, calamint, betony, sage and similar ones hold the chief praise. The Swedes and the other peoples of the North are far happier than we are, who place on their hearths and stoves logs of fir and of other resinous trees, of which there is the greatest abundance there (for oaks are rarer there and therefore highly prized), and which, when kindled, give off a very sweet odour resembling frankincense, which strikes the nose and brain and strengthens and preserves them in vigour in wonderful ways.

units.la: illic abundantia maxima, (quercus enim raríores ibi visuntur, ob idq; in magno pretio) quæ postea suauissimum, thuriq; similem odorem ex resina accensa fundunt, qui nares & cerebrū feriens miris id modis corroborat, inq; vigore conseruat. Solent autem & eiusdem cœli populi liquorem illum pinguem & flagrabilem ex arboribus prædictis affatim refudante colligere, colle&tum exiccare & thuris instar advsum reseruare. Ipse ego ex Suecia redeuntes imperitioribus quibusdam pharmacopœis imponens pro thure eum prædicaui, postea admonens, vt in simplicibus probe dignoscendis & discernendis sint cautiores.
units.tr: The people of that same climate also usually collect that fat and flammable liquor which flows out in plenty from the aforesaid trees, dry it once collected, and keep it for use in place of frankincense. I myself, returning from Sweden, recommended it as frankincense to some rather inexperienced druggists, and afterwards warned them to be more careful in properly recognising and distinguishing simple drugs.

units.la: In Calidiori vero nobis offuso aere floribus frigidis, vt nymphæ rosarum, violarum anemones, hyacinthi, cichorii, balaustii, &c. herbis item frigidis, vt parietaria, chondrilla, lactuca, endiuia, acetosa, plantagine, trifolio acetoso, portulaca, & similibus vti conuenit.
units.tr: But when the air around us is warmer, it is fitting to use cooling flowers, such as water lilies, violets, anemones, hyacinths, chicory, pomegranate flowers, and so on, and likewise cooling herbs, such as pellitory, chondrilla, lettuce, endive, sorrel, plantain, sour trefoil, purslane and similar ones.

units.la: Verum ventulum facere flabello optimum iudico. Ventilatio enim in aere calidiori quibusdam peculiaris est. Vbi tamen obseruandum vitiatum & corruptum aerem ventilandum non esse, nisi adapertis in conclaui fenestris, ex ea parte, qua ventus spirat Septentrionalis vel Orientalis, & si conclaue ab illa parte adapertile non est, corrigatur aer garyophyllis, baccis iuniperinis, masticheque, thurecque, vel detineatur in ore paulatim, & sensim masticando. cando radix angelicæ, Zedoariæ, galangæ, nux moschata, garyophyllus, vel simile quid odoriferum, de quibus paulo post exinstituto, vbi de veneno aeris, dicetur commodius.
units.tr: Yet I judge that making a little breeze with a fan is best. For ventilation is particularly suited to warmer air for some people. Here, however, it must be observed that polluted and corrupted air should not be ventilated unless the windows of the room are opened on the side from which the north or east wind blows; and if the room cannot be opened on that side, the air should be corrected with cloves, juniper berries, mastic and frankincense, or held in the mouth and gradually chewed. Chewing the root of angelica, zedoary, galangal, nutmeg, cloves, or something similar and fragrant, about which a little later, when we discuss the poison of the air, I shall speak more conveniently.

units.la: Accidit autem frequenter, vt per vrbium oppidorumq; angustos, flexuofosq; vicos comeanti putris e sterquilinii svel cloacali vapor in nares & os obreptet, qui postea in cerebrum delatus spirituum animalium consortium disgregat & conturbat. Quibus igitur necessario per eiusmodi foetentia loca est eundum, vel ftrophioli nodo ex garyophyllis & similib^9 aromatis admoto naribus, vel spiritu fortiter retento, vel si quid inopinato inspiratum fuerit, fortiter expirando, efflandoque a contagione possunt euadere immunes. Vnde videre est intempestiuas, exuperantesq; aeris immoderantias prorsus esse fugiendas.
units.tr: It often happens that as one passes through the narrow, winding streets of cities and towns, a foul vapour from a dunghill or a sewer creeps into the nose and mouth, and afterwards, carried to the brain, it scatters and disturbs the association of the animal spirits. Those who must necessarily go through such foul-smelling places can escape unharmed from the contagion by holding a little bag of cloves and similar aromatics to the nostrils, or by holding the breath firmly, or, if something has been breathed in unexpectedly, by breathing it out forcefully. Hence it is seen that untimely and excessive intemperances of the air are altogether to be avoided.

units.la: M. Aurelius Imper. diei pensum certis horis partiebatur, maneq; non vigente adhuc calore deambulabat, meridie vero in capitolio quiescebat. Augustus Cæsar natura valetudinarius domo non exibat, nisi prius aerem Sol colluftraffet.
units.tr: The Emperor Marcus Aurelius divided the day's work into fixed hours, walking in the morning while the heat was not yet strong, and resting at midday in the Capitol. Augustus Caesar, being sickly by nature, did not go out of his house unless the sun had first warmed the air.

units.la: Iccirco aer temperatus, vt matutinus, est omnium salubertrimus, Sole videlicet horofcopum, duodecimumq; cœli locum occupante: meridianus calore exuperans, vt nocturnus vapore exhalationeq; humescens, insalubris & noxius. Vespertinus, Sole videlicet Cardinem occi-
units.tr: Therefore the temperate air of the morning is the most healthful of all, when the sun occupies the horoscope and the twelfth place of the heavens. The midday air, which is excessive in heat, and the night air, which grows damp with vapour and exhalation, are unhealthful and harmful. The evening air, when the sun is traversing the western quarter of the heavens,

units.la: occidentis peragrante, quanto cum desiderio pro cordis refrigerio à contentius æstate pete-spertim grinantibus, vel subdiali ardore Solis nimioue salubris, exercitio labefactatis, hauriatur, nemini non est notum.
units.tr: is well known to everyone: with what longing it is breathed in, for the refreshment of the heart, by those especially toiling through the summer, and how healthful it is for those weakened by exercise and by the excessive burning heat of the sun in the open air.

units.la: Cauendum tamen est, ne frigidior aer extrinsecus ad cutim, detecto scilicet capite pectoreq; denudato, admittatur, densat enim cogitq; cutim, ac putredinosorum excrementorum, humorumq; effluxum transpirare prohibet, unde sæpe febres accendi videmus, aliaq; incommoda excitari. Qui tamen in continuo immodicoue sunt motu & exercitio, ne ob nimiam pororum cutaneorum relaxationem calor nativus nimium expiret, his extrinsecus cutis spiracula perflari non est noxium, hoc enim modo cutanei meatus quodammodo densantur, calorque intus detinetur, qui aliàs perhalaret magno cum facultatum & actionū incommodo.
units.tr: Still, one must take care that the colder air from outside does not reach the skin, that is, when the head is uncovered and the chest bared; for it thickens and compresses the skin and prevents the putrid excrements and the outflow of humours from passing off through perspiration, whence we often see fevers kindled and other troubles stirred up. Yet for those who are in continual or excessive motion and exercise, lest the native heat escape too much because of the excessive relaxation of the cutaneous pores, it is not harmful to let breezes blow over the skin's openings from outside; for in this way the cutaneous passages are somewhat thickened, and the heat is kept within, which otherwise would evaporate with great harm to the faculties and actions.

units.la: Insolitæ etiam & subitæ mutationes tempestatum, & maximè austrinæ, graues sunt & periculosæ, corpusq; nostrum offendunt, testimonioq; Hipp. mentem percellunt: has igitur sanitatis studiosus præcaucbit, aut saltem se foras non debebit conferre, præsertim qui à rerum externarum, tempestatumq; immoderatarum occursatione prompte conflictantur.
units.tr: Unusual and sudden changes of weather, especially southerly ones, are also grievous and dangerous, and they injure our body, and, as Hippocrates testifies, they shake the mind. The person who studies health will therefore guard against these, or at least ought not to go abroad, especially one who is readily afflicted by the encounter with external things and immoderate weather.

units.la: Hic vero & mundi regiones, regionum varietatem, ventorum vim, & quatuor anni tem-porta
units.tr: Here it is indeed worth weighing carefully the regions of the world, the variety of regions, the force of the winds, and the four seasons of the year, together with the mildness or harshness of the air. ## Caution.

units.la: Cautela. pora cum aeris temperie, vel intemperie diligenter perpendere expedit, vt quisque pro peculiari & vernacula natura aere competente & conueniente fruatur, noxiumq; euitet.
units.tr: So that each person may enjoy air that suits and agrees with his own particular and native nature, and avoid what is harmful.

units.la: Primum mundi regiones seu cardines I V. vt Oriens calidus & siccus, Occidens frigidus & humidus. Septentrio frigidus & siccus, Meridies calidus & humidus: quibus cardinibus venti temperamento & natura correspondent, quod hi naturam loci, per quem spirant, induant & affumant, auster videlic. calidus & humidus omnium insalubberrimus, pernitiosus n. semper, morborum namq; seminaria maligna ex meridionalibus illis locis & regionibus, vt Italia, Gallia, & bona parte Hispaniae secum exportare, ac in Germaniam nostrã deponere sat testatur experientia, quãuis & apud nos radices & seminaria malignorum morborũ immutabilia, quaq; interdum sua fede & loco excludi nõ possint, sponte generari nõ negârim.
units.tr: First, the four quarters or cardinal points of the world: the East is hot and dry, the West cold and moist, the North cold and dry, the South hot and moist. The winds correspond to these quarters in their temperament and nature, because they take on and assume the nature of the place over which they blow. The south wind, being hot and moist, is the most unwholesome of all and always pernicious. Experience amply shows that it carries deadly seeds of disease from the southern lands and regions, such as Italy, France, and a good part of Spain, and deposits them in our Germany. Yet I would not deny that the roots and seeds of malignant diseases, which cannot be shut out from their own seat and place, are also generated spontaneously among us.

units.la: Zephyrus frigidus est & humidus. Boreas, iudicio Plinii, & testimonio populorum Septentrionis saluberrimus, vt & Eurus qui ab Oriente flat.
units.tr: The west wind is cold and moist. The north wind, in the judgment of Pliny and the testimony of the peoples of the North, is most wholesome, and so is the east wind, which blows from the East.

units.la: Itaq; saluberrimi sunt dies sereni, meliores pluuiosi quam nebulosi, optimiq; hieme qui omnino vento carent, aestate quibus Fauonius perflat. Occidentalem enim ventum, non plane insalubrem esse & noxium testantur populi Occidentis: Imo Euro saepe salubriorem eum inspirari æstiua docent experimenta.
units.tr: Therefore, clear days are the most wholesome, rainy days are better than foggy ones, and the best in winter are those that are wholly free of wind, and in summer those in which the west wind blows. For the peoples of the West testify that the west wind is not altogether unwholesome or harmful. Indeed, summer experience teaches that it is often healthier to breathe than the east wind.

units.la: De anni temporibus, horumq; temperie, intemperieq; supra in quæstione, an autumnus recte dicatur frigidus & siccus, abunde dictum est, quare lectorem eo remitto.
units.tr: Concerning the seasons of the year and their mildness or harshness, we have said enough above, in the question whether autumn is rightly called cold and dry. I therefore refer the reader to that discussion.

units.la: Mundi Regiones sequuntur, Asia, Africa, Europa, America.
units.tr: The regions of the world follow: Asia, Africa, Europe, America.

units.la: Europæi ob calidi innati & influentis vbertatem sunt audaces, robusti, longioris q; vitæ, inter quos Germani, vt placuit Gale. 2. de temp. & Seneca sunt iracundi, fortes, audaces, graues, armorumque cupidi.
units.tr: Europeans, because of the abundance of innate and inflowing heat, are bold, robust, and long-lived. Among them the Germans, as Gale. 2. de temp. and Seneca have thought, are quick-tempered, brave, bold, serious, and eager for arms.

units.la: Per Europæos intelligo Britannos, Germanos, Gallos, Hispanos, Italos. Sarmatas (h e. Polonos, Boruffos, Effluos, <bl>Liefflender/Letuanos Littawer/Russos, Reussen/Pomeranos Pommern/</bl> Danos, Suecos, Dacos, <bl>Walachen/</bl> Tranflyluanos, <bl>Siebenbürger</bl> / Pannonęs, <bl>Ungern/</bl> Tartaros, <bl>Tartern/</bl> Mœsos, <bl>dietn Bulgarey/</bl> Pannonib. vicinos, Thraces, Macedones, Græcos, Dalmatas, Istros <bl>Histerreich/</bl> Italiā attingentes ad mare Adriaticū, &c.
