units.tr: By Europeans I mean the British, Germans, French, Spaniards, and Italians; the Sarmatians (that is, Poles, Prussians, Estonians, Livonians, Lithuanians, Russians, Pomeranians, Danes, Swedes, Dacians, Wallachians, Transylvanians, Pannonians, Hungarians, Tartars, Moesians, Bulgarians, Thracians, Macedonians, Greeks, Dalmatians, the Istrians, and the Austrians bordering on Italy and on the Adriatic Sea), and so on.

units.la: Verum vt aerem & cœlum non habent hi vnum & idem, sic etiam vita & moribus sunt diuersissimis. Galli suffragiis Justini, Cæsaris, Herodiani & Galeni sunt bellicosi & audaces, sed sitis impatientes. Pannonii teste Plin, sunt hebeti & tardo ingenio, sed ad bellum paratissimi. Itali, teste Vitruvio, prouidi & sapientes sunt, compositi scilicet factiq; ex Mercurio Venere, unde etiam Veneri plus quam caeterae Europae gentes indulgere videntur. Ligures montani Cic. teste sunt agrestes. Graeci leues & mendaces, sed ob aeris siccitatem sapientiores, quod siccitas, vt Plato prodidit, ingenium, humiditas vero stuporem gignat. Vides diuersas in diuersis terrae partibus, seu sub diuerso coelo habitantium hominum proprietates. Hae autem cum magnam partem ab influxu coelesti dependeant, varientque secundum diuersitatem in lineis parallelis & angulis mundi, qui sunt Oriens, Occidens, Meridies, Septentrio, lege iustitiae admonitus, quae regiones, prouinciae, populi, quibus sideribus, stellisque subiiciantur & gubernentur in tractatu meo astrologico, quem adornandum iam sum aggressus, commodius & uberius paulo quae acturum polliceor.
units.tr: But just as these peoples do not all have one and the same air and sky, so also their ways of life and customs are very different. According to the testimony of Justin, Caesar, Herodian, and Galen, the Gauls are warlike and bold, but impatient of thirst. Pannonians, according to Pliny, are dull and slow of wit, but most ready for war. Italians, according to Vitruvius, are provident and wise, being made, as it were, of Mercury and Venus; whence they also seem to indulge in Venus more than the other peoples of Europe. The mountain Ligurians, according to Cicero, are rustic. The Greeks are light and lying, but wiser because of the dryness of their air, since dryness, as Plato has taught, produces wit, while moisture produces stupidity. You see the different characteristics of men living in different parts of the earth, or under different skies. These depend largely on the influence of the heavens and vary according to the differing positions of the parallel lines and angles of the world, namely East, West, South, and North. Reminded by the law of justice, I promise that in my astrological treatise, which I have now begun to prepare, I shall more conveniently and fully treat which regions, provinces, and peoples are subject to and governed by which constellations and stars.

units.la: De Asianis, Africanis & Americae incolis eorundemque variis naturis & moribus, mira sunt & fidem vix impetrare valentia, quae a Cosmographis literis mandata reperiuntur.
units.tr: Concerning the Asians, Africans, and the inhabitants of America, and their various natures and customs, there are wonders that can hardly be believed, which are found recorded in the writings of the cosmographers.

units.la: Ex Asianis ob aeris temperiem quidam, sunt clementiores & humaniores: quidam contra sylvestres, feriqueque humanorum corpora eis gaudentes.
units.tr: Among the Asians, some, because of the temperature of the air, are milder and more humane; others, on the contrary, are savage and wild, and delight in the bodies of men as food.

units.la: Africani minus vitam producunt, ob caloris innati & fluentis penuriam, unde & plaeriqu sunt timidi, reperias tamen & inter eos vix homines magisque semiferos.
units.tr: Africans generally live shorter lives, because of the scarcity of innate and flowing heat; hence most of them are timid, though among them one may find men hardly human but rather half-beasts.

units.la: Americanos inter crudelissimi sunt Antropophagi in sagittando certissimi, currendo velocissimi, nudi incedentes, nulliq; obedientes, vniones aurumq; nihili facientes. Qui regionem Peru incolunt, feruntur humaniores & prudentiores, diuersarumque artium non expertes, ac coloris crocei, cujusmodi sunt regio morbo seu ictero laborantes. Hos commercia & humanitatem excolere testantur, qui mercatura amicè & perhumaniter, cum illis peracta, velis remisq; inde rediturunt.
units.tr: Among the Americans, the cannibals are the most cruel, most accurate in shooting arrows, and swiftest in running; they go about naked, obey no one, and make nothing of pearls and gold. Those who inhabit the region of Peru are said to be more humane and prudent, not without skill in various arts, and of a saffron colour, such as are people suffering from jaundice in that region. Trade and merchants testify that they cultivate commerce and humanity; those who have carried on trade with them in a friendly and most courteous manner return home by sail and oar.

units.la: Per Asianos intellige Ægyptios, Æthiopes sub Ægypto, Arabes, Syros, (qui in medio orbis sunt constituti, coelumq; habent temperatissimum, adeo vt nec nimio calore torrean-tur, nec nimio frigore horreant:) Indianos, Chaldæos, Idumæos, Samaritanos, Interamnos, Galilæos, Persas, Scythas, Armenios, Parthos, Albanos, Colchos, (maximi veneficii autores) Cilices, Pamphylios, Lycios, Jones, Lydos, Phryges, (inter quos Trojani claruerunt) Lycaones &c.
units.tr: By Asians I mean the Egyptians, the Ethiopians under Egypt, the Arabs, the Syrians (who are situated in the middle of the world and have the most temperate sky, so that they are neither scorched by excessive heat nor shivering with excessive cold), the Indians, Chaldeans, Idumeans, Samaritans, Mesopotamians, Galileans, Persians, Scythians, Armenians, Parthians, Albanians, Colchians (the greatest authors of poisoning), Cilicians, Pamphylians, Lycians, Ionians, Lydians, Phrygians (among whom the Trojans were famous), Lycaonians, and so on.

units.la: Per Africanos, Mauros, Numidas, Libes, Cyrenæos, Carthaginenses, Æthiopes, Tingitanos, Cæsariensis, Ægyptios, Æthiopiæ conterminos, &c.
units.tr: By Africans I mean the Moors, Numidians, Libyans, Cyrenaeans, Carthaginians, Ethiopians, Tangerines, Caesariensians, Egyptians bordering on Ethiopia, and so on.

units.la: Regionum denique varietas, prout calida, humida, frigida vel sicca est, varias temperamentorum, humorumq; differentes producit naturas.
units.tr: Finally, the variety of regions, according as each is hot, moist, cold, or dry, produces different natures of temperaments and humours.

units.la: Regio aspera & montosa homines alit ingratos, stupidos & inhumanos, corpora magna, aspera, crudelia, pertinacia, morbis calidis obnoxia: concava pratis & latifundiis abundas, corpora mollia, animos molles, morbos putridos & frigidos vt plurimum procreat. Vehementi & ancipiti temporum varietate flatuumq; incursione crebro infestata corpora magnitudine diuersa, robusta, animos audaces, induftriosq; sed instabiles, varios morbos, moresque inducit, vt in Gallia videre est. In locis aquosis degentes & humidis stupidi evadunt, carnosi, pingues, laborum impatientes, manfuetiores, morbisq; pituitosis obnoxii. In locis vero siccis contra sunt acuto ingenio, proni ad iracundiam & febres ardentes. Regionem in ostiis sitam incolentes, vbi maximi fluuii mare vastum ingrediuntur, variis morbis corripiuntur, quod aqua retenta in halitum convertatur, vnde postea aer conspurcatur & infici-tur.
units.tr: A rough and mountainous region breeds men who are ungrateful, dull, and inhumane, with large, rough, cruel, and stubborn bodies, prone to hot diseases. A region full of marshes and wide plains usually produces soft bodies, soft minds, and putrid and cold diseases. A place constantly troubled by violent and uncertain changes of weather and by the onset of winds produces bodies of differing size, robust, with bold and industrious but unstable minds, and various diseases and customs, as may be seen in France. Those who dwell in watery and damp places become dull, fleshy, fat, impatient of labour, gentler, and liable to phlegmatic diseases. In dry places, on the contrary, people have a sharp wit, are prone to anger, and suffer burning fevers. Those who inhabit regions situated at river mouths, where the greatest rivers enter the vast sea, are seized by various diseases, because the water that is held back turns into vapour, whence the air is afterwards polluted and infected.

units.la: Morbosa est Regio, quae magna antra, palides & loca halitibus tetris infecta recipit: Locus quoq; nulla ventorum vi exagitatus facile corrumpitur, per flabilis vero & liber salubberrimus est.
units.tr: A region is unhealthy if it contains large caves, marshes, and places infected with foul vapours. A place also that is not stirred by any force of winds is easily corrupted, but one that is open and free to the breeze is most wholesome.

units.la: Hactenus de aere, ejus essentia & proprietatibus &c. Sequitur de veneno & peste aeris.
units.tr: So far concerning air, its essence and properties, and so on. Next follows concerning the poison and plague of the air.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: SAnitatis studio omnes tenieri non posse, ut navigantes, peregrinantes & castra sequentes, ostendunt contagiosi gravissimique morbi, in quos sape incidunt: Horum praecipuum seminarium est aer malignus, pestilentiique qualitate infectus, per quem iter affectant, qui necessario cum spiritu attractus, inspiratusque pulmones primo, & postea (cor invadit, cum maxima inflammatione, & carbunculatione cito multos interimens, passimque per expirationem & inspirationem in vulgus involans, interdum multas peragrans regiones, frequentius unam, saepe unicum oppidum, vel etiam domum, quamuis frequenti pestiferorum habituum expiratione transpirationeque tandem accidit, ut aer totius urbis vel oppidi evadat venenatum. Saepe etiam delitescit includiturque in linteis, lana, indumentis pannis, locisque obscuris, minimeque patentibus. Est in historiis ex arcula in templo quodam Graecia, sepe thesauri inveniendi a quibusdam perfracta, latens evolasse venenum, totamque fere Graeciam infecisse. Scribit Bened. Alex. tempore patris sui, tegumentum, in quo venenum fuisse suspicio erat, in abditiore quodam loco fuisse repositum. & post 7. annum expromtum, probeque ventilatum uni ex servis pro tegmine impositum mortem accelerasse, pluresque alios infecisse. Unde patefecit venenum extra etiam corpus humanum posse subsistere, contagionemque ac mutua communi-tate tate contaminare ab ea parte primum, quà fit contactus, ut quotidiana id docent experimenta.
units.tr: Since all people cannot keep to the care of their health, as sailors, travellers and those who follow the army show, contagious and very grievous diseases, into which they often fall, make plain. The chief seed of these is a malignant air, infected with a pestilential quality, through which those who must travel are exposed. Drawn in with the breath and inhaled, it first invades the lungs and afterwards the heart, with the greatest inflammation and carbuncles, quickly destroying many. Flying about among the common people through breathing out and breathing in, it sometimes passes through many regions, more often through one, often through a single town, or even a single house. Yet by the frequent breathing out and exhaling of pestilential vapours, it at last happens that the air of a whole city or town becomes poisonous. Often too it lies hidden and is enclosed in linen, wool, clothing, rags, and dark places that are little open. In histories there is an account of a little chest in a certain temple in Greece, which, broken open by some who sought treasure, released a hidden poison and infected almost all of Greece. Benedictus Alexandrinus writes that in the time of his father a covering, in which poison was suspected to be, had been put away in a rather hidden place, and after seven years, taken out and well aired, was laid as a cover upon one of the servants, and hastened his death and infected several others. From this he showed that poison can subsist even outside the human body, and by mutual communication contaminate, first in that part where the contact occurs, as daily experience teaches.

units.la: Quibuscunque igitur necessario per ejusmodi infectum aerem vltro citroque est peregrinandum, quique ejusmodi habitacula, quæ à maligni aeris contagio sint libera, habere non possunt, ut ne in periculum quoddam deveniant, causas prius probè diligenterque perpendentes, quæ aeri contagium & corruptelam inferant, suffitibus, odoramentis & masticatoriis, contra extrinsecus ambientis aeris contagium se munire omni studio conabuntur.
units.tr: Therefore, for those who must necessarily travel back and forth through such infected air, and who cannot have dwellings free from the contagion of malignant air, they should first weigh carefully and diligently the causes that bring contagion and corruption to the air, and with all zeal try to protect themselves against the contagion of the surrounding air by fumigations, perfumes and things to chew.

units.la: Loquor de peste aeris seu veneno aerio ad differentiam veneni cuius contagium vel seminaria effunduntur ex aqua, terra, igne, & humanis et-iam corporibus, humoribus, scilicet in iis ad summum putredinis gradum permutatis, cujusmodi fuit pestis quæ anno 1605. pervadere capit Francofurtum, & loca tandem vicina.
units.tr: I am speaking of the plague of the air, or aerial poison, as distinct from the poison whose contagion or seeds spread from water, earth, fire, and even from human bodies, namely from humours in them changed to the highest degree of putrefaction, such as was the plague which in the year 1605 began to invade Frankfurt and at last the neighbouring places.

units.la: Hinc pestis, aeris, ignis, terra, aqua, & quæ ex humoribus in animantium corporibus corruptis & putrefactis effluit, potest pestis hominum appellari.
units.tr: Hence the plague of the air, fire, earth, water, and that which flows from humours corrupted and putrefied in the bodies of living things, may be called the plague of men.

units.la: Non enim contagium vel seminaria pestis in solo aere ponenda sunt, nec ex humanis tantum corporibus ea effundi arbitrandum est, ut falso quidam opinantur ex arte myrepsica alimoniam magis & turpe lucrum, quam agri salutem quaerentes.
units.tr: For the contagion or seeds of plague are not to be placed in air alone, nor is it to be thought that they flow only from human bodies, as some falsely hold, seeking food and base gain by the art of the cook rather than the health of the sick.

units.la: Sed hoc mirari subit etiam justissimo titulo Medi-
units.tr: But this too may fairly astonish the Medi-

units.la: Medicinam facientes hæc peste lentia seminaria confundere, parum referre existimantes, num pestis sit hominis, aeris, aquæ vel terræ.
units.tr: Making medicine, they think it matters little whether these pestilential seeds are confused, whether the plague belongs to man, air, water or earth.

units.la: Quidam falsò opinantur pestis contagium ex aere semper primario effundi. Verum de his & similibus Pseudodoxis in tractatu meo de peste prolixè disserui.
units.tr: Some falsely think that the contagion of plague always flows primarily from the air. But about these and similar false opinions I have discussed at length in my treatise on the plague.

units.la: Unum hic meminisse oportet, pestis vocabulum æquinocum esse, aerium enim venenum, morbum ab eo illatum, necnon bubonem morbi comitem, (a quibus rursus diversa est febris pestilens) denotat.
units.tr: Here one must remember that the word plague is equivocal, for it denotes the aerial poison, the disease brought on by it, and also the bubo, the companion of the disease (from which again the pestilential fever differs).

units.la: Est enim pestis propriè seu Pestilentia nunc cupatâ ab aere venenato & corrupto, venenosus vapor in aere conceptus animantium generi perniciosissimus: is inspiratus spiritus cordis primùm invadit, alteratque, qui amissâ temperie à natura imperio emancipati putrere incipiunt, aq; aliena caliditate occupati vnà attenduntur, & cum his ipsa cordis substantia, hinc per vniversum corpus venenum serpens in digniora viscera facit impetum, quia tantam malestiam ferre non possunt, in emissaria propria vel corporis habitum venenum protrudunt, vnde buboines, carbunculatio, herpetes & erysipelata, & hæc est origo febris propriæ pestilentialis dicta: Sed est & alia ex simili vdine pestilentialis dicta, quod scilicet est eiusdem ideæ & characteristici, similiaque edit symptomata, perindeq; habetur nonnunquàm le: halitus hoc fere distinguuntur, quod in vera pesti-
units.tr: Plague, properly speaking, or pestilence as it is now called, is from air that is poisoned and corrupted: a poisonous vapour conceived in the air, most destructive to the race of living things. When this breathed-in spirit first invades and alters the heart, the temperature being lost, the parts, freed from nature's rule, begin to rot, and, seized by a foreign heat, are at once consumed together with these, and with them the very substance of the heart. From here the poison creeping through the whole body makes an assault on the more noble viscera; because they cannot bear so great a malice, they push the poison out into the outlets of the body or its surface, whence come buboes, carbuncles, herpes and erysipelas. And this is the origin of the fever called properly pestilential. But there is also another fever called pestilential from a similar cause, because it is of the same kind and character and produces similar symptoms, and is often taken for the same thing. These two differ in this, that in true plague there must necessarily be some bubo, carbuncle or even papule, whether hidden or manifest, which always has as its common cause poisoned air; whereas the other is accustomed to be excited in the body by bad, corrupt foods and putrid humours. For that a substance close to poison can be excited, or rather generated, in us from the proper life of each person, is manifest from experience and reasoning.

units.la: pestilenti necessario sit aliquis bubo, vel carbuncu- lus, (vel etiam papula) siquâ latens vel manifestus, semper communem caujam habeat aerem vene- natum: illa autem ex pravis corruptisq; alimen- tis, putridisq; humoribus in corpore excitari con- sueuerit: posse enim in nobis excitari, vel potius generari substantiam venenô proximam, ex cuiusq; vitæ proprio, experientia & rationibus manife- stum est.
units.tr: Now the signs of the differences of plague must be set out, which I notice are neglected by most today to the great loss of patients and of the art. The sympathies and antipathies are a mystery to be explored here: those which, by a certain divine law of association, agree, and those which disagree with one another.

units.la: Nunc signa differentiarum pestis propo- nenda sunt, quæ à plerisque hodie negligi sum- ma cum ægrotorum & artis jactura animad- uerto. Sympathias verò & antipathias myste- rium hic explorandum, quæ videlicet diuina quadam consortii lege conspirent, quæque in- ter se dissideant.
units.tr: Signs of earth plague are abscesses with pestilence, difficult sleep, and a livid colour of the skin. In this case all remedies that share in the nature of earth are useful, such as the flesh of the mole, fox, wolf, cat, and so on.

units.la: Signa pestis terra sunt apostemata cum pe- stilentia, difficilis somnus, color cutis lividus: in hac prosunt omnia medicamenta naturam terra participantia, ut caro talpæ, vulpis, lupi, felis, &c.
units.tr: The signs of pestilence from earth are abscesses with plague, difficult sleep, and a livid colour of the skin. In this case all remedies that share the nature of earth are useful, such as the flesh of the mole, fox, wolf, cat, and so on.

units.la: Pestis aeris signa sunt tibiarum hinc inde jactatio, tumores circa humeros, & infra brachia, astma siccum, cephalalgia ingens cum phrenitide: in hac prosunt passeres, merula, gallina, pavones, cornices, corvi.
units.tr: The signs of pestilence from air are jerking of the legs back and forth, swellings around the shoulders and under the arms, dry asthma, and severe headache with phrenitis. In this case sparrows, the blackbird, the hen, peacocks, jackdaws, and ravens are useful.

units.la: Pestis aquæ signa sunt sitis ingens; paucus so- mnus, tumor pedum & signa circa pudenda, potare nolunt, pedesq; intumescunt, in hac prosunt pisces, rana, bufones, inprimis verò carnes ciconiæ & anatum, locis affectis applicatæ. Secretum. Pestis ignis signa sunt, somnus continuus & in-desinens, calor intensus, humores magni post aures, sitim non habent: in hac venenum extrahendum est per alium & cepas, vel aliud specificum: atq; hic laudatur Xenechdon Theophrasti. Has differentias diligenter expendere decet bonum & fidelem medicum, ex his enim cura instituenda est cum veris prognosticis, per quæ medicus in sua arte, testimonio Hippocr. admirabilis censetur.
units.tr: The signs of pestilence from water are great thirst, little sleep, swelling of the feet, and signs around the genitals; the patients refuse to drink and their feet swell. In this case fish, frogs, and toads are useful, and above all the flesh of storks and ducks, applied to the affected places. Secret. The signs of pestilence from fire are continuous and unceasing sleep, intense heat, and large humours behind the ears; the patients have no thirst. In this case the poison must be drawn out by another, using onions or some other specific; and here the Xenechdon of Theophrastus is praised. A good and faithful physician ought to weigh these differences carefully, for from them the cure must be undertaken with true prognoses, through which the physician is judged admirable in his art, by the testimony of Hippocrates.

units.la: Aerem autem dupliciter immutari, velin primis qualitatibus, vel in tota substantia, cum vi-delicet Extremam prauitatem maligntatem sortitus est, Physicorum documentum est.
units.tr: That the air is changed in two ways, either in its primary qualities or in its whole substance, namely when it has acquired extreme depravity and malignity, is a teaching of the natural philosophers.

units.la: In peste putrens & corruptus est non calore tantum, sed maligna et venenata etiam qualitate.
units.tr: Therefore plague of the air does not happen unless the air is corrupted in its substance.

units.la: Non igitur accidit pestis aeris, nisi aere se-cundum substantiam corrupto.
units.tr: Therefore pestilence of the air does not occur unless the air has been corrupted in its substance.

units.la: Corrumpitur aer a corporibus cœlestibus & terrestribus, ab illis, ut causa remota, ab his, ut propinqua.
units.tr: The air is corrupted by heavenly bodies and by earthly bodies: by the former as a remote cause, by the latter as a proximate cause.

units.la: Ab astris corrumpitur aer 1. Cum siunt coniunctiones magnæ, ut Saturni, Iouis & Martis, sicut anno elapso 1604. in Sagittario. 11. Cum plures stellæ tam fixæ, quam erraticæ Soli coniunguntur; cumulatur enim & intenditur calor illis locis & populis, ad quos coniunctio spectat. 111. Virtus cœlestis fortius agens in virtutes patientes terrestres aerem sensibiliter immutat & alterat, vel in naturam & statum ipsi homogeneum, ut cum naturali temporis caliditas mutatur in calidatem
units.tr: The air is corrupted by the stars: (1) when great conjunctions occur, such as of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars, as in the past year 1604 in Sagittarius; (2) when several stars, both fixed and wandering, are conjoined with the Sun, for the heat is then heaped up and intensified in those places and peoples to which the conjunction relates; (3) the heavenly power, acting more strongly upon the passive earthly powers, changes and alters the air perceptibly, either into a nature and state homogeneous with itself, as when the natural warmth of the season is changed into heat

units.la: C vehevehementem, vel heterogeneum & oppositum, ut fi astas mutetur in frigiditatem & humiditatem lædentem & contra communem naturæ cursum. Ejusmodi mutationes temporum inquit Hipp. 3. aphor. Si magna fuerint, subita & vehementes pariunt morbos, & quandoq; mortem. A subita enim mutatione qualitatum aliarum vehementer imprimentium forisq; occurrentium, ut caliditatis in astate, frigiditatis in hieme, mortem infirmis aliquando accidisse, & etiamnunc accidere posse patet, nam mortem, quæ infirmis astate contingit & hieme, potissimum à virtute cœlesti agente naturali aeris statum supra modum & subito immutante dependere animaduersum est, in vere vero & autumno magis à causa inferiori & terrestri.
units.tr: vehement, or into a heterogeneous and opposite state, harmful cold and moisture, and contrary to the common course of nature, as when summer is changed into cold and damp. Hippocrates, in the third Aphorism, says of such changes of the seasons: If they are great, sudden and violent, they produce diseases and sometimes death. For it is clear that from a sudden change of other qualities that strongly impress themselves and rush in from outside, such as heat in summer or cold in winter, death has sometimes come to the sick and can still come; for it has been observed that the death which comes to the sick in summer and winter depends chiefly on the heavenly natural agent, which changes the state of the air beyond measure and suddenly, but in spring and autumn more on the lower and earthly cause.

units.la: Inter causas inferiores, à quibus aer promtius corrumpi potest, sunt vapores, halitusque maligni e terra quibusdam cavernis et aperturis expirantes, exhalantesq;, tum etiam fœda hominum & animalium strages, aquarum stagnantium & putridarum corruptela, tetraq; & contagiosa aliarum putrescentium evaporatio, ut ex pecorum stabulis & cloacis, tum animalibus etiam quibusdam venenosis.
units.tr: Among the lesser causes by which the air can more readily be corrupted are vapours and noxious breaths that rise and exhale from the earth through certain caves and openings. Also the foul slaughter of men and animals, the corruption of stagnant and putrid waters, and the foul and contagious evaporation of other decaying things, such as from cattle stalls and sewers, and also from certain poisonous animals.

units.la: Verum locus sive regio, regionis altitudo & humilitas montium marisq; vicinitas, ipsiusq; regionis terra hic perpendenda est. Non enim in omni regione, & ubiq; semper, sed cateris terra cavernis eiusmodi veneno si halitus concluduntur, qui eruentes aquam & aerem illius loci inficiunt, præcipue vero per terra motum exclusi animalia inter-ficiunt & inter ea primum oves pascentes, qui in locis p[?]cuis vbi vapores paulatim erumpunt, con-tinuo quasi cum pastu exhalantem quandam pu-tredinem hauriunt. Testatur Seneca, in terra mo-tu tempore Neronis Imp. grigem fexcentarum o-vium esse deletum, vnaq; homines aliaq; animan-tia contagio huic vicina.
units.tr: But the place or region must be considered here as well: the height or lowness of the region, the nearness of mountains or sea, and the nature of the soil itself. For it is not in every region, nor at all times, that such caves release poisonous exhalations, which, bursting forth, taint the water and air of that place. Especially when they are shut in by an earthquake, these exhalations kill animals, and above all the sheep that graze there. In places where the vapours seep slowly out, the sheep, as they feed, take in with the pasture a kind of putrid exhalation. Seneca reports that in an earthquake in the time of the emperor Nero, a flock of six hundred sheep was destroyed, and that men and other living things near that place were affected by the same contagion.

units.la: Idem ve[?] o halitus seu vapor intra terra cauter-nas repulsus exitu videlicet ei interclusus, infernalis evadit & maxime pestiferus, ad auripigmenti e-nim aluminis & sulphuris specus venaq; detrusus ignescit, qui postea erumpens subito & cito, quic-quid comprehenderit, adurendo corrumpit atq; in terficit, a qua etiam maligni a e a quibusdam in-fernalem eum dictum reperio.
units.tr: The same breath or vapour, when it is driven back into the caverns of the earth and so has its exit closed off, becomes infernal and most pestilential. For when it is forced into veins and caves of orpiment, alum and sulphur, it catches fire, and afterwards it bursts forth suddenly and quickly, and by burning it corrupts and kills whatever it seizes. For this reason some have called it "infernal" and "malignant."

units.la: A vivis animalibus quoq; aerem infici & cor-rumpi praeter experientiam nostri huius seculi ex-emplo sunt duo dracones, tempore Philippi Regis Macedoniae inter duos Armeniae montes viam-du a multis salubriter tritam ita inficientes, ut transeuntes illico et subito e medio tollerentur. Ac-cersitus a Rege Socrates, ut infectionis huius con-tagiique causam diceret, iussit adificium aliud erigi juxta montes fecitq; speculum chalybeum planum, ut ad illud ex omni parte montium fierent reflexo & reuerberatio. Ex qua radiatura catoptrica ap-paruerunt in speculo species draconum didutiis a-pertisq; faucibus ex aduerso se aspicientium, aeris intermedium oris ventrisq; ipsorum halitu mali-
units.tr: Living animals too, as well as the air, are known to infect and corrupt it, as our own age also shows. In the time of Philip, King of Macedon, two dragons, between two mountains of Armenia, infected the road that many people had used to their benefit, so that those who passed by were at once and suddenly carried off. The king summoned Socrates to say what the cause of this infection and contagion was. Socrates ordered another building to be erected near the mountains and made a flat bronze mirror, so that reflections and echoes from all sides of the mountains would strike it. From this catoptric radiation, images of the dragons appeared in the mirror, with their jaws open and their throats wide, facing one another, and the air between their mouths and bellies, tainted by their breath, was made harmful. Afterwards, by the king's command, the dragons were killed, and the place no longer took its name from the sudden deaths of passers-by, and did not hand down that memory.

units.la: C 2 gu gno vitiantium, quibus postea jussu Regis interemptis factum est, ut is locus ex subita transeuntium inter necione nomen non amplius ceperit, memoriamq; prodiderit.
units.tr: (Omitted: this unit consists only of a printer's signature mark, followed by the continuation of the sentence given in unit 1.) The place no longer took its name from the sudden deaths of passers-by, and did not hand down that memory.

units.la: Ventos deniq; quosdam pestilentes ferosque esse nemo erit qui inficias iverit. Constat ventos naturam & qualitates locorum, per quae spirant, suscipere & induere, aeremq;, sive salubrem, sive insalubrem & corruptum secum deferre, inq; oppositam sibi plagam locumq; deponere. Exempli gratia, aere corrupto & infecto in plaga occidentis vel meridiei, ventus contagium defert in plagam orientis vel septentrionis. Sed hic latitudines, altitudinesq; locorum & civitatum perpendisse oportebit. Contagium enim quod per ventos defertur promptius subsidit in locis sublimioribus & editioribus, quod vero ex stagnantium aquarum, terra, aliarumq; rerum putrescentium contagiosTo tetroq; halitu emanat atq; effunditur, loca utplurimum in cavis vallibus sita infestare solet.
units.tr: Nobody will deny that some winds are pestilential and savage. It is agreed that winds take on and assume the nature and qualities of the regions through which they blow, and carry with them air, whether healthy or unhealthy and corrupt, and set it down in the region opposite to them. For example, when air in the western or southern region has been corrupted and infected, the wind carries the contagion into the eastern or northern region. But here one must weigh the latitudes and altitudes of places and cities. For contagion carried by the winds settles more readily in higher and loftier places, whereas that which rises and spreads from stagnant waters, earth, and other putrefying things, with its foul, poisonous breath, usually infests places lying in hollow valleys.

units.la: Iter igitur per publicas strages facientes, paludes, stagna, locaq; foetentia & veneno infecta praetereuntes, Pomambris, odoriferis oleis, odoratis sacculis vel trocisci mastrcandis adversus eiusmodi foetentes exhalationes se debent munire.
units.tr: Therefore, those who make journeys through public pestilence, passing marshes, ponds, foul places and places infected with poison, should protect themselves with pomanders, fragrant oils, scented sachets, or lozenges to be chewed against such stinking exhalations.

units.la: POMAMBRUM.
units.tr: POMAMBRUM.

units.la: Recip. laudani pinguis drachm. unam semis, styracis calamitae scrupulos duos, benzoi, storacis liquid. singulorum drachm. unam gariophylorum, cinnamomi; nucis mofchatæ» macis,fantali citrini, Zedoariæ, rofarum rube- arum fing,drachm.femis, balfami garyophyl- lorum fcr. femis, terebinthinæ quantum fuffi - cit ad incoiporationem,
units.tr: Take fat laudanum, one and a half drachms; two scruples of Styrax calamita; of benzoin, liquid storax, each one drachm; of cloves, nutmeg, mace, citron sandalwood, zedoary, and red roses, each half a drachm; of balsam of cloves, half a scruple; turpentine, as much as suffices to bind them together.

units.la: Ditiores, quique cupiunt fragrantius & carius, addant mofchi & ambræ, fing.grana ij. vel iij.
units.tr: Those who are wealthier, and who wish for something more fragrant and costly, should add two or three grains each of musk and ambergris.

units.la: Aliud minus pretiosum pro pauperibus veltenacium.
units.tr: Another, less costly, for the poor or those of slender means.

units.la: Recip.radic.enulæ,angelicæ, majoranæ, rorifmarini,rofarum rub.ruthæ.Saluiæ,garyo- phyllorum, thymi vel fatureiæ, fingulorum partes æquales, camphoræ parum, fiat puluis & incorporetur pro Pomambro.
units.tr: Take roots of elecampane, angelica, marjoram, rosemary, red roses, rue, sage, cloves, thyme or savory, equal parts of each, and a little camphor. Make a powder and mix it into a pomander.

units.la: Sacculi fiunt ex rofis, violis, majorana, pulegio.bafilicone,thymo,Satureja,radice iri- dis,calamo aromatico,garyophyllis, lauendu- la,feropillo,origano,rutha,Itechade,coriandro, baccis juniperi,melilla,floribus hiflopi,lauen- dulę,falyiæ,rorifmarini,& fimilibus,ferico infu- endis.
units.tr: The same ones used in the same way are of value against infection, but they are disapproved in treatment. For because they are very strong, and of thin and hot parts, they increase feverish heat. This should be noted: nevertheless they may be allowed at the first onset and before the fever.

units.la: Ego nullum ingredior iter abfq; Zedoaria, garyophyllis,corticibus citri,arantiarum,radi- ce angelicæ, enulæ, valerianæ, vel galangæ, hæc enim & fimilia ore detenta & masticata venenatos halitus potenter difcutiunt & avertunt. Certum enim est fimplici veneno fimplex medica- mentum esse optimum,sed specificum,nam angeli- cain pefte aqua improbatur. Possunt etiam prædicta fimplisimplicia medicamenta contundi, & in electuarii formam cum melle, vel sirupo consistente, ut rosarum, acaciae, atque citri, acetosae, scabiosae, concinnari. Acetum ex huiusque concinnata ipsum iustissimum fuit. Sequens in praesertim autem ratione celebra iustissimum est, paratum quoque vtilis, prae-sertim ...
units.tr: I never set out on a journey without zedoary, cloves, citron peel, orange peel, root of angelica, elecampane, valerian or galangal. For these and similar things, held in the mouth and chewed, powerfully dispel and turn away poisonous breath. For it is certain that for a simple poison a simple remedy is the best, but a specific one; for angelica water is disapproved in plague. These simple ingredients may also be pounded and made up into an electuary with honey or a thick syrup, such as of roses, acacia, citron, sorrel or scabious. Vinegar prepared from these was most useful. The following preparation, especially, is very celebrated and most useful, and also easy to make, especially ...

units.la: Recipe baccarum iuniperi, cortici bus nigris detractis, quantum libet: folia ruthae, juglandis vel plures: Zedoariam, angelicam: quibus omnibus contusis in mortario & cum mellis electuario admodum croci integri, sicci & boni, iterumque miscentur. Sumatur mane vel etiam tempore coquendo pulsante, quantitas avellanae majoris singulis vicibus.
units.tr: Take juniper berries, with the black skins removed, as much as you like; leaves of rue, walnuts or more; zedoary and angelica. Crush all of these in a mortar and mix them with an electuary of honey, together with entire, dry and good saffron, and mix again. Take it in the morning, or even at the time of pulsing cooking, in the quantity of a large hazelnut each time.

units.la: Eodem etiam modo usurpata theriaca & mithridati cum infigres praestant usus, sed in curatione improbantur. Quia enim magna sunt alliuitatis, tenuiumque ac calida arum partium, calorem febrilem augent, quod notandum est: in primo tamen infultu & ante febrim concedantur.
units.tr: Theriac and mithridate, used in the same way and with the same ingredients, are of benefit, but they are disapproved in treatment. For since they are heavy and of thin and hot parts, they increase febrile heat, which must be noted. Nevertheless, they may be allowed at the first onset and before the fever.

units.la: Consuenti quoque praedictorum simplicium fasraginem quandam in crassiorem puluerem redigere, sericoque infucre & interiori pilei vel tiara partim, vbi cerebellum contingit & verticem annectere, non tam vitiati aeris emendandi, & a cerebro repellendi, quam eiusdem corroborandi gratia.
units.tr: These simples, too, may be reduced to a rather coarse powder, sewn into a little sack and placed in silk, and partly sewn into the inside of a cap or hat, where it touches the crown and top of the head. This is done not so much to correct the vitiated air and repel it from the brain, as to strengthen the brain itself.

units.la: Olea quoque; & odorifera vnguenta naribus temporibusque admota vel inuncta, sicut & cartapolas quas manus, Spiritus ab omni contagione seruant immunes.
units.tr: Oils and fragrant ointments, applied or rubbed on the nostrils and temples, as also scented gloves for the hands, keep the spirits immune from all contagion.

units.la: Ex Oleis magis probantur, Oleum ex baccis juniperi, lauri, feminę anisi, fœniculi, cymini, ex hyssopo, thymo, spica, cinnamomo, garyophyllis (hæc duo pretiosissima sunt) nucę moschata, macę, succino albo, terebinthinū, &c.
units.tr: Among oils, the following are more approved: oil of juniper berries, laurel, seed of anise, fennel and cumin; of hyssop, thyme, spike, cinnamon, and cloves (these two are most precious); nutmeg, mace, white amber, turpentine, etc.

units.la: Quia vero olea facile diffluunt, præstat in unguenti consistentiam ea redigere, vasculoq; in auro vel argenteo inclusa conseruare.
units.tr: Since oils flow away easily, it is better to reduce them to the consistency of an ointment and keep them enclosed in a little vessel of gold or silver.

units.la: Unguentum odoriferum pro delicatioribus.
units.tr: A fragrant ointment for the more fastidious.

units.la: Recip. ambrę, moschi, zibetti, singul. granarum, olei garyoph. vel cinnamomi, &c. guttas iij, cum oleo amygdalarum dulcium fiat unguentum.
units.tr: Take ambergris, musk and civet, a grain of each, oil of cloves or of cinnamon, three drops, and make an ointment with oil of sweet almonds.

units.la: Aliud pretiosissimum.
units.tr: Another, most precious.

units.la: Recip. moschi, gr. vj. ol. garyoph. guttas iij. ambr. gr. ij. zibetti gr. viij. cum oleo è nuce moschata expresso ad drachm. unam, f. unguentum.
units.tr: Take musk, six grains; oil of cloves, three drops; ambergris, two grains; civet, eight grains. With oil pressed from nutmeg, one drachm, make an ointment.

units.la: Aliud.
units.tr: Another.

units.la: Minus earum, & tamen efficax.
units.tr: Less costly, yet still effective.

units.la: Recip. ol. thymi, hyssopi, fing. guttas iij, ol. spicæ gutt. ij. ol. ex nuce moschata expressi drachm. semis vel scrup. duos, f. unguentum.
units.tr: Take oil of thyme and hyssop, three drops of each; oil of spike, two drops; oil pressed from nutmeg, half a drachm or two scruples. Make an ointment.

units.la: Qui vero eiusmodi habitacula obtinent, quæ vel plaudum, vel stagnorum rancori, vel etiam limi inquinamentis obnia sunt, & subiecta, ut dent operam, ut domus valuę sint perflabiles & vento quidem septentrionis, vel orientis, vel aør rećt sirectificetur & corrigatur accenso igne, suffumi-gius ex ligno & baccis juniperi, thus e, mastiche, Igne enim contra aerem infectum nihil efficacius; vapores enim absorbet & dissipat. Unde Hippo-crates, magnam illam lucem Athenis & totius fere Graecia ignepublicis in plateis & compitis accenso propulsavit: idemque Thaletem Milesium fa-bitasse reperio. Ignes debent construi ex lignis juniperi, abietis, cypressi, betularum, tamarisci, quernis, fagi-nis & similibus. Ligna resiniferarum arborum omnibus aliis praestant.
units.tr: Those who occupy dwellings that are exposed to marshes, to the foulness of ponds, or even to the filth of mud, and that lie low, should take care that the houses are airy and open to the wind, whether from the north or the east, or that the air is corrected and rectified by a lit fire, with fumigations of juniper wood and berries, frankincense and mastic. For nothing is more effective than fire against tainted air, since it absorbs and disperses the vapours. Hence Hippocrates drove away that great pestilence at Athens and throughout almost all of Greece by lighting fires in the public squares and crossroads; and I find that Thales of Miletus did the same. Fires should be made from wood of juniper, fir, cypress, birch, tamarisk, oak, beech and similar trees. The wood of resinous trees surpasses all others.

units.la: Praestat etiam in ipso sanitatis statu praeser-tim literis operam navantibus, singulis horis matutinis os & palatam diligenter aqua pura cum aceti modico vel pura rosacea abluere, vel aceto aqua rosarum mixto, vel vino aqua rosarum con-temperato quod postremum oculis clarificandis optimum est. Frontis denique temporum nariumque aspersio aqua rosar. vel lauendula, vel etiam aceto rosarum optimum spirituum fomentum est: & tum de aere nobis offuso, ac invitis etiam ad corporis vigorem tutelamque inspirando dixisse sufficiat.
units.tr: It is also advisable, even when in good health, especially for those who devote themselves to study, to wash the mouth and palate carefully with pure water every morning, either with a little vinegar, or with rosewater alone, or with vinegar mixed with rosewater, or with wine mixed with rosewater; the last is best for clearing the eyes. Finally, sprinkling the forehead, temples and nostrils with rosewater or lavender water, or even with rose vinegar, is an excellent fomentation for the spirits. And let what has been said about the air that surrounds us, and that we breathe in even against our will, suffice for the vigour and protection of the body.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: De cibo, & potu, secundum locum inter Sanitatis praecepta & capita obtinentibus.
units.tr: Concerning food and drink, which hold the second place among the precepts and heads of health.

units.la: Constat quotidie aliquid de corporis nostri substantia decedere, viuereq; ho-minem
units.tr: It is agreed that something of the substance of our body wastes away every day, and that a man cannot live long

units.la: minė diu non posse, nisi cibo & potu q̃ deflu-xit, reparetur, cibo quidem quicquid solidio-ris & liccioris suit substantiæ, potu vero quic-quid humidioris ac spiritusosæ exhaustum est, vt ita absque cibo & potu 7. vel ad longissimū 8. dies vitam protrahere nemo possit. Quod si à corporibus animantium nihil effluereret, sem-perque eadem substantiæ moles perduraret, cibis opus non esset.
units.tr: unless what has flowed away is restored by food and drink. By food he restores whatever was of a more solid and firm substance, and by drink whatever was moist and spirituous. So no one can prolong life beyond seven, or at most eight, days without food and drink. If nothing flowed out of the bodies of living creatures, and the same mass of substance always endured, there would be no need of food.

units.la: Est enim cibus, quem nutrimentum, & ali-mentum appellant, substantia similis illi, quæ è corporibus defluxit, resarciens atque re-staurans, quod deperiit. Triplicis enim sub-stantiæ nostræ fluor perpetuus cibo & potu re-stauratur.
units.tr: For food, which they call nourishment and aliment, is a substance like that which has flowed from the bodies, making good and restoring what has been lost. The constant flow of our threefold substance is restored by food and drink.

units.la: Itaque in legitimè & salubriter assumendis esculentis & poculentis, habitâ diligenti ra-tione qualitatis, quantitatis, vtendiqué modi, obseruentur proæmii loco sequentes præce-ptiones.
units.tr: Therefore, in taking solid and liquid food lawfully and healthfully, with careful regard to quality, quantity and manner of use, the following precepts are to be observed by way of preface.

units.la: I. Esculentorum & poculentorum quanti-tas non debet esse intempestiua, importuna, molesta & indecens, sed mediocris: Tantum enim cibi & potus, inquit Tullius in libr. de se-nect, adhibendum est, vt reficiantur vires non opprimantur. Reficiuntur autem, si edentes & bibentes modum teneant, qui est inter nimi-um & paucum: suffocantur vero & opprimun-tur, si in alterutram partem à mediocritate su-erit aberratum. Vnde Lycurgus Lacædemo-
units.tr: I. The quantity of food and drink should not be untimely, unseasonable, troublesome or unbecoming, but moderate. For, as Tully says in his book On Old Age, only so much food and drink is to be taken that the strength is restored and not oppressed. Strength is restored if those who eat and drink keep to a measure between too much and too little; but they are choked and oppressed if they stray from the mean in either direction. Hence Lycurgus, giving laws to the Lacedaemonians,

units.la: C niis leges ferens tantum ciborum vnicuiq; distribui iussit, quantum ad bonam corporis valetudinem tuendam satis esset.
units.tr: ordered that each man be given only as much food as would be enough to preserve good health of body.

units.la: Galenus in arte parua vere & sapienter docet, certam cibi exhibendi mensuram ex naturali appetentia & coctione sumendam esse.
units.tr: Galen, in his Ars Parva, truly and wisely teaches that the fixed measure of food to be given is to be taken from natural appetite and digestion.

units.la: Huc accedit quod quantitas porrigendi cibi commodissime sumitur a calore magis vel minus concoquente, qui pro varia corporum, humorum, aetatum, temporum, coelique natura variat & mutatur. Vnde pro aetatum, temperamentorum, temporum & regionum varietate, proq; vniuscuiusq; conditione & natura, cibi assumedi occasio sumeda est. Robustiores enim multum & frequentius comedunt ob caloris innati & influentis copiam: imbecilliores vt senes pauco & frequenti ob calorem elanguescentem alimento indigent: Biliosi & macilenti difficilius, obesi & pituitosi facilius inediam perferunt, illic igitur pastus crebrior: hic rarior vtilior est. Æstate ob calorem influentem exiguum paucus cibus, sed potus dilutior offerendus est, hieme liberalius & meracius ob aeris frigidam & humidam constitutionem vescendum & bibendum est. Pueri etiam frequentius ob copiam caloris innati & influentis, iuuenes ob caloris influentis acrimoniam dilutius, senes ob calorem imbecillum alantur frequentius. Itaque sanitati optime consulere volentes decentem ciborum mensuram, naturaliter . raeq; conuenientem sibi praescribant, eamque accuratè, vel quoad fieri poterit, seruent, hic enim iucundè & salubriter totum vitae cursum absq; morborum inuasione peracturi, corporisq; ac animi vires integras sunt conseruaturi.
units.tr: Moreover, the quantity of food to be offered is most conveniently judged by the heat that digests more or less, which varies and changes according to the nature of bodies, humours, ages, seasons and climate. Hence, according to the variety of ages, temperaments, seasons and regions, and according to each person's condition and nature, the occasion for taking food must be chosen. Stronger people eat much and more often because of the abundance of innate and incoming heat; weaker people, such as the old, need little and frequent nourishment because their heat is failing. Bilious and lean people bear fasting with more difficulty, while the obese and phlegmatic bear it more easily; so for the former more frequent meals, for the latter rarer ones, are more useful. In summer, because the incoming heat is slight, little food but more diluted drink should be offered; in winter one should eat and drink more freely and undiluted because of the cold and moist constitution of the air. Children too are fed more often because of the abundance of innate and incoming heat; young people more diluted, because of the sharpness of the incoming heat; the old more often, because their heat is weak. Therefore, those who wish to consult their health best should prescribe for themselves a fitting measure of food, natural and suited to themselves, and keep to it carefully, or as far as possible; for in this way they will pass the whole course of life pleasantly and healthily, without invasion of disease, and will keep the strength of body and mind intact.

units.la: Unde qui temperantiam & frugalitatem vitae constituerunt fundamentum, diutius vitam produxêre, illustresq; euasêre virtute & ingenio.
units.tr: Hence those who have made temperance and frugality of life the foundation have prolonged their lives, and become illustrious for virtue and talent.

units.la: Pythagoras Philosophus Samius, à multis escis sibi temperasse fertur, quoniam animo ad temperantiam eas incommodare arbitrabatur. Ad vitem quoque non ingrediendum monuit, non ad ipsam scilicet vitem, sed vinolentiam fugiendam praeceptum dirigens. Vinum enim non attigisse aiunt, quin & parcissimi fuisse potus nullumq; obsonium degustasse, crebrius verò exiguo melle victitasse, omninoq; moderatissimè vitam produxisse ab optimis autoribus proditum est.
units.tr: Pythagoras the Samian philosopher is said to have abstained from many foods, since he thought they hindered the temperance of the mind. He also warned against entering the vine, not meaning the vine itself but directing the precept at shunning drunkenness. For they report that he never touched wine, and that he was most sparing in drink and tasted no delicacy; he often lived on a little honey, and the best authors record that he lived most moderately.

units.la: Socrates Philosophus Atheniensis, parcissimi cibi extitisse & continentissimi victus omnium consensu fertur: famem scambulando obsonare dictitabat.
units.tr: Socrates the Athenian philosopher is by general agreement said to have been the most sparing in food and the most abstemious in diet; he used to say that he procured his relish by walking, that is, with hunger.

units.la: Plato Phil. Atheniensis, à praeceptoris frugalitate non discessit, quod testatur dictum Timothei, qui superiori die apud Platonem coenaverat, muscam tenuemque coenulam dixit, quiqueque coenassent apud Platonem postero eos die bene agere. Mensas Italicas & Syracusanas nas vt opiparas & luxuriosas damnauit: quin morem illum, quo bis die statutum fieri liceret, detestatus est. Ficuum fuit amator, vnde φιλόσυκος dictus fuit.
units.tr: Plato the Athenian philosopher did not depart from his teacher's frugality. This is shown by the saying of Timotheus, who had dined the day before with Plato: he called it a fly and a thin little supper, and said that those who had dined with Plato were well off the next day. He condemned the Italian and Syracusan tables as lavish and luxurious, and detested the custom by which a meal might be set out twice a day. He was a lover of figs, and so was called philosykos.

units.la: Ariftotelem huius discipulum non sibi adeo moderatum constat, Alexandrinae proculdubio illius victoriae aut Perlici potius luxus contagione imbutum.
units.tr: Aristotle, his disciple, is not recorded to have been so temperate himself, being no doubt tainted by the contagion of Alexander's victories, or rather of Persian luxury.

units.la: Epaminondas Thebanorum dux clarissimus, sic in vita frugalis erat, vt è vicino ad coenam vocatus, cum obsoniorum & bellariorum summum apparatum inuenisset, è vestigio abiit, dicens, Ego te sacrificare non lasciuire putabam, vnde in exercitu ventricosis obesisq; infensus erat, eosq; pellebat. In vestium vero moderatione laborumq; tolerantia clarum eu extitisse Plutarchus testis est.
units.tr: Epaminondas, the most famous leader of the Thebans, was so frugal in life that, when invited to dinner by a neighbour and finding a great display of dainties and sweetmeats, he at once left, saying, "I thought you were sacrificing, not feasting." Hence in the army he was hostile to paunchy and fat men and drove them away. Plutarch bears witness that he was famous for moderation in dress and for endurance of labours.

units.la: Agesilaum illum Magnum Spartanorum Regem, a satietate vinolentiaq; penitus abstinuisse Historiae tradunt. Huic Thespii per summ agrum iter cum exercitu facienti, farinam, anseres, bellaria, libaq; & mellita opera aliasq; omnis generis escas, vina simul generosissima miserunt. Verum is farina tantum recepta caetera recusauit: tandem vero precibus accipere coactus mancipiis distribuit, afferens ingenuos & fortes ganeae operibus non indigere.
units.tr: Histories hand down that Agesilaus, the great king of the Spartans, abstained entirely from satiety and wine. When he was marching with his army through the territory of Thespiae, the people sent him meal, geese, sweetmeats, cakes, honey-cakes and foods of every kind, together with the finest wines. But he accepted only the meal and refused the rest. At last, compelled by entreaties to accept them, he gave them to his servants, saying that free and brave men had no need of the works of gluttony.

units.la: Chrysippus Philosophus Assianus Solensis ad alendum homines nihil praeter Cereris munera & aquae poculum opus esse ... Euripides afferebat.
units.tr: Chrysippus, the philosopher of Assos and Soli, said that nothing but the gifts of Ceres and a cup of water is needed to nourish men... Euripides used to assert this.

units.la: Bion Boryfthenes sapiēnter dixit non oportere voluptates ab epulis menfisq; proficisci, sed à sobrietate.
units.tr: Bion of Borysthenes wisely said that pleasures ought to come not from feasts and tables but from sobriety.

units.la: Crates Philosophus ille Thebanus Demetrium Phalereum reprehendit, quod panes in pera, & lagenam vini ad fe misisset, dicens iis minimè fe indigere vbi effent fontes: pecunias suas omnes abiecit in mare, vt philosophare-tur liberius.
units.tr: Crates, that Theban philosopher, reproached Demetrius of Phalerum because he had sent him bread in a bag and a flask of wine, saying that he had no need of them where there were springs. He threw all his money into the sea so that he might philosophize more freely.

units.la: Cleomenes Lacedæmoniorum dux, omnium aliarum virtutum gloria floruit, coenandique apparatum quotidianum exiguum habuit laconicæ parsimoniæ conuenientem. Quod fi seniores quosdam hospitesue conuiuio excepisset, paulò lautius mensam struebat, non aromatum iucunditate, aut saporum coarctatione conditis dapibus, sed tantum vt copia largior paulò & vinum aliquanto effet suauius: Aurum non magnoperè expetebatur, nec alia oblectatio aderat vlla, ipse enim oratione animos conuiuarum fatis delectabat atque demulcebat.
units.tr: Cleomenes, leader of the Lacedaemonians, flourished with the glory of all other virtues, and kept a small daily preparation for dinner, suited to Laconian thrift. If he had entertained some older men or guests at a banquet, he set a somewhat more generous table, not seasoning the dishes with the delight of spices or with a riot of flavours, but only so that the abundance was a little larger and the wine a little sweeter. Gold was not greatly sought, and no other pleasure was present; for he himself, by his conversation, delighted and soothed the minds of his guests well enough.

units.la: Alexander quoque ille Macedo ventris cibiq; temperatissimus fertur, ad prandia enim, nocturna itinera, ad coenas verò prandiorum tenuitatem optima esse condimenta putabat, vnde coquos ab exercitu suo remouit. In rebus gerendis cum magnus inprimis fuit, tum verò sobrius & vigilans, non temulentus, nec imperii licentiâ bacchabundus.
units.tr: Alexander the Macedonian, too, is said to have been most temperate in belly and food. He thought that for lunch night marches were the best seasoning, and for dinner the slenderness of lunch; hence he removed cooks from his army. In conducting affairs he was great above all, and also sober and watchful, neither drunken nor raving with the licence of power.

units.la: Adeò autem exquisitorum ciborum conditor extitit, ut abe e longinquo transmissa obsonia elegantissima inter amicos partiretur, nihilque ex iis sibi reliquum faceret. Graues tamen autores tradunt, tum Philippum patrem, tum Alexandrum filium vinolentos extitisse, multaque per temulentiam crudelitet perpetrasse. Alexandrum ad vinum pronum fuisse, & apud Mediam vini fortis bibisse congios duos, paulo{q}; post extinctum Plutarchus autor est.
units.tr: Yet he was so much a connoisseur of exquisite foods that he shared the most elegant dainties brought from afar among his friends, and kept nothing of them for himself. Serious authors nevertheless relate that both his father Philip and his son Alexander were heavy drinkers and committed many cruelties through drunkenness. Plutarch is the authority that Alexander was prone to wine, and that at Media he drank two congii of strong wine, and died shortly afterwards.

units.la: Demosthenes Atheniensis Orator aquam bibit, noctes vigilauit, totus curis sollicitudinibus{q}; intentus, unde orationes eius lucernæ olere prouerbio iactatur, vitamque egit longè contrariam vitæ Demadis oratoris æqualis fui. Hic enim scortabatur, ebrietati ac vinolentiæ totus deditus, singulisq; diebus in concionibus & conciliis distentus discumbebat, plenoque ventre accubabat.
units.tr: Demosthenes the Athenian orator drank water, kept vigil at night, and was wholly intent on cares and anxieties; hence the proverb that his speeches smell of the lamp. He lived in a way quite contrary to the life of Demades the orator, his contemporary. For Demades consorted with prostitutes, wholly given over to drunkenness and wine, and, distracted every day by assemblies and councils, he reclined at table and lay down with a full belly.

units.la: Cato Censorius in amplissima fortuna tenuissime vixit, ex rapis sua sibi manu iucundissimum parans obsonium, eoq; ut saluberrimo vescebatur.
units.tr: Cato the Censor lived most frugally though he had great wealth, preparing for himself with his own hand a most pleasant relish from turnips, and eating it as most wholesome.

units.la: In Hispaniam nauigans, unde cum triumpho rediit, non aliud bibit vinum quam regimes: mensam amicorum parentem & procreatricem dixit. A puero, laboribus, moderata viuendi ratione, & ex rei militaris consuetudine bonam valetudinem & constantissimum tissimum nactus est corporis habitum. In exercitu siciens fere semper bibit aquam. Quod si æstu graviori tentaretur, aceti haustu crebriori sitim leuabat & calorem, si vero infirmior sibi videretur pro pristinis viribus recuperandis leuiusculi vini aliquid degustabat, eodemq; pane & vino vsus est, quo sui, Imperator & Consul.
units.tr: Sailing to Spain, from which he returned in triumph, he drank no wine except the thinnest kind; he called the table of friends the parent and mother of its guests. From boyhood, through labour, a moderate way of life and the habits of military life, he gained good health and a very firm bodily constitution. In the army, when thirsty, he almost always drank water. If he was tried by a more severe heat, he relieved his thirst and the heat by frequent draughts of vinegar; if he seemed too weak, to recover his former strength he tasted some rather light wine. He used the same bread and wine as his soldiers, though he was their general and consul.

units.la: Curius Dentatus Romanorum Imperator frugalitate & felicitate victoriarum clarissim• rapis vixisse fertur. Quare Samnitum legatis aurum ei plurimum offerentibus, respondet, auro illi non opus esse qui talia cœnaret, ostendens rapam quam foco torrebat in cibso.
units.tr: Curius Dentatus, the Roman general, is said to have lived with great frugality and, for all his successes, to have been happy. When the envoys of the Samnites offered him a great deal of gold, he replied that a man who dined on such fare had no need of gold, and he pointed to the turnip he was roasting over the hearth for his meal.

units.la: Pompeius Virad omnia summa natus, multis felicissime confectis bellis & victoriis clarus, insignis in victus ratione fuit, de qua re hoc tantum commemorasse sufficit quod cum morbo d. cumbeti, & cibos fastidieti medicus turdum illi apponi iussisset, huncque venalem non inuenirent famuli, quoniam id temporis non ferebat, a quodam indicatum est apud Lucullum posse reperiri, qui eos toto anno in auiariis educaret: verum Pompeius respondisse fertur, nos igitur sine Luculli luxu viuere non possumus? aliumque cibum facile parabilem sumpsit.
units.tr: Pompey the Great, born to every kind of distinction, was famous for his many brilliant wars and victories, and he was also notable for his way of eating. It is enough to record one story about this. When he was ill and had lost his appetite, his doctor ordered that a thrush be served to him. His servants could not find one for sale, since it was not the season for them, and someone reported that they could be found at Lucullus's house, where they were reared all year round in aviaries. Pompey is said to have replied: "So we cannot live without Lucullus's luxury?" and he took another food that was easy to get.

units.la: Ciceronem cibi potusq; fuisse temperatissimum: nemo opinor ambiger, qui scripta eius euoluerit.
units.tr: I suppose that no one who has read Cicero's writings doubts that he was most temperate in his food and drink.

units.la: Augustus Cæsar cibo minimo atque vulgari vsus est, pisces enim minusculos, panem secundarium & caseum bubulum manu pressum, ficus q; virides maxime expetiuisse aiunt. Vini natura erat parcissimus, pro potione sumebat perfusum aqua frigida panem, aut cucumeris fructum aut lactucæ thyrsum, aut recens acidumue pomum succi vinosioris. Vesceba-tur quocunque tempore & loco, quod stomachus desiderabat. Querentem de inopia & caritate vini populum Romanum seuerissima obiurgauit oratione, vtpote satis prouisum à genero suo Agrippa, productis pluribus aquis, ne homines sitirent.
units.tr: Augustus Caesar ate the plainest and most ordinary food. They say he was especially fond of small fish, second-quality bread, cow's cheese pressed by hand, and green figs. He was very sparing with wine. For his drink he took bread soaked in cold water, or a cucumber, or a lettuce stalk, or a fresh sour apple, which was less winey. He ate whenever and wherever his stomach wanted food. When the Roman people complained of the shortage and high price of wine, he rebuked them in a very severe speech, saying that his son-in-law Agrippa had provided well enough, since he had brought in many waters so that men would not go thirsty.

units.la: Agrippa Augusti generi in victu rusticitati potius, quam delitiis fuit propior.
units.tr: Agrippa, Augustus's son-in-law, inclined more to country simplicity than to pleasures in his way of living.

units.la: Tiberius Augusti successor integra fuit valetudine, eaque vsus est toto imperii sui secundi tempore, sineque consilio & medicorum adiumento octauum & septuagesimum annū attigit. Annonam macelli quotannis tempe-randam censuit, dato ædilibus negotio, popi-pas ganeasque eousque inhibendi, vt ne opera quidem pistoria venalia sinerent. Et vt parsi-moniā publicam exemplo quoq; corroboraret atque iuuaret, solemnibus ipse cœnis pridiana sæpe ac semesa obsonia apposuit, dimidiatūq; aprum, affirmans hæc omnia eadem habere quæ totum, quamuis à vini auidi-tate pro Tiberio Biberium eum dictum reperio.
units.tr: Tiberius, Augustus's successor, enjoyed unbroken health, and he kept it throughout the whole of his reign. Without medical advice or help he reached his seventy-eighth year. He decided that the price of provisions in the market should be regulated every year, and he gave the aediles the task of restraining the lavish display and gluttony so far that they did not even allow bakers' goods to be sold. To strengthen and support public thrift by example, he himself often served at his public banquets food that had been left over from the day before and half-eaten, and half a boar, declaring that all these things had the same value as the whole. Yet I find that, because of his greed for wine, he was called Biberius instead of Tiberius.

units.la: Marcus ille Crassus Romanorum ditissi- mus, P. Crassi iurisperiti filius, Licinii Crassi Pontificis nepos, in omni victu frugalis fuit atque modestus. Parua in domo tenui censu vna cum fratribus parce admodum educatus est, viuisq; adhuc parentibus vxores ducentes vnà & domo & mensa simul omnes vsos repetrio. Ad cœnas atq; conuiuia homines plerumq; ex media plebe vocare consuesse Crassum historiæ prodiderunt. Neminem Romanorum debere esse, dixit, quibusdam de eius liberalitate conquerentibus, qui parum se possidere arbitretur, cum tantum habeat soli, quod ad victum præbendum abundè sufficiat, dederat enim iis singulis 14. agri iugera.
units.tr: Marcus Crassus, the richest of the Romans, son of Publius Crassus the jurist and grandson of Licinius Crassus the Pontifex, was thrifty and modest in all his living. He was brought up very sparingly in a small house on a modest income, together with his brothers. While his parents were still alive, all of them, even after they married, used the same house and the same table. Historians record that Crassus used to invite to his dinners and parties people who were mostly from the common people. When some complained about his generosity, saying that he did not think himself the owner of enough, he said that no Roman ought to be counted poor who had enough land to support himself, and he had given each of them fourteen acres.

units.la: Tanta fuit Prisci illius seculi Imperatorum & illustrium virorum temperantia & frugalitas.
units.tr: Such was the temperance and frugality of the generals and illustrious men of that early age.

units.la: Contra verò, qui intemperantiæ voluptatisq; illecebris & lenociniis diffluxerunt, miserè vixerunt, mortemq; præcipitem matura-runt, vel veneno sublati, alioque mortis violentæ genere, vt suffocatione, prolapsu ex equis, reuixerunt (vinum enim in prælia trudit inermem) igne, aqua, decollatione, strangulatione, & vt plurimum morbosâ corporis dispositione, quæ luxum continuum comitatur, vel denique ventrem in amplitudinem pinguissimum & distentissimum adepti.
units.tr: On the other hand, those who gave way to intemperance and were seduced and enticed by pleasure lived wretched lives and hastened a headlong death. Some were carried off by poison, others by violent deaths of other kinds: by suffocation, by falling from horses (wine drives an unarmed man into battle), by fire, by water, by beheading, by strangling, and most often by a diseased condition of the body, which goes with continual luxury. Some finally acquired a belly swollen to an enormous size and stretched very tight.

units.la: {y} Intemperantes, luxui deditæ, rantes & viuent, NB.
units.tr: {Note in the margin, garbled in the scan:} Intemperate men, given over to luxury ... and they live. NB.

units.la: Euergetes 7. Ægyptiorum Rex, ab Alexandrinis dictus Κακεργέτης ob luxuriosam & delicatam victus rationem ventrem adeptus est pinguissimum & distentissimum: quin & filius huius Alexander, qui matrem regni sociam interfecit. Hi fuere adeo ventricosi, ut vix pedem efferre possent, raroque in conspectum prodirent.
units.tr: Euergetes, the seventh king of Egypt, called by the Alexandrians Kakergetes [Κακεργέτης] because of his luxurious and pampered way of living, acquired a belly that was enormously fat and stretched. So too did his son Alexander, who killed his mother, the queen who shared his throne. These men were so bloated that they could scarcely lift a foot and seldom appeared in public.

units.la: Dionysius Heracleorum Tyrannus ad immodicam corporis molem adoleuit ob intemperatissimas voluptates & quotidianam voracitatem.
units.tr: Dionysius, tyrant of Heraclea, grew to an immoderate bulk of body because of his most intemperate pleasures and his daily gluttony.

units.la: Fuit item Pitho Bizantius, Rhetor obesissimo aqualiculo, pariterque vxor eius, gulæ sc. vitio & ventris intemperantia.
units.tr: Pitho of Byzantium, a rhetorician, likewise had a very big paunch, and so did his wife, through the vice of gluttony and the intemperance of the belly.

units.la: C. Caligula portentissimorum ciborum atque epularum fuit autor, omniumque ganeforum gulosorumque ingenia superasse dicitur. Pretiosas Margaritas aceto liquefactas absorpsit, panesque ex auro atque etiam obsoniaappofuit.
units.tr: Gaius Caligula was the author of monstrous foods and feasts, and he is said to have surpassed the cleverness of all gluttons and guzzlers. He dissolved precious pearls in vinegar and swallowed them, and he set before his guests bread made of gold and even food made of gold.

units.la: Claudius Cæsar vinum cibosque quocunque tempore appetebat avidissimè, conuiuia celebrabat assidua & ampla, nec triclinio abscessit nisi madens & distentus. Erat boletorum cupidissimus. Quare per hanc ei occasionem venenum datum ab Agrippina coniuge: quo facto illa terris venenum alterum sibique ante omnes Neronem dedit.
units.tr: Claudius Caesar craved wine and food most eagerly at any time. He held frequent and lavish banquets and never left the dining couch except drunk and stuffed. He was very fond of mushrooms. Because of this, poison was given to him by his wife Agrippina, on this occasion; after this deed she gave another poison to the world, and to herself, before all others, to Nero.

units.la: Nero ad principatum eucetus vulgaria cibaria baria recusauit, sordidum enim ei oblatum panem fame etiam stimulante aspernatus est, in tantum dissimilis clarissimis illis Regibus & Ducibus, qui cruentas aquas & coenolas, pa-nesq; atros & cibarios assumpserunt.
units.tr: Nero, raised to the principate, refused the common and ordinary food. Even when hunger goaded him, he disdained the dirty bread offered to him, so unlike those most famous kings and generals who ate bloody water and porridge, and black and coarse bread.

units.la: Vitellius trifariam semper, quandoque etiam quadrifariam epulas dispertiebat, in ientaculà, prandia, coenas & commessationes, qui-bus vt sufficeret, vomitibus vtebatur assiduè, quod etiam Claudium factitasse reperio pinnâ & in os indita. Famosissimam illam vero supra alias Vitellio à fratre datam coenam quis non miretur, in qua duo millia electissimorum piscium, & y. alium appositae traduntur? Pati-nam Vitellii, cui faciendae fornax in campis exaedificata est non minoris quam ducentis sestertiis, hoc est, quinque millibus aureorum cô-stitisse proditur, in qua scarorum iecinora, Phoenicopterorum linguae & murenarum lactes commisçebantur: erat autem Phoenicopterus auis rarissima, & primum M. Apitii mensis cognita: Murenarum lactes etiam in ipso Italico mari frequentes reperirentur, nihilominus ab externis littoribus asportatae gratiores videbantur: à Carpathio enim vsque, fretoque Hispaniae petitae sunt. Unde manifestum est, quadrigas for-didissimae & profusissimae Vitellium fuisse vi-tae, cum nouies millies sestertium paucis eum mensibus interuertisse, Tacitus auctor sit.
units.tr: Vitellius always divided his feasts into three parts, and sometimes into four: breakfasts, lunches, dinners and drinking parties. To keep up with these he constantly used vomiting, which I find Claudius also practised, by putting a feather into his mouth. Who would not marvel at that most famous dinner given to Vitellius by his brother, above all others? It is said that two thousand of the choicest fish and y. others were served at it. Vitellius's platter, for which an oven was built on the Campus at a cost of not less than two hundred thousand sesterces, that is, five thousand gold pieces, is reported to have contained a mixture of the livers of parrot-fish, the tongues of flamingos and the milt of lampreys. The flamingo was a very rare bird, first known at the table of Marcus Apicius. Lampreys were common even in the Italian sea itself, yet those brought from foreign shores seemed more pleasing: they were fetched all the way from the Carpathian sea and the Strait of Spain. From this it is clear that Vitellius was of the most filthy and extravagant kind of life, since Tacitus tells us he squandered nine hundred million sesterces in a few months.

units.la: Lucullus, qui primus luxum Romam in-troduxit, D I uexit & auxit, ingentes opes, quas deuictis duobus potentissimis & maximis Regibus Tigrane & Mithridate, sibi comparauerat, conterere Romam regressus omnino studebat, quod tamen efficere non potuit, seu hortorum spectes amoenissimorum impensam intolerabilem, seu piscinarum, praetoriorum, aedium & coenationum amoenissimarum structuram, seu deniq; lautissimorum conuiuiorum quotidianum apparatum. Vnde in proverbium abierunt delitiae LucullI. Vnicuiq; loco coenarum taxata & ordinata erat summa: quod testatur apparata coena illa impendio quinquaginta millium, hoc est, mille & ducentorum quinquaginta aureorum, tanta celeritate & lautitia, ut Cicero & Pompeius, quibus illa dabatur, obstupescerent.
units.tr: Lucullus, who first introduced luxury into Rome, spread it and increased it. Having conquered the two most powerful and greatest kings, Tigranes and Mithridates, he acquired immense wealth, and on his return to Rome he was entirely eager to squander it. He could not, however, accomplish this, whether one looks at the intolerable expense of his most delightful gardens, or the building of his fishponds, his palaces, houses and dining rooms, or finally at the daily preparation of his most lavish banquets. From this the delights of Lucullus passed into a proverb. For each dining room the total cost was fixed and determined in advance. This is shown by the dinner prepared at a cost of fifty thousand, that is, one thousand two hundred and fifty gold pieces, with such speed and such elegance that Cicero and Pompey, to whom it was served, were astonished.

units.la: Apitius Marcus nepotinis helluationibus hunc longe superauit, Hinc coenae Apitianae proverbii loco circumferuntur. Sexcenties enim sestertium, id est, quindecies centena aureorum millia in explebili illa ingluuie helluatus est: cumq; potuisset adhuc ducentis quinquaginta millibus vitam lauto victu producere, tamen venenum misér hausit, ne patrimonio tanto superesset, quod iam se defecturum videbatur. Plinius aptissimum omnium nepotum gurgitem appellauit. Suidas in luxum & infusitatos sumtus multas eum argenti myriadas in ventrem abstumpsisse autor est. Degebat autem crebrius in Campaniæ vrbe Minturna-rum, vt caricas, quæ illic amplissimæ gignuntur, luxuriosè manderet. Quin tanta erat hominis huius gulæ insania, vt in Lybiam navigarit ventrem ficubus explendi graria: merces vero sociis comportantibus, cum ad reditum iam omnia spectarent, Apitius sparteis aliquot corbibus ficus bene compactas, in naui comportari iussit, vt & domi, si venter desideraret, earum possit esse copia. Verum exorta subito turbulentissima tempestate, nulla salutis spe affulgente, morte, vt saxum Tantalo, impendente, Apitius, ne vacuo ventre interiret, ficubus probè & ad saturitatem vsq; eum farsit, reliquas in mare proiectis, quibus postea sedatâ tempestate, ægerrimè carere ipsum oportuit. Signum ingenii ad omnem luxum mirandi.
units.tr: Marcus Apicius far surpassed this man in his extravagant gluttony, and from him his Apician dinners are passed around as a proverb. He squandered six hundred million sesterces, that is, fifteen hundred thousand gold pieces, on that insatiable gorging. Although he could still have lived in splendour on two hundred and fifty thousand, he wretchedly drank poison, so as not to be left with an estate that he saw was about to run out. Pliny called him the most fitting whirlpool of all spendthrifts. Suidas reports that in luxury and unbounded expense he swallowed many myriads of silver into his belly. He often lived in the Campanian city of Minturnae, where he ate the figs that grow there in great abundance, with a luxurious appetite. Indeed, this man's gluttony was so insane that he sailed to Libya simply to fill his belly with figs. His merchants brought goods, and when they were all looking towards the return voyage, Apicius ordered several baskets of woven broom to be carried aboard ship, packed tight with figs, so that he would have a supply of them at home too, if his belly wanted them. But a most violent storm broke suddenly, with no hope of safety shining out, and death hung over them like the rock over Tantalus. Apicius, so that he would not die with an empty belly, stuffed himself well and to the full with figs, and threw the rest into the sea. Afterwards, when the storm had calmed, he was forced most painfully to go without them. A sign of a mind amazing in every kind of luxury.

units.la: M. Antonius exquisitissimis quotidiè epulis se saginabat, & per luxum insusitatum deBacchabatur, exhausisseq; fertur & impendisse ducenta millia talentum, hoc est, centies & viciès millies mille aureos.
units.tr: Mark Antony stuffed himself every day with the most exquisite banquets and indulged in unheard-of luxury. He is said to have spent and squandered two hundred thousand talents, that is, two thousand million gold pieces.

units.la: Cleopatra Ægypti Regina lautitiam eius omnem apparatusque splendorem fastu meretricio detrectabat, dicitans vna se cœna centies sestertium absumturam. Condicta cœna Regina magnificam alias epularem struem, sed quotidianam posuit. Irridente autem & computationem Antonio expostulante, confirma-bat. bat in ea se coena taxationem confumturam. Quare mensam secundam inferri iubens, dictitans totum alium apparatum corollarium vel proœmium saltem esse, detractumq; auribus vnionem aceto merlit, & liquefactum absorpsit.
units.tr: Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, scorned all his extravagance and splendour of display with a harlot's pride, declaring that she alone would spend a hundred thousand sesterces on a single dinner. When the dinner was agreed, the queen set out a magnificent feast, though otherwise an ordinary daily one. Antony laughed and demanded the reckoning, but she insisted that the dinner would cost exactly that sum. Then, ordering a second course to be brought in and saying that all the rest of the display was merely a prelude or at least a garnish, she took one of her pearl earrings, put it in vinegar, and when it had dissolved, swallowed it.
