units.la: Singulare & fere vnicum naturæ opus, ait Plinius, aurib. gerebat Cleopatra, quis quisquam non obstupescat, vno ferculo secundæ mensæ centies sestertium, h. e. ducenta & quinquaginta millia aureorum abfumta? Experta hæc certè est, quid in gloria palati saperent margaritæ. Quis dubitet in aulis huiusmodi perditissimorum principum multos fuisse, qui sese non vitæ sui solum, sed cæteris etiam eorum moribus accommodarent? Quin & nostra memoria in aulis Magnatum inueniuntur non infimum obtinentes locum, gulæ ganeæque deditissimi, nullusque iam fere habetur pluris, quam qui peritissimè censum Domini mergit. Videmus nostra ætate prisċm illum morem pertinacissimè perdurare.
units.tr: "A singular and almost unique work of nature," says Pliny, was the pearl earring Cleopatra wore. Who would not be astonished that a hundred thousand sesterces, that is 250,000 gold pieces, was spent on one dish of the second course? She certainly found out what pearls taste like in the glory of the palate. Who can doubt that in the courts of such utterly depraved princes there were many who conformed not only to their way of life but to their other habits as well? Indeed, in our own memory, men holding no low place are found in the courts of the magnates, given over most completely to gluttony and gorging, and hardly anyone is now held in higher esteem than the one who most skilfully drowns his lord's estate. We see in our age that ancient custom stubbornly persisting.

units.la: Vina enim hac nostra ætate tam profusè prodiguntur, vt videantur ad perdenda ea geniti, ita vt nullam operosiorem lautioremque vitam nostro seculo inueniamus, quam in proluendis vinis. Apud nos enim sine lege, sine modo bibitur.
units.tr: Wine is nowadays squandered so lavishly that men seem born only to waste it. In our century we find no more elaborate or refined way of life than washing down wines. Among us wine is drunk without law and without measure.

units.la: Germanorum bibacitas ante cunctas aliae gentes nobilitatur, atque inter miracula celebratur. tur,cum singuli quaternos quartarios vno prā-dio haurirunt.& hodie vasa cernūtur potoria, quæ plus quam vnam mensuram ciuilem capiant, quibus hospites externos liberalissimè inuitant & proluunt. In conuiuiis enim nostris omnes certamus pro luxus patina & principatu. Nam quò quisque exquisitissimorum obsonioꝝ varia genera, epularumq; varios apparatus & lautos dat profusius, eò magis commendatur. Dolendum sanè nos eo venisse, vt cibis maximè pereamus. Innumerofissimum illud morborum agmen & satellitium nouum, quod indies gulæ culpâ emergit, quâ plurimū plurimi funeris ante diem intereunt, ad temperantiam & vitæ modestiam deberet nos incitare. Tantum verò abest, vt hoc fiat, vt etiam luxus Luculli, Cœnæ Apitianę, & quadripartita Vitellii Epularum, in ientacula, Prandia, Cœnas, & commessationes dimensio maiorem longè hodie quam olim laudem in Magnatum aulis mereatur, vtq; asoti illi crudi postridie rursus ingurgitent, vt cum Cic. de finibus loquar, de mensa & conuiuiis auferuntur, pinnaq; inos inditâ vomitum proritât, quod à multis hodie factitari more Epicuri de grege porcorum animaduertitur magno sæpe&corporis & animi damno. Verum de vomitu morboso & non morboso suo loco.
units.tr: The drinking capacity of the Germans is famed above all other peoples and celebrated among wonders, since individuals drain four quarts at a single draught. Even today drinking vessels are seen that hold more than one civic measure, with which they most generously invite and drench foreign guests. At our feasts we all compete for the prize and the leading place in luxury. The more lavishly a man provides the many kinds of exquisite delicacies and the varied and sumptuous preparations of food, the more he is commended. It is truly to be lamented that we have come to the point of dying chiefly by food. That countless host of diseases and new retinue, which daily arises through the fault of gluttony, and by which very many perish in great numbers before their time, ought to urge us to temperance and moderation of life. But so far is this from happening that even the luxury of Lucullus, the Apician dinner and the fourfold banquets of Vitellius, measured in breakfasts, lunches, dinners and carousings, deserve far greater praise today in the courts of the magnates than they once did. The crude sots gorge themselves again the next day, and so, to use Cicero's words in de finibus, they are carried away from the table and the feast, and a feather inserted into the throat provokes vomiting. Many today are observed doing this, in the manner of Epicurus' herd of pigs, often with great damage to body and mind. But of morbid and non-morbid vomiting, more in its place.

units.la: Non tamen hic prætereundum est, voraci-tatis & bibacitatis quoddam vitium à natura quidam quiqaibusdam innasci,aliis etiam ab ipsa consue- tudine proficisci,cum saepe videamus alios a-liis esse edaciores à tenero, eosq; vitae processu moderantiores fieri. Sed de externa & intem-peratissima voracitate & ingluuie hic sermo est: Cuiusmodi fuit Milonis Crotoniatae athletae robustissimi,qui in certamine Olympico taurum viuum circumtulisse stadio vnius curriculi praedicat,ipsumq; postea ictu nudae dextrae iugulatum ipso die solum vorasse, Quin & vno conictu carnium xx. pondo, totidemq; panum absumere,vini vero choas tres exhausisse consuevit,teste Athen.lib.10. Verum in prodigioso robore prodigiosa certe minus vi-debitur gula.
units.tr: Yet it must not be passed over here that a certain vice of voracity and drinking is innate in some by nature, and in others arises from habit itself, since we often see some more greedy from childhood and others becoming more moderate as life goes on. But the discussion here concerns external and most intemperate voracity and gluttony. Such was that of Milo of Croton, the most robust athlete, who is said at the Olympic contest to have carried a live bull around the stadium for the length of one course, and afterwards to have struck it dead with a blow of his bare right hand and eaten it all on the same day. Indeed he was accustomed to consume twenty pounds of meat and as many loaves at one sitting, and to drain three chous of wine, as Athen. lib. 10 attests. But in prodigious strength, prodigious gluttony is seen less clearly.

units.la: Omnes autem athletas assuevisse plurimo cibo ad corporis vires ampliandas Hippocrates etiam & interpres eius Galenus in aphorismis non tacuerunt. Habitum enim corporis ipsorum periculosum esse confirmant,quorum etiam sententiam Hieronymus contra Iovianum vsurpauit. Athletas,inquit Galenus, in exhortatione Medicinae, nec posse viuere diu nec sanos esse, animasque eorum in nimio sanguine & adipibus quasi luto inuolutas nihil tenue,nihil coelestc, semperque de carnibus & ructu,ventris ingluuie cogitare.Suillam itaq; Galenus suadet vt valenter alentem.
units.tr: That all athletes are accustomed to much food in order to increase their bodily strength, Hippocrates and his interpreter Galen did not fail to note in the Aphorisms. For they affirm that such a bodily condition is dangerous, and Jerome also used their opinion against Jovinian. Galen says, in the Exhortation to Medicine, that athletes cannot live long nor be healthy, and that their souls, wrapped up in excess blood and fat as if in mud, have nothing fine and nothing heavenly, and always think of meat and belching and the gluttony of the belly. Galen therefore advises pig's flesh as a strongly nourishing food.

units.la: Theagenes Thasius athleta taurum solus edebat.
units.tr: Theagenes of Thasos, an athlete, ate a bull by himself.

units.la: Aftidamas athleta Milefius, qui terin Olympia euasit victor, deuorabat, quantum novem hominibus aliis satis esset: & plerumque omnia quæ apud Ariobarzanem Persarum Regem in conuiuio parata offenderet, solus abluebat.
units.tr: Astydamas of Miletus, the athlete who won the victory at Olympia, devoured as much as would be enough for nine other men; and for the most part he alone washed down everything he found prepared at the banquet of Ariobarzanes, king of the Persians.

units.la: Herodorus Megarensis tibicen & saltator, trium plus minus cubitorum altitudine & proceritate, aliàs tamen bonis lateribus constans, panis sex chœnices, carnis libras 20. edebat, viniq; duas choas, h.e. 12. Sextarios seu congios 2. hauriebat uno conuictu. Dignahercle gula harpiis rapacibus,
units.tr: Herodorus of Megara, a flute-player and dancer, about three cubits tall and of stature, though otherwise well built, ate six choenices of bread and twenty pounds of meat, and drank two chous of wine, that is twelve sextarii or two congii, at one sitting. Truly a gullet worthy of the rapacious Harpies.

units.la: Gulosus ille Phago, cujus meminit Flauius Vopiscus, Aureliano Imperatori fuit in delitiis, quod uno prandio integrum aprum deuoraret, veruecem unum, præterea porcellum & panes 100. exiccaretq; vini orcam, quibus omnibus in ventrem exceptis, percon&atus est coquum, quanam hora sit redeundum ad cœnam. Sed an capacitati ventriculi ejusq; amplitudini id sit acceptum ferendum, an vero ventriculi infirmitati vel firmitati, quod Budæus voluit, quæritur? Capacitatem certè & amplitudinem ventriculi cibi & potus majorem copiam expetere, firmioremque viscçris constitutionem arguere, contra verò angustiâ & paruitatem, imbecillitatem, esculentorumque ac potulentorum parsimoniam præter jam dicta etiam consuetudo ipsa suadet, plurimum enim eam valere exemplo sunt Parthi, qui quanto plus biberint, tanto plus sitiunt.
units.tr: That gluttonous Phago, whom Flavius Vopiscus mentions, was a favourite of the Emperor Aurelian, because at one meal he devoured a whole boar, a wether, a piglet and a hundred loaves, and drained a jar of wine. When all of this had gone into his belly, he asked the cook at what hour he should return for supper. But is this to be credited to the capacity and size of his stomach, or rather to the weakness or strength of the stomach, as Budaeus preferred? Certainly capacity and largeness of the stomach seek a greater quantity of food and drink and indicate a firmer constitution of the bowels. On the contrary, narrowness and smallness, weakness and sparing use of food and drink, custom itself also suggests, apart from what has been said already; for that custom has great power the Parthians are an example, who the more they drink, the more thirsty they become.

units.la: Graeci poculis certarunt, praesertim diebus festis agentes inferias, quinque caeteris praebibebat, promachus dicebatur quasi prepugnans, quatuorque choas ebibebat. Alexander aliquando conuocatis & amicis & ducibus solenne constituit conuiuium, in quo vinariae potationis certamen indixit, victori proponens coronam: bibacissimus omnium Promachus quatuor ingurgitans congios palmam retulit, vniusque talenti coronam accepit, h.e. aureorum sexcentorum. Romani Tricongium Torquatum appellarunt a tribus vno impetu congiis exhaustis, & Bicongium a duobus congiis Ciceronis filium.
units.tr: The Greeks competed in drinking cups, especially on festival days when they performed funeral rites. The man who drank five congii before the others was called Promachus, as it were "fighting in the front rank", and he would drain four chous. Once Alexander, having summoned both friends and commanders, established a solemn banquet, at which he proclaimed a contest of wine drinking, offering a crown to the victor. Promachus, the most bibulous of all, swallowed four congii, carried off the palm and received a crown worth one talent, that is six hundred gold pieces. The Romans called Torquatus "Tricongius" because he had drained three congii at a single gulp, and Cicero's son "Bicongius" for two congii.

units.la: Xenarchus Rhodius Metretes dictus est ab immodica potione.
units.tr: Xenarchus of Rhodes was called "Metretes" from his immoderate drinking.

units.la: Maximinus Pater amphoram Capitolinam siccabat saepe in die, teste Capitolino, amphora vero 8. capiebat congios.
units.tr: Maximinus the father often drained the Capitoline amphora in a day, according to Capitolinus; the amphora held eight congii.

units.la: Tiberius ignotissimum quendam nobilissimis anteposuit, ob epotam in conuiuio, propinante se, vini amphoram: quin & eodem nomine atque prodigiosa bibendi ostentatione L. Pisonem urbis curatorem delegit, quod biduo duabusque noctibus per potationem continuasset apud ipsum jam Principem.
units.tr: Tiberius preferred a certain most obscure man to the most noble, because at a banquet, when he himself proposed the toast, the man had drunk a whole amphora of wine. Indeed, under the same title and for the same prodigious display of drinking, he appointed Lucius Piso curator of the city, because he had kept on drinking for two days and two nights in the company of the Prince himself.

units.la: De quodam vini potatore reperitur Syracusis tandiu potare solitum, donec ab eo cooperta perta ova in terra fœtum ederent, teste Aristotele & Plin.
units.tr: It is recorded that at Syracuse a certain wine-drinker used to drink for so long that eggs covered by him hatched chicks in the ground, according to Aristotle and Pliny.

units.la: Bonosus imperator, vt scribit Flavius Vopiscus, bibit, quantum alius nemo: & si quando legati barbararum gentium vndecunq; venissent, ipsis propinauit, vt eos vino obrueret, sicque ab ebriis consilia eliciebat.
units.tr: Bonosus the emperor, as Flavius Vopiscus writes, drank more than anyone else. And if ever ambassadors of barbarian nations had come from any quarter, he would give them drink to overwhelm them with wine, and so drew out their counsels from them while they were drunk.

units.la: Protheas Macedo apud Alexandrum bibacissimus fuit, & valenti corporis robore, tamen vino periit.
units.tr: Protheas the Macedonian was the most addicted to drink at Alexander's court, and although of strong bodily vigour, he perished through wine.

units.la: Illyrii cubantes cœnabant & bibebant, teste Periandro, &c.
units.tr: The Illyrians reclined and dined and drank, according to Periander, etc.

units.la: Scythas, Iberos, Thraces, Gallos, Persas & Lydios vinolentiæ deditos fuisse Plato prodidit.
units.tr: Plato has recorded that Scythians, Iberians, Thracians, Gauls, Persians and Lydians were given over to drunkenness.

units.la: Ariæi conuiuia celebrabant quotidie, & inebriabantur, quare Galli, qui bellum aduersus eos gerebant, id animaduertentes, dolum comenti sunt. Singuli enim Gallorum duces prandium exquisitissime in tabernaculis suis apparauerunt, cibariisq; adjecerunt herbam quandam medicamentosam quæ aliuum deiiciendi & violenter purgandi vim obtineret: vnde quotquot ex iis edissent, ad vnum extincti sunt omnes. Præterea & flumina eadem herba infecerant, quæ postea hausta aliuum immodice purgarunt. Constat certe multos & inuictos exercitus militum vinolentia fuisse prostratos. Germanis nostris olim in bello Gallico simile quid accidisse plus quam notum est.
units.tr: The Ariaei celebrated feasts every day and grew drunk, and the Gauls who waged war against them noticed this and devised a trick. Each of the Gallic leaders prepared a lunch most exquisitely in his tent, and added to the food a certain medicinal herb which had the power of causing diarrhoea and violent purging. So all who ate of it died, every one of them. Moreover, they had infected the rivers with the same herb, which, once drunk, purged the bowels immoderately. It is certain that many and unconquered armies have been laid low by the drunkenness of soldiers. That something similar happened to our Germans in the Gallic war long ago is more than well known.

units.la: Cap.
units.tr: Chap.

units.la: Carthaginenses non sinebant in castra vinum deferri. Contra vero Neftor vel graui instante pugna à vini potu non abstinuit, quam etiam gloriam nostri seculi duces & milites quaerunt pertinacissime, vt adeo in confesso sit, neminiq; dubium, maximam prisca illius luxuriae ad nos fluxisse partem, inueniriq; qui eam avidissime sectentur, non tam in virorum quam foeminarum tribubus. Foeminarum genus vini auidum fuisse & etiamnunc esse, forsan quispiam dubitet. Dubitare autem desinet Romanorum annales qui euoluerit.
units.tr: The Carthaginians did not allow wine to be brought into their camps. Nestor, by contrast, did not abstain from drinking wine even when a battle was pressing hard. Our own age's commanders and soldiers seek this same glory most stubbornly, so that it is generally agreed and no one doubts that the greater part of that ancient luxury has flowed down to us. And people are found who pursue it most eagerly, not only among the men but among the women. Perhaps someone may doubt that the female sex has been, and still is, greedy for wine. But whoever reads through the annals of the Romans will cease to doubt it.

units.la: Romulo regnum obtinente Egnatius Mecentinus vxorem, quod vinum e dolio bibisset, interfecit, cuius etiam caedis à Romulo fuit absolutus.
units.tr: When Romulus held the kingdom, Egnatius Mecentinus killed his wife because she had drunk wine from the cask. He was acquitted of this killing by Romulus himself.

units.la: Est quoq; inter exempla, mulierem à Cneo Domitio dote multatam, quod viro inscio, plus vini hausisse visa esset, quam valetudo exposceret.
units.tr: Among the examples is also a woman whom Gnaeus Domitius fined with the loss of her dowry, because, without her husband's knowledge, she was seen to have drunk more wine than her health required.

units.la: Polybius apud Athenaeum scribit non licuisse Romanorum foeminis vinum bibere. Apud Massilienses lex quoq; fuit, qua mulieres aquam potare jubebantur, hancq; eandem legem Mileti sua aetate floruisse Theophrastus autor est.
units.tr: Polybius, as reported by Athenaeus, writes that Roman women were not permitted to drink wine. There was also a law among the Massilians by which women were ordered to drink water, and Theophrastus is the authority that this same law flourished at Miletus in his own time.

units.la: Cato censuit oflculum foeminis dari debere à propinquis, vt scil. scirent an vinum olerent. Nostrae certe hodie cautiores sunt & callidiores quę à vini hausta aromata commanducant aut anisum, coriandrum, vel fœniculum sac-charo intectum, quo diuerticulo imponunt maritis suis atq; adulteris. Vidi in inferiori Germania potissimum vero Coloniç tam pro-fuse vina à fœminis prodigi, vt vino pleniffim ç velut attonitæ in plateas conciderint, ac pub-licum propudium extiterint, quo tamen op-probrio cæteræ se abstererì minimè patiun-tur, sed potius moti morem gerere pertinaci-ter pergunt, parique sæpe ebrietatis vitio con-spiciuntur viri & fœminæ, vt merito antiqui prouerbii veritas hic locum tenere videatur, Cascus Cascam ducit, Cœcus Cœcam, Ebrius Ebriam. Sed mirum, in tanta Colonia tot esse leges bene viuendi, & inter eas nullam quæ sa-cram illam vinolentiam puniat, hac enim im-punitate efficitur luxus ille quotidie capitalis.
units.tr: Cato held that a kiss should be given to women by their relatives, so that they could know whether they smelled of wine. Our women today are certainly more cautious and more cunning: they chew aromatic herbs after drinking wine, or aniseed, coriander or fennel coated with sugar, by which little trick they deceive their husbands and lovers. I have seen in Lower Germany, especially at Cologne, women so lavish with wine that, quite stupefied by it, they have fallen down in the streets and become a public disgrace. Yet they do not allow themselves to be deterred from this reproach by the other women; rather, moved by it, they obstinately persist in their custom. Men and women are often seen with the same vice of drunkenness, so that the truth of the old proverb seems to hold its place here: the one-eyed man leads the one-eyed woman, the blind man the blind woman, the drunk man the drunk woman. But it is remarkable that in so great a city there are so many laws for living well, and among them none that punishes this sacred drunkenness. For it is by this impunity that that luxury, deadly every day, is maintained.

units.la: Apud Persas quidem pignus & fœdus ho-spitii habebatur, mulieres vxores filiasq; con-uiuiis adhibere, si quando hospites laute & splendide excipere vellet, qui etiam mos apud nos durat, verum illis propinare vt vino intu-mescant, sicut Periander scriptum reliquit, Il-lyrios in vsu habuisse, & ipsæ postea è conui-uiis viros exturbent, vt nostra ætate sæpius contingit, hoc, inquam, an egregium sit & pul-crum, facile quilibet prudens secum reputa-verit.
units.tr: Among the Persians, to bring wives and daughters to their banquets was regarded as a pledge and bond of hospitality, when someone wished to entertain guests handsomely and splendidly; and this custom survives among us too. But to give them drink until they swell with wine, as Periander left written that the Illyrians practised, so that afterwards they drive the men out from the banquets themselves, as happens fairly often in our own age: anyone sensible may easily consider for himself whether this, I say, is a noble and fine thing.

units.la: Illyricæ potantes aluum sibi fasciis zonisq; cingunt: primum quidem leuiter & modice, postea verò cum liberalius bibunt, astius validiusq;: quem morem Scythis etiam fuisse in bello, vt diutius & constantius famem tolerarent, graues autores tradiderunt. Nostræ, ne mentem animumq; vinum nimium obtundat atq; etiam adimat, ciborum luxuriæ vna vacant, pluris vinolentiam, quàm opes facientes.
units.tr: Illyrian drinkers bind their bellies with bands and belts, at first lightly and moderately, but later, when they drink more freely, more tightly and firmly. Grave authors have handed down that the Scythians too had this custom in war, so that they might endure hunger longer and more steadily. Our people, so that wine may not overwhelm and even take away the mind and spirit, abstain from luxurious food, and value drunkenness more than they value their resources.

units.la: Non possum silentio hic præterire memorabilem bibacitatem, quâ apud nos tres mulieres ciuicæ se nobilitarunt, vno prandio quindecim mensuras vini ciuiles in ventrem absumentes, constanté adhuc mente & animo, vt ita in totum dixisse liceat, fœminarum genus vini auidissimum esse.
units.tr: I cannot pass over in silence here the memorable drinking capacity by which three citizen women have made themselves famous among us, consuming fifteen civic measures of wine in the belly at a single lunch, and still keeping their mind and spirit steady. So that one may say, without exaggeration, that the female sex is the most greedy for wine.

units.la: Sed cesso ne insanis illis Bacchis fiam Archilochicus.
units.tr: But I will stop, lest I become an Archilochus to those mad Bacchantes.

units.la: Hactenus de quantitate cibi.
units.tr: So much concerning the quantity of food.

units.la: Sequitur præceptio II. de tempore cibum sumendi seu corpus reficiendi: Non vescendum prius quàm appetitus & fames adsit.
units.tr: Follows precept II, on the time of taking food, or of refreshing the body: one should not eat before appetite and hunger are present.

units.la: Non intelligo hic famem morbosam, quæ cibum expetit corpore non indigente. Præsente igitur fame cibus non est protrahendus, juxta illud vulgatum: Non toleranda fames nam ventrem humoribus implet.
units.tr: Here I do not mean morbid hunger, which craves food when the body has no need of it. So, when hunger is present, food should not be delayed, according to the common saying: hunger is not to be endured, for it fills the belly with humours.

units.la: Ventriculus enim vacuus à venis proximis & membris alimentum experentibus stimulatur & impellitur, vtque eorum desiderio morem gerat, lacessit Oesophagum vnde, alimento non subsequente, viciosis eum humoribus impleri necesse est, è vicinis partibus eos ad se allicientem.
units.tr: For the empty stomach, deprived of nourishment, is stimulated and driven by the nearby veins and by the limbs that are in need of nourishment. To satisfy their desire, it irritates the gullet; and then, if no food follows, the gullet must be filled with bad humours, drawing them to itself from the neighbouring parts.

units.la: Certissimus igitur & fidus cibi noui ingerendi index est fames seu appetitus edendi. Unde non approbo, quod quidam certam, opportunam & consuetam in iumendo cibo horam sibi eligunt, persuasum habentes naturâ felicius sic coctioni indulgere. Saepe enim contingit, vt hora illa ordinaria & consueta ventriculum exinanitum cibisq; vacuum, purumq; non reperiat, nullumq; edendi adsit desiderium, vt ita certum edendi tempus praeferri bene non facile audiam, sed potius suadeam, vt qui suae sponte est, edat bibatque quoties & quandocunq; cibum ventriculus efflagitat, idque naturae instinctu.
units.tr: The most certain and trustworthy sign that new food should be taken in is therefore hunger, or the appetite for eating. Hence I do not approve of those who choose for themselves a fixed, convenient and customary hour for taking food, being persuaded that nature digests more happily in this way. For it often happens that this ordinary and customary hour finds the stomach not empty, not free of food, and with no desire for eating at all. Thus I can hardly bring myself to hear that a fixed time for eating is to be preferred. Rather I would advise that whoever is in good health should eat and drink whenever and as often as the stomach demands food, and that by the impulse of nature.

units.la: Quapropter reprehensione non immerito digni sunt, qui, sine vllo appetitu, ventriculo non postulante, priori alimento nondum plene concocto, nouum cibum ingerunt, studiose procurato jentaculo, prandio mox subsequente, non neglectis etiam coenis & commessationibus, quae saepe in aulis magnatum, vbi praeceptur hodie merentur laudem, in multam notem protrahuntur nec sine corporis dispendio. Fieri enim non potest, vt in tanta ingluuie vites corporis possint constare integrae. Sunt multi qui, voluptatis tantum gratia, vt sibi hoc nomine alios deuincant, famæ etiam non stimulante, jentant & commeffantur, qui postea molestam totius corporis graunedinem sentiut & lassitudinem. Ego illis edonibus aureum illud Gorgiæ Rhetoris Siculi respondum tanquam saluberrimum sanitatis custodiendæ remedium imitandum & custodiendum suase-rim: is enim interrogatus, quanam ratione tantum temporis, hoc est, centum & nouem annos salubriter optimeq; vixisset, respondit, nihil voluptatis gratia faciendo. Hippocrates conseruationem sanitatis esse dixit, veluti citra satietatem. Galenus nunquam satur de mensa surrexit, quâ etiam ratione vitam in extremam vsq; produxit senectam. Nunquam igitur salutum de mensa surgere, est frugaliter & temperanter viuere.
units.tr: Therefore those are rightly worthy of reproach who, without any appetite, while the stomach does not ask for it and the previous food is not yet fully digested, take in new food: they carefully arrange a breakfast, with lunch soon following, and do not neglect suppers and carousing, which, often in the courts of great men (where such things are today thought worthy of praise), are drawn out late into the night, and not without loss to the body. For it cannot be that the powers of the body remain intact amid such gluttony. There are many who, for the sake of pleasure alone, and to bind others to themselves by this means, eat and carouse even when hunger does not urge them; afterwards they feel a troublesome heaviness and weariness of the whole body. I would advise that, as a most wholesome remedy for keeping health, one should imitate and observe that golden answer of Gorgias the Sicilian rhetorician to such gluttons. Asked by what method he had lived so long, that is a hundred and nine years, healthily and very well, he replied: by doing nothing for the sake of pleasure. Hippocrates said that the preservation of health consists in living without satiety. Galen never rose from the table satisfied, and by this method he also prolonged his life into extreme old age. Therefore to rise from the table never fully satisfied is to live frugally and temperately.

units.la: Concoctu facilia, liquida, & quæ facile putrescunt primum sunt ingerenda, citius enim è ventriculo elabuntur, nam si extremis epulis sumerentur, præposteroque ordine concoctu difficilia præcederent, concoctionis opus impediretur, prohiberetur; ne concoctu facilia è ventriculo exirent: adde quòd liquida, & quæ facile corrumpuntur, primis mensis sunt offerenda, vt citius è ventriculi officina depelluntur, autequam putrescant. Unde ciborum varievarietas, menfæq; dubiæ (in quibus dubitatur potissimum, quid fit fumendum) illaudantur, diuersæ enim naturæ cibi eadem mensa aslumati contumaciter à naturæ robore edomantur, magnoq; negotio à ventriculo concoquuntur, faciliufq; putredinis labem induunt. Unde Homerus vnam & simplex alimentum, vt carnem bubulam assam Principibus seduci-bus appositam esse prodidit. Hoc nomine Chrysippus Euripidis sæpe sententiam in ore habebat, qui ad hominum alimentum nihil præter Cereris munera & aquæ poculum opus esse contendebat.
units.tr: Foods that are easy to digest, liquid, and those that rot easily should be taken first, for they pass more quickly out of the stomach. For if they were taken at the end of the meal, and hard-to-digest foods came first in the wrong order, the work of digestion would be hindered and prevented, and the easily digested foods would not pass out of the stomach. Add that liquid foods, and those that spoil easily, should be served at the first courses, so that they are driven out more quickly from the workshop of the stomach before they rot. Hence a variety of foods, and doubtful meals (in which one is uncertain above all what ought to be eaten), are not praised. For foods of different natures eaten at the same table are stubbornly overcome by the strength of nature, are digested by the stomach only with great effort, and more easily take on the stain of putrefaction. Hence Homer reported that a single and simple food, such as roast beef, was set before the leading princes. For this reason Chrysippus often had on his lips a saying of Euripides, who maintained that for human nourishment nothing more was needed than the gifts of Ceres and a cup of water.

units.la: Quid tibi deesse potest, modicus sipanis & vnā, Prandia, vel cœnam si tibi præbet olus.
units.tr: What can be lacking to you, with a modest sip of wine and one dish, whether it is lunch or supper that vegetables provide for you?

units.la: Quanquam consuetudinis hic ratio habenda est, tanquam alterius naturæ. Etenim cibi præter consuetudinem plurimum, aut repentè ingesti ventriculum aggrauant, & non paum offendunt. Ventriculus enim consuetis gaudere solet, cibumque familiarem majori cum voluptate amplectitur. Ubi tamen memineris consuetudinem sanitatis tempore esse immutandam, si sit praua, cibisq; omnino mali succi quispiam vesci consueuerit, vt fungis, oleribus quibusdam, & leguminibus. Non tamen derepente & subitò immutanda est. Mala enim victus ratio, inquit Hippocrates, modo sit familiaris & aslueta, tutior est, quam si repentè in aliam, & quidem meliorem fiat transmutatio:
units.tr: Yet the custom of the individual must be taken into account here, as though it were a second nature. For foods eaten in quantity beyond custom, or suddenly, weigh down the stomach and offend it not a little. The stomach is accustomed to enjoy what it is used to, and embraces familiar food with greater pleasure. Yet you should remember that a habit must be changed in health if it is bad, as when someone has been accustomed to eat foods of bad juice, such as mushrooms, certain herbs and pulses. Yet it must not be changed suddenly and all at once. For a bad diet, says Hippocrates, if it is familiar and accustomed, is safer than if a sudden change is made to another and better one.

units.la: E tio: quin tantam consuetudinis esse vim idem nos monet. 1. & 2. aphorifm. vt, quae longo tempore consueta sunt, licet sint deteriora, minus laedant insuetis: quem locum enarrans Galenus consuetudinem videtur aequalle naturae, cibos & potus consuetos dicens naturam facere aduentitiam. Hac consuetudinis efficacia, ingenitaq; solidorum & similiarum membrorum temperatura & proprietate, non solius natiui caloris virtute, venena & pharmaca digerinq; alimentum conuerti exemplo sunt natos, & palumbi hyoscyami pastillis inescati, praeterea coturnices & sturni ex hellebori & cicutae pastu obesi, ac pisces nuce vomica capu, struthio ferrum digerens, pastores plerique; in Graecia integros hellebori manipulos citra noxam, & Turcae opium deuorantes. Hac lente primum & moderate acquisita assuetudine puella Indica puellari Venere decora, praesentissimo Napelli veneno enutrita est, à Rege Indorum Alexandro Magno, dolo, muneri data, cujus scintillantes & serpentum more nictantes oculos cum Aristoteles ipsius praeceptor vidisset, Caue tibi ab hac, inquit, O Alexander, hac nempe tibi exitium paratur. Nec judicio Aristotelis defuit euentus, nam fere omnes proci virginis concubitu intoxicati interierunt. Sic venena quotidie fere hausta, praesumptis tamen remediis, Mitridati à consuetudine fuerunt innoxia adeo, vt captus à Pompejo M. in vinculis veneno se interimere non potuerit. Cicutæ autem succum esse venenum soporiferum, & puluerem quoq; lethalem, Athenienses indicant supplicia, qui morte condemnatos sorbitione cicutæ intereme-runt, quam & Socrates condemnatus in carcere hausit. Ex quibus patere arbitror, quid consuetudo cum ingenita totius substantiæ membrorum similarium proprietate citra etiam natiui, & à corde influentis caloris auxilium valeat. Illa autem proprietas cum sit diuersa in diuersis corporibus & animalibus, accidit, vt hic caseum, alius vinum naturâ abhorreat, coturnices & capræ Elleboro, struthi cicuta vescantur. De qua re doctè ceci-nit Lucretius l.4.& 5. Est vtiq; serpens, hominis qua tacta saliua Disperit, ac sese mandendo conficit ipsa. Praterea nobis veratrum est acre venenum, At capris adipes & co ni nicibus augeT. Quippe videre licet pinguescere sape cicutā Barbigeras pecudes, hominiq; quae est acre venenum.
units.tr: Hence the same authority warns us how great the power of custom is (Aphorisms 1 and 2): that things long accustomed, even if they are worse, harm those unaccustomed to them less. Commenting on this passage, Galen seems to equate custom with nature, saying that customary foods and drinks make nature into something acquired. Through this power of custom, and not by the native heat alone, people have been known to digest poisons and drugs and to turn them into nourishment, given the inborn temperament and property of their solid and similar parts. Doves fed on pellets of henbane, quails and starlings fattened on hellebore and hemlock, fish fed on nux vomica, the ostrich digesting iron, most shepherds in Greece eating whole bundles of hellebore without harm, and the Turks devouring opium. In this way, a girl of Indian birth, lovely in the manner of a maiden, was nourished by the most deadly poison of aconite, acquired slowly and gradually at first. King Alexander the Great of the Indians gave her as a gift, by treachery. When Aristotle, his teacher, saw her sparkling eyes, blinking like a serpent's, he said: "Beware of her, Alexander, for she is prepared as your destruction." Aristotle's judgment was not without its outcome, for nearly all her suitors died poisoned by her embrace. So too Mithridates, who daily took in poisons almost constantly, though with antidotes applied, was made so immune by habit that when he was captured by Pompey the Great and held in chains he could not kill himself with poison. That the juice of hemlock is a soporific poison, and its powder deadly, the Athenians show by their executions, who killed condemned men by drinking hemlock; and Socrates, condemned, drank it in prison. From these things, I think, it is clear how much custom can do, together with the inborn property of all the substance of the similar parts, even without the aid of the native heat flowing from the heart. Since this property differs in different bodies and animals, it happens that one naturally shrinks from cheese, another from wine; quails and goats eat hellebore, ostriches eat hemlock. On this matter Lucretius has sung learnedly, in Book 4 and 5: There is indeed a serpent whose spittle, touching a man, destroys him, and it wastes itself by biting. Moreover, hellebore is a sharp poison to us, yet it fattens goats and quails. Indeed one may often see hemlock fatten bearded flocks, though it is a sharp poison for man.

units.la: Plura vide apud Plin. l. 10. c. 23. Arist. l. 1 de hist. plant. Gal. lib. 3. de simplic. med. l. 2. de alim. Theoph. l. 9. de hist. plant c. 18. Arist. in l. de regimine principum. Averrh. in procem. 3. phys.
units.tr: See more in Pliny, Book 10, chapter 23; Aristotle, Book 1 of the History of Plants; Galen, Book 3 On Simple Medicines and Book 2 On Foods; Theophrastus, Book 9 of the History of Plants, chapter 18; Aristotle in the book On the Governance of Princes; Averroes on the Proem of the Physics, Book 3.

units.la: De Eudemo illo Chio tradit Theophrastus, quod neque vomitu, neque alui dejectione purgatus purgari potuerit. Multi aluum habent sequacem, pharmacoq; facile cedentem. Nouiin regio Haffniensi myropolio quendam, qui, quotiescunq; volebat, solo pillularum formadarum olfactu aluum irritabat,vt ita congenitae totius membrorum substantiae proprietati, quae in indiuiduis variat, hae diuersitates indiuiduificae sint acceptae ferendae,struthionumque ventriculum ferrum & numismata, quae vix igne domari possunt, feruentisq; aquae calor ventriculo calidior liquefacere aptus non est, concoquere ob eandem rationem sit credendum.
units.tr: Theophrastus relates of that Eudemus of Chios that he could not be purged either by vomiting or by the evacuation of the bowels. Many people have a loose bowel that yields easily to medicine. I know of a certain man in the apothecary's shop at Copenhagen who, whenever he wished, irritated his bowels merely by smelling pills being shaped. Thus, since the inborn property of the whole substance of the parts, which varies among individuals, must be accepted and borne, so these individual differences must be accepted. It must also be believed that the ostrich's stomach digests iron and coins, which can hardly be tamed by fire, and that the heat of boiling water, hotter than the stomach, is not fit to melt them, for the same reason.

units.la: Occasio noui cibi ingerendi aliquando humorum cruditate interturbatur.
units.tr: The opportunity to take in new food is sometimes disturbed by the crudity of the humours.

units.la: Itaq; qui laborant ex cruditatibus,& calorem ventriculi habent imbecilliorem, minusque vigentem,videant, ne assumtione noui cibi ventriculi vigorem vel opprimant,planeue prosternant.
units.tr: Therefore those who suffer from indigestions and have a weaker and less vigorous heat of the stomach should take care that the intake of new food does not overwhelm or utterly prostrate the vigour of the stomach.

units.la: Verum cum cruditas literarum studiosos plerumq; infestare soleat,iisq; inimica sit,plurimumq; morborum radix, teste Cicer. de fato operae pretium me hic facturum putaui, si hu-manioribus literis operam dantibus, quorum in gratiam hic potissimum de tuenda sanitate tractatus est conscriptus, de cruditate ejusque causis & signis breuiter & perspicue aliquid adiicerem.
units.tr: But since crudity usually troubles students of literature and is harmful to them, and is the chief root of many diseases (as Cicero says in his work On Fate), I have thought it worthwhile to add briefly and clearly something about crudity, its causes and signs, for those who devote themselves to the humane letters, for whose sake this treatise on preserving health has been chiefly written.

units.la: Cibus in ventriculo vel plane non alteratur, & dicitur ἁπλῶς, id est, simpliciter eruditas, vel alteratur, non tamen sicut oportet,& dicitur cruditas κατὰ τί, id est, secundum quid, vel alteratio depravata. Hæc alteratio depravata vel fit tarde, cum videlicet cibi conuenientem mutationem nondum fuscepepunt, & dicitur βραδυπεψία, id est, tarda coctio: vel fit corrupte, cum videlicet cibi corrumpuntur, & dici potest chylificatio corrupta: mutatio enim cibi in chylum, id est, eam substantiam quæ in epate in sanguinem potest converti, à medicis dicitur chylificatio, sicut chyli in sanguinem conuersio sanguificatio.
units.tr: Food in the stomach is either not altered at all, and is called crudity simply [ἁπλῶς], that is, absolutely; or it is altered, but not as it should be, and this is called crudity in some respect [κατὰ τί], that is, in a certain respect, or depraved alteration. This depraved alteration either occurs slowly, when the food has not yet undergone its proper change, and is called tardy digestion [βραδυπεψία], that is, slow concoction; or it occurs corruptly, when the food is spoiled, and it may be called corrupt chylification. For the change of food into chyle, that is, into the substance which in the liver can be converted into blood, is called chylification by physicians, just as the conversion of chyle into blood is called sanguification.

units.la: Causarum magna differentia est. Contra-huntur potissimum ex ciborum copiosa varietate, commessationibus & compotationibus assiduis, vnde ventriculus frigidior evadit, vel calidior, nativúsque calor imminuitur, vel opprimitur.
units.tr: There is a great difference in causes. They arise chiefly from a copious and varied diet, from constant feasting and drinking, whence the stomach becomes either colder or hotter, and the native heat is diminished or suppressed.

units.la: Signa in genere sunt flatus, ructus, morsus & ventriculi pondus, grauitas, & circa diaphragma compressio.
units.tr: The signs in general are flatulence, belching, gnawing, a heaviness and weight of the stomach, and pressure around the diaphragm.

units.la: In specie verò, signa cruditatis sunt excrementa mutata. Si cibi ingesti nullam suscipiunt alterationem, vt cum integra ova iterum deiiciuntur, signum coctionis ablatæ est: Sicut imminutæ coctionis signum est, cum cibi longo tempore concoquuntur: corruptæ denique signum cognoscitur è ructibus tum aci-
units.tr: In particular, the signs of crudity are altered excrements. If the food taken in undergoes no alteration at all, as when whole eggs are passed again, this is a sign that digestion has been taken away. A sign of diminished digestion is when food takes a long time to be digested. Finally, the sign of corrupt digestion is recognised from the belchings, which are

units.la: E distum nidorulentis,illi frigiditatis, hi calidi-tatis noxam denunciant.
units.tr: sour, or smelling of rottenness; the former announce the harm of coldness, the latter the harm of heat.

units.la: Crudi tates vel admittunt coctionem, vel non admittunt.Si non admittunt, (vt in ascite aqua, quæ omnem coctionem respuit) euacuandæ sunt. Si crudi humores coctionem admittunt,vel quiescunt vel mouentur. Si quiescunt, conducit primum digerere, postea purgare. Si mouentur,mouentur ad loca conuenientia vel non conuenientia. Si ad conuenientia,promouendi sunt & expurgindi. Si ad non conuenientia, h. e,ad partem aliquam principem vel principi cognatam,ilico,negleta concoctione, exturbandi sunt, pillulis ex hiera simplici, alephangineis, mastichinis vel similibus.
units.tr: Crudities either admit concoction or do not. If they do not admit it (as in dropsy, where the water rejects all concoction), they must be evacuated. If the crude humours admit concoction, they either remain still or are moved. If they remain still, it is best first to digest them and afterwards to purge them. If they are moved, they are moved either to suitable places or to unsuitable ones. If to suitable places, they must be moved onward and purged. If to unsuitable places, that is, to some principal part or one akin to a principal part, they must immediately be driven out, without waiting for concoction, by pills of simple hiera, alexipharmic pills, mastic pills, or the like.

units.la: Præsentissimum remedium est vomitus, qui si spontaneus non est, irritabitur hausta olei,aquæ & aceti tepide mixtorum, vel digito oleo intincto acin fauces immisso: quo facto ventriculus statim roborandus est nuce mo-schata condita,corticibus citri vel arantiarum conditis, Zinzibere vel galanga condita, vino absinthite,vel similibus.
units.tr: The most ready remedy is vomiting; if it does not occur spontaneously, it is provoked by drinking a mixture of oil, water and vinegar, warmed, or by putting a finger dipped in oil into the throat. After this the stomach must at once be strengthened with preserved nutmeg, preserved citron or orange peel, preserved ginger or galangal, wine of wormwood, or similar remedies.

units.la: Qui vero caloris congeniti & natiui im-becillitatem & defectum per se sentiunt,omni studio conabuntur, substantiam caloris adaugere, pro rato & firmo habentes, omnia ea, quæ calorem innatum adaugere experientia testatur, etiam ventriculi concoctionem promouere. mouere,vt sunt:aromata deglutita, fomentationes,cataplasmata, frictiones, inunctiones, exercitia, balnea & id genus temperata fomenta,vt catellus,aut puer,puellaue senili flaccido-que stomacho accumbens. Sic Dauid septua-genarius cum senili torpore frigeret,nec pelli-bus coopertus incalescceret,in spectati decorispuellae amplexibus caste condormiuit, vt ejuscalore stomachi robur foueretur. Est in expe-rimentis, quosdam jam fere tabe & atrophiaconfumptos solo lacte ex vegetae & florentismulieris uberibus sucto esse restitutos, vt ita constet,calorem naturalem & a corde infusum non modo esse spirituum vehiculum,sed praecipuum concoctionis organum, facultatumq; animae instrumentum,teste Arist.2.de anima.
units.tr: But those who feel in themselves the weakness and defect of the innate and native heat must strive with all zeal to increase the substance of the heat, holding as certain and firm that all those things which experience shows increase the innate heat also promote the concoction of the stomach. These are: swallowed aromatics, fomentations, poultices, rubbing, anointing, exercise, baths, and such gentle warmings, as well as a little dog, or a boy or girl lying beside an old, flaccid stomach. So David, being seventy years old, when he was chilled by senile torpor and could not grow warm even when covered with skins, slept chastely in the embrace of a beautiful girl, so that the strength of his stomach might be cherished by her warmth. There is experience that some who were already nearly wasted by consumption and atrophy have been restored by sucking milk alone from the breasts of a vigorous and flourishing woman. Thus it is established, as Aristotle teaches in Book 2 On the Soul, that the natural heat, infused from the heart, is not only the vehicle of the spirits but the chief organ of concoction and the instrument of the faculties of the soul.

units.la: Hactenus fuerunt generales praeceptiones de cibo & potu:
units.tr: So far these have been the general precepts about food and drink.

units.la: Sequitur de variis cibi & potus generibus, quae in vsum hominum admittuntur, cum primis vero quae nostras mensas subeunt.
units.tr: It follows concerning the various kinds of food and drink that are admitted for human use, and especially those that come to our tables.

units.la: HIC vero me non inanem plane operam sumpsisse arbitrabor, si sequentes prius quaestiones in medicorum & philosophorum Scholis etiamnunc controversas, difficultate, utilitate & jucunditate non carentes discutiendas propulserim, quam varia cibaria degustanda exhibuerim.
units.tr: Here I shall think I have not spent my effort entirely in vain if, before setting out various foods to be tasted, I first put forward the following questions, which are still disputed in the schools of physicians and philosophers and which are not without difficulty, usefulness and interest.

units.la: 1. An coena prandio debeat esse liberalior, hoc est, an largius sit coenandum, quam prandendum?
units.tr: 1. Ought supper to be more generous than dinner, that is, should one eat more at supper than at dinner?

units.la: 2. Virum magis laedat valetudinem, vorando an potando modum excedere?
units.tr: 2. Does excess in eating or excess in drinking do more harm to a man's health?

units.la: 3. An omnino sit abstinendum a potu inter medio inter coenam & prandium tempore?
units.tr: 3. Should one abstain altogether from drink in the interval between supper and dinner?

units.la: 4. An hieme propterea plus esitandum quam aestate, quod ventres sint calidiores?
units.tr: 4. Should people eat more in winter than in summer, because their stomachs are warmer?

units.la: 5. An alimentum sit tantum dicendum quod nutrit?
units.tr: 5. Is only that to be called food which nourishes?

units.la: 6. An nutritio sit assimilatio:
units.tr: 6. Is nutrition the same as assimilation?

units.la: 7. An morbi communes etiam oriantur a ciborum malorum copia & culpa?
units.tr: 7. Do common diseases also arise from a surplus and fault of bad foods?

units.la: 8. An ciborum natura & potestas ad varia gentium ac populorum ingenia morefq; aliquid confera? ubi & de singulari alimentorum vi.
units.tr: 8. Do the nature and power of foods contribute anything to the varied dispositions and customs of nations and peoples? Here also belongs the special power of foods.

units.la: 9. Morbi quod quibusdam gentibus peculiariter accidant, an victus ratio in causa sit? & cur quidam repente hominibus nascantur in certis membris?
units.tr: 9. Do the diseases that befall certain peoples in a peculiar way have their cause in the manner of their diet? And why do some growths suddenly appear in certain parts of the body in some people?

units.la: In his quaestionibus ventilandis apud me valebit prisccum illud: In sententia permaneto, ni alia sit melior. Itaque si quid rectius & verius videro vel audiuero, lubenter id amplectar. Neque enim inconstantis est, repudiatis falsis vera amplecti & defendere. Veritatem vel infirmare vel obscurare, aq; viris sapientibus & doctis temere disseTire euidentissimum stultitiae & infscitiae argumentu est. Omnia sibi tritribuere, reliquis nihil vel parum, superciliosę fatuitatis est. Turpes & ridiculas potius causas & rationes quærere, quam de ignorantia conuiteri improbum nec ingenuum est, cum sapientissimi & doctissimi quique multa se ignorare, & multa sibi etiam atque etiam dicenda esse, sint confessi, referente Cic. 3. Tusc. ingenuè suam imbecillitatem indicabat Fallopius, cum se ignorare causam, cur argentum viuum gallicam luem sanet, scriberet: Hippocrates sclertissimus Medicinæ instaurator, cum popularium & incurabilium morborum causas & curationes explicare nequiret, ipsum Deum quasi ad hominum errores explicandos accire non dubitauit, seu diuina potestate illos cieri modestè confessus est, quem secutus fidelissimus eius interpres Galenus, cum seminis vim admirabilem intueretur, nec causas animaduerteret, diuinum quid in eo latitare scripsit. Aristoteles ignorantiæ se palam accusare non erubuit. Socrate inter Græcos iudicio Apollinis nemo erat sapiens, & tamen assiduè discens plurima fiebat senex, vt de se ipso refert.
units.tr: In examining these questions, the old saying will hold good with me: Stay with your opinion unless another is better. So if I see or hear anything more correct and true, I shall gladly embrace it. For it is not the mark of an inconstant man to reject what is false and to embrace and defend what is true. To weaken or obscure the truth, and to dispute rashly before wise and learned men, is the clearest sign of folly and ignorance. To claim everything for oneself and little or nothing for others is the mark of a haughty foolishness. To seek base and ridiculous causes and reasons rather than to complain of one's ignorance is wicked and not becoming a free man, since the wisest and most learned men have all confessed that they know many things not, and that much must be said and said again about them, as Cic. 3. Tusc. reports. Fallopius frankly admitted his weakness when he wrote that he did not know why quicksilver cures the French pox. Hippocrates, the most skilful restorer of medicine, when he could not explain the causes and cures of epidemic and incurable diseases, did not hesitate to summon God himself, as it were, to explain human errors; he modestly confessed that such diseases were stirred up by divine power. His most faithful interpreter Galen followed him, and when he looked upon the admirable power of semen and did not perceive its causes, he wrote that something divine lies hidden in it. Aristotle did not blush to accuse himself openly of ignorance. Among the Greeks, by the judgment of Apollo, no one was wiser than Socrates, and yet, as he himself reports, he became an old man while constantly learning many things.

units.la: Verè igitur eruditi & sapienter literati intra hominem consistunt & naturam.
units.tr: Truly, then, the learned and wisely lettered remain within the limits of man and of nature.

units.la: Verum cum præsidium in nobis sit diuinæ imaginis, hoc est, artificiosus & rationalis igniculus, non plane etiam is nullus putandus est, licet graduum sit diuersitas, adeò vt nimaduers…
units.tr: But since there is in us a safeguard of the divine image, that is, a skilful and rational spark, it should not be thought wholly absent, although there is a difference of degrees, so that one notices some things in the keen and superior men which are inferior to them, things which they can indeed admire but can hardly imitate.

units.la: E stant aliquid in acutis & superioribus inferio-res,quod admirari quidem,imitari vero vix valeant. Quod quidem ego in magni ingenii viris lubens agnosco, naturaeq; praestantiam in illis magnificio, me ad illorum exemplum, quantum per naturae genium mihi licebit, totum conformans. Sapere vltra hominem ex se nulli concessum esse.
units.tr: I gladly acknowledge this in men of great genius, and I magnify the excellence of their nature, shaping myself wholly after their example, as far as the spirit of nature allows me. To be wise beyond man is granted to no one by himself.

units.la: QVÆSTIO I. An largius sit coenandum quam prandendum? Disting.
units.tr: QUESTION I. Ought supper to be more generous than dinner? A distinction is needed.

units.la: VEtus & constans opinio est parcius prandendum esse quam coenandum, pluraq; & valentiora alimenta in coena, quam in prandio esse offerenda, quod quies, somnus & nox calorem naturum ad centrum revocant, unde adauctus ad coctionem excitatur, ventriculum & viscera corroborat, siccq; coctio magis completur, quā in vigilia, in qua calor ad cutim & partes corporis externas exprimaq; revocatur & influit, unde ex immodicis vigiliis cruditates coacervantur. In somno autem interiora omnia calent magis, virtutes spiritusq; naturales plus vigent quam in pervigilio, in quo magis dissipantur.
units.tr: It is an old and settled opinion that one should dine more sparingly than one sups, and that more and richer food should be offered at supper than at dinner, because rest, sleep and night draw the natural heat back to the centre; from there it is increased and roused to digestion, strengthens the stomach and the inner organs, and so digestion is more fully completed than in waking hours, when the heat is drawn out and flows back to the skin and the outer parts of the body, whence crudities accumulate after excessive waking. In sleep, moreover, all the inner parts grow warmer, and the natural powers and spirits are more vigorous than in long wakefulness, when they are more dissipated.

units.la: Nam quoq; cibum melius digeri argumento est mentis ingeniiq; acumen mane longe expeditius, quo uno nocturnam ferculorum coenā concoctionem diurnā longe vegetiorem esse magisq; exastam demonstratur. Huc accedit nosturnus & humidus Lunæ splendor. Luna enim astrum ad cibariorum concoctiones multum conferre nemo negauerit nisi Lunam e cœlo suo deturbans. Est enim putrefactiui, ococtio autem quædam putrefactio est. Victima certè nosturnæ sunt digestibiliores, ną & ligna ad Lunæ splendorem casa citius putrescunt.
units.tr: That food is digested better at night is shown also by the keenness of mind and wit, which is far readier in the morning; by this alone it is demonstrated that the digestion of a night supper of dishes is much more vigorous than the daytime digestion, and more fully done. To this is added the moist light of the moon at night. No one would deny that the moon, a heavenly body, contributes much to the digestion of foods, unless he is thrusting the moon out of its own heaven. For it is putrefying, and digestion is a kind of putrefaction. Indeed, night-killed victims are more digestible, and wood cut by moonlight rots more quickly.

units.la: Hæc sententia vetustissima & saluberrima Heorum vitæ ratione corroboratur. Magis enim opiparè & maiori ferculorum apparatu instruxisse cœnas quam prandia veteres, istatur apud Homerum Eumæus subulcus, Vlyssi adueniënti duos mastans porcos, carneq; suilla in verù tosta cœnam ei, addito vino optimo, instruens. Gracifru-gi fere semper ientare & prandere solitisunt. Athleta quoq; & palæstrita, quamuis varius palæstra exercitus valentiori alimento corporis robur sibi comparare omnibus modis studerent, interdiu-tamen à ferculis varijs sibi caueba̅t, & in prandio soli panem coliphium (Krafftbrodt) edebant: at in cœna liberali genio indulgebant, præcipuè vescitu carnæ suilla, quia copiosè nutriret.
units.tr: This most ancient and most wholesome opinion is confirmed by the way of life of the heroes. Homer shows that the ancients furnished suppers more lavishly and with a greater display of dishes than dinners: Eumaeus the swineherd, when Ulysses arrived, was roasting two pigs and, with pork roasted on the spit and the finest wine added, set supper before him. The Greeks, too, were accustomed to take their breakfast and dinner almost always on grain. Athletes and wrestlers also, although they trained in the wrestling school and by every means strove to gain bodily strength from more nourishing food, nevertheless kept themselves from various dishes during the day, and at dinner ate only bread and coliphium (Krafftbrodt). At supper, however, they indulged their generous spirit, especially by eating pork, because it nourished abundantly.

units.la: Antoninus Pius Cæsar iam senex, mane antequam saluta̅ores venirent solo pane sicco robur virium conseruauit, Capitolino teste. Pythagoricos non aliud quam panem cum melle attico prandere solitos, referri Aristoxenus. Quid? quod Galenus ipse 7. methodi copiosè docet, semper studiostudendum vt valentius alimentum vesperi exhibeamus, quoniam non solum quia & somnus, verum etiam longius tempus naturalem huius concoctionem excipit. Et Corn. Celsus lib. i. c. 3. inquit: plus edere hieme conuenit, sed minus & meracius bibere, prandenti vero vtilius esse exiguum quid, & ipsum siccum sine carne, sine potione sumere: quae certe Celsi sententia plurimum in se habet momenti. Inter stentandum enim vel prandendum potando & vorando modum excedens, cumprimis vero bibendo, dic amabo te mihi, an non toto illo die somnolentia corripiaris, acfacile abdormiscas (nisi colloquio somnum impediatur,) & ad quaestus negotia obeunda reddaris ineptus? nemo opinor inficietur: Et licet somno meridiano vel diurno medelam male quaeras, expergefactus tamen ita capiti vaporibus repletum cum tanta gravedine sentias, vt cyclopas tibi in id migrasse iuret qui alternatis illud feriant stibus: quae certe corporis lassitudo capitisq; grauedo nō contingit largiùs cœnantibus (nisi commessationes & potationes ad mediam vel vltra noctem protrahantur, & horis subluctantis iterum sit surgendum cœtione scilicet non perasta, vaporibus non discussis,) quies enim somnumq; noctumus, calorq; intro compulsus reliquias meri in venis turgentibus humoresq; crudos exactius concoquunt digerunt: quod perquam norunt potatores.
units.tr: The emperor Antoninus Pius, already an old man, kept up his strength in the morning, before the morning callers came, with only dry bread, as Capitolinus testifies. Aristoxenus reports that the Pythagoreans were accustomed to dine on nothing but bread with Attic honey. And what of Galen himself, who in book seven of his Method teaches at length that we should always take care to offer a more nourishing food in the evening, since not only sleep but also a longer time follows and receives its natural digestion? Cornelius Celsus, book one, chapter three, says: it is fitting to eat more in winter, but to drink less and more undiluted; for the one who dines, it is more useful to take something small, and that dry, without meat and without drink. This opinion of Celsus certainly carries great weight. For when, in eating or dining, one exceeds the measure in drinking and gorging, especially in drinking, tell me, I beg you, will you not be seized with drowsiness the whole day and easily fall asleep (unless sleep is prevented by conversation), and become unfit for performing your business? No one, I think, will deny it. And although you may seek a remedy in a midday or daytime sleep, when you wake you will feel your head so full of vapours and so heavy that you would swear the Cyclopes had migrated into it and were striking it with alternating hammers. Such weariness of body and heaviness of head do not come to those who sup more generously (unless their revelries and drinking bouts are prolonged to midnight or beyond, and one must get up after a few hours with the drinking unfinished and the vapours not dispersed). For the quiet and the night's sleep, and the heat driven inward, digest more exactly the remains of wine in the swollen veins and the crude humours; this is well known to drinkers.

units.la: Hi enim ob noctu rnam hesternamq; erapulam, corporis capitisq; lassitudinem grauedinemq; persentiscensentiscentes totum fere diem stertunt somnoque inde dulgent, sicque male medentur: & recte quidem præ-stat enim ad coctionis vsque complementum dormire, quam crudo ventriculo surgere, h.e. cibo nondum coctto eque ventriculo egressa. Pro quantitate enim & qualitate alimentorum & coctrices robore citius aut serius concoquitur. Percipitur autem cibum è ventriculo elapsum esse, (quod fit ǒ. vel 7. plerumque horis) sinullis sitibus, nullis ructibus, nulla gravitas, morsus, tumor inflatione circa ventriculi regionem vexigant: horum signorum vero maior pars si sentiatur, signum est non tantum cibum è ventriculo non egressum, sed ad dimidium etiam vix coctum esse. Talem quibus contingit, id est, qui vel nimium se replerunt, vel parum concoxerunt, vomitus utilis est, inquit Cornelius Celsus.
units.tr: For these men, sensing the weariness and heaviness of body and head from last night's and yesterday's excess, snore away almost the whole day and indulge in sleep, and so they cure themselves badly. And indeed it is better to sleep until digestion is complete than to rise with a crude stomach, that is, with food not yet digested having left the stomach. For according to the quantity and quality of the foods and the strength of the digestive powers, digestion proceeds more quickly or more slowly. It is perceived that the food has left the stomach (which usually happens after four or seven hours) when no thirst, no belching, no heaviness, no gnawing, and no swelling with wind troubles the region of the stomach. If most of these signs are felt, it is a sign that the food has not only not left the stomach but is scarcely half digested. For those who have this condition, that is, who have either filled themselves too much or digested too little, vomiting is useful, says Cornelius Celsus.

units.la: Recentiores quidam, inter quos est clarissimus Philosophus & Medicus Ioh. Pincier, veterum illam prandendi, cœnandique rationem videntur impugnare non infirmis rationibus. Primo concedunt vigilantes extrinsecus plus calere, dormientes vero frigere, eo quod vigilantes plerumque corpus exerceant, dormientes non item: calorque revocetur quidem ad summum principium videlicet cor venasque, non vero ventriculum, qui caloris principium & subiectum non est; ideoque meliorem etiam coctionem non fieri in ventriculo noctu affirmant: Exercitio autem calorum natium non tantum re-focillari in nobis & excitari, verum etiam quamquam diffribui omnibus non est notum, per motum auctio calore melius absolui collionem probant qui labore corporis victum sibi quaeritant, fabri lignarii, ferrarii, agricolae, qui prandio & coena non contenti tenuaculum etiam & merendam sibi dari postulat. (Sed & Troiani belli tempore Graeci 4. comedendi tempora observabant, ut sunt acratissima seu tenuaculi, aristos prandii, hesperitina merenda, & dipnos coena, quae adeo illis fragi institutebatur, ut in acratismate solo pane mero macerato vescerentur, sub vesperam institutebatur merenda, post vero occasum solis coena.) Praeterea cum etiam illis, qui vigilantes a corporis agitatione & exercitio abstinent, idem quod dormientibus evenire solet, sequitur non ideo in somno frigere exteriora, quia homo dormiat, sed quod corpus non exerceatur. Adde quod tunc praecipue est somno indulgendum, cum ventriculus calore maxime indiget: atque nunquam eo magis indiget, quam mox a cibo, cum videlicet adhuc crudus est, ut ita saturi somno se dare quam primum debeant. At vero eos, qui id faciunt, male cibos coquere & liquefacere, documenta sunt, nausea, rustus, inflatio doloris ventriculi: & qui profundo tanquam ventriculi coquentis adiutore tantopere decertant, duarum horarum spatium inter coenam somnum interuenire oportere & debere praecipiunt, quo mandato nihil aliud testatum faciunt, quam somnum chylificationis impedimentum potius esse quam adiumentum, alioquin confestim a somno dormire inherent.
units.tr: Some more recent writers, among whom is the most distinguished philosopher and physician Johann Pincier, seem to attack the ancients' practice of dining and supping on grounds that are not weak. First, they concede that waking people are warmer on the outside and sleeping people colder, because waking people usually exercise their bodies and sleepers do not. The heat is drawn back to the chief source, namely the heart and the veins, and not to the stomach, which is neither the source nor the seat of heat. They therefore affirm that digestion is not better in the stomach at night. Moreover, exercise does not merely refresh and rouse our innate heat. Though not everyone knows it, those who earn their living by bodily labour, such as carpenters, smiths and farmers, prove that by motion the heat is increased and digestion is better completed. Not content with dinner and supper, these men ask for a light meal and an afternoon snack. (The Greeks in the time of the Trojan war also observed four times for eating: the light breakfast [ἀκρατισμα], the lunch [ἄριστον], the afternoon snack [ἑσπερίτινα], and the supper [δεῖπνον]. They were so frugal that at the akratisma they ate only bread soaked in unmixed wine; the snack was taken towards evening, and the supper after sunset.) Furthermore, since those who keep from bodily movement and exercise while awake suffer the same as sleepers, it follows that the outside does not grow cold in sleep because a man sleeps, but because the body is not exercised. Add that one should especially indulge sleep when the stomach most needs heat. It never needs heat more than just after food, while the food is still raw; so the sated should give themselves to sleep as soon as they can. But that those who do this digest their food badly is shown by nausea, belching and pain and swelling of the stomach. And those who contend so fiercely for sleep as the deep helper of the digesting stomach direct that two hours should, and must, lie between supper and sleep. By this precept they show nothing else than that sleep hinders chylification rather than helps it; otherwise they would fall straight into sleep after supper.

units.la: Deinde, quo tempore maior fit resolutio, eo maiori opus est refectione.
units.tr: Next, the greater the loss of strength at a given time, the greater the refreshment needed then.

units.la: A tempore prandii, ob vigilias praecedentes & subsequentes, resolutio fit evidentior & maior, quam tempore coenae. Ergo in prandio maiori opus est refectione, ante enim prandium & diu a prandio exercitiis fessi lent homines obleflare.
units.tr: From the time of lunch, because of the waking before and after it, the loss is more evident and greater than at supper. Therefore more refreshment is needed at lunch, for men worn out by exertion before lunch, and long after it, are apt to grow faint.

units.la: Ad ex rerum experientia, se muniunt, quae testatur vigiliam concoctionem maturare, vigilantes enim plus cibi & horarum spatio conficere, q. 15. vel 16. horis domientes: adducitur quoque auctoritas Plinii, qui perunigilio cibos peracipue vinei ait. Et Hippocr. 6. Epid. vigiliam homines reddere edaces afferentis, quod motu, quo vtuntur vigilantes excitetur calor & augetur. In hac controuersia quid statuendum? Ante omnia hic quemlibet nosse co-poris sui naturam oportet: mihi perinde est, sive largius coenem sive parcius, modo bene coenem, hoc est, citra virium corporis iactuaram: prout plura pauciorave, mala vel bona alimenta in prandio vel coena, sive domi sive mea, sive aliena, offerantur, ita & efficio, nunc in prandio largius, nunc in coena, pro appetitus desiderio.
units.tr: They also support themselves by experience, which shows that waking hastens digestion: those who are awake take in more food and digest it within a space of hours, fifteen or sixteen, than sleepers do. The authority of Pliny is also cited, who says that food is digested especially by wakefulness and wine. And Hippocrates, in the sixth book of the Epidemics, says that wakefulness makes men voracious, because the heat is aroused and increased by the motion that the waking employ. What is to be decided in this controversy? Above all, each man must know the nature of his own body. For my part it makes no difference whether I eat more or less at supper, provided I eat well, that is, without loss of strength. According as more or fewer, good or bad foods are offered at lunch or supper, whether at home or at my own or another's table, so I act: now more largely at lunch, now at supper, according to the desire of my appetite.

units.la: Ego vitius rationem eam esse optimam existimarem, quae neque plura, nec pauciora, nec valentiora alimenta in prandio apponerentur, quam coena, utroque aequabilitas mereretur laudem, quae sicut in omni vita polara est, ita esset hic maxime. Quorsum enim quasi prodest, exquisito se sagine prandio, in coena vero ieiunare, vel exquisitè cœnare, & postero prandio atrum ex hesterno iure devorare panem? Verum vberius cœnandum esse sanis & amorbo conualescentibus veteres medici, paleftrita, gymnastica ac pancratia-stà summopere approbárunt, (nisi à puero alia edendi consuetudo obstiterit) frugalius verò prandendum. Valetudinariis verò, quibus ventriculo sunt infirmo, cerebrumque habent frigidum humidumque, liberalius prandere quam cœnare expedit: ex larga enim illis cœna vapores sursum elevati cerebrum imbrium instar humectant, qui postea suffusiones aliaque capitis symptomata producunt.
units.tr: I would consider the best rule to be the one in which neither more, nor fewer, nor stronger food is set out at lunch than at supper. In both, evenness deserves praise, which, as it is pivotal in all of life, is most of all so here. For what good is it to stuff oneself with rich food at lunch, and then fast at supper, or dine richly and next day at lunch wolf down dry bread with yesterday's broth? But the ancient physicians, together with the wrestlers, the gymnastic trainers and the pancratiasts, greatly approved that the healthy, and those recovering from illness, should sup more copiously, and dine more sparingly (unless an older habit of eating from boyhood stood in the way). For the infirm, whose stomach is weak and whose brain is cold and moist, it is more expedient to dine more freely than to sup. For from a large supper, vapours rising upward moisten the brain like rain, and these afterwards produce suffusions and other symptoms of the head.

units.la: Valetudinariorum enim longe alia est ratio quam sanorum. Quibusdam enim venter est imbecillis & frigidus adeo, ut copiam ciborum noctu digerere non possit, id quod postero die ventriculum ciborum odorem eructans, & hypochondria flatu turgentia indicant: quibusdam ob venarum in visceribus obstructionem alimentum per corpus non distribuitur, excrementaque cibi humida & cruda per alvum deiiciuntur, unde atrophia & absumptio totius: illis diu ob humorum cruditatem dormire, ac corpus stragulí tepore fouere & exercere, plus meri bibere, parciusque eo die cœnare suadet. Hipp. l. de salubri diæt. in sin. Hospanem bene in furno tostum ac vino intinctum comedere, vinumque bene temperatum bibere, ac semel tantum comedere, vel uno tantum cibariorum genere vesci, & a cibo quiescere iubet idem. Quibus verò semel, bis aut crebrius in die, parum vel plus cibi osseofferendum, id valetudinis natura, anni tempus, aetas, eaendi assuetudo, virefq; perito Medico facile indicabunt. Antiochus Medicus Ascalonita ea ratione vitium in senio suo usus est, ut sensibus illaesis membrisq; omnibus integris ad extremum usque vitae duraverit. Plus quam octogenarius ter in die comedebat, nec tamen desidem domi vitam agens, sed quotidie in forum ad cuium concilium, et ad visendos agros, ad trium stadiorum iter pedes conficiens: et si qua longius erat progrediendum, in sella deferebatur, aut vehiculo vehebatur: postea, deinde primo alio, in aliquo fori loco, remotis arbitris circa horam diei tertiam vel quartam, panem cum melle Attico esitabat. Deinde aliquid legens ipse, aut cum aliis de rebus gravioribus communicans, usque ad horam diei sextam in foro perseveravit: deinde in balneo publico frictione et exercitiis senili suae aetati opportunis curatus domi mediocriter prandebat, primum hus assumptis qua alium laxaret, posthac piscibus, maxime saxatilibus vel in alto mari degentibus, vescebatur, at in coena piscibus abstinuit aliquid boni succi, quod non facile putresceret, ut aliquam ex mulso, aucmq; iure simplici coctam edebat, merumq; bibebat.
units.tr: The regimen of the infirm is indeed very different from that of the healthy. For some have a stomach so weak and cold that it cannot digest a quantity of food at night; the next day their belching of the smell of food and their hypochondria swollen with wind show this. In others, because of an obstruction of the veins in the viscera, nourishment is not distributed through the body, and the moist and raw residues of food pass out through the bowels, whence come wasting and emaciation of the whole body. For those whose humours are crude, he advises sleeping long, warming and exercising the body with the heat of blankets, drinking more unmixed wine, and supping more sparingly that day. Hippocrates, at the end of his book On Salubrious Diet, bids the guest eat bread well toasted in an oven and dipped in wine, drink well-mixed wine, eat only once, or eat only one kind of food, and rest from eating. For those to whom food must be offered once, twice, or more often in the day, and in what amount, the state of their health, the season of the year, their age, their habits of eating and their strength will easily show to a skilled physician. Antiochus, the physician of Ascalon, followed such a diet in his old age that he endured to the end of life with his senses unimpaired and all his limbs intact. Though he was more than eighty, he ate three times a day. Nor did he lead an idle life at home: every day he walked on foot to the forum, to the council, and to inspect his fields, covering a distance of three stades; and if he had to go further, he was carried in a chair or driven in a carriage. Afterwards, in some place in the forum, with onlookers removed, about the third or fourth hour of the day, he ate bread with Attic honey. Then, reading something himself or conferring with others on weightier matters, he stayed in the forum until the sixth hour of the day. Then, in the public bath, cared for with rubbing and exercises suited to his old age, he dined moderately at home. First he took something that loosened the bowels, afterwards he ate fish, especially rock fish or those living in the deep sea. But at supper he abstained from fish and ate something of good juice that does not readily putrefy, such as some fowl boiled in plain broth, and he drank unmixed wine.

units.la: Telephus Grammaticus Antiocho aetate proUectior natus 100. annos, diebus quibus non lavabatur, tertiam circa diei horam cum exigua frictione oleo inunctus, mox mel optimum crudum aliceaqua coctapermixtum edebat, quo solo pro
units.tr: Telephus the grammarian, who was born in the time of Antiochus and lived to be 100, on the days he did not bathe, was anointed about the third hour of the day with a light rubbing of oil. Soon afterwards he ate excellent raw honey mixed with some boiled water, and was content with this alone as his breakfast.

units.la: suta ientaculo fuit contentus : prandebat hora 7, aut paulo citius primum oleribus, deinde piscibus aut avibus comestis : vesperi pane tantum vino diluto madidum edebat, vinumque senilis ætatis nectar bibebat. Hac de horum fenu vitæ Gal. l. 5. salubr. &c.
units.tr: He dined at the seventh hour, or a little earlier, first on vegetables and then on fish or birds. In the evening he ate only bread soaked in diluted wine, and he drank wine, the nectar of old age. Thus far on the manner of life of these men: Gal. bk. 5, On Hygiene, etc.

units.la: De calore in somno & noctu per antiperistasin ad summ fontem & principium confugiente videl. cor venasque, non ventriculum, expeditiorem, propterea fieri in venis concoctionem noctu & in somno quam in die, assentior, interim tamen caloris ad centrum suum repulsi portionem etiam ventriculo per venas & arterias impertiri negari non potest, & per consequens calorem ventriculi robustiorem evadere. Vide quæst. 4.
units.tr: I agree that in sleep and at night the heat, driven back by antiperistasis to its chief source and origin, namely the heart and the veins, and not the stomach, is more active, and therefore digestion in the veins takes place more quickly at night and in sleep than by day. Meanwhile, it cannot be denied that a portion of this heat, repelled to its centre, is also imparted to the stomach through the veins and arteries, and consequently the heat of the stomach becomes stronger. See question 4.

units.la: Noctu autem cibos & alimenta melius & vegetius digeri, eò quòd metus ingenii, vis manet fit vegetior & acutior, non est de omnibus universaliter verum. Mihi, quoties à cœna eduliis abstinee omnino, idfere semper contingit. Musis meus amicissima Lucubratio est: non aurora. Non à me dissentient, quibus lucubratoria sunt lecticula.
units.tr: It is not universally true that food and nourishment are digested better and more vigorously at night, because the power of the mind remains and becomes more vigorous and sharp. For me, whenever I entirely abstain from supper and dainties, this almost always happens. My study is my dearest friend in the Muses' service: lamplight, not dawn. Those for whom a little reading couch is a lamplit place will not disagree with me.

units.la: QVÆSTIO II.
units.tr: QUESTION II.

units.la: Vrrum magis sit noxium, potando an vorando excedere modum?
units.tr: Whether it is more harmful to exceed the measure by drinking or by eating?
