units.la: Vi potus intemperantiam nocentiorem existimant quàm cibi, sequentibus id astruunt rationibus. 1. quòd potus venas omnes confestim penetret, subeatque crudus & plane incoctus, unde sanguini infer-cuc tut noxa. II. quod neruos tentet & cere-brum mentemque perturbet. Verum potum citius meatus corporis penetrare quam cibum facilè datur, interim tamen non sequitur, plane incoctum & crudum eum permeare, dum enim e ventriculo per venas transfit, alterari cum aliqua ex parte, (licet non perfecte) negari non potest: idque ostendunt color, odor, qui in celeri etiam & frequenti eius emissione bi-bacibus vsitatissima, deprehenduntur longè diuersi, quam in materia ipsa potulenta, cum primum ingurgitatur. Adde quod plus laffitu-dinis, grauedinis, incommodiq; persentiscunt, qui nimia fe ciborum copia vel semel inferse-runt, quàm qui dies etiam continuos vinum cereuisiamque plenis buccis absque vlla etiam molestia in fe ingurgitant, propterea quod li-quida citius descendunt, penetrant, & in vesica collecta excernuntur, solida verò & cibaria tardius & secedunt, & digeruntur, & nutriunt, vt ita longè securius sit grauari potu quàm cibis. Potum autem quod quidam nutrire negant, mirari subit. Siquidem ipsius Hip-pocratis iudicio & autoritate facilè conuin-cuntur.
units.tr: Some judge intemperance in drink to be more harmful than intemperance in food, and they support this with the following reasons: (1) drink penetrates all the veins at once and passes through them raw and quite undigested, whence harm comes to the blood; (2) it attacks the nerves and disturbs the brain and mind. It is readily granted that drink penetrates the bodily passages more quickly than food, but it does not follow that it passes through quite raw and uncooked. For while it passes from the stomach through the veins, it cannot be denied that it is altered in some part, though not perfectly. Colour and smell show this: even in the quick and frequent discharge most common among drinkers, they are found to be quite different from the drink itself when first swallowed. Add that those who have eaten an excess of food, even once, feel more weariness, heaviness and discomfort than those who gulp down wine and beer by full mouthfuls for days on end without any trouble at all. This is because liquids descend more quickly, penetrate, and are collected in the bladder and excreted, while solids and food descend more slowly, are digested and nourish. So it is much safer to be burdened by drink than by food. It is surprising that some deny that drink nourishes, for they are easily refuted by the judgment and authority of Hippocrates himself.

units.la: Facilius enim est impleti cibo quam potu, An potus inquit aph. 11. sect. 2. Galenus hoc explicans, nutriat? humida, etsi non nutriunt vt solidiora, supe-rare tamen ait nutriendi celeritate. Quod ite-rum cofirmat Hipp. l. de alimento, quicunq; veloci appositione indigent, his humidum ad reficiendas vires optimum medicamen, quicunq; vero adhuc velociori opus habet, rectissimè reficiuntur per olfactum. Quibus autem tardior appositio est necessaria, solido alimento vtantur: vnde potum esse alimentum, faciliusque digeri quam esculenta & cibaria manifesta est, etiam exinde, quod qui hesterna cœna largius biberunt, parcius autem esitarunt, longè melius postero die se habere testantur, quam si vna cum copioso potu copiosum etiam cibum deglutiissent: quamuis id non semper probari poterit, cum in larga potatione ventriculo (sed per interualla & vices) aliquid sit obiiciendum in quod agat, & quod meri viribus resistit, quæ alias confertim irrepérent in cerebrum idq; conturbarent. Verum de dolore capitis à tumulentia & brietate excitato, apud multos non parum gratiæ me initurum persuasum habeo, si in præsentia aliquid dixero.
units.tr: "It is easier to be filled with food than with drink," says Hippocrates in Aphorisms 2.11. Galen, explaining this, says that liquids, though they do not nourish as solids do, surpass them in the speed of nourishing. Hippocrates confirms this again in his book On Nutriment: those who need quick application, for them moisture is the best remedy for restoring strength; and whoever needs an even quicker one is best restored through smell. But for those who need slower application, let them use solid food. Hence it is clear that drink is nourishment, and is digested more easily than solid and substantial food. This is also shown by the fact that those who drank more heavily at last evening's dinner and ate less testify that they feel far better the next day than if they had swallowed a copious amount of food along with copious drink. Yet this cannot always be proven, since in heavy drinking something must be worked on in the stomach (but by intervals and in turns), and this resists the strength of the wine, which otherwise would creep at once into the brain and disturb it. But I am persuaded that I will win no small favour with many if I now say something about the headache caused by bloating and drunkenness.

units.la: Sunt multi, & inter hos viri temperantiæ & frugalitati deditissimi quidem, sed tamen incidentur dente & postulante occasione largius se quoq; expridia- mero perfundentes, qui post a capite vini vapori bus cruditatibusque repleto languent vel ... rieq; afficiuntur, afferentes, omnibus se Creti fidelitiis carere potius malle, quam eiusmodi molestiet? semper dolores ex crapula perpeti.
units.tr: There are many, and among them men most devoted to temperance and frugality, who, when an occasion invites, indulge too freely in wine too; afterwards, with their heads filled with the vapours and crudities of wine, they languish or are troubled in various ways. They declare that they would rather go without all the pleasures of the Cretans than endure such troubles, which they always suffer after excess.

units.la: Symptomata adsunt varia, dolor capitis, ... suffusiones, obscuritas visus, oculorum caligo, nausea, fastidium, cor palpitans, venæ inflatæ & turgentes, ructus, flatus, & similia. Quidam Zinzibere condito, brodio gallinæ, piscium, vel vini saccharati, aromati que vt cinnamo-mo, cubebis, garyophylis, cardamomis, galan-ga, piperibus & similibus, symtomata, vel mi-tigari vel propulsari sibi plane habent perfua-sum. Quidam generosa vina, vt maluatica, Hi-spanica, ali i lulapia, lilmantib. expetunt buc-cis. Sed fallaci experimento & iudicio cæco. Primo enim sciendum, num malum hæreat in ventriculo nec ne? Si malum hæretin ventri- culo cruditasque tuiget, male faciunt, qui bro- diis aromatisque conditis, vel vinis generosis quærunt leuamen, hæc enim cruditates in ventriculo magis faciunt effumare, vnde dolor recrudescit.
units.tr: There are various symptoms: headache, ... suffusions, dimness of sight, darkness of the eyes, nausea, loathing of food, a palpitating heart, swollen and distended veins, belching, wind, and the like. Some are fully persuaded that these symptoms are either eased or driven off by candied ginger, chicken broth, fish, sweetened wine, and spices such as cinnamon, cubebs, cloves, cardamom, galangal, pepper and the like. Others crave strong wines, such as Malmsey and Spanish, and others julep, with their mouths. But this is a deceptive experiment and a blind judgment. For first it must be known whether the evil sticks in the stomach or not. If the evil sticks in the stomach and crudity oppresses it, those do badly who seek relief from broths and spiced drinks or from strong wines; for these make the crudities evaporate more within the stomach, whence the pain revives.

units.la: Si malum cruditasq; non est in ventriculo sed venis, quæ ex meri reliquiis turgent, frustra brodia, aromata, maluatica, lulapia, & simi-lia affumuntur in ventriculum, non tantum e-nim prius malum non aufertur, sed nouû sub-inde oboritur, noua scilicet vaporum genera-tione & conturbatione. Itaq; malo hærente in ventriculo indeq; vaporibus in caput & cere-brum repentib*, vomitu expurgandum quic-quid in ventriculo vel permansit, vel in eû re-sorbuit, postea verò ventriculus aromatis con-ditis, & vino generoso venit corroboratus pa-ne videlicet tosto vel aromatis consperso, vel vino imbuto, prout quisq; voluerit vel assue- uerit. Vacuato enim ventre & tamé dolore nó remittente, vini noxam potum vini eiusdem (non quidem specie) eluere nó sine ratione as- seuero: quia nimirū, quæ mala calidæ tenuisq; suæ substantiæ copia inuexit, eadem sua quali- tate & vi calefaciendi exiccandiq; vicissim tol- lit, eo inquam modo vapores crassos nebulo- sosq; dispergit, quo dolores oculorum inde ortos scripsit Hip.feẞ.6.l.2. Epidem. meraca po- tione discuti. Contrarium verò si euenerit, id est, si vini noxam vini potio non tollit, malum & recrudescit & augetur.
units.tr: If the evil and crudity are not in the stomach but in the veins, which swell with the remnants of the neat wine, then broths, spices, Malmsey, julep and the like are taken into the stomach in vain. For not only is the earlier evil not removed, but a new one soon arises from a fresh generation and disturbance of vapours. Therefore, when the evil sticks in the stomach and vapours creep up into the head and brain, whatever remains in the stomach or has been reabsorbed there must be purged by vomiting. Afterwards the stomach, strengthened, may be restored with spiced things and generous wine, namely toasted bread sprinkled with spices or soaked in wine, as each person prefers or is accustomed. Once the belly is emptied, yet the pain does not abate, I assert, not without reason, that the harm of wine is washed out by drinking the same wine (though not of the same kind). For what evil the warm and thin substance of wine has brought in, the same substance removes again by its own quality and its power of warming and drying. In this way, I say, it scatters thick and misty vapours, just as Hippocrates wrote that eye pains arising from them are dispelled by neat wine in the sixth section, second book of the Epidemics. But if the opposite happens, that is, if drinking wine does not remove the harm of wine, the evil revives and grows.

units.la: * Vomere autem vel non valentibus, vel mo- leste & difficulter vomentibus ieiunium & in- ediam optimum esse remedium experientia te- stis est, somnum præterea, quietem optimam, ventriculi fomentū & linimentum, quibus e- go addo leuem frictionem capitis & ventris. Sæpe frustra tentantur omnia vaporibus scili- cet crassis & crudis in venas, cerebri profun- dum, & neruorum substantiam relapsis, cumq; spiritibus mixtis, unde torpidi, obscuri, ingna- uiqueredditi lassitudinem illam membrorum tantisper fouent, dum per motum vapor ille fuerit dispersus atque resolutus. Itaq; mo- tionem & obambulationem diuturniorem & paulo celeriorem ante cibum plurimum plurimis hic prodesse & profuisse in experi- mentis est, à cibo autem lentiorem & bre- uiorem
units.tr: * For those who cannot vomit, or who vomit with difficulty and discomfort, fasting and abstinence are the best remedy, as experience testifies. Besides these, sleep, the best rest, a fomentation and liniment for the stomach, to which I add gentle rubbing of the head and belly. Often everything is tried in vain, because the crude, thick vapours have slipped back into the veins, the depths of the brain and the substance of the nerves, mixed with the spirits. Hence the sluggish, dim and dulled feel that heaviness of the limbs and nurse it for a while, until that vapour has been dispersed and dissolved by motion. Therefore I find from experience that walking about and moving for a longer time, and somewhat more briskly, before food helps very many; after food, a slower and shorter movement ...

units.la: Ad vini noxam eius dem potio per- sanetî uiorem commendari reperio, idq; duabus aut tribus horis post. Posteroigitur die hesterna crapula dilturbati diligenter animaduertent, num excrementa in illis & humores crudi sint reuocati & propulsi ad centrum, an vero ventriculum eiusque orificium afficiant? illic exercitium & motus ante cibum, vel somnus ad tertiam etiam diei partem, teste Hipp. absque interruptione extractus laudatur: hic vomit", inedia, fomenta, linimenta vel frictiones circa ventriculi regionem magis commendantur. Vnde male sanitati consulunt, qui ventriculo ex immodica fortioris meri potione aestuanti & sitienti refrigerium quaerunt potu frigido aquae vel cereuisiae, quam ad aliquot saepe mensuras a Germanis ingurgitari ieiuno stomacho, passim videas.
units.tr: For the harm of wine, I find it recommended that the same wine be drunk again, and that this be done two or three hours afterwards. So on the following day, those disturbed by yesterday's drunkenness should carefully observe whether the excrements and crude humours in them have been called back and driven to the centre, or whether they affect the stomach and its orifice. In the former case, exercise and movement before food, or sleep, even uninterrupted to a third part of the day, as Hippocrates witnesses, is praised. In the latter case, vomiting, fasting, fomentations, liniments or rubbing around the region of the stomach are more strongly recommended. Hence they consult badly for their health who, when the stomach is heated and thirsty from immoderate drinking of stronger neat wine, seek refreshment in a cold drink of water or beer. Everywhere you may see Germans gulping this on an empty stomach, several measures at a time.

units.la: Sed dum calorem eo remedio deferbere putant, feruentiorem eum paulo post & auctiorem deprehendunt, quo enim plus bibunt, eo plus sitire incipiunt, non secus ac in lapidibus excalfactis videmus, qui, si aqua frigidissima asperguntur, multo sentiuntur calidiores, nutriente videlicet in ipsis humida substantia aridam caliditatem, vt ita hoc medicandi ventriculo excalfacto modo nihil sit nocenti*. Qui de nocte sitiunt, decenti & conuenienti vtantur potu, & postea redormiant, id enim bonum esse ipse Hipp. asseruit. Qui tamen adhuc graviori siti tentantur atque premuntur post redormitionem,iis potum non interdico, cum omnino ab eo abstinere insalubre prorsus est, ob adustionem humidi, intemperieique siccæ,quâ nihil periculosius, metum. Vehementius igitur sitientes ventriculum æstuantem potione diluent & irrigabunt, potione inquam, in qua panis tosti frusta puluere nucis moschatæ vel cinnamomi aspersò macerata sint, sic enim ventriculus minus offendetur.
units.tr: But while they think the heat is cooled by that remedy, they find it afterwards more fervent and increased. For the more they drink, the more they begin to thirst, just as we see with heated stones, which, if sprinkled with very cold water, are felt to be much hotter, the dry heat being fed by the moisture in them. So this way of treating a heated stomach is in no way harmless. Those who are thirsty at night should take a fitting and suitable drink and then go back to sleep, for Hippocrates himself asserted this to be good. Yet those who are still tormented and pressed by a more severe thirst after going back to sleep, I do not forbid drink, since to abstain from it altogether is quite unhealthy, because of the burning of moisture and dry intemperance, than which nothing is more dangerous, I fear. So those who thirst more vehemently should dilute and bathe the heated stomach with a drink, I mean one in which pieces of toasted bread have been steeped, sprinkled with powdered nutmeg or cinnamon, for in this way the stomach will be less offended.

units.la: Apud Septentrionis gentes vidi in frequenti vsu esse crapulosis, potum ex vino vel cereuisia Roftochiana cum sufficiente saccharo, cinnamomo, nuce moschata, cubebis, & similibus concinnare, adiecta panis bis cocti sufficiente quantitate, æstum enim ventriculi mirificè extinguit, ipsumq; ventriculum roborat, cum panis ipse, tum etiam aromata.
units.tr: Among the Northern peoples I have seen that drunkards commonly make a drink from wine or Rostock beer, with enough sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg, cubebs and the like, and with a sufficient quantity of twice-baked bread added. This quenches the heat of the stomach wonderfully and strengthens the stomach itself, both the bread and the spices doing this.

units.la: Mirum in modum me sæpius eo refectum sensi, meos primo mores ad illum morem conformans. Saccharo destitutus fumo eius loco mel despumatum, & panis nostri cibarii inuetterati medullam, quæ in micas friatur conteriturq;, ac postea aromatis in puluerem redactis commiscetur. Ad extremum optime sibi consulent profpicientq; potatores, frequenter in ter potandum sale vtentes. Sal enim torpentem ventriculi excitat appetentiam, teste Plinio lib.31.c.9. & Plutarch. l.de causis naturae. quaest.9. & salsugo illa naturam stimulat ad celeriorem excretionem, ne vasa & vtres nimium distendantur.
units.tr: I have often felt myself wonderfully refreshed by it, adapting my own habits to that custom. Lacking sugar, I use skimmed honey instead, and the crumb of our ordinary stale bread, rubbed and crushed into crumbs, then mixed with spices reduced to powder. Finally, drinkers look out for themselves best by using salt, frequently during the drinking. For salt rouses the sluggish appetite of the stomach, as Pliny witnesses (book 31, chapter 9) and Plutarch (On the Causes of Nature, question 9). That saltiness also stimulates nature to quicker evacuation, so that the vessels and bladders are not overstretched.

units.la: Consilia autoris, ut immodicus potus minus noceat. dantur: salsuginem enim illam fero permiscer i testantur, qui crebrius falsis cibis vtentes sal- fiorem mingunt vrinam, & contra. Quamuis haec non à me dicuntur, vel in apertum prose- runtur, vt ansam alicui ministrem aut fenestra aperiam ad potandum, sed vt aut moderatè bi- bere omnes assuescant, aut fi occasione inci- dente liberalius & meracius fit bibendum, id fiat citra noxam & incommodum corporis. De Ebrietatiautem naturali quadam proprietate repugnantibus, inter quae amygdalas amaras, brassicam, cardamomum, persicorum nucleos, succum foliorum persicæ arboris expressum, absinthii pontici dilutum, & nostrum etiam vulgare absinthium præcipuam obtinuisse lau- dem reperio, suo dicetur loco & ordine.
units.tr: The author's advice, so that excessive drinking may do less harm, is given as follows. They testify that this saltiness is tolerated, since those who more often eat salty foods pass saltier urine, and conversely. I do not say these things, nor set them forth in public, to give anyone an occasion or open a window for drinking. Rather, I say them so that either everyone gets used to drinking in moderation, or, if on some occasion one must drink more freely and undiluted, that it be done without harm or discomfort to the body. Concerning drunkenness, however, I find that some natural properties are reckoned as remedies against it. Among these, bitter almonds, cabbage, cardamom, peach kernels, the juice pressed from peach-tree leaves, Pontic wormwood diluted, and our common wormwood have obtained the chief praise. This will be discussed in its place and order.

units.la: QUAESTIO III. An à potu omninò fit abstinendum in- termedio prandii & coenæ tempore?
units.tr: QUESTION III. Should one abstain entirely from drink in the interval between lunch and dinner?

units.la: HIC vero modeste discedo ab iis, qui quasi prætorio edicto inter prandium & coenam omnem potum interdicunt, putantes clausum ventriculum potu frigido crudoq; aperiri, coctionemq; interturbari. Rigidam nimis hanc in victu præceptionem vix ab vno inter millenos video obseruari, imo verius dixerim à nullo mortalium.
units.tr: Here I modestly depart from those who, as if by a praetorian edict, forbid all drink between lunch and dinner, thinking that the closed stomach is opened by cold, raw drink and that digestion is thereby disturbed. I see this overly strict rule of diet observed by scarcely one in a thousand; to speak more truly, by no mortal at all.

units.la: Quis enim potu omninò abstinere juberet falsuram vel suillæ carnis, vel haleces ex muria, aliosque piscesaut carnes infumatas, vel etiam aromatis conspersos & conditos cibos devorantem in prandio? haec enim vehementiorem excitabunt sitim. Constat salsum saporem linguam quidem non admodum calefacere, sed acriter siccando corrodere, sincerumq; salso-rum esum nimium humores & sanguinem labefactare, ob siccitatem quae in salso sapore major est quam caliditas. Id quod chymico-rum salsus sapor vi chymica elicitus demonstrat, nullum enim fere corpus est e quo & calx & proprius sal non extrahi potest arte vulcania, at vero ejusmodi acerrimi caloris esse ac in plerisque caustic-um, id est, vi adurendi praedi-tum, gustus vnicuiq; indicabit. Quapropter cibum in ipso etiam coctionis opere humectare, ne exuratur, aletur & corrumpatur, optimum & saluberrimum judico, non secus ac coqui inter elixandum solidioribus obsoniis, quae tardius coctionis terminum aequuntur, affundere aquam consueuerunt, priori ante perfectam coctiram abfumta, minus interesse experientia edocti, elixationem paulum interturbare quàm concedere, vt cibus in lebete comburatur. Verum quemadmodum aquam saepe & multum affundere elixationem non interpellat tantum, verum ipsam coctionem impedit, suffocato scilicet ob nimiam humectationem calore, vel potius actione seu operatione ejus laesa ac retusa: sic & cibus in ventri-
units.tr: For who would bid a man abstain entirely from drink if at lunch he eats salted pork, or salt-meat, or herrings in brine, or other fish or smoked meats, or even foods sprinkled and seasoned with spices? For these will stir up a stronger thirst. It is established that salty taste does not heat the tongue much, but corrodes it by drying sharply, and that eating pure salty things in excess weakens the humours and the blood, because the dryness in salty taste is greater than its heat. The salty taste elicited by the chemists' chemical force demonstrates this. For there is almost no body from which both lime and its proper salt cannot be extracted by the art of fire. But that these are of such bitter heat, and mostly caustic, that is, endowed with the power of burning, anyone's taste will show. Therefore I judge it best and most wholesome to moisten food even during the process of cooking, so that it is not scorched, burnt and spoiled. Cooks, when boiling solid dishes which take longer to finish cooking, are accustomed to pour in water, the former portion having been used up before cooking is complete. Taught by experience, they know it matters less to disturb the boiling a little than to let the food burn in the pot. But just as pouring water often and in quantity does not merely interrupt boiling but actually hinders the cooking itself (the heat being suffocated, of course, by excessive moistening, or rather its action and operation being impaired and blunted), so also food in the stomach...

units.la: NB.
units.tr: NB.

units.la: NB. ventriculo immoderatius humectandus non est ob causas easdem.
units.tr: NB. The stomach is not to be moistened immoderately, for the same reasons.

units.la: Quos praeterea grauis inter prandium & coenam fitis non vrget, iis (nisi sint temperamenti cholerici, hoc est, calidioris & siccioris, ii enim vt plurimum sunt siticulosi) vt à potu abstineant plane, suasor sum. Si quando tamen voluptatis vel officii gratia bibendum est, decenter id fiat & conuenienter, &c.
units.tr: For those whom no heavy thirst oppresses between lunch and dinner, I advise that they abstain from drink altogether (unless they are of a choleric temperament, that is, hotter and drier, for these are mostly thirsty). If, however, one must drink for pleasure or out of duty, let it be done decently and suitably, etc.

units.la: QVAESTIO IV. An hieme plus edere conueniat quam aestate, propterea quòd ventres sint tempore hiberno calidiores, aestate vero frigidiores?
units.tr: QUESTION IV. Is it fitting to eat more in winter than in summer, because stomachs are warmer in winter and colder in summer?

units.la: Opiofitra alimenta offerenda esse hieme quam aestate, tempore hiberno cibum melius facilius digeri, plus etiam homines appetere, vetus a vetustissimis repetita autoribus, & per multa secula sapientum judicio & ratione confirmata sententia est. Causa, ob quam haec ita se habeant, assignatur ab Hippocrate lib. 1. aphor. 15. Cum ait ventres natura calidissimos esse hieme & vere, obq. id copiosius cibandos. Calidissimi sunt non absolute & simpliciter, sed calido naturali influente, quod tempore hiberno propter circumstantiam extrinsecus frigiditatem, continentur, cohibetur, & ad inte... interiora refugit, ob quod coctiones, sanguificationes & nutritiones magis procedunt, tempore vero æstivo idem calidum a sibi affinibus videlicet exterioribus ad extimas corporis partes evocatur, & ssoluitur atq; dissipatur, unde natura opera magis languent æstate, quàm hyeme. Cum enim calor innatus sit omnium naturalium operationum causa, s quitur, vbi is plurimus est & superabundat, cibi appetentiam intendi, coctionesq; melius procedere & felicius absolui.
units.tr: That more food is to be offered in winter than in summer, that in winter food is better and more easily digested, and that people desire more, is an opinion repeated from the most ancient authors, and confirmed through many centuries by the judgment and reason of the wise. The cause why these things are so is assigned by Hippocrates, Aphorisms book 1, aphorism 15, where he says that stomachs are by nature hottest in winter and spring, and therefore should be fed more abundantly. They are hottest not absolutely and simply, but by the natural heat that flows in, which in winter, because of the external cold, is held in, confined and retreats to the interior, whence concoctions, sanguification and nutrition proceed more. In summer, by contrast, the same heat is drawn out by its related exterior parts to the outer parts of the body, and is loosened and dissipated, whence the operations of nature are more languid in summer than in winter. For since innate heat is the cause of all natural operations, it follows that where it is most abundant and overflowing, the appetite for food is increased, and digestions proceed better and are completed more happily.

units.la: At vero plurimum eum esse hiberno tempore validiores, atq; indicio sunt natura opera fortiora, coctiones enim augentur, plus generatur sanguinis, corpus efficitur crassius, superfluitatesq; in somno longioribus expurgantur, & omnia melius in corpore animalis administrantur tempore hiberno quàm æstate, quà calor circumfusus non tantum inutilia, sed etiam ea, quæ secundum naturam in corpore continentur, una diffluitionem quàm calor innatus operatur. Huius enim beneficio non tantum alimentum conficitur, singulisq; partibus proprium agglutinatur, verum etiam omnes superfluitates huius excernuntur atq; extenuantur, quedam exquisite per cutim, quæ vero in vapores convertuntur per expirationem, suffientem vero habentes crassitudinem per vrinas, in quibus etiam plus sedimenti est quàm per æstatem, propterea quod coctio felicius perficitur, corpora secundum carnem plus augentur, plus etiam boni sanguinis cumulatur. tur hieme mediocritate seruante qua omnia vigorem et robur caloris innati denunciant. Ad-de quo ad occulta perspiratio seu diffusio, quo magis efficit sensum, eo fortius arguit calidum innatum; unde sudores praeter natum am sunt, quia sensibilis humor sensibiliter per cutem non excenitur, si in animalis corpore rite omnia administrantur, alimentum mq; probe a natura conficitur: (Sudores enim in balneis, vehementioribus exercitiis, vel astuo calore excitati a raufis violentis habent originem) probe au em omnia administrari in animalis corpore, alimentumq; a natura bene confici tempore hiberno praeter sensum, rationem, experientiam, oftendun supe fluitates qua insensibiliter per occulta spiracula magis diffluntur et expurgantur hieme quam aestate, ut ita in totum dixisse liceat, vere et ab Hipp. dictum esse ventres hieme et vere esse calidissimos, quare per ea tempora alimenta copiosiora exhibenda: enim tunc calor innatus plurimum est, intus q; viget, unde et pluribus opus est al mentis.
units.tr: But indeed, that in winter the body is much stronger is shown by the operations of nature being stronger: concoctions are increased, more blood is generated, the body becomes denser, superfluities are purged more in the longer sleep, and everything in the animal body is better managed in winter than in summer. In summer the surrounding heat dissolves and disperses not only useless things but also those that are naturally kept in the body, more than the innate heat does. For by its benefit food is not only made up but is joined to each part proper to it, and all its superfluities are excreted and thinned out: some exquisitely through the skin, those which turn into vapours through breathing out, and those of sufficient thickness through urine, in which there is also more sediment than in summer, because concoction is more happily completed, bodies grow more in flesh, and more good blood is accumulated. in winter, with moderation preserved, by which all things announce the vigour and strength of the innate heat. Moreover, the more the hidden perspiration or diffusion is perceptible, the more strongly it proves the innate heat. Hence sweats are unnatural, because perceptible moisture is not excreted perceptibly through the skin when everything in the animal body is duly managed and food is properly made up by nature. (Sweats in baths, from more violent exercises or from excessive heat, have their origin in violent exertions.) That all things are properly managed in the animal body, and food well made up by nature, in winter, beyond sense, reason and experience, is shown by this: superfluities which flow away insensibly through hidden pores are more diffused and purged in winter than in summer. So that, to say it in general, it may be permitted that Hippocrates said truly that stomachs are hottest in winter and spring, wherefore more abundant food should be given in those seasons, for then innate heat is greatest and flourishes within, whence more food is needed.

units.la: Accedunt nox et somnus longissimus, in quo interna omnia magis calent, ut tutes et Spiritus naturales plus vigent, qui in vigilia corporis sensum laboribus magis diffiuntur.
units.tr: Add to this the night and the longest sleep, in which all the inner parts grow warmer, so that the natural powers and spirits are more vigorous, which in the waking of the body are dissipated more by labours.

units.la: Quid? quod hi me quo dam parcius pauca comedentes, r frugi arti atq; offendi, liberalius vero ac copiosius vescentes in nullos tamen ex re letiae morbos incidere ipsa experientia ostendit manifeste.
units.tr: What of the fact that these men, who eat a little more sparingly and only small amounts, and who live frugally, and who are offended by nothing, yet those who eat more freely and abundantly, experience itself clearly shows, fall into no diseases from that cause.

units.la: Rationem addit Galenus in comment. quod nimirum corpora diffluentur promptius per sensui occulta foramina & spiracula, unde alimento egent quoniam evacuantur: quod si enim nihil a corporibus nostris effueret, sed semper aqua substantia nostra moles seruaretur, nulla foret alimenti necessitas. Hac veterum sententia tot seculis tanto consensu ab antiquitate approbata, habetur quoque stans inconcussa a recentioribus quibusdam argute improbatur.
units.tr: Galen, in his commentary, gives the reason: bodies are dissipated more readily through the hidden pores and openings of the senses, and so they need food because they are emptied. For if nothing flowed out of our bodies, but our substance always kept the same mass, there would be no need of food. This opinion of the ancients, approved for so many centuries with such unanimous agreement from antiquity, is held to stand unshaken, though some more recent writers cleverly reject it.

units.la: Ac primo adducunt autoritatem Hippoc. & Galen. qui volunt corpora calidissima esse aestate, quoniam id anni tempus calidissimum est, frigidissimum hieme, quoniam hiberno tempore frigidum nullum. Hippocr. l. 3. de diaet. Tempore existente frigido ac compacto, consimilia patiuntur etiam animalia ipsa: (scilicet extrinsecus, sicut aestate extrinsecus calent) & de salubri diaeta, sic his, ubi aestas fuerit, uti oportet, ut frigidum sit corpus & molle, tempus enim calidum est & sic cum, reddit que corpora aestuosa & squalida. Ubi, inquit Hippocrates, fuerit aestas, curare oportet ut corpus sit frigidum, quid ita? quia tempus calidum est: jubet igitur ac vult Hippocrates, ut tempore aestivo, cum aestu flagrat totum corpus, applicemus adhibeamusque frigida, ut nimirum cutis spiracula porique paululum paulatim que condensentur atque constringantur, ne ob caloris interni nimium diffluxum (ab externo enim evocatur, dissipatur, disperditurque) totum corpus, cumprimis vemis vero interiora marcescant viresq; labascant, quod certè aestate crebrerrime accidere vidimus peregrinantibus, dum potu destituuntur : Una enim cum calore exhalante etiam humidum diffluere, ob idq; siccitura magisq; frigida, reddit corpora, quis est qui inficias ibit? Adducitur quoq; Galenus, quem idem asserere ajunt in comm.in l. Hipp.de natura humana, cum circumfuso fcil. aeris flatu vna animalium corpora affici, siccari in sicco humectari in humido, &c. Unde concludunt nihil aliud voluisse Hipp.& Gal. quam nostra corpora hieme frigere, aestate vero calere, propterea quod hieme pituitam augeri, aestate bilem. Hippocrates & experientia testentur, hieme enim homines pituitosissima expuere atq; emungere, unde sequi ajunt corpus aestate calidius esse, hieme frigidius. Verum Galenus comment. in l.Hipp. de natur.human. copiosioris pituita per hyemem hanc affert causam, quod homines id tempore multis pituitosis vescantur cibis, ut oleribus, rapis, leguminibus, fructibus, carnibus agninis & porcinis, & id genus aliis quae facile in pituitam vertuntur : quod item bibant vinum novum, ex quo non minus promte generetur pituita.
units.tr: And first they cite the authority of Hippocrates and Galen, who hold that bodies are hottest in summer, because that is the hottest season of the year, and coldest in winter, because in winter nothing is cold to the same degree. Hippocrates, Book 3 On Diet: "When the weather is cold and compact, living creatures themselves suffer similar things (namely from without, just as in summer they are heated from without), and on a healthy diet, for those for whom it is summer, one ought to use what makes the body cool and soft, for the time is hot, and so it makes bodies fiery and squalid." Where it is summer, says Hippocrates, one must take care that the body be cool. Why so? Because the season is hot. Hippocrates therefore orders and wishes that in summer, when the whole body burns with heat, we apply and use cold things, so that the pores and openings of the skin are gradually condensed and constricted, lest through an excessive outflow of internal heat (for it is drawn out by the external heat, dissipated and dispersed) the whole body, and especially the inner parts, waste away and their strength fail. We have certainly seen this happen most often in summer to travellers deprived of drink. For together with the exhaling heat the moisture also flows away, and so it makes the bodies drier and colder. Who will deny it? Galen is also cited, whom they say asserts in his commentary on Hippocrates' On the Nature of Man that the bodies of living creatures are affected by the surrounding air-stream: dried in dry air, moistened in moist air, and so on. From this they conclude that Hippocrates and Galen meant nothing else than that our bodies grow cold in winter and warm in summer, because phlegm increases in winter and bile in summer. Hippocrates and experience bear witness, they say, for in winter men spit out and blow their noses most of all phlegm; whence they infer that the body is hotter in summer and colder in winter. But Galen, in his commentary on that book of Hippocrates, gives a different cause for the greater abundance of phlegm in winter: people at that time eat many phlegmatic foods, such as vegetables, turnips, pulses, fruits, lamb and pork, and other kinds that are easily turned into phlegm; and they likewise drink new wine, from which phlegm is generated no less readily.

units.la: Sed illi regerunt etiam per aestatem talibus cibis nos vesci & pituitosioribus, omnis scilicet generis fructibus, iisq; crudis, ut fragis, cerasis, prunis, pomis, pyris, & in acetariis lactucâ, endiuia, acetosa, portulacâ, &c.
units.tr: But they reply that in summer we also eat such foods, even more phlegmatic: all kinds of fruits, and raw ones at that, such as strawberries, cherries, plums, apples, pears, and among salad herbs lettuce, endive, sorrel, purslane, and so on.

units.la: Hic
units.tr: Here.

units.la: Hīc vero quaeritur cur horum ciborum pitui-toforum immoderatus vsus sit noxius magis aestate quam hyeme, ac vt plurimum diarrhoeas procreet ac dysenterias? an id fit ob caloris natiui penuriam ac imbecillitatem, quae maior est aestate, quàm vt exsuperantiam illam ciborum moderari possit ac domare, vnde pituita crassa ac viscida in intestinis colligitur, cruditates cumulantur, quae prauam qualitatem adepta à calore nec superari, nec mitigari possunt? Nemo opinor existet, qui contradicturus sit.
units.tr: Here, however, the question is why the immoderate use of these phlegm-producing foods is more harmful in summer than in winter, and usually produces diarrhoeas and dysenteries. Is it because the natural heat is scarcer and weaker in summer, so that it is not strong enough to moderate and subdue that excess of food, whence thick and viscid phlegm gathers in the intestines and crudities pile up, which, having taken on a bad quality from the heat, can neither be overcome nor softened? I think no one will arise to dispute it.

units.la: Illa enim omnia aestino calore promptius putrescunt, intestina horumque venas vellicant atque exulcerant, complexionem ventriculi intestinorumque immutant, quam complexionis mutationem praedicta symptomata subsequuntur: contra vero hieme melius omnia in animalis corpore administrari supra demonstratum est. Praeterea vero & recte ab Hipp. dictum esse I. de salubr. diaet. oportere & ad aetatem, & ad anni tempus & ad corporum habitum diaetas constituere, ita vt caloribus & hiemibus nos opponamus, sic enim homines maxime fore sanos, ipse Galenus scribit in commentar. Et licet eundem pro se adducant scribentem in eodem commentario, corpus, quod immoderatius excalfactum est, aut calefit, refrigerandum esse, refrigeratum calefaciendum: Et Celsum l. de re medica c. 3, dicentem, naturale esse potione aestuantem ventriculum refrigerari, frigentem calefieri: Item calidum hominem refrigerare se debere: inde tamen non elicitur, propterea aestate sstate nos magis vesci cibis frigidis & humidis, quod ventriculus fit calidior secundum essentiam primo & per se sed potum ut ventriculus flaccidus, humido scil. in eo per resolutionem & evaporationem tenuium partium absumto, refrigerando & humectando co roboretur, villiq; resoluti ac relaxati astringantur: his enim laxatis appetitus perditur, qui iisdem astrictis restituitur. Cum enim calorem immodicum & redundantem consecutive & necessario comitetur siccitas, quæ in corpore humano nihil periculosius, (ut vidimus in corporibus tabidis & emaciatis, quæ sunt sicca absumto videlicet humido radicali) ad hanc præcavendam ventriculum frigido humidis roboramus, cujus aliàs vires prorsus concidèrent atq; resolverentur. Deinde calor æstate sentitur magis in exterioribus evocatus scilicet a centro suo ad circumferentiam ac per universum corpus differsus. &Atq; hoc est quod Hipp. l. 3. de diæt. inquit, cibis mollioribus & paucioribus utendum esse ob debilem ventriculi calorem, & maza magis quam pane, potionibusq; albis, mollibus & aquosis sc. ad humectandum. Consentiunt cum his quæ habentur l. de salubr. diæt. Æstate maza molli alioportet & potione aquosa multa, obsoniisq; omnibus elixis: & his ita utendum est, ut corpus sit frigidum & molle. Huc accedit auctoritas Celsi, qui inquit, æstate potione & cibo corpus sæpius egere quia videlicet calor externus multum depascitur: calorem externum nominat & circumfusum non internum,
units.tr: For all those things putrefy more readily under the burning heat, irritate and ulcerate the intestines and their veins, and alter the constitution of the stomach and bowels, and the aforementioned symptoms follow this alteration of constitution. On the contrary, in winter everything is better managed in the animal body, as was shown above. Moreover, Hippocrates rightly said in his first book On Healthy Diet that diets must be arranged according to age, the season of the year and the habit of the body, so that we set ourselves against heats and winters; for so, says Galen himself in his commentary, men will be most healthy. And although they cite the same writer in the same commentary, that a body which has been overheated or is becoming overheated must be cooled, and one that has been cooled must be warmed; and Celsus, in his book On Medicine, chapter 3, saying that it is natural to cool a stomach that burns from drink, and to warm one that is chilled; likewise that a hot man ought to cool himself: yet from this it does not follow that we eat cold and moist foods more in summer because the stomach becomes hotter, in essence and primarily in itself. Rather, the stomach, being flaccid, since the moisture in it is consumed by the dissolving and evaporation of its thin parts, is strengthened by cooling and moistening, and its villi, loosened and relaxed, are drawn together. For when these are relaxed the appetite is lost, and when they are drawn together it is restored. For since excessive and redundant heat is necessarily and consequently accompanied by dryness, which in the human body is nothing more dangerous (as we see in wasted and emaciated bodies, which are dry because the radical moisture has been consumed), we strengthen the stomach with cold and moist things to guard against this; otherwise its powers would utterly collapse and dissolve. Further, in summer heat is felt more in the exterior, being drawn out, namely from its centre to the circumference and spread through the whole body. And this is what Hippocrates says in Book 3 On Diet: softer and fewer foods must be used because of the weak heat of the stomach, and barley-porridge rather than bread, and white, soft and watery drinks, namely to moisten. They agree with what is held in his book On Healthy Diet: in summer one should use soft barley-porridge and much watery drink, and all boiled dishes, and these should be used so that the body is cool and soft. To this is added the authority of Celsus, who says that in summer the body more often needs drink and food because the external heat is greatly consumed: he names the external and surrounding heat, not the internal, which is weaker.

units.la: G qui debilior est. Ad morbos pergunt sensum & experientiam attestari aientes, astate vtplurimum grassan-es morbos calidio es & ardentiores esse, negari non potest. Verum hoc quaeritur num hoc fiat propterea quod ventriculus cateraq; viscera calore abundent? an vero quia calor internus e cetro suo & sede dimot p vniuersum corpus quasi volitans tenuiores sanguinis partes & ichores inflammat & accendit, bilem puto, secundum Hippocratis judicium ad eiusmodi præ reliquis humoribus exarsionem & incendium astate & sua natura quæ calida & sicca est, aptissimam: calescente enim sanguine exhalat maxime per hunc aquosum humor s bruli incendio infistissimus, relinquitur au empinguis & seuus, qui biliosus est & febris astuæ potissimum nutrimentum, copiosius enim & accommodatius nutrimentum febri bilis ipsa suppeditat inquit Hipp. 4. de morb,
units.tr: Quod: they go on to claim that sense and experience attest that in summer the prevailing diseases are for the most part hotter and more ardent; this cannot be denied. But the question is whether this happens because the stomach and the other viscera abound in heat, or rather because the internal heat, moved from its centre and seat and flying through the whole body, inflames and kindles the thinner parts of the blood and the serum. I think bile, according to Hippocrates' judgment, is most apt above the other humours for such a flaring and burning, by its nature in summer, which is hot and dry. For when the blood heats, the watery humour, the most fiery of all, is exhaled most, and what remains is fat and tallowy, which is bilious and the chief nourishment of a burning fever. For bile itself supplies more abundant and suitable nourishment to fever, says Hippocrates in Book 4 On Diseases.

units.la: Quid? an propterea calidiores morbi generari dicentur, quod corpus sit calidius, aliis dijudicandum relinquo. Hippocrates enim l. de veter. med. calidum vult, quā calidum, non esse morbi causam, nam inquit, ego hoc maximum signum esse puto, quod non propter calidum hominess febricitent simpliciter, neq; hoc sit simpliciter affectionis causa, sed est amarum & calidum idem, & calidum ac acidum & salsum, sic & frigidum cum aliis facultatibus coniunctum.
units.tr: Well, whether diseases are said to be generated hotter because the body is hotter, I leave to others to judge. For Hippocrates in his book On Ancient Medicine holds that heat, as heat, is not the cause of disease. For he says: "I think this is the greatest sign that people do not fall ill with fever simply because of the heat, nor is this simply the cause of the affection; but the bitter and the hot are the same, and the hot and the sour and the salty, and likewise the cold, when joined with other qualities."

units.la: Bilis autem calida est & amara maximè vigens astate, ac propter pinguedinem tenuitatem emq adsead febrilem exacerbationem promptissima est calore scite excitato atq; per omne corpus sursum & deorsum volitante, putredinemq; in humore primum pinguiori tenuiorique, ad inflammationem longe aptiori accedente, non secus ut in aedificio incenso palea primo flammam concipere, postea trabes, auctio vero incendio non solum paleas, & ligna, sed & lapides rumpi videmus: calidiores igitur & ardentiores morbi contingunt aestate ratione bilis flammae facile ac prompte concipientis, sua etiam natura non simpliciter calida, sed calida ac amara. Antiperistasi denique nihil vel parum fonderis & virium hic concedunt. I. quod qui gelu enecantur, in illorum se corpora ambiens frigus penitissime insinuet caloremq; natiuum extinguat. Sed hoc ipsum frigoris intensissimo afferibendum est: frigiditas enim ἀσύμμετρος & redundans altissime & violenter penetrans calorem quasi in suo centro quiescentem extinguat, quod nequaquam fieret si calor esset per universum corpus distributus, quod certissimum argumentum est calo is ad intima pene ratio animadversio hoste efugientis.
units.tr: Bile, however, is hot and bitter and is most vigorous in summer. Because it is thin and fatty, it is very quick to give rise to a feverish flare-up when its heat is stirred up and flies about through the whole body, up and down. Putrefaction begins first in the moister and thinner humour, which is much more apt for inflammation. Just as in a burning building the chaff catches fire first, then the beams, and once the blaze grows we see not only straw and wood but even stones split, so hotter and fiercer diseases occur in summer, because bile catches fire easily and quickly. Its nature is not simply hot but hot and bitter. Lastly, here they grant little or nothing to antiperistasis as a source of strength. Those who die of frost are an example: the cold surrounding their bodies penetrates deep inside and extinguishes their native heat. But this must itself be ascribed to the most intense cold. Cold that is excessive and superabundant, penetrating deeply and violently, extinguishes the heat as if it were resting in its own centre. This would not happen if the heat were spread through the whole body, and it is a most certain proof that heat retreats to the innermost parts when it senses the enemy.

units.la: Cum enim calor & frigus sint contraria, ut de se mutuo prohibent, fugant, & fugiunt, necesse est debiliorem a fortiori fugari & vinci. Praeterea calorem refugere quidem ac repelli ob antiperistasin, sin ad interiora concedunt, verum ad suum principium videlicet cor, non vero ventriculum. Sed quis caloris ad principium suum repulsi partem etiam per venas arteriasq; ventriculo communicari neganegabit? ad insitum enim ventriculi calorem, quo plus accesserit caloris influentis eo evadit fortior, & felicius cibus conficitur. Instant, multos hiberni frigoris saevitiam interemisse & valde frigentes sen-mortuorum instar rigere, cibumque, a potum aversari quam diu non recalfacit. fuerint, ergo calori innato tanta vires non sunt, ut frigori ambienti resistat, seu eo intendatur. Hic responderi potest, hoc fieri ratione nervorum, musculorum & extremorum, in quae frigus penetravit, seque insinuavit, unde extrema rigida & congelata deprehenduntur, motus sensusque expertia: quod si vero intensius, frigus est, diutiusque durans, ulterius etiam penetrando calorisofficinam ita coarctat atque occludit, ut calor extinguatur atque suffocetur. Reliqua negantis partis argumenta aequo ac erudito lectori perpendanda relinquo, liberum cuique faciens, hoc ne an illud approbet, sed natura: veritas ipsa se non quaesita prodet.
units.tr: For since heat and cold are contraries, each drives out, repels and flees the other, it must follow that the weaker is driven out and conquered by the stronger. Besides, they admit that heat does retreat and is repelled by antiperistasis, but they say it withdraws to the interior, that is, to its source, the heart, and not to the stomach. But who will deny that a part of the heat driven back to its source is communicated to the stomach through the veins and arteries? For the stomach's innate heat grows stronger the more of the incoming heat it receives, and food is digested more successfully. They object that many have died from the savagery of a winter frost, and that those who are very chilled stiffen like the dead and shrink from food and drink as long as they have not warmed up again. Therefore, they say, the innate heat has no such strength as to resist the surrounding cold or to be intensified by it. Here it can be answered that this happens because of the nerves, muscles and extremities into which the cold has penetrated and insinuated itself, whence the extremities are found stiff and frozen, lacking motion and sensation. But if the cold is more intense and lasts longer, then by penetrating further it constricts and shuts up the workshop of heat, so that the heat is extinguished and suffocated. I leave the remaining arguments of the other side to be weighed by the fair and learned reader, leaving it to each to decide whether he approves this or that. Nature, the truth itself, will reveal itself without being sought.

units.la: 1. Si, inquiunt, hieme constricta cute calor interior corpore cohibetur & intensior fit, aestate autem caloris extra evocato frigus succedit, sequitur aestate generari pituitam, hieme vero bilem, aestate vitandum esse calido, hieme frigido, aestateque calidas naturas bene se habituras, hieme frigidas, quae Hip. & Galeni placitis sunt adversa. Ego vero sum in ea sententia & pituitam & bilem tam aestate, quam hieme generari, illam tamen copiosius hieme, hanc aestate: pituitam aestate generari ostendunt alui profluvia ex crudorum ciborum immodico esu, quæpostea pituita æstiuo calore putrescens acris evadit & corrosiua: bilem verò etiam hiemegenerari manifestò ostendunt biliosi vomitus, Idem Iudicium sit de bile atra, quam non minus æstate, vere, hiemeq; quam autumno generari certum est.
units.tr: 1. They say: if in winter the skin is constricted and the inner heat is held in by the body and becomes more intense, while in summer the heat is called outward and cold follows, then it follows that phlegm is generated in summer and bile in winter. Thus in summer one must avoid hot things, in winter cold ones, and in summer hot natures will do well, in winter cold ones. These views are opposed to the opinions of Hippocrates and Galen. I myself hold that both phlegm and bile are generated in summer as well as in winter, though phlegm more abundantly in winter and bile in summer. That phlegm is generated in summer is shown by the diarrhoeas that follow immoderate eating of raw food, which afterwards, as the summer heat putrefies the phlegm, become sharp and corrosive. That bile is generated even in winter is clearly shown by bilious vomiting. The same judgement holds for black bile, which is certainly generated no less in summer, spring and winter than in autumn.

units.la: II. Quod hieme quàm æstate sumus edaciores, escamq; minori negotio digeramus, aiunt non esse certum signum abundantis in ventriculo caloris, qui enim laborant canina appetentia, voracissimi sunt, quorum tamen ventriculi omnium medicorum judicio sunt frigida intemperie affecti. Hic ignoratur Elenchus.
units.tr: II. They say that we eat more in winter than in summer and digest our food with less effort, but this is no sure sign of abundant heat in the stomach. For those who suffer from canine appetite are most voracious, and yet, by the judgement of all physicians, their stomachs are afflicted with a cold intemperature. Here the fallacy is overlooked (ignoratur Elenchus).

units.la: Quod enim pro confesso ac demonstrato assumitur adhuc probandum restat. An enim frigidus ventriculus plus appetat quàm calidus, rationum & argumentorum viribus ponderandum est. Pueri certè plus cibi appetunt, augmentum mq; capiunt non quòd longius profundiusq; dormiant, ut quidam putant, sed quòd plurimo calido innato abundent. Appetitus igitur nec omnis, nec semper a frigido est, sed modera, e seu temperatè calido. Phlegmatici & pituitosi parum & tardè appetunt, ob calorem remissum & torpidum: contra qui natiui caloris qualitatem acriorem experiuntur inediam nocentissimè ferunt, identidemq; iterato pastu uti coguntur ut sunt biliosi, quæ cer è expr se conradicunt posterioris sententia patronus, contrariumq; satis demonstrant.
units.tr: For what is assumed as admitted and proven still remains to be proved. Whether a cold stomach desires more than a warm one must be weighed by the force of reasons and arguments. Children certainly desire more food and gain in growth, not because they sleep longer and more deeply, as some think, but because they abound in native heat. Appetite, then, does not always and not in every case come from cold, but from a moderate or temperate heat. Phlegmatic and phlegmy people have little appetite and desire food slowly, because their heat is slack and sluggish. On the other hand, those who experience the sharper quality of native heat bear fasting very badly, and are often forced to eat again and again, as the bilious are. These things plainly contradict the defender of the latter opinion and show the contrary.

units.la: III. Quod æstate ciborum sumus minus appetentes aut assumtos difficulter concoquimus, non frigofrigoris aiunt fieri culpa, sed immoderati caloris, id enim nobis astuantibus euenire quod fibri-citantibus, qui cum maxime ardeant, cibos tamen auersantur, aut si comedant, grauantur magis quam refocillantur. Hoc vero ipsum est, quod volui, appetentiam silicet oriri a calore moderato seu temperato: quo etiam sensu potest concedi a frigido posse excitari appetentiam, non simpliciter & absolute seu quà frigido, sed quatenus cum calore contemperatum, adq; natura conuenienstem-peramentum redactum est.
units.tr: III. They say that in summer we have less appetite for food, or digest with difficulty what we have eaten, and that this is the fault not of cold but of excessive heat. For this happens to us in the heat of summer just as to feverish people, who, though they burn most fiercely, nevertheless shun food, or if they do eat, are weighed down rather than refreshed. But this is precisely what I wanted: that appetite arises from a moderate or temperate heat. In this sense it may be conceded that appetite can be aroused even by cold, not simply and absolutely, or as cold, but insofar as it has been tempered with heat and brought into a mixture agreeable to nature.

units.la: IV. Quod deniq; hieme potu frigido minus delectemur, magis autem edulis calidis, argumento esse contendunt, ventriculum hieme frigidum esse, non calidum. Item quod appetamus vina calidiora & generosa ad ventriculum calefaciendum. Vera hac esse concedo de iis qui liberiori aeri crebro se exponunt, horum enim ventriculos edulis calidioribus generosisq; vinis foueri expedit, ut a violenti penetrantisq; frigoris ambientis iniuria interiora sint tutiora, fortiusq; circumfusa frigiditati resistant. Deinde quibus ventriculus est infirmus, generosis vinis edulisq; calidis quocunq; loco & tempore vti innoxium erit, vt scilicet calor innatus sibi affini & simili adauctus atq; adjutus in vigore & operationibus con-seruetur.
units.tr: IV. Finally, they contend that because we take less pleasure in cold drink in winter and more in warm food, this is evidence that the stomach is cold in winter and not warm. Likewise, that we desire warmer and stronger wines to warm the stomach. I concede that these things are true of those who often expose themselves to the open air, for it is useful to nourish their stomachs with warmer food and strong wines, so that their insides may be safer from the harm of a violent and piercing surrounding cold, and so that they may better resist the chill that surrounds them. Then, for those whose stomach is weak, it will be harmless to use strong wines and warm food at any place and any time, so that the innate heat, increased and aided by what is akin and similar to it, may be preserved in its vigour and its operations.

units.la: AD QVAEST. V. An alimentum sit tantum dicendum quod nutrit?
units.tr: Question 5: Is only that which nourishes to be called food?

units.la: A Limentum familiare, simile, proprium, facultateq, idem cum eo esse quod nutritur, aq; naturæ majestate vaicuique animantium proprium atque peculiare tributum esse, nulli est dubium. Verum cum triplex sit apud Galenum & Medicos alimentum, sciendum quodnam vere & proprie dicatur nutrire.
units.tr: That food should be familiar, similar and proper, and of the same faculty as the thing nourished, and that by the majesty of nature a proper and peculiar allotment is given to each living creature, is beyond doubt. But since, according to Galen and the physicians, food is threefold, we must know which is truly and properly said to nourish.

units.la: Primum enim alimentum iis dicitur quod vere & jam actu nutrit: Secundo quod velut nutrimentum est, nondum tamen nutriuit. Tertio quod futurum est, seu aliquando alitu-rum est.
units.tr: For the first kind of food is that which truly and already actually nourishes. The second is that which is, as it were, nutriment but has not yet nourished. The third is that which will be, or will at some time nourish.

units.la: Alimentum igitur quod proximè & proprie nutrit, exquisitè assimilatum esse oportet: quod autem veluti nutriens est, nondum vero nutriuit, cujusmodi est quod agglutinatur & apponitur, æquiuocè nutrimentum est. In venis autem ac in ventriculo magis existens, si probè pleneq, conficiatur, alimentu futurum nuncupatur: atq; hoc est, quod Galenus aphor. 29. l. 5. ait, alimentum non nisi coctum nutrit; qua ratione & modo cibi omnes nutrimenta possunt appellari, non quòd animal iis proximè jam alatur, neque quod tales sint, qualia vere nutrimenta esse oportet, sed quòd probè conseconfecti & subacti nutrituri sint: vbiadno- tandum paucos admodum medicos praeter v- num Galenum ejusque sectatores has alimen- torum distinctiones nouiße & explanaße.
units.tr: Food that nourishes most closely and properly must be exactly assimilated. But what is only as it were nourishing and has not yet nourished, such as what is merely stuck on and applied, is nutriment only in an equivocal sense. Food that is more in the veins and in the stomach, if it is properly and fully digested, is called food that will be; and this is what Galen means in aphor. 29. l. 5., when he says that food nourishes only when it has been cooked. By this reasoning and manner, all foods can be called nutriments, not because the animal is nourished by them directly now, nor because they are such as must truly be nutriments, but because, when properly concocted and prepared, they will nourish. Here it should be noted that very few physicians, apart from Galen alone and his followers, have recognised and explained these distinctions of foods.

units.la: Ex his facile patebit alimenti simpliciter sic dicti, alimenti medicamentosi, & medica- menti differentia. Ex propria enim cujusque substantia & forma ea innotescit. Alimen- tum corpori nutriendo ita simile est, vt id nu- triat,augeatque: exuperante vero aliqua qua- litate id immutante, licet substantia quodam- modo sit simile, alimentum medicamentosum est, vt lactuca, vina generosa, mala cotonea, &c. Nulla autem qualitate corpus manifeste afficiente praeditum, substantiaque corporia- lendo plane dissimile, neque inter alimenta, neque medicamenta censeri debet. Quod denique in substantia nobis prorsus dispari qualitates ab alimenti natura omnino remo- tas obrinet, corpusque nostrum manifeste immutare aptum est, vsquequaque medica- mentum est, vt hyoscyamus, pirethrum, alu- men, sena, aloe, rhabarbarum, &c. Manife- sta qualitate homines jugulantes, venena sunt & deleteria, vt euforbium, arsenicum, scammonium, antimonium male praeparatum, &c.
units.tr: From these points it will easily become clear what distinguishes food simply so called, medicinal food, and medicine. For each is known from the proper substance and form of the thing itself. Food is so similar to the body to be nourished that it nourishes and augments it. But when some quality predominates and alters it, then, although it is somewhat similar in substance, it is medicinal food, such as lettuce, generous wines, quinces, etc. Nothing endowed with no quality that manifestly affects the body, and wholly unlike in substance to what nourishes the body, should be counted either among foods or among medicines. Finally, what is wholly unlike us in substance, has qualities entirely remote from the nature of food, and is apt to alter our body manifestly, is altogether medicine, such as henbane, pellitory, alum, senna, aloe, rhubarb, etc. Those which kill men by a manifest quality are poisons and deadly things, such as euphorbium, arsenic, scammony, badly prepared antimony, etc.

units.la: AD QVÆST. VI. An nutritio sit assimilatio?
units.tr: CHAPTER 6: Is nutrition assimilation?

units.la: VEram nutritionem nihil aliud esse, quam eius quod nutrit assimilatione ad id quod nutritur, seu repositionem, instaurationem vel repletionem eius quod effluxit, in Medicorum scholis tritum est. Verum an nutritio sit assimilatio vel vnio, ad vnguem nosse poterit nemo, nisi nutritionis modum, eius instrumenta ac gradus praenoverit: hoc enim ignorare, homine, qui eruditus perhiberi vult, nihil turpius. Nempe qua ratione ex pane devorato generetur sanguis, depositio sanguinis albore, sensim rubore accipiente: sanguine enim facto non ita magno negotio generabitur caro, cum in id, quod natura illius, quod mutatur vicinius est, facilior semper est mutatio. At vero vt sanguis fiat os, multo labore et mutatione opus est, longoque temporis interuallo. Vnde nemini mirum videri debet, ea quae nutriuntur singula proprium e sanguine suscipum primum trahere, to[?]q[?] instrumentis in alendo prouidam naturam esse vsam, ad mutandos, alterandos, perficiendos, deducendosque cibos idoneis. Ac quidem os primus meatus est, quo cibi in ventriculum ingrediuntur, siue prima quasi praeparatio cibi in ore masticando, dentibus conterendo, qui postea per oesophagum seu gulam in ventriculum (vulgo stomachum) delabitur ac deducitur.
units.tr: It is a commonplace in the schools of the physicians that nutrition is nothing other than the assimilation of what nourishes to that which is nourished, or the replacing, restoring or refilling of what has flowed away. But no one can know exactly whether nutrition is assimilation or union unless he has first learned the manner of nutrition, its instruments and its stages. For to be ignorant of this is the most disgraceful thing for a man who wishes to be thought learned. Consider how blood is generated from devoured bread: the blood is deposited first white and then gradually takes on red. Once blood has been formed, flesh is generated without great difficulty, since a change into what lies nearer to the nature of the thing changed is always easier. But for blood to become bone, much labour and change are needed, and a long interval of time. Hence no one should think it strange that the parts being nourished first draw their own proper nourishment from the blood, and that nature, in nourishing, makes use of suitable instruments for changing, altering, perfecting and conveying the food. The mouth is the first passage by which food enters the stomach, and it is, as it were, the first preparation of the food, in chewing it and grinding it with the teeth. From there it passes down through the gullet, or oesophagus, into the stomach (commonly called the belly), and is conveyed onward.

units.la: Hic primum subit in cibis laborem, ac insita
units.tr: Here the first labour upon the food arises, and the innate

units.la: quadam facultate cibum in substantiam quandam adeptus qualitatem, in epate postea in sanguinem convertitur, atque haec prima concoctio est, quae fit una vice in ventriculo, s. aut 6. 7. etiam in quibusdam horarum spatio. Huius coctionis excrementa sunt alvi seces.
units.tr: faculty, by which the food, having acquired a certain quality as a certain substance, is afterwards converted in the liver into blood. This is the first concoction, which takes place at one time in the stomach, that is, in six or seven hours, or in some people over a span of hours. The excrements of this concoction are the dregs of the bowels.

units.la: Ventriculus igitur chylo satiatus in intestina superiora eum deponit, ubi venae mesaraicae sensim hunc exugunt, et ad epar amandant, in cuius ossi-cina fit secunda concoctio, quae sanguificationem conficit: qua confecta et peracta tertia subsequitur in singulis membris. Ut autem ventriculum primum ea, quae in ea sunt impura et inutilia diligenter repurgat, ita quoque iecoris munus est, utile ab inutili secernere.
units.tr: The stomach, therefore, having been filled with chyle, deposits it into the upper intestines, where the mesaraic veins gradually draw it out and send it on to the liver. In the workshop of the liver the second concoction takes place, which completes the making of blood. When this is completed and finished, a third follows in the individual limbs. Just as the stomach first carefully purges out what is impure and useless in it, so too it is the office of the liver to separate what is useful from what is useless.

units.la: Dum enim succus ille a ventriculo in epar diffusus in sanguinis probi massam alteratur et convertitur, gignuntur duo excrementa, quorum alterum tenue, et quasi innatans spuma, alterum crassum, lutulentumque est, virumque in fabricatum a natura receptaculum segregatur, lene illud, spumosum et flavum vasculo recipitur Epati adhaerenti, Vesicalam fellis vocant, coenosum et faeculentum in lienem recipitur, aquosus vero serosusque liquor, qui sanguini semper admistus est, eiqque privihiculo existit (ob angustiam enim venarum exilitatemque sanguis facile permeare non posset, nisi fluidum quid et aquosum esset permistum) munere suo functus, naturaque animantis non amplius plius utilis, noxius (scilicet & molestus vasorum generi, per renes à sanguine secernitur, perq; exi-tus meatus ureteres dictos in vesicam demissus, & laxatum ibi musculum effunditur excernitur q, sicq; sanguis ab omni alieno & inutili liquore re-purgatus totum corpus sursum permeat atq; deorsum.
units.tr: For while that juice, poured from the stomach into the liver, is altered and turned into the mass of good blood, two excrements are produced. One is thin and like a floating foam, the other thick and muddy. Each is separated into the receptacle that nature has fashioned for it. The light, frothy and yellow one is received into a little vessel attached to the liver, which they call the gall bladder. The muddy and dregs-like one is received into the spleen. The watery and serous liquid, which is always mixed with the blood and which exists for its sake (for the blood could not easily pass through the narrowness and thinness of the veins unless some fluid and watery matter were mixed with it), having performed its office, and being no longer useful but harmful to the nature of the living creature (and troublesome to the kind of vessels), is secreted from the blood by the kidneys. It is sent down through the passages called the ureters into the bladder, and is discharged there when the muscle is relaxed. So the blood, purged of every foreign and useless liquid, passes through the whole body, upward and downward.

units.la: Atq; tantum de nutritione & nutritionis mo- do, ubi & gradus annotasse oportebit, nam ipsam naturam gradatim in ea procederé ss̃ stratur, sic-cus enim illi, qui omnes animalis partes nutriuntur e-st, in eas primum diffunditur, seu apponitur, seu dispergitur, mox agglutinatur, deinde assimilatur & unitur.
units.tr: And this is enough about nutrition and its manner. Here it will also be necessary to note its stages, for it is shown that nature proceeds through them gradually. The juice that nourishes all the parts of the animal is first diffused into them, or applied to them, or spread out; then it is agglutinated, and afterwards it is assimilated and united.

units.la: Sunt itaque ad nutritionem gradus necessarii appositio, agglutinatio, assimilatio & unio. Vl-timus igitur nutritionis gradus est unio eius, quod nutrit cum parte nutrienda. Si enim, quod nutri-re carnem debet, in locum eius, quæ abiit, succedere, a quo idipsum fieri, quod illa fuerat, oportet, necessario sequitur, illud ipsum carni quæ nutritur, primo assimilari, deinde uniri, hoc est, carnem specie & natura fieri eandem cum ea, quæ nutritur, & quod talis caro fieri non potest, nutrimentum eius esse non potest. In vera igitur nutritione idem restituitur in locum euacuati, & quod in vacuati locum per nutritionem succedit, proprium est & familiare, unde alimentum dicitur facultate idem cum eo esse quod nutrinutritur, idq; veritas pronunciati illius Physici confirmat, vnumquodq; fcil. eo nutriri, ex quo de principio confiterit, cuius saepe apud Galen. & Aristot. fi mentio.
units.tr: There are therefore four stages necessary to nutrition: apposition, agglutination, assimilation and union. The last stage of nutrition is the union of what nourishes with the part to be nourished. For if what ought to nourish the flesh is to succeed into the place of what has departed, and this must be done by becoming the same as what it replaces, it necessarily follows that it must first be assimilated to the nourished flesh and then united with it. That is, the flesh must become the same in kind and nature as that which nourishes it. And since such flesh cannot be made, what is not of this kind cannot be its nourishment. In true nutrition, therefore, the same thing is restored into the place of what has been emptied, and what succeeds by nutrition into the place of what was emptied is proper and familiar to it. Hence food is said to have the same faculty as that which it nourishes, and this is confirmed by the truth of that saying of the natural philosophers, that each thing is nourished by that from which it has been constituted in its beginning, a saying often mentioned in Galen and Aristotle.

units.la: Nec obstat, quod diuersis reb. vescamur, quod q; multis esculentis vtamur, quib. diuersa animalia gaudent, nam de vltimo alimento, videl. sanguine accipienda esi praedicta enunciatio. Sanguis enim, licet ex variis cibis conficiatur, natura tamen in eius collione partes tantu cognatas & homogeneas colligit, nostris vero corporibus inimica separat & secernit, & sis nobis reddit familiarem. Idem de aliis animalibus iudicandum est. Etsi enim suea & canes pane nobiscum vescerentur, non tamen eundem specie sanguinem cum nostro generarent, quia non eodem modo coccoquunt, nec easdem partes segregant, quas noster calor separat: quod manifestum primo euadit ex specie excrementorum qua qualitatibus & subitantia sunt dissimilia: de- inde quod nostris deleantur, sua abominantur: nunquam vero id facerent, si non in nostris relinquerentur partes ipsis gratae: quare alias partes non- habent ac reiecit, alterq; omnes coxit & mutauit, vt vita idem sanguis non sit, qui ex eadem materia genitus est. Causa haec est, quod idem agens res diuersas non solum alteret & mutet, sed eadem quae res a diuersis agentibus eodem modo non alterat & immutatur.
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way that we eat different things, and use many foods in which different animals delight. For the aforementioned statement must be understood of the ultimate nourishment, namely blood. For blood, although it is made from various foods, nevertheless in its collection nature gathers only parts that are akin and of one kind, and separates and secretes those that are hostile to our bodies, and so makes them familiar to us. The same must be judged of other animals. For even if swine and dogs ate bread with us, they would not produce blood the same in kind as ours, because they do not cook it in the same way and do not separate the same parts that our heat separates. This is clear, first, from the kind of excrements, which differ in quality and substance. Next, because things that are harmful to us they reject, and what is harmless to them they abominate. Yet they would never do this if parts agreeable to them were not left in ours. Hence they do not have the same parts; they reject some and cook and change others, so that the blood of one living creature is not the same as that which is generated from the same matter in another. The cause of this is that the same agent not only alters and changes different things, but also does not alter and change the same thing in the same way when it is acted upon by different agents.

units.la: Nunquam igitur calor ignis ex pane faciet sangui-
units.tr: Therefore the heat of fire never makes blood out of bread

units.la: Cur ex e- adein materia & alime- to in di- uersis a- nimalib nongenneretur idem san guis? sanguinem & chylum, quod ventriculi calorfacit. Nunquam epar expane chylum, sicut nec ex chylo venter unquam producet sanguinem. Idem chylus aliter ab eodem epate sano & agro permutatur sanum chylum in sanguinem bonum, agrum, vt in hydrope, in aquam conuertit.
units.tr: Why would the same blood not be generated from the same matter and food in different animals? from blood and chyle, as the heat of the stomach makes it. The liver never makes chyle from bread, just as the stomach never produces blood from chyle. The same chyle is changed differently by the same liver, whether healthy or diseased: a healthy liver converts healthy chyle into good blood, but a diseased one, as in dropsy, converts it into water.

units.la: Et tantum de hac quæstione.
units.tr: And this is enough on this question.

units.la: AD QVÆST. VII.
units.tr: On Question 7

units.la: An morbi communes etiam oriantur à malorum ciborum copia & culpa?
units.tr: Whether common diseases also arise from an abundance of bad foods and from fault in diet?

units.la: MOrbus communis dicitur, non tantum qui causam habet communem, sed etiam qui ad plures alios sese per contagium potest extendere & promouere. Causa communis est nō solus aer, verum etiam aqua putris, cibus aut potus vitiosus. Hic igitur quæritur, num morbi communes, puta pestis, origine trahant à malorum ciborum culpa? Sunt qui pestis seminaria in solo aere ponunt. Alii ex humanis tantum corporib. pestis contagia effundi arbitrantur. Alii hoc ipsum negant. Quidā ex aeris cœliq; iniuria, vt magnis & insolitis tempestatibus, magnis planetarū coniunctionibus. Verum neque in solo aere pestis seminarium contineri, neque ex aeris semper iniuria cœliq; inclementia dependere, neq; ex hominum corporibus tantum erumpere ostendunt dunt putridi illi halitus ex lacubus, spelunci̇s, brutorum cadaueribus putrefactis exhalantes corporaq; nostra inficientes. Qui vero ex humanis corporibus, diæteq; culpa, vt prauis aliimeutis humoribusq; putridis, comunes morbos oriri posse inficiantur, contendentes morbum communem esse, cuius semper commu-nis fit causa, videlicet aer venenatus, contagiosus, non considerant posse in nobis generari substantiam quandam eiusdem cum veneno ideæ & characterismi, æquè pernitiosam contagiosamq; vt ipsa pestilens est. In annonæ æstuantis caritate quot sunt qui alimentis prauis, vt bulbis, brássicis, raphanis, cæpis, oleribus agrestibus, radicib9, arborumq; foliis & germinib9, vescetes grauissimis postea morbis correpti sunt? eiusmodi cibis magnos sæpè exercitus deletos esse constat. Validos exercitus fœdarum aquarum potu concidisse, quin etiā frugū viriatarū vsu, historię tradunt. Fit namq; interdū vt diutissimè seruata frumenta ac cerealia femina putrescant, & male condita repositaq; humore contrahant atq; sitū. Hipp. refert, eos qui leguminib9 in Æno fame premente in cibatu vsi fuissent, cruri b. debilitatos, genuūq; dolore tentatos: quasdam n. terras iniqui succi legumina oleraq; producere in cōfesso est. Sed quid multis? Ex variis cibis diuersarū qualitatum viriūq; contrariarū difficiles & contumaces gritudines generari nemo inficiabit, qui ali-acres, acres, alios falsos, alios summe frigidos, calidos, humidos, siccos, austeros, astringentes, amaros, alios deniq; venenosis qualitatibus esse praeditos, vt cicutâ, ferulâ, tytimallô, hyoscyamô, quib. saepe homines in famis inclementia vescuntur praenouerit. Sic Gal. ex semiputrido tritico morbû ortû communé asseruit. Ex vitiosæ cereuisiæ potu, quæ ex semiputrido hordeo parata fuerat, vidi vno in loco tempore eodem, multos decubuisse eodé morbo, aliis sic nuspiâ affectis. Aliquot ab hinc annis celebratæ sunt nuptiæ in quedâ pago, in quib. cû carnes ob æstum putrescere cœpisset, quidâ ex illis, q eas auidius comedissent, decubuerunt, plures verò ex contagione in eundem morbû lapsi perierunt. Proinde cauendû vnicuiq; imprimis est, ne improbi succi cibos vsurpet, vnde tot valetudini vitæq; ipsi incommoda impendent.
units.tr: A common disease is called one that not only has a common cause but can also spread and be passed on to many others by contagion. The common cause is not only the air but also putrid water, or tainted food or drink. The question here is whether common diseases, such as the plague, take their origin from the fault of bad food. Some place the seeds of the plague in the air alone. Others think that the contagion of plague flows only from human bodies. Others deny even this. Some ascribe it to an injury of the air and sky, such as great and unusual storms or major conjunctions of the planets. But they show that the seed of the plague is not contained in the air alone, nor does it always depend on an injury to the air or the harshness of the sky, nor does it break out only from human bodies, since those foul vapours rising from lakes, caves and rotting animal carcasses infect our bodies. Those, however, who deny that common diseases can arise from human bodies and from a fault of diet, such as bad foods and putrid humours, contend that a common disease always has a common cause, namely a poisonous and contagious air.
