They do not consider that a substance of the same form and character as the poison, and just as deadly and contagious as the pestilence itself, can be generated within us. In the dear years of grain, how many have been seized by grievous diseases afterwards, having eaten bad foods such as bulbs, cabbages, radishes, onions, wild herbs, roots, and the leaves and shoots of trees? It is established that great armies have often been destroyed by such foods. Histories also relate that strong armies have been brought low by drinking foul water, and even by eating spoiled grain. For it sometimes happens that grain and cereal seeds, kept for a very long time, rot, and when badly stored they draw in moisture and mustiness. Hippocrates reports that those who, in a time of famine at Aenus, lived on pulses as food, were weakened in the legs and afflicted with pain in the knees; for it is agreed that certain soils produce pulses and herbs of a bad juice. But why say more? No one will deny that difficult and stubborn diseases are generated from various foods of different qualities and contrary powers, who knows that some foods are sharp, some acrid, some false, some extremely cold, hot, moist, dry, astringent, bitter, and others, finally, endowed with poisonous qualities, such as hemlock, giant fennel, spurge and henbane, which men often eat in the harshness of famine. Thus Galen asserted that a common disease arose from half-rotten wheat. I myself have seen that, from drinking bad beer brewed from half-rotten barley, many in one place at the same time were laid low by the same disease, while others, who had not drunk it, were in no way affected. A few years ago a wedding was celebrated in a certain village, in which, when the meat had begun to putrefy from the heat, some of those who had eaten it more greedily fell ill, and more who caught it from contagion sank into the same disease and perished. Therefore, above all, everyone must take care not to consume foods of bad juice, from which so many discomforts for health and life itself hang over them.

units.la: AD QVÆST. VIII.
units.tr: AD QVÆST. VIII.

units.la: An ciborum natura & potestas ad varia gentium ingenia moresque aliquid conferat?
units.tr: Does the nature and power of foods contribute anything to the varied dispositions and customs of nations?

units.la: Admiranda plane gentium populorumq; deprehenduntur ingenia, variique animorum mores. Hos autem temperatu-ram corporis sequi, temperaturam vero consonare spirituum confusione, atque commoderamoderatione testes praeter Platonem sunt Philosophi & Medici. Pro ciborum autem diversitate ac mutatione temperamenta variari a'q; immutari non inficias iturus est, qui alimentorum vim memorabilem ac singularem ab omnibus Philosophis celebribusq; Medicis proditam consideranti. Persae pro montana sua & in hospita regione planam ac fertilem occupare cupiuerunt: Vetuit Cyrus, quod sciret, ut plantis femina, sic hominum vitas regionibus similes fieri.
units.tr: Truly admirable are the dispositions of nations and peoples, and the varied habits of their minds. That these follow the temperament of the body, and that the temperament in turn corresponds to the confusion and moderation of the spirits, is attested by the philosophers and physicians, Plato among them. Whoever considers the remarkable and singular power of food, as handed down by all the philosophers and the famous physicians, will not deny that temperaments vary and change with the diversity and change of diet. The Persians, who had a mountainous homeland, wished to occupy a flat and fertile region that was foreign to them. Cyrus forbade it, because he knew that, as plants are, so human lives become like the regions in which they grow.

units.la: Planta enim qua transferuntur, saepe toto genere immutari conspicuuntur. Causam praecipuam nutrimento assribunt naturae prudentes, quanquam & coeli virtus hic non est proscribenda, plurimum enim referre testis quotidiana experientia est. Ex ferocibus & sylvestribus quis negabit urbanas fieri & mites plantas? Coeli solique mutatione naturam immutare tam est verum quam quod verissimum. Exigui namque intervalli mutatio atque translatio, hoc est, duorum, trium, pluriumve passuum transitus maximas efficit differentias. Arbores translatas mutari, satis testatur Persea, quae in Persidem nata pestilens esse fertur, deportata vero & translata in Aegyptum mutata natura in cibos recipitur, succosq; noxios deponit. Saepe arbor laeta ac nitens in alium translocata locum deteriorus terra succo & alimento deperiisse visa est. Aristoteles, Plato, Theophrastus, caeterique Philosophi, quique de situ orbis literis mandarunt, ipsa animantia ab alimentis immutari testantur, in primis vero aqua-
units.tr: For plants are often seen to change in their whole kind when they are transplanted. Wise natural philosophers ascribe the chief cause to nourishment, although the power of the climate is not to be rejected here either; daily experience testifies how much it matters. Who would deny that wild and woodland plants become cultivated and gentle? To change nature by a change of sky and soil is as true as any truth. For even a small shift and transplanting, that is, a passage of two, three or more paces, produces the greatest differences. That trees change when transplanted is sufficiently shown by the persea, which is said to be harmful when born in Persia, but when carried over and transplanted into Egypt its nature changes, it is taken as food, and it lays aside its harmful juices. Often a flourishing and shining tree, transplanted to another place, has been seen to perish for lack of the juice and nourishment of its land, which is worse. Aristotle, Plato, Theophrastus and the other philosophers who committed to writing the description of the world testify that animals themselves are changed by their food, and above all by the waters.

units.la: Persea non est vulgaris pomi Persici arbor, ut quidam putant. aquarum mirabili vi id contingere prodiderunt. Traduntur & inveniuntur fontes, amnes, lacus, quorum haustu memorabiles & insignes fiunt alterationes: sunt quaedam aquae quae nigredinem, quaedam quae canorem potu pecoribus afferunt.
units.tr: The persea is not the common peach tree, as some think. They have also reported that this comes about through the wonderful power of waters. Springs, rivers and lakes are found and recorded whose drinking brings about remarkable and striking changes: some waters bring blackness, others a white colour, to the cattle that drink them.

units.la: Apud Æthiopes Macrobios quib. dimidio vita protensior est quam nostra, est lacus, quo perfusa corpora velut oleo nitescunt, adeoque nitidum est, ut ne caducas quidem vehat frondes, sed illico folia lapsa ad fundum demittat laticis tenuitate.
units.tr: Among the Ethiopian Macrobians, whose lives are longer by half than ours, there is a lake in which bodies bathed in it shine as if with oil. It is so bright that it does not even carry falling leaves, but at once lets them sink to the bottom through the thinness of its water.

units.la: In oppido Garamantum Debri fons est alternis vicibus die frigens, noctu feruens: ac per eadem venarum comerciai nerdum igni to vapore aestuat, interdum glaciali horrore algescit. Quis non miretur fontem frigere calore, calere frigore? occasio enim mundum a calore temperante it a incipit incalescere, ut, intactu abstineas, contigisse noxiu sit. Rursus cum ortus solis incanduerit radiis, feruenta sint omnia, sic glaciales eu omit scaturigines, ut hauriri etiam a sitientibus nequeat. Supendis sane & incredibile memoratu, quod tam breui temporis curriculo natura tam dissonam sui faciat mutationem. Scamandrus ille Homericus exiguus amnis Xanthus appellatus, existimatur, quod flauus redderet oves. Euenire autem id a succo, quem ex terris, per quas transeunt fluunt, concipiunt, manifestum est. Nam & arborum plantarum radices succos ex terra viscerib. sugere trahere, ing alimentum conuertere ostendunt alii atq. alii saporem differentiaque fructuum. Quod si enim sic nutri
units.tr: In the town of the Garamantes there is a spring, Debri, which by turns is cold by day and boils by night; and through the same veins, its flow is now heated by fire and vapour, and at other times it grows cold with an icy chill. Who would not marvel that a spring grows cold from heat and hot from cold? For the world begins to grow warm from the tempering heat, so that, if you refrain from touching it, it would be harmful to have touched it. Again, when the rising sun has grown hot with its rays, all things are scorching, and so all the icy springs become so cold that they cannot even be drawn by the thirsty. Truly it is a wonder and incredible to relate that nature in so brief a course of time makes so discordant a change. That Homeric river Scamander, a small stream, was called Xanthus, and is thought to have been so named because it made the sheep yellow. That this happens from the juice which they take up from the lands through which they flow is clear. For others, and others again, show that the roots of trees and plants suck and draw juices from the earth into their inner parts and turn them into nourishment, and that from these comes the taste and difference of the fruits.

units.la: {H} nutrirentur, unum esset omnium in omnibus sapor frugum, fructuum, aliorumq; seminum. Arabia, India, Syria, caeterarumq; regionum poma & fruges tanta gustus odorumq; varietate non distinguerentur, nisi terra dissimilia succorum genera continerent. Hinc tot vinorum genera prodigiosa. Vinum in Arcadia foecunditatem foeminis apportare, viris autem rabiem, in Arcadia quoddam genus esse, quo abigatur partus, Trochenium potum non generare, aliud quod somnum conciliet, alterum quod perunigilium faciat, etiam unam esse, quae abortus faciat, & haud dubie terrarum maleficos pestilentesq; succos, aquas & fruges fructusq; omnes noxios insalubresq; reddere, ut a quibus alantur, & nutrimentum capiant, apud grauissimos autores Aristotelem, Theophrastum, Athenaeum, Plinium, & alios scriptum reperitur. Differentiam aquarum quotidie sentimus, de quib. alibi seorsim, Deo dante, & copiosius differemus.
units.tr: {H} For if they were nourished in this way, there would be one taste for all fruits, produce and other seeds alike. Arabia, India, Syria and the other regions would not be distinguished by such variety of flavour and smell for fruits and crops, unless the earth contained kinds of juices unlike one another. Hence come so many prodigious kinds of wine: wine in Arcadia brings fertility to women but madness to men; there is a certain kind in Arcadia by which birth is driven out; a drink from Trochenium does not produce offspring; another induces sleep, another causes sleeplessness for a whole night; there is also one that causes miscarriage. And undoubtedly the poisonous and pestilent juices of the earth make waters, crops and all fruits harmful and unwholesome, so that those by which they are fed and draw their nourishment are noxious; as is found written by the most weighty authors, Aristotle, Theophrastus, Athenaeus, Pliny, and others. We perceive the difference of waters every day; about these we will speak separately elsewhere, God willing, and more fully.

units.la: Sed ad animalia pergamus, quae quibusdam in locis carent felle, praesertim in parte quada agri Chalcidici. In Euboea pecora eo carent, quod non aliunde quam a pabulo accidere indubitatum putatur. In Ponto quoq; eo carent, quae vescuntur absinthio, cum tamen illo eximie pinguescant.
units.tr: But let us go on to animals, which in some places have no gall, especially in a certain part of the Chalcidic region. In Euboea the cattle lack it, which is thought beyond doubt to come from nothing other than their pasture. In Pontus too they lack it, those that feed on wormwood, although they fatten excellently on it.

units.la: Gallis gallinaceis in officinis Ferrariis educatis, lienem non reperiri certissimi autores tradunt.
units.tr: Certain authors report that chickens reared in the poultry yards of Ferrara are found without a spleen.

units.la: Pecora, quae in alveis aut canalib. ex Tamarisco fabricatis bibunt, sine splene inveniuntur, cum primis sues. Unde praeceptum est lienosis & melancolis cibum potumq; dare in vasis ex eafactis.
units.tr: Cattle that drink in troughs or channels made of tamarisk are found without a spleen, the pigs above all. Hence the rule is given that those who suffer from the spleen and melancholy should be given food and drink in vessels made of it.

units.la: In Naxo fere omnib. quadrupedib. adeo gran-desel esse Aristot. scripsit, ut qui sacra fecerint ad-uenae, stupescant, rem scil. prodigii loco arbitrari, quam sane amplitudinem, vel a potu, vel a pabulo contingere verisimile est.
units.tr: Aristotle wrote that on Naxos almost all the four-footed animals are so large that foreigners who have come to perform sacrifices are amazed, and regard the thing as a marvel. It is indeed likely that this size comes from either their drink or their pasture.

units.la: In suibus & anseribus dulcibus cibariis enutritis iecur incredibile pene incrementum assumere omnib. non est nō noxium: unde veteres culinae in operibus ganea mirifice id commendarunt.
units.tr: In pigs and geese fed on sweet foods, the liver takes on an almost incredible growth, and this is not without harm to anyone; hence the old cooks commended it wonderfully in their works on the making of delicacies.

units.la: Melle vescentes populos longam aetatem agere & sanam, Athenaeus testis est. Septentrionis quidam populi id optime norunt, mulsam bibendam iis praecipientes, qui animi sunt praeparti & pusilli, quasi eius miti leniq; succo vis anima robo-retur atq; augeatur. Celebre est Pollionis Romuli exemplum, quem centesimum excedentem annu, cum Augustus Caesar hospes interrogaret, quanam ratione maxime vigorem illum animi corporisq; custodiuisset, ille respondit, intus mulso, foris oleo.
units.tr: Athenaeus is witness that peoples who eat honey live long and healthy lives. Certain peoples of the North know this very well, prescribing mead to drink for those who are dejected and feeble of spirit, as if by its mild and gentle juice the strength of the soul is restored and increased. The example of Pollio Romulus is famous: when he had reached a hundred years, and Augustus Caesar, as his guest, asked by what means he had so greatly preserved that vigour of mind and body, he answered: "With mead inside, with oil outside."

units.la: In Hispaniola insula gregis pecorum ex nostris terris in ea deportatos, papulo quidem illius soli pinguescere, verum carnes eorum in cibis infuauses esse & sentiri testantur, qui de situ orbis nuper inuenti literis mandarunt: Quin ossa eorum aut medullae expertia inueniri, aut si contineant, aquosiore omnino spectari, fuesq; eadem in insula egregie obesari a-greshib. pomis, carnesq; gustui incundiores nancisci, cicures item sues in sylvis feros effici, & sylvestres quibusdam in locis suis nostris minores, cauda pe-dibusq; dibusq; dissimiles carnes prabere maxime salutares praecipuiq; saporis experimento compertu habent. Id quod cibariorum praestantia & natura tribui vere potest.
units.tr: Those who have recently written about the world, and about the new discoveries, testify that herds of cattle carried from our lands to the island of Hispaniola grow fat on the pasture of that soil, but that their flesh is found and tasted to be insipid as food. Moreover, their bones or marrow are found to lack substance, or if they contain it, it is seen to be altogether more watery; and in that same island pigs grow remarkably fat on wild fruits, and get meat more pleasant to the taste; likewise tame pigs become wild in the woods, and in some places the wild ones are smaller than ours, unlike them in tail and feet. They have found by experiment that their flesh is most wholesome and of peculiar flavour. This can truly be attributed to the excellence and nature of their food.

units.la: In hominibus memorabilis horum natura non minus conspicua est, cum pro ipsorum diversitate & mutatione temperamenta immutentur. Quis enim ignorat, temperatas esse cas, boniq; succi cibos, temperatos humores spiritusq; puriores gignere, indeq; mentem puriorem, defecatiorem & prudentiorem euadere, rationemq; constantiorem & solidiorem effici. Animum adipe & sanguine suffocatum nihil coeleste sublimeq; meditari posse, Galen* asserit.
units.tr: The remarkable nature of these things is no less evident in human beings, since their temperaments change with the diversity and change of their diet. For who does not know that foods that are temperate and of good juice produce temperate humours and purer spirits, and from these the mind becomes purer, clearer and wiser, and the reason is made more steady and firm? Galen asserts that a mind choked with fat and blood cannot think of anything heavenly or lofty.

units.la: Vinum praestantissimum nutrimentum utentium moribus sese applicare non negabit, qui, tardiores eo incendi & excitari mobilioresque reddi, contra vero mobiliores dissolui pigrosq; reddi, observarit, ut ita nunc retardos, nunc superbos, nunc insanibundos efficiat. Zeno dicere solitus est, se a vino perinde affici atq; lupini ab aqua, qui in ea macerati omnem amaritudinem deponunt, dulcesq; reddantur.
units.tr: Whoever has observed that wine, the most excellent nourishment, adapts itself to men's customs, will not deny it: that it makes the slower kind more quick and stirred up, and on the contrary renders the more mobile kind loose and sluggish, so that it now makes men sluggish, now proud, now frenzied. Zeno was accustomed to say that he was affected by wine in the same way as lupine beans by water: when they have soaked in it they lay aside all bitterness and become sweet.

units.la: Coelum, solumq; maximum momentum ad faciliores diffisilioresq; cibos generandos obtinere, natura rerum prudentes unanimi asserunt consensu. Nec dubium est pro caeli aerisq; clementia ac benignitate solum quoq; succos benignos adipisci atq; salubres, quibus deinde enutrita planta alimenta exhibet salubriora. Unde caeli, quo necessario cun-
units.tr: Those who understand the nature of things agree unanimously that the heaven and the soil hold the greatest importance in producing foods that are easier or harder to digest. Nor is there doubt that, through the mildness and kindness of the sky and air, the soil too acquires kindly and wholesome juices, by which the plant, once nourished, then supplies more wholesome food. Hence the heaven, with which it is necessarily…

units.la: Ita alluntur, aerisq; sub Luna concavo temperatura statusq; imprimis animadvertenda. Tempora enim anni si sunt constantia, & tempestiue tempestiua in iis omnia reddentur, fructus quoque terra melior es proveniunt atq; utiliores. Quod si praepostera sint tempora & intempestiua, terra etiam fundet dabitq; alimenta insalubriora, ut si frigora sint intempestiua, imbres & calores intempestiui & immoderati. Ab his enim corporis temperationem depravari, animiq; mores mirum non est. Observatur hoc in tractibus & regionibus, in quib. caelum adeo est iniquum & inuidum, ut temporum anni temperatum ordinem non seruet, unde incolarum ingenia animiq; mores necessario etiam intemperantiam non mediocrem sortiuntur. Hippocrates morum temperaturas locis aeriq; acceptas retulit. Vult enim mores temperatos & probos fieri in locis & terris temperatis, contra in intemperatis. Ideoq; Europaeos feros, indomitos, iracundos & insociabiles asserit: Asianos mitiores, ignavos, imbelles animisq; abiectiores: quod etiam a Lucano dictum eleganter reperio,
units.tr: Thus they are nourished, and the temperature and condition of the air beneath the concave of the Moon must be considered above all. For if the seasons of the year are steady, and everything comes in its proper time, the fruits of the earth also turn out better and more useful. But if the seasons are reversed and untimely, the earth too will yield food that is less wholesome: for example, if the cold is untimely, and the rains and heats are untimely and excessive. It is no wonder that the constitution of the body is spoiled by these, and the morals of the mind as well. This is observed in regions and countries where the sky is so harsh and hostile that it does not keep the orderly sequence of the seasons, and so the natures and morals of the inhabitants necessarily acquire no small intemperance. Hippocrates attributed the temperaments of men's characters to places and airs. For he holds that morals become temperate and upright in temperate places and lands, but the opposite in intemperate ones. Hence he calls Europeans fierce, untamed, irascible and unsociable, and Asians milder, slothful, unwarlike and more spiritless. I find that Lucan also said this elegantly:

units.la: Emollit gentes clementia caeli.
units.tr: The mildness of the sky softens nations.

units.la: Temporibus autem anni omnia haec imputantur. Faba, teste Theophrasto, quodam in loco ab afflatu quodam incoctilis est: fruges item & reliqua semina cerealia a succo telluris, in quam seruntur, incoctilia proveniunt. Haec igitur in cibatu probu alimentum minime dabunt, corpus namq; atq; animum depravabunt.
units.tr: All these things are attributed to the seasons of the year. According to Theophrastus, the bean is spoiled in a certain place by some blast of wind; likewise grains and the other cereal seeds come forth spoiled by the juice of the soil into which they are sown. These, then, will by no means give good food for eating, for they will corrupt both body and mind.

units.la: H
units.tr: H

units.la: Gallis leuitatem innasci, & audaciam omnib* fere Romanis historiis proditum est, cuius causam nullam aliam crediderim, quam coeli inconstantiam. Intemperatam enim Galliam esse, assiduis flatibus agitari constat, quin & crebrioribus imbribus obnoxiam. Proinde licet vinorum omnium fere cibariorum ad vitam sustinendam necessariorum feracissima sit, non tamen adeo salutaria alimenta suggerit, quod patet in tritici probatione apud Theophrastum & Plinium.
units.tr: It is recorded in nearly all Roman histories that levity and boldness are innate in the Gauls, and I can believe no other cause for this than the inconstancy of their sky. For it is established that Gaul is intemperate, shaken by constant winds, and moreover exposed to frequent rains. Therefore, although it is almost the most fertile of all lands in the foods needed to sustain life, it does not supply foods so healthful, as is clear from the testing of wheat in Theophrastus and Pliny.

units.la: Aphros & maxime Carthaginenses perfidos omnium consensu dictos inuenimus, Memorabile illud Cic. est in Orat. pro l. Agraria, dum ait, ingenerari hominibus mores non tam a stirpe generis & feminis, quam ex his rebus, quae ex ipsa natura loci, & a vitae consuetudine suppeditantur, quibus alimur & vivimus. Chartaginenses mendaces sunt ac fraudulenti non genere sed natura loci, quod propter portus suos multis & variis mercatorum adventarum sermonibus ad studium fallendi studio quaesitus ducebantur.
units.tr: We find the Africans, and especially the Carthaginians, called faithless by the agreement of all. That famous passage of Cicero in the speech on the Agrarian Law is memorable, where he says that morals are produced in men not so much by the stock of their birth and their women as by those things which come from the very nature of the place and from the custom of life, by which we are fed and live. The Carthaginians are deceitful and fraudulent, not by birth but by the nature of their place: because of their harbours, they were drawn by eagerness for deceit to the many and varied talk of foreign merchants.

units.la: Ligures montani duri atq; agrestes sunt, quod docet ager ipse nihil ferendo, nisi multa cultura & labore quaesitum.
units.tr: The Ligurians are rough and rustic mountain people, as the land itself shows, which bears nothing unless it is won by much cultivation and labour.

units.la: Campani semper superbi, ob agrorum bonitatem, fructuum magnitudinem, urbis salubritate.
units.tr: The Campanians have always been proud, on account of the goodness of their fields, the abundance of their fruits, and the healthfulness of their city.

units.la: Hispanos ac Lusitanos iactabundos & astutos videmus, quae partim a solo coeloq;, partim a vitae accidere dubium non est.
units.tr: We see the Spaniards and Portuguese boastful and crafty, and there is no doubt that this comes partly from the soil and sky and partly from their way of life.

units.la: Aristot. in animantibus a sanguinis consistentia & & substantia petere videtur prudentiam, sortitu-dinem, timiditatem. Tenuem enim & purum atq; mundum sapientiores efficere credidit. In quibus e-nim humor subtilior atq; purior, iis sensus quoque subtiliores puriores atq; insunt: timidiores qua aquo-sum nimis & dilutum obtinent: animosos, irasun-dos, faribundos, quibus crassus biliosus & feruens sanguine Sanguis enim quia ultimum corporis alimentum habetur, alimentu aute materia est, facit ut per-multa animalib. eueniant, tum per mores, tum per sensum, si calidus aut frigidus existat, tenuis & cras-sus, turbulentus, splendidus aut nitidus. Hac Arist. Plato huic suffragatur, improbos succos corporis anima noxios esse volens, indeq; varios & multi-plices, graviores & leviores agritudines exoriri, quae eam pro loco adque resederint, afficiunt. Un-de ad principem eius facultatem deuenientes obli-uiones, atq; hebetudines, conuulsiones, stupores, tre-mores, phrenitidem, melancoliam, vertiginem, a-poplexias, lethargos: sin ad cor, iracundias, audá-cias, timiditates, febresq; inferent. Idem animam corporea humiditatis potestate in obliuionem labi eorum, quae ante, quàm corporis esset coercita vinculis, coperta habebat, videtur q; sentire, nimiam hanc humiditate esse causam de-mentia & stultitia, siccitatem vero ad prudentiam adipiscendam plurimum conferre. Quorum igi-tur corpora sunt humidiora, vt in terris frigidis & humidis, minus sunt prudentes callidiq;, sed sim-plices: at calidarum & siccarum terrarum H 4 populus populi versuti & prudentes iudicantur. Hinc graeci leves & mendaces quidem, sed ob aeris siccitatem sapientiores. Itali pronidi ingeniosi & Venerei sunt, teste Vitruuio. Gasconez iracundos & furibundos dicunt non aliam ob causam, quam quod biliosi imprimis vtantur vitulo, aliis scilicet, capris, raphanis, vinisque vehementissimis.
units.tr: Aristotle, in his work on animals, seems to derive prudence, courage and timidity from the consistency and substance of the blood. For he believed that thin, pure and clean blood makes men wiser. Those in whom the humour is finer and purer have finer and purer senses as well; those who have too much watery and diluted humour are more timid; those who are spirited, irascible and quarrelsome have thick, bilious and fiery blood. For since blood is regarded as the last nourishment of the body, and is the matter of nourishment, it causes many things to happen to animals, both in their morals and in their senses, whether it is hot or cold, thin or thick, turbulent, bright or clear. So far Aristotle. Plato supports him, holding that the bad humours of the body are harmful to the soul, and that from these various and manifold diseases, graver and lighter, arise, which afflict the soul according to the place where they have settled. Hence, when they reach its principal faculty, they bring forgetfulness, dullness, convulsions, stupors, tremors, phrenitis, melancholy, vertigo, apoplexies and lethargies; but when they reach the heart, they bring anger, boldness, timidity and fevers. Plato also seems to hold that the soul, by the power of bodily moisture, slips into forgetting those things which it had held before it was bound by the chains of the body; he thinks that excessive moisture is the cause of madness and folly, while dryness contributes greatly to gaining prudence. Therefore those whose bodies are more moist, as in cold and wet lands, are less prudent and shrewd, but simple; while the peoples of hot and dry lands are judged clever and prudent. Hence the Greeks are light and deceitful, but wiser because of the dryness of their air. The Italians, according to Vitruvius, are quick-witted, clever and fond of love. The Gascons are said to be irascible and furious for no other reason than that the bilious especially use veal, that is, goats, radishes and very strong wines.

units.la: Verum ingeniorum morumque varietatem, non natura loci tantum, vitae consuetudini, aeris temperiei intemperieque, verum etiam generis sexus & feminini non raro acceptam ferendam esse, fatebitur, qui animum ad similitudinem causas retulerit. Deprehendet certe mirum naturae artificium ingenium.
units.tr: Yet the variety of talents and morals is to be attributed, as one who considers the causes by likeness will admit, not only to the nature of the place, to the custom of life, and to the temperateness or intemperateness of the air, but also not rarely to the kind and sex of the parents. Certainly the wonderful craft of nature is discovered in talent.

units.la: Saepe in familias transitus fit per sobolem. Videmus plerumque parvulos modo cicatrices, modo qualescunque originis suae notas referre.
units.tr: Often a transmission into families happens through the offspring. We see that small children commonly bear scars, or whatever marks of their origin.

units.la: Biz antius nobilis pugil, qui matrem habuit ex Aethiope per adulterinum conceptam, qua nihil patri comparandum reddidisset, in Aethiopem atrum degeneravit.
units.tr: Bizanthius, a noble boxer, who had a mother conceived by an Ethiopian through adultery, having no resemblance to his father, degenerated into a black Ethiopian.

units.la: Regem Antiochum Arteon quidam ex plebe Syriaca sic facie emula mentitus est, ut postmodum Laodice uxor regia obiecta popularis isto tamdiu dissimulavit defunctum maritum, quoad ex arbitratu eius regni successor ordinaretur.
units.tr: A certain man from the common people of Syria so falsely pretended to be King Antiochus Arteon in appearance that afterwards Laodice, the royal wife, pretended for so long that her husband was dead, until a successor was appointed at the discretion of that kingdom.

units.la: Inter Cn. Pomp. & Vibium humili loco natum, tantus error extitit de paribus lineamentis, ut Romani Vibium Pompeii nomine, Pompeium Vibii vocabulo cognominarent. Oratorem L. Plancum Rubrius Histrio sic expressit, ut & ipse Plancus à populo nominaretur.
units.tr: Between Gnaeus Pompey and Vibius, who was born of humble rank, there was such an error about the likeness of features that the Romans called Vibius by the name of Pompey, and Pompey by the name of Vibius. The actor Rubrius portrayed the orator Lucius Plancus so exactly that Plancus himself was called by the people.

units.la: Armentarius Mirmillo & Cassius Severus oratoriu ita se reddiderunt mutuo ut si quando pariter viderentur, dignosci non possent, nisi discrepantiam indicaret habitus.
units.tr: The armourer-gladiator Mirmillo and the orator Cassius Severus made themselves so alike to each other that if they were ever seen together, they could not be told apart, unless their dress showed the difference.

units.la: M. Messala Censorius & Menogenes ex facie vulgi, hoc fuerunt uterq;, quod singuli, nec alium Messalam quam Menogenem, nec Menogenem alium quam Messalam putarunt.
units.tr: Marcus Messala the censor and Menogenes were, from the face of the common people, both of them such that each thought there was no Messala other than Menogenes, nor any Menogenes other than Messala.

units.la: Quid? quod nostro etiam seculo nostrisq; interris indiscreti vultus corporisq; miracula extet. At licet pleriq; sentiant, nullum posse excedere 7. pedū longitudine, quod intra hunc modum fuerit Hercules, deprehensum tamen est Romanis temporib. sub D. Augusto Pusionem & Secundillā denos pedes & amplius habuisse proceritatis, quorum reliquiæ adhuc in conditorio Sallustianorum ante annos aliquot visæ sunt: Sicut postmodū sub D. Claudio principe nomine Gabbaras ex Arabia advest nouem pedum fuit & totidem unciarum quamuis annis ferme mille ante Augustū huiusmodi forma non apparuit, sicut nec post Claudium visa est.
units.tr: Why? In our own age and in our own lands there are also wonders of indistinguishable faces and bodies. Although most people think that no one can exceed seven feet in height, since Hercules was of that measure, it has nonetheless been found that in Roman times, under the deified Augustus, Pusio and Secundilla had ten feet and more of stature, whose remains were seen some years ago in the burial place of the Sallustians. Likewise, afterwards under the emperor Claudius, a man named Gabbaras came from Arabia who was nine feet and as many inches tall; yet about a thousand years before Augustus no such form appeared, and it was not seen again after Claudius.

units.la: Scripta quoq; ex antiquitate memorias reuo- eant in fidem veri, quod bello Cretico, cum elata slumina impetu plus quam vi amnica inuecta terras rupissent, post fluctuum discessum inter pluri- ma alia humanum cadauer repertum sit cubitū trium atq; triginta, cuius spectandi cupidine L. Flaccum Legatum, atq; Metellum ipsum, quod H s andiauditu refutarant, cum oculis aspicerent, miracu-lo quasi captos, eadem memoria receptum est. Non omiserim Euthymenis filium Salamiam, qui in triennio creuit in sublimitatem tria cubita, sed incessu tardo, sensu hebeti, robusta voce, pubertate festina, verum morbis statim plurimis vexatus immoderatis aegritudinum suppliciis praecipitem incrementi celeritatem compensavit.
units.tr: Writings from antiquity also recall memories worthy of belief: in the Cretan war, when swollen rivers, carried by an impetus more than a river's force, had broken into the lands, after the waters withdrew a human corpse was found among many other things, thirty-three cubits long; and it is recorded in the same memory that Lucius Flaccus the legate, and Metellus himself, because they had refused to believe it on hearsay, were seized as if by a miracle when they looked at it with their own eyes. I would not omit the son of Euthymenes of Salamis, who grew in three years to a height of three cubits; but his gait was slow, his sense dull, his voice strong, and his puberty hasty; yet he was at once beset by very many diseases, and by the immoderate torments of illnesses he made up for the headlong speed of his growth.

units.la: Possem hic multa adducere, quae fastidio parcens praetereo. Vide Solinum cap. 5.
units.tr: I could bring forward here many more things, which I pass over, sparing the reader's weariness. See Solinus, chapter 5.

units.la: AD QVAEST IX.
units.tr: Question IX.

units.la: Morbi quod quibusdam gentib. peculiariter accidant, an victus ratio incausa sit? & cur repente quida hominib. exoriantur in certis membris? consuetudinem deniq; plurimum valere.
units.tr: Whether the diseases that befall certain peoples in particular are caused by their manner of diet; why some people suddenly break out in certain limbs; and, finally, how greatly custom prevails.

units.la: MOrborum plurimorum causam vel abundantiam, vel cibariorum diversitatem esse, potissimam vero rerum naturalium abusum, illegitimam intempestiuamq; earum administrationem, (ut cum bona dieta negligitur, aerq; male affectus non corrigitur, cum euacuatio, retentio, somnus, vigilia, & affectus animi finistre & immoderate se habent) inter omnes Medicinae peritos conuenit. Quosdam etiam morbos terris quibusdam & populis peculiares esse, quos aeris coeliq; inclementior status improborumq; alimentorum visus excitare consueuit, notius est quam ut explicari fusius debedebeat. Quofdam vero repete certis membris innafci,hominib. optima etiam conftitutione praeditis a natura, mirabile aliquib,videbitur, praefertim iis qui ignorant cibaria, per quae vi- uunt. Elephantiafin Aegypti peculiare malum effe, Alexandrinofq; magis infeftare, vt quorum victus ex farina elixata eft &lentib. quae illic in magna copia proueniunt, teftatur ille, qui Ele- phantiafin morbu effe fcripfit nafcente ppter flumina Nili in media Aegypto. Vefcuntitem cochleis &falfamctis largiffime, afininis quoq; nonnulli carnib.quecraffos fuccos atramq; bilem pariunt, qui poftmodu humores ob coeli feruidam conftitutionem ad cutim euocati ea foeda ficcaq; fcabie deformant, evaditq; morb, plane deteftandus, elephantorum cuti fimilis, per multa durans fecula, & quafi haereditario jure pertinaciter etiam in pofteris haerens. Brit- tones, Nortmanni & Narbonenfis prouinciae populi huic malo funt oportuniores. Apud Pleumofios, vulgoFlandros, frequentiffimu eft. Caufae adfcribuntur efui pifciu creberrimo & liberaliori, tu potib.ex corruptis frugib.cocin-natis, operi ite lactario, quo imodice eos vti conftat: quamuis Gal.nufquam hunc morbum apud Scythas, quos ... nucuparut, vagari cenfet: quin & in Germania haereditaria eam effe, rariffime fentitur, vt plurimum vero per contagium inducitur. Italiae ante Pompeii Magni aetate ignota fuiffe Elephantiafin Plin. conconstanter asserit, vt ita nullum hodie sit dubium Alexandrinorum mores, delitiasque oēs Asianas Italiam inuasisse.
units.tr: Almost all physicians agree that the cause of most diseases is either excess or a variety of foods, but above all the abuse of the natural things and their unlawful and untimely management: when good diet is neglected, when the air is not corrected where it is bad, and when evacuation, retention, sleep, waking, and the affections of the mind are disordered or immoderate. That certain diseases are peculiar to certain lands and peoples, which the harsher state of the air and sky and the use of bad foods are wont to provoke, is too well known to need to be explained at length. That some diseases grow in particular limbs, even in men endowed by nature with the best constitution, will seem wonderful to some, especially to those who do not know the foods on which they live. Elephantiasis is a peculiar disease of Egypt and attacks the Alexandrians more, as he testifies who wrote that elephantiasis is a disease arising in the middle of Egypt because of the rivers of the Nile. Their diet is largely of boiled meal and lentils, which grow there in great abundance. Some also eat snails and salted fish very freely, and the flesh of asses, which produce thick juices and black bile. Afterwards these humours, drawn to the skin by the hot constitution of the sky, disfigure it with a foul and dry scab; and the disease, truly dreadful, like the skin of elephants, lasts through many ages and clings stubbornly, as if by hereditary right, even in descendants. The Britons, the Normans, and the people of the province of Narbonne are more open to this evil. Among the Pleumosii, commonly called Flemings, it is very frequent. It is ascribed to the very frequent and abundant eating of fish, and to their drinking of sour foods, cooked from corrupted grain, and of milk products, which they are known to use immoderately. Although Galen thought that this disease does not wander among the Scythians, whom ... they call nucuparutes, yet in Germany it is seldom felt to be hereditary; for the most part it is introduced by contagion. Pliny steadily asserts that elephantiasis was unknown in Italy before the age of Pompey the Great; so there is now no doubt that the customs and all the Asian luxuries of the Alexandrians have invaded Italy.

units.la: Carbunculum Narbonensi provinciæ peculiarem, & Parthis obindiscretos cibos, grauem oris halitum esse testatur idem.
units.tr: The same author testifies that the carbuncle is peculiar to the province of Narbonne, and that the Parthians have a grave breath of the mouth because of their indiscriminate foods.

units.la: In Alpibus aliisque regionibus aquarum vitio atq; culpa homines gutturosos effici testis experientia est.
units.tr: Experience is witness that in the Alps and other regions people become goitred through the fault and defect of the waters.

units.la: Strumosi magis Lusitani.
units.tr: The Lusitanians are more subject to scrofula.

units.la: Hippocr. Eunuchos podagra non laborare scripsit in Aphor. quod tamen Galen. diligentissimus ejus interpres suo ævo aliter contigisse vidit, ob malam scilicet viuendi rationem. Podagram Italiæ incognitam aliquando fuisse traditum est, colicumq; dolorem Tiberii principatu irrepsisse, nec quenquam priorem ipso Imperatore id malum sensisse : Nunc per oës gentes disseminatum pertinacissime durat.
units.tr: Hippocrates wrote in the Aphorisms that eunuchs do not suffer from gout. Yet Galen, his most diligent interpreter, saw that in his own age it happened otherwise, namely because of a bad manner of living. It is recorded that gout was once unknown in Italy, and that colic pain crept in under the rule of Tiberius, and that no one before the emperor himself had felt that disease. Now it is spread through all nations and lasts most stubbornly.

units.la: Lues Venerea, quæ ab Hispanis ortum habuit, Hispanis primum & Gallis peculiaris fuit, nunc ex Venereo concubitu vniusq; impuritate & inquinamento sensim in vniuersum orbem est disseminata.
units.tr: The venereal plague, which had its origin among the Spaniards, was at first peculiar to the Spaniards and the French. Now, from venereal intercourse and the impurity and pollution of each person, it has gradually spread through the whole world.

units.la: Scorbutus, pessimus corporis humani inquilinus, non ita pridem Septentrionis gentē & loca maritima arctica inhabitantes coepit affligere, germ. Schurbock/Schurmund, alocis in quibus externis signis primo malitiam suam & contagium prodidisse compertum est:
units.tr: Scurvy, the worst inhabitant of the human body, not long ago began to afflict the peoples of the North and the arctic maritime places. In German it is called Schurbock or Schurmund. It has been found that it first revealed its malice and contagion by external signs in the places where it appeared.

units.la: Veteres de eo nihil certi prodiderűt,nisi quòd gingiuarum affectum ftomacacen dixerunt, cum videlicet illis corrosis & putrefactis den- tes cum fœdo odore, vel sponte excidunt, vel digitis apprehensi abscq; villa molestia & den- tifrangibulo eruuntur. Origo hujus mali non aliunde est quàm ex rancidorum, falidorum, indurator um infumatorumque alimentorum continuo esu vsuq;,cereuisiæq; præpinguioris & dulcioris potu,vnde sensim & paulatim, af- fiduaq; vitæ assuetudine primum sanguinis of-ficinam lienemq; adoritur inficitq;,tandem ir-repit absq; vllo etiam doloris sensu in omnes partes,gingiuas tamen primum & dentes inua-dens, liuidis etiam quandoq; & fuscis maculis crura circa tibias inprimis deformans cum ge-nuum dolore,quod malum scelotyrbe dicitur certissimum & confirmati scorbuti signum, non enim quæuis gingiuarum putrilago fœ-torq; scorbuti index est,vt temerè & imperite chirurgi opinantur,cum sæpe gingiuæ exacri-um calidorumq; humorum superno affluxu inflammentur,& putrescant, scorbuticæ vero gingiuarum putrilaginis origo ab epate sem-per ac liene dependet, meatuumq; inter hæc viscera obstructione.
units.tr: The ancients reported nothing certain about it, except that they called the affection of the gums stomacace [στομακάκη], namely when the teeth, corroded and rotten with a foul odour, either fall out of their own accord or, when caught by the fingers, are drawn out without any trouble and with a tooth-forceps. The origin of this disease is nothing other than the continual eating and use of rancid, salted, hardened, and smoked foods, and the drinking of beer that is too fat and sweet. From this, gradually and little by little, through constant habit of life, it first attacks and infects the workshop of the blood, the spleen; finally it creeps without any sense of pain into all parts, attacking the gums and teeth first, and deforming the shins especially with livid and dusky spots, with pain in the knees. This disease is called scelotyrbe [σκελοτυρβή], and it is a most certain sign of confirmed scurvy. For not every putrid decay of the gums and every foul smell is a sign of scurvy, as surgeons rashly and unskilfully think. The gums are often inflamed and rot from the upper inflow of sharp and hot humours. But the origin of scorbutic putrid decay of the gums always depends on the liver and the spleen, and on obstruction of the passages between these viscera.

units.la: Quamobrem minime mirum videri debet, si noui quotidie & priori ævo incogniti acci-dunt morbi, ex terrisq; in alias terras transfe-runtur ac deportantur,& peculiariter quibus-dam dam gentibus contingunt: etiam quosdam ho- minib. repente nasci & exoriri in certis mem- bris posse. Cum enim ratio viuendi noua vsur- petur, & ex alienis terris in nostras introduca- tur, quis inficias ibit, vel non censebit à cibo- rum improbitate gulæq; intemperie certis et- iam membris morbos importari posse? Ab In- dis cibum petentes contagium simul sperare oportet. Nam quis salubritatem in peregrinis illis & incognitis spondeat? Quot sunt, quorū renes grauiter tentantur calculo? Colica quot torquentur? quot vehementissimis capitis do- loribus? quot stomachi dolore debilitateque? oculorum hebetudine atq; caligine quot? quot digitorū manuumq; sæuissimis tormentis ex- cruciantur? Immodicum horum omnium v- sum improborum ciborum auctorem esse ar- gumento est, quod ipsa anima ciborum vitiis inficitur, id quod Parthis præcipue accidere ob cibos indiscretos, di&um est.
units.tr: Therefore it ought to seem least surprising if new diseases, unknown in earlier ages, arise every day, and are carried and transported from lands to other lands, and happen in particular to certain peoples; and that some may suddenly be born and arise in certain limbs of men. For when a new way of living is adopted and introduced into our lands from foreign ones, who will deny, or not think, that diseases may be brought in to certain limbs from the badness of foods and the intemperance of the palate? Those who seek food from the Indians must hope to receive contagion at the same time. For who will promise healthfulness in those foreign and unknown things? How many are there whose kidneys are grievously tormented by stone? How many suffer from colic? How many from most violent headaches? How many from pain and weakness of the stomach? How many from dullness and darkness of the eyes? How many are racked with the most savage torments of their fingers and hands? That the immoderate use of all these is caused by bad foods is shown by the fact that the soul itself is infected by the vices of food, which, as has been said, happens especially to the Parthians because of their indiscriminate foods.

units.la: Sed id nunc terris etiam nostris familiare est: & verisimile est ejusmodi animas pestilen- tes fieri haud aliter atq; innocua quædam ani- malia, quæ venenis pasta noxia fiunt & ipsa, vt apri in Pamphilia. Ergo vitæ multum interest, diligenter considerare quibus alamur cibis. Siquidem qualis naturę succiq; cibi extiterint, talem quoq; sanguinem, h.e. ipsos corporis hu- mores præstabunt, crassos, lentos, viscidos, te- nues, calidos, frigidos, mordaces, acres, qui in partes aliquas imbecillas delapsi illicq; confi- stentes dolores excitant & morbos, quifq; pro naturæ suæ & loci etiam cui impactus & infar- ctus est, conditione, vt mirum non sit quam- obrem, qui sine delectu cibos ingerunt nul- lamq; rationem alimentorum habentinsignes corpore mutationes sentiant, varisque mor- bos. Corpus scatens atra bile hanc reserer, morbisque atrabiliariis obnoxium est: pituitâ refertum carnem pituitosiorem referet, & se- rosam.
units.tr: But this now is familiar even in our own lands. It is likely that such souls become pestilential no differently from certain harmless animals which, fed on poisons, become noxious themselves, as the boars in Pamphylia do. Therefore it matters greatly to life to consider carefully with what foods we are nourished. For just as the nature and juice of food have been, so will they produce the blood, that is, the very humours of the body: thick, sluggish, viscid, thin, hot, cold, biting, and sharp. These, having slipped into some weak parts and lodged there, excite pains and diseases, each according to the nature of its own kind and the condition of the place into which it is driven and stopped. So it is no wonder that those who swallow foods without choice and take no account of diet feel remarkable changes in the body and various diseases. A body abounding in black bile shows this, and is liable to melancholic diseases; a body filled with phlegm produces flesh that is more phlegmatic and watery.

units.la: Verum consuetudinem, vt in aliis multis, itaincibis plurimum valere non est dubium. Id quod peregrinantes, & continuas commes- sationes voluptatis & honoris gratiâ agentes, dum à domestica assuetudine recedere cogun- tur crebrò experiuntur.
units.tr: But that custom, as in many other things, has great power over food too, is beyond doubt. Travellers often experience this, and so do those who keep up continual feasting for the sake of pleasure and honour, when they are compelled to depart from their domestic habits.

units.la: Nec in hominum solùm genere, sed & in pecoribus quoq; id spectatur. Insueta enim pa- bula, tota plerumq; armenta totosq; greges p- diderunt. Peregrina namq; licet suauia sentiā- tur & facilia, vescentibus tamen insignem asse- runt mutationem & perturbationem. Alexan- dri exercitum in India ciborum nouitate penè deletum historia proditum est: quin & in ea- dem India apud Arianam gentem repertus est frutex pestilens, lauri folio, odore equos invi- tante atq; alliciente, qui penè omni equitatu Alexandrum orbauit, & quidem primo in- troitu. Incolis autem iste propter assuetudinem minus noxius,adeò à teneris assuescere multum est.
units.tr: This is observed not only in the human race but also in cattle. For unfamiliar pastures have often destroyed whole herds and whole flocks. Foreign foods, though they seem pleasant and easy, nevertheless cause remarkable change and disturbance in those who eat them. History records that Alexander's army in India was nearly destroyed by the novelty of foods. Indeed, in the same India, among the Arian people, a pestilent shrub was found, with a laurel-like leaf, whose odour invites and allures horses; at the first contact it deprived Alexander of almost his whole cavalry. For the inhabitants, however, it was less harmful through habit; so much does it matter to become accustomed to things from tender years.

units.la: Qui nostra memoria de situ orbis Indici nuper patefacti scripserunt, variis ægritudinibus incommodisque affectos primo introitu prodiderunt eos,qui illuc commeârant, tum ob cœli mutationem,tum vero & inprimis ob pomorum radicumq;,quibus salubriter vescebantur incolæ, atq; etiam ipsorum animalium esum.
units.tr: Those who in our memory have written about the situation of the recently discovered Indian world reported that those who had gone there were, at their first arrival, afflicted with various sicknesses and discomforts. This was due partly to the change of air, and especially to the fruits and roots on which the inhabitants fed healthily, and also to their eating of the animals themselves.

units.la: Quid? quod mirabilius possit videri quod Mithridates maximus sua ætate Regum quotidiè bibere venenum excogitauit, vt scilicet consuetudine redderetur innoxium,clandestinasque epularum insidias euitaret, quo etiam pacto tutum corpus aduersus veneni pericula effecit. Sic enim de eo Martialis l. 5.
units.tr: What is more remarkable still: Mithridates, the greatest king of his age, devised a way to drink poison every day, so that by habit it would become harmless and he could avoid secret plots at his banquets. In this way he also made his body proof against the dangers of poison. Martial says of him in book 5.

units.la: Profecit poto Mithridates sæpe veneno Toxica ne possent sua nocere sibi.
units.tr: Mithridates, by often drinking poison, made progress, so that poisons could not harm him.

units.la: Consuetudine præterea venena in alimoniam conuerti Indica testatur puella, ab Indorum Rege Alexandro Regi dono missa, illius contagioso concubitu vt inficeretur, & anus illa attica, quæ à momento cicutæ, quod natura euincere & concoquere posset assueuit integros cicutæ manipulos innoxiè deuorare, cũ cicutæ succus eiusq; puluis fit lethalis, alias & soporiferum venenum, id quod Atheniensium supplicia indicant, qui morte condemnatos sorbitione cicutæ interemerunt, quam & Socratem cratem impietatis condemnatum in carcere hausisse ferunt.
units.tr: Habit also turns poisons into food, as an Indian girl bears witness. She was sent as a gift to a king by Alexander, king of the Indians, so that she might infect him through her poisonous embrace. And that old Athenian woman, who had grown accustomed to swallowing whole bundles of hemlock without harm, was able to digest it, though hemlock juice and its powder are otherwise deadly and a soporific poison. The Athenian executions show this, since they killed condemned men by making them drink hemlock. They also say Socrates, condemned for impiety, drank it in prison.

units.la: Eadem pene ratio Pharmacorum & medicamentorum quorundam est,quorum vires in assuetis debiliores deprehenduntur, in nonnullis etiam plane inertes. Quicquid enim à natura,calore,aut cogenita vel ex consuetudine acquisita corporis proprietate alteratum in corporis alimoniam conficitur & digeritur, id alito venenum esse non potest,adeo plurimum pollet consuetudo & natura acquisititia,vt scil. qui venenorum esui sensim assueuere, congeniti caloris substantia existente forti, ea tandé digerant,iisq; alantur,sicque in nutrimentum versa medicamentorum nomen plane amittant, id quod non in Attica illa anu tantum, quæ ab initio cicutæ momentum hauriens, ad liberalissimum haustum progressa sine vllo valetudinis incommodo diu superstes mansit, manifestum est, sed etiam id factitasse aliós in historiis reperitur,& quidem, qui Elleborum, opiumq; in magna quantitate deuorárunt innoxiè, teste Theophrasto, quod hodie adhuc ipsos Turcas factitare audio. Refert Theophrastus, quosdam totos Ellebori manipulos esitasse, nihilq; affectos esse, Chiumq; Eudemum viginti duos aliquando haustus Ellebori vno etiam die sumpsisse. Anus attica triginta cicutæ succi potiones tolerauit, vt ita manifestum sit, omnem cibum similem debere esse nutrinutrito, nec omnem cibum omnibus conue-nire, ob proprietatem quandam temperaméti quæ omnibus cibariis inest, huicque naturæ consentiens est, illi vero auersatur atq; contraria est. Sic suibus serpentes aprisque pro pabulo sunt: generi gallinaceo bufones, araneæ & colubri: coturnicibus & sturnis helleborus & cicuta: anatibus hyoscyamus, bufones, serpentes, ranæ, &c. Sibi igitur conueniens & familiare alimentum asluméns calorisq; beneficio in suam naturam conuertens natiui caloris substantiam augeri sentiet: quod enim secundum naturam est, suaue est & gratum, & carum cuique suaueque est, quod per & secundum naturam habetur. Sic biliosis mel est infestum, pituitosis suaue & familiare: acria, salsa, amara pituitosis magis quam biliosis conueniunt, ut non tàm vescendorum, quàm vescentium ratio hic habenda sit, &c.
units.tr: The same reasoning applies to certain drugs and medicines, whose force is found to be weaker in those who are accustomed to them, and in some cases plainly inert. For whatever is changed by nature, by heat, or by the body's inborn or acquired properties, and is then prepared and digested into the body's nourishment, cannot be a poison to the one who feeds on it. So powerful is habit and acquired nature. Those who have gradually grown accustomed to eating poisons, while their innate natural heat is strong, finally digest them and are nourished by them, and so the poisons, turned into nutriment, entirely lose the name of medicines. This is clear not only from that old Athenian woman alone, who began with a small dose of hemlock and advanced to very large draughts, and lived on for a long time without any harm to her health. It is also found in histories that others have done the same. Theophrastus, for example, reports that some ate hellebore and opium in large quantities without harm, and I hear that the Turks still do this today. Theophrastus relates that some swallowed whole bundles of hellebore and were not affected, and that Eudemus of Chios once took twenty-two doses of hellebore in a single day. The old Athenian woman endured thirty draughts of hemlock juice. It is therefore plain that every food must be similar to the one nourished, and that not every food suits everyone, because of a certain property of temperament that is present in all foods, and which agrees with one nature but is opposed to and hostile to another. Thus pigs feed on snakes and wild boars, fowl on toads, spiders and snakes, quails and starlings on hellebore and hemlock, and ducks on henbane, toads, snakes, frogs, and so on. So whoever takes in food that is suitable and familiar to him, and by the help of his heat converts it into his own nature, will feel the substance of his native heat increase. For what is according to nature is pleasant and agreeable, and whatever is held through and according to nature is dear and sweet to each person. Thus honey is harmful to the bilious, but sweet and familiar to the phlegmatic. Sharp, salty and bitter things suit the phlegmatic more than the bilious. So the question here concerns not so much the foods to be eaten as the people who eat them, and so on.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: De Primo, & vario mirabiliq; diuersissimarum gentium victu.
units.tr: Concerning the first and varied, and remarkable, diet of very diverse peoples.

units.la: Ibariorum facultates nosse ad unguem, vita hominum, supra quam cuiquam credibile est, utile erit. Sunt enim non morborum tantum, sed & secunda valetudinis communia præsidia: nec valetudo nostra stabiliri firmariq; potest, si fundamenta corporis, h.e. succi, quib. & nutritio ipsa & vita subsistit, vitiosa sint. Itaq; in alimentorum variis generib. viribus & natu- studiosè enucl andis atq; explicandis animus occupatus est, quantum per naturam li ebit ei esse sagaci & industrio. Sed prius de primo mortalium & postea vario gentiū quā nostro vitu & in cibis delectu disserendum est, vt sc.palam fiat, vitu hominū gradus quosdam habuisse, quibus à summa rusticitate & feritate ad humaniore elegantio: eq, & tandem ad celsa luxuria fastigia deuentum sit.
units.tr: It will be useful to know thoroughly the resources of the Ibarii for human life, more than anyone could believe. For they are common aids not only against diseases but also for keeping health. Nor can our health be established or strengthened if the foundations of the body, that is, the humours on which both nourishment and life depend, are faulty. Therefore my mind has been busy with carefully unfolding and explaining the qualities and natures of the various kinds of food, as far as nature allows me to be perceptive and diligent in this. But first we must discuss the original diet of mortals, and then the varied diets of the nations, compared with our own, and the choice of foods, so that it may be plain that the human diet passed through certain stages, from the utmost rusticity and savagery to a more refined civility, and at last to the lofty heights of luxury.

units.la: Constat autem inter omnes tum Philosophos tum historiarum scriptores, primum hominum genus in syluis & nemorib. vt feras degisse, ac glandiferis baccifer, arboribus vitam sitasse, h.e. syluas arboresq; prima m rtalibus alimenta suppeditasse in glandibus, pomis ac baccis.
units.tr: Now it is agreed among all philosophers and writers of history that the first human beings lived in woods and groves like wild beasts, and lived on acorn-bearing and berry-bearing trees; that is, that woods and trees first supplied mortals with food, in acorns, fruits and berries.

units.la: Deinde ex hac vita in aliam descenderunt pastoritiam s. etenim ex animalibus ob eandem vtilitatem syluestria deprehenderunt: atq; mansuefecerunt, inter quas oues primum assumtas verisimile est, tum propter placiditatem, aptissima enim sunt ad vitam hominis, ad cibos, caseum ac butyrum, tum propter corporis tutelam & vestitum, ad quem vellera adhibuerunt.
units.tr: Then from this life they went down into another, a pastoral one. For from the animals they caught the wild ones for the same usefulness and tamed them. Among these, sheep were probably taken up first, both for their gentleness (they are very well suited to human life, for food, cheese and butter) and for protection of the body and clothing, for which they used the fleeces.

units.la: Tertio à vita pastorali ad agriculturam animum adhibuerunt, quā maximè accepta vita s isse sa tustestan·ur populorum erga eam amor ingens & diligentia admirabilis, cum illis s. culis nihil anti- quius habuerint, quam agros studiosè excolere, il- lumq; amplissimè laudatum existimabant, quæ vi- rum
units.tr: Third, from the pastoral life they turned their minds to agriculture. The people who lived this life, as the ancient writers attest, had an immense love for it and a remarkable diligence, since in those ages they held nothing more important than cultivating their fields with care. They thought that man was most highly praised who heard himself called a good farmer,

units.la: Ioha. 21. rum bonum colonum appellari audirent, tuncq; pascua & fruges sola regum & gentium vectigalia erant, annonaq; vilitas erat incredib lis: haudq; dubie aurea illa secula vere extiterunt, in quibus tam innocenti victu homines vteretur, iis vt d. quae benigna tellure prouenirent vescentes, eoq;, quod honestis excultum effet manibus.
units.tr: Ioha. 21. and at that time pastures and crops were the only revenues of kings and nations, and food was incredibly cheap. Undoubtedly those golden ages truly existed, in which men lived on such innocent food, eating what the kindly earth produced, and what was cultivated by honest hands.

units.la: In hoc coelesti munere quantum vita postea profecerit, & quantum soleri ia ingeniaq; hominum curam eam per gula irritamenta auxerint, satis superq; testatur aureum illud vitae genus sublatu, luxuria gradu repente inuecto & subsecuto: atq; hic postremus gradus nostri seculi est: hac vltima vita, quam beatiorem solent dicere, quinouis morib. & luxui fauent. Hinc tot panificii gene a, tot pul es, tot pulmenta, tot esca, totq; obsonia parantur atq; conflantur in vsus vitae hominum, tot deniq; videas lautitias atq; delitias fine quib. vita vixpos- se consistere credi ur, a ganeo forum portentosis ingeniis excogitatas. Verum non vnum olim fuisse gentium victum sed varium mirabilemq;, imo innumeros & totidem pene quot gentes hominum q; lingua, testatur inter alios, qui res populorum historia prodiderunt, quiq; de situ orbis monumenta reliquerunt, Iul. Caes. in Clarissimis illis suis commentariis de rebus bellicis. Non solum enim Gallorum alium fuisse victum, alium Britannorum, alium vero Germanorum prodidit, verum etiam inter ipsos Germanos varium exm extitisse mirabilemq; atq; etiam inter ipsos Gallos.
units.tr: How far life has since advanced through this heavenly gift, and how much the skill and talents of men have increased their care for it through the incentives of gluttony, is sufficiently and more than sufficiently shown by that golden way of life having been abolished, and luxury having suddenly been introduced and followed step by step. This is the last stage of our age: this final life, which people usually call happier, favours every kind of moral laxity and luxury. Hence so many kinds of bread, so many dishes, so many sauces, so many foods and so many delicacies are prepared and made for the uses of human life. Finally you may see so many delicacies and pleasures, without which people believe life cannot exist, devised by the monstrous talents of the gluttons. But that the diet of the nations was once not one but varied and remarkable, indeed innumerable and almost as many as the nations and languages of men, is attested among others by Julius Caesar, who wrote of the affairs of peoples in those famous commentaries of his on war, and who left records of the situation of the world. For he reported not only that the diet of the Gauls was one thing, that of the Britons another, and that of the Germans yet another, but also that among the Germans themselves there was great and remarkable variety, and even among the Gauls themselves.

units.la: Apud Petragonos & Lemouicos castanea & rapa a vino & melle tertium honorem adipi-scebantur: rapa etiam Allobrogibus & Subaudis in cibis mirifice grata, sicut & castanea montanis Lugdunensibus fuere.
units.tr: Among the Petragorii and the Lemovices, chestnuts, turnips, wine and honey held the third place of honour. Turnips were also wonderfully pleasing in the food of the Allobroges and the Subaudi, just as chestnuts were to the mountain people of Lyon.

units.la: Montium Cemannorum populi Aruernis & Velleis proximi vice panificii utebantur, & exiamnunc vtuntur, castaneis, quippe festis tantum diebus, vel non infima fortis ac fortuna homines panificium illic ex frugibus vsurpant.
units.tr: The peoples of the Cemmenian mountains, neighbouring the Arverni and the Velavi, used chestnuts in place of bread, and they still use them, chiefly on feast days. Or, men of no low rank or fortune there take bread made from grain.

units.la: Gasconum gens Aquitaniae nobilissima inter praecipua pulmentaria alia habet & cepas, quorum olfactum & gustatum in delitias gula vertit & suauia condimenta: hi nunc quoque pra caeteris Gallis ventri indulgere magis creduntur: vulgatum enim & maxime nobilitatum apud eos jactatur prouerbium, satius esse ventrem belle farcire epulis, quam corpus vestire molli & pretiosa ornare, adjunctq; Burgundioni venirem esse fericeum.
units.tr: The people of Gascony in Aquitaine, most noble, have other chief delicacies: onions, whose smell and taste turn into a pleasure for the gullet, and pleasant seasonings. These people, even now, are believed to indulge their belly more than other Gauls. For a common and very famous proverb is bandied about among them, that it is better to stuff the belly well with feasts than to clothe the body in soft and costly garments; and they add that a Burgundian's belly is made of silk.

units.la: Aruerni Cafeo frequentius vtitare consue-uerunt.
units.tr: The Arverni were accustomed to use cheese rather often.

units.la: Nortmanni malis pyrisq; crudis ac coctis vescebantur liberaliter, fuosq; ex illis concinnabant potus, carnibus praeterea omnigenis utebantur.
units.tr: The Normans ate apples and pears, raw and cooked, freely, and made drinks from them; besides, they used all kinds of meat.

units.la: Narbonensis Gallia pisces habet frequentes, tum sale conditos, ante cunctea autem oleas condita capparisq; manducat, ficus item vuasq; recentes, mala citria, aranaria, limones inter lautiores cibos habet & gulae irritamenta: vina apud eos generosissima: oues pascuntur thymo, quo pabulo mire pinguescunt.
units.tr: Narbonese Gaul has many fish, salted, and above all it eats olives preserved in brine and capers, and likewise fresh figs and grapes, and citrons, bitter oranges and lemons, which they count among the choicer foods and incitements to the gullet. Their wines are very fine. Their sheep are pastured on thyme, by which fodder they grow wonderfully fat.

units.la: Armonicarum regionum populi inter se vi-vendi ratione differunt.
units.tr: The peoples of the Armorican regions differ among themselves in their way of living.

units.la: Brittones enim & Brittonifantes victu magis vtuntur fero & barbaro : at Gallobrittones maximam ciuilitatis vrbanitatisque Francica partem seruant, apud quos panificia lauta ex frugi-bus parantur, vinaque non ignobilia absorbentur.
units.tr: For the Britons and the Little Britons follow a wild and barbarous diet more. But the Gallo-Britons keep the greater part of French civility and urbanity, among whom fine breads are made from grains, and not ignoble wines are drunk.

units.la: De moribus Germanorum prodidit Cornelius Tacitus, quod cibi illis olim fuerint simplices, agrestia poma, recens feraque aut lac concretum sine appara tu, sine blandimentis ad famem sedandam, sed aduersus sitim non eandem fuisse tempe-rantiam, quoniam diem noctemque in potu continuarent, qui mos apud illos nostra etiam memoria pertinacissime perdurat, ut videantur ad perdenda vina geniti eoque nomine nunc apud Romanos, Hispanos & Gallos male audiant, quamvis certum est totam Germaniam a Romanis minime fuisse cognitam : & hodie, licet longe mitiori vrbanoreque victu degant, vinantque, nihilominus tamen ferina & prisca illius vita vestigia quaedam retinuerunt, maxime quo propius accedunt ad Septentrionem.
units.tr: Cornelius Tacitus wrote of the customs of the Germans that their food was once simple: wild apples, fresh game, or curdled milk, without preparation and without delicacies, to satisfy hunger. But their restraint in drink was not the same, since they kept on drinking day and night. This custom, even in our own memory, has persisted most stubbornly among them, so that they seem born to waste wine; and for this reason they now get a bad name with the Romans, Spaniards and Gauls. Yet it is certain that the whole of Germany was little known to the Romans. And today, although they live on a far milder and more urbane diet and drink wine, they have nonetheless kept certain traces of their old, savage life, most of all the nearer they come to the north.

units.la: Britanni qui nunc Angli, pecorum magnum numerum alebant, leporem vero, gallinam, anserem quoque gustare fas non putabant, animi tantum voluptatisque gratia educabant. Hodie a prisinis illis moribus longe recesserunt, humaniores facti, in-queomni exercitiorum genere (corporis puta & animi) sportabiles. Caelum temperatium illis esse quam Gallis, frigoris aspernitatem ab iis abesse experientia abunde testatur.
units.tr: The Britons, who are now the English, kept large herds of cattle, and they did not think it lawful to taste hare, hen or even goose; they raised these only for the sake of pleasure and amusement of mind. Today they have departed far from those old customs, have become more civilised, and are fit for every kind of exercise, both of body and of mind. That their climate is more temperate than that of the Gauls, and that the harshness of cold is absent from them, experience sufficiently attests.

units.la: Scoti, quibus Diuus Hieronymus feritatem & barbariem asscribit, in quorum etiam numero habentur Septentrionis quidam populi, ut Dani, Sueci, Effui, quos omnes feros adhuc & agrestes inveneris ni aliae gentes eos cicu arint atq; expoliierunt. Nunc urbanitate & humanitate nemini fere cedunt. Miseram olim autem vitae conditionem Scotis fuisse historiae testantur, frumentis enim adventi iis ut plurimum utebantur, bubulamq; in cibis largissime assumebant.
units.tr: The Scots, to whom Saint Jerome ascribes wildness and barbarity, and among whom are counted certain peoples of the north, such as the Danes, the Swedes and the Esthonians, all of whom you will find still wild and rustic, unless other nations have tamed and civilised them. Now they yield to almost no one in urbanity and humanity. History attests that the life of the Scots was once miserable, for they mostly used grain of the wild kind, and they ate ox flesh very freely.

units.la: Italia pro tractuum differentia imperiique incremento vitae mutauit. Romani enim qui initia imperio dederunt, tum etiam qui id provexerunt, cibos expetebant tantum qui vitam sustinerent, famemq; depellerent. Capitale erat bouem mactasse gulae causa: piscibus statim a Roma condita praesertim marinus vios esse constat ex antiquorum scriptorum monumentis: carnes omnino parcius esitasse quam cateros populos verum videri potest, nam & nostra memoria parcissime iis vescuntur. Vini obseruationes memorabiles apud Romanos fuerunt, auctoritatem enim post centesimum urbis annum coepisse aiunt, Romulumq; ipsum latte non vino libasse, & Numam sanxisse, ne rogum vino respergerent, nec licuisse foeminis primum id bibere, postea concessum valetudinis tantum causa: eorum au:erm
units.tr: Italy changed its way of life according to the difference of regions and the growth of empire. For the Romans, who gave the beginnings of the empire, and those who advanced it, sought only such food as sustained life and drove away hunger. It was a capital offence to slaughter an ox for the sake of gluttony. It is established from the records of the ancient writers that the Romans, from the founding of the city, lived especially on fish, especially sea fish; and it can be seen as true that they ate meat more sparingly than other peoples, for even in our own memory they eat it very sparingly. There were remarkable regulations about wine among the Romans. For they say that wine was first admitted only after the hundredth year of the city, and that Romulus himself poured libations with milk, not wine, and that Numa ordained that they should not sprinkle the funeral pyre with wine; and that women were at first not allowed to drink it at all, and afterwards it was permitted only for the sake of health. Of these things the later writers...

units.la: NB. autem qui secuti sunt cura fertilior feliciorq; industria in vitibus fuit excolendis: vini quidem in universum sunt auidi, sed modum potionibus adhibent, sicut & Hispani.
units.tr: Those who came after, however, devoted more care and more diligent effort to cultivating vines. They are indeed generally fond of wine, but they keep to moderation in drinking, as the Spaniards also do.

units.la: Vitius autem Romanorum rationem variasse pro Reipub. recta depravatave gubernatione, & siquidem Imperatorum virtute temperantia, atq; etiam libidine ac luxuria, dubium nullum est: inde enim tot emerserunt leges sumtuarias & censorias, quibus non exotica solum cibaria sed & domestica quaedam prohibebantur, atq; etiam ex sue pernae coenis detrahebantur. Pisces simul cum carnibus una in patella seu lance, mensis veteres Romani apponebant, pariterq; herbas quasdam ut asparagum: panificia varii generis conficiebant: lepusculi & perdices raro illorum mensas subibant ob inopiam scilicet, catera autem alium genera frequentius. Vitulina nulla illic caro pretiosior, Veruecina non admodum grata.
units.tr: That the Romans' habits varied with the sound or corrupt government of the commonwealth, and that under their emperors they moved between temperance, lust and luxury, is beyond doubt. From this came the many sumptuary and censorial laws, which forbade not only foreign foods but also certain domestic ones, and even removed sausages from dinners. The ancient Romans served fish together with meat on one dish or platter, and likewise certain herbs such as asparagus. They made bread of various kinds. Hares and partridges seldom appeared on their tables, certainly because of scarcity, while other kinds of game were more common. No veal was more prized there, and mutton was not very pleasing.

units.la: Hispani sordes in victu pecculiares habebant, quoniam, si suis alebantur loculis, domi esuriebant, & famelici hiabant, at quando alienna quadra illis frui licebat, nulla gens aeque vorax cernebatur, quem etiam morem nostra aetate in quibusdam Hispaniae locis perdurare animadversum est. Viuunt praeterea carnibus immodicis, piscibusq; tum amnicis, tum marinis: pomorum vbertas apud eos varia atq; multiplex, maxime citriorum omne genus, punicorum, ficuum, suarum, quas siccatas in alias terras mittunt.
units.tr: The Spaniards had a peculiar meanness in their diet: if they were fed from their own purses, they went hungry at home and gaped with hunger, but when they could feast at another's expense, no nation was seen to be so greedy. It has been observed that this custom persists in some places in Spain even in our own time. Moreover, they live on immoderate quantities of meat and on fish, both river and sea fish. Their fruit is abundant and varied, especially every kind of citrus, pomegranates, figs and plums, which they dry and send to other lands.

units.la: NB. tunt : vina illis vehementissima: secundis mensis quernas glandes adhibent dulcedine praestantes.
units.tr: They drink very strong wines. At the second course they serve acorns of the oak, which are excellent in sweetness.

units.la: Lusitaniae montanas gentes quernas glandes vesci Strabo autor est.
units.tr: Strabo is the authority that the mountain peoples of Lusitania eat acorns of the oak.

units.la: Graecis diversa victus & studiorum fuit ratio: aliter n. Lacedaemonii vinebat, aliter Athenienses. Lycurgus leges Lacedaemonis condens tantum cibi vnicuiq; elargiri iussit, quantum ad bona corporis valerudine effet satis: certum itaq; numerum frumenti singulis, in singulos annos emetiri madauit, & liquores pro ratione, atq; id uberius viris, foeminis parcius. Instituit praeterea publica convivia, in quibus nulla, praeter vulgares, esca apponebantur, probrosu exisitimas & inutile animis corporibusq; coquorum condimentis, & saporu coacervationib. Saginari. Solebant praeterea Lacaedemonii epulas suas condire laboribus in venatu, sudore, cursu, fame, siti: unde Dionysio Siculo neganti, se iure illo nigro (erat enim inter obsonia hoc illis celebratissimum) quod caput coenae fuerat, delectatum, respondisse fertur, quia illud coxerat, minime mirum, condimenta n. defuerunt.
units.tr: The Greeks had different ways of life and of study. The Lacedaemonians lived one way, the Athenians another. Lycurgus, when framing the laws of Sparta, ordered that each person be given only as much food as was sufficient for the good health of the body. He therefore commanded that a fixed measure of grain be apportioned to each person each year, and liquids in proportion, more generously for men and more sparingly for women. He also established public dinners, at which no food was served beyond the common fare, since he judged it shameful and harmful to minds and bodies to be fattened by the seasonings of cooks and by heaps of flavours. Besides, the Lacedaemonians were accustomed to season their feasts with toil in hunting, with sweat, running, hunger and thirst. Hence it is reported that when Dionysius of Sicily said he did not enjoy that black broth (for among their dishes this was most celebrated), they replied that this was hardly surprising, since it had been cooked without seasonings.

units.la: Sybaritae gloria virtutisq; loco d. litis mollitieq; dediti vitam despiciebant. Spartani vero & viuendum liberaliter & moriendum censebant, utrumq; cum virtute, teste Plutarcho. Verum Athenienium longe alia fuit viuendi ratio, quippe luxui omnino deditos fuisse graeci fere omnes testati sunt, ipsique Poeta Comici Atticas inprimis coenas riserunt. Socrates cibos detrahebat, quinque esurienti inuitaret ad edendum, similiter & potum, qui non sitientes ad bibendum. Est in exemplis parasitum quendam interrogatum, num cœnæ Atticæ (Chalcidicis lautiores essent), an vero hæc Athenien-sibus præstarent, respondisse, Chalcedonicum præmium pretiosius esse & suavius, quam Atticorum totum apparatum, appellant præmium cœnarum, ostrearum multitudinem & varietatem.
units.tr: The Sybarites, who gave themselves to luxury and softness in place of glory and virtue, despised life. The Spartans, however, thought that one should live freely and die freely, both with virtue, as Plutarch testifies. But the Athenians had a very different way of living, for almost all the Greeks have testified that they were wholly given to luxury, and the comic poets especially mocked the Attic dinners.
