Socrates would take away food, and would invite the hungry to eat, and likewise to drink those who were not thirsty. There is an example of a certain parasite who, when asked whether Attic dinners were more lavish than those of Chalcis, or whether these surpassed the Athenians, replied that the Chalcedonian prize was more costly and more agreeable than the whole Attic display; they call the prize of dinners the great number and variety of oysters.

units.la: Persas præter nasturtium ad panem nihil adhibuisse Xenophon testis est. Sed de eorundem luxu ganeaque apud omnes fere scriptores passim complura traditia leguntur.
units.tr: Xenophon bears witness that the Persians used nothing with their bread except cress. But many things about their luxury and gluttony are read scattered through almost all the writers.

units.la: De aliarum gentium victu, quæ a grauissimis autoribus literis sunt assignata, scio permulta esse, quæ vix fidem merentur, multique ea videantur incredibilia, præsertim iis qui a patrio solo nō multum discesserunt.
units.tr: I know that there is a great deal about the diet of other peoples, recorded by very serious authors, which hardly deserves belief, and many think it incredible, especially those who have not travelled far from their native soil.

units.la: Sed quia ex illis mundi partibus, quarum gentium ritus mirabilemque victum sum enarraturus, homines, fruges, legumina, animalia, aues, nobis incognita, creberrimæ ad nos terra marique conuenientur, fidem facile iis adhibendam esse censeo. Ferinum ante annos aliquot apud nostrates habitum est, cochleis, vesci, ranis, testudinibus. At in universa fere Gallia & Italia inter præcipuas mensarum delitias reponuntur. Thraces quosdam canibus victitasse Picus Francisceus autor est. Hircani vescebantur venatibus, quorum varietate abundabant, teste Marcellino. Getis quibusdam vini usu omnino ignotum, quin & frugum victum illum quendam ... omnillum pecus comodat, ex quo Nomadū Getarū plurimi Columella teste, galactopotæ dicuntur.
units.tr: But since, from those parts of the world whose peoples' customs and marvellous diet I am about to describe, men, crops, pulses, animals and birds unknown to us are very often brought to us by land and sea, I think they should be believed without difficulty. Some years ago it was reported among our countrymen that people eat snails and frogs and tortoises. Yet these are placed among the chief delicacies of tables throughout almost all of Gaul and Italy. Francesco Pico is the authority that certain Thracians lived on dogs. The Hyrcanians fed on the game of their hunts, of which they had an abundance, as Marcellinus testifies. Some Getae are entirely unacquainted with the use of wine, and even that food of grains... every herd provides, from which, as Columella testifies, very many of the nomadic Getae are called milk-drinkers.

units.la: Orientis populi plurimi, q imperio Magni Cham parent, potusfuos ex oryza & genere aromatu cocinnant, carnesq; crudas cōritas primū, deinde aromatis respersas, oleisq; odoratis imbutas vorāt: serpentib. etiamnunc, q illic nascuntur copiosissima & grandissima in cibis viuntur, inq; delitiis habēt carnes humanas, hominis scil. morbo non extinctli, sed in bello ab iis trucidati. Matthias Michon de Sarmatia Asiana scribens, Tartarorū quoq; meminit, omniq; frumento carere asseuerat, omni quoq; leguminū genere, excepto milio, quod magna cura ab iis seri idem tradit: equorum præterea greges educant, quorum carnes manducant, sanguine vero equinum milio commiscent, coquuntq; simul ac vorant, quin etiam ipsum solum potāt, idq; & barbaris olim placuisse testatur Virg. carm. Bucolico: Et lac concretum cum sanguine potat equino.
units.tr: Most of the peoples of the East, who obey the empire of the Great Khan, prepare their drinks from rice and a kind of spice, and first eat raw meat cut into pieces, then sprinkled with spices and soaked in fragrant oils. They also eat serpents, which grow there in great abundance and size, and they count human flesh a delicacy, namely of men slain by them in war, not of those dead of disease. Matthias Michou, writing about Asian Sarmatia, also mentions the Tartars, and asserts that they lack all grain and every kind of pulse except millet, which he says they sow with great care. Moreover they keep herds of horses, whose flesh they eat, and they mix horse blood with millet, cooking and devouring them together; indeed they even drink the blood alone. He testifies that this pleased barbarians of old, as Virgil says in his Eclogue: "and drinks milk curdled with horse blood."

units.la: Acido lacte obletantur, id namq; stomacho tum salutare esse persuadent, tum aluo deiiciendæ idoneum experimentis comprobarunt: si quando vero epulari splendidius illis animus est, lac equinum sublimatum bibunt, quod mirabile dictu, promtissime atq; ocyssime in cerebrum penetrans inebriat. A Tartaris Turcas Oriundos censet idem, quare ab eorum vitu non procul recedere.
units.tr: They smear themselves with sour milk, for they assert that this is healthy for the stomach and suitable for loosening the bowels, and they have confirmed it by experience. But if at any time they wish to feast more splendidly, they drink sublimated horse milk, which, marvellous to say, penetrates the brain most readily and quickly and intoxicates. The same author thinks the Turks are descended from the Tartars, and therefore they do not stray far from their way of life.

units.la: Qui de Rhodi expugnatione historiā scripserūt, omnino gentē illam immundam atq; obscœnā tradunt. In Sarmatia Europæa Podoliæ fertilitate nobilinobilitata est: potus illic ex melle concinnantur, quod ibidem abundantissimè gignitur, atq; etiam in Rufcia. Moscouiæ idem Matthiâs faciens mentio-nem potum incolis esse scribit, ex aqua & melle con-sectum: aromatis vtuntur crebrius, nam & ea cum melle arte chymica sublimant, existimantes (& vere) hac potione viscerib. calore excitari adeo in-signem & salutarem, vt possit inclementissimis frigoribus fortiter repugnare: auenam ipsam subli-mant, ex qua sublimatione elicitur liquor, quem aquâ ardentem vocant aquæ ac apud Germanos, Italos, Gallos, ex vinis vehementioribus. Mosco-uitis parent Scythæ humanis corporib. vescentes, sine vllo degentes panificio, vino aliúq; potibus: vi-scera ossaq; humana vorare, ipsumq; sanguine gla-diatorum bibere, & quidem ex homine ipso, ex ipsa venasectâ calentem adhuc & spirante adhuc sor-bere efficacissimum putant. Paulus Iouius testatur Moscouiam Melopeponem ferre, quod mirari subit, quippe gelidissimis Boreæ flatib. tenerrima quæq; exuruntur. Certissima illic messis in melle atq; cera est, namq; illic apes in arborum cannis mella conficiunt, & probatissima, & copiosissima: domi opi-pare & lau-è epulantur, gallinæ siquidem & anates singulæ profingulis argenteolis numm̃is venëut: venatio & aucupia mensas magnarum opulen-tant, vina nesciunt præter exotica, itaq; vtuntur in sacrificiis & conuiviis luxuriosioribus ostenta-tionis gratiâ. Lapponum gens supra quam credi-bile est fera & agrestis, neq; enim frugæ, neq; vina, neq; poma nouit, sagittandi sola arte viSlum qua-rita, & ferarum occisarum tergoribus vestitur. In Oriente porro traditur quosdam esse populos, qui sine vllis arboribus, sineq; frutice degant. Plurima quoq; gen. es frugum, arborum, quin & pecorum innumeruntur expertes. Fuerunt & apud Graecos, qui scrupulose hominum viscera sunt persecuti, eorumq; sapores. Æthiopum gens, cuius regio a Meroe ad fluuium Hydaspin porrigitur, scorpionibus vescebatur & aspidibus. Quintinus Herodus scribit, se vidisse in insula Melita, qui scorpionem ederet innoxie. Supra Boryslhenem Scythae fluuium maximum esse gente Saucomatum, qua tertio semper die capiat cibum: ad extremes vero Indos gente aßomorum fuisse fine ore, corpore toto hirsutam, vestitam frondium lanugine, halitibus tantum viuentem & odore quem narib. trahebant, memoriaprodit u est: quae sit vera sunt, quos mirentur Democritum melius odore vixisse? Qui Athon monte incolebant, viperinis carnibus alebatur, itaq; nec capiti nec vestibus eorum noxia corpori animalia innascebantur. Gens Medunnorum animalium, quae Cynophalos appellabant, laeste vi- uebat * Arimphaei gens baccis alebatur.
units.tr: Those who wrote the history of the capture of Rhodes report that that nation was altogether unclean and obscene. In European Sarmatia, Podolia is ennobled by its fertility: drinks are prepared there from honey, which is produced in great abundance in that place, and also in Russia. Matthias, writing about Moscovy, mentions that the inhabitants drink a beverage made of water and honey; they often use spices, for they also sublimate them with honey by chemical art, believing (and truly) that by this drink the viscera are so strongly stirred to heat and health that it can bravely resist the most severe frosts. They also sublimate oats themselves, from which sublimation is drawn a liquor which the Germans, Italians and French call burning water, aqua ardens, made from stronger wines. The Scythians who obey the Muscovites eat human bodies, living without any bakery, wine or other drinks; they devour human viscera and bones, and drink the very blood of gladiators, and indeed they think it most efficacious to sup warm blood drawn from a man himself, from a vein just opened, while he still breathes. Paulus Jovius testifies that Moscovy produces the melon, which is surprising, since the tenderest things are scorched by the most icy blasts of the north wind. The surest harvest there is in honey and wax, for there the bees make honey in the hollows of trees, and it is both excellent and abundant. They feast richly and sumptuously at home: a hen and a duck each sell for a small silver coin. Hunting and fowling enrich the tables of the great, and they know no wines except foreign ones; therefore they use them in sacrifices and in more luxurious banquets for the sake of display. The race of the Lapps is wild and rustic beyond what is credible: they know neither grain, nor wine, nor fruit, but procure their food by the art of archery alone, and clothe themselves with the hides of slain beasts. Further, it is said that in the East there are certain peoples who live without any trees or shrubs. Countless kinds of grain, trees and even livestock are also unknown to them. There were also among the Greeks some who carefully investigated the viscera of men and their flavours. The Ethiopian nation, whose country stretches from Meroe to the river Hydaspes, fed on scorpions and asps. Quintinus Herodus writes that he saw on the island of Malta a man who ate a scorpion without harm. Beyond the Borysthenes, a great river of the Scythians, there is a people of the Sauromatae who take food only every third day. It is recorded that among the farthest Indians there was a people of the Aśomori, without mouths, whole-bodied and hairy, clothed in a down of leaves, living only on breath and on the odour they drew in through the nostrils. Whether these things are true, what would they wonder at, that Democritus lived better on odour? Those who lived on Mount Athos fed on the flesh of vipers, and so no animals harmful to the body were bred on their heads or in their clothes. The race of the Medunni, which they called Cynophali, lived wickedly. The Arimphaei were nourished on berries.

units.la: Celenophagi tesludinib. vescebantur, quarum vsq; Lemtestis casas suas intagebant, id genus hominum nouarum non porta India. Candei serpentibus vesci assueti, & ob id ophiophagi dicti. Libes ouillam non gustabant, erat enim apud eos id inexpiabile, si quis edisset. * Cynocephali Iudaei atq; Ægyptii non vescebantur suilla. Trogloditae ferae sunt
units.tr: Chelonophagi fed on tortoises, and roofed their huts with the tortoise shells. This race of men is not found in India. The Gandi were accustomed to eat serpents and were therefore called Ophiophagi. The Libyans did not taste sheep's flesh, for among them it was an unforgivable crime if anyone ate it. The Cynocephali, the Jews and the Egyptians did not eat pork. The Troglodytes are wild.

units.la: * Cyno-
units.tr: Cyno-

units.la: in æthio- gloditæ specus subibant, alebanturq; serpentibus pia cani- Kiphæis bacca erant alimenta. Nonnullis India na habe- populis casorum parentu viscerib.epulari fas erat. tes capi- *Carmani sine fruge ac veste, sine pecore, sine sedi- ta,cætera bus degebant,piscib.vescebantur,eorumq; cute sese hominis velabant. Pharusi pecoribus alebantur tantum. In similes, Æthiopia cu hominu multiformes miraq; effigies violentæ reperiuntur, tu vitlus ratio incredibilis: illic enim ad saltu, gentes sse ore concreto naribusq; carentes, vnoq; morsu & tantuforamine spirantes, & potu auena calamus lacratu trahere, tradiderunt prisci. Acridophagi vermib. ferx. alūtur, iisdemq; necatur, cibus illorum omne tempus * Carma est locustarū victus, q veris tempore Zephyrus in nia regio maxima copia ad eos ex deserto defert. Hassale, Indiscō- qui apud eos plurimus est seruant. Vitasunt bre- termina, uissima, annosissimus enim 40. non excedit annos. populi Quibusdam ignotum fuisse ignis vsum narrat toto cor- ante Ptolomæum Latyram Ægypti regem, atq; pore præ illic fuisse Nomades, qui Elephantis vescerentur. ter capi- Agriophagi Pantherarum carnes leonumq; ede- ta hirsuti bant. Pamphagi omnia vorabant. Alii Orientis sunt. populi piscibus viuunt tum siccatis tum recentib, quorum captura vberrima fit Martio, Aprili, Maioq, contritos eos & in massam redastos in panificia cogunt, siccataq; in annua cibaria repo- nunt. Fortunatarum insularum incola beatiores sunt, quibus sua sponte tellus abundantissime sup- peditat alimenta. De victu & cibo nouæ Indiæ, siue noui orbis non ita pridem a Christianis pa- fasli constat varium eum esse, fertilitate soli alibi, alibi albi vero infæcunditate nobilem: alij autem oves, aliaq; pecora, aprosq; affatim, melle, saccharo, vitibusq; abundat, quæ illic plus funduntur uuarum quam foliorum.
units.tr: The Troglodytes went down into caves, fed on serpents, and their food was berries. Among some peoples of India it was lawful to feast on the entrails of their dead parents. The Carmanians lived without grain, clothing, flocks or homes; they ate fish and covered themselves with the skin of a man. The Pharusii were nourished only by cattle. Similar monstrous and strange human shapes are found in Ethiopia, and the ancients tell an incredible story: there, they say, are tribes without a mouth or nostrils, who breathe through a single bite-sized hole and draw their drink through a hollow oat stalk. The Acridophagi feed on wild worms, and are killed by them; their food at all times is locusts, which the west wind brings to them from the desert in spring, in great numbers. Their lives are very short, for the oldest of them does not exceed forty years. Some relate that the use of fire was unknown until Ptolemy Lathyrus, king of Egypt, and that there were Nomads there who fed on elephants. The Agriophagi ate the flesh of panthers and lions. The Pamphagi devoured everything. Other peoples of the East live on fish, both dried and fresh, whose catch is most plentiful in March, April and May; they pound the fish, press them into a mass, form it into cakes, and dry and store them as food for the whole year. The inhabitants of the Fortunate Islands are happier, for the earth of its own accord supplies them with abundant food. Concerning the food and diet of New India, or the New World, lately opened up by Christians, it is known that it is varied: in some places it is noted for the fertility of the soil, in others for its barrenness. It abounds in sheep and other cattle, and in wild boar in plenty, and in honey, sugar and vines, which there yield more grapes than leaves.

units.la: Qui terras incolunt, prima Americi Vespucii navigatione visas, omnino frumenta ignorant, cibariaq; iis sunt poma atq; herba, ac quoq; pisces, radicem quandam in farinam redigunt, quæ vice panis utuntur, hanc alii Iuccam, alii Chambi appellant: carnes nullas attingunt præter humanas. Qui primi e nostro orbe in eas terras habitatum sunt deducti, duraruntquidem aliquot annis solis herbis, pomis, radicibusq; viuentes, verum postea ad alia cibaria descenderunt, inuenerunt q; cibos, quos primum exitiales expertisunt, innoxios reddere. Etenim iucca radix, primum degustata illis mortifera fuit, verum procedente tempore, cum id venenum in radicis solo succo delitescere comperisset, aqua coctâ ac igne totam madere coperunt absq; noxa.
units.tr: Those who inhabit the lands first seen on the voyage of Amerigo Vespucci know nothing at all of grain. Their food is fruit and herbs, and also fish; they grind a certain root into flour, which they use in place of bread; some call it yuca, others chambi. They touch no meat except human flesh. The first people led there from our world survived for some years on herbs, fruit and roots alone, but afterwards they moved on to other foods, and found ways of making harmless the foods which at first had proved deadly to them. For the yuca root, when first tasted, was fatal to them; but as time went on, having discovered that the poison lay hidden in the juice of the root alone, they began to boil the whole root in water and cook it over the fire, without harm.

units.la: Navigatione Iosephi Indi compertum habetur, regionem Indicâ, quæ Carangonora dicitur, sitâ inter æstuum tropicum & æquatorem, nucib. Indicis abundare, incolasq; herbarum 24. radicib. vesci, ex oryza vero panes conficere: sunt etiamnum Palmeta, quorum ex fructibus panes conflant, vinum elicient: acetum temperant, oleum exprimunt, atque etiam saccharum, quod ideo minus mirabile videtur, quod Strabonem auctorem grauem, eadem pene in libris suis de orbis situ tradidisse reperitur. Ex palma enim fieri panem, mel, acetum oleum scripto mandauit. Calechutani lacte & butyro vescuntur, panesq; faciitant sine frumento in foco tantum coctos & cinere. Oryza apud eos abundantia summa, eaq; cymbalis, saltationib. omniq; laetitia genere ferunt, daemonia sua praeca es vt sit oryza uberrimus prouentus, hac n. varias epulas conficiunt, ex palmis potant liquore, carnibus piscibusq; promiscue vescuntur, a bubala tame abstinent, bones namq; sacrosanctos putant. Qui colunt Insula, quae S. Iohannis porta dicta est, canes alut saginantq; in vsum cibarium, verum nullus illis latratus est, rostrumq; habent vulpinu. Infima plebs piscatu nutritur, muriumq; venatu. Mameluchi, qui Sultano parebant Aegyptio, equorum, camelorum, bubalorumq; carnib. vicli arunt. Arietes in illis locis grandes & memorabiles visuntur magnitudine asinos aequantes, quorum aliqui cauda gestant libraru 40. adeo obesi vt pgredi vix valeant: capras praeterea grandes illic reperiri traditur, quae vno partu quatuor haedos enitantur. Apud quasdam Orientis gentes sunt gallinae, quae pro pennis pilos gerant nigricantes, quib. vescuntur, pariter q; ipsarum carnes q sunt saporis suauissimi. Liquores ex sauciatis arboribus emanantes in potum assumunt: quin & sub earum corticibus farina reperiri praedicat, q prabeat incolis pulmenta suauiaq; cibaria.
units.tr: By the voyage of Joseph the Indian it is known that the Indian region called Carangonora, which lies between the tropic and the equator, abounds in Indian nuts, and that its inhabitants feed on the roots of herbs and make bread from rice. There are also palm groves, whose fruit they make into bread and from which they draw wine; they prepare vinegar, press oil, and even make sugar. This seems less surprising because the grave author Strabo is found to have related almost the same things in his books on the geography of the world: he wrote that bread, honey, vinegar and oil are made from the palm. The inhabitants of Calechut eat milk and butter, and make loaves without grain, baking them only on the hearth and in the ashes. Among them rice is very plentiful, and they celebrate it with cymbals, dancing and every kind of joy, invoking their demons so that the rice harvest may be abundant. They make various feasts of it, drink a liquor from palms, and eat meat and fish indiscriminately, but they abstain from buffalo, for they regard cattle as sacred. Those who inhabit the island called St John's feed dogs and fatten them for eating; yet these dogs never bark, and they have fox-like snouts. The lowest common people live by fishing and by gathering shellfish. The Mamelukes, who obeyed the Egyptian Sultan, live on the flesh of horses, camels and buffaloes. In those regions rams are seen which are large and remarkable, equal in size to donkeys; some of them carry tails weighing forty pounds, so fat that they can hardly walk. Moreover, it is related that large goats are found there which bring forth four kids at a single birth. Among certain peoples of the East there are hens which have dark hairs in place of feathers; they are eaten, and their flesh is of most delicious flavour. They take into drink the liquors that flow from wounded trees; indeed, it is said that under their bark meal is found, which provides the inhabitants with pulse and sweet foods.

units.la: Pygmei, (quorum tota cohors cubito non est altior vno, vt ait Iuuenalis) profrugib. aduerso gruies dimicabant: na & tantillos homunculos mitioribus alimentis vti natura docuit: fabulosam aute & filitiam pygmæorum gentem non ffe Aristote- les in illis suis præclaris de animalib. historiis scri- psit. Atq; hæc de vario mirabilíq; gentium victu a- spergere placuit, ut scil. comperium quis habeat, si forsan rudis in istiusmodi rerum auditionib. repe- riatur, quantum exoticus ille victus à nostro diffe- rat: vbi hoc adnotasse oportebit, si ab exoticis istis abscesserimus, adq; domestica exempla venerimus, permulta futura, quæ visa primum admiratione attatura sint, ut fide carere quis ea existimet, etiam ab homine probo audita & grauì.
units.tr: The Pygmies (whose whole troop is no taller than a cubit, as Juvenal says) fought with cranes over grain. For nature has taught even such tiny men to use gentler foods. But that the race of Pygmies is fabulous and fictitious, Aristotle did not write in those famous books of his on the history of animals. I have been pleased to scatter these remarks on the varied and wonderful diet of the nations, so that anyone who may be a novice in hearing such things may know how far that foreign diet differs from ours. Here it will be necessary to note that if we leave these foreign examples and come to domestic ones, there will be very many things which, at first seen, will astonish us, so that one might think them unbelievable, even when heard from an upright and serious man.

units.la: Multi, cum quis ab Italis colubras tuto edi re- fert, minimè credent: cum item in Alpinis iugis & Septentrionis quibusdam locis, ut Norvegia, Suecia, Liuonia, &c. cadidos lepores, vrsos & vul- pes conspici, atq; ab illorum locorum incolis edi au- dierint. Vt enim externa illa & exotica nobis mi- raculo sunt ita vicissim nostra illis. Et vt homines equo insidentes antiquitas Centauros dixit, ita & Indi illi nostros equites, nostra nauigia, remiganti- dq; artem sunt demirati.
units.tr: Many people, when someone reports that snakes are eaten safely by the Italians, will not believe it at all; likewise, when they hear that on the Alpine ridges and in certain northern places, such as Norway, Sweden, Livonia and so on, white hares, bears and foxes are seen, and are eaten by the inhabitants of those places. For just as those foreign and exotic things are a wonder to us, so in turn our things are a wonder to them. And just as the ancients called men riding on horses Centaurs, so those Indians marvelled at our horsemen, our ships, and the art of rowing.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: De alimentorum diuisione, generibus, & differentiis generatim, deq; mirâ ter- rarum quarundam fertilitate.
units.tr: On the division of foods, their kinds and differences in general, and on the remarkable fertility of certain lands.

units.la: Primus mortalium victus, & exotica gen- tium quarundam cibandi ratio exhibita est, quæ si cui ganeofo forsan saluiam K mouemouerit,videatis quomodo vlteriore atq; lauti- tiore quodam ferculo palatum explere possit: auribus percipiendam,oculisq; lectitandam e- am proposui,non etiam degustandam.
units.tr: The first food of mortals, and the strange ways of feeding practised by certain peoples, are set out here. If these perhaps stir the appetite of some glutton, you may see how he could satisfy his palate with a more refined and sumptuous dish. I have proposed to set this before the ears to be heard and the eyes to be read, not also to be tasted.

units.la: Nos melioribus(vtinam non peioribus)vi- viuedi institutis deliniti placidiorefq; reddiri, quod ex cibis ferum omnino est, relinquamus illis,alimentorumq; vim ac naturam memora- dam,diligenter perpendamus,vt suauia,fami- liaria & amica distinguamus ab iis,quæ naturę ac vitæ hominum noxia sunt & inimica.
units.tr: Let us, charmed by better (I wish not worse) ways of living and made gentler, leave to those peoples what is altogether savage in food. Let us carefully weigh the power and nature of foods, so that we may distinguish the pleasant, familiar and friendly from those that are harmful and hostile to human nature and life.

units.la: Omne autem animans sibi conueniente nutritur alimento. Alimentum est quo alimur, vel fine quo corpus ali non potest. Conueniens vnicuiq; alimentum est, cp assimilari cor- pori alendo potest: ciborum enim ratio est,af- similari & vniri substantiæ corporis cibandi.
units.tr: Every living thing is nourished by food suited to it. Food is that by which we are fed, or without which the body cannot be fed. The food suited to each is that which can be assimilated to the body in feeding, for the nature of food is to be assimilated to and united with the substance of the body.

units.la: Alimentum affimilandū vel efculentū est vel potulentum. Esculentum est cp esui est aptum.
units.tr: Food that can be assimilated is either edible or drinkable. Edible is that which is fit for eating.

units.la: Esculenta fiue cibi quæ in hominum vsus ad- mittuntur,veniunt vel à vegetabilibus,vt fru- gibus,leguminibus,fructibus: vel ab animali- bus horumq; partibus, vel ab iis, quæ ab ani- malib. ‚pueniunt, vt sunt oua,lac,mel,sanguis.
units.tr: Edibles, or foods admitted to human use, come either from plants, such as grains, pulses and fruits; or from animals and their parts; or from those things which come from animals, such as eggs, milk, honey and blood.

units.la: De omnib.autem & fingulisin specie efcu- lentis,quæ vel à vegetabilib*, vel ab animalib* depromi possunt in vsus humanos,tractare in- ftituti,& consilii mei non est, sed deiis solum- modo,quę nostra ætate crebrius veniunt in ci- bos & mensas. Ac qui de cibis hominū tractarunt, ab arborum pomis & baccis, quæ prius vitam mortalium aluerunt, vt vitæ ordinem sequerentur, exordiri maluerunt. Verum nos, quoniam salubriora subsecuta sunt secula, mitioraq; cibaria ex frugibus inuenta sunt, frugū naturas prius persequemur atq; inde cabimus, præsertim cum ex iis firmissimum & probatissimum cibi ac potus vinculum videl. panis conficiatur, & præcipua hominū cibaria. Mira profecto frugū natura & eximia gratia, quod sine iis vix villa esca placere potest. Vnde nō immerito agriculatio ab antiquis Romanis adeò commendata est, vt quæ non solum fanis, sed etiam ægrotantibus alimenta suggerat. Romanorum aratores triumphales extiterunt & laureati, qui femina non leuiori cura tractabat quam bella, qui eâdem diligentia agros disponebant atque castra: vnde tunc in Italia annonæ vilitas erat incredibilis, nulla enim prouinciatum Italiam alebat. Athenienses licet pascuo magis indulgere visi sunt quâ agricolationi, maximo tamē in honore agricolas habuerunt frugū; inuentores. Quid? quod optimi quiq; pariterq; disgnissimi rei rustice operā dabant, nam nec Imperatores pudebat manibus triumphalibus tum agros colere, tum femina tractare ipsosq; ligones: & cum viri boni laudabant, eum bonum agricolam bonumq; colonū appellitabat. Hodie ita abiecta est, vt tellus aranda committatur in seruitute quasi reddis, prouentuq;
units.tr: I have undertaken to treat each and every kind of food that can be drawn from plants or from animals for human use, but that is neither my purpose nor my plan. I will deal only with those foods that are more commonly brought to our tables in our own age. Those who have written about human food have preferred to begin with the fruits and berries of trees, which fed mortals first, following the order of life itself. But since more wholesome ages have followed and milder foodstuffs have been discovered from grains, I shall first examine the natures of grains and proceed from there, especially since the firmest and most approved bond of food and drink, namely bread, is made from them, and grains are the chief food of humankind. Truly, the nature of grain is wonderful and its grace remarkable, since almost no food can please without it. Hence agriculture was rightly commended so highly by the ancient Romans that it supplies nourishment not only to the healthy but also to the sick. The Roman ploughmen were triumphant and crowned with laurel, who handled the plough with no less care than they gave to war, and who arranged their fields with the same diligence as their camps. Therefore in Italy at that time the price of grain was incredibly low, for no province fed Italy. The Athenians, although they seemed more inclined to pasturage than to tillage, nevertheless held the inventors of grain-growing in the greatest honour. What more? The best and most distinguished men of every rank devoted themselves to rural work. Even generals were not ashamed then to till the fields with triumphal hands, to handle the plough, and the hoes themselves; and when they praised a good man, they called him a good farmer and a good husbandman. Today it is so despised that the land to be ploughed is committed to servitude, as it were, and a tax is taken from its yield.

units.la: K abiis & vectigal accipiatur. Felicissimum rerum statum tunc fuisse, cum aranti Cincinnato viator afferret dictaturam, & Serranum serentem oblati inuenirent honores, extra dubium est. Sed ad propositum.
units.tr: That the state of affairs was most fortunate then, when a messenger brought the dictatorship to Cincinnatus at the plough and offices were found offered to Serranus while he sowed, is beyond doubt. But to my purpose.

units.la: Omnes frugum species & differentiae auctore Theophrasto, Columella, & aliis, sub frumentis & leguminibus tanquam summis generibus comprehenduntur. Varias autem cerealium seminum differentias inueniri, testantur, qui per Italiam, Galliam, Indiam, Aegyptum, Hispaniam, Angliam, Germaniam, Daniam, peregrinationes suscepepunt. Causas coelo soloque tribuerunt naturae solertes, ad frugum enim fructuumque nobilitatem autignobilitatem, facilitatem aut difficultatem in cibis foecunditatem aut sterilitatem, coelum aut solum plurimum valere animadverterunt.
units.tr: All the kinds and differences of grains, according to Theophrastus, Columella and others, are comprehended under wheat and pulses as their highest genera. Moreover, those who have undertaken journeys through Italy, Gaul, India, Egypt, Spain, England, Germany and Denmark testify that there are various differences among the cereal seeds. Skilled students of nature have ascribed the causes to climate and soil, for they have observed that the climate or the soil has the greatest power over the nobility or baseness of fruits and grains, over the ease or difficulty of their use as food, and over their fertility or barrenness.

units.la: Differentias itaq; frugum scire & cognoscere inprimis oportet vitae salubritati consulturum & peregrinationes suscepturum. In quibusdam enim locis quaedam praecoces cernuntur, quaedam ferae: quaedam multum ferentes, quaedam parum, quaedam pauciores intra dies consummantur, vt Euboicae, quae intra 40. dies perficiuntur, quaedam ponderosae sunt & firmae, quaedam leues, quaedam parum obtinent furfuris, quaedam multum, quaedam Spicam effundunt, quaedam cristam, &c. Sunt etiam quaedam loca quae semper cochlia & cibo facilia ferant. ferât, alia verò perpetuò incoctilia & cibis dif-sicilia: quin & in eadem interdū segete nonnul-la coctilia inueniri, alia autem incoctilia, sulço tantum discernente, mirabile alicui videretur, nisi in victib id quoq; spectaretur. Coctile hic dicitur, quod resolui facile potest, & coctura frumenti celeriter immutari: incoctile contra, plane non vel aegre immutatur: prius molle tarumq; est, caliditatem & humiditatem, quibus resolutio fit, suscipere valens: alterum sua densitate repugnat & resistit: atq; haec omnia eueniunt coeli solisque ratione. In Lemno non nisi coctilia proueniunt, quoniam ager calidus, stercorosus, tenuis, soliq; expositus est. Ægyptus coeli soliq; gratiâ coctilia affert, caliditas enim coctilitati atq; digestioni perutilis est atque pnecessaria. Quę igitur agro feruéti & leni proueniunt, coctilia erunt: quae algido, spisso, lento, atq; etiam madido & palustri erumpunt solo, incoctilia sententur omnia, ob vberi nimirum alimentum validiusq;. nam & frequentioribus imbrib. incoctilia fieri constat, & deteriora, putri edinique magis obnoxia. Pluuia certè à satione protinus secuta incoctilitatè affert, Solis siccitas, licet minus reddat suauia, coctilia tamen efficit. Certissimû autéin proban- dis frumentis & leguminib. experimentu est, quod vnicuique debet esse ad manum, siqui- dem ad vire salubritatem optimum funda- mentum: estque huiusmodi. Seminaaquâ per- K funduntur aut madescunt, & quae ocyus ex his fcil bonu intumescunt, mollioraq; euadut, ariditatemq; corpori ac duritiem statim eximunt, praestantiora iudi- praestens cabuntur: quae vero pristinam ariditatem duri- alimentu tiemq; diu retinent, necin coquendo tumef- nec ne? cunt, necinfigniter mollescunt, cibis abdican- da sunt, constant enim terrestri & crassa effen- tia, ac difficulter a ventriculo & venis confi- ciuntur ac digeruntur, quamobrem crudus succus in vescentium corporibus procreatur, qui variorum morborum causa existit: quae vero ocyus videmus intumescere & mol- lefcere, cibis idonea & facilia iudicantur, nam a ventriculo facile digeruntur, & coficiuntur.
units.tr: It is therefore above all necessary to know and recognise the differences among grains, for the sake of preserving health and of undertaking journeys. For in some places certain grains are seen to be early and others late; some bear much, others little, and others are finished in fewer days, as the Euboic grain, which is ripened within forty days. Some are heavy and firm, some light; some yield little bran, some much; some shed their ear, some their crest, and so on. There are also some regions which always produce grain that is easily cooked and easily digested, while others always produce grain that is hard to cook and hard to digest. Indeed, in the same crop sometimes some grains are found to be easily cooked and others not, the furrow alone separating them; this would seem a wonder to someone, unless in our way of life this too were observed. Grain is called "cookable" here if it can easily be dissolved, and its cooking changes it quickly; "uncookable", on the other hand, is that which is not changed at all, or only with difficulty. The former is soft and loose at first, able to take in the heat and moisture by which dissolution occurs; the latter resists and withstands by its density. All these things happen by reason of climate and sun. In Lemnos only cookable grains are produced, since the field is warm, dunged, thin and exposed to the sun. Egypt yields cookable grain by the favour of climate and sun, for warmth is most useful and necessary for cookability and digestion. Therefore what grows in a warm and gentle field will be cookable; whatever bursts forth in a cold, dense, sluggish, and even wet and marshy soil will be judged uncookable, no doubt because of its richer and stronger nourishment. For it is agreed that grain becomes uncookable and inferior by frequent rains, and is more liable to rot and to mildew. Rain that follows directly after sowing certainly causes uncookability; dryness from the sun, though it makes grain less pleasant, nevertheless makes it cookable. The most certain test for judging grains and pulses, which everyone ought to have at hand, since it is the best foundation for health, is this: seeds are steeped or soaked in water, and those which swell more quickly and become softer, and at once shed their dryness and hardness, are judged the better. But those which retain their former dryness and hardness for a long time, and neither swell nor soften noticeably in cooking, must be rejected as food; for they consist of an earthy and thick substance, and are digested and processed with difficulty by the stomach and veins, and therefore raw juice is produced in the bodies of those who eat them, which is the cause of various diseases. Those which we see swelling and softening more quickly are judged suitable and easy as food, for they are easily digested and processed by the stomach.

units.la: Haec diligenter obseruare oportebit eum, cui vitae salubritas, qua inter omnia dona & bona nihil praestantius, curae est: quis vero inter mor- tales est, qui eam non expetat? Hanc ne- gligere, quid aliud est quam morbis ipsis prae- bere initia? Caeterum de frugum satione, agricolatione, frugum ipsarum permultis dif- ferentiis, earum messe, & repositione, plura qui desiderat, consulat rei rusticae scriptores, naturaeq; prudentes & inter alios. Varronem, Columellam, Theophraftum, Plinium, &c. Vnum hic praeterire minime decet, quae vide- licet terrae in Europa foecunditate magis sint nobilitatae? Europam terrarum pulcerrimam esse, saluberrimam iuxta ac fructuosissi- mam, adq; colendum magis idoneam, quam caeteras exteras orbis partes, qui de situ orbis literis mandarunt, propemodum affruunt omnes.
units.tr: Whoever cares for the healthiness of life, which among all gifts and goods is nothing more excellent, must observe these things carefully; and who among mortals does not desire it? To neglect it is nothing other than to offer the beginnings of disease itself. As for the sowing of grain, its cultivation, the very many differences of grains, their harvesting and storage, whoever wants more should consult the writers on rural matters and those skilled in nature, and among others Varro, Columella, Theophrastus, Pliny, and so on. One point it is by no means fitting to pass over here: which lands in Europe are more ennobled by fertility? Nearly all who have committed the description of the world to writing agree that Europe is the most beautiful of the lands, as healthful as it is most fruitful, and more suited to cultivation than the other foreign parts of the world.

units.la: In hac Germania nostra sitae sit, hodie plu- rimis suis partibus agrorum cultu insignis, frugum abundantia commendabilis, genero-fisq; vitibus consita, dives clarorum virorum, animosisque populis frequens, ferarum, alio-rumque animalium, qui in cibos hominum pro nutrimento admittuntur, foecundissima, quibusdam tamen in locis magnis fyluis multisq; fluminibus inuia cernitur: olim non ad-modum ferax frugum fuit, quia teste Caesa-re, agrorum cultum neglexerunt, nolen-tes studium gerendi belli agricultura commutare, vitaq; omnibus erat in venationibus. Unde maior pars illorum victus in caseo, la-cte, carne, consistebat, neque quisquam apud eos agri modum certum aut fines proprios habebat. Hodie quoque plerasque Germaniae gentes vinum ignorant, ut quae sub coelo frigidiore & alperiore sitae sunt, externa tamen conquirunt terra marique, qualia sunt Galli-cum, Hispanicum, Rhenanum. Sed certum est totam Germaniam a Prisciis non fuisse cognitam. Hodie certe in victus urbanitate, morum; comitate nullis aliis populis Germani cedunt.
units.tr: Our Germany, which lies here, is today remarkable for the cultivation of many of its parts, commended for its abundance of grain, planted with noble vines, rich in famous men and populous with spirited peoples; it is most fertile in wild beasts and other animals which are admitted as nourishment for human food. Yet in some places it is seen to be impassable because of great forests and many rivers. Formerly it was not very productive of grain, because, as Caesar testifies, its people neglected the cultivation of the fields, being unwilling to exchange the pursuit of waging war for agriculture, and their life consisted entirely of hunting. Hence the greater part of their food consisted of cheese, milk and meat, and no one among them had a fixed measure or proper boundaries of land. Today too most of the peoples of Germany do not know wine, since they dwell under a colder and harsher sky; yet they seek out foreign wines by land and sea, such as the Gallic, the Spanish and the Rhenish. But it is certain that all Germany was unknown to the Greeks. Today, certainly, in refinement of diet and courtesy of manners, the Germans yield to no other people.

units.la: Galliam florentissimam regionem esse, foliisque vbertate felicissima, amoenam, salu-berrimam, frumenti pabuli; feracem, quin & vitisbus maxima ex parte consitam, omnium fere scripta prædicant. Vnum non leue incommodum habet, quod assiduis agitatur flatibus, humoribusq; & pluuiis plurimum obnoxia cernitur, algoribusque premitur vehementibus. Quidam tam opulentam hodie Galliam esse existimant, quàm Prisci temporibus Hispania fuisse aut Persis perhibetur. Vndecimi Galliarum Regis Ludouici elegans dictum hic vt surpare libet, pratum enim graminosum & late patens Galliam nominabat, quod toties sit restibile, quoties visum fuerit fœnisecio opus esse, quo dicto omnium aliorum regum opes suis minimè æquandas intellexit.
units.tr: Many writers declare that Gaul is a most flourishing region, remarkably fertile, pleasant, very healthful, and rich in grain and pasture, and indeed for the most part planted with vines. It has one considerable drawback: it is constantly buffeted by winds, is very exposed to moisture and rain, and is oppressed by severe cold. Some think Gaul is as wealthy today as Spain was in ancient times, or as Persia is said to have been. It is pleasant to borrow here the elegant saying of Louis XI, the eleventh king of the French. He called France a broad, grassy meadow, which can be mown again whenever there is need for haymaking. By this saying he made clear that the wealth of all other kings was not to be compared with his.

units.la: Italiæ veterum, tum Latinorum, tum Græcorum scriptis admirabilis fertilitas celebratur, inq; frugibus, vitibus, arboribus, aliisq; ad vitam necessariis cibis beatissima semper habita est. Ipsam tamen Romam Venetiasq; finealiarum vicinarumq; terrarum frumentis stare non posse constat.
units.tr: The admirable fertility of Italy is celebrated in the writings of the ancients, both Latin and Greek, and it has always been regarded as most blessed in grain, vines, trees and the other foods necessary for life. Yet it is well established that Rome and Venice themselves cannot survive without grain from neighbouring lands.

units.la: Hispaniam quoq; fertilitate mirè commendabilem graues autores tradiderunt, maximè verò ob metallorum copiam, quibus vniuersa scatet: frugibus enim non vbique abundare, & præsertim vbi metallorū est ferax, Strabo prodidit: rarum enim est inuenire regione vtroq; munere claram. Solinus nihil in ea ociosum, nihilq; sterile inueniri affirmat, siue foli vbertatem, siue vinearum prouentus, siue arborarios rios respicias. Sed hæc felicitas cœli aerisque temperationi non parum accepta ferenda est, quippe flores, rosæ scilicet, violæ & asparagus etiam tribus tantum menfib.in anno illis defi-ciunt. In quibusdam etiam locis agros fertiles este adeò traditur vt,cum semel fata frumenta sint, subinde recidiuis feminibus segetem no-uantibus septem minimum, interdum plures etiam ferant mefles.
units.tr: Grave authors have also commended Spain for its remarkable fertility, but above all for its abundance of metals, with which the whole country teems. Strabo has reported that crops do not abound everywhere, and especially not where the land is rich in metals, for it is rare to find a region famous for both gifts. Solinus affirms that nothing idle or barren is to be found there, whether you look at the richness of the soil, the yield of the vineyards, or the trees. But this happiness must be credited in no small part to the temperate climate and air, for roses, violets and even asparagus fail there for only three months of the year. In some places the fields are said to be so fertile that, once the grain has been sown, the fallen seed springs up again and renews the crop, bearing at least seven harvests, and sometimes more.

units.la: Hæc Romanis ante Dictatorem Cæsarem patu fuit cognita,vt ex historiis patet: plæriq; enim fictâ eam, nusquamq; extare omninoq; fabulosam contenderunt, teste Plut. Tempe-ratius in ea & salubrius cœlum est quâ in Gal-lia:imbribus tamen ac nebulis crebriorib.ma-didum. Frugum pecorumq; fœcundum eftibi solum, Fruges citò proueniunt,sed tardè mite-scunt, omnibusque iis quæ tàm pecora, quàm hominibus benignius alant, præclarè abundat. Hibernia iniquum habet ad maturanda femi-na cœlum, verùm herbis lætis & dulcib. adeo luxuriat, vt se exigua diei parte pecora imple-ant,& nisi pabulo prohibeantur,difficiliant diu-ti° sc.pasta. Vina in Anglia nulla,àGallis enim Germanisque ea petunt, & quidem fortiora, quia imbecilla vectuam non ferunt.
units.tr: These things were known to the Romans before the dictator Caesar, as the histories show. For many maintained that it was a fiction, nowhere existing and wholly fabulous, citing Plutarch as witness. The climate there is more temperate and healthful than in Gaul, though with more frequent showers and mists. The soil is fruitful in crops and herds. Crops come up quickly but ripen slowly, and the land abounds splendidly in all those things that nourish cattle and men more richly. Ireland has an unfavourable climate for ripening grain, but its meadows are so lush with pleasant, sweet herbs that cattle fill themselves in a small part of the day, and unless they are kept from the pasture they can scarcely digest what they have eaten for a long time. England has no wine; it fetches wine from Gaul and Germany, and indeed the stronger kinds, since the English cannot bear weak wine.

units.la: Sicilia, cui Anglia maxime similis nonnul-lis videtur figura sc.triquetra, fertilitate nullis pene terris comparanda venit. Tulit Cererem frugum inuentricem : Unde fit vt quicquid gignat, optimum esse judicetur. Hujus felicitas ex orat. Cic. in Verr. manifesta euadit. Theophrastus autor est in quadam ejus parte celerem quandam fieri consummationem feminum ferorum, esse namque sementem eorum sex mensis, pascua quoq; habere mirifica, frumentiq; omnino perfertilem praedicant: horreum Romanorum jure nominatae st, ut quae in singulos annos ingentem frumenti copiam penderet, ut quidam non sibi sed Romanis agros arare atq; ferere eam dixerit. Leontinorum in ea ager ante cuncta fœcunditate nobilitatus reperitur centesimum granum reddens.
units.tr: Sicily, to which England in some people's view is most similar in shape, being triangular, is hardly to be compared in fertility with any lands. It bore Ceres, the inventor of grain, and so whatever it produces is judged the best. Its happiness is plain from Cicero in the Verrines. Theophrastus states that in one part of it wild seed ripens quickly, the sowing period being only six months. They also say it has wonderful pastures and is altogether very rich in grain. It was rightly called the granary of the Romans, since it paid a huge quantity of grain every year. So someone said that its farmers ploughed and sowed the fields not for themselves but for the Romans. Among its places the field of the Leontini is found to be the most renowned for fruitfulness of all, yielding a hundredfold.

units.la: Sed & cæteras Europæi orbis terras fertiles esse opimisq; segetibus non deficere testantur qui in illas iter adornarunt, & ad tempus in iis moram fecerunt, vel visendarum illarum gratia, vel etiam certorum negotiorum expediundorum causa. De Suecia & Dania hoc vere possum affirmare, licet sub asperiore & algidiore sint coelo sita illa loca, nihil tamen, quicquid ad hominum vitam humaniter & benigne sustentandam pertinet, naturam iis denegasse. Brabantiam, Flandriam, Hollandiam, Frisiam totam, &c. Multis nominibus earum rerum vbertate & fœcunditate, quae salubritati hominum conducunt, nobilitatas reperimus.
units.tr: But the other lands of Europe are also testified to be fertile and not lacking in rich crops, by those who have journeyed into them and stayed there for a time, either to see them or to transact certain business. About Sweden and Denmark I can truly affirm this: although those places lie under a harsher and colder sky, nature has nonetheless denied them nothing that pertains to sustaining human life humanely and kindly. Brabant, Flanders, Holland, all of Friesland and so on are found to be renowned in many respects for the abundance and fruitfulness of those things which serve human health.

units.la: Sed ob tumultus bellicos frumentorum aliarumq; rerum pretium plus justo adauctum, annonæq; caritas major.
units.tr: But because of warlike disturbances the price of grain and other goods has risen beyond what is just, and the dearness of provisions is greater.

units.la: Sed quid memorem Africæ, Asiæque loca quædam fœcunditate adeo nobilitata ab auctoribus grauissimis, vt fidem pene excedat omnem. Inprimis vero Babylonica felicitas commendatur. Etenim, Theophrasto prodente, bis illic in anno semper & quasi ordinatè tondent triticum, tertiò verò pecus admittunt, sic enim caulem mittit, cum alioquin foliis tantum lasciuiat. Quod negligentius colentib. quinquagesimo cum fœnore messes reddunt, diligentius vero cum centesimo quinquagesimo. Refert Curtius inter Tygrim & Euphratem jacentia tam vberi & pingui esse solo, vt à pastu repelli pecora dicantur, ne suffocentur. Causam memorandæ huius fertilitatis tradit, humorem ex vtroque manantem amne per certas aquarum venas.
units.tr: But why should I mention certain places in Africa and Asia, so renowned for fertility by the most weighty authors that it almost exceeds all belief? Above all, the fortune of Babylon is praised. For, as Theophrastus reports, there they always mow wheat twice a year, as if by regular order, and the third time they turn cattle in, since otherwise the stalk would only run to leaves. Those who farm carelessly get back fifty-fold at harvest, but those who farm more diligently get a hundred and fifty-fold. Curtius reports that the land lying between the Tigris and the Euphrates is so rich and fat that cattle are said to be driven from pasture lest they choke. He gives as the cause of this remarkable fertility the moisture that flows from both rivers through certain veins of water.

units.la: Theophr. Asiæ quodam in loco adeo grande frumentum produci ait, vt grana singula magnitudine sua oliuę nucleis æquiparentur, illicq; omnia rore coalescere. Mirabile dictu & auditu, q; Procurator in Byzantia Africæ campo Diuo Augusto ex eo loco misit ex vno grano quadringenta paucis minus germina. Misit & Neroni similiter trecentas quadraginta stipulas ex grano vno. Cetinetin circuita eximię fertifertilitatis illius tractus ducentos quinquaginta millenos passus, cum centesima fruge agricolis fœnus reddens. Oleo tamen ac vino caret satis gloriæ in messibus exhibens.
units.tr: Theophrastus says that in a certain place in Asia the grain grows so large that the individual grains equal olive stones in size, and that there everything thrives on dew alone. It is wonderful to say and to hear that the procurator in the African plain of Byzacium sent to the divine Augustus from that place about four hundred shoots from a single grain, a few fewer. He likewise sent to Nero three hundred and forty stalks from a single grain. The circuit of that tract of remarkable fertility is two hundred and fifty thousand paces, yielding a hundredfold return to the farmers. Yet it lacks oil and wine, though it displays enough glory in its harvests.

units.la: Mauritaniæ oram exteriorem adeò fertilem esse traditur, soloq; diuitem, vt frugum genera & benignissimè proferat, & vitem biferam ostendat, duasq; messes, teste Strabone. Mirabilissimum est, quod in Chalcia Rhodiorum insula fieri proditum est Theoph. & Plin. auctoribus, locum videlicet illic repertum præcocem fertilemq; adeò, vt hordeum in eo satum, cum cæteris seeretur in locis, meterentque coloni, iterumq; ferere, atque cum reliquis vna frugibus rursus metere possent. Sed beatiores longè sunt Insulæ fortunatæ, in mari Caspio, quæ sine cultu fertiles, omni frugum genere fructibusq; abundant sua sponte genitis, subindeq; aliis super aliis innascentibus.
units.tr: The outer coast of Mauretania is said to be so fertile and rich in soil that it bears all kinds of grain most generously and shows a vine bearing fruit twice a year, with two harvests, according to Strabo. Most remarkable is what is reported, on the authority of Theophrastus and Pliny, of Chalcia, an island of the Rhodians: a place is found there so early and fertile that barley sown there, while in other places it is still being reaped, is reaped by the farmers, and then sown again, so that they can reap it again together with the other crops. But far happier are the Fortunate Islands in the Caspian Sea, which without cultivation are fertile, abounding in every kind of grain and fruit produced of their own accord, one growing upon another.

units.la: In Hispaniola insula ejusdem orbis (sc. Nouæ Indiæ) ter anno maturescere demetiq; segetes testantur qui de situ nouæ Indiæ scripserunt: expertes enim sunt algoris hiemalis ob lineæ æquinoctialis viciniam: illic præterea ocyssimè erumpere hortensia femina, fructusq; mitescere ac maturari tradunt: Cucumeres enim pepones & id genus, vigesimo a jacto semine die maturescunt, aut ad summum 18.
units.tr: In Hispaniola, an island of the same world (namely New India), those who have written about the situation of New India testify that crops ripen and are harvested three times a year, since the island lies near the equinoctial line and so is free from winter cold. There, moreover, garden seeds sprout very quickly, and fruits are said to ripen and mature. Cucumbers, melons and the like mature on the twentieth day after sowing, or at most the eighteenth.

units.la: Theophraft in Melo Insula intra 30. aut 40. dies meti fruges testatus est.
units.tr: Theophrastus recorded that on the island of Melos crops are harvested within thirty or forty days.

units.la: Arabes beati felicefq; appellati sunt, quod frugibus, palmitibus, odorum suauitate multiplici, fluuiorumq; perspicua multitudine abundent, reste Marcell. Temperies praeterea apud eos coeli terraeq; admirabilis, adeo vt adeo extremam eis felicitatem nihil videatur deesse: quin & pretiosissimae ex mari apud eos margaritae petuntur, habent enim mare felicissimum. Thus illic duplici colligitur vindemia, primo circa canis exortum hinc verno tempore.
units.tr: The Arabs were called blessed and happy, because they abound in grain, vines, a manifold sweetness of perfumes and a clear abundance of rivers, as Marcellinus rightly says. Moreover, the temperature of their air and land is admirable, so that no extreme happiness seems to be lacking to them. Indeed the most precious pearls are sought there from the sea, for they have a most fortunate sea. Frankincense is gathered there in a double vintage: first around the rising of the Dog Star, and then in spring.

units.la: Iudaeam terram fertilitate insigniem, nulliq; alteri inferiorem esse inter Historicos orbisq; scriptores pene omnes conuenit. Solum apud eos feracissimum est, maximeq; balsamo nobilitatum. Insulam, in qua Meroe ciuitas cerni tur, triticum ferre atq; hordeum, quae in tanta adolescant proceritatem, vt facile homo equo aut Camelo insidens occulteretur eorum segetibus, & a nemine conspici possit, Heliodorus testis est. In Olynthia agros quotannis reftibulos esse Varro scripsit. Vix in nostris foecundissimis etiam atq; maxime opimis latifundiis agros reftibulos inuenire est, ac in summa etiam terratum vbertate rariflime ac fere nunquam semen cum decima fruge reddi, quod partim hominum negligentia, praecipue vero telluris ac temporum culpa accidere manifestum est. Hactenus de mirabili terrarum quarundam fertilitate, redeamus nunc ad ipsa frumentacea, quibus potissimum aluntur homines, & ex quibus præcipua hominum cibaria constant atque conflantur. Ubi tamen adnotandum de frumentorum speciebus inquisitionem ambiguam valde esse, quod, referente Plinio, non eadem vbiq; sint frumenti genera, & si eadem, neque tamen vbique iisdem nominibus appellentur: proindeque superfluum puto, frumentorum nomina præcipere, quæ aut loco subinde, aut ætate mutantur, satisque esse, ea eligere acexplorata habere, quæ nostris in regionibus vel fata prouenium vel aliunde aduehuntur.
units.tr: Almost all historians and writers of the world agree that the land of Judea is distinguished for fertility and inferior to no other. The soil there is most fertile and especially famous for balsam. Heliodorus bears witness that on the island where the city of Meroe is seen, wheat and barley grow to such a height that a man sitting on a horse or camel can be hidden by their crops and seen by no one. Varro wrote that in Olynthia the fields lie fallow every year. Scarcely can one find fallow fields even on our most fruitful and richest estates; and even in the greatest fertility of lands, it very rarely, almost never, happens that seed is returned with a tenfold yield. That clearly happens partly through human negligence, but above all through the fault of the soil and the seasons. So far on the remarkable fertility of certain lands. Let us now return to the grains themselves, on which men chiefly live and from which their principal foods are made and prepared. Yet it should be noted that inquiry into the kinds of grain is very uncertain, since, as Pliny reports, the kinds of grain are not the same everywhere, and even where they are the same they are not called by the same names everywhere. I therefore think it superfluous to set out the names of grains, which change from place to place or from age to age. It is enough to choose and to know well those which either grow in our regions or are brought in from elsewhere.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAP. VI.

units.la: De alimentis quæ veniunt à vegetabilibus & plantis.
units.tr: On foods that come from vegetables and plants.

units.la: INexorsu huius capitis meminisse velim lectorem amplioris vlteriorisq; intelligentia gratia, varias alimentorum diuisiones apud autores occurrere, pro variis atq; diuersis eorum facultatibus & viribus. Primo enim quædam proprie dicuntur alimenta, alendi tantum corporis potestatem habentia, non etiam alterandi: quædam non solum alunt, sed alendo etiam alterant & immutant & nutrimento sua alimenta appellantur, immutant, inquam calefaciendo, vel refrigerando, vel humectando, vel exiccando. Deinde quædam sunt εὐχυλα bonifucci, quadam κακοχυλα mali succi, quæ quoq; difficulter concoquuntur & perficiuntur, sicut priora facile digeruntur & nutriunt. ariunt. Tertio quædâ sunt infirma parū sed promptè nutrientia, quædam firmissima ex quibus plurimum alimenti coaceruatur, vt succolenta crassa & grauia: quædam inter hæc ambigunt nullâ in emperie donata, optimum frugiue succum efficientia, in quorum numero sunt panis benè iuba-tus & fermentatu gallinarum, capo-num, phasi-anorum, perdicum, columbarum, turturum, tur-dorum, merularum, omniumq; generis auicularum carnes, aliaq; laudabiles succi, vt vitulina, veruecina, pisces saxatiles, vinum generosum, mel, lac, & ovaforbilia. Quædam vero insitâ quadam sympathia & familiaritate alunt, vt elleborus co-turnices, ferrum Stru hiocamelum. Deniq; à condimentis differunt alimenta. illa enim ad obsonia condienda fiunt, græcis ὀψώνια, ὀψωνίσματα, dicuntur, alimenta vero proprie sunt, sine quib. corpus alino potest. Nunc de singulis seorsim & speciatim pertractare instituti operis ratio requirit. Et primo quidè explanatis in cibū veniunt aut semen, aut radix, aut folia, aut fructus, aut flos, quib. addi possunt tubera & fungi quos terra spon-te ut supernacua protrudit.
units.tr: At the start of this chapter I would have the reader keep in mind, for the sake of a fuller and deeper understanding, that authors divide foods in various ways, according to their different properties and powers. First, some foods are properly called nourishments: they have only the power to feed the body, not to alter it. Others not only nourish but also change and transform what they feed on, and these are called nutriments; they change things by warming, cooling, moistening or drying. Next, some foods are easily digested and of good juice (εὐχυλα), others of bad juice (κακοχυλα), which are digested and assimilated with difficulty, while the former are easily digested and nourish. Third, some foods are weak but quick to nourish, others very firm, from which a great deal of nourishment is gathered, such as thick and heavy juicy foods. Some lie between these, with no excess of any quality, producing the best and most wholesome juice. Among these are well-leavened bread, the flesh of hens, capons, pheasants, partridges, pigeons, turtle-doves, thrushes, blackbirds and all kinds of small birds, and other commendable juices such as veal, mutton, rock fish, good wine, honey, milk and eggs. Some foods nourish by a certain inborn sympathy and affinity, as hellebore nourishes quails, and iron nourishes the ostrich. Finally, foods differ from condiments: condiments are made to season dishes, and in Greek are called ὀψώνια or ὀψωνίσματα, whereas foods properly so called are those without which the body cannot be sustained. Now the plan of the work requires that I treat each kind separately and in detail. And first, of those foods that come to the table, some are seeds, some roots, some leaves, some fruits, some flowers; to these may be added the truffles and mushrooms that the earth pushes up of its own accord as superfluous growths.

units.la: Inter feminina primas obtinent frumenta & legumina.
units.tr: Among the seeds, grains and pulses hold the first place.

units.la: Frumenta (sic dicta à frugendo, id est, vescendo, frumen enim summa pars gulæ est) spicas habent cū arista, aut spica mutica: Legumina (sic dicta à legedo, vnde etiam legumeta dicuntur, non n. secatur, sed vellendo legitur) siliquis seu thecis includuntur. Inter cerealia præcipuè numerantur triticum, &c. Siligo, hordeum, zea, far, oryza, avena, milium, ocymum, panicum, sesamum.
units.tr: Grains (so called from frugere, that is, to eat, since frumen is the chief part of the appetite) have ears with awns, or ears without awns. Pulses (so called from legere, whence they are also called legumina, since they are not cut but gathered by plucking) are enclosed in pods or husks. Among the cereals the chief are wheat, etc.: rye, barley, maize, spelt, rice, oats, millet, basil, panic grass, sesame.

units.la: Triticum alendis hominibus accommodatissimum est, inter quas fruges primam semper obtinuit autoritatem: Plurima eius notantur genera, Africum, Thracium, Assyrium, Ægyptiacum, Italicum, Gallicum, Germanicum, &c. Non aliunde quam a terris sortita nomina, colore tamen, specie, magnitudine & proprietate differentia.
units.tr: Wheat is most suited to feeding people, and among all grains has always held the first place of authority. Many kinds of it are noted: African, Thracian, Assyrian, Egyptian, Italian, Gallic, German, etc. They take their names from the lands they came from, but differ in colour, appearance, size and properties.

units.la: Optimum probumque triticum est ponderosum, denstum, tota substantia adeo compacta, ut dentib. vix teri dividique queat: quod item plus farinæ reddit, quod aqua maceratum vel etiam præcoctum ocyus intumescit, (hoc enim modo agricolationis naturaque rerum periti cerealia semina probare solent, probitatisque vel improbitatis indubitatum id habent experimentum.) Dentib. vero facile cedens facileque frangibile, fractumque sirarum & laxum cernitur, magna mole & quantitate exiguum prabet alimentum. Non enim superfluum tantum externa consideranda est, sed frangi debet & divi-di. Usu enim venire solet, ut quoad extra flauum ac densum fit, pinsitum postea fractumque rarum, leve, intusque album appareat. Plurimum enim vita interest, tritico uti electo, vescique quod non sit mucidum, situm corruptione mutato redolens, aqua gurgulionibus arrosum, quod bene pinsitum ac molitum, quod lolio, melampyro, aliisque feminum quisquiliis careat, id siquidem permitti-sum vescentibus graves autores cum experientia tra-
units.tr: The best and most approved wheat is heavy and dense, its whole substance so compact that it can scarcely be ground or split by the teeth. Likewise it yields more flour, and when soaked in water or even parboiled it swells more quickly (for in this way those skilled in husbandry and the nature of things usually test cereal seeds, and they have this as an unfailing proof of good or bad quality). But wheat that yields easily to the teeth, is easily broken, and when broken appears loose and porous, gives little nourishment for its great bulk and quantity. For one must consider not only the outward appearance, but the grain must be broken and split. For it often happens that, while it looks yellow and dense on the outside, once ground and broken it appears thin, light and white within. It matters greatly to health to use selected wheat, and to eat what is not mouldy, not spoiled by decay, not smelling of age, not gnawed by weevils in water, which is well ground and milled, and is free from darnel, cockle and other rubbish of seeds. For serious authors, with experience, hand down that this is the only kind permitted to those who eat it.

units.la: Triticum salubre & insalubre.
units.tr: Wheat, wholesome and unwholesome.

units.la: tradunt: panificia enim ingrata, tum odore & colore, tum gustatu reddit. Non igitur parum vitæ interest pistorum diligentia aut negligentia: negligentius enim ventilata & expurgatæ fruges, lolio aliisq; id genus vitiis mixtæ plerumq; in cibos assumtæ ingentes morborum causas præbent. Quoties panificum & frumentariorum aviaritia fraud-q; accidere videmus, vt in pani-ficia veniat triticum mucidum atq; gurgulio- nibus arrosum? frumenta scilicet impurgata relinquuntur, ne mensuræ aliquid destrahatur, quas imposituras quidam hodie ad unguem tenent, & per experimenta ducunt. Lolii pessimi esse succi, caput ferire, & vertigines ciere multis exemplis probare superuacaneum iudico: hinc proverbium, Lolio vitiari vsurpatur in eos, qui cacutiunt, & de rebus peruerse iudicant. Æram quoq; inter frugum vitia numerat Plinius, & cum est in pane, celerrime ait, vertigines facere. In Asia, Græciaq; balneatores, cum volunt turbam pelle-re, carbonibus id semen inticiunt. Melampyrum in siculo tritico peculiariter innasci traditur, nō tamen æque noxium ac lolium. In nostri segeti-bus prosilis herba, quæ nigella dicitur, cuius semé pinsitum, & in panificia redastum, non admodū ingratum gustu est, est enim tota planta sine odore, excepto semine, quod odoratum solum est. ideoq; panibus potest compinsi, sicut fœniculum & carui. Porro vitiari & corrumpi semina fre-quentioribus imbribus, imprimis vero triticum corru-
units.tr: They report that spoiled grain makes bread unpleasant in smell, colour and taste. So it matters a good deal to health whether bakers are careful or careless. Grain that has been winnowed and cleaned carelessly, and that is mixed with darnel and similar faults and then eaten, provides large causes of disease. How often do we see, from the greed and fraud of bakers and grain dealers, mouldy wheat gnawed by weevils ending up in bread? Clearly the grain is left unclean so that nothing is taken from the measure, as some who now keep the weights exact to a fingernail and test them by experiment. That darnel's juice is very harmful, causing headache and dizziness, I judge superfluous to prove with many examples. Hence the proverb "spoiled by darnel" is used of those who are dull-witted and judge matters perversely. Pliny also counts the weed called aera among the faults of grain, and says that when it is in bread it very quickly causes dizziness. In Asia and Greece, bath attendants, when they want to drive off a crowd, fumigate this seed with charcoal. Melampyrum is said to grow especially among Sicilian wheat, though it is not as harmful as darnel. In our fields there grows a plant called nigella, whose seed, when pounded and put into bread, is not very unpleasant in taste. The whole plant is without smell except the seed, which alone is fragrant, so it can be ground into bread, as fennel and caraway can. Moreover, that seeds are spoiled and corrupted by frequent rains is confirmed by experience, especially for wheat and

units.la: L & & hordeum, stercoratione quoque quandoque, tum cantharidibus, quae tritico, dum adhuc in spica est, innascuntur, experientia compertum est. Ex stercoratione virus redolere, cantharides grana erodere, exindeque contagione fruges infici, plane verisimile est. In frequentioribus pluviis & imbribus plus prosilire lolium quam in siccitatibus testantur praeter experientiam naturae rerum agricolationisque prudentes. Quid? quod ipsa femina cariosa, arrosa, & imbecilla fruges vitiant? Quapropter summa diligentia adhibenda est, ut fruges a tempestiva messe rite condantur: recentes enim & ventilatae & pulcriores sunt & ponderosiores, diu vero in horreo afficiuntur exustae deprehenduntur & leviores, minusque farinam reddunt. Plurimum etiam refert ante exactam & completam maturitatem fruges, cumprimis vero triticum & hordeum non demetere: ante enim tempus decisae molae maiori conflare deprehenduntur, multoque meliores ac laxiores: Superuacua humiditatis indubitatum argumentum: Sic enim recondita humore tepo concalescente corruptionem contrahunt & putrescunt: unde deteriores evadunt tum ad semen, tum ad usum cibarium. Intempestive igitur demessa fruges incorrupta servari non possunt, etiam in intensissima aruitia & perditissime frumentariorum dolo & fraude. Caeterum pura frumenta, quae in annos reponuntur, repurgari iubet Columella: quanto enim sunt expolitiora minus
units.tr: barley, and sometimes also by manure, and by the blister beetles that grow on wheat while it is still in the ear. That manure gives off a foul smell, that beetles eat away the grains, and that the crop is thereby infected by contagion, is plainly probable. Experience and the nature of things, and wise farmers, attest that darnel springs up more in wet and rainy seasons than in dry ones. What of the fact that the grain itself, decayed, gnawed and feeble, also spoils the crop? For this reason the greatest diligence must be applied so that the crop is properly stored after timely harvest. Fresh grain that has been winnowed is finer and heavier, but if it stays long in the granary it is found to be dried out, lighter, and gives less flour. It also matters greatly not to reap wheat and barley before the grain is fully and completely ripe, for grain cut too early is found to be much more bulky when ground, and much better and softer. This is an undoubted sign of excess moisture, for stored in that state, as the moisture warms, it contracts corruption and rots, and so becomes worse, both as seed and for food. Grain cut at the wrong time therefore cannot be kept sound, even in the driest weather, and even against the trickery and fraud of corn dealers. Columella, moreover, orders that clean grain which is stored for years be cleaned again, for the cleaner it is, the less it is gnawed by weevils. But if it is taken into use at once, it will be easy to

units.la: Cautela necessaria. minus à gurgulionibus arroduntur : sin vero protinus ad usum assumantur, sacile erit in vmbra refrigerari, in granarium reponere.
units.tr: Necessary caution. cool it in the shade and then put it back in the granary.

units.la: Nec statim à messe in vsum cibarium sunt affumenda, vt maior fere pars nostris temporibus & locis facere consueuit, sed loco sicco condenda sunt ac reponenda, modicèque sitcanda, al sum-ta sic, alieria in iis humiditate post adepta quadam excoctione. Cauendum quoque diligenter, ne praeter modum arescant, decedente sc. ab iis & exhalante natiua humiditate: immodicè enim sicca-ta in cibis dant nantur, quamuis absolute improba dici non possint. Certum est, quae in annos multos reposita durauerunt, vires inualidiores habere : vetusta autem & diutissime seruata sequenti experimento discernes, quippe dinifa ac fracta pulniseulum quendam tenuissimum o-ftentant atque emittunt, taliaq; in vsu cibario ingratissima sunt, sicut & erosa à noxiis ani-malculis valetudini obesse non dubitandum : ad diuturnitatem vero & durationem in mul-tos annos plurimum facit frugum matura deci-fio & colletio in siccitatibus, repositioq; in loco sicco, quo aer humorq; nō pertingit, nisi cū adu-stum promuntur, vnde auster damnatur & me-ridiei, auraq; humidiores nonnunquam propinquis locus aut amnibus expirates: laudatur aura a-quilonaris frigida & sicca, hac enim perennitate affert conditus frugibus. Vnde mirari non subit in Germania nostra fruges tam diu durare non posse ob imbrium f. abundantiam, quà robustissi-ma etiam grana corrumpi videmus. Fruges enim repositæ, si diu incorrupta manere debent, quotannis ventilandæ sunt & repurgandæ, monente Columella. Qui denique de re rustica post acceptam reliquerunt, in vniuersum iubent omnes messem fieri, antequam ex toto grana indurescant, æqualiter sicca flauescentibus, sic enim necimmodicè siccata, nec etiam nimis madida deprehenduntur. Hactenus de variis frugum cerealium & seminum corruptionis causis internis & externis, remotis & propinquis: redeamus nunc ad triticum.
units.tr: Grain should not be taken into food straight from the harvest, as most people in our times and places are wont to do. It should be stored and kept in a dry place, and dried moderately, so that it is taken after a certain kind of cooking, the moisture in it having been gone through. Care must also be taken not to let it dry out beyond measure, since its native moisture departs and evaporates. Grain dried excessively does not make good food, although it cannot be called absolutely bad. It is certain that grain which has lasted long in storage has weaker strength. You will tell old and very long-kept grain by this test: when crushed or broken, it gives off and releases a very fine dust, and such grain is most unpleasant for food, and, since it is gnawed by harmful little animals, there is no doubt it harms health. For durability and lasting many years, the most important things are timely gathering of the grain and harvesting it in dry weather, and storing it in a dry place where air and moisture do not reach it, and bringing it out only when it is dry. For this reason the south wind and the midday are condemned, and winds that are more humid, sometimes blowing from nearby places or rivers, while the cold, dry north wind is praised, for its steady air preserves the stored grain. Hence it is no surprise that in our Germany the grain cannot last so long, because of the abundance of rains, through which we see even the most robust grains corrupted. For stored grain, if it is to remain sound for long, must be winnowed and cleaned every year, as Columella advises. Finally, those who wrote on farming after Columella, all bid the harvest be made before the grains harden completely, while the stalks are equally dry and turning yellow, for thus the grain is found neither excessively dried nor too damp. So far concerning the various internal and external, remote and proximate causes of corruption in cereal grains and seeds. Let us now return to wheat.

units.la: Natura tritici est mediocriter siccare & calefacere, hominique præbere alimentum inter omnia frumenta familiare & salutare. Vsus eius præcipuè & maximè in pane sentitur: quippe aliter efficitur, siue crudum, siue elixum, succum crassum generat & lentum. Esu enim crudi tritici inflari aluum indubitatum est, ex voluptate verò & dulcedine plus effectum durumpit. Elixato rustico Asiaplarosq, vti Galenus testis est, concoctu tamen esse difficile & crassi succi afferat, ideoq; cibis abdicandum: quæ sita sunt, videant qui frumentatam, vt vocant, hoc est, Prisanam ex tritico confectam liberalius assumunt, olim enim hanc sorbitionem, & etiam-num quibusdam admodum placuisse & placere, infimamq; plebem in ieiunijs quadragenariis quandoque se ea solari atque reficere confuesse ebserobseruatum est. Olim celebrata ex tritico Ptisana est ad eadem commoda ad quae hordacea, scilicet ad asperitatem arteriae exulcerationem, nisi Ptisana quod triticea valentiora alimenti, et ad ciendas urinas efficacior perhibetur, hordacea vero gluti- tinosior, obiid pulmonis trachea ad ulcerationi utilior. Cum itaque non ex tritico tantum, sed hordeo, oryza et similibus Ptisana fieri consuevit, et in libris omnium Medicorum Ptisanae sorbitione nihil sit magis protritum atque decantatum, praesertim infebrium acutorum morborum cura, non ἀλόγως me hic fecisse existimauerim, si de Ptisana huiusmodi confectionibus generatim aliquid adiecero.
units.tr: The nature of wheat is to dry and warm moderately, and among all grains it provides food that is familiar and wholesome for humans. Its use is felt most especially and most strongly in bread, for when it is prepared otherwise, whether raw or boiled, it produces thick and sticky juice. It is certain that eating raw wheat causes flatulence in the bowels, and the pleasure and sweetness of it cause more harm by hardening. Boiled wheat, the rustic kind, as Galen testifies, is nonetheless hard to digest and yields thick juice, and so it must be excluded from food. Let those who take freely the frumentry, as they call it, that is, the ptisan made from wheat, see to these matters. It has been observed that this kind of broth was once, and still is, much liked by some, and that the lowest common people, during the forty days of fasting, were sometimes accustomed to comfort and refresh themselves with it. The ptisan made from wheat was once celebrated for the same benefits as that made from barley: namely, for roughness of the windpipe and its ulceration. It is said that the wheat ptisan is the more nourishing and more effective for promoting urine, while the barley one is more glutinous and more useful for ulceration of the lungs and trachea. Since the ptisan is customarily made not only from wheat but from barley, rice and similar grains, and since nothing is more often repeated and praised in the books of all physicians than the broth of ptisan, especially in the treatment of acute fevers, I think I shall not be acting without reason if I add something here about such preparations of ptisan in general.

units.la: Sciendum vero Ptisanam proprie, sicut ex antiquis et recentioribus scriptoribus liquet, dici de hordeo vel de corticato solum atque degluba-to, vel etiam de hordeo decoctio, vita Ptisana proprie nihil aliud sit, quam pulmentarium, sorbitio vel cremor ex hordeo in mortario contusoo et decorticato. Cremor vero lac seu succus ex grano macerato elicitus. Unde in consuetudine dipnosophistarum griphus ialabatur, succum hordei decorticati depsitum bibe. Athen. l. 10. dipno- sophi.
units.tr: It must be understood that, as is clear from ancient and recent writers, ptisan properly means only barley that has been husked and hulled, or a decoction of barley.
