Properly, the ptisan is nothing other than a pottage, a broth or a gruel made from barley pounded in a mortar and husked. The gruel is the milk, or juice, drawn from the macerated grain. Hence in the custom of the Deipnosophists the riddle ran: "Drink the juice of husked barley that has been pounded." Athenaeus, book 10, Deipnosophists.

units.la: Improprie vero et generaliter Ptisana appellatione veniunt omnia frumentacea, deglubata ac pistillis decorticata, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀλήσεως, fana, de hoc est, tundere vel decorticare, hinc Ptisanam quibus ex dicatur? ex zea, tritico, hordeo & oryza apud Galenum, Plin. & Hippocrat. concinnatam legimus. Tertio, dicebatur de omnibus his non crudis sed tum & deglubatis, sed etiam aqua coctis, Plin. l. 18. c. 17. Galen. 8. meth. & 7. c. 6.
units.tr: Improperly and in general, however, the name ptisan covers all grains that are hulled and husked with pestles, from ἀπὸ τῆς ἀλήσεως [from the grinding or threshing]. We read that ptisan was prepared from spelt, wheat, barley and rice by Galen, Pliny and Hippocrates. Thirdly, the name was applied to all these grains when they were not raw but hulled, and also boiled in water. Pliny, book 18, chapter 17; Galen, Method, book 8, and book 7, chapter 6.

units.la: Genuina autem & antiqua Ptisana confectionis ratio hæc erat: hordeum maturum, medulla plenum, non strigosum, sed crudum adhuc aqua irrigatum manibus fricabatur fortiter, donec exterior cortex bene abstergeretur: hoc ita aliquoties manibus subactum, sole siccatum in pilam coniiciebatur, vel usq; in mola trusatili pinsebatur, contusumq; suo cum polline ad necessarios usus in vase fictili condebatur, ex quo ptisanæ sorbitiones, pultem & cremorem concoquebant.
units.tr: The genuine and ancient method of preparing ptisan was this. Ripe barley, full of pith, not shrivelled but still moist from water, was rubbed vigorously with the hands until the outer husk was well rubbed off. Having been treated this way several times by hand and dried in the sun, it was put into a mortar, or pounded in a hand mill, and the crushed grain, together with its flour, was stored for the needed uses in an earthen vessel. From this, they boiled the ptisan broths, the porridge and the gruel.

units.la: Pollen tenuissimum est & purissimum in farina pulueris instar melis adhærescens, & proprie est in tritico, sicut flos in siligine.
units.tr: The pollen is the finest and purest part, clinging to the meal like dust, like honey, and it is properly found in wheat, as the flower is in fine wheat flour.

units.la: Porro simplex hordei decoctio per colum tracta ptisana colata, succus hordei & hordeata dicitur. Item aqua hordei, pars enim succulenta retinetur, terrestrior vero abicitur: In qua vero grana hordei colo vel cribro ab eorum succo segregata non sunt, ptisana non colata dicitur & sorbitio.
units.tr: Further, a plain decoction of barley strained through a sieve is called strained ptisan, barley juice, or barley water. For the succulent part is retained, while the more earthy part is thrown away. Where the barley grains have not been separated from their juice by a strainer or sieve, it is called unstrained ptisan, or a pottage.

units.la: Varij autem modis ptisanam condire solebant, vt aceto, melle, sapa, cymino, amygdalis, piperē, & similibus præsertim magis vel minus nutritientem. trientem, refrigorantem, abstergentem, pracordia humectantem, asperitatem pectoris demulcentem, ventrem lubricantem, sitisque extinguendam reddere eam studebant. Optima conditura est cum lacte feminis peponum vel amygdalarum dulcium & saccharo, pro plus vel minus nutriendi ac refrigerandi scopo. Si enim magis eam nutrire optamus, multa portio hordei adiicienda erit, multumque bullire permittendum: Si vero maior cura refrigerandi est, paucior erit hordei portio, atque non tam diu bullire concedendum. Fuerunt quoque alia operosiores & lautiores ptisanae decoctiones, ut cum melle, aceto, oleo, porro, anethoque, quas Apitius (qui arte culinaria pa-terna abligurierat bona) & Galen passim mentionem faciunt, sicut & Aegineta lib. 1. & Oribasius in Euporistis, qui tamen minus aquae accipit, unam nempe hordei praeparati heminam, hoc est, dimidium sextarii in X. tantum aquae heminis coquit, donec medulla hordei fuerit eliquata, tum mel, acetum & salinicit, & postquam in ebullitione hordeum detumuit, porrum & anethum quoque addere solitum est.
units.tr: People used to season ptisan in various ways, with vinegar, honey, must syrup, cumin, almonds, pepper and similar things, especially to make it more or less nourishing, warming, cooling, cleansing, moistening the heart, soothing roughness of the chest, loosening the bowels, and quenching thirst. The best seasoning is with the milk of pumpkin seeds or of sweet almonds, and sugar, according to whether the aim is more or less nourishment and cooling. For if we wish it to nourish more, a large portion of barley must be added, and it must be allowed to boil for a long time. But if greater care is taken to cool, the portion of barley will be smaller, and it must not be allowed to boil for so long. There were also other more elaborate and more luxurious decoctions of ptisan, with honey, vinegar, oil, leek and dill. Apicius, who had squandered his father's goods on culinary arts, and Galen mention them frequently, as do Aegineta, book 1, and Oribasius in the Euporista. Oribasius, however, takes less water: he boils one hemina of prepared barley, that is half a sextarius, in ten hemina of water only, until the pith of the barley is dissolved. Then he adds honey, vinegar and salt, and when the barley has swelled up in the boiling he is accustomed to add leek and dill too.

units.la: Aegineta vero accipit aquae partes XV. paululum oloei, & post ebullitionem acetum addebat, post vero exactam coctionem parum salis friabilis inspergebat: atque hoc modo ptisana etiam extrinseco & oryza ad varios usus coquinari praeparari potest. Ad extremum vulgaris nostra ex hordeo aqua, quae frequenter utimur in febrium cura, conficiendi modus non est apud omnes vnus & idem: quidam simpliciter aquâ macerant, quidam tam, vt ex hordeo {y}hum præparant. Galeno fuisse eam ignotam inde constare quibusdam videtur, quod quidem explicaturus Hippocratem 4. acutorum libro, iubentem, vt febricitantes ad sedandam sitim aquâ hordeacea potum bibant, dicit, hordei poculum esse ἀδιψον, hoc est, sitis extinctivum, sed non docet qua ratione hordeum præparetur. Oribasius V. Galiani Imp. medicus id videtur docere, quan-do, inquit, non oportet febrientibus hordeum in pila tundere, sed grana compressa dilatare & coquere in aqua, hordeumque in aqua tepida bis abluere, deinde illius hordei herminam, hoc est, dimidium sextarii (eine halbe Maß) in x. aquæ heminis ad hordei vsque crepaturam coquere, tandemque colare: in fine decoctionis quiddam addunt cinnamomum, nucem moschatam, zinziber vel galangam, vel etiam post decoctionem modicum croci integri prout morbus requirit, habita ratione simul naturæ patientis, ætatis & temporis.
units.tr: Aegineta takes fifteen parts of water, a little oil, and adds vinegar after boiling, and after the cooking is finished he sprinkles in a little crumbly salt. In this way ptisan can also be prepared from extrinsic barley and from rice, for various uses in the kitchen. Finally, our common barley water, which we often use in the treatment of fevers, is not made in the same way by everyone: some simply macerate the barley in water, while others prepare it from barley in a more elaborate way. It seems to some that Galen did not know it, and he indeed, explaining Hippocrates in the fourth book of the Acute Diseases, where Hippocrates bids feverish patients drink barley water to quench thirst, says that a barley drink is ἀδιψον [thirst-quenching], that is, it extinguishes thirst, but he does not teach how the barley is prepared. Oribasius, physician to the emperor Julian, seems to teach this in book 5, when he says: "It is not right to pound barley in a mortar for feverish patients, but the grains should be pressed, softened and boiled in water; the barley should be washed twice in lukewarm water, then a hemina of this barley, that is half a sextarius (eine halbe Maß), should be boiled in ten hemina of water until the barley bursts, and finally strained." At the end of the decoction they add something: cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger or galangal, or after the decoction a little whole saffron, as the illness requires, having regard at the same time to the nature of the patient, their age and the season.

units.la: Depultibus, placentis, paneque ex tritico, & hordeo, de cereuisia, huiusque coctione commodius dicetur (suo loco post frugum sc. tractationem.
units.tr: Concerning poultices, cakes and bread made from wheat and barley, and concerning beer and its brewing, this will be more conveniently discussed in its own place, after the treatment of grains.

units.la: Hucusque igitur de Ptisana, sequuntur nunc vires quædam iritici speciatiores, quas hic negligere, effet glori a illud sua f audar
units.tr: So far, then, concerning ptisan. Now follow certain more particular powers of wheat, which it would be shameful to neglect here.

units.la: Annotatum vero supra est naturam eius esse modice calfacere & exiccare, propterea pra- stantissimum & delicatissimum ex eo panem concinnari. Expertum praeterea est farinam eius in aqua vel laȼte cum butyro bene decoȼ-ȼtam, vel etiam cum oleo amygdalarum dul-cium (quodin experimentis habeo, licet non a-pud omnes in vsu sit) contra tussim, arteriam exasperatam, cruentas & sanguinolentas excreationes pectorisque catera vitia efficacem esse.
units.tr: It has been noted above that its nature is to warm and dry moderately, and therefore the most excellent and most delicate bread is made from it. It has also been found by experience that its flour, well boiled in water or milk with butter, or also with oil of sweet almonds (which I have tested, though it is not in use among all people), is effective against cough, a roughened windpipe, bloody and blood-streaked spitting, and other diseases of the chest.

units.la: Sextum Pompeium in tritico coȼto adge-nua uq; sedendo podagra liberatum historia tradunt.
units.tr: Histories relate that Sextus Pompeius, freed from gout, was cured by sitting on his knees on boiled wheat.

units.la: Farinam triticeam cum aqua & melle decoȼlam, quamuis phlogosin & inflammatio-nem discutere, emplastri vice illitam atq; appo-sitam, qui dubitat, experiatur.
units.tr: Wheat flour boiled with water and honey, though it disperses inflammation and swelling, applied and laid on like a plaster: let whoever doubts it try it.

units.la: Furfures tritici aqua cum melle decoȼti, percolatiq;, colli palatiq; inflammationes sa-nant, gargarizatu & collutione: colluatur au-tem os tepide: si vis, adde flores malvae hortensis, qui Germanis dicuntur, Ehrnrosen/Herbst-rosen; hi enim maxime in oris colliq; inflammationibus commendantur: si adhst oris exulceratio coȼlioni adde alumen.
units.tr: Wheat bran boiled in water with honey and strained cures inflammations of the throat and palate, by gargling and rinsing. Let the mouth be rinsed with it lukewarm. If you wish, add the flowers of the garden mallow, which are called by the Germans Ehrnrosen or Herbstrosen, for these are especially recommended for inflammations of the mouth and throat. If there is an ulceration of the mouth, add alum to the rinse.

units.la: In aceto vero & vino tritici furfures de-coȼti utilissime adhibentur membris neruoq; luxatis, sanant serpigines, pruriginem, & mam-marum inflammationes: efficacius operantur si pigines. Addideris ruthaam & agrimoniam: si vero luxa-tionitionibus illorum decoctum tantum adhibendum est, in fine decoctionis adde crocum, vel, quod melius est post remotionem abigne.
units.tr: Wheat bran boiled in vinegar and wine is most usefully applied to dislocated limbs and sinews; it heals creeping ulcers, itching and inflammations of the breasts. It works more effectively if you add rue and agrimony. If, however, only the decoction is to be applied to dislocations, add saffron at the end of the boiling, or, what is better, after it has been removed from the fire.

units.la: Fermentum ex ritico extenuandi, extrahendi, maturandi, concoquendi aperiendi qq vi pollere ostendunt furunculi caeteraq; tubercula cutanea maturanda, concoquenda atq; aperienda, ut materia putris intus conclusa egrediatur: adiiciendum vero modicum falis est, emplastriq; vice applicandum.
units.tr: Bran of wheat, made into a ferment, shows the power to thin, draw out, ripen, digest and open. It ripens, digests and opens boils and other cutaneous tubercles, so that the putrid matter enclosed inside comes out. A small amount of salt must be added, and it is applied in the manner of a plaster.

units.la: Tritici quoq; proles est amylum, farina fc.ex tritico sine mola confecta: dictum enim quod sine mola conficiatur: optimum ex trimestri fit tritico, huius qq inuentionem deberi insula Chio prodidit Plinius; idq; sua aetate fuisse laudatissimum. Dioscorides laudat Creticum & Aegyptium. Probatur leuitate, & ut candidum ac recens sit, nec tactu asperum. Emplasticum vere est, hoc est tenacius adhaerescendo obstruit & infarctu implet, siccat & absorbet, quare sanguinis reiectiones potu cohibet, cum saccharo & modico croci prodest tussientibus & asthmaticis, faucibus item exasperatis, cum oleo vero amygdalarum dulc. decoctum admixto saccharo Candi pectoris apostematum sanat, imbuendum autem, antequam coquatur in aqua per noctem est: contra oculorum deniq; fluxus, pustulas cavaq; ulcera illitum efficax est. Confidendi modum antiqui satis satisq; tradiderunt. Aegineta ex purgato tritico fieri sub Canicula feruoribus tradit. Vulgaris modum talis est. Triticum in aquam frigidam recentem iniicitur, s-piusq; in die agitatur, indies recentem affun-dendo: quinto die effunditur aqua sensim, cum sc. triticum fuerit emollitum, vasculoq; puro ex-cipitur, contusumq; triticum per pannum cola-tur, aqua autem effusa nonnihil ei admiscea-tur ob facilitatem penetrationem, colatum in sole siccatur, aquam vero innatantem omnem ef-fundes vel effluere sines, & ita confectum est.
units.tr: Starch is also an offspring of wheat: amylum, flour made from wheat without a mill, for it is said to be made without a mill. The best comes from trimester wheat. Pliny reports that its invention is owed to the island of Chios, and that in his day it was most highly praised there. Dioscorides praises the Cretan and the Egyptian. It is tested by its lightness, and by whether it is white and fresh and not rough to the touch. It is truly emplastic, that is, by adhering more tenaciously it obstructs and fills up blockages, and it dries and absorbs. Therefore, taken as a drink, it checks spitting of blood. With sugar and a little saffron it helps those who cough and those with asthma, and likewise roughened throats. Boiled with sweet almond oil and candied sugar, it heals apostemes of the chest. It must be steeped in water overnight before it is cooked. Finally, applied to the eyes, it is effective against fluxes, and against pustules and hollow ulcers. The ancients have handed down enough about the method of preparing it. Aegineta says it is made from cleaned wheat under the heat of the Dog Star. The common method is this: the wheat is put into fresh cold water and stirred often during the day, with fresh water poured on each day. On the fifth day the water is gradually poured off, once the wheat has softened, and it is received in a clean vessel. The crushed wheat is strained through a cloth, and a little of the poured-off water is mixed in to make it pass through more easily. The strained matter is dried in the sun, and any water floating on top is poured off or allowed to drain away, and so it is finished.

units.la: Ex triticis denique aliud præcocius, aliud se-rius prouenit, aliud plures, aliud pauciores emit-tit culmos. Legitur vno ex tritici grano 30. aut 40 quandoq; exiisse spicatos culmos, quod tamen terra bonitati, fertilitati & diligenti cultura ac-ceptum ferendum est: atq; huc respexisse Sal-uatorem nostrum extra dubium est, cum dicit in parabola ad populum, sementem quæ in bo-nam terram cecidisset, aliam quidem centu-plum, aliam sexagecuplum aliam deniq; trige-cuplum tulisse fructum. Eandem habet ratio-nem, quod quadam loca adeo præcocia & ferti-lia deprehenduntur, vt circa Thracium Si-num & in Chalcia Rhodiorum insula & c. vt quadragesimo à satione die triticum mature-scat, testante Plinio & Theophr. lib. 9. hist. Plant. quoddam 9. mens. in agris moratur, vt in quibus-dam locis hibernis: quoddam 7. à satione mense hor-reis mandatur, unde septimestre dici meretur: quoddam 3. à satione mense erumpit, vt sitanium amelcoan/ex quo optimum fit amylum, et trimestre Diofcoridi appellatur. Sed eiusmodi beneficium fertilitasq; nostro solo denegata est, apud nos enim quinto demum mense maturatur, adeo fruges alio atq; alio solo inter se distant, alio a q; alio gaudent cœlo, suum q; cuiq; frumento tempus, quo ad maturitatem perducitur, pro terrarum diuersitate in singulis regionibus deputatum cernimus. Tantum de tritico.
units.tr: Some wheat ripens earlier and some later, and some sends up more stalks and some fewer. It is reported that from a single grain of wheat as many as thirty or forty ears of stalks have sometimes come up. This, however, must be credited to the goodness of the soil, its fertility and careful cultivation. Our Saviour certainly had this in mind when, in the parable to the people, he says that the seed which fell on good ground brought forth fruit, some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, and some thirtyfold. For the same reason, some places are found to be so early and so fertile that, around the Thracian Gulf and in Chalcia, an island of the Rhodians, wheat ripens on the fortieth day after sowing, as Pliny and Theophrastus (Book 9 of the Historia Plantarum) attest. Some wheat stays in the fields for nine months, as in certain places with winter climates. Some is stored in barns seven months after sowing, whence it deserves to be called septimestre. Some sprouts three months after sowing, such as the sitanium amelcoan, from which the best starch is made, and which Dioscorides calls trimestre. But such a benefit of fertility has been denied to our soil. For among us wheat ripens only in the fifth month. So far do crops differ from one soil to another, and so far do they enjoy different skies, that we see a time for each kind of grain, by which it is brought to ripeness, assigned in each region according to the diversity of lands. That is enough about wheat.

units.la: A tritico proximam sibi dignitatem vendicant Siligo & Hordeum.
units.tr: Rye and barley claim the rank of dignity next to wheat.

units.la: De Siligine non parua controuersia inter doctos reiq; frumentarie scriptores exorta est, quo pasto videl. veteribus fuerit hoc frumenti genus appellatum? quid? quod & nostra ætate doctissimi quiq; medici in frugibus antiquorum discernendis non parum ambigere video, cum de vulgatissimo & notissimo hordeo dubitare illos animaduertam. Plinius vir alioquin acerrimi ingenii plurima hic confuse tradidit. Galenus de frumentis & feminibus, quæ in vsu cibario erant, diligenter admodum sed tamen non vsquequaq; aperte disseruisse visus est. Veteribus Siligo non tantum altera tritici species erat, in quam triticum tertio anno degenerabat, sed quoq; depuratissima a furfuribus farina, Starschön Weitzenmehl/ quam Plinius obid tritici delitias appellat. l.18.c.8. & 10. ac 11. Et Cornelius Celsus l.2.c.17.ex tritico inquit firmissima siligo. Et idem Plinius, ex Siligine ait firmissimus panis, qui pistus dicebatur Siligi-tisicut Semidalitiŭ, hoc est, Simila, qui conficiebatur ebatur extritico non exquisite a furfuribus de-purato, & syncomistus a Dioscoride appellaba-tur a farina cum furfuribus commixtione, nihil enim furfuris cribro ab eo excussum est, ut ita exquisite pura tritici farina, & ex ea panis siligo, similago, & semidulis dicta si veteribus. Fuisse autem siliginem frugem I alii notissimam, magnamque in panificiis gratiam obtinuisse ostendit Iuvenalis carmine Satyrico Romanorum diuitum morem reprehendens, qui alium sibi ac delicatiorem quam communem panem apponi iubebant:
units.tr: Concerning rye, no small controversy has arisen among the learned and among writers on grain: by what name, namely, did the ancients call this kind of grain? Indeed, I observe that in our own age the most learned physicians, in distinguishing the crops of the ancients, are not a little uncertain, and I notice that they doubt even about the most common and well-known barley. Pliny, a man otherwise of very sharp mind, has here delivered many things in a confused way. Galen, in his work on grains and seeds that were used for food, seems to have discussed them very carefully, but not everywhere clearly. For the ancients, rye was not only a second species of wheat, into which wheat degenerated in the third year, but also flour purified of bran, Starschön Weitzenmehl, which Pliny calls the delicacy of wheat (Book 18, chapters 8, 10 and 11). And Cornelius Celsus, Book 2, chapter 17, says: "from wheat comes the firmest rye." And Pliny himself says that from rye comes the firmest bread, which was called pistus Siligitis, as well as semidalitium, that is, simila, which was made from wheat not exquisitely cleared of bran, and syncomistus, as Dioscorides called it, from flour mixed with bran, for nothing of the bran had been sifted out by the sieve. Thus from the ancients come the names siligo, similago and semidulis for bread made from exquisitely pure wheat flour. That rye was a well-known grain, and held great favour in baking, is shown by Juvenal in his Satires, rebuking the custom of the rich Romans, who ordered that a bread finer and more delicate than the common bread be set before them:

units.la: Ecce alius quanto porrexit murmure panem
units.tr: Look, how loudly the other one called for bread

units.la: Vix fractum solidae jam muccida fructa farinae,
units.tr: Hardly broken, already mouldy, of solid flour,

units.la: Quae geminum agerent non admittentia morsum:
units.tr: Which would not admit a double bite:

units.la: Sed tener & niueus molliq; siligine factus
units.tr: But soft and snow-white, made of soft rye,

units.la: Seruatur Domino.
units.tr: Is kept for the master.

units.la: Panis hic siliginei meminit ut lautissimi ac primarii, venustecq; & eleganter Romanos luxum in pane quaerentes exagitat.
units.tr: Here he speaks of rye bread as the most elegant and first-rate, and he charmingly and elegantly censures the Romans who sought luxury in their bread.

units.la: Alii in hoc consentiunt siliginem vetē-rum esse quod Germani Korn oder Roggen appellant. Et ex omnibus testimoniis veterum congestis liquido constare arbitror, siliginem, triticum, sicut & Speltam congeneres esse frugem, nam & Columella l. 2. c. 6. siliginem secundum dum tritici genus facit, & Theophrastus Siligi‑nem tritico similem esse dixit, vocans eam ho‑rayopyron : Dioscorides quoq; Spelta generi eam annumerat. l. 2. c. 82. ut ita in totum dixisse lice‑at, Siliginem nostram, quam German Rocken appellant, cuius grana in molis tunduntur, quodq; crassius est pro pecorum nutrimento a farina separatur, furfures nominant, a vete‑rum siligine longe esse diuersam, cum siligo illa non tantum sit granum delicatissimi tritici, ve‑rum etiam interdum medulla siliginei grani: Summa enim panis laus siliginis bonitate & praestantia apud illos constabat, ac panis ex ea conficiebatur delicatissimus & dulcissimus, cu‑ex nostra siligine insuauior, crassior ac atrior e‑nadat pro locorum tamen terrarumq; ac coeli temperatura varia. hucusq; de siligine.
units.tr: Others agree on this point, that the rye of the ancients is what the Germans call Korn or Roggen. And from all the testimonies of the ancients gathered together, I think it clearly established that rye, wheat, and likewise spelt are kindred grains. For Columella (Book 2, chapter 6) makes rye a second kind of wheat, and Theophrastus said that rye is similar to wheat, calling it [ὡραιόπυρον]. Dioscorides also counts it among the spelt kind (Book 2, chapter 82). So one may speak in general terms: the rye we have, which the Germans call Rocken, whose grains are ground in mills, and whose coarser part is separated from the flour for feeding livestock, they call bran. This is very different from the rye of the ancients, for that rye was not only the grain of the most delicate wheat, but sometimes also the marrow of the rye grain. For the highest praise of bread among them rested on the goodness and excellence of rye, and the bread made from it was most delicate and sweetest, whereas our rye is less agreeable, coarser and darker, though this varies with the temperature of places, lands and skies. So far on rye.

units.la: Submonitio ad locum de Siligine.
units.tr: Note on the passage on Siligo.

units.la: Sunt qui existimant, quod Germani tocken nominant, id esse siliginem veterum & jecale, nec non triticum secundum Columellam, olyram vero appellatam Theophrasto & Dioscoridi. Sunt praterea qui siliginem Romanorum eandem esse cum olyra Graecorum esse putant, nam Theodorus Gaza fidelissimus Aristotelis et Theophrasti interpres pro olyra siliginem vertit. Plinius seorsim de siligine & olyra tractat, unde cadit illorum sententia, qui olyram siliginem esse Plinium prodidisse scripserunt. Alii Germanorum siliginem antiquorum typham esse cen‑tendunt: alii esse diuersa coniuncunt, quod triticum, siligo & hordeum teste Plin. in area ex- eruntur, Zea vero cuius species est olyra mola exterirur & cum suis folliculis feritur. At olyrä Africanam siliginem esse Plinius sequenti, af- firmat verbis l.18.c.10 Ex ea dulcissimus sit pa- nis,inquit spissiorq; est ipsa quam far, & ponde- rosior,raroq; modicus granorum eius non sexde- cim libras farina admplet, exteritur in Gracia difficulter,propterea iumentis dari Hom. tradi- dit, hac enim est inquit quam vocant olyram.
units.tr: Some think that what the Germans call tocken is the ancient siligo and jecale, and also triticum according to Columella, but that Theophrastus and Dioscorides called it olyra. Others think that the Roman siligo is the same as the Greek olyra, for Theodorus Gaza, the most faithful interpreter of Aristotle and Theophrastus, translates olyra as siligo. Pliny treats siligo and olyra separately, so the opinion of those who have written that Pliny reported olyra to be siligo falls away. Others hold that the German siligo is the typha of the ancients, and others judge them to be different, since wheat, siligo and barley, as Pliny attests, are threshed on the threshing floor, while zea, of which olyra is a species, is ground in a mill and beaten with its husks. But that African siligo is olyra Pliny asserts in the following words, book 18, chapter 10: "From it the sweetest bread is made," he says, "and it is thicker and heavier than far itself, and rarely does a modest amount of its grains fill sixteen pounds of flour. It is threshed with difficulty in Greece, and for that reason he taught that it is given to the beasts of burden; for this is what they call olyra."

units.la: Olyra v. Ægypto peculiaris est,sicut & Gal- lis,qui eam arincam nominant,Italisq; Theoph. l.de plantis,olyram inter ea,quæ tritico hordeoq; sunt similia,retulit,matureq; feri prodidit, quin & multiplici folio includi, molliore; atq; infir- miorem typha,avena, Zea, colore item candido. Non desunt qui nostra siliginem typhä potiu esse q olyr a suspicantur: Est nam q; typha Galeno te- ste 2 de alim.cereale frumentiu, cuius granum gluma sine innuolucro velut triticu & hordeum vestitur,pinsituq; totum in panes densatur,color illi tritico flauior,corpus strigosum,tritico exili unde & parum tritici quibusdam appellatur. Ha- ttenus de sil'gine,cuius disceptatio,sicut & cate- rorum frumentorum ideo ambigua est,quod,sicut aliquoties memini,non eadem ubiq; sint frumeti genera,&si eadem,neq; tamen iisdem nominib. appellitentur,sufficit illa frumentorum genera ex- ploratu habere, quæ in nostris regionib. fata pro- nuntiant, quorumq; vsus ac vires sunt perspecta atq; probata.
units.tr: Olyra is peculiar to Egypt, as it is to the Gauls, who call it arinca, and to the Italians. Theophrastus, in his book on plants, lists olyra among those plants that are similar to wheat and barley, and reports that it ripens late, and moreover that it is enclosed in several husks, softer and weaker than typha, oats or zea, and likewise of a white colour. There are those who suspect that our siligo is rather typha than olyra. For typha, according to Galen's testimony in book 2 of On Foods, is a cereal grain whose kernel, like wheat and barley, is clothed in a husk without an outer covering, and when ground is made into dense bread. Its colour is more yellow than wheat's, its body is meagre, and from its thinness some call it "little wheat". So far on siligo. Its dispute, like that of the other grains, is ambiguous for this reason: as I have often mentioned, the kinds of grain are not everywhere the same, and even where they are the same they are not called by the same names. It is enough to know accurately those kinds of grain which our regions produce, and whose uses and powers have been observed and proven.

units.la: Hordeum ad varios medicina vsus vsur-patum ab antiquis inuenitur, & nobilissimum ab iisfrumentum appellatum est. Hodie raro lautiorum atq; magnatum mensas subit, nisi cortice suo castratum, mundatum hordeum ap-pellatum. Tundendo enim deglubitur, gerolte oder gescheite Gersten / elixum enim primo cibo sumi solet, stomacho non ingratum praser-tim si aceti modicum fuerit permixtum: quod si vero diu fuerit elixum non fuerit, inflat, & ventriculo noxium est, minus enim abstergit. Plurimum eo in papatu vescuntur in ieiunio illo quadragenario. Caeterum cum hordeum cuiq; notissimum sit, hic illud delineare operae pretium esse non puto, nisi, quod, sicut & in aliis, meminisse & hic oportet, omnia femina, praecipue vero frumenta pro locorum natura varia, coeli statu in quo sata sunt & enata, bonitatem adipisci vel malignitatem. Maturius feritur quam triticum, & primo ex omnibus frumentis erumpit a primo satu, die vt plurimum septimo, magis quam festinat quam tritici nam. In Aegypto tertio quartoque die provenit, sexto vero a satu mense metitur, in Hellade septimo, in Peloponneso octaue. Hiopes non aliam quam milii & hordei frugem nouerc. Melius autem deteriusq; fit cultura & soli natura. Terram requirit optimam & bene stercoratam, quae si destituitur, facile in lolium transit & degenerat praesertim pluuiosa tempestate. Causam huius
units.tr: Barley, used in ancient medicine for various purposes, was called by the ancients the noblest of grains. Today it rarely enters the tables of the wealthier and the great, unless it has been stripped of its husk and cleaned, and is then called pearl barley. For it is peeled by pounding (German: <bl>gerolte oder gescheite Gersten</bl>). It is usually eaten first, boiled, and is not unpleasant to the stomach, especially if a little vinegar is mixed in. But if it has not been boiled for long, it causes bloating and is harmful to the stomach, for it cleanses less. In Papacy they eat much of it during that forty-day fast. Otherwise, since barley is known to everyone, I do not think it worth the trouble to describe it here, except that, as with other things, it is also right to remember here that all seeds, and especially grains, vary according to the nature of the place, and gain goodness or badness from the condition of the sky under which they are sown and grow. It is sown earlier than wheat, and of all grains it comes up first from the sowing, usually on the seventh day, and comes up faster than wheat. In Egypt it comes up on the third or fourth day, and in the sixth month after sowing it is reaped; in Hellas on the seventh, in the Peloponnese on the eighth. The Ethiopians know no crop other than millet and barley. Cultivation and the nature of the soil make it better or worse. It requires the best soil, well manured; if this is lacking, it easily turns into darnel and degenerates, especially in rainy weather. The cause of this

units.la: Hordeu. munda-tum. N. Frumenta omnia pro coeli statu variant. huius rei assignat Galenus aliquam 1. de alim. cum ait, a patre suo agricolationis peritissimo, longo usu observatum fuisse, femina tritici, cum infirmiora fuerint et imperfectiora, diutius intra humum delituerint, non facile fructum bonum edere posse, sed potius converti in lolium herbam sc. segetibus inimicam. Theophrastus aut hordeum primum in triticum, in hordeum vero triticum mutari, atque ita deinceps ex utroque generari lolium. Sed id fortasse in agro Asiatico aut Atheniensi, ubi maximum optimum et firmissimum hordeum reperitur, euenire solet. Noster sermo de germanico hordeo est. Porro laudatissimum hordeum id est, quod fractum et pinsitum candorem repraesentat, quod densum, planum ac ponderosum est, laxum enim, gracile et leve improbatur. Sed certissimum vitiosi hordei indicium est, quando e fracto et diviso excidit pulmusculus quidam, quo significatur interna corruptio, caries, situs ac putredo.
units.tr: Barley, cleaned. N. All grains vary according to the state of the sky. Galen gives some reason for this in book 1 of On Foods, where he says that his father, most skilled in farming, had observed from long experience that grains of wheat, when weaker and less perfect, lie hidden longer in the ground and cannot easily produce good fruit, but are rather turned into darnel, a weed hostile to crops. Theophrastus says that barley first changes into wheat, and wheat into barley, and so in turn both produce darnel. But this usually happens in the Asian or Athenian field, where the largest, best and firmest barley is found. Our discussion is about German barley. Moreover, the most praised barley is that which, when broken and pounded, shows whiteness, which is dense, flat and heavy; for loose, slender and light barley is disapproved. But the most certain sign of faulty barley is when a small dust falls out of a broken and split grain, which signifies internal corruption, decay, mould and rot.

units.la: Verum quaestio hic occurrebat, quae discutienda est, an hordeum sicut et alia femina, protinus a messe et tritura sint meliora, an vero certo tempore post? Quosdam non pati exiccari triticum et hordeum Theophrastus meminit, propterea quod ad reddendam farinam meliora minus arefacta putantur, unde in aceruos tam triticum quam hordeum reponere solent: in hac etiam sententia agricolationis periti quidam esse reperiuntur. Alii femina non protinus a tritura meliora
units.tr: But here a question arises that must be discussed: whether barley, like other grains, is better straight after harvest and threshing, or only after some time? Theophrastus records that some do not allow wheat and barley to dry out, because less dried grain is thought better for producing flour; for this reason they usually store both wheat and barley in heaps, and some skilled farmers hold this view too. Others hold that grains are not better straight after threshing

units.la: Notae hordei laudatissimi.
units.tr: Marks of the most praised barley.

units.la: An frumenta nouella annicullis praesentiu, an vero haec illis? meliora esse quam certo tempore post, nec nouella anniculis praestare inde conuincunt, quod necesse sit, ut veluti excoctionem quandam atque potestatem capiant, exacto sc. quod fuerit in illo alienum: humor enim superuacuus conco-quendus erit in loco sicco & minime humenti primumque in vsum cibarium veniant, mediocriter siccata, salutaria sunt & cibis idonea. Columella affirmat frumenta decisa tempestate inc ementum postea capere, qua si pura deinde in annum reconduntur, repurgari debent, quanto enim sunt expolitiora, tanto minus a gurgulionibus exeduntur, sin protinus vsui destinantur, satius est in vmbra refrigerari, & ita granario inferi: intempestiue vero demessa incorrupta diutius seruari non posse videmus, sic enim condita concalescunt & putrescunt. Prior sententia vera esse potest de cento tritici & hordei genere: est namque tritici sicut & hordei genus trimestre, sic appellatum quod trium mensium spatio possit perfici, idque in cibo hominis facilius est gratum, quod videl. minus terra infit propter temporis breuitatem, germ. Sommergersten. Hocobiter notandum frumentarius negotiatoribus &
units.tr: Are new grains better than those a year old, or the reverse? Those who hold that they are better than after a certain time, and do not concede that new grain surpasses that a year old, argue from this that they must undergo, as it were, a certain cooking and strengthening once whatever was foreign in them has been driven out; for superfluous moisture must be dried off in a dry and not at all damp place, and only then do they come into use as food. Moderately dried, they are wholesome and fit for food. Columella affirms that grains cut at an unseasonable time acquire, afterwards, ... if they are then stored pure for the year, they must be cleaned again, for the cleaner they are, the less they are eaten by weevils. But if they are destined for immediate use, it is better to cool them in the shade and then put them into the granary. We see that grain reaped at the wrong time cannot be kept uncorrupted for long, for so stored it heats up and rots. The former opinion may be true of a certain kind of wheat and barley: there is a kind of wheat, and of barley, called trimestre, so named because it can be completed in a space of three months, and this is more easily pleasing in human food, since it is less infected by the earth on account of the shortness of time (German: Sommergersten). It should be noted here that I leave to grain merchants and

units.la: annonam flagellantibus relinquo frumenta im-modice sicca, quaeque repositia in multos annos duraverunt, vires inualidiores & imbecilliores habere, cuius rei, ut ante meminisse indicium euolans dimissis ac fractis granis puluisculus: Sed eiusmodi Da danarios, sic enim Vlpianus eos appel-
units.tr: to those who drive up the price of grain: grains that are excessively dry, and those kept in storage for many years, have weaker and feebler powers. Of this, as I mentioned before, the sign is the dust that flies out when the grains are released and broken. But such men, for so Ulpian calls them,

units.la: Censura appellat, qui omnia praemunt ut carius ea postea distrahant, capite de vinis, verioribus coloribus depingam.
units.tr: Censure: they are those who hoard everything so that they may sell it later at a higher price. I shall describe them in more accurate colours in the chapter on wines.

units.la: Apud Campanos κατ' ἐξοχὴν ἀνόβιλιtatem scilicet & frugis praestantia Semen appella-tum est: quin ex ea praestant jimmam atq; [alu-bersimam alicam confici prodidit Dioscor. l. 2. c. 80. & Plinius l. 18. c. 8. In Campania provincia laudatissima, ac in multis quoq; Italiae locis. Typhae pe-quam similem esse scribit Theophrastus; matureq; seri dicitur solo pingui & læto: granum multiplici tunica includitur, facilimum, omnibusq; animantibus gratissimum. Qui far non habent, loco eius utuntur Zea. Quidam tamen far eam esse putant. Duorum autem est genernm, una simplex, altera in binis putaminibus bina grana ichia gerens, unde dicoccos appellatur. Scribit Dioscorides (chondron ex ea, quae dicoccos dicitur, & Crimnon, hoc est, farinam crassiorem seu crasulentam confici, ex qua faciebant pultes abunde alentes, sed quae agre conficiuntur. Galenus rerum natura prudentissimus 1. de alimentis, nihil certi videtur de Zea statuere, ait enim se nusquam vidisse nec ab ullo alio audivisse semen esse aliquod frumentaceum, quod vulgo appellatur Zea, inq; totum vult, nullam aliam esse exquirendam praeter olyras & typhas.
units.tr: Among the Campanians, grain was called "semen" by way of eminence, from its excellence and quality of produce. Indeed, Dioscorides in book 2, chapter 80, and Pliny in book 18, chapter 8, report that from it they make the finest and most nourishing alica. It is most praised in the province of Campania, and in many places in Italy too. Theophrastus writes that it is similar to typha; it is said to be sown late, in rich and fertile soil. The grain is enclosed in a manifold husk, is very easy to prepare, and is most pleasing to all animals. Those who lack far use zea in its place. Some, however, think it is far. There are two kinds: one simple, the other bearing two grains in each of two husks, whence it is called dicoccos. Dioscorides writes that chondros, and crimnon, that is a thicker or coarser flour, are made from what is called dicoccos, and from it they made porridges that nourish abundantly but are hard to prepare. Galen, most prudent in the nature of things, in book 1 of On Foods, seems to establish nothing certain about zea. For he says that he has nowhere seen, nor heard from anyone else, that any grain-like seed is commonly called zea, and in general he wants no other grain to be sought beyond olyra and typha.

units.la: Alica seu Chondrus. Crimnho. Ex Crimno pultes. Galeni de Zea dubium. Idem quaedam esse femina testatur, quae partim in hordei aut typha, partim in typha oly aq, aut olyra aut tritici medio sunt loco, quaedam vero esse quae ad oly a, alia ad hordei aut typhæ, alia ad tritici, alia ad panici, alia quae ad milii naturam proximè accedant quae nomina habent, alia simplicia, ut in Italia, alia composita, ut in Cappadocia γυμνόχεμον, hoc est, ho deum nudum ac corticis expers in Bithynia autem minoris Asiæ regione Zeopyron, hoc est, ex Zea & tritico nomen conflatum est, ut ita adeo difficillimum sit de iis feminibus exquisite differere, quae in nostro orbe non feruntur, e quibus etiam in usum nostrum cibarium nihil ad nos venit.
units.tr: Alica or chondrus. Crimnon. Pultes from crimnon. Galen's doubt about zea. He himself testifies that there are certain grains which lie midway, partly between barley or typha, partly between typha or olyra and wheat. Some are close to olyra, others to barley or typha, others to wheat, others to millet, and others come nearest the nature of millet. Some of these have names, some are simple, as in Italy, and some are compound, as in Cappadocia, where it is called gymnochemon [γυμνόχεμον], that is, naked and without husk. In Bithynia, a region of Asia Minor, it is called zeopyron, that is, its name is blended from zea and wheat. So it is very hard to write exactly about those grains which are not grown in our part of the world, and from which nothing comes to our food.

units.la: Quidam Galeni interpretes Chondrum far verterunt, ut Linacer vir utraque literatura clarissimus. Quid hodie sit parum constare video. Ruellius scribit in Gallia farris duo genera esse: unum rutilo colore, a rusticis & agricolis rutilum frumentum appellatum, german. Kern, alterum candidum, quod clausum putatur, germ. Spelt oder Dinkel. Columella farris 4. describit genera, Venuculum rutilum, venunculum album germ. Teutsch Rieß, orysage manica, clausum germ. Spelt, semen devia, trimestre alias hal-cast um, german. Ammelkorn, quod ponde e bonitateq; praecipuum est: unde non cadit illorum sententia, qui Chendron, hoc est, alicam & far adoreum Columella
units.tr: Some interpreters of Galen rendered chondrus as far, as Linacre did, a man most distinguished in both literatures. I see that what it is today is little agreed. Ruellius writes that in Gaul there are two kinds of spelt: one with a reddish colour, called by country folk and farmers rutilum frumentum (German Kern); the other white, which is thought to be enclosed (German Spelt or Dinkel). Columella in book 2 describes four kinds of far: the reddish venuculum, the white venunculum (German Teutsch Rieß), orysage manica, which is enclosed (German Spelt), and semen devia, a three-month grain, otherwise called halicastrum (German Ammelkorn), which is the most valuable for weight and quality. Hence the opinion of those does not hold, who take chondros, that is alica and far adoreum, to be the same as Columella's

units.la: Dhoc lumella, Spelta seu Zea faciunt speciem. Exi- mum autem fuisse farri a prisca Romanus honorem tributum, ex eo corstat, quod ipsam gloriam a farris honore adoreamvocarunt: Tanta autem erat farris copia, vt nulla prouinciarum Italiam pasceret, modiusq; farris ad singulos asses redactus erat. Numa instituit fa ipsum torrere, tunc enim salubrius censebatur, vnde fornacalia farris torrendi feriasinstituisse fertur: arista caret, interq; hiberna frumenta annumeratur: omnium frumentorum durissimum, contraq; hiemes firmissimum est. Romanis far triticumq; vulgatissima fuisse frumenta comperio, quamuis & aliis terris communia. Varro Campanum praestantissimum appellauit. Ex omnibus autem veterum testimoniis colligere est & concludere licet, far adoreum, alicam & chondrum idem significare, & nunc quidem pro frumento peculiari, nunc pro mola, hoc est, farre tosto ex Zea confecta accipi. Far autem factitium an fuerit apud antiquos disceptatur. Archigenes apud Athen. l. 9. c. 45 manifeste monstrat, Romanos far ex frumento madefactum, siccato, & in craffores partes diffracto, parasse: alii & quidem recentiores, inter quos est Hero. Mercurialis l. 2. variar. lect. contra afferunt, nullum, far aliud praeter natiuum adoreum vocatum, vnquam nominasse: In his & similibus parum iuuat diutius immorari, quare relinquo illis litem: nolo enim hic esse ambitiose diligens.
units.tr: Columella's spelt or zea, which make one kind. The ancient Romans paid far special honour, as is shown by the fact that they called the glory itself by the name of the honour of far, adoreum. Yet there was such an abundance of far that no province fed Italy, and a modius of far was sold for a single as. Numa ordained that it be parched, for it was then thought more wholesome; whence it is said he instituted the Fornacalia, the festival of parching far. It has no awn, and is counted among the winter grains; it is the hardest of all grains, and the firmest against the winters. I find that far and wheat were the most common grains among the Romans, though they were common in other lands too. Varro called Campanian far the most excellent. From all the testimonies of the ancients one may gather and conclude that far adoreum, alica and chondrus mean the same thing, and are taken now for a particular grain, now for mola, that is, parched far made from zea. Whether far was artificial among the ancients is disputed. Archigenes, in Athenaeus book 9 chapter 45, clearly shows that the Romans prepared far from grain soaked, dried and broken into coarse pieces. Others, and indeed more recent writers, among whom is Hieronymus Mercurialis (Variae lectiones, book 2), contend that no far other than the natural kind called adoreum was ever so named. Little is gained by lingering long over these and similar questions, so I leave the dispute to them; for I do not wish to be ambitiously exact here.

units.la: Submonitio.
units.tr: Preliminary remark.

units.la: Plinius tragum cerealem et typham cerealem inter frumentacea genera reponit, & quidem ab Oriente aduehi prodidit, atq; ex ipsa typha in Iuo orbe oryzam fieri retulit: dicitur tragus cerealis ad differentiam tragi herba. Ex tritici femine fieri tragum in Campania tantum & in Aegypto Plinius affirmat: Galenus vero ex nobilissima olyra decorticata: tragum ex Chondro fieri scriptores graeci tradiderunt. Columella c.6.lib.2. far candidum tragum cerealem nominat, aliu oryzam germanicam, Dioscorides tragum frumentaceum l.2.c.85.& 86. Eiusdem cum chondro natura est, nisi quod difficilius in ventriculo conficiatur. De typha Dioscorides omnino tacuit, quod mirari subit, cum Theophrastus lib.de plantis multa de typha prodiderit. quin & Plinius nihil praeterea de ea notatu dignum reliquit. Hoc adiicere unum opera est pretium, quod Theophrastus scribit, nullum frumenti genus comperiri, quod totum in aliud transfire aptum sit, atq; typha & Zea. Galenus large in Asia provenire testatur, regionibus praecipue quae supra Pergamum sunt: hanc que ab agricolis in panificia cogi, quoniam triticum in oppida deportetur. Adhaec panes typhinos olyrinis longe praestantiores praedicat, illi calen ti nimirum sint calentes. Si enim diutius asseruntur, seipsis evadunt deteriores, ventriculum
units.tr: Pliny places tragus cerealis and typha cerealis among the grain kinds, and reports that it is brought from the East, and that rice is made in our world from typha itself. Tragus cerealis is so called to distinguish it from the herb tragus. Pliny affirms that tragus is made from wheat only in Campania and in Egypt; Galen says it is made from the noble olyra, husked. Greek writers have handed down that tragus is made from chondros. Columella in book 2 chapter 6 calls white far tragus cerealis, and another kind German rice. Dioscorides describes tragus frumentaceus in book 2 chapters 85 and 86. It is of the same nature as chondros, except that it is digested with more difficulty in the stomach. Dioscorides said nothing at all about typha, which is surprising, since Theophrastus in his book on plants wrote much about typha. Indeed Pliny too left nothing else about it worth noting. It is worth adding one thing: Theophrastus writes that no kind of grain is found that turns wholly into another, except typha and zea. Galen testifies that it grows abundantly in Asia, especially in the regions beyond Pergamum, and that farmers press it into bread because wheat is carried into the towns. He further praises typha bread as far better than olyra bread, provided it is warm; for if it is kept longer it becomes worse, and weighs down the stomach and bowels like clinging mud. So Galen.

units.la: NB. culumq; instar concreti luti grauant. Hac Ga-lenus.
units.tr: N.B. and the bowels like a lump of set clay. So Galen.

units.la: De alica velim in hac submonitione le-gerem in transcursu quasi meminisse eam nunc frugis genus esse, nunc ex fruge factam fari-nam, indeque pulticulam velsorbitionem. Pro fruge accipitur a Plin. l. 18. c. 7. vbi de frumen-tis per tempora satis inquit, aliqui verna, myli-um, panicum, lentem, cicer, alicam appel-lant.
units.tr: I would like to note in passing, in this preliminary remark, that alica is now a kind of grain, now a flour made from grain, and from that a little porridge or sorbition. Pliny, book 18 chapter 7, where he speaks of grains sown in different seasons, says that some call spring crops milium, panicum, lentil, chickpea and alica.

units.la: Et Celsus l. 2. c. 17. inter frumenta expresse numerat alicam. Cap. item 19. inquit: Boni succi sunt triticum, Siligo, Zea, Alica, Amy-lum: ut ita quartum farris genus Columella halicastrum si alica.
units.tr: Celsus too, book 2 chapter 17, expressly counts alica among the grains. In chapter 19 he also says: wheat, siligo, zea, alica and amylum are of good juice. So, as Columella says, halicastrum, if it is alica, is the fourth kind of far.

units.la: Ab eodem quoque Plinio alica propulte accipitur, sicut et ab aliis, in sanitatis quidem statu locum habens, sed diuersis locis diuersimode praeparata, ut patet ex Plin. l. 18. c. 11. vbi varia eius genera conficiendique modos ponit, et ex Zea fieri tra-dit, &c.
units.tr: By the same Pliny, alica is also taken in a broader sense, as it is by others. It has a place in a healthy diet, but is prepared in different ways in different places, as is clear from Pliny, book 18 chapter 11, where he sets out its various kinds and methods of preparation, and relates that it is made from zea, and so on.

units.la: De Secali hoc sub huius submonitionis finem adiiciendum exstimo, quod latinis quibusdam ut Plinio fuerit notum, a graecorum vero nullo proditum. Rei scriptores rusti-ca Romani, Cato, Varro, Columella et Pal-ladius nullam fecerunt de ea mentionem, vel quia usum eius ingratissimum putarunt, fo-lisque Subalpinis familiarem, aut quia non dignam arbitrati sunt quae posteris vulgaretur, Plinius farraginem vocat: gratissimus eius usus in panificiis est rusticis, sicut & infima media plebi, potentiorum enim & procerum mensis abdicatur, nisi quod quandoque miscetur tritico, ut panis inde confectus firmitudinem quandam recipiat, cum aliās panis, exsolafecalis farina ater sit & ponderosus: quidam Secale vulgarem nostram siliginem esse existimant de quo cap. de Siligine dictum est.
units.tr: At the end of this preliminary remark I think it should be added about secale that it was known to some Latin writers, such as Pliny, but mentioned by no Greek. The Roman writers on farming, Cato, Varro, Columella and Palladius, made no mention of it, either because they thought its use most disagreeable and familiar only to the Subalpine peoples, or because they did not think it worth making known to posterity. Pliny calls it farrago. Its most welcome use is in rustic bread-making, and also among the lower middling commons, for it is banished from the tables of the powerful and the great; except that sometimes it is mixed with wheat, so that bread made from it gains a certain firmness, since otherwise bread made from bran-stripped flour is dark and heavy. Some think secale is our common rye, of which something was said in the chapter on siligo.

units.la: O yzam peregrinam Galenus inter legumina numerat, Plinius & Celsus inter frumenti genera. Indica terra populis vulgatissimus & gratissimus cibus est, apud quos magna cum superstitione feritur. Hodie in quibusdam Italiae locus feritur. Orientis Indiaeque populi potissimum Calechutani oryzam in panes cogunt, potus ex ea concinnant saccharo variisque aromatis conditos, quibus facilius occiusque capita grauari aiunt, quam vini potentioris hausturi. Oryza aut apud eos summa abundantia, eamque cymbalis ac saltationibus, omniq; laetitiae genere ferunt, sua daemonia precantes, ut sit oryza uberrimus proventus, hac enim varias epulas conficiunt. In regione quoque Indica quae Carangonora dicitur, panes ex oryza confici navigatione Iosephi Indi compertum est. Duo faciunt eius genera, unum gramino rubente quod rarius est, alterum candido aque nonnullis hordeum galaticum appellatur, hoc elegantiorum mensis subit, variisque praeparatur modis, estq; boni succi edulium, crassiorem tamen pituitam generat non, ut decet praparatum: de pultibus & sorbitionibus eius agetur infra cap. de pultibus. In Germania nondum nasci est deprehensa, quam enim nos vulgo vocamus orysam, aliud simenti genus est, totasque bstantia oryza illa peregrina minus, nostra tamen ex Syria, & Asia, & Ægypto, vbi copiosissimè provenit translata in multis quoq; Europæ locis hodie seritur, vnde ad nos exportatur.
units.tr: Galen counts foreign rice among the pulses, while Pliny and Celsus count it among the grain kinds. In the Indian land it is the most common and most welcome food of the peoples, among whom it is sown with great superstition. Today it is sown in some places in Italy. The peoples of the East and of India, especially those of Calicut, press rice into bread, and make from it a drink sweetened with sugar and flavoured with various spices, by which, they say, heads are weighed down more easily and quickly than by drinking stronger wine. They have rice in extreme abundance, and bring it in with cymbals, dances and every kind of rejoicing, praying to their demons that the rice may yield most richly, for from it they prepare their varied feasts. In the Indian region called Carangonora too, the making of bread from rice was learned from the voyage of Joseph the Indian. They make two kinds of it: one of reddish grain, which is rarer, and the other white, which some call Galatic barley. The white kind comes to the tables of the more refined, is prepared in various ways, and is a food of good juice, though it generates thicker phlegm unless it is properly prepared. Its porridges and sorbitions will be discussed below, in the chapter on porridges. It has not been found to grow in Germany; for what we commonly call oryza is another kind of seed, and that foreign rice is somewhat less in substance. Our rice, however, is brought from Syria, Asia and Egypt, where it grows most abundantly, and today it is sown in many places in Europe too, whence it is exported to us.

units.la: Milium frumentum est non contemnendum, multis enim gentibus in cibis fuit gratissimum, & hodie quoq; esse inter omnes constat. Festus à milliaria summa derivatum latinis putat. Varro à Græco id deducit, melinemq; ab iis nuncupari voluit, licet alii melinem panicum intellexerunt. Bis in anno feritur, vere & initio Iunii: quidam sub Vergiliarum exortum Maio scmense seri felicius suadent. Aduersus iniuriam auicularum indispensum existit, sicut & auena ocymum q. Omnia enim frumenta armatur, vel aristis acutis & asperis, vt triticum, hordeum, siligo, vel gluma & folliculis includuntur, vt spelta, huiusmodi genera: milium vero, auena, & ocymum femina sua in tenuissimis continent membranis, vnde etiam facilius auicularum iniuriis obnoxia redduntur. Omnium autem frugum fertilissimum est milium, ex vno enim grano ternos sextarios signi affirmat Plin.l.18.c. 17. seriq; debere locis vliginosis & humidis. Idem loco milium. loco citato multos ad mihi remedia noxia rubetam aruo circumferre solere, priusquam farria-tur, defodiq; in medio inclusam vase fictili tubeum, ne a-re, tegatur, ita nec passerem nec vermes nocere. Hoc vero remedium an superstitione careat, non est huius loci inquirere, dicetur de hac alibi: hac de nostro vulgari milio.
units.tr: Millet is a grain not to be despised, for it was most pleasant food for many peoples, and it is agreed that it is still eaten by everyone today. Festus thinks it is derived from the Latin milliaria summa. Varro derives it from the Greek and wanted it called melinē by them, though others understood melinē to mean panic grass. It is sown twice a year, in spring and at the beginning of June, though some advise that sowing in May, at the rising of the Pleiades, is more fortunate. It is unprotected against the harm done by small birds, as are oats and likewise ocymum. All grains are either armed with sharp, rough awns, like wheat, barley and siligo, or enclosed in husks and pods, like spelt and similar kinds; but millet, oats and ocymum keep their seed in very thin membranes, which is why they are more easily exposed to the injuries of birds. Of all grains millet is the most fertile, for Pliny (book 18, chapter 17) affirms that from a single grain come three sextarii. It should be sown in marshy and damp places. In the same place Pliny says that many people, before they grind it, carry a toad around the field as a remedy against harmful things, and bury it in the middle, enclosed in an earthen vessel covered with earth, so that neither sparrows nor worms harm the crop. Whether this remedy is free from superstition is not a matter for this place to inquire; it will be discussed elsewhere. So much for our common millet.

units.la: Est & aliud consimile, quod Indicum appellatur, in Italiam sub Neronis principatu con-uectum, colore nigrum, granoq; amplum, sed hoc nihil ad nos, cum peregrinum sit.
units.tr: There is also another similar grain, called Indian, brought into Italy under the principate of Nero. It is black in colour and large in grain, but this has nothing to do with us, since it is foreign.

units.la: Provenit quoq; in quibusdam asperioribus Germaniae locis frumentum, cuius semen tritum milio adeo simile est, ut discerni vix possit, huius saltem semen altero magis exiguum apparet, unde & milium exiguum seu agreste dicitur, ab aliis panicum, & typha à iuba illa paniculata, seu quia spicas fert inter typha aquatica praedensis acervatas granis, verum quia typha appellatio aliis frugibus nimi u tritico & oryza attribuitur, milium agreste dici potest.
units.tr: In some rougher parts of Germany there also grows a grain whose seed, when threshed, is so like millet that they can scarcely be told apart; only its seed appears somewhat smaller than the other. For this reason it is also called small or wild millet, by others panic, and "typha" from that plumed panicle, or because it bears ears with grains packed densely among water reeds. But since the name typha is given to other grains, namely wheat and rice, wild millet may be the better name.

units.la: Quod vero ex Italia nouum frumenti genus in Germaniam aduectum est, semen habens lenticulas nostras forma & magnitudine referentia, paululum tamen acuminatum, quia Germanico nomine destituitur, milium Italicum appellari potest, & Panicum, cuius Plinius 4. facit genera lib. 18. cap. 7. & 8. candidum, nigrum, russum, & purpureum, nobis non nisi russum cognitum est. Eodem modo quo quo multum in panis subiguntur, minus tamen nutrit.
units.tr: As for the new kind of grain brought into Germany from Italy, whose seed resembles our lentils in shape and size, though it is slightly pointed, it can be called Italian millet, since it has no German name, and also panic. Pliny, in books 18 chapters 7 and 8, makes four kinds of it: white, black, reddish and purple; to us only the reddish kind is known. In the same way it is worked much into bread, yet it nourishes less.

units.la: In er peregrina quoq; frumenta recenseetur Turcicum, a mercatoribus primum in nostras terras exportatum, nostrumq; solum coepit esse liciter affectere: requirit autem solum pingue & benestercoratum. 4. autem huius frumenti reperiuntur genera: quaddam enim grana russa, quaeddam purpurea, quaedam lutea quaeddam candida grana profert phaseoli agrestis, magnitudinem obtinentia. Culmi in hoc frumento virides adhuc & succulenti dulcedine saccharum superant. In Asia vltra Bastram fluuium adeo grande fieri tradunt (Theophrast. lib. 9. c. 4.) vt nucleo solum sua aquiparet magnitudine: non inepte etiam hoc frumentum typha magna appellari potest.
units.tr: Among the foreign grains is also counted Turkish corn, first brought into our lands by merchants, and it has begun to be well received in our soil. It requires rich, well-manured ground. Four kinds of this grain are found: some grains are red, some purple, some yellow, and some white, bearing grains of the size of a wild bean. The stalks of this grain are still green and juicy, and in sweetness they surpass sugar. In Asia beyond the river Bactra they report that it grows so large (Theophrastus, book 9, chapter 4) that its kernel alone equals the other in size. It is not inappropriately called a great typha.

units.la: Sesamum à veteribus inter fruges fuit numeratum, hodie paucis cognitum. Ægyptii oleum exeo prastantissimum tum ad cibos, tum ad alia confecerunt, oleo communi longe prastantius: hoc deuenit in contemtum, vbi primum Italia oleas plantare coepit. Apud veteres fuit in magno pretio, quia pani compsitum iucundum et dulcem saporem conciliat, quamprimum vero saccharum coepit vsurpari, non solum magnò aestimatum est, sed neplantatum quidem postea. Caeterum, quae assatim inter lini segetes vbique locorum, maxime vero in Alsatia & trattu Rheni prouenit planta, sesam nostrū.
units.tr: Sesame was counted among the grains by the ancients, but today it is known to few. The Egyptians made from it an oil most excellent both for food and for other uses, far better than common oil. This fell into disrepute as soon as Italy began to plant olives. Among the ancients it was held in great esteem, because it gives bread a pleasant and sweet flavour. As soon as sugar began to be used, not only was it valued less, but it was not even planted afterwards. Our sesame plant, which grows widely among flax fields everywhere, but especially in Alsace and the region of the Rhine, is what remains.

units.la: Calamus huius frumenti viridis saccharo dulcior. sesami genus est, quod ipsa ratio & descriptio indicat, excepto quod Ægyptiacum efficacius est & candidius. Hoc nostrum sesamum ab omnibus aunlsa tanquam inutile reiicitur, cum tamen ipsum mel emollire & calfacere, plantam vero viridem vino decoctam inflammationem doloreque oculorum certo sedare expertum sit. Quin & pani commixtum iucundum & dulce et iaporem conciliat: per se vero usurpatum stomacho non admodum confert, est enim oleosum & pingue, unde pingue alimentum praestat, crassumque succum. Cum melle crudo placentas ex eo conficiebant, quas κοπτίδας vocabant. Apud Athenaeum lib.14. huiusmodi placentae finguntur ex melle & sesamo torrefactis addito oleo: meminit praeterea & aliarum, quas ab universa Sicilia μυῤῥίνας appellatas asserit, quae ex sesamo & melle muliebris pubis formam fingebantur, has enim feminae Dearum altaribus circumferebant.
units.tr: The green stalk of this grain is sweeter than sugar. It is a kind of sesame, as its own nature and description show, except that the Egyptian kind is more effective and whiter. Our sesame is rejected by everyone as useless, although experience has shown that it softens and warms honey itself, and that the green plant boiled in wine reliably soothes inflammation and pain of the eyes. Indeed, mixed with bread it gives a pleasant and sweet flavour, but used by itself it does not greatly benefit the stomach, for it is oily and fatty, and so provides rich nourishment and thick juice. With raw honey they made cakes from it, which they called koptidas [κοπτίδας]. Athenaeus, book 14, describes such cakes made of honey and roasted sesame with oil added. He also mentions others, which he says were called myrrhinas [μυῤῥίνας] throughout all Sicily, shaped from sesame and honey in the form of female genitals, for women carried these around the altars of the goddesses.

units.la: Auena.
units.tr: Oats.

units.la: Auena haud poenitendum frumenti genus est. In Insulis quibusdam sola auena homines vitare memoriae proditum est, ut poenitente proveniente. Moscovita, ut scribit Matthias Michon, auenam sublimant, ex qua sublimatione elicitur liquor, quem aquam ardentem vitaeque vocant, aeque ac apud Germanos, Italos, Gallosque ex vinis vehementioribus, bancq; in summo eos habere pretio testantur, qui legatione functi ist incredierunt domum. Quidam ex eā leniter leuiter tusa pinsitaq; edulium ægrotis parant, eoq; quadragenario tenuno quoq; diutes ac pauperes patiter utuntur. Ægrotu edulia auenacea non facile obtinentur, nisi sint sorbitiones rite prapara ta, & ad certum vsum destinata exmedicipræscripto atq; consilio. Eiusmodi enim sorbitiones (cum crota & melle) suffientibus vi-ter propinantur. Cogitur quoq; in panis in aspera qui bus dam & montosis regionibus, alias pro pabulo equorum præcipue bodie feriatur. Certum est pulsus auenacea, as prote confecta optime convenire sanis, licet enim alium sintant, nutriunt tamen mediocriter propter calorem quem habet suana ura auena, ut enim cibus calidæ temperatura est, ut ve o medicamentam frigida & sicca. Quod vero Plinius Germanos nonnihil notat barbarias nescio cuius, ob pultem auenacæam quæ frequenter & plurimum vtuntur, non morandum, cum ii, qui auenaceæ pulte victitant, se auenaræ asuerunt, non solum prosperiori vtantur valetudine, validi sint, bene curati, formaq; egregia confpicuntur, sed etiam diutius viuant, quam Plinius vixerit, quam ii qui vel in Italia vel Gallia ipsius tritici delitias vinoq; generosissimi ceis pulmo affatim vtuntur. Putaui forsan vir alias acerrimo iudicio, eiusmodi pulses ex mera aqua & pura farina confici. Si fuerit reduiuus atque diutius probe confectas degustaret sponsionem facerem, & falu-ni palato stomachoq; cas gratas esse sit assuera-brius vi-turus. Idem plane indicum sit de pulsibus ex uut aliis. ocymo, quibus in quibusdam nostris terris nihil vulgatius. Quidam farinam torrere solent, & in pulte empostea cogere: videoid multis in locis iesse vulgatum, vt etiam cā aunde & alacriter vscen-tes ad estandum me vna pulte xerint. Verum melancholicum succum exinde generari, obstru-ctionesq; viscerum manifeste deprehendi atq; ob-seruari in iis, qui largius & sapius eā sunt vsi. Cauteant igitur sibi ab eiusmodi pultibus, quibus humor melancholicus non expurgatur in sple-nem, vt proprium receptaculum, qui laborant calculo, ventriculoq; frigido. Cum latte, sale, & butyro copiosè probantur: quidam delicatio-res addunt saccharum, qui butyro destituuntur, loco eius vsurpent lardum, quod in stilli vel sar-tagine torrendum est: quibus non innuisum est mel, possunt id permiscere, hæc enim singula effi-ciunt, vt & iucundius & salubrius edantur: hoc etiam modo parandæ sunt pultes ex ocymo, cate-riuq; frumentis, quæ in usum cibarium admit-tuntur. Inprimis vero hic opera danda, ne consistentia harum pultiacularum sit nimis cras-sa, densa & compacta, sed mediocris, hac enim-ratione firmant ventriculum & valenter alunt, nimis crassæ, solidæq; meatus obstruunt, difficul-tergq; concoquuntur: Si vei ò contigerit, vt fame-licus quispiam ex aliorum eduliorum defeciu crassiorem quam par est, devorarit, is largiore vini haustu eam imbuat, ita enim condensatio dissoluetur, prohibebiturq;, nelentore tunicis ad-harę-
units.tr: Oats are not a kind of grain to be despised. It is recorded that on certain islands people avoid oats alone, as if they caused sickness. The Muscovites, as Matthias Michou writes, distil oats, and from this distillation a liquor is drawn which they call burning water or aqua vitae, just as the Germans, Italians and French do with stronger wines. They report that those who return home from an embassy hold this in the highest esteem. Some people lightly crush and pound oats and prepare a food from them for the sick, and the rich and the poor alike use this thin gruel during the forty days of Lent. Oat foods are not easily obtained for the sick unless the gruels are properly prepared and intended for a particular use, according to the prescription and advice of a physician. For such gruels, made with cream and honey, are given to sick people to drink. Oats are also made into bread in some rough and mountainous regions, while elsewhere they are used mainly as fodder for horses. It is certain that oat porridge, if well made, suits healthy people very well. Although it is thin, it nourishes moderately because of the heat that oats contain. For just as food is of a warm temperament, so medicine is cold and dry. As for Pliny's remark that the Germans, because they eat oat porridge often and in quantity, are somewhat barbarous, I need not dwell on it. Those who live on oat porridge and have accustomed themselves to oats not only enjoy better health, are strong, well cared for and conspicuous for their fine appearance, but also live longer than Pliny did. This is so compared with those who in Italy or Gaul feed freely on wheat delicacies and very fine wine. Perhaps the man, otherwise of keen judgement, thought that such porridges are made of plain water and pure flour. If he came back and tasted them when they had been properly and long prepared, I would wager that he would find them pleasant to the palate and stomach, and that he would live the more healthily for it. The same must be said plainly of porridges made from ozymum, which are very common in some of our lands. Some people are in the habit of toasting the flour and then thickening it in the porridge afterwards. This custom is widespread in many places, so that even those who are eager and quick to eat have often praised this porridge to me. Yet it is clear that a melancholic humour is generated from it, and that obstructions of the viscera are plainly detected and observed in those who have used it more freely and frequently. Therefore let those who suffer from stone and a cold stomach beware of such porridges, by which the melancholic humour is not purged into the spleen, its proper receptacle. They are commonly prepared with milk, salt and butter. Some who are more refined add sugar, and those who lack butter use bacon instead, which must be melted in a pan or frying-pan. To these, honey is not unwelcome, and they may mix it in. Each of these makes the food both more pleasant and more wholesome. In this way porridges of ozymum and of the other grains admitted for food are also to be prepared. Above all, care must be taken here that the consistency of these porridges is not too thick, dense and compact, but moderate. For in this way they strengthen the stomach and nourish it well, whereas if they are too thick and solid they block the passages and are digested with difficulty. If it happens that someone, through lack of other foods, has eaten a porridge thicker than it ought to be, let him soak it with a larger draught of wine. For in this way the thickening will be loosened and prevented, and it will slip down more easily without sticking to the coats of the stomach, and will swell and distend the belly less.

units.la: Pultis a-uenaceæ incommoda, si non probe fit parata. Censura. hærefcatifacilius etiam descendet, minusque infla- bit atque diffendet ventrem.
units.tr: Disadvantages of oat porridge if it is not properly made. A note.

units.la: De ozymo miror quod controuersia sit, cum denominepotius quam re ipsa contentio sit. Qui dicunt id esse basilicum, nostrum hallucinantur, siquidem basilicum in magno habetur à nobis pretio, nec pecoribus saginandum ut ozymum adhibetur, sed lætificans corda appellatur à Galeno. Ozymum igitur est illud, quod vulgo appellatur <bl>Speydenforn</bl>, multis gentibus, cumprimis Sep-tentrionalibus, frigidiora item ac aspera loca inhabitantibus notissimum. Pultes ex eo confi-ciunt cum lacte et butyro, et ad arcendam etiam famem panem. Pultes probe paratæ, consistentiam mediocrem nactæ, non ingratæ sunt palato, ventre enim firmant et corroborant, valentiorque alunt. Nam magni nominis Reges et Principes, quibus amenaceæ et ex ozymo pultes in cibum sunt gratissimæ, cumprimis vero venatu, sturnis, vel ultro citroque peregrinantibus. Prisanam quoque exutis granorum putaminibus e grano, et ex iure carnium decoquunt ad esum. Quapropter qui hoc frumenti genus cibis abdicandis existimant, infcienter id palam facere offenero. Videmus homines pultib. ex ozymo frequentius vivitantes, validos esse, bene curatos, ac laudabiliter corporis habitu, præcipue in Lugdunensi monte tractu Foresti et Aruerno, Suecia, item Danicq, et in nostri etiam Comitatu Ifenburgici parte, quæ septentrionem, vulgo Bogelsberg, ubi hoc frumentum vulgatissimum est.
units.tr: I wonder why there is a dispute about ozymum, since the disagreement is about the name rather than the thing itself. Those who say it is basil are mistaken, for basil is held by us in high value and is not used to fatten cattle as ozymum is. It is called by Galen "the heart-gladdening herb." So ozymum is that which is commonly called Speydenforn, and it is very well known to many peoples, especially the northern ones and those who live in colder and harsher regions. They make porridges from it with milk and butter, and also bread to keep off hunger. Porridges properly made, of moderate consistency, are not unpleasant to the palate. For they firm and strengthen the belly and nourish it more vigorously. Indeed, kings and princes of great name, to whom oat and ozymum porridges are most welcome as food, especially those who hunt or travel back and forth, eat them. They also boil barley, with the husks removed, in the broth of meats for eating. Therefore those who think this kind of grain should be banished from food are plainly doing an injury by saying so openly and without knowledge. We see people who live more often on ozymum porridge to be strong, well cared for, and of a praiseworthy bodily habit. This is especially so in the Lyonnais mountain region, in Forez and in Auvergne, and also in Sweden and Denmark, and in part of our own county of Isenburg, the northern part commonly called the Vogelsberg, where this grain is very common.

units.la: Ozymum dicitur ab ζύμη, i.e. citò, celeriter; n. erumpit, tertio die pridie ab ozymo diuersum loge est, dicitur n. ab ὀζῳ, i.e. oleo, maxima- que indiget cura, alias basilicum. Regibus pultes ex auena ozymoque familiares. Ego soleo adiicere modicum boni croci, cum debita quantitate piperis trii, (quamuis crocus in omni pultis genere laudatur) butyro salito super natante, sic enim parata ne tantillum quidem noxa inferre valent: pipere enim calor ventriculi excitatur, prohibeturq; ne venter infletur atq; distendatur: crocus obstructionem prohibet, ventriculoq; ex humiditate debili succurrit, metatuq; urinarios seruat apertos: butyrum salitu est quasi vinculum totius massa, vehicul emq; virtutis crocea, piperis ipsiusq; esculenti assimilandi: additur praterea crocus, ad prohibendam oculorum caliginem, quam ocymum per se sepiùs commestum inferre creditur. Otiosis tamen & sedentariam vitam agentibus non adeo esse utile semper dixerim. Consuetudinis nihilominus hic magna vis. In Dania, & Suecia vidi magni nominis fœminis inter multa alia cibaria pulte ex ocymo nihil vulgatius, eaq; prosperrima valetudine ac nitidissima forma confbiciuntur. Ad hoc ipsum in causa est, quod rustici & agricolae longiorem aetatem cum firmiori valetudine attingant, quia nimirum innocentia ac simplici cibo sunt contenti & aqua potu, quam quisplendidissimè, delicatissimeq; viuunt, quotidiemq; magna & lauta epularum struè mensas suas opulentant: quin potius consta & sole ipso clarius est, e luxuriosis illis coquinis & culinis plures morbos quam ulla alia ex causa promanare, & licet manifestum hoc sit omnibus, nemo tamen men est, qui delitiis his carere velit. O fortunatos nimium, (inquit Maro) sua si bona norint Agricolas, quibus ipsa procul discordibus armis Fundit humo facilem victum iustissima tellus.
units.tr: Ozymum is said to derive from zymē [ζύμη], that is, quickly, speedily; for it sprouts up on the third day, and it differs greatly from ozymum in... It is said to come from ozō [ὄζω], that is, oil, and it needs the greatest care, otherwise it is basil. Oat and ozymum porridges are familiar to kings. I am accustomed to add a little good saffron, with the due quantity of ground pepper (although saffron is praised in every kind of porridge), and butter salted and floating on top. For prepared in this way they bring not the slightest harm. For pepper stirs up the heat of the stomach and prevents the belly from being swollen and distended. Saffron prevents obstruction and helps the stomach when it is weakened by moisture, and keeps the urinary passages open. The salted butter is as it were a bond holding the whole mass together, and a vehicle for the saffron-like virtue of the pepper and of the food itself to be assimilated. Saffron is further added to prevent dimness of the eyes, which ozymum, when eaten often by itself, is believed to cause. Nevertheless I would say it is not always very useful for those who lead idle and sedentary lives. Yet custom has great force here. In Denmark and Sweden I have seen women of great name, among many other foods, eating porridge of ozymum, nothing being more common, and they are made with the best health and the neatest figure. The cause of this is that country people and farmers reach a longer age with firmer health, because they are content with simple innocent food and water to drink, while those who live most splendidly and luxuriously load their tables every day with great and sumptuous banquets. Indeed, it is clearer than the sun itself that more diseases come from those luxurious kitchens and cookshops than from any other cause. And although this is plain to everyone, there is no one who wishes to be without these delights. "O too fortunate farmers," says Maro, "if only they knew their own good, for whom the most just earth pours forth an easy living from her soil, far from the clash of arms."

units.la: Hodie, Deum immortalem, quam omnia in peius eunt, deteriorag; quotidie euadunt? Infra- ne gula irritamentis & nepotinis helluationibus interire videmus homines, regna, urbes.
