Inipsos urbium agros luxuriam penetrasse spectamus, quippe & India ipsa in cibos aduocatur, cum etiam nullam escam lautam probeq; paratam arbitrantur multi, quae zinziber, cinnamomo, macere, piperibus, croco, caterisque id genus non condiatur. An non vesani luxus argumentum est, cibes ita aromatis condire, ut etiam in paroffidum margnibus luxurient, & quod inprimis deplorandum est, apud infimam et iam & exhaustam plebem, qui non minus in conuiuiis suis pro luxu patina certant ac principatu, quam magnates & diuitiores. Constat quibusdam in Germania, ostrea locis celebrari conuiuia, quae puerperialia seu baptismalia vocantur, & lustrica a die quo infantes lustrantur nomen accipiunt, adeo luxuriosa ac sumtuosa, vt, sicut infans aquae fuit extrinsecus aspersus, ita viri pariter atque mulieres vino immodico intrinsecus sumptuo ita se abluunt, ita baptizantur, vt neque mens se celeque.
units.tr: Today, immortal God, how everything goes from bad to worse, and grows worse every day! Do we not see men and kingdoms and cities perishing by the incitements of gluttony and the riotous feasting of the young? We see luxury penetrating even into the fields of the cities themselves. Indeed India itself is summoned for food, since many people think no food is elegant or properly prepared unless it is seasoned with ginger, cinnamon, mace, pepper, saffron and the like. Is it not a sign of mad luxury to season foods with spices in such a way that the luxury runs riot even in the pans of the poor? And what is especially to be lamented is that among the lowest and most exhausted common people, who in their feasts vie for pre-eminence over the cooking pot no less than the great nobles and the richer folk do. It is well known that in some places in Germany feasts are celebrated which are called childbed or christening feasts, and take their name, "lustral," from the day on which infants are purified. They are so luxurious and sumptuous that, just as the infant was sprinkled with water from outside, so men and women alike wash and baptise themselves inwardly with immoderate wine, so that neither the mind nor the senses can perform their office.

units.la: N brari fo- neque sensus officium suum munus obire am- lita im p- plius possint. Hic quo quisq; exquisitissimorum banda, & obsoniorum varia genera, epularum q; varios multis apparatus dat profusius, eo magis commendan- nomini- tur, vt ita nihil aliud ista conuiuia dicere lice- buscasti- at, quam ad perdenda vina operosum inuen- ganda tum ac sumtuosum gula irritamentum: hanc sunt. vita intemperantiam etiam hic apud nos quoti- die adhuc debacchari videmus magna cum rei Plebsin- familiaris detrimento: sunt enim multi qui fima per conuiuia eiusmodi celebraturi tanto id faciunt cotinua- cum luxu & sumtu, tantis cum expensis, vt co- ta ista co gantur postea atrum ex hesterno iure denorare uiuia ex- panem, vix anno vno atque alio meritoria hauritur: manu recolligentes, quantum vna cæna pran- opesque dione profundebatur. Sic itaque miseri illi necessa- quod vnciatim comparserunt, vno cœnit; ioab- riæ abfu- liqurunt. Darnach gehen sie zum Brunnen/ muntur. fauffen Wasser/ vnd fressen Salat. Con- sue udo igitur lustricum illum diem luxu riosis conuiuiis celebrandi vel abroganda est, vel pu- blica animadversione legum q; sanctionib. mul- Rationes, Standa & coercenda, vitium vero moderatur ut at- cur luxu- que sobrius iisdem custodiendus atq; confirmandum riosa co- dus: quo nomine magistratus amicet ntum co- uiuia sint pellandus venit, non admonendus: primo enim abroga- maxima in Deum sit iniuria, cuius veneranda da, vel le sacramentum, quo infans in sanctorum album gibus co est affcriptus, fœdissime pollutur ac contamina- ercenda? tur, dum videl. nos eodem statim die, quo & infantis & nostro nomine, sanctè spondimus, e- brietatis gulæ, sordibus nos inquinamus, suis instar lutulentæ ad pristinum prorsus lutum, cœnumq; se volutantis. 2. Insanis istis ac sumptuo- sis conuiuiis opes ad infantis & puerperæ sustentationem necessariæ absumuntur in impurissimum ventrem, sicq; miserabile infantulus ino- piæatq; famiʀ relinquitur. quid? quod sæpe propter insanum baptismalium huiusmodi epularum apparatum baptismus differtur, magna cum in Deum, tum in infantem iniuria. Tertio notissimum est, luxuriosas istas ac sumptuosas com- messationes contentionum, rixarum, conuitio- rumq; esse semina, ex quibus funesta sæpe odia, inimicitiæ, cædesq; oriuntur, adq; tuendam & confirmandam amicitiam nihil, sed distur- bandam potius, pacemque ac concordiam dirimendam valere plurimum. Quod ele- ganter celebri Epicharmi disto, cuius me- minit Atheneus libr. 1. notatur, ex sacri- ficio conuiuiuz, ex conuiuio potio, ex potione lasciuia, ex hac insania, ex insania iudicium, à iudicio condemnatio, hinc compedes, sideratio- nes, multæ.
units.tr: Nor can the senses any longer perform their proper function. The more someone lavishes the most exquisite dishes, the most varied courses and elaborate preparations on a feast, the more he is praised, so that these banquets can be called nothing other than a laborious and costly invention, a stimulus to gluttony for wasting wine. We see this same intemperance still raging among us every day, to the great ruin of family fortunes. Many people who hold such feasts spend so much on luxury and expense that afterwards they are forced to gather up the black bread left over from yesterday's broth, scarcely able to make a living for a year or more, picking up whatever one dinner cost them. So those wretches, who scraped together their wealth bit by bit, are left with nothing but the crumbs of their money. Afterwards they go to the well, drink water and eat salad. The custom of holding those luxurious feasts on the day of the child's purification must therefore either be abolished, or be restrained and checked by public penalty and the sanctions of law, while sober conduct should be preserved and confirmed by the same means. The magistrate ought to see to this, rather than merely be urged to it. First, it is a very great wrong against God, because the venerable sacrament by which the infant is enrolled in the register of the saints is most foully defiled and polluted: on the very day on which we solemnly promised in the child's name as well as our own, we soil ourselves with drunkenness and gluttony, like a pig that wallows in mud and dirt and returns to its former filth. 2. In these mad and sumptuous feasts, the means necessary for the support of the infant and the mother are consumed by the most filthy belly, and so the poor little child is left in want and hunger. What is more, because of the mad preparations of such baptismal feasts, baptism is often postponed, a great wrong both to God and to the infant. Third, it is well known that these luxurious and costly carousals are the seeds of quarrels, brawls and insults, from which deadly hatreds, enmities and murders often arise, and that they do the very most to disturb friendship, rather than to preserve and confirm it, and to break up peace and harmony. This is elegantly expressed in the well-known saying of Epicharmus, which Athenaeus mentions in book 1: from sacrifice comes feasting, from feasting drinking, from drinking wantonness, from wantonness madness, from madness judgement, from judgement condemnation, and from that come fetters, ruin and many penalties.

units.la: Ne itaque insanum vulgus ita helluetur, & familiam pecuniamque prandiorum gurgitibus proluat, certis legibus, ac edictis luxus coercendus est, quibus decernendum q3, quantum cuiq3 in singulas coenas & conuiuia insumere conueniat. Hinc illustres illae Romanorum sumtuariae access-ibariae leges sunt promulgatae. Lege enim Phanía canebatur, ne quis carius obsonaret. Lex Fannia ludis Romanis, item Plebeis & Saturnalibus in singulos dies centenos asses insumi concessit, decemq3 aliis diebus in singulis mensibus tricenos, caeteris vero omnibus denos. Lex Licinia nuptiis ducenos induisit, caeterisque diebus tricenos, tum & carnis aridae & salsamentorum certa pondera in singulos dies constituit. Orchia (quae omnium, quae de coenis lata sunt, fuit prima) conuiuarum tantum numerum praescribebat, luxui nihil derogabat. Lege Didia, prandia coenasque maiori sumtu parantes tenebat ut. Lex Aemilia non sumtus coenarum, sed ciborum genus & modum praefiniebat. Postremo vnuit Iulia ad populum, quae profestis diebus ducentos permisit, Calendis, Idibus & nonis trecentos, nuptiis accrepotiis, h. e. postridie nuptiarum fester tios mille, qui quinq3 & 20. aureis coronantur. Nostra nuptia nostra aetate longe sunt luxuriosiora & sumtuosiora, qui pro quotidiana conuiuia hanc taxationem excedunt, fester uenim ducenti in singulas coenas quinq3 aestimantur coronariis aureis. Optandum saneiss, ut Christianis rerum publicarum moderatores ad Ethnicorum illorum exemplum & imi annonam infamia illam & immanem conuiuiorum luxuriam sensu.
units.tr: So that the mad crowd may not gorge itself in this way and wash away its household and money in the whirlpool of banquets, luxury must be restrained by fixed laws and edicts, which also decide how much each person may properly spend on individual dinners and feasts. From this came those famous Roman sumptuary and anti-extravagance laws. By the Lex Fannia it was ordained that no one should buy costlier provisions. The Lex Fannia allowed a hundred asses a day to be spent at the Roman Games, likewise at the Plebeian Games and the Saturnalia, thirty on ten other days of each month, and ten on all the rest. The Lex Licinia set two hundred for weddings and thirty for other days, and also fixed certain weights of dried meat and salted fish per day. The Orchian law (the first of all laws passed on dinners) prescribed only the number of guests and did not curb luxury at all. By the Didian law, those who prepared lunches and dinners at greater expense were restrained. The Aemilian law regulated not the cost of dinners but the kinds and quantities of food. Finally the Julian law, passed to the people alone, allowed two hundred on ordinary days, three hundred on the Kalends, Ides and Nones, and a thousand on wedding days and the day after a wedding, at which people are crowned with twenty-five gold pieces. In our own age weddings are far more luxurious and costly than that, and those who exceed this limit for ordinary feasts are valued at two hundred crowns per dinner, with gold crowns. Certainly it is to be wished that the rulers of Christian commonwealths would, after the example of those heathen, restrain and punish with true sanctions of law the shameful and monstrous luxury of feasts, and above all that they would encourage sober living by the example of the law.

units.la: Votum autoris. ueris legum sanctionibus, atq; inprimis sobria vi-tam atq; viua legis exemplo refrenarent atq; coercerent. Id si fieret, melius cum Respubl. Christiana multius in locis ageretur, pretia omnium rerum non quo idie adaugrentur, nulla esset annona flagellatio, aroma opolarum q; crumena minus turgeret. Verum enim uero ne quis xifti-net, me omnem epularum apparatum abicere, velliq; vt Christiani ab omni prorsus continuali confusdine tanquam mono bagifin alin, et ex multis hoc unicum dico, tantum abesse, vt ia-le quid sentiam, vt etiam, in veteri & nouo testa-mento pios & religiosos homines conuiuia & alia apparatus, & inuitatos aliorum conuiuia adui-se, quin & Deum ipsum conuiuia lata populo suo praescripsisse atq; mandasse, non ignorem, facileq; si opus esset, id probari posse. Ipse Christus cum omnium exemplorum rationum q; loco nobis debet esse, quem Euangelica historia tradit, & conuiuio alios excepisse, & ad aliorum conuiuia accessisse, atq; adeo cum improbis famis hominibus, publicanis & meretricibus saepe numero conuiuia inire minime dubitasse, non libidine quadam immoderata q; cibi potusq; auiditate, sed, vt Hieron. c.9. Matth. differret, vt occasionem haberet docendi, vt quorum inuitationes cum spiritualibus epulis compensaret, illosq; hac occasione ab improba vita ad bonam frugem perduceret. His adde Salomonis in Ecclesiaste testimonium, nihil, dicentis, hominis fere oprabilius esse, quam latari, conuiuari, & soluta quadam animi libertate. Ibid. nec non Sirac. c. 31. & 32. docentis conuiuia iucunda esse &c. Si igitur Christus cum Pharisaeis, publicanis atque meretricibus conuiuari solitus est, nobis quoque an hoc liceat, quaeritur? Respondetur non simpliciter: in vniuersum omnem conuiuandi cum impiis liberum esse, sed in sacris literis interdici, quam etiam ipse Paulus reliquit liberam, 1. Cor. 10. Sed nimium conuiuium prohiberi, cum videlicet quis amide magno studio & voluptate consuetudinem eorum sectatur, cum dictis vel factis illorum superstitionibus impietatique praebet assensum, cum religionem veram criminandi submittit occasionem, & Christi exemplo contrarium, in impietate & superstitionibus ipsos confirmat, cum praecipuum conuiuiorum finis sit, omnia facere ad Dei gloriam. Inordinata igitur, immoderata, luxuriosa, monstrosa, portentosa, & sumptuosa conuiuia damnantur, quae non ex honestatis & caritatis erga Deum & proximum studio, sed ex ambitione, & inexplebili quadam voluptatum cupiditate instituuntur.
units.tr: The author's wish. If this were done, the Christian commonwealth would be better governed in many places; the prices of all things, which now rise every day, would not be so high, there would be no scarcity of food, and the purses of merchants and traders would not swell so much. But lest anyone think that I reject every preparation for feasts, and wish Christians to abstain altogether from every kind of convivial gathering, I say this on just one point among many: far from holding such a view, I know well that in the Old and New Testaments pious and religious men held feasts and other gatherings, and were invited to the feasts of others, and that God himself commanded and prescribed feasts for his people; this could easily be proved if need be. Christ himself, whom the Gospel history presents as the model for us in every case, both received others at feasts and went to the feasts of others, and so he did not hesitate often to sit at table with wicked, infamous men, tax collectors and prostitutes, not out of any unrestrained desire or greed for food and drink, but, as Jerome says on Matthew 9, so that he might have an occasion to teach, and by repaying their invitations with spiritual feasts, lead them from a wicked life to good living. To this add the testimony of Solomon in Ecclesiastes, who says there is nothing better for a man than to rejoice, to feast and to live with a certain freedom of mind (Eccles. 8). Likewise Sirach chapters 31 and 32 teach that feasts are pleasant, etc. If Christ, then, was accustomed to dine with Pharisees, tax collectors and prostitutes, the question is whether we too may do so. The answer is: not simply. In general, it is free to eat with the ungodly, but Scripture forbids it in some cases, though Paul himself left it free (1 Cor. 10). But excessive dining is forbidden, namely when someone pursues their company with great eagerness and pleasure, when by word or deed he gives assent to their superstitions and impiety, when he gives occasion to slander the true religion, and when he confirms them in impiety and superstition, contrary to Christ's example, since the chief end of all feasts is to do everything for the glory of God. Therefore disorderly, immoderate, luxurious, monstrous, portentous and costly feasts are condemned, those held not from a zeal for honesty and love towards God and neighbour, but from ambition and an insatiable desire for pleasure.

units.la: Contra vero frugalia, munda, parca, moderata, iucunda, suauia (quae honestis & liberalibus locis sunt condita, quales vere elegantes ac eruditi homines solent afferre e musarum sacrario) maxime probantur, sunt enim luxus exotici deliciae ignara. In horum censu fuit coena Saturnia, quae a poetis aureo seculo tribuitur, proverbialiq; tropo dicitur pro beata. {a}Coena Icci Medici Tarentini, cuius vitae parsimonia in proverbium abiit. Meminit Æliani alterius cuiusdam Icci Tarentini luctatoris, quem toto certaminis tempore temperatissime vixisse, venereq; omnis fuisse expertem scribit. Inter frugales quoque & moderatas coenas referuntur philosophicae frugalissime Athenis a Diogenisto, Antipatristis, & Panetiastis instructa, ut moderate & erudite de rerum natura dissererent. Conuiuium quoq; musicum pro mediocri temperatoq; passim apud authores accipi testantur Atheneus libr. 10. dicens, conuiuio exceptus mediocri & musico: & Plutarch. in praec. salubrib. Timotheum αθηναίου ducem coenasse dicit in Academia apud Platonem musicam & frugalem coenam: atque hinc Lucianum conuiuium sapientium virorum μουσικών appellasse puto.
units.tr: On the other hand, frugal, clean, sparing, moderate, pleasant and agreeable feasts, such as are arranged in honourable and liberal places (the kind that truly refined and learned men are accustomed to bring from the shrine of the Muses), are most approved, for they know nothing of the delights of exotic luxury. Among these is the Saturnian feast, which the poets assign to the golden age and which is proverbially used of a blessed life. The feast of Icchus the Tarentine physician, whose sparing life passed into a proverb. Aelian mentions another Icchus of Tarentum, a wrestler, whom he writes lived most temperately throughout the whole time of the contest and was free from all sexual indulgence. Among frugal and moderate feasts are also reckoned the philosophical dinners arranged most frugally at Athens by Diogenes, Antipater and Panaetius, so that they might discuss the nature of things moderately and learnedly. Authors everywhere testify that a musical feast is also understood as one of moderate and temperate character: Athenaeus in book 10 says he was entertained at a moderate and musical feast, and Plutarch in the precepts on health says that Timotheus the Athenian [Αθηναῖον] general dined in the Academy with Plato on a musical and frugal meal. I think this is why Lucian called the gathering of wise men a musical [μουσικῶν] feast.

units.la: Coenam quoque Platonicam proverbialiter & paroemiace pro mediocri & frugali usurpatam inuenio, propterea quod is Philosophus eiusmodi coena fuisse delectatus scribitur. Unde Timotheus Cononis filius summa tuosis coenis indulgens, a Platone exceptus Coena tenui, musico ac moderato vitta, dixit, eos qui apud Platonem coenarent, ca.
units.tr: I find that the Platonic dinner was used proverbially and as a saying for a moderate and frugal meal, because the philosopher is recorded to have delighted in such a dinner. Hence Timotheus, son of Conon, who indulged in very lavish dinners, when he was entertained by Plato with a thin dinner, with music and moderation, is said to have remarked that those who dined with Plato were well fed the next day.

units.la: N 4 postrida posteridie bene se habere. Horatius lib. 2. Satyr. 5. cœnas quoque rusticas vocat tenues minimiq; sumptuosas, dici q; post eas se noctes ducere quietas & tranquillas. De his conuiuiis vere & concenter dicitur, quod sint mutua hominum caritatis, amicitiae, beneuolentiaq; vincula & symbola. Unde recte à conuiuendo dicuntur, vitæq; coniunctione & quasi conuictu, quod hunc maxime simul viuatur, teste Cicerone l. de senectute. Nonius Marcell. epularem amicorum accubationem vocat. Aristoteles in Ethicis communiones hominum amicitiis tuendis ac stabilendis perquam accommodatas esse scribit. Cicero Patum monet, ut cum viris bonis, iucundis, suauiq; amantibus viuat, sermone enim fami- liari, qui in conuiuiis est dulcissimus, vita nihil aptius esse, nihilq; ad beate viuendum accommodatius: ac plurima alia praeclara doctissimorum testimonia ad hunc conuiuiorum finem demonstrandum extant: vnum tantum producam, quod est Plutarchi lib. 4. Symposiaco problem. 1. vbi conuiuii finem esse dicit amicitiae vel generationem, vel confirmationem iunctam cum voluptate, vnde conuiuium definit viuendi rationem per vini vsum in amicitiam definentem.
units.tr: Horace, Satires book 2, poem 5, calls rustic dinners thin and of little cost, and says that people spend the nights after them quietly and calmly. Such dinners truly and harmoniously serve as bonds and tokens of mutual human love, friendship and goodwill. Hence they are rightly called after living together (convivium), and a sharing of life, as it were a living together, because people live together most of all in them, as Cicero says in his book on old age. Nonius Marcellus calls them the reclining of friends at a feast. Aristotle, in the Ethics, writes that shared meals are very well suited to preserving and strengthening friendships. Cicero advises Patus to live with good, pleasant and affable men, for nothing is more fitting to life, nor more suited to living happily, than familiar conversation, which is sweetest at dinners. There are many other excellent testimonies of the most learned men that demonstrate this purpose of dinners; I will cite only one, from Plutarch's Symposiacs, book 4, problem 1, where he says that the end of a dinner is the generation or strengthening of friendship together with pleasure, and so he defines a dinner as a way of life, by the use of wine, ending in friendship.

units.la: Hinc fit hanc admodum Romanus ille solus aliquando cœnans eo die se non cœnasse dixit, sed edisse tantum, innuens cœnam semper commucommunione & amicitia veluti condimento indigere. Neq; vero ad amicitiam tuendam, stabiliendamq; tantum conuiuia valent, sed & ad simultates inimicitiasq; auferendas: graues enim diuturnasq; priuatorum hominum simultates, odiaq; conuiuiis extincta legimus ac etiamnunc hodie sepe homines capitalibus à se inuicem odiis diffidentes conuiuiorum occasione sibi inuicem reconciliari. Sic M. Crassus Cicero-ni reconciliatus conuiuio est. Scipio & Hasdru-bal conuiuio sibi inuicem reconciliati: vt vere dixisse liceat, mensa posita contentionem tolli, hoc est, mensa communione sepe tolli rixas, inimicitiasq; gratiamq; reconciliari, cuius rei exemplum profertur de Isbosetho filio Saulis, in cuius adibus cum exarsisset altercatio, seruus eius adornato conuiuio dicitur eam diremisse. habet enim nescio quid philtri in se vinum ad amorem reconciliandum.
units.tr: Hence that Roman, who once dined alone, said that on that day he had not dined but only eaten, implying that a dinner always needs communion and friendship as its seasoning. Nor do dinners serve only to preserve and strengthen friendship, but also to remove quarrels and enmities. For we read that grave and long-standing quarrels and hatreds between private men have been ended at dinners, and even today men who distrust each other with deadly hatred are often reconciled through the occasion of a dinner. Thus Marcus Crassus was reconciled to Cicero at a dinner. Scipio and Hasdrubal were reconciled at a dinner. So one may truly say that when the table is set, strife is removed; that is, by the shared table quarrels are often ended and enmities and favour are restored. An example of this is told of Ishbosheth, son of Saul: when a quarrel had flared up in his house, his servant is said to have settled it by preparing a dinner. For wine has I know not what love-charm in it for reconciling affection.

units.la: Atq; haec de conuiuiis frugalibus & moderatis, quae si nimis sunt sordida & parca, recte appellantur Cynica & Timonia: Cynicorum enim Philosophorum vitus erat vilissimus, tenuissimus & sordidus, si liquae videl. & legumina. Timonia à Timone, cui humanum genus exosum erat, dicta sunt, is enim vitam sequebatur feram, in cibisque vilissimis & à reliquis hominibus propemodum damnatis acquiescebat. Huc referuntur coenae terrestres, quae nil nisi terra producium continent, quas Horatius coenas sine sanguine vocat. vocat: & pafferinum conuiuium, pro exigue bolo & minuto, quantum vel pafjer abjumat. Sordidum denique nimisque tenue conuiuium est absque fumo, in quo nihil coctii obsoni quapponitur. Quemadmodum igitur, qui nimia conuiuiorum crebritate atque frequenta, eorumque profusi, splendido ac sumptuoso apparatu gaudent, in excessu peccant, ita contra in defectu sordide delinquunt, I. qui tam a conuiuiali consuetudine abhorrent, ut neque alios ad se epularum communionem vnquam inuitet, neque inuitati ad aliorum conuiuia accedant, id quod fera cuiusdam immanitatis esse videtur, quippe cum ipsa natura atque humanitas, hanc vitae coenarum consuetudinem postulet.
units.tr: These are the things to say about frugal and moderate dinners. If they are too mean and sparing, they are rightly called Cynic and Timonian. For the diet of the Cynic philosophers was very cheap, very thin and squalid, consisting of lentils and beans. Timonian dinners are named after Timon, who hated mankind; he lived a savage life and was content with the cheapest food, which the rest of mankind almost despised. To this category belong the earthly dinners, which contain nothing but what the earth produces, which Horace calls dinners without blood. Also the sparrow's dinner, for a very small and meagre morsel, as much as a sparrow could swallow. Finally, a squalid dinner that is too meagre is one without smoke, in which nothing cooked is set before the guests. Just as those who rejoice in too frequent and crowded dinners, and in their lavish and splendid display, sin by excess, so on the other hand those who shrink from the custom of dining together, sin by defect in a squalid way. They avoid the custom of feasting so much that they never invite others to share a meal with them, nor, when invited, do they go to others' dinners. This seems to be the mark of a savage brutality, since nature itself and humanity demand this custom of living and dining together.

units.la: II. Cum quis inuitatus liberiter quidem & prote aliorum conuiuio se sistit, at ille inuitat neminem, id quod anaritia ingratitudinisque cuiusdam sigitiofissima vitium est, quo quis laborans αλλοτριοφαγος recte dicitur, cui nimirum dulce est aliena viuere quadra. Horum passim reperiuntur plurimi, quos neque pudet, neque piget, neque poenitet inconuiuientia sua & monophagia sordidissima, & si quando honestis ribus liberalioribusque conuiuiis adhibentur, alienamque quadram arrodere ac lingere illis licet, tanta ciborum ingluuie se infarciunt vno prandio coenaue, quanta vix decem alii accusarifa natura & genio existimantes, si in tanta epularum strue apparatuque eum defrauda-rent.
units.tr: II. When someone, invited, gladly presents himself at another's dinner but invites no one in return, this is a most shameful vice of a certain stinginess and ingratitude. A person suffering from it is rightly called an allotriophagos, one who likes to live on other people's table. Many of these are found everywhere; they are not ashamed, nor sorry, nor repentant of their unsociable and most squalid solitary eating. And when they are admitted to honourable and more generous dinners, they are allowed to gnaw and lick another's dish. They stuff themselves at one lunch or supper with such a gluttony of food that ten others could scarcely manage it, thinking that nature and their genius are wronged if they were cheated of such a feast and display of dishes.

units.la: Parasiti cum & fordum: monophagi, αλλοτριοφαγοι, ἀρπαγαί (side-note glosses in Greek and Latin). rent. III. Cum quis ad conuiuium a se in- uitatos nimis tenuiter fordideq; tractat, eosq; se- mifamelicos atque sitientes dimittit, qui μικροτεχνίζων [?] potest appellari, hoc est, par- nam & angustam mensam ponens : vbitamen excipiendi, qui aduersa valetudine impediti, vel negotiorum multitudo ne distrahi, vel denique ex inopia & egestate conuiuali huiusmodi ossi- cio fungi minime possunt : quamuis & hic a- uaritia sordibus polluti inueniantur, qui, con- uiuia quidem symbola, quae solita conuiuatoris sumtibus constant ac apparantur, biante ore ac promptissima mente accedunt, ad symbolica ve- ro & collatitia, ad quae singuli conuiua certas quasdam portiones, vel esculentorum, vel pocu- lentorum, vel etiam pecuniae certam summam, amoris, amicitiaeq; mutua declarandae ac conci- l andae gratia, conferre solent, inuitati, quouis vel leui etiam praetextu se excusant, interesse, se conuiuio nunc non posse, iam iam accepisse se li- teras, ad quas protinus nullaque interpolita mo- ra sit respondendum, tentari se, nescio, qua capi- tis grauedine, vertigine, oculorumque caligine, sentire se insignem corporis alterationem, vel oc- cupari se necessariorum negotiorum mole: his & similibus praetextis multi hodie, trygobii, tryfi- bii, ac quouis lutulentiores, legitima & hu- manitora conuiuia refugere norunt, ne scilicet de suo in eandem aliquid conferant, cyclopica quaquadam misanthropia, vel anaritia dulci, fuce vitare, anxiequ viuere, ficiq; arboris foliis vesci, fordideq; coenare malunt, quam mutua beneuolentia amicitiaq; cum aliis conjungi, quam certas quasdam portiones adsympofia illa collatitia conferre.
units.tr: Parasites, also the squalid, the solitary eaters, the allotriophagoi, the rapacious (side-note glosses in Greek and Latin). III. When someone entertains those he has invited too meanly and squalidly, and sends them away half-starved and thirsty, setting a small and narrow table, he may be called a petty-craftsman (micro-technizon), that is, one who does little. Yet this is not to be applied to those who, prevented by poor health, or by the press of business, or finally by poverty and want, cannot discharge such a duty of hospitality at all. Still, there are also people stained by the squalor of greed, who, when a dinner is a shared meal, paid for from the usual expense of the host, come to it with open mouth and ready mind. But when invited to shared and contributory dinners, to which each guest is accustomed to bring a certain portion of food or drink, or even a certain sum of money, for the sake of declaring and gathering mutual love and friendship, they excuse themselves on any slight pretext: that they cannot attend the dinner now, that they have just received a letter to which they must reply at once without any delay, that they feel themselves tempted by some heaviness of the head, dizziness, or dimness of the eyes, that they feel a marked change in their body, or that they are weighed down by the burden of necessary business. With these and similar pretexts many today, more muddy than any Trygobii or Trifibii, know how to flee lawful and humane dinners, so that they need not contribute anything of their own to the same. They prefer, with a certain Cyclopean misanthropy or a sweet stinginess disguised as something else, to avoid, to live anxiously, to feed on fig-tree leaves and to dine squalidly, rather than to be joined with others in mutual goodwill and friendship by bringing their fixed portions to those contributory feasts.

units.la: Huiusmodi collatitiarum coenarum illustria exempla fuerunt dilectiones illa Christianorum primitiua Ecclesia, qua quidem inter diuites & pauperes, amicos, vicinos & propinquos agitarit promisfcue etiamnunc consueuerunt ex collectis fiue symbolis, qua a singulis coferuntur. Paschales similiter epula, qua apud Christianos nonnullos summa cum hilaritate & laetitia quotannis celebrantur ex collectis constant fiue symbolis, dona enim atq; munera, vt oua, placentas, panes saccharatos, & mellites, carnes, & vina ad festivitatis illius celebrationem, colliguntur atq; conferuntur. Legislatores denique sapientissimi publica olim conuiuia & quotidiana etiam, fyfitia dicta, & phiditia, vt facilius ciues in officio, parsimonia frugalitatiq; studio, imprimis vero mutuo amore benevolentia atq; concordia continerent, instituerunt. Hanc quoq; victus quotidianam communionem probat Plato f. de legibus, vbi singulis in locis oportere esse fyfitia, in quibus simul omnibus conuiuandum fit, aferit: quin & Aristoteles politic. 7. Syfitia approbat, conducibilia esse in-quiens communi omnium consensu bene confti-tutis tutis ciuitatibus Syssitia, multitudinemq; opor-tere in syssitia siue sodalitates esse distribuiam, probatq; ibidem antiquam esse syssitiorum ταξιν, omnium-que antiquissima esse Italica, a quibus reliquorum populorum syssitia fuerunt deducta, vt Cretensium, Spartanorum, Lacedæmo-nio-rum, quorum meminit Cicero 6. Tuscul. Chartaginensium, Atheniensium, quibus non inepte Germanorum syssitia collegia, siue sodalitates comparari posse existimo, in democraticis pra-sertim Rebuspublicis publicas commessationes ac quotidianas in frequenti usu esse nemini non est notum, in quem etiam usum ampla & splen-dida cœnacula extrui cernuntur, qua vulgo a potatione gentilitia lingua appellantur Trinckstuben/Gesellstuben / sodalium domus, in qua eiusdem muneris atq; officii artifi-ciq; homines, eadem vita genere vtentes conue-niunt atq; coeunt, tum ad mutuam benevolen-tiam atq; amicitiam tuendam, tum etiam ad honesta legitimaq; fœdera atq; conuenta sancien-da atq; confirmanda. Vbi vero commessatio-num & compotationum existit intemperantia, quam in pluribus hodie ciuitatibus & oppidis debacchari, imo maximam fere orbis partem perbacchari videmus, cumq; factionis cuiusdam metu suspicioq; subest, syssitia magistratus autoritate iunt abolenda, evertenda, & dis-soluenda, vt illicita, noua illegitima, & intem-pestiva, in quibus sc. mensis sumtuosis accum-bentes
units.tr: Illustrious examples of such contributory dinners were those love-feasts of the early Christian Church, which were held among rich and poor, friends, neighbours and relatives alike, and which even now are customarily kept among some people from collections or contributions made by each one. In the same way the Paschal feasts, which some Christians celebrate every year with great cheer and joy, are made up of collections or contributions. For gifts and presents, such as eggs, cakes, sugared and honeyed breads, meats and wines for the celebration of that festival, are gathered and brought together. Finally, the wisest lawgivers established public dinners, also daily ones, called syssitia and phiditia, so that citizens might more easily be kept in duty, in the pursuit of thrift and frugality, and above all in mutual love, goodwill and harmony. Plato too in the Laws approves this daily communal meal of food, where he states that there ought to be syssitia in every place, in which all must dine together. Indeed Aristotle in the Politics, book 7, approves the syssitia, saying that in well-ordered states by the common consent of all, syssitia are useful, and that the multitude ought to be distributed into syssitia or fellowships. He also states that the order of syssitia is ancient, and that the oldest of all is the Italian, from which the syssitia of the other peoples were derived, such as those of the Cretans, the Spartans and the Lacedaemonians, of whom Cicero speaks in book 6 of the Tusculan Disputations, and of the Carthaginians and Athenians. I think the syssitia or fellowships of the Germans may fittingly be compared with these. That public feasts and daily meals are in frequent use, especially in democratic commonwealths, is known to everyone. For this purpose large and splendid dining-halls are seen to be built, which in the vernacular of the Germans are commonly called by the name of drinking-houses: <bl>Trinckstuben/Gesellstuben</bl>, the houses of companions, where men of the same office and craft, living the same kind of life, meet and gather, both to preserve mutual goodwill and friendship, and also to ratify and confirm honest and lawful agreements and covenants. But where intemperance of feasting and drinking arises, which we see running riot in many states and towns today, indeed raging through nearly the greater part of the world, and where some fear or suspicion of faction lies beneath, the syssitia must be abolished, overthrown and dissolved by the authority of the magistrate, as unlawful, new, illegitimate and untimely, in which men reclining at sumptuous tables, like voracious beasts and, in the manner of Epicurus' herd of swine, so gorge and stuff themselves with wine and food that they lose all use of mind and reason, making impious and wicked pacts against God and their neighbour.

units.la: Syssitia summis philosophis approbantur. Germanorum syssitia. Verus Syssitiorum finis. Illicita syssitia abroganda. bentes voracium instar pecudum Epicurique de grege porcorum vino ciboq; adeo se obruunt atque infarciunt, vt omnem mentis rationisque vsum amittant, impiis nefariisque contra DE-VM & Proximum pactis foedera buc q; se obstrin-gant atque denunciant, vnde maxima mala atque calamitates necessario enascuntur. Verum_ sat commessatum est, sat prolixe coenatum_; adeo pollucibiles coenas conuiuiaque varia vario ferculorum apparatu exhibuit vnicum illud ocymum, ex eoq; puls: saluam fi forsan alicui monerim, case saturet, vlteriore enim & lau-tiore ferculo palatum explere non valeo. Et ha-benus de frumentis eorumque variis differen-tiis, sequuntur nunc panificia, pultes, placenta & libamina, qua ex iis conficiuntur.
units.tr: Common meals are approved by the greatest philosophers. The common meals of the Germans. The true end of common meals. Unlawful common meals are to be abolished. reclining at their sumptuous tables like voracious beasts, and like the herd of Epicurus's pigs, they so overwhelm and stuff themselves with wine and food that they lose all use of mind and reason, and they bind themselves by impious and wicked pacts against God and their neighbour, from which the greatest evils and calamities necessarily arise. But enough of drinking, enough of long dinners! Such lavish dinners and banquets, with their varied display of dishes, have produced that single dish of basil and pottage, if I may say so in good faith, which is enough to fill anyone; for I cannot satisfy my palate with a further and more sumptuous course. Having spoken of grains and their various kinds, there now follow breads, porridges, cakes and offerings made from them.

units.la: CAP. VII. Depane, placentis, pultibus, variisq; eduliis.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. Of bread, cakes, porridges, and various other foods.

units.la: X frugibus hactenus commemoratis fiunt panificia. Inter omnia enim alimenta primas tenet panis, esculentorum potulentorumque firmissimum & probatissimum vinculum.
units.tr: From the grains mentioned so far, bakers' goods are made. Among all foods, bread holds the first place, the firmest and most approved bond of solid and liquid nourishment.

units.la: Vnde & facrę literę sub nomine pa-nis omne genus alimenti comprehendunt: qua de re etiam Eŭripides impulsus ad alimentum hominum nihil pręterCereris mu-nera & aquę poculum opus esse pronuncia-uit.Et quę quæfc pulmentariis aliisq; cibariis vtilitas esse potest atq; voluptas , si citra panem edantur. Animam iis grauiter infici, qui pane in cibis abstinent,vulgi opinioquę-dam est: quin iis quoq;, qui parcius eum mi-scent cæteris eduliis, fœtere ora manifestum est.Vidi & nouiipse multos,quibus hoc peculiare fuit , multis carnibus , pauco autem pane vesci, vnde illis in pœnam contigit fœtidissimus oris halitus. Complures nihilominus inuenias, quib.à juuenta carnes, aliis quibus oua, aliis quibus pisces,multos quib. casei fuerint fastidio, quib. vero panes, pau-cos. Certissimum est maximam hominum partem,vel solo pane, vel ex vino, vel ex jure aliquo contentam viuere,nulloquealimento magis contineri vitam, quam optimo pa-ne. Est in exemplis senes quosdam panem ex melle edifle , eoque cibo vitam diutius protraxisse. Permulti,cum per occupationes non licet vberiores ingerere cibos , panem ex vino mandunt cum saccharo: Saluberrimum & suauissimum inuentum, hoc est, literarum studiosis & vitam sedentariam agentibus commodissimum.
units.tr: For this reason Holy Scripture also uses the word "bread" to cover every kind of food. Hence Euripides, moved to say what men need for food, declared that nothing is needed except the gifts of Ceres and a cup of water. And what use or pleasure can relishes and other victuals have if they are eaten without bread? It is a popular opinion that those who abstain from bread in their meals have a grievously tainted breath, and it is plain that the mouths of those who use bread sparingly with other foods also smell. I myself have seen many people who had this peculiarity, that they ate much meat but little bread, and so as a punishment they had a most foul breath. Nevertheless you will find many who from youth have loathed meat, others eggs, others fish, many who disliked cheese, and few who disliked bread. It is quite certain that the greater part of mankind lives on bread alone, or on bread with wine, or with some broth, and that life is sustained by no food more than by the best bread. There are examples of some old men who ate bread made with honey and by that food prolonged their lives. Many people, when their work does not allow them to take in more substantial food, eat bread soaked in wine with sugar: a most healthful and pleasant invention, and especially suited to students of letters and to those who lead a sedentary life.

units.la: De modo autem fumendi, panis certi alli- quid singulis constitui non facile potest, quippe alii minori contenti viuunt, alii ma-iorem expetunt, intense enim laborantes vt fossores, messores, helcijarii, bajuli, athletae-que copiosiorem edunt, iifq; inutilis est can-didus & qui celeriter conficitur, vtiles Vero iis sunt ejusmodi panes, qui neq; bellissime co&ti, neq; plurimum fermentati sunt, crassi enim lentiq; succi alimentis indigent, quae haud facile exhalent & corrumpantur. Candidi autem panes probe parati ac co&ti exi-mie conueniunt liberaliorem vitam fequen-tibus : qua de causa Sacerdotibus & Monachis lautissima panificia constituta sunt, aliquin otio marcidi, frequentissime aegrota-rent. Ele&ti igitur probiq; panes sunt eligendi, pondusq; pro pulmentariorum aliorumq; cibatiorum natura & copia augeri mi-nuiue potest, vbi etiam laborum hominum-que varietas consideranda venit. Vetusta- tem in panificiis medicina damnat: calen-tes item recentioresque : veteres supra mo-dum ficciores redduntur, proinde aegrius conficiuntur, qui calent. Siticulosi sunt, fla-tufq; pariunt, & obstru&tiones insignes : re-centes jucunde & salubriter efficiuntur : he-sterni ab illis sunt fecundi, id est qui jam consederunt, ab his biduani triduanique qui vltra durarunt, inutiliter eduntur. Quapro-pter pter illarum gentium morem improbo,quae in aliquot menses coquunt panes & in esum recondunt, nullam aliam ob causam, quam quod parcius votantur ob duritiem & siccitatem. Locus quoque in quo feruantur panificia non parum addit detrahitve bonitati vel malignitati, calentes enim in locum graveolentem repositi, facile virosam vim alliciunt, vi caloris trahentis, locis autem humentioribus facile mucescunt, situmque contrahunt, redolentque: apud quosdam gentes in subterraneis cellis vinariis innoxie feruantur, alii in tabulatis & locis foco proximis, panes suos recondunt, sed hanc curam matribus vel patribus familias relinquimus suscipiendam.
units.tr: As to how much bread should be taken, a fixed quantity cannot easily be set for everyone, since some live content with less, others desire more. Those who labour hard, such as diggers, reapers, haulers, porters and athletes, eat more copiously, and for them white bread that is quickly digested is unsuitable; the breads suited to them are those that are neither very finely made nor much fermented, for thick and heavy juices need foods that are not easily exhaled and corrupted. Indeed, well-prepared and carefully baked white bread suits those who lead a more luxurious life, and for this reason the most refined breads have been provided for priests and monks, who otherwise, wasting away in idleness, would very often fall ill. Choice and good breads, therefore, should be chosen, and the weight can be increased or diminished according to the nature and quantity of other relishes and foods, and also where the variety of men's labours must be considered. Medicine condemns old bread in these foods, and likewise hot and very fresh bread: old bread becomes excessively dry and so is digested with more difficulty, and hot bread causes thirst, flatulence and marked obstructions; fresh bread is digested pleasantly and healthfully. Bread from the day before is wholesome, that is, bread that has already settled; bread two or three days old, which has lasted longer, is eaten to no purpose. Therefore I disapprove of the custom of those peoples who bake bread for several months and store it for eating, for no other reason than that they swallow it with less ease because of its hardness and dryness. The place, too, in which bakers' goods are kept adds to or takes away from their goodness or badness: bread put while still warm into a foul-smelling place easily takes up the noxious quality, by the drawing power of heat, while in damper places it quickly grows mouldy, contracts a mustiness and smells. Among some peoples they are kept harmlessly in underground wine cellars; others store their bread in lofts and in places next to the hearth. But this care we leave to be undertaken by mothers and fathers of families.

units.la: De panibus furnaceis & clibanitis.
units.tr: On oven bread and bread baked in a clibanus.

units.la: Cum panis furnaceus inter ea quae nutriunt primum tenet locum, nonq; parum ad valetudinis vitaeq; conseruationem eius costura refert, operae pretium erit, de eo pauca hic inferere.
units.tr: Since oven bread holds the first place among the foods that nourish, and contributes no little to the preservation of health and life, it will be worth while to set down a few words about it here.

units.la: Panes autem ipnitas seu furnaceos à clibanitis differre Plinius l.8. & Athen.l.3. clare indicant. Furnacei enim in magnis furnis coquuntur, clibanite in testis aut furnis portatilibus, illi innocentiores sunt magisq; nutriunt bi[?] ficcissimi sunt, ob testa nimiam humiditatem exugentis calorem, quam etiam sententiam expresse expressit Hipp. 2. de diat. Ignita igitur magis nutriunt, quam verubus aut craticulis coctis, quod minus ab igne, quam illi aduruntur.
units.tr: That oven-baked or hearth-baked bread differs from bread baked in a clibanus, Pliny in book 8 and Athenaeus in book 3 clearly show. For oven bread is baked in great ovens, bread in a clibanus in pans or portable ovens. The former are more harmless and nourish more... they are driest, because the pan draws out the heat by its excessive moisture, which opinion Hippocrates also expressly states in the second book On Diet. Bread baked in the fire therefore nourishes more than bread cooked on spits or gridirons, because it is burnt less by the fire.

units.la: Ad clibanitas panis biscoctus refertur & nauticus, quo praecipue utuntur vinctis atque ad scalmum redacti in triremibus: Item milites & nautae in longioribus navigationibus: in septentrionalibus regionibus a nonnullis etiam sub testis coquitur, non ingratus ut quidam putant ob nimiam siccitatem, sed famelicus & melioris inopia pressis acceptissimus, cuius rei ipse possum esse testis: coctus autem in partes scinditur ac recoquitur, ut perduret, non mucescat, situmque minus contrahat.
units.tr: To bread baked in a clibanus belongs the twice-baked bread, sea biscuit, which is used above all by prisoners in chains reduced to the rowing bench in triremes, likewise by soldiers and sailors on longer voyages. In the northern regions some also bake it under a tile. It is not pleasant, as some think, because of its excessive dryness, but it is most welcome to the hungry and to those pressed by lack of anything better, of which I can myself be a witness. It is cut into pieces when cooked and baked again, so that it lasts, does not go mouldy, and contracts less mustiness.

units.la: Quidam torretur sub cratícula, & sub finem coenae apponi solet, diu iuxta Eschoritis, Ante inventionem clibanorum & furnorum veteres torrebant panes suos ferventi loco, vel fictilibus patinis, cinere & carbone, qui adhuc mos barbaris quibusdam gentibus peculiaris est, subcineritiis panibus maxime vescentibus.
units.tr: Some bread is toasted on a gridiron, and is usually served at the end of a meal; it has long been near the hearth. Before the invention of ovens and furnaces, the ancients toasted their bread on a hot spot, or in earthen dishes, in ashes and embers. This custom is still peculiar to certain barbarous peoples, who eat mostly bread baked under the ashes.

units.la: Quin & nostra atate saepius nunc fornaces, seu furni, nunc ligna, omnibus locis & temporibus, maxime vero in bellis ac maris, item itineribus haberi nequeunt, ut ita subcineritiis panibus ad focum vel cacabum aut prunas coctis esurientes vesci cogantur. In laminis quoq; ferreis aut aneis &c. ci-tissime panes coquuntur, Unde lixæ in militia ta-les laminas ut & farinam, in sacculis coriaceis, ne scilicet peruolet, secum gerunt, ut fugati vel exitinere defatigati, cibum in eiusmodi laminis cito possint parare. Sed & furnos subter-raneos ad colles scil. & montes, vbi glebosum solum est, quidam fodiunt, quod hodie Turcas factitare audio: alii vero fornaces cupreas pen-siles secum vehunt curruum instar suspensi-lium.
units.tr: Even in our own age, when furnaces or ovens and wood cannot be had in all places and at all times, especially in wars, at sea and on journeys, hungry men are compelled to eat bread baked under the ashes by the hearth, in a pot or among the embers. Bread is also baked very quickly on iron or bronze plates, etc. Hence in the army camp followers carry such plates, and flour too, in leather bags, lest it blow away, so that when put to flight or worn out by the march they can quickly prepare food on such plates. But some also dig underground ovens into hills, that is, into mountains where the soil is clayey; I hear that the Turks do this today. Others carry with them portable copper ovens, hung like carriages.

units.la: Damnantur autem omnes qui feruenti loco, cineribus atq; carbone torrentur, intus autem crudi existunt. Subcineritius vero coctura ratione omnium improbatur maxime, barbaris & a cultu humanitatis remotis conuenientes: minus ab igne vsti, aeque intus & extra colti innocentiores deprehenduntur, ut sunt panes nostris furnis cocti. Non hic prætereundum est, ab vrbe condita annis super quingentis oblogin-ta Pistores Romæ non fuisse mulierum, id tunc opus fuisse, ipsosq; Quirites panes finxisse. Vxor Catonis, autore Plutarcho, pinsendi munus a sua dignitate alienum non putauit: Denique vero Persia atq; Asia omnis generis delitiæ Romam confluxerunt, vnde adhuc pistores illi dulciarii, qui placentas & catera dulcia panificia formant, carneq; incrustant, ut in amplis vrbibus, magnatum q; familiis videre est.
units.tr: All those who bake in hot place, in ashes and embers, and remain raw inside, are condemned. Baking under the ashes is most of all disapproved of by every reasoning, and suits barbarians and those removed from the culture of humanity. Bread that is less burnt by the fire and equally cooked inside and out is found more wholesome, as are the breads baked in our ovens. Here it must not be passed over that for more than five hundred years after the founding of the city, there were no bakers at Rome who were women; that work was then done by men, and the citizens themselves made their bread. Cato's wife, according to Plutarch, did not think grinding corn beneath her dignity. At last, however, all kinds of luxury from Persia and all Asia flowed into Rome, and from this come those confectioners who still shape cakes and other sweet bakers' goods and cover meat with pastry, as may be seen in great cities and in the households of the great.

units.tr: O a

units.la: De coctura panis.
units.tr: On the baking of bread.

units.la: Coctura quoque ratio diligenter ei, qui vitæ salubritati studet, tenenda est, Pistorum storum enim intolerabili auaritia atq; negligentia fit, ut identidem panes justam coctionem non adipiscantur, quia minus coctos ponderosiores existere certum est ob humoris copiam intus manentis: sæpe torrentur potius quam coquuntur; quo errore haud dubie valetudo tentatur, immodico enim ignis calore non alienus tantum humor absumitur, sed etiam lentus ille, genuinus & dulcis succus, qui velut anima farinæ est exhalat atque deuritur. Quamobrem urbium præfecti inprimis debent cauere ne in hac rei cibariæ parte adeo grauiter & frequenter peccetur, sed potius, qui ex jurisdictione hoc habent inquirere pœnis multisque in eos debent animaduertere, quos tantas vitæ insidias moliri compererint.
units.tr: Care must also be taken in the baking, by anyone who studies the wholesomeness of life. Through the intolerable greed and carelessness of bakers, loaves repeatedly fail to achieve proper baking, because it is certain that underbaked loaves are heavier on account of the abundance of moisture remaining inside. They are often scorched rather than baked. This error undoubtedly endangers health: excessive heat not only consumes the foreign moisture but also drives off and burns away that sluggish, native and sweet juice which is like the life of the flour. Therefore the magistrates of cities above all should take care that this part of the food is not so gravely and so often neglected. Rather, those who hold jurisdiction in this matter should inquire into it and punish with penalties and fines those whom they find plotting such great dangers to life.

units.la: De farina & aqua qua subigitur.
units.tr: On the flour and the water with which it is kneaded.

units.la: Farina quoque natura viresque non sunt negligenda: ut enim panis sit optimus, optimeque nutriat, facilliusque conficitur, requiritur I. frumenti bonitas. II. Iusta eius molitura ac pistura. III. ut farina fit tenuis, non vermiculosa, ut fit candida & ab omni furfure pura, ficenim facilius in ventriculo alteratur, probius concoquitur, facilius in corpus distribuitur, promtiusque alit. IV. miftio fermenti plurima, falis modica. V. Subactio exacta. VI. Proba coctura.
units.tr: The nature and strength of the flour must also not be neglected. For bread to be the best, to nourish best, and to be more easily prepared, the following are required: (1) goodness of the grain; (2) its proper milling and grinding; (3) that the flour be fine, not wormy, white and free of all bran, for such flour is more easily changed in the stomach, more properly digested, more readily distributed into the body, and nourishes more promptly; (4) a large quantity of leaven and a moderate amount of salt; (5) exact kneading; (6) proper baking.

units.la: Quod igitur in farina durum relinquitur atque furfureum, ut in aqua id extrinsecus dissolui non potest, eadem ratione nein ventre quidem madefactum dissoluetur, sed totum ut fuit ingestum, indiuiduum permanet atque indigestum, unde etiam panes furfuracei & crassi, maiorem stercoris copiam conficiunt quam necesse est propter subsidentiam furfurumque vim abfterforiam.
units.tr: Therefore whatever in the flour remains hard and bran-like, since it cannot be dissolved from outside in water, by the same reasoning will not be dissolved even when moistened in the belly. It remains whole and undigested just as it was swallowed. Hence bread that is bran-rich and coarse also produces a greater quantity of excrement than is necessary, on account of the sediment and the cleansing power of the bran.

units.la: Aqua porro maximam habendam esse rationem, non dubitandum est, vitiosa enim insalubres panes reddit, ut plurimum continget hieme: largiori etiam aqua farina perfundi debet, ut sua spongiosa inanitate panis multum admittat aerem.
units.tr: Moreover, there is no doubt that the greatest regard must be had for the water, for faulty water makes bread unwholesome, which will mostly happen in winter. The flour should also be wetted with rather more water, so that by its spongy emptiness the bread may admit much air.

units.la: Panificum grex peruersus neque aqua, neque salis, neque fermenti etiam habet rationem. Salitos enim panes salubriores esse iucundioresque in cibo eruditi palati homines iudicant omnes. Salenim exiccat omnem humorem, qui a calore solet putrescere, quod manifeste indicant sale imbuta conditaque carnes, quae quas in vsum cibarium salitas diu videmus per- durare, qua ratione etiam in panificiis humor a sale consumetur, qui si insideret pondus addi- ceret. Praterea sal modicum in omni cibo excitat auiditatem, coctionemque iuuat.
units.tr: The perverse tribe of bakers pays no regard either to water, to salt, or even to leaven. For all men of refined palate judge that salted breads are more wholesome and more pleasant to eat. For salt dries up all moisture, which is wont to putrefy through heat, as salted and seasoned meats clearly show, which we see lasting a long time when salted for use as food. By the same reasoning, in bakers' goods too the moisture is consumed by the salt, which, if it remained, would add weight. Besides, a moderate amount of salt in every food stirs up appetite and aids digestion.

units.la: Panis denique fermentatus esse debet, qui zymitis dicitur: fermentum enim panificiis sa- lubritatem affert et gratiam. Infermentatus dicitur ἄζυμος, qualis fuit Iudaicus panis. Cornelius tamen Celsus panem sine fermento stomacho idoneum dicit, fermentatum vero a- lienum, facilimque intus corrumpi, cui Galenus caeteri posteriores medici contradicunt, panes plurimum fermentatos facillime concoqui, eos vero qui sine fermento finguntur nemini omnino utiles esse constanter asseuerantes; quin et utiliores fieri si cafeum admiscetur, constatque hoc panificii genus tum apud maiores, tum no- stra atate agricolis et rusticis in summo honore fuisse inque usu frequentissimo etiamnunc esse: a quibus tamen panibus literarum studiosi omnes quique otioediti vitam transigunt, iubeo abstinere, namque fossores, messoresque ipsos bains- losque esu illorum ladi constat.
units.tr: Finally, bread ought to be leavened, which is called zymitic, for leaven gives bakers' goods wholesomeness and agreeableness. Unleavened bread is called azymos [ἄζυμος], such as the Jewish bread was. Yet Cornelius Celsus says that bread without leaven suits the stomach, while leavened bread is unsuitable and easily goes bad inside. Galen and the other later physicians contradict him, steadily asserting that well-leavened breads are most easily digested, while those made without leaven are utterly useless to anyone; and that they become more useful if cheese is mixed in. It is established that this kind of bread was held in the highest esteem among farmers and country folk, both among our ancestors and in our own age, and is still in very frequent use. But from these breads I bid abstain all who spend their lives in literary study or in leisure, for it is clear that diggers and reapers themselves are harmed by eating them.

units.la: Esse autem fermentatos panes non inutiles inde constat, quod fermentum sit tenuum partium, modiceque calidum, et ut verius dicam ex contrariis facultatibus temperatum, quip-
units.tr: That leavened breads are not useless is evident from this, that leaven consists of fine parts and is moderately warm, or, to speak more truly, is tempered by contrary qualities,

units.la: quippe propter aciditatem frigida cuiusdam naturae particeps est, & calliditatis etiam expu- tredine oborta, quin & aliquid a sale accipit & farina natura.
units.tr: since on account of its acidity it partakes of a certain cold nature, and also of a cunning arising from putrefaction. Moreover, it receives something from the salt and from the nature of the flour.

units.la: Protritu autem gentium fermentum va-riis fit mediis, quos, nimis laboriosum esset, hic recensere: teneamus nos nostram faciendi fer-menti rationem nobis obviam: hoc unum observandum, subactum fermentum plus mi-nus quindecim dies seruari posse, ultra vero vi-tiari.
units.tr: Leaven is made among the peoples in various ways, which it would be too laborious to recount here. Let us keep to our own method of making leaven, which is familiar to us. This one thing must be observed: kneaded leaven can be kept for about fifteen days, but beyond that it spoils.

units.la: Modus quoque statuendus: modicum enim fermentum totam massam corrumpit, plurimumque deperdit gratia.
units.tr: The quantity must also be set, for a little leaven corrupts the whole mass and loses most of its grace.

units.la: Per se denique fermentum cum primis ex farina tritici extrahendi maturandique virtute pollere experimentis constat, callos enim pedum clavosque extenuat, cateraque tubercula & furunculos ex sale concoquit aperitque.
units.tr: Finally, leaven by itself is known from experience to have especially the power of drawing out and ripening: it thins calluses on the feet and corns, and by means of salt it softens and opens other swellings and boils.

units.la: De variis panis generibus & differentiis.
units.tr: On the various kinds and differences of bread.

units.la: PAnis varia genera ac differentias omnes literis mandare ut superuacuum, ita difficilimum est, discrimina tamen ad rem nostram pertinentia, asseribam.
units.tr: To commit all the kinds and differences of bread to writing is as superfluous as it is difficult. Nevertheless, I shall set out the distinctions that pertain to our purpose.

units.la: O
units.tr: (page signature)

units.la: Conuenit autem inter omnes delica- tissimum præstantissimumq; panem fieri ex tritico, qui tamen pro tritici natura non exiguas sortitur differentias : alii enim purissimi, alii furfuribus paucis, alii multis, quidam polline furfuribusque simul confusis finguntur, pro gentium ritu, hominumque peculiari viuendi ratione : alius enim hoc, alius illo panis genere delectatur. Ut enim olim apud antiquos, tum Græcos, tum Romanos multiplex fuit panis varietas, sic nostra quoque ætate hic & alibi permulta sunt discrimina, quippe primarii, vt regii, procerumque ac magnatum, secundarii, tertiarii & quartarii cernuntur, quanquam magnos imperatores & magnates secundario etiam pane obleQatos fuisse constat, & hodie in plurium Dominorum mensis atri panes conspiciuntur.
units.tr: It is agreed among all that the most delicate and excellent bread is made from wheat. Yet, according to the nature of the wheat, it has no small differences. For some is made from the purest flour, others with few bran, others with many, and some is shaped from fine flour and bran mixed together, according to the custom of peoples and the particular way of life of men. For one delights in this kind of bread, another in that. For just as formerly among the ancients, both Greeks and Romans, there was a manifold variety of bread, so in our own age too there are very many distinctions, here and elsewhere. For primary bread, as of kings, nobles and magnates, secondary, tertiary and quaternary are seen. Although it is established that great emperors and magnates were also fed on secondary bread, and today black breads are seen on the tables of many lords.

units.la: Siligineus summæ fuit auctoritatis in mensis Romanorum, quorum mos hodie quoq; in amplis familiis pertinaciter durat.
units.tr: Rye bread (siligineus) was of the highest authority on the tables of the Romans, a custom which even today persists stubbornly in large households.

units.la: Porro doctrinæ gratiâ talis panis dichotomia, instituì potest, vt quidam dicuntur extremi, quidam intermedij. Extremi triticei seu purissimi, & furfuracei : inter hos Interjecti sunt hordeacei, siliginei nostri, auenacei, farracei, spleltacei & ex ocymo.
units.tr: Moreover, for the sake of instruction, such a division of bread can be made, so that some are called extreme and some intermediate. The extreme kinds are wheaten or purest, and bran bread. Between these are interposed barley, our rye, oat, emmer, spelt, and bread made of ocymum.

units.la: Triticei omnium sunt purissimi. Furfuracei furacei omnium sordidissimi, leuissimeque alunt,ocyffimè per aluum deiiciuntur, quos nisi summa vrgente inopia edi non videmus.
units.tr: Wheaten bread is of all the purest. Bran bread is of all the most sordid; it nourishes very lightly and is most quickly voided through the bowels. We do not see these eaten except under extreme and pressing want.

units.la: Hordaceos & reliquos,qui antiquis fue-runt vsitatissimi, cibis quidam abdicandos iubent, quadrupedumq; refe&ibus tantum idoneos, sed nullo iudicio.
units.tr: Barley and the rest, which were most in use among the ancients, some order to be cast out of food, fit only for the feeding of four-footed beasts, and even that without judgment.

units.la: Hordaceus namq; tritico feré nihil cedit, ita vt etiam Hipp. teste, proximum ab eo oc-cupet locum. Siquidem ipsi saluatori nostro panes hordacei miraculi materiam praebue-runt,non igitur ex humana vita panes hordacei sunt proscribendi. Constat eos qui pani-bus hordaceis vescuntur,morbo pedum non tentari. Experimenti via facilis,quibus res est cum podagra. Experimentum cuiq; sit libe-rum &obuium. Multos certè reperias in no-stris etiam regionibus & locis illis asperis monrofisq; acsyluis illis, quas Germani Westerwalde vnd Odenwalde vocant, vt & in nostrae etiam ditionis & Comitatus 1-senburgici parte,quae auimontium appellari potest, Bogelsberg/auenâsola, ocymoque plurimum victitantes,melius nutriri satiari-que,quam qui tritico abundant, (praesertim vbi farina auenacea pollinario cribro exacte fuerit cribrata,furfuribusque purgata) imò non tantum prosperiori vti eos valetudine, sed diutius etiam viuere iis constat,qui vel in
units.tr: For barley bread yields almost nothing to wheat, so that, as Hippocrates testifies, it holds the next place after it. Indeed, barley loaves supplied the matter of a miracle for our Saviour himself; therefore barley bread is not to be banished from human life. It is agreed that those who eat barley bread are not troubled by gout of the feet. The way to test this is easy for those who have to do with podagra, and the experiment is open and free to anyone. Certainly you will find many in our own regions and in those rough, mountainous places and forests which the Germans call Westerwald and Odenwald, and also in part of our own territory and county of Isenburg, which may be called Avimontium, the Vogelsberg. These people, living mostly on oats, barley and spelt, are better nourished and satisfied than those who abound in wheat (especially where oat flour has been carefully sifted through a fine sieve and cleansed of bran). Indeed, it is agreed that they not only enjoy a healthier constitution but also live longer than those who have plenty of wheat and wine in Alsace or Italy, and who every day devise new dishes after the manner of Apicius.

units.la: Alfatia, vel Italia tritici & vini habent copiam, quique Apitii more quotidie noua fercula excogitant. Quare prudenter gladiatores & athletæ veteres ab hordei tanquam optimi cibi ad nutriendum accommodatissimi visu, ie deterreri non sunt passi, licet à plerisque contumeliosè hordearii appellarentur.
units.tr: Therefore the ancient gladiators and athletes wisely did not allow themselves to be deterred from barley, which is the most suitable food for building up strength, by its appearance, although they were insultingly called barley-men by many.

units.la: Ac vt multa paucis expediam, omnia frumenta mutuo in hominibus alendis sibi succedere posse visus docuit: quemadmodum enim qui vinum non habet, cereuisiam, qui hac destituitur, aquam bibat, ita cui per vitæ suæ rationem, triticum, speltam, hordeumque vsui pare concessum non est, is vulgarem siliginem, auenam, ocymumue vsurpet, non minus enim his quam tritico natura contenta est, præsertim si iis quis assuerit, non enim assuetis grauitatem ventriculo inferunt, difficulterque concoquuntur, malleatoribus verò, phalangariis, agricolisque conuenientissima sunt.
units.tr: To set out many things in few words: experience has shown that all grains can serve in turn for feeding men. For just as one who has no wine drinks beer, and one who lacks beer drinks water, so one for whom, by the manner of his life, wheat, spelt and barley are not available for use may take common rye, oats or ocymum. He is content with these no less than with wheat, especially if he has been accustomed to them; for they weigh heavily on the stomach of those not used to them and are digested with difficulty, but they are most suitable for mallet-men, carriers and farmers.

units.la: Ex siligine nostra seu secali, sale fermento bono, aquaque simplici præstantissimum fit tetraphapмacum famis, vbiuis vsitatissimum ac longo vsu probatissimum, Roggenbrodt. Rite autè & proportionaliter inter se quatuor illa sunt contemperanda & percoquen-
units.tr: Of our rye or common grain, with salt, good leaven and plain water, is made the most excellent four-ingredient bread for famine, in use everywhere and long proven by experience: Roggenbrodt. These four must be mixed together properly and in due proportion, and then baked thoroughly.

units.la: quenda. Salubrior panis efficitur, si bene fer-mentatus est, & probè salitus.
units.tr: Bread is more wholesome if it is well fermented and properly salted.

units.la: Romani & delicati Græci hunc panem sordidum appellarunt, sed iniquè. Vtinam eiusmodi sordibus horrea & penuaria tempore caritatis annonæ plena essent.
units.tr: The Romans and the fastidious Greeks called this bread coarse, but unjustly. Would that granaries and storehouses were full of such coarseness in a time of dear grain.

units.la: Verum, ne vnquam alicui aliquid dura riffimæ etiam & miserandæ famis, nec non h. e. abfq; summæ frumentaceorum feminum penuriæ magno la tempore deesse videatur, subsidia quædam bore & aut saltem subleuamina, naturaliaque & arti- sumptu ficiosa simul cibi vicaria seu locum tenentia, parabi- annotabo, pauperculis & egenis fameque lia.fame, perituris pernecessaria.
units.tr: That is, without any great shortage of grain seeds at any time, lest anyone should seem to be left with nothing in the most severe and pitiable famine. I will note certain aids, or at least alleviations, both natural and artificial, which are also substitutes or stand-ins for food and cost little, and which are most necessary for the poor and needy who are perishing from hunger.

units.la: Ac primò quidem paupertas in frumen-torum penuria artificiosè didicit concinna-re panes ex pisis, fabis, cicerbus, lupinis, vi-ciis, lentibus, milio, oryza, orobis, glandibus, &c. horum enim farina frumentaceæ vel parte media, vel etiam largius admissetur: fa-melicorum autem stomachum sufficienter replent, famem retardant, paucitate satiant, firmiusque præbent nutrimentum, præsertim glandini, caftaneati, cicerini, quique ex eryza fiunt & milio, hi enim nec inusitati sunt, nec insalubres. Pulcriores autem & gratiores erunt eiusmodi panes, si feminibus excorticatis prius parentur.
units.tr: First, poverty, when grain is scarce, has learned to make bread skilfully from peas, beans, chickpeas, lupins, vetches, lentils, millet, rice, orobus, acorns and so on. Their flour may be mixed in with grain flour, either in part or even in larger amounts. These foods sufficiently fill the stomachs of the hungry, delay hunger, satisfy with small quantities and provide firmer nourishment. This is especially so for acorn, chestnut, chickpea, and breads made from rice and millet, for these are neither unusual nor unwholesome. Such breads will be finer and more pleasant if they are first made from husked seeds.

units.la: Legumi-nofi. Quibus vero leguminum flatulentia su-specta est,ii carui,fœniculi, anisi vel cymini feminę adiecto eam emendare possunt,morbidisq; corporibus sunt accommodatiores, quia hac ratione medicati euadunt.
units.tr: Of the pulses: where lentils and beans are suspected of causing flatulence, caraway, fennel, anise or cumin seeds added to them can correct this, and they are more suitable for sickly bodies, since in this way they become medicinal.

units.la: Dira quoque,tabida & rabida fames panes ex siliquis cereuisiariis <bl>Drabern/inesu</bl> hominum transferre coegit:quin & ex furfuribus, qui tamen extra annonæ caritatem in Magnorum aulis in paltum canum & altilium pinsuntur. Minimè enim hi panes tam propter extremam paganorum famem lethalem (quam Deus auertat) quam ob vtilitatem ac comparandi facilitatem fuerunt prætereundi. Carius enim vita nihil est, quomodocunque illa tandem conseruetur. Lupulus siliquis adiectus earum fœculentiam facile corriget, putredinem enim arcet, sanguinemq; mundificat.
units.tr: Dire, wasting and raging hunger has also forced people to turn to bread made from brewers' husks, <bl>Drabern/inesu</bl>, and even from bran, which otherwise is ground for the tables of the great, for dogs and fattened fowl outside times of dear grain. Indeed these breads should not be passed over, whether because of the extreme and deadly famine of the common people (which God forbid) or because of their usefulness and ease of obtaining. For nothing is dearer than life, however it may be preserved. Hops added to the husks will easily correct their muddiness, for they ward off putrefaction and cleanse the blood.

units.la: Fit quoq; panis laudabilis ex pomis concisis,siue excorticatis,siue non , vel elixis in forma pultis. vel furno tostis,sic vt farina prius probe fermētata & salita subigatur,& mane media pomorum præparatorum pars admisceatur.
units.tr: A praiseworthy bread is also made from apples, cut up, whether peeled or not, or boiled into a pulp, or toasted in an oven, in such a way that the flour, first well fermented and salted, is kneaded and a portion of the prepared apples is mixed in in the morning.

units.la: Rectius tamen coquuntur in pulmenti formam,coloque traiiciuntur, & postea farinæ subiiciuntur. Tot autem sunt huius panis differentiæ, quot & pomorum. Ex dulcibus fiunt meliores & ξυχυμοι.
units.tr: However, they are better cooked into the form of a pottage, strained through a sieve, and afterwards added to the flour. There are as many kinds of this bread as there are kinds of apples. Those from sweet apples are better and succulent [ξύχυμοι].

units.la: Eodem modo ex pyris tam sylueftribus quàm domesticis, prout libet, panes confici possunt.
units.tr: In the same way, breads can be made from wild or cultivated pears, as one pleases.

units.la: Fiunt quoq; panes ex cerasis, prunis, aliis nostris cotoneis, amygdalis, castaneis, nucibus iuglandibus & auellanis, baccis iuniperinis & lauri.
units.tr: Breads are also made from cherries, plums, our quinces, almonds, chestnuts, walnuts, hazelnuts, juniper berries and laurel berries.

units.la: Cerasati sic conficiuntur. Exiccata cerasa per totum annum in hunc & alium vsum reponuntur, postea recocta praebentur, vel electuarium farinae commiscetur, vel per se in pane triticeo & pane placentarum piftato devorantur. Nuclei vero, sicut & confimiliū fructuum, cum cortice pistrino moli, & in pollinem redigi possunt albicantem, farinae subigendae addendum pro pane augendo, & largius exiguâ massa cibando: talesq; panes inutiles plane & noxii esse non possunt, eiusmodi enim nuclei cum suis ossibus & corticibus contra calculum colicamq; commendantur.
units.tr: Cherry breads are made as follows. Dried cherries are kept for the whole year for this and other uses; afterwards they are offered after being cooked again, either mixed with the flour as a paste, or eaten whole in wheaten bread or in bread of pastry-cakes. The stones, and likewise those of similar fruits, can be ground with the shell in a mill and reduced to a whitish powder, to be added to the flour when kneading, to increase the bread and to make a small mass go further. Such breads cannot be entirely useless or harmful, for such stones, with their bones and shells, are recommended against stone and colic.

units.la: Eodem modo coquuntur myrtilli, moras, fraga, similesque fructus in formam electuarii adq; vsum reseruantur.
units.tr: In the same way, bilberries, mulberries, strawberries and similar fruits are cooked into the form of an electuary and kept for use.

units.la: Amygdalae cum corticibus suis si moluntur, farinam replentem exhibebunt & nutrientem.
units.tr: Almonds ground along with their husks will yield a filling and nourishing flour.

units.la: Sunt & panes faginei, rosacei, rosis cum farinae particula contemperatis, suntq; vtilissimi & saluberrimi, efficati enim omnes alui cruen-
units.tr: There are also breads of beech-mast and of roses, with a little flour mixed in with the roses. These are very useful and wholesome, for all of them check bloody discharges from the bowels and excessive menstrual flow.

units.la: cruentas deiectiones mensiumque immodi- cum fluxum sistunt. Ficulnei, passulati, qui fiunt ex ficubus caricisque præpinguibus & passulis, si videlicet cum farina subigantur, suntque non inutiles: sed ne hi panes aluum citius soluant, solido & stiptico medicamento sunt distemperandi, vt pisis glandibus, vel salrem aquâ chalybeata.
units.tr: Fig breads and raisin breads, made from very plump figs, dried figs and raisins, are also not useless, provided they are kneaded with flour. But so that these breads do not loosen the bowels too quickly, they must be tempered with a firm, astringent ingredient, such as pine nuts or acorns, or salt in chalybeate water.

units.la: Ex floribus quoque sambuci coctis, in ele- ctuarii formam fit panis in dysenteria celeberrimus. Recipiantur baccæ sambuci contusæ, in mortario & farina è mola iam iam calens adhuc allata, hæc inter se miscentur, coquantur vel pinsantur: frustum de hoc pane vino optimo iniicitur, & pro restinguenda siti exhibitur saluberrimo experimento.
units.tr: Bread that nourishes and moistens well can be prepared by kneading flour with cooked or roasted plums of every kind, wherever there is an abundant crop of them. They can very conveniently be dried and stored, so that bread may be ready for the whole year, when necessity presses and demands it.

units.la: Ex omnis generis prunis coctis vel tostis, vbi scilicet vberior eorum prouentus est, sarinæ subactis, panis bene nutriens humestansque parari potest. Possunt commodissime torreri & reponi, vt toto anno panis in promtu, necessitate vrgente & postulante, esse queat.
units.tr: Moreover, country people have been accustomed to prepare bread and food from mushrooms, dried and ground into powder; but they must be gathered with the greatest care, since some are poisonous. To guard against such danger, and so that edible mushrooms can be had at every season of the year, a white poplar's bark is cut through to the ground and soaked in warm water which has received leaven; after four days this yields most suitable mushrooms for eating.

units.la: Ex fungis præterea rustici exiccatis, & in pollinem tritis panes cibosq; parare consueuerunt: verum cautissimè sunt colligendi, quia quidam venenosi sunt: eiusmodi tamen periculum præcauendum, vtque omnianni tempore edules fungi haberi possint, albi populi cortex humotenus sectus, aquaque calida, quæ fermentum excepit, perfulus, quatriduo spatio fungos esui proferet aptif-limos.
units.tr: Besides this, country folk have commonly made breads and food from dried mushrooms ground into meal. These must be gathered with great care, since some are poisonous. To guard against this danger, and so that edible mushrooms can be had at any season, cut the bark of the white poplar into pieces at ground level and soak it for four days in warm water that has received leaven; this will produce the most edible mushrooms.

units.la: Sed ne vnquam cuiquam aliquid deesse vi deatur, in famis & penuriæ tempore fcien-dum,etiam ex radicibus,vt rapis,napis,petro-felino,iride,cæpis,& ex ipsis stagneis arundi-netis panem parari facilè salubrem posse: I-tem,ex herbis,vt cichoriis,acetosis,rosis, be-tis,blitis,brassicis,buglossis,lactucis, & simi-libus polychrestis simplicibus.
