Ex arborum quoque foliis,vt prunorum,pyrorum,fago-rum,quercuumque torridis,inque pollinem redactis, cotritis scilicet vel pistrino molitis, quin & arborum quarundam corticibus, vt betulæ,(quod vidi ipse in Suecia anno 98.cū annonæ caritas grauissima flagellaret totum regnum)molere farinam inque panis vsum spissare incuitabilis fames famelicos coegit. Folia quoq; coxerunt atq; devorarunt.
units.tr: But so that no one may think anything is ever lacking, it should be known that in times of famine and shortage a wholesome bread can easily be made even from roots, such as turnips, rape, parsley, iris, onions, and from the stalks of reeds in marshes. Likewise from herbs such as chicory, sorrel, roses, beets, blites, cabbages, bugloss, lettuce and similar simple herbs of common use. Also from the leaves of trees, such as plum, pear, beech and oak, dried and reduced to powder, that is, crushed or ground in a mill. Even from the bark of certain trees, such as birch (which I saw myself in Sweden in the year 1598, when the scarcity of grain was scourging the whole kingdom), grinding it into meal and thickening it for bread was forced upon the starving by unavoidable hunger. They also boiled and devoured the leaves.

units.la: Ex fœno quoque & cordo in extrema necessitate pistrino molito,& cum farina laudabili vsitata commixto,panem paratum inuenio. Nec id absurdum est, aut penitus inauditum,cum Hierosolymis id factum esse, Josephus testetur. Sed malum hoc paternè auferat,auertatq; Deus.
units.tr: Bread can also be found made from hay and bark, ground in a mill in extreme necessity and mixed with the usual good flour. Nor is this absurd or entirely unheard of, since Josephus testifies that it was done at Jerusalem. But may God mercifully avert and remove this calamity.

units.la: Sunt quoque panes vinosi, acetati, saccha- rati, melliti. Spissantur & panes ex piscibus sole siccatis, tostis etiam vel assis inque pul- uerem attritis & cum farina subactis, vt in Norvvegia, Islandia, Finlappia. Quibus et- iam populis caseati panes in frequenti sunt vsu.
units.tr: Milk bread is excellent and very nourishing. It is made from milk, either unleavened [ἄζυμος] or fermented, and is most useful for those who waste away. It should be noted here that these milk breads satisfy much more if fried bacon is added; in Wetterau they are called <bl>Speckkuchen</bl>. The Dutch and the Swiss, even apart from famine, eat fresh cheese or plenty of pressed curds with their bread, and those of the wealthier country folk, whose property is valued at 5000 florins, hardly use finer bread even on Sundays. It is therefore not absurd if in a time of dear grain these breads are brought into use.

units.la: Panis lacteus optimus est, & valde nutri- ens: fit ex lacte ἀζυμος vel fermentatus, ta- bidis vtilissimus. Notandum hic, lacteos hosce panes multo magis satiare, si laridum frixum addatur, vocanturque; in Wetterauia <bl>Speckkuchen</bl>. Holandi & Heluetii etiam extra famem caseum recentem seu pressi co- piam lactis cum pane interunt, & vix purio- re pane etiam diebus dominicis vtuntur ii, qui ex rusticis ditioribus sunt, quorum cen- sus aestimatur 5000 flor. Non ergo absurdu, sitempore caritatis hi panes trahantur in v- sum.
units.tr: Milk bread is excellent and very nourishing; it is made from milk, either unleavened (azymos) or fermented, and is most useful for the sick. It should be noted here that these milk breads satisfy much more if fried bacon is added; in the Wetterau they are called Speckkuchen. The Dutch and the Swiss, even outside times of famine, eat fresh cheese or a quantity of pressed curds with their bread, and those who are of the richer country folk, whose wealth is reckoned at 5000 florins, hardly use finer bread even on Sundays. It is therefore not absurd that these breads should be taken up in a time of dearth.

units.la: Neque vero praetereundi sunt panes, qui ex ouis fiunt saluberrimi ac praestantissimi, magis enim caeteris panibus satietatem in- ducunt, laudabilissimumque corpori praebent nutrimentum, cumprimis quando fa-ce cere- uisiae melioris fermentatus aut subactus fue- rit, quod optime norunt matresfamilias o- mnes in Wetterauia, quae ob pinsendi (heb- doatim enim in magna id faciunt copia, ma- xime vero diebus dominicis & sacris) artifi- cium.
units.tr: Nor should bread made with eggs be passed over; these are most wholesome and excellent, for they induce satiety more than other breads and provide the body with most commendable nourishment, especially when they have been leavened or kneaded with a good beer yeast. All housewives in the Wetterau know this well, since they make it in great quantity every week, and especially on Sundays and holy days, through the skill of baking.

units.la: Piscini. Lactens panis. Ouati. Vvettera. Haffia. Fraco-furto. teriacens. annona. felicitate. bonita-te clarus. cium conterminis sibi populis omnibus prę-ripuerunt palmam.
units.tr: Fish bread. Milk bread. Oats. Wetterau. Hesse. Frankfurt. Theriac... Famous for abundance, for good harvest and for happy fortune, they have carried off the palm from all the neighbouring peoples.

units.la: Inter non naturales denique panes Cinerei sunt, qui ex cineribus radicum, item arborum & gleba- condensantur, quibus vsi sunt in nauigatio-cei panes, ne Indica, vt a famelica sese morte vindica-rent. Cineres autem cum aqua subegerunt & comederunt. Sic fieri potest panis ex puriori terræ gleba, vt bolo armeno, terra sigillata, quorum in defectu & paucitate commode vsurpari potest bolus Hungen-Bolus sis, Niddanus, vel Laubacensis. Hi enim Hungen- in summa penuria farinæ commiscentur: li-ris, Lau- cet enim plus replent quam nutriant, ine-bacenfis uitabilis tamen penuria & fames victum et-materia iam horrendum sapidum reddit. Sic anno panis pre- 98. in Suecia pauperes ob intolerabilem fa-bere pof- mem glebam furnorum deuorasse, cortices-sunt. que betularum in panificium redegisse meis vidi oculis, quam tamen plus quam lupinam famem Deus paterne & clementer postea mitigauit.
units.tr: Finally, among the non-natural breads are ash breads, which are made from the ashes of roots and of trees, and also from clods of earth. Sailors on voyages to the Indies have used them so that they might save themselves from starving to death. They mixed the ashes with water and ate them. Bread can likewise be made from purer clods of earth, such as Armenian bole or sealed earth. When these are lacking or scarce, the bole of Hungen, Nidda or Lau-bach may conveniently be used. In great shortage of flour these are mixed in, for they fill the belly more than they nourish, and although they are unpleasant, hunger and want still make them palatable. So in the year 1598 I saw with my own eyes poor people in Sweden, driven by unbearable hunger, gobble up the clay of ovens and turn the bark of birches into bread. Yet God, in his fatherly mercy, afterwards relieved that hunger, which was worse than famine by lupins.

units.la: De peculiaribus quibusdam panis vsi-bus, saluberrimisq; inuentis ad sani-tatem conseruandam.
units.tr: On certain special uses of bread, and the most healthful inventions for preserving health.

units.la: Quibusdam torreatur in tenuissimas lamina dissectus nouitio medicina inuento, po-P Premoq ftremoq; loco sumitur prasertim ab obesioribus, putant enim corpora obesiora esu huius frequentiori gracilescere, abjumiq; pituitam ventriculo infarctam.
units.tr: Some toast bread, cut into very thin slices. This is a newly discovered remedy and is taken especially by the stouter, for they think that bodies grow slimmer by frequent eating of it, and that it drives out phlegm lodged in the stomach.

units.la: Panem alii tostum vino inungunt, deinde pulueres excinnamomo, nuce mofchata, mace, laudatissimoq; saccharo conspergunt, eoq; tum in secunda tum in aduersa valetudine plerique vtuntur ad cibi auiditatem torpescentem, excitandam atque titillandam, ipsumque ventriculum corroborandum. Compertum quoque vstum panem grauitatem odorum in cubiculis emendare, sicut ✠ oris foetorem, quo nihil est certius, vini item ingratum odorem & saporem in sacculis additum.
units.tr: Others smear toasted bread with wine, then sprinkle it with powders of cinnamon, nutmeg, mace and the most highly prized sugar. Many use this both in good health and in bad, to rouse and tickle a jaded appetite and to strengthen the stomach itself. It has also been found that toasted bread corrects the heaviness of smells in bedrooms, as it does the bad breath of the mouth, which is most certain; likewise the unpleasant smell and taste of wine, when it is added to the bag.

units.la: Elotum panem miris celebrat laudibus medicina, leuiter enim alit, obstructionesq; viscerdibus non creat, quicquid enim in eo antea lentoris atq; crassi ici continebatur, omnino exactum est, leuissimus scilicet ac aerius saltus. Subteris autem in molem in aquam coniectus supernatat, superfluitque, post lotionem si appendatur, mirabere singularem leuitatem.
units.tr: Medicine praises washed bread with wonderful praise: it nourishes lightly and does not produce blockages in the viscera, for whatever sluggishness and thickness it held before has been entirely removed, leaving a very light and airy substance. If it is ground into powder and thrown into water, it floats on top, and after washing, if it is weighed, you will be amazed at its singular lightness.

units.la: Fit praeterea edulium ex pane sanis aegrisque summè expetitum, Panatellam vocant seu panem friatum: friatur enim manibus panis, deinde aliquot horis sinunt aqua madescere calida vel frigida, quae ter quaterue mutatur, exinde oleo. ellis inditur, leni ︎oq igne coquitur ex aqua bury-ro adiecto, alioue pinguiusculo liquor elautius fit autem, si carbonibus decoquatur ex iure gallina-cei pulli aut gallina, sape & diutius cochleari versando, adiecto pulueris cinnamomi, zinzibe-ris modico, laudatissimo facchar o, confert esum cruditatibus stomachi eximmodica crapula con-tractis, iisq; qui a cibo largiori abstinere cupi-unt.
units.tr: Besides, a dish is made from bread that is most sought after by the healthy and the sick alike, which they call panatella, or crumbled bread. The bread is crumbled by hand, then left for some hours to soak in warm or cold water, which is changed three or four times. Then it is put into oil, or into butter or some other slightly fatty substance, and simmered over a gentle fire with broth added, made from a chicken or a hen. The liquor becomes more refined if it is boiled down over coals, often and for a long time stirred with a spoon, with a little powdered cinnamon, ginger and the most highly praised sugar added. It helps against indigestion of the stomach, contracted from excessive gorging, and for those who wish to abstain from a heavier meal.

units.la: Huc pertinet panis distillatus optimum nu-tritium & refectuum, inter extracta nutritiua merito principem obtinens locum, tabidi morbo exhausto conuenientissimum.
units.tr: To this belongs bread distilled, the best nourishment and restorative, deservedly holding the first place among nutritive extracts, most suitable for a wasting disease that has worn a person out.

units.la: De panificiis quae dicuntur pla-centae.
units.tr: On pastries called cakes.

units.la: AD panis categoriam proxime accedunt placentae, Graece τρίμματα & τλακούντες, & bellaria, quorum omnium rationem, numerum & differentias, nominaque conscribere infinitii esset operis.
units.tr: Next to the bread family come cakes, in Greek trimmata [τρίμματα] and tlakountes [τλακούντες], and sweetmeats. To write down the method, number, differences and names of all of these would be an endless task.

units.la: Pro locorum enim & gentium viru vario, proque temporum varia diuersitate & ratione variare ea certum est.
units.tr: For indeed it is certain that they vary according to the various places and peoples, and according to the varied differences and customs of the times.

units.la: Ex farina autem tritici, ouis, lacte, flore eius, melle, saccharo, caseo ac butyro praecipue confici & subigi con- stat.
units.tr: It is agreed that they are mainly made and kneaded from wheat flour, eggs, milk, its flour, honey, sugar, cheese and butter.

units.la: Quae ex lacte, caseo, ouis, butyro, melle, aut saccharo subactis conflantur, totum fere annum in vsu esse possunt. Quaedam aestate fiunt ex fructibus arboreis, cerasis, prunis, malis, pyris, atque id genus aliis: ex fragis item ineunte aestate, vere vero ex grossulis, vuisque passis, quae stomacho non ingratae sunt.
units.tr: Those made by mixing milk, cheese, eggs, butter, honey or sugar can be in use almost the whole year. Some are made in summer from tree fruits: cherries, plums, apples, pears and other such fruits; also from strawberries in early summer, and in spring from gooseberries and raisins, which are not unpleasant to the stomach.

units.la: Hyssopus, thymus, saluia, cinnamomum, rosmarinus, maiorana, piper, huiusmodi quae alia mediocriter admixta acriores eas faciunt & salubriores.
units.tr: Hyssop, thyme, sage, cinnamon, rosemary, marjoram, pepper and such other things, mixed in moderately, make them sharper and more wholesome.

units.la: Erunt itaque placentae vernae, hiemales, autumnales & aestiuae.
units.tr: There will therefore be spring, winter, autumn and summer cakes.

units.la: Vernae ex farina butyro, ouisque, absyn- thio, chelidonia, violis, mentha, hedera terrestri, porro, allio, cepisue admixtis concin- nantur, saluberrimaeque existunt ac probatissimae.
units.tr: Spring cakes are made from flour, butter and eggs, mixed with wormwood, celandine, violets, mint, ground ivy, leek, or onion, and they are most wholesome and most approved.

units.la: Aestate admisceantur, rosae, flores borraginis, buglossae, rosmarini, hyssopus, melissa, nasturtium hortense &c. Autumno anisum, apium, cyminum, foeniculum, rutha, fumaria, centaurium, lingua cerulina, &c.
units.tr: In summer, roses, borage flowers, bugloss, rosemary, hyssop, balm, garden cress and so on are mixed in. In autumn, anise, celery, cumin, fennel, rue, fumitory, centaury, blue bugloss and so on.

units.la: Hiemenasturtium aquaticum, piper, thymus, satureia, saluia, galanga, radix arizinziber, & similia : hæc enim moderatè & mediocriter admixta, palato eas gratiores reddunt minusquè noxias.
units.tr: In winter, water cress, pepper, thyme, savory, sage, galangal, the root of ginger and similar things. For when these are mixed in moderately and in small amounts, they make the cakes more pleasing to the palate and less harmful.

units.la: Quæ ex amygdalis, pistaciis, nucibusque pineis conficiuntur,atrophia laborantibus pthificisquefaluberrimæ sunt,possuntque & melle condiri, quas placentras Græci, credo, μελίπηκτα appellant,apud antiquos enim mel placentis & tragematis fingendis obtinebat primas,hodie sacchari polline nihil feré est, quod non conficiatur vel falrem conspergatur.
units.tr: Those made from almonds, pistachios and pine nuts are very wholesome for those suffering from atrophy and for consumptives, and they can also be seasoned with honey. The Greeks, I think, call these honey-set cakes [μελίπηκτα]; for among the ancients honey held the first place in shaping cakes and sweet cakes, whereas today there is almost nothing that is not made with sugar powder or sprinkled with salt.

units.la: Fiunt quoque pugillares pastilli ex nucleis pineis, & saccharo : ex pistaciis item & amygdalis saccharoque conficiuntur placentulæ, quas vulgus panes martios appellat. Quid? quod similago & saccharum in omnes figuras duci possunt atque trahi.
units.tr: Little lozenges are also made from pine kernels and sugar; little cakes made from pistachios and almonds and sugar, which the common people call Mars' breads. What then? Fine flour and sugar can be drawn and shaped into all sorts of figures.

units.la: Pythagorici non aliud quam panem cum melle Attico prandere soliti sunt, fuitq; placentæ genus, quod ex butyro, femidale & melle conficiebatur, gratum palato obsoni-um,ac salubre.
units.tr: The Pythagoreans used to eat nothing but bread with Attic honey at their lunch. There was also a kind of cake, made from butter, fine flour and honey, a dish pleasing to the palate and wholesome.

units.la: In placentarum quoque albo est panis ille absque fermento dulciarius leu infermenta- tus, quem Hebræi septem diebus in azymo- rum festo edebant: coquebatur autem ex fa- rina tritici, caseo & meliè in clibano sub te- staceo operculo, censeturque inter Græco- rum pemmata. Vnde Galenus libr. 1. de alimen. ait, quæcunque azymorum pemmata in clibano coxerint, exemta statim in mel ca- lidum coiiciunt, vt penitus melle imbuatur, & hæc, inquit, de placentorum genere sunt. Et lib. de alimen. boni & mali succi, ait, omne ex tritico pistorium sine fermento opus pemma dictum, præcipuè addito caseo len- tos crassosque humores generat, succosque crudos.
units.tr: Among the cakes too is that bread without leaven, or unfermented and sweeter, which the Hebrews ate for seven days at the feast of unleavened bread. It was baked from wheat flour, cheese and honey, in an oven under a clay lid, and it is counted among the Greek pemmata [πέμματα]. Hence Galen, book 1 of On Foods, says: whatever pemmata of unleavened bread they have baked in the oven, they immediately take out and throw into warm honey, so that it is thoroughly soaked in honey; and these, he says, belong to the kind of cakes. And in On Foods, of good and bad juice, he says that every baked work made of wheat without leaven, called pemma, especially with cheese added, generates thick and gross humours and raw juices.

units.la: Quare saluberrimus panis est is, qui plu- rimum salis & fermenti participat, cuius ma- za primum manibus bene subacta ac depsita tandem probe in clibano decocta fuerit. At panis infermentatus, quamuis corpus impin- guat, si bene digestus fuerit, quo & athletæ ob id saginabantur, viscidos tamen humo- res generat, aliquamque & viscera obstruit, cum fermentum contra suo feruore maz- zam panis friabilem reddit insumpta e- ius viscositate, illiusque dum turget sta- tus discutit, faciliusque digeritur. Omnes ta- men panes azymi venerem languentem & frigescentem excitant.
units.tr: Therefore the most wholesome bread is that which takes in a great deal of salt and leaven, whose dough is first well kneaded and pressed by hand, and finally thoroughly baked in the oven. Unleavened bread, although it fattens the body if it is well digested (which is why athletes were fattened on it), nevertheless generates sticky humours and also blocks the viscera somewhat; whereas leaven, by its heat, makes the dough of bread crumbly, its stickiness being taken in, and while it swells it breaks up the condition of the dough, and so it is digested more easily. Yet all unleavened breads arouse a sluggish and cold lust.

units.la: Sunt & alia pemmatum apud veteres genera, quæ liba appellarunt, ac ex caseo, farina siliginea aut tritica, quidam addunt crocum lactisque pinguedinem.
units.tr: The ancients also had other kinds of pemmata, which they called liba, made from cheese, fine or wheat flour, and some add saffron and the fat of milk.

units.la: Huius generis est itrion dictum, cuius sæpe mentionem facit Galenus & aliii, componiturque ex sesamo & melle, hodie loco sesami sumunt amygdalas.
units.tr: Of this kind is what is called itrion, which Galen and others often mention. It is made from sesame and honey; nowadays almonds are used in place of sesame.

units.la: Est Tracta, mixtura quædam ex fermento & farina compacta, manibus sæpius in formam longam planamque tracta, unde etiam nomen emanavit. Itali Tiratas à trahendo nominant, si subigitur vuæ passæ succo, melior fit & suavior.
units.tr: There is the tracta, a certain mixture of leaven and flour kneaded together, often drawn by hand into a long, flat shape, whence it also got its name. The Italians call them tiratas from drawing (trahendo); if it is kneaded with the juice of raisins, it becomes better and sweeter.

units.la: Infitiaetiam huc referre licet, sive insicia, quæ fiebant ex variis carnibus tritis pereque commixtis, vel etiam ex piscibus diversis, teste Alexandro Tralliano.
units.tr: Nor may we fail to refer here to the infitia or insicia, which were made from various meats minced and mixed together, or also from different fishes, as Alexander of Tralles testifies.

units.la: Simile huic edulium tetrapharmacum est Adriano Imperat. carum, quod ex phasiano, fumine, perna, & cruštulo compositum fuisse, narrat Spartanus.
units.tr: Similar to this is the dish called tetrapharmacum, which Spartianus reports was made of pheasant, sow's womb, ham and crust, and was a favourite of the emperor Hadrian.

units.la: Qui primò Itria, Tractam, & id genus liba in mensis ponunt, illaudandi sunt: nam certum est eiusmodi panificiorum genera nullo tanda.
units.tr: Those who first put itria, tractae and that kind of liba on the table deserve no praise, for it is certain that such kinds of pastry, not steeped in leaven, are unwholesome.

units.la: P fermento imbuta insalubria esse, quin & coquendi apparandique modo. Videmus plerunque, quod foris est retorridum, intus esse incoctum, ideoque vix conficiuntur, stomacho enim negotium facessunt, crudumque succum ac flatus generant.
units.tr: Bread steeped in leaven is unwholesome, and so is the way it is cooked and prepared. We often see that what is baked hard on the outside is undercooked inside, so it is scarcely digested; it troubles the stomach and generates crude juices and wind.

units.la: Fiunt quoque panificia celebratissima ex medulla tritici aqua vinoque albo diligenter macerata agitataque, deinde ouorum luteis pluribus adiectis, sale modico ac saccharo: ferramenta autem habent peculiaria qui hos panes expetunt, non tam alte, neque tam patenter exsculpta, sed tantum ad fauorum rudimenta, quę oleo aut butyro illinuntur, Germani vocant <bl>Kuchensen/ Eisenkuchen.</bl>
units.tr: The most celebrated pastries are also made from the marrow of wheat, carefully soaked and beaten in water and white wine, then with several egg yolks added, with a little salt and sugar. Those who desire these breads have special moulds for them, not very deep or broad, but only shallow enough to give the rudiments of a honeycomb; these are smeared with oil or butter. The Germans call them <bl>Kuchensen/ Eisenkuchen.</bl>

units.la: Apud quosdam ex similagine, alios ex polline tritici conflantur opera pistoria, butyro, ouis, lacte, melle aut saccharo subigentes, quidam crocum adiiciunt, gustuque sunt suauissima.
units.tr: Among some people they are made from fine flour, among others from wheat meal, by the baker's craft, kneaded with butter, eggs, milk, honey or sugar; some add saffron, and they are most pleasant to the taste.

units.la: Alii similam triticeam adiecto melle aut saccharo subigunt, quibus postea cinnamomum, piper, aliaque id genus confundunt. Quidam anisum, fœniculum & cyminum inspergunt, grati optimique saporis, quibus etiam communis nostep panis siligineus salubriter perspergi potest.
units.tr: Others knead wheat semolina with added honey or sugar, and afterwards mix in cinnamon, pepper and similar spices. Some sprinkle on anise, fennel and cumin, which give a pleasing and excellent flavour; even ordinary rye bread may be wholesomely sprinkled with these.

units.la: Plura panificiorum placentarumq; generȝ exhibent in inclytis vrbibus aulifq; magnatum pistores dulciarii, cupedinarii, libarii, scriblitarii, mira subtilitate & elegantia va- ria panificia concinnantes: hinc ferinam o- pera piftoria incrustatam cernimus, hincin- crustatos gallos, capones, pisces, variasque formas, quarum quaedam triangulae, quae- dam oblongae sunt, quaedam sphæricæ, quae- dam pudenda muliebria repræsentant, quae- dam virilia, adeo degenerârunt mores Chri- stianorum, vt obscœna & pudenda in cibis hodie delectent, sunt enim quos cunnos siccharatos vocant. Sed longum foret in his- ce singulis enumerandis tempori inseruire, p- sertim cum ad gulæ irritamenta pertine- ant luxuriamque, in qua ita Christiani pro- fecerunt, vt eorum culinæ monstrificarum potius epularum, quam necessariorum stru- sturam doceant.
units.tr: In famous cities and at the courts of great lords, bakers of sweetmeats, confectioners, pastry-cooks and makers of wafers prepare many kinds of breads and cakes, arranging various pastries with wonderful skill and elegance. Hence we see game meat encrusted in pastry, hence encrusted cocks, capons and fish, and various shapes, some triangular, some oblong, some round, some representing female private parts, some male; so far have the morals of Christians degenerated that obscene and shameful things now delight them in their food. For there are those who call them sugared cunts. But it would be long to list each of these here, especially since they pertain to incitements of gluttony and luxury, in which Christians have advanced so far that their kitchens teach the construction of monstrous banquets rather than of necessary food.

units.la: Hactenus de placentis.
units.tr: Thus far concerning cakes.

units.la: De Pultibus.
units.tr: On Porridges.

units.la: PVlte non pane longo tempore vixisse Romanos certum & manifestum est, vnde pulti- phagi fuerunt appellati. Ex farina autem aqua vel laëte, melle, caseo, ouisq; vt plurimum concinnantur. Ex diuersis vero fiunt seminibus tritico, hordeo, siligine, milio, oryza, avena, ozymo. Certum est omnes pultes bene probeq; co- stas ac praparatas valenter nutrire, ac firmare corpus: praftant tamen triticea, qui enim saepius ut vtantur, melioris esse habitus deprehenduntur, facilius enim coquuntur & conficiuntur, ingg crudos humores non convertuntur. Ex ocymo avena, milio, oryza confecta pultes putantur cruditates gignere, exiccare atque astringere, quod de improba & non exacta coctione concef- fero: crassiorem enim consistentiam nacta valide laborantibus, ut sunt baioli, agricolae, mesores, fossores, apprime conueniunt, liberaliorem vero victum sectantes ac sedentariam vitam agentes, butyro, lactiq; pinguedine, croco vel saccharo eas reddent lautiores, molliores, ac delicatiores, qua etiam ratione salubriores evadent. Apud quosdam infrequentissimo vsu est pulticula genus, quod concinnatur expane friabili (sine triticeo sit, sine sil gineus, cui tamen ille praefertur) lacte & butyro: lautius evadit, si vino saccharo roq, adiecto cinnamomi modico, praparetur: salubberrimum hoc edulium est stomachoq; vtilissimum, quod ipse sapius comperi, licet mulierum & opus sit & inuentum.
units.tr: It is certain and well attested that the Romans lived for a long time on porridge rather than bread, which is why they were called pultiphagi, porridge-eaters. Porridges are usually made from flour cooked with water or milk, and with honey, cheese, or eggs. They are made from various grains: wheat, barley, rye, millet, rice, oats, and unleavened grain. It is certain that all porridges, when well and properly cooked and prepared, nourish vigorously and strengthen the body. Wheat porridges are nonetheless the best, for those who use them regularly are found to be in better condition: they are cooked and digested more easily, and they do not turn into crude humours. Porridges made from unleavened grain, oats, millet, or rice are thought to produce indigestion, to dry out and constrict, and this arises from poor and imperfect cooking. Thicker in consistency, they are especially suitable for those who labour hard, such as porters, farmers, reapers, and diggers. Those who live a more refined diet and a sedentary life will make them richer, softer, and more delicate with butter, the fat of milk, saffron, or sugar, and in this way they will also become more wholesome. Among some people there is a very rarely used kind of small porridge, made from crumbled bread (whether of wheat or rye, though wheat is preferred), with milk and butter. It becomes richer if it is prepared with wine, sugar, and rose water, with a little cinnamon added. This is a very wholesome food and most useful for the stomach, as I have often found myself; although it is both the work and the invention of women.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De Leguminibus.
units.tr: CAP. VIII. Of Pulses.

units.la: HActenus fuerunt semina Cerealia, & quae ex his conficiuntur, alimenta, sequuntur legumina & legumenta à legendo dicta, quod videl. non secentur, sed vellendo legantur. Horum tractatio jure à frumentis proxima est, quia secundas in vsu cibario tenere videntur, & aliquando vicem panis excoctaimplent, inquemultiplices ci-bariorum vsus à plebeis conuertuntur. Quin etiam magnatum mensas frequenter exornant, praesertim in papatu tempore juniorum. Complura autem leguminum sunt genera, de singulis hic scribere nihil attinet, multo minus de eorundem satione, & vni-uersa cultura, quorundam duntaxat nobis scilicet magis vsitatorum ac familiarium, naturam & mirabiles vires persequemur, vt intelligatur, quae noxia sint, quae innoxia.
units.tr: So far we have treated the cereal seeds and the foods made from them. Next come the pulses, called legumina from legendo (gathering), because they are not cut but plucked by hand. Their preparation is rightly placed next to that of grain, since they seem to hold second place in the diet and often take the place of bread when baked, and since the many uses of food are commonly turned to the common people's fare. Indeed they often adorn the tables of the great, especially in the time of the papacy, among the young. There are many kinds of pulses, and there is no point in writing here about each one, still less about their sowing and general cultivation. We shall only examine the nature and remarkable powers of certain ones that are more common and familiar to us, so that it may be understood which are harmful and which are harmless.

units.la: Vbi in transcursu notandum, legumina incoctilia, coctilibus deteriora semper esse, propterea quod aegre conficiuntur, ac difficulter mutantur. Salubriora evadunt omnia, si inter coquendum sinapis momentu adijciatur, tunc enim resoluta penitus tabescunt, & cocyssime fatiscunt, alias cacochymia ac flatus parere, continuatus eorum vsus doçet. Verum coctura hic diligentissima habenda ratio: nimium enim coquendo & ad lucu-lenta flamam, exorbet atq; exhalat, quicquid nutrimentalis humidi in eis continetur, juftu vero coctionis termini non adepta, retinent quiequicquid flatulentum est & crudum, quod imprimis prosperâ valetudine frui cupientes, sedentariamque vitam agentes observabunt.
units.tr: In passing, it should be noted that pulses that must be boiled are always worse than those that are easily cooked, because they are hard to digest and slow to change. All of them become more wholesome if a little mustard is added during cooking, for then they dissolve completely and fall apart thoroughly; otherwise, long experience shows, they produce cacochymia and wind. Still, cooking must be done with great care. If they are boiled too long, or over a fierce flame, whatever nourishing moisture they contain boils away and evaporates; if they are not cooked to the proper point, they keep whatever is windy and raw. Those who wish above all to enjoy good health and lead a sedentary life will take note of this.

units.la: Ex leguminibus quædam sunt culinaria, quorum maxime vsus in culina est & cibo, quædam medicamentosa, quorum vsus est potissimum in medicina; & ex his quædam medium obtinere locum videntur, ob idq; mixta appellari possunt.
units.tr: Of the pulses, some are culinary, whose main use is in the kitchen and for food; some are medicinal, whose use is chiefly in medicine; and some seem to hold a middle place and so may be called mixed.

units.la: Culinaria legumina sunt faba phaseoli, pisa, lentes.
units.tr: The culinary pulses are beans, kidney beans, peas, and lentils.

units.la: Medicinalia, semen lini, cannabis, cymini, sesami, fœnugræci, papaueris, orobus, lupinus, cicer: hæc licet olim fuerint inter alimenta numerata, hodie tamen in medicamentorum magis habentur censu.
units.tr: The medicinal ones are linseed, hemp, cumin, sesame, fenugreek, poppy, vetch, lupin, and chickpea. Although these were once counted among foods, today they are rather regarded as medicines.

units.la: De Fabis.
units.tr: On Beans.

units.la: Neque tam leguminum sagaciter disquirere vitæ plurimum interest. De Fabis sciendum, maximam semper eorum fuisse auctoritatem inter legumina, quippe ex iis tentatus panis apud quosdam populos. Dicta faba q. phaga, ἀπὸ τῆς φαγεῖν a comedendo, quod primum hoc legumine homines sint usi. Diversæ autem de fabis inueniuntur eruditorum opiniones. Pythagoras omnino ab illorum esu abstinuisse, eumque vetasse multorum monumentis traditraditur, tum quod mentem eoperturbari, sensus obtundi, somnoq; sopitu tumultuosa somnia excitari existimarent, tum quod comestæ mulieres infœcundas redderent. Aristoxenus apud Gell. l. 4. c. 11. hanc opinionem refellit, affirmans nullo legumine sæpius vsum Pythagoras quam fabis, quod is cibus & alnum sensim subduceret & levigaret. Galen. quoq; meminit fabas, si belle nutriunt, & flatulenta sunt, fœcunditatem potius, quam sterilitatem inducere debere. In tanta opinionum diuersitate attendendum, quid vero sit simile. Theophrastus l. 5. de causis plantarum c. 21. scribit, fabarum putaminia radicibus aut germinibus plantarum novellarum appositæ earum vitam penitus tollere, quæ etiam sententia à Clemente Alexandrino & Apollonio in mirabilibus histor. citata invenitur, qui addunt, domesticas gallinas iisdem putaminibus iugiter vescentes sterilescere. Quæ sita se habent, facile à fabarum esu frequentiore aliquem deterrere debent. Alii quocunq; etiam modo ac ratione paratam, atq; conditam fabam noxiam proclamant, eo quod vim generandi flatus coctura non amittat, quod equidem miror, cum nihil sit tam noxium, quod coquendi arte ac vi ignis non efficiatur innoxium, quin & venenati serpentes ac vipera arte coquendi artificio, condiendi innoxie in cibos vsurpari posse, præter experimentum testantur leprosi, qui propotu bibunt vinum, in quo vipera viva sit exextincta, iubentur que earum carnem abscissa pte & cauda ad putrilaginem coctam cum iure conuenienti edere, insuculum q; sorbere. Quid? quod gentibus quibusdam peculiare est vesci serpentibus, quod Nomadas Scythas q; facere a- pud Scriptores i eperio, est enim illorum regio serpentum fertilissima. Gentem Æthio- pum, cuius regio a Meroe ad fluvium Hyda- spin porrigitur, scorpionibus & aspidibus vesci, literis proditum est. Sed forsan illis minus venenati sunt, vel etiam veneni omnino expertes, ut in quibusdam locis scorpiones. Certum est in nostris regionibus virus mortiferum terrestres omnes continere, mitiores vero esse colubros & aquaticos, qui anguillis cognati sunt. Verum si quis forsan vel voluptatis gratia vesani luxus palatij gloria proletatus iis delectaretur, aut ex contagiosa ac maligna scabiei metu vesci iisdem cogeretur, in sequentem cotionis modum obser-vabit, quem a quibusdam, sponsione ac stipulatione certa pecunia se provocantibus, orta videl. inter ipsos quæstione an coctura venenum expel-latur, ipse adhibitum vidi. Coquatur serpens, vel vipera aqua fontana, abiiciatur ius ex coctione reliquum, verissimum enim est, maximam veneni partem in illud deponi: affundatur aqua pura recens, secundo fiat decoctio, iterum q; vt prius, ius abiicien-dum, coquatur tertio vino & aqua, vel si mauis, vino tantum, aromatis q; convenientibus, vt cinnaélænamomo, corticibus arantiarum vel citri, ga-ryophyllis, piperibus & similibus ius condiatur -esui referuandum. Ferinum multis videbitur vesci serpentibus, cochleis, ranis, testudinibus, asininum vero carduis: at in vniuersa fere Italia & Gallia inter praecipuas mensarum delitias reponuntur. In longis obsidionibus vrbium canes ac feles, mures ac glires, gratum palato obsonium extitisse testantur, hoc sunt. Qui a patria solo nunquam discesserunt, non sine fastidio ac admiratione etiam, haec legent, tanquam veritatis fidem excedentia.
units.tr: It is not of great importance to inquire with too much subtlety into the pulses. Concerning beans, it should be known that they have always held the greatest authority among pulses, since among some peoples bread was made from them. The bean is called faba, from [ἀπὸ τῆς φαγεῖν] "from eating," because men first used this pulse for food. Learned men hold differing opinions about beans. It is handed down in the records of many that Pythagoras abstained altogether from eating them and forbade others to do so, both because they thought beans disturbed the mind, dulled the senses, and, when one was asleep, stirred up troubled dreams, and because women who ate them became barren. Aristoxenus, quoted in Gellius, book 4, chapter 11, refutes this opinion, affirming that Pythagoras used no pulse more often than beans, since they gradually thin and smooth the blood. Galen also mentions that beans, if they nourish well and are windy, ought rather to produce fertility than sterility. Given such great diversity of opinion, we must consider what is most likely. Theophrastus, book 5 of On the Causes of Plants, chapter 21, writes that bean husks placed against the roots or shoots of young plants completely destroy their life. This opinion is also found cited by Clement of Alexandria and by Apollonius in his Marvellous Histories, who add that domestic hens which constantly eat those same husks become barren. Since matters stand so, they ought to deter anyone from eating beans too frequently. Others declare that beans are harmful however they are prepared and seasoned, because cooking does not remove their power to produce wind. I am surprised at this, since there is nothing so harmful that it cannot be made harmless by the art of cooking and the power of fire. Indeed, even poisonous snakes and vipers, by the skill of cooking and seasoning, can be safely used as food; lepers testify to this from experience, for they drink wine in which a live viper has been drowned, and they are ordered to eat the flesh of these creatures, with the head and tail removed, boiled down to a pulp with a suitable broth, and to sip the liquor. What of the fact that some peoples make a point of eating snakes? I find in writers that the Scythian Nomads do this, for their region is very rich in serpents. It is recorded in writing that the Ethiopian people, whose land stretches from Meroe to the river Hydaspes, feed on scorpions and asps. Perhaps these are less poisonous for them, or even quite without poison, as scorpions are in some places. It is certain that in our regions all land creatures contain deadly venom, while the water snakes, which are related to eels, are milder. But if anyone, perhaps for pleasure, or from the vain glory of a lavish palate, takes delight in these, or is compelled to eat them out of fear of a contagious and malignant itch, he shall observe the following method of cooking. I myself have seen it used by some who challenged one another, under a wager and a stipulated sum of money, over whether cooking drives out the poison. Let the snake or viper be boiled in spring water, and let the broth from this first boiling be thrown away, for it is very true that the greater part of the poison settles into it. Then pour on fresh clean water and boil a second time; again, as before, throw away the broth. Boil a third time in wine and water, or, if you prefer, in wine alone, with suitable spices such as cinnamon, the peel of oranges or citron, cloves, pepper, and the like, and season the broth and keep it for eating. [8a] (continued) It will seem a wild thing to many to eat snakes, snails, frogs, and tortoises, but to eat thistles is for asses. Yet throughout almost all of Italy and France these are placed among the chief delicacies of the table. During long sieges of cities, it is reported that dogs and cats, mice and dormice, became a welcome dish for the palate. Those who have never left their native soil will read these things with disgust and wonder, as if they went beyond the bounds of truth.

units.la: Ego lectorem relego ad autores, qui de his dubiis regati certi aliquid affirmabunt, inter quos Athenaeum & Plinium studiosiores ac copiosiores reperiet. Sed adrem. Si igitur noxia & venenata cultura & conditura reddunt-ur innoxia, esuiq; apta, quid quasi prohibebit, quominus & fabis per coctionem visgenerandi flatus, ventremq; diffendendi adimatur? Vt- rides tamen & recentes magis commendantur in re esculenta, auidissime enim a gula proceri-bus quibusdam in regionibus, praesertim Gallia & Italia, expetuntur. Siccata relinquuntur ope-rariis.
units.tr: I refer the reader to the authors who make certain assertions about these doubtful matters; among them he will find Athenaeus and Pliny more studious and fuller. But to the point. If harmful and poisonous things are made harmless by cooking and seasoning and so become fit for eating, what would prevent beans from losing, by cooking, their power to produce wind and distend the belly? Yet fresh beans are more highly recommended as a food, for in certain regions, especially France and Italy, they are eagerly sought by the greedy among the great. Dried beans are left to the labourers.

units.la: Parantur autem ex iis iusculā: quandoq; in sartagine, ex lardo, butyro, aut oleo, adiectā Saturea, apio, thymo, anethi vel cymini semine friguntur, prius tamen decorticata.
units.tr: Soups are made from them: sometimes they are fried in a pan with lard, butter, or oil, with savory, celery, thyme, dill, or cumin seed added; but first they are shelled.

units.la: Viridia Virides post carnes loco bellariorum olim efita-tas fuisse. Athenæum & Mercurialis l.4. variarum lect. docent: affumebantur quoq; parentum-do. In quibusdam Galliæ & Italiæ locis mola parum prius franguntur, deinde delibrantur ac percoquuntur, inq; album quoddam crassamentum formantur ac rediguntur, quod per vrbis compita, dieb. quadragesima venale prostat, idq; postea in patinis ex butyro aut oleo lento igne paratur ad esum, nonq; ingratum est e-dulium, plebi, quæ familiariter eo vtitur. Ut vt sit, studiosi literarum ab immodico fabarum esu abstinebunt, præsertim vero pueri, qui gravem inde ingeniorum patiuntur ialluram, in otio quoq; degentes, ac ventriculi imbecillitate laborantes ab illarum esu se continent, inflatu enim agreq; conficiuntur, cuius rei argumentum est, quod frequentius colico dolore, ructibus crepitibusq; confliguntur, qui Pythagoræ præceptis non obtemperant.
units.tr: Green beans were once eagerly eaten after meat in place of sweetmeats, as Athenaeus and Mercurialis, in book 4 of Various Readings, teach; they were also taken with bread. In some places in France and Italy they are first lightly crushed in a mill, then steeped and cooked thoroughly, and made into a kind of white paste, which is sold at street corners during Lent; afterwards it is prepared in pans with butter or oil over a gentle fire for eating. It is not an unpleasant dish, and the common people, who use it as an everyday food, enjoy it. However that may be, students of letters will abstain from excessive eating of beans, especially boys, who suffer serious loss of their mental powers from them. Those who lead an idle life and are weak in the stomach should also keep away from them, for they are troubled by wind and sickness; a sign of this is that those who do not follow Pythagoras's precepts are more often afflicted with colic pains, belching, and farting.

units.la: Hinc trita illa & celebrata de faba proverbia, à fabis abstineto: fabas ne comedas: faba alba, hac enim antiquitas in fortibus vsa est, cui enim contigisset ei permittebatur in conuivio & ocio agere aliis laborantibus: faba numinmus, fabis enim olim ferebantur suffragia, ac denotantur proverbio corrupta suffragia: Sic fabarum arrosor dicebatur, qui in creandis magistratibus vendebat sua suffragia accepta pecunia, quod certe & hodie fieri atq; vsu venire vividemus in proceribus & orbis monarchis creandis: fabilibus denique vitiitare diceba-tur de homine nimis sordido, qui qui-busvis cibis vilissimis etiam fabarum furfuri-bus & repurgamentis pra nimia parsimonia ve-scitur. Hactenus de fabis, quarum maxi-mam fuisse inter legumina olim autoritatem, expraditis facile est coniicere: vnum hic no-tandum venit quod, quae de vulgaribus nostris fabis hic sunt assignata, eadem quoq; de phaseo-lis seu fabis Italicis, quarum species quoq; est Smilax hortensis, sint intelligenda: faba vero Aegyptia nostras longe amplitudine superat, humidioriq; est temperatura, radixq; eius lau-te ab incolis cruda atq; decoctu adhibetur.
units.tr: Hence the well-worn and famous proverbs about beans: "Abstain from beans"; "Do not eat beans"; "A white bean," for in ancient times the bean was used in voting: whoever had been given a white bean was allowed to live at ease at banquets and leisure while others laboured. "A bean-coin": for beans were once used to cast votes, and by a proverb corrupted votes are so named. So a "bean-gnawer" was said of a man who sold his vote for money when creating magistrates, which we see done and practised even today in the choosing of great men and monarchs of the world. Finally, one was said to be "bean-bran" of a man too mean, who, out of excessive thrift, eats the cheapest foods, even the bran and sweepings of beans. So far concerning beans, whose great authority among pulses in former times may easily be gathered from what has been said. One thing must be noted here: what has been said about our common beans applies equally to kidney beans, or Italian beans, of which the Smilax hortensis is also a kind. The Egyptian bean, however, far surpasses ours in size; its nature is moister, and its root is eaten by the inhabitants, raw or boiled.

units.la: De phaseolis in specie notetur, quod secun-dum Galenum, Aetium & Paulum, medium inter alimenta boni maliq; succi obtineant lo-cum, & inter ea quae exiguum corpori praebent, nutrimentum, & quae plurimum, inter ea, quae flatus gignunt, & quae non gignunt, & inter ea, quae facile & difficulter concoquuntur. Colu-mella vero Phaseolum inter legumina maxime grata & in vsu cibario posuit, quod nostri coqui testantur, quibus nunc familiares esse coeperunt, miris modis phaseolum coquentes in iure galli-naceo: In cibis crebrius vsurpati melancoliam augent, atrum reddentes sanguinem, unde Ga-lenus exacte siccatos atq; repositos tutioris esse vs-us tradidit, & vt pisa vsurpari possit.
units.tr: Concerning the kidney bean in particular, it should be noted that, according to Galen, Aëtius and Paul, it holds a middle place between foods of good and of bad juice, and among those that give the body little nourishment and those that give much; among those that generate wind and those that do not; and among those that are digested easily and those that are digested with difficulty. Columella, however, placed the phaseolus among the pulses most pleasing and useful as food, as our cooks bear witness, who have now begun to be familiar with it, preparing the phaseolus in wonderful ways in chicken broth. Eaten too often, it increases melancholy, making the blood black; hence Galen related that it is safer to use when carefully dried and stored, and that it may be used like peas.

units.la: Q InInnocentiores quoq; in cibis reddunt' ur, si cum sinapi aut cari femine edantur, adiecto piperis momento. Semen deniq; generare, venerem, stimulare, praesertim si ex latte bubalo conquantur experimentum est. Quidam, ut leguminum omnium noxas vitent, cepas simul decoquunt, & quidem prudentissime, licet alii aliter sentiant, concalfaciunt enim, pariter, atttenuant, discutiunt simul ac dissipant, quod adest flatulentum, idq; a coquis & culinis vellem diligenter observari, escarum enim notare noxas cauti & prudentis est.
units.tr: Even the milder kinds are made harmful when eaten with mustard or caraway seed, with a pinch of pepper added. Finally, it is an established experience that it generates seed and stirs up lust, especially if it is cooked in buffalo milk. Some, to avoid all the harms of pulses, cook onions along with them, and indeed most wisely, though others think otherwise: for onions warm, thin, break up and dissipate together, and so disperse what is windy in the pulse. I would wish this to be carefully observed by cooks and kitchen-workers, for it is the mark of a cautious and prudent person to note the harms of foods.

units.la: Hactenus de Phaseolis.
units.tr: So far concerning kidney beans.

units.la: De Pisis.
units.tr: On Peas.

units.la: INter omnia leguminum genera nostra memoria vix vllum pisis praestantius reperitur atque vsitatius: lautissimas enim mensas ea subire, magnatesque gratissime mandere videmus: quin & nobile foeminarum genus auidissime iis praesertim suilla incoctis vescitur ac delectatur, ex lautissima etiam ac magnifica variarum epularum strue ambabus quasi manibus ea praeripiens.
units.tr: Among all kinds of pulse, I scarcely find any in our time more excellent or more commonly used than peas. We see them served at the most lavish tables and eaten with great pleasure by magnates. Indeed the noble sex too eagerly eats and enjoys them, especially when cooked with pork, snatching them up with both hands from the rich and splendid array of various dishes.

units.la: Apud veteres quoq; in gratia fuisse dubium non est, quippe de iis ab antiquis & medicis & rei rusticae scriptoribus traditum est. Hodie fabis longe praeferuntur. Satiandi enim alendi, nutriendique vi praepollent,
units.tr: There is no doubt that they were also held in favour among the ancients, since physicians and writers on agriculture from antiquity have handed down accounts of them. Today they are generally preferred to beans, for they excel in their power to satisfy, nourish and sustain.

units.la: Pisa fabis longe praestant. lent, nec perinde ac fabæ flatus gignunt, quod præter experientiam ipse Galenus pi-stribuit, licet Hippocrates lib.2.de rat.vict. in morbis acut. fabam minus inflate afferat, quod tamen contra experientiam dictum videtur. Ratio Hippocratis videtur esse hæc, quod nimirum fabæ facilius descendant & celerius, ob substantiam earum gravem & densam, unde concludit, ob celerem illum descensum minus inflare. Galenus contra censet pisa minus inflare, seriusque peraluum excerni, ventremque permeare quam fabas, ob leuem & fungosam illorum substantiam, quàfit vt pigre descendant, meliusque nutriant quam ipsæ fabæ. Hæc Galeni sententia confirmatur sequente syllogismo.
units.tr: Peas are far superior to beans. They do not produce wind in the same way as beans do, a point which Galen himself observed from experience, although Hippocrates, in book 2 of On Diet in Acute Diseases, says that beans cause less inflation. This, however, seems to be said contrary to experience. Hippocrates' reasoning appears to be this: beans pass down more easily and quickly because of their heavy and dense substance, and from that rapid descent he concludes that they inflate less. Galen, on the other hand, holds that peas inflate less and are evacuated more slowly and pass through the belly more slowly than beans, because of their light and spongy substance; so they descend sluggishly and nourish better than beans themselves. This opinion of Galen is confirmed by the following syllogism.

units.la: Quod celeriter per ventrem & intestina dilabitur, id minus nutrit, requiritur enim diuturnior cibi commoratio in intestinis, ne facilis transitus causam præbeat voracitati, vénisq; mesaraicis necessarius succus inter-cipiatur: fabæ celerius per ventrem descendunt ob grauitatem & densitatem, Ergo minus nutriunt, & qua vix aut raro & fere nunq; viqita sunt expeditæ & lubricæ, & ab infastib. liberę, vt cib. cum impetu possit dilabi & permeare, cosequés est, fabas, cu transitu phibetur, plusq; iusto detinetur crassorum humorum colluvie pcreare flatuumq; copia maiorem. rem, quam vel vnquam vlla pila, quae ob substantiam raram & leuem, viis etiam impeditis & obstructis, penetrando possunt permeare. An vero quod celeriter descendit, inque intestinis non diu commoratur, possit in transitu flatus excitare ac procreare, quaesitum est vtile ac difcuffu dignum, cum potius contrarium quis verum dixerit, videlicet ex diuturniore cibi in ventre mora flatus excitari.
units.tr: What passes quickly through the belly and intestines nourishes less, for the food needs a longer stay in the intestines, lest easy passage give occasion to gluttony, and so that the nourishing juice may be taken up by the mesenteric veins. Beans pass down the belly more quickly because of their heaviness and density; therefore they nourish less. Peas, which are seldom or never so clear, slippery and free from obstructions that food can rush through and pass with force, are on the contrary light and spongy, so that they can pass through even blocked and obstructed passages by penetrating. It follows that beans, when their passage is hindered and they are detained longer than is right by a mass of thick humours, produce a greater quantity of wind than any peas ever do. Whether what descends quickly and does not linger in the intestines can excite and produce wind in its passage is a question that is useful and worth examining, since one might rather maintain the opposite, namely that wind is excited by the longer stay of food in the belly.

units.la: Hanc quaestionem enodandi occasionem dabit tractatus de potu & inprimis cereuisia. Vide cap. de potulentis. Porro omnia juscula & brodia ex pisis commendantur: multipliciter vero & varijs modis a coquis praeparantur.
units.tr: This question will give occasion for treating of drink, and especially of beer. See the chapter on drinks. Moreover, all broths and soups made from peas are commended, and cooks prepare them in many ways and by various methods.

units.la: Spina suis sale condita pisis decocta suauis est: grata etiam palato est Lucanica cum lardo, gratissimum si pani in frusta reuiter dilecto, butyroque torrefacto, jusculum pisorum affundatur, vtque salubrius eaadat lautiusque, crocus sufficiente quantitate cum cymini vel cari femine & similibus, adiiciendus est, habetque insignem corroborandi ac nutriendi vim, ex grato odore, sapore, & colore, odorem conciliat crocus sicut & colorem, saporem panis butyro tostus & cyminum, quod etiam flatuum discutiendorum gratia adjectum est. Viridia cum siliginis cocta maximam in mensis & aulis ma-
units.tr: Pig's spine seasoned with salt and boiled with peas is pleasant, and Lucanica sausage with lard is agreeable to the palate. Most pleasing of all is when pea broth is poured over bread cut into pieces and toasted in butter. To make it more wholesome and elegant, saffron in sufficient quantity is added, together with cumin or caraway seed and the like. It has a notable power to strengthen and nourish. The saffron gives a pleasing smell and colour, and the buttered toast and cumin give flavour; the cumin is also added to disperse wind. Green peas cooked with rye hold the highest authority at the tables and courts of magnates.

units.la: Laupi-forum. Pisorum brodium saluber-rimum. Viridia celebrantur. magnatum ohtinent autoritatem: defidera-tiffima funt,fi cum pullaftris coquantur, aut plateffis. Id veroin infantia fieri oportet, nam vbi jam adoleuerint,duriora euadunt & ingratiora. Gratiffimi deniq; faporis ac odo-ris funt, falubritatiq; maxime conducunt,fi cum radice petrofelini,mace,rofmarino,thy-mo,aut faluia coquantur : thecis autefuis & valuulis fint fpoliata fic enim multipliciter præparari & condiri poffunt.Ridendi igitur potius funt quam refutandi, qui pifaconco-ctu difficilia effe fcribunt,craflumq; fuccum parere , eumq; flatulentum contendunt,de adultis & durioribus, rutilis ac rubentibus, eximiæq; amplitudinis, inq; plenum perco-ctis id verum effe fcitur ratione & experi- entia, in plenum enim percocta &ad perfe-ctum maturitatis terminum perducta,admi-niculis item vel palis non fulta deteriora ea euadere minufque durare conflat, eo quod hac ratione foli terræq; humorem attrahant imbibantq;. A gurgulionibus (à quibus ina* xime infeftantur) arrofa cibis abdicanda funt,licet fationi fic corrofa idonea effe agri-colationis periti affirmant, quod mirum eft.
units.tr: Pea broth is most wholesome. Green peas are highly esteemed. They are most desirable if cooked with young chickens or pullets, or with capons. This must be done in their infancy, for once they have grown up they become harder and less pleasant. Finally, they are most pleasing in taste and smell, and most conducive to health, if cooked with parsley root, mace, rosemary, thyme or sage, with the pods and shells removed, for in this way they can be prepared and seasoned in many ways. Therefore those who write that peas are difficult to digest and yield thick, flatulent juice are to be laughed at rather than refuted. They speak of mature and harder peas, reddish and ruddy, of exceptional size; and it is known by reason and experience that this holds true of peas that are fully cooked. For peas fully cooked and brought to the perfect term of ripeness, not supported by props or stakes, are known to turn out worse and to last less, because in this way they draw in and soak up moisture from the soil. Peas gnawed by weevils (which attack them most), must be rejected as food, although skilled farmers affirm that peas so corroded are fit for sowing, which is strange.

units.la: Quodigitur Auicenna lib. 2. capite de eo quod comeditur ac bibitur,nulla legumi-na, quatenuscibi rationem fubeunt, fanis conducere fcribit,& Galenus lib.4. de vi&ta morb.acut.legumina vniuersa,ceu suam sin-gula malignitatem habentia,à consortio bo-norum ciborum sejungit, nonabsolute & τῶς sed, κατὰ τὶ accipiendum est, de adul-tioribus enim & durioribus, crudeque in-gestis ac comestis eos locutos esse mani-festum est, cum omnibus fructibus & legu-minibus, quæ cruda viridiaque comedun-tur, hoc commune sit, vt alimentum præ-stent humidius,superfluitatibusq; abundans, vnde cruditates & flatus generari necesse est. Manifesto exemplo sunt faba ipsa & pisa cruda & viridia commesta, persica quoque, pruna, pepones, cucumeres, de quibus sin-gulis vide suo loco.
units.tr: Therefore, when Avicenna, in book 2, in the chapter on what is eaten and drunk, writes that no legumes, insofar as they take the place of food, are good for the healthy, and when Galen, in book 4 of On Diet in Acute Diseases, separates all legumes from the company of good foods, as each having its own malignity, this must be understood not absolutely but in a certain respect. For it is clear that they spoke of older and harder legumes, eaten raw and crude. For it is common to all fruits and legumes that are eaten raw and green that they provide a moister nourishment, abundant in superfluities, whence crudities and wind must necessarily be generated. Clear examples are beans, peas, peaches, plums, melons and cucumbers when eaten raw and green, each of which should be considered in its own place.

units.la: De Lentibus.
units.tr: On Lentils.

units.la: LEntes philosophis olim in cibo maxime placuisse,& apud Græcos magno in pretio fuisse, passim ex antiquis literarum mo-nimentis constat. Apud Atheneum Zenonem lentes coxisse inuenitur, vnde stoicorum dogma erat, (teste Atheneo l. 4) Sapientem omnia rectè agere,& lentem diligenter condire, persuasum enim sibi habebant vescentibus iis æquanimita-tem sieri, quam opinionem, nec probo, nec im-probo, natura enim huius leguminis sagacius in-quisita veritatem autoritati præferet.
units.tr: That lentils once greatly pleased the philosophers as food, and were highly valued among the Greeks, is clear from many ancient literary records. Athenaeus reports that Zeno was found to have cooked lentils, whence it was a dogma of the Stoics (as Athenaeus says in book 4) that the wise man does everything rightly and seasons a lentil dish carefully, for they were persuaded that equanimity came to those who ate them. I neither approve nor disapprove of this opinion, for a more careful investigation of the nature of this pulse will set truth above authority.

units.la: Est autem lens leguminum omnium fere minimum, sed fertilissimum, teste Theophrasto
units.tr: Indeed the lentil is almost the smallest of all pulses, but the most fertile, according to Theophrastus.

units.la: lib.9.cap.3. Coctu pertinax est, ac inuenias, quae non mollescant, nisi aqua coelesti cocta, cuius rei rationem reddit Theophrastus libr.9.c.9. affirmans fabam & lentem maxime coctu difficiles, idque fieri coeli conditione, quae in his duobus leguminibus maiorem mutationem pariat. Hac etenim Theophrastus. Unde etiam rarius apud nos in mensas magnatum veniunt, frequentiori enim earum esu atram bilem, & ex hac peruicaciores morbos, ut Cancrum, Lepram, Scorbutum, generari existimatur, crassa enim & arida alimenta humori atrabiliario procreando sunt aptissima: oculorum quoque acie alimenta natura siccis b betare, humentioribus vero vitam tueri compertum habetur, unde utilissima putantur iis, qui cachexia conflictantur, inutiles vero arido aequalore laborantib. Aqua Lentium cocta, ius culumque illud sale aut gaco conditum, contrahaustumque aluum haud dubie soluet, gratiores concoctuque faciliores euadent, si pulegium, thymum vel satureiam adiecerit. Bisco cta & terobsec percocta si comedantur aluum sistunt, ventriculum egregie corroborant aceto perfuso. Optimae sunt quae facillime coquuntur, maximeque aequae sorbent: cum carnibus suillis sale conditis cocta stomacho gratiores sunt, licet crassos humores augeant: peculiare enim salsis carnibus est sanguinem melancholicum gignere, praesertim in autumno, hieme enim eduntur tutius. Optima nasci circa oppidum Pelusium, unde les Pelusiaca diuina. dicta videtur, Inq; Ægypto maximeq; Alexandria peculiarem eius fuisse vsum certissimi autores tradunt, unde non mirandum si elephantiasis morbus in Ægypto fuerit vulgatissimus.
units.tr: Book 9, chapter 3. It is stubborn in cooking: you will find some that do not soften unless they are boiled in rainwater. Theophrastus gives the reason in book 9, chapter 9, asserting that beans and lentils are especially hard to cook, and that this comes from the condition of the sky, which brings about a greater change in these two pulses. So far Theophrastus. For this reason they are also rarer on the tables of great men among us, since by frequent eating of them black bile is thought to be generated, and from this more obstinate diseases such as cancer, leprosy and scurvy; for thick and dry foods are most apt to produce melancholic humour. It is also known that by nature dry foods sharpen the keenness of the eyes, while moister foods preserve life; so they are thought most useful to those suffering from cachexia, but unsuitable for those troubled by dry intemperance. Lentils boiled in water, with the broth seasoned with salt or garum, will undoubtedly loosen a constipated bowel; they become more pleasant and easier to digest if pennyroyal, thyme or savory is added. Lentils boiled twice and cooked thoroughly, if eaten, check the bowels, and when drenched in vinegar they strongly strengthen the stomach. The best are those that cook most easily and are most readily sipped. Cooked with salted pork they are more agreeable to the stomach, although they increase thick humours, for it is peculiar to salted meats to generate melancholic blood, especially in autumn; in winter they are eaten more safely. The best grow near the town of Pelusium, whence the lentil seems to have been called "Pelusiac" and "divine." Certain reliable authors record that its use was especially common in Egypt, and above all in Alexandria, so it is no wonder that elephantiasis was most widespread in Egypt.

units.la: Heraclidi Tarentino edulium ex beta & lentibus dicebatur πυτλοφάκη, quem citrum bene, tum male valentibus exhibebat, constatq; expugnantibus naturis, beta enim minus, lens autem magis subducitur, unde & alimentum, quod ex his in corpus distribuitur, vtriusq; naturam referre necesse est. Panis denique ex lentibus rarissime aut nunquam confectus inuenitur.
units.tr: For Heraclides of Tarentum a dish of beet and lentils was called pytlophake [πυτλοφάκη], which he gave both to those in good health and to the sick; and it is agreed that it suits even strong constitutions, for beet is digested less and lentil more, so the nourishment distributed from these into the body must partake of the nature of both. Finally, bread made from lentils is found very rarely or never.

units.la: Hactenus fuerunt culinaria legumina, sequuntur medicinalia: (De vicia enim, eruo, & similibus hic multum differre, opera pretium non est, cum inter pecudum pabula magis enumerentur, quam alimenta hominum, ac non nisi annona aestuante & fame vrgente meliorumq; penuria in hominum cibatum admittantur) qua Medicorum schola & pharmacopolis committimus, in humaniorum enim & nitidioris vita hominum mensis, nullum hactenus obtinuisse locum certum est, quare abdicanda sunt.
units.tr: So far these have been the culinary pulses; what follows are the medicinal ones. (For vetches, bitter vetch and similar plants it is not worth the labour to say much here, since they are counted among cattle fodder rather than human food, and are admitted into people's diet only when grain is scarce and hunger presses and better things are lacking.) These we commit to the school of physicians and apothecaries, for it is certain that they have never held a fixed place on the tables of more refined and civilised living; therefore they must be renounced.

units.la: Lupinos protogeni piçori comedendos relinquimus. Cicer seu pisum rubeum raro opipaѓas mensas subit, in medicina autem & lupinum, & cicer praclaros habere vsus compertum est. Semine (cannabino antiquitatem olim vice bel-lariorum & tragematum vsam constat, quas tamen delitias nostrum seculum penitus ignorat, nisi in annona difficultatibus, vt in retrodi-ctis pramonitum est, vti eo cogamur. Idem iudicium esto de femine lini, fœnugraci, &c.
units.tr: We leave lupins to be eaten by the painter Protogenes. Chickpea, or red pea, rarely enters elegant tables, but both lupin and chickpea are known to have notable uses in medicine. Hemp seed, as is established, was once used in place of biscuits and sweetmeats, which our age entirely ignores, unless, in the difficulties of grain supply, as was warned above, we are forced to use it. The same judgement is to be made about flaxseed, fenugreek, and so on.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAP. IX.

units.la: De alimentis, quæ sumuntur ex radicibus.
units.tr: On foods that are taken from roots.

units.la: Hucusq; de leguminibus, sequuntur radices.
units.tr: Thus far on pulses; now follow the roots.

units.la: MAxime iucundas ac vitæ mortalium salutares cibos ex hortis peti, nemini non est notum : ideoque vbique terrarum hortorum cultus nostra ætate celeberrimus habetur, quin & apud antiquos auctore Plinio, in magno honore fuerunt horti, damnabat enim antiqua frugalitas pulmentaria, quæ egerent alio pulmentario. Hodiè Magnates & Principes quidam herbis cognoscendis non modò impensè dant operâ, verum etiam nullis sumtibus parcunt, nullisq; impensis, quò horti variarum arborum plantarumque famâ percelebres extruantur.
units.tr: That the most pleasant foods, and those most healthful to human life, are sought from gardens is known to everyone. So the cultivation of gardens is held in the highest esteem in our age everywhere in the world. Indeed, even among the ancients, according to Pliny, gardens were held in great honour, for ancient frugality condemned those side dishes that needed another side dish to go with them. Today certain magnates and princes not only devote great effort to learning about herbs, but also spare no expense or outlay, so that gardens famous for their varieties of trees and plants may be built.

units.la: Ex radicibus præcipuam laudem obtinet, rapa, napus, pastinaca, petroselinum, raphanus maior & minor,caepa,allium,por-rum.
units.tr: Among the roots, turnip, rape, parsnip, parsley, the greater and lesser radish, onion, garlic and leek obtain the chief praise.

units.la: De rapis.
units.tr: On turnips.

units.la: INter Romanos Plinius rapis tantam tribuit autoritatem,vt à frumento protinus, aut certè faba de iis dixisse (inquit) conueniat. Et certè gentium multarum opes sunt, inque cibis commendantur plurimis modis, omnibus animalibus non in nouissimis:quapropter pluribus commoditates raporum hic commemorare operae pretium esse non puto,vt quae vulgò notissimae sint. Crescunt autem quibusdam in locis amplitudine mirabili, Plinius lib.13.cap 18. fe vidisse testatur 40. libras excedentia, id quod credibile est, cum & apud nos ingentis amplitudinis inueniantur. Quaedam inlatitudinem finguntur, & amplitudinem rotunditatemque maximâ glomerantur, idque rariore satu, densiore enim mafculefcunt,hoc est,in oblongam excrescunt figuram. Cum laete cocta palato gratissima sunt,ac bene nutriunt satiantque. Cum veruecina percocta nutriunt, multisq; gentibus desideratissimus cibus sunt, magnatum etiam mensas exornans. Venerem languentem stimulant,visumque clarificant : brodium & iusculum eorum modice crocacrocatum tussi eximie conferre experimento didici. Flatus generare eofdemque vicissim expellere constat.
units.tr: Among the Romans, Pliny gave turnips such authority that he said it is fitting to speak of them straight after grain, or at least after beans. And indeed many peoples have their wealth in them, and they are commended in foods in many ways, and not least for all animals. Therefore I do not think it worth the effort to recount here at length the advantages of turnips, since they are generally very well known. They grow in some places to a wonderful size: Pliny, in book 13, chapter 18, testifies that he saw some weighing more than 40 pounds, which is credible, since among us too they are found of huge size. Some are shaped broad and rounded and grow to a great size when sown more thinly; when sown more densely they grow long, that is, they run into an oblong shape. Cooked well with milk, they are most pleasant to the palate, and they nourish and satisfy well. Cooked with mutton, they nourish, and they are a most desired food for many peoples, adorning the tables of magnates too. They stimulate faded desire and sharpen the sight. I have learned by experience that their broth and soup, moderately seasoned with saffron, is remarkably good for coughing. It is established that they produce wind and also in turn expel it.

units.la: Cruda noxia sunt cumprimis edacibus pueris, ideoque ab iis abstinendum. Percocta manducantur vtilius. Quidam cinere calido torrent vel carbonibus, tosta permixto butyro & modico sale, salubriter efficantur.
units.tr: Raw, they are harmful, especially to greedy children, so one should abstain from them. Cooked, they are eaten more healthfully. Some roast them in warm ashes or embers; dressed with melted butter and a little salt, they are made wholesome.

units.la: His victitasse Curium Imper. Romanum historiae testantur, & inuentum a Legatis Samnitum aurum offerentibus rapum torrentem in foco. Apud Septentrionis gentes vidi ex iis cum lacte percoctis & butyro, concinnari pulticulam suauissimi & saluberrimi saporis, procerum mensis commendatissimam, qua saepe palatum egregie expleui. Pruinis & frigore rapa ali, dulcioraque & grandiora fieri constat: ne autem tabescant & putrescant, scrobes & foveas fodiunt, quibus hieme appropinquante conduntur & seruantur incorrupta: ad restim enim quaedam gentes rem rediisse clamant, vbi rapa gelu fuerint exusta, aut alia iniuria aliqua coeli soliue perierint. Ad raporum quoque catalogum refertur napus & rapunculus seu rapum sylueftre.
units.tr: Historians testify that the Roman emperor Curius lived on these, and that when the envoys of the Samnites came bearing gold as a gift, he was found roasting a turnip on the hearth. Among the peoples of the North I have seen them boiled with milk and butter and made into a little porridge of most pleasant and healthful flavour, most commended at the tables of the great, and I have often enjoyed it greatly. It is established that turnips are nourished by frost and cold and become sweeter and larger. But lest they wither and rot, people dig pits and trenches in which, as winter approaches, they are stored and kept uncorrupted. For some peoples cry out that matters have come to the last extremity when turnips have been burnt by frost or have perished by some other injury of sky or soil. To the catalogue of turnips is also referred the rape, and the little turnip or wild turnip.

units.la: Napus radices habet praelongas, tres fere palmos in terram descendentes crassitudine staphylino luteo pares, in cibo propter infi-gnem dulcedinem gratissimae, suaues ac falu-bres, praesertim cum carnibus praecipue fuil-lis & veruecina coctae, has enim mira suaui-tate condiunt: fi quis vero flatuum prouen-tum ex crudo illarum succo pertimescat, is ex sinapi coctas edat, hoc enim modo flatus dissipabuntur. Sabulo in subterraneis cellis incorruptae feruantur, durant enim sic con-ditae in multos menses. Has edunt ex butyro in Papatu, diebus quibus carne vesci vetitum est, praesertim ieiunio illo quadragenario.
units.tr: The rape has very long roots, descending nearly three palms into the earth, as thick as a yellow parsnip. They are most welcome as food for their remarkable sweetness, pleasant and wholesome, especially when boiled with meats, above all with fowl and mutton, for they season these with wonderful sweetness. But if anyone fears a rise of wind from the raw juice of these, let him eat them boiled with mustard, for in this way the wind will be dispelled. They are kept uncorrupted in sand in underground cellars, for they last in this way for many months. The Papists eat these with butter on days when it is forbidden to eat meat, especially in that forty-day fast.

units.la: Rapunculus rapum exiguum seu mini-mum napi genus, estur vere in acetariis. Sed tenendum vsum huius ante primum ver esse noxium, frigore scilicet terrae meatibus adhuc occlusis, foliisq; nondum apparenter e-rumpentibus: vere quoque tepido & humido, certum est elum huius minus salutarem esse. Videant igitur, qui liberalius eo vtuntur. Cocta radix cum planta gustui in acetariis magis arridet, minusque est noxia, quamque in terrae visceribus malignitatem contraxit, eam coctionis vi amittit.
units.tr: The rapunculus, a small turnip or the smallest kind of rape, is eaten in spring in salads. But its use before early spring is harmful, namely because the ground is still cold, its pores still closed and its leaves not yet appearing. And in a warm and damp spring too, it is certain that its use is less wholesome. Let those who use it too freely therefore take care. The root cooked with its plant pleases the taste more in salads, and is less harmful, since by the force of cooking it loses the malignity it has contracted from the bowels of the earth.

units.la: De
units.tr: On

units.la: De Pastinaca.
units.tr: On Parsnip.

units.la: Pastinaca quoq; suus in hortis & cibis honos est, feritur enim studiosissimè. Candida & lutea in summa apud gentes quasdam sunt autoritatis: cum carnib. decoctæ salubriores sunt ac suaviores, habent enim aromaticum quid, stomachoq; haud inutiles sunt, vrinam quoque promoveni, veneremq; stimulant. In miram autem crescunt amplitudinem, praesertim si folia reseentur, durantq; in veris tempora in sua terra, unde insignes visus praebent circa id tempus diuitibus & pauperibus solenni ieiunio quadragesimali.
units.tr: The parsnip also has its own honour in gardens and in food, for it is cultivated most eagerly. The white and yellow kinds are held in highest esteem among certain peoples. When boiled with meat they are more wholesome and pleasanter, for they have a certain aromatic quality, are not useless to the stomach, also promote urine and stimulate Venus. They grow to a remarkable size, especially if the leaves are cut off, and they keep into spring in their own soil, whence at that season they provide notable fare for rich and poor alike during the solemn Lenten fast.

units.la: Huc pertinent Carota, Satiua, Pastinacæ species, culinis notissimæ, Germani vocant, rothe und gelbe Rüben / magni apud nos visus & gratia in cibus, vrinæ Veneriq; stimulanda acco- modatæ. Rubram coquunt aquam, tesselatim q; incisam in acetariis cum pipere, aniso vel fœniculo mandunt. Albain cibos frequentius assumitur, verum cocta in iure aliquo, cruda enim e- stata inflat, ac concoctu difficilis est, unde proba- re non possum, quod quidam hæc incommoda etiam concoctæ attribuant. Non protinus enim damnandum, aut cibis abdicandum est, à quo quis vel abhorret natura, vel errore quodam externo.
units.tr: To this group belong the carrot and the cultivated parsnip, species of pastinaca, very well known in kitchens; the Germans call them rothe und gelbe Rüben . Among us they are much esteemed and pleasing as food, and suited to stimulating urine and Venus. They boil the red kind in water, and cut into little cubes they eat them in salads with pepper, anise or fennel. The white kind is taken more often in food, but cooked in some broth; raw, it is windy and difficult to digest. That is why I cannot approve of those who attribute these discomforts even to the cooked kind. For one should not straightaway condemn or reject as food something from which one shrinks either by natural aversion or by some external error.

units.la: Censura.
units.tr: Remark.

units.la: De
units.tr: Of

units.la: De petroselino, seu apio hor-tensi.
units.tr: Of parsley, or garden celery.

units.la: Vix reperias in Germania nostra culi-nam, in qua herba & radix huius, su-um inter praecipua olera locum non occupet. Quid? quod apud Romanos & Graecos in maxima autoritate fuisse propter renum calculos & vrinae difficultatem, ad quae maxime radix & semen expetuntur, graues autores literis mandarunt. Apitius nepotum gurges, vt eum appellat Plinius, & Platina magno in honore petroselinum semper habuerunt. Carnes elixas & assas mire commendat praecipue veruecinas, quin etiam piíces atque oüain sartagine tosta: aegris pariter atque bene valentibus datur: vina reddit gratiora & suauiora, sicut & aquas, in-coctum. Stomacho & suaue & gratum esse testatur Galenus. Lactucis quoque in acetariis miscetur, vt earum frigus contemperet. Peculiaris quoq; gratia crudo est, foetidum enim illum halitum e frustis esculentis vinum redolentibus, oreque vino nimium foetente exhalantem retundit atque hebetat. Graues autores, inter quos est Plinius, literis mandarunt frequentiorem eius vsum Comitiales & epilepticos facere, visusque claritati obesse, quod si vetum est, mirari subit, cur in cibis tam frequens eius fit vsus. Verum de nostro petrolelino seu apio hortensi id minime accipiendum esse puto, sed de fylueftri & aquatico, licet Manardus lib.18.Epistol. dubitet, quodnam genus fit, quod in Comitiali morbo damnatur. Alexander damnat Smyrnium, Plinius vero indiscriminatim alimenti ratione, apium omne, quod non probatur, siquidem nemini non constat, nostri petrolelini radices & folia in cibis vtilissima esse peculiaremque obtinere gratiam, id quod Galenus expresse testatur, cum scribit, stomacho & suaue & gratum esse: Veteres namque id ex aceto & sale & garo mandebant, qui tamen mos an quibusdam adhuc gentibus fit peculiaris, an vero exaruerit, affirmare vere non ausim. Hactenus Petroselinum.
units.tr: Hardly anywhere in our Germany would you find a kitchen in which the herb and root of this plant do not hold a place among the chief vegetables. Indeed, serious authors have written that among the Romans and Greeks it was held in the highest esteem for kidney stones and difficulty in urinating, for which the root and seed are especially sought. Apicius, the glutton of the spendthrifts (as Pliny calls him), and Platina always held parsley in great honour.
