It wonderfully commends boiled and roasted meats, especially mutton, and indeed fish and eggs fried in a pan. It is given equally to the sick and the healthy. It makes wines and waters, once boiled in, more pleasant and agreeable. Galen testifies that it is both sweet and pleasing to the stomach. It is also mixed into lettuce salads to temper their coldness. It has a special grace even when raw: it blunts and dulls the foul breath that comes from food smelling of wine, and from a mouth too foul with wine. Serious authors, among whom is Pliny, have written that its more frequent use causes convulsions and epilepsy and harms the clarity of sight. If this is true, one wonders why it is so often used in food. But I think this should not be taken of our parsley, or garden celery, at all, but of the wild and water kinds. Manardus (Epistles, book 18) doubts which kind it is that is condemned in the falling sickness. Alexander condemns smyrnium, while Pliny, judging by its use as food, condemns indiscriminately every kind of celery that is not approved. For it is known to everyone that the roots and leaves of our parsley are most useful in food and have a special grace, as Galen expressly attests when he writes that it is both sweet and pleasing to the stomach. The ancients ate it with vinegar, salt and garum. Whether this custom is still peculiar to some peoples, or has died out, I would not dare to affirm. So much for parsley.

units.la: De raphano vtroq.
units.tr: Of both kinds of radish.

units.la: Omnibus fere orbis gentibus admodum placere in cibatu raphanum minorem, (German. Rettich) seu radiculam, nemo est, opinor, qui ignoret. Plebs infima et lautiores mensa mire eo delectantur. Quidam eo solo ex sale cum pane sese sustentant. Eligendus autem est qui modice dulcescit, mitiorque est, est, nec adeo vehementer acrimonia linguam vellicat, quam coctione amitti expertum est: In probandi autem raphano spectandum maxime est, si frangenti sit contumax, fragilis namque facile commendatur. Pralongus napis similis, dulcior & minor est. Verum quaestionem, an radiculam ante vel post alios cibos mandere conuenientius sit & utilius, opera pretium est hic disputare, tum quia graues autores hic differentiunt, tum quod in omnibus fere liberalioribus conuiuis a doctis eam proponi animaduerti. Galenus eum vult alios cibos praecedere, atque ex garo, cui modicum aceti permixtum sit, edendum praecipit, alii facilicet eiciendae gratia, facilius enim sic aliquem subire exireq; dicit, ac citius & minori cum incommodo ex ima ventriculi parte, in qua coctio praecipue coficitur, ad intestina transfire, hacque ratione ori ventriculi minus nocumentu inferre: debet n. q aliu facile subeunt, q corruptibilia sunt, & humida omnia in principio mesa dari, teste Gal. 1. & 3. l. de ratione victus in morb. acut. praesertim ubi intentio est mollire alvu ne sia cibo dentur, eum corrumpant. Qua autem ventrem stomachum q corroborant, ut poma acerba, aut pyra cineribus calidis mediocriter affata, statim a cibo sunt offerenda. Hac Galenus. Diofcorides contrarium asserit videlicet radiculam, quia stomacho adversetur, a cibo dandam esse, hoc enim modo digestionem eam adiuvare, contrario vero coctionem impedire & suspendere, crudosq; humores mores attrahere, qui postea orificium ventriculi laedant a q; lac essant. Galeni sententiam confirmant Paulus Aegineta, Aetius, & nonnulli alii, Dioscorides patrocinantem habet Trallianus. Sed Galenus medicos illos miratur, qui radiculam crudam a cœna ad cibi ione iuuandam ingerunt.
units.tr: I suppose there is no one who does not know that almost all nations of the world are very fond of the smaller radish (German: Rettich), or little root, as food. The lowest common people and the better-off at table delight in it greatly. Some sustain themselves on it alone, with salt and bread. One should choose the kind that is mildly sweet and milder, which does not sting the tongue too sharply; experience shows that its sharpness is lost in cooking. In judging a radish, one should chiefly look at whether it resists when broken, for a brittle one is easily spoiled. The long kind, similar to the turnip, is sweeter and smaller. But whether it is more fitting and more useful to eat the radish before or after other food is worth discussing here, both because serious authors differ on this and because I have noticed it is put forward by learned men at almost all the more generous banquets. Galen wants it to precede other foods, and prescribes that it be eaten with garum mixed with a little vinegar. Others do so for the sake of expelling it, for he says that in this way one enters and leaves more easily, and passes more quickly and with less discomfort from the lower part of the stomach, where digestion is chiefly accomplished, into the intestines, and so does less harm to the mouth of the stomach. For corruptible and all moist things should be given at the beginning of a meal, as Galen testifies in books 1 and 3 of his work on the regimen in acute diseases, especially where the aim is to soften the bowels, lest they be given after food and corrupt it. But things that strengthen the belly and stomach, such as sour apples or pears gently warmed in hot ashes, should be offered straight after food. So Galen. Dioscorides asserts the contrary: that the radish, since it is opposed to the stomach, should be given after food, for in this way it aids digestion, whereas if taken before food it impedes and suspends digestion, draws up raw humours which afterwards harm the mouth of the stomach, and causes belching. Paulus Aegineta, Aetius and several others support Galen's opinion; Trallianus has Dioscorides as his advocate. But Galen marvels at those physicians who swallow raw radish after supper to help digestion.

units.la: Simon Sethi cap. de radicula hanc controversiam breviter dirimit, vult enim, si ventriculus facile fluat, nec ad inflationem seu flatuum generationem sit dispositus, radiculam ante cibum dari commodius, sin contrarium fuerit a cibo. Ex quibus colligitur ventriculum humidum esse flatulentum, quia flatus generantur ex materia humida non sicca, calor enim tanquam causa efficiens in cibos quidem & humores agit, sed dimi-nuté, respectu scilicet ipsius materiæ, quam qui-de aliqua ex parte attenuat atq; dissoluit, nota-men perfectè conficit. Vndequi duriore sunt alii, & ventriculum habent flatulentum, radicu-la cum sale & modico aceto vesci debent a cibo, ante vero si contrarium fuerit. Verum quia quo-modocunque modo sumta cruda eructationes & flatus excitat, cerebrum oculosq; turbat, ac con-coctu difficilis est ex oleo comedenda est, sic enim de ventriculo eructationis ciere non potest. Quae corticem habet tenuem, modicamq; acrimoniæ, eamq; ita temperatam, ut vix sentiatur, cæteris præfertur: nō tamen debet esse omnes acrimoniæ expers: quoddam genus est quod corticem habet crassissimum, cui subest amaritudo plurima (quae tamen
units.tr: Simon Seth, in his chapter on the radish, briefly settles this controversy. For he holds that if the stomach empties easily and is not disposed to swelling or the generation of wind, the radish is more conveniently given before food, but if the contrary, after food. From this it is gathered that a moist stomach is windy, since winds are generated from moist, not dry, matter. For heat, as the efficient cause, acts on food and humours, but diminished, namely with respect to the matter itself, which it partly thins and dissolves, yet does not perfectly digest. Therefore those of harder constitution who have a windy stomach should eat the radish with salt and a little vinegar after food, but before food if the contrary holds. Yet because, however it is taken, raw, it excites belching and wind, disturbs the brain and eyes, and is difficult to digest, it should be eaten with oil, for thus it cannot raise belches from the stomach. The kind that has a thin skin and moderate sharpness, so tempered that it is barely felt, is preferred to the others. Yet it should not be wholly free of sharpness. There is one kind that has a very thick skin, beneath which lies much bitterness (which

units.la: NB. Raphani boni notæ. tamen salsugine eximitur,) ac cibis abdicandu. Quare rustica & stupida palata sunt, quae eius-modi amaritudinem acremq; illum saporem in raphano quaerunt.
units.tr: NB. Marks of a good radish. is removed by salting), and it is to be rejected from food. Hence those are rustic and dull palates that seek such bitterness and sharp flavour in the radish.

units.la: Raphanus maior, seu thlaspi maius ger-man. Merrettich / feruentior in omnibus & efficacior est, adsalsamentarios vsus cum sale & aceto tusa radix conditur, embammatus enim seu condimentis ex aceto, quae ad condienda fiunt obsonia, ut pisces, carnes, adiungitur, & maxime idonea est ad excitandam appetentiam, pellendam vrinam & calculum, sed immodicus eius vsus capiti noxius est, quare aliis conuenientibus contemperanda est. De raphano minori, germ. Rettich / hoc minime praetereundum est, quod ieiuno stomacho manducatus cum sale & pane veneno potenter resistit, experimenti via facilis & certa.
units.tr: The greater radish, or horseradish (German Merrettich ), is more fiery in all respects and more effective. Its root, pounded with salt and vinegar, is preserved for use in sauces, for it is added to the embamata, or condiments made of vinegar, prepared for seasoning dishes such as fish and meat. It is most suited to arousing appetite and driving out urine and stones, but immoderate use of it is harmful to the head, so it must be tempered with other suitable things. Of the lesser radish (German Rettich ) this must by no means be passed over: eaten with salt and bread on an empty stomach, it powerfully resists poison. This is an easy and certain test by experience.

units.la: De Caepis.
units.tr: On Onions.

units.la: Apud Aegyptios piaculum ducunt vesci caepis aut allio, propterea quod haec illorum sint numina, qua de re extant in 5 iuuenalis Satyr. elegantes versus Oppida tota canem venerantur, nulla Diana Porrum & Caepe nefas violare ac frangere morsu, O sanctas gentes quib. haec nascuntur in hortis Numina. Causam hujus superstitionis ex fequen- tibus verbis Ruellii in historia cepæ, facile quis intellexerit. Id mirandum, inquit, occurrit, quod apud Plutarchum 4. in Hefiod. commentario legitur, Cepa enim reuirescit & congerminat luna decedente, contra autem marcescit eădem adolescente : eam causam dicunt Sacerdotes Ægyptii, cur Pelufiotæ Cœpam non edant, eo quod solum olerum omnium contra fyderis incrementa & decrementa vices minuendi & augendi habeat contrarias, cum omnia quæ crescente Luna gliscunt, eădem senescente tabescunt, quod in ostreis & cancris aperte cognoscitur, quos fyderis juuenta complet & vberiores facit, senium deplet macrosque reddit. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Among the Egyptians it was considered sacrilege to eat onions or garlic, because these were their gods. On this account there are elegant verses in Juvenal's fifth Satire: Whole towns worship a dog, and no town reveres Diana. It is wrong to harm the leek and the onion, or to bite into them. O holy nations, in whose gardens such deities grow! The cause of this superstition can easily be understood from the following words of Ruellius in his history of the onion: "It is remarkable," he says, "what is read in Plutarch, in the fourth book of his commentary on Hesiod: the onion revives and sprouts again when the moon is waning, but on the contrary withers when the moon is waxing. The Egyptian priests give this as the reason why the people of Pelusium do not eat onions: that this alone of all vegetables has the opposite course of diminishing and increasing against the increase and decrease of the star, since everything that swells when the moon grows wastes away when it wanes. This is clearly seen in oysters and crabs, which the youth of the star fills and makes plumper, while old age empties them and makes them thin." So far he.

units.la: Nos vero Germani acribus istis Ægyptiorum Diis carere non possumus, in nostris enim culinis cepis nihil fere frequentius, aliumque cultum Ægyptiacis Diis præstare non possumus, quam vt iis mane & jejuno stomacho cum sale & pane deuoratis à peste & veneno nos præferuemus.
units.tr: We Germans, however, cannot do without those sharp things that the gods of the Egyptians had. In our kitchens nothing is more common than onions, and we cannot offer the Egyptian gods any better worship than this: by eating them in the morning on an empty stomach with salt and bread, we fortify ourselves against plague and poison.

units.la: De cepis porro notandum, quod coctæ salubriores sint crudis, tum quia magis nutriunt, tũ quia coctione acre illum afperumq; sapore deponunt. Russę & rubicundę albis acriores sunt & calidiores, Carnib. aut. R piscibus, quibus condiendis accommodatissimae sunt. Feruenti cinere coctae atque ex oleo, saccharo, acetiq; momento comeltae ad difficiles tusses praestant: aliquam quoq; emolliunt, vrinamq; pellunt continuo sitatae. Vnicum hic omnib. praeceptum esto omni auro praestantius, videl. quod vnumquemq; suii psius medicum esse deceat, obseruareq;, iuuerturne an offendatur ceparum vsu, actum demum ab iis, vel abstinere, aut eas vsurpare. Idem de allio, & id genus aliis intelligas.
units.tr: It should further be noted about onions that cooked ones are healthier than raw, both because they nourish more and because cooking removes their harsh, rough sharpness. Red and reddish onions are sharper and hotter than white ones, and they are most suitable for seasoning meats and fish. Onions roasted in hot ashes, or cooked in oil with sugar and vinegar, help with difficult coughs; they also soften some, and when taken continually they drive out urine. This one rule is worth more than any gold to everyone: each person should be his own doctor, and should observe whether the use of onions agrees with him or offends him, and then either abstain from them or use them. The same is to be understood of garlic and similar things.

units.la: Aridae deniq; & coctae virentibus & crudis vtiliores sunt, namin his sapor ille mordax & acris, odorq; lacrymosus (qui tamen tempore elanguescit) oculorum caliginem, capitisq; dolores gignit. Idem & nonnunquam salutaris est, oculorumq; caliginem pellit, id quod expertus sum in me ipso, capitis grauedinem ex narium obstructione sentiens. Cepam autem vel mando cum pane, vel per medium scindo, odoremq; exhalantem ad oculos penetrare sino, verum caute obseruandum est, tabidis natura aridisq;, flaccidis & languidis, ac biliosis, hunc vtendi modum noxium esse, humiditas enim radicalis & nutrimentalis eo absumitur, contrario autem modo se habentibus vsui est. Leguminibus, vt fabis, pisis, lentibus, salutariter cepas adiectas expertus sum, ad flatus discutiendum, dissipandumque crassum, qui ab his gignitur, succum. Somnum quoque conciliare viui-dumque colorem creduntur. Hæc de ce-pis.
units.tr: Finally, dried or cooked onions are more useful than green and raw ones, for in the latter there is a biting, sharp taste and a tear-provoking smell (which however fades with time), and these cause dimness of the eyes and headaches. Sometimes the same is also beneficial and drives away dimness of the eyes, as I have experienced myself when I felt heaviness of the head from a blocked nose. I either chew an onion with bread or cut it in half and let its exhaling smell reach my eyes. But it must be cautiously observed that this manner of use is harmful to those of wasting and dry constitution, to the flabby and languid, and to the bilious, for the radical and nutritive moisture is consumed by it; but it is useful to those disposed in the opposite way. I have found that adding onions to pulses, such as beans, peas and lentils, helps to dissipate wind and to disperse the thick humour that these generate. They are also believed to induce sleep and a lively colour. So much on onions.

units.la: De allio.
units.tr: On Garlic.

units.la: NOn minor vero allio autoritas est apud gentes quasdam. In algidioribus quibus-dam regionibus ab ipsius esu non possunt arceri incolæ. Rusticorum quoque theriaca est. Qui natura sunt calidiori ac biliosiori pernitio-so errore co vuntur, infigniter enim calefacit, quare oleum addunt igni. Vini auiditatem qua-runt nonnulli vno atq; altero nucleo commanducato. Galenus, Ægineta, Aetius q; minimè esse siticuli sum constanter affirmant. Dioscorides vero & Plinius sitim gignere prodiderunt, quod experimento constat. Siticulosi enim allii esu reddutur & sommiculosi, caput enim tentatur, oculorumq; hebetudo infertur, quod tamen de crudo potius quam elixo intelligas velim, cosium enim crudo, elixumq; tosto, Plinio teste, utilius. Elixatur ut acrimoniam amittat, succi q; fit melioris. Nihil enim tam est medicamentosum, quod coctione & elixatione aliqua ex parte non fiat alimentosum. Contra aquarum autem & quorumlibet locorum mutationes insignem prestat utilitatem, quod nautis optime esse notum scio, qui navigantes in lintea id coniiciunt. Qui carnes & cum primis veruecinam torrentes verubus, verubus, allio eam implent ac infigunt, non fa-ciunt infalubriter. Hoc miror principes quasdam foeminas allio plurimum gaudere. Quin & magnates quidam (cum primis in Gallia) ineunte vere cum butyro recenti eo vntuntur, valetudinis per totum annum custodiendæ gratia. Colico doloři nobile & præsens medicamentum esse Ga-lenus promisit, inueterata quoq; tussi, & vrinæ ciendæ, mensibus & fecundinæ extrahendæ. Vnū detestandum in allio est, fœtidus videl. ac ingra-tus ille odor cerebro officiens, ob quem Horatium puto, illud tantopere execratum esse, cum scribit lib. epodon ode 3.
units.tr: Garlic's authority is no less among certain peoples. In the colder regions some inhabitants cannot be kept from eating it. It is also the theriac of the peasants. Those of hotter and more bilious natures fall into a harmful error, for it warms remarkably, so they add oil to the fire. Some seek a desire for wine by chewing one or two cloves. Galen, Aegineta and Aetius constantly affirm that it does not in any way cause thirst. Dioscorides and Pliny, however, have reported that it produces thirst, which is confirmed by experience: for those who eat garlic become thirsty and drowsy, since the head is affected and dullness of the eyes is brought on. I would have this understood, however, of raw rather than boiled garlic, for according to Pliny raw garlic is more useful than cooked. It is boiled so that it loses its sharpness and its juice becomes better. For nothing is so medicinal that it does not become in some measure nourishing through cooking and boiling. Changes of water and of place bring a notable benefit, which I know sailors understand very well, since they put garlic into their linen when they sail. Those who roast meats, especially mutton, on spits, and stuff and insert garlic into them, do not act unwholesomely. This I wonder at: certain princely women take great delight in garlic. Indeed some magnates (especially in France) anoint themselves with it and fresh butter at the beginning of spring, to keep their health through the whole year. Galen promised that it is a noble and effective remedy for colic pain, also for long-standing cough, for provoking urine, and for drawing out the menses and afterbirth. There is one thing to be detested in garlic: its foul and ungrateful smell, which is harmful to the brain. On account of this, I think Horace so greatly execrated it, when he writes in Epode 3:

units.la: NB. Parentis olim si quis impia manu Senile guttur fregerit, Edat cicutis allium nocentius O dura messorum ilia.
units.tr: If anyone with impious hand has ever broken the aged throat of his parent, let him eat garlic, more harmful than hemlock, O hard bellies of the reapers!

units.la: Est in exemplis multos odore allii non secus atq; pestilentis rei olfactu affici. Didymus asse-rit, allium, si luna infra terram exist ente, sera-tur, idemq;, luna sub terra latente, vellatur, o-doris fœditatem amittere & dulcescere. Alii apii liberaliori esu, halitum eius reflingui pro-diderunt.
units.tr: There are examples of many people being affected by the smell of garlic no less than by the smell of something pestilential. Didymus asserts that garlic, if sown while the moon is below the earth, and likewise if pulled up while the moon lies hidden under the earth, loses the foulness of its smell and becomes sweet. Others have reported that by freer eating of celery, its breath is blunted.

units.la: Didymus crudæ fabæ manducationem probat: alii beta radicem in prunis tostam: alii rutha folia: ego laudo panem tostum aceto vel vi-no intinctum. Antipathiam magnetis & allii hic silentio praeterire nefas est, ille enim hoc affirmat
units.tr: Didymus approves of eating raw beans; others of beet root roasted on coals; others of rue leaves; I commend bread toasted and dipped in vinegar or wine. It would be wrong to pass over here in silence the antipathy between the magnet and garlic, for he affirms it.

units.la: Alli odor quomodo corrigendus. catus fert um non trahit. Sed de hoc mysterio dicetur alibi.
units.tr: How the smell of garlic is to be corrected: a cat carries it, it does not drag it. But this mystery will be spoken of elsewhere.

units.la: De porro.
units.tr: On the leek.

units.la: EIusdem cum caepis & allio est naturae, quare no incouenienter de eo hic verba fiunt. Culinę carnes eo decoquūt, vt gallinas, capones, veruecinamq;, quibus adiiciunt crocum, suaui & grato sapore: Itaque certum est in cibis admodum esse vtile, licet in huius viribus & natura autores varient. Thadeus Florentinus experimento compertum habebat, porrum crudum ex sale primo cibo efitatū ventriculū à crassis lentisq; humoribus, crudisq; succis liberare. Biliosas vero ac calidiores naturas, eosq; qui infirmiori sunt capite, grauiter ab illius esu affici certū est. Alii venerem irritare, ebrietatemque discutere praedicant. Quaedam rura edunt ex sale, panemque eo aequè atque allio fricant, ad condiendum panis atri ingratitudinem. Alsatiae agricolae & vinitores allium, caepam & porrum inter prima & vltima habent fercula. Praestat autem allium, antequam caules faciat, si intorqueatur ac humi prosternatur, quod Iulio faciendum est, hoc enim pacto cauetur, ne in frondem luxuriet, vnde grandiora fiunt capita. In Germania nostra foliis porri, sicut & absynthii, melissae, R menthae Sarracenicae, rosmarini, amenthae vulgaris, matricariae, & similibus ad placentas quas taganitas vocant (Pfannkuchen) coquendas vsus frequentissimus est, praeterea in verno tempore, estque harum vsus & esus sto tempore non infalutaris, ventriculo enim & medicamento & alimento sunt. Hactenus de alimentis quae veniunt ex radicibus, quibus, quia ciborum potius codimenta sunt, quam cibi, qui proprie alimentum praestare existimantur, annumerari possunt, femina, quae in praecipuis ac laudatissimis saluberrimisque hodie condimentis escarum variarum habetur, vt sunt, anisi, foeniculi, cari, apii, anethi, sinapi, quod praecipuam nobilitatem in condimentis carnium, vt bubulae praesertim infumatae, item piscium obtinuit: matres familias obsonatricis artis non imperitae per vindemias musto id diluunt temperantque, ad acrimoniam eius retundendam, vnde adhuc mustardae nomea musto & ardore retinuisse videtur. Insigniter autem prodest, quibus palatum torpescit, quosque cibi fastidium molestat, cerebrum quoque purgat, sed inualidioribus aridisque oculis insigniter noxium: aridos oculos voco tabidos, flaccidos, debiles, roridae sc. humiditatis ratione, ea enim deficiente oculos aridos existere debilesque necesse est.
units.tr: It is of the same nature as onions and garlic, so it is not out of place to discuss it here. Cooks boil meats with it, such as hens, capons and mutton, and add saffron for a pleasant and agreeable flavour. It is therefore certain that it is very useful in food, although authors differ on its powers and nature. Thaddeus of Florence had found by experience that raw leek, eaten with salt as the first food, frees the stomach from thick, viscous humours and raw juices. But it is certain that bilious and hotter natures, and those who have weaker heads, are seriously harmed by eating it. Others claim that it arouses lust and dispels drunkenness. Some country folk eat it with salt, and rub bread with it just as they do with garlic, to season the unpleasantness of black bread. The farmers and vine-growers of Alsace count garlic, onion and leek among their first and last dishes. It is better, however, that the leek, before it runs to stalk, be twisted and laid flat on the ground, which should be done in July; for in this way it is prevented from running to leaf, which is why the heads grow larger. In our Germany, the leaves of leek are very commonly used, as are those of wormwood, balm, Saracen mint, rosemary, common mint, feverfew and similar herbs, for baking the cakes they call taganitae (Pfannkuchen); and in spring, the use and eating of these in season is not unwholesome, for they serve the stomach as medicine and as food alike. So far concerning foods that come from roots, which may be counted among condiments rather than foods, since they are seasonings of food and not what is properly thought to supply nourishment. Seeds, which today are held to be among the chief, most praised and most wholesome seasonings of various dishes, such as anise, fennel, caraway, celery, dill and mustard, may be counted here too. Mustard has gained particular distinction among seasonings for meats, especially smoked beef, and likewise for fish. Housewives, not unskilled in the art of cookery, at vintage time dilute and temper it with must to blunt its sharpness, and so mustard seems to have kept its name from must and its heat. It is notably beneficial to those whose palate is dull and whom loss of appetite troubles; it also purges the brain, but it is notably harmful to weak and dry eyes. By dry eyes I mean wasted, flabby, weak eyes, lacking dewy moisture; for when this moisture is lacking, the eyes must become dry and weak.

units.la: CAP. X. De alimentis, quæ sumuntur ex plantarum foliis.
units.tr: CHAPTER X. Of foods taken from the leaves of plants.

units.la: Hæc pluraque sunt hortensia, ut brassica, caulis capitatus, lactuca, endivia, seu cichorium hortense, atriplex, beta, spinachium, Hæc cæterum oleribus, agrestibus & domesticis magis salutaria utiliorque iudicantur, tum quia natura illorum longo experimento vitæ hominum est probata, tum quia rem alimentariam eximie augent.
units.tr: These and many more are garden plants, such as cabbage, head cabbage, lettuce, endive or garden chicory, orache, beet, and spinach. Yet these are judged more wholesome and useful than the wild and cultivated herbs, both because their nature has been proved by long experience of human life, and because they greatly increase the food supply.

units.la: De Brassica.
units.tr: On Cabbage.

units.la: IN Græcia Crambe vocitabatur, quasi Coramble, quod oculis inimica existimabatur, pupillam enim oculorum, quæ κώρη gr. dicitur, hebetare dicitur. Galenus exciccandi vim insignem obtinere, ideoque visum hebetare, nisi quis oculos habeat humentiores, scriptum reliquit. Alii solam interolera atram bilem procreare, eamque; iniqui & graveolentis succi esse prodiderunt. Sunt qui plurimis mirisque laudibus eam celebrent cum primis vero sativam crispam, hinc enim probe paratam stomacho imbecillo conuenire, concoctionem adiuuare, bilem & phlegma sensim educere assueerant. rant, ad quod posterius adhuc magis com-mendantur cymata seu cauliculi brassicæ te-neriores & delicatiores. Sexcentis annis po-pulum Romanum brassica vsum esse, nul-lumque extitisse morbum, quem non hoc o-lere curarent graues autores testantur. Se-ptentrionis gentes, sicut & Westphali, apud quos magna in copia optima prouenit, brassicam in gloria palati habent, coquunt eam cum perdicibus, columbis, carnib° pinguio-ribus, & anseribus insumatis, quidam adiici-ciunt piper salutari inuento, sic enim infalu-brior & asperior succus salubrior euadit & mitior. Hibernis frigoribus & gelicidiis me-dullam caulium quidam in delitiis habent, parăturq; eodem modo quo pastinacæ: lautior quoq; & suauior ipsa brassica redditur in fri-goribus & rigoribus hiemis, teste experien-tia. Qui humaniorem ac nitidiorem sequun-tur vitam, caules leuiter coquunt, coctos paropsidibus imponunt, salequeac oleo co-diunt, quo apparatu gustatu gratissimi eua-dunt. Ebrietatem arcere, crapulamque dis-cutere bina aut terna brassicæ folia cruda cū sale & aceto, ante & post cibum comesta, ex-perimento haud fallaci constat, ob antipa-thian quæ est brassicæ cum vitibus, quæ iuxta consitæ non coalescunt. Podagri-cos, neruosque paralyticos & tremu-los brassicæ esu plurimum iuuari Erasistrati schola testatur, annotante Plinio, vt itanon necesse fit exotica, peregrina & pretiosa expetere, cum vulgaribus sæpe ac notissimis remediis auxilium sentiamus.
units.tr: In Greece it was called crambe, as if coramble, because it was thought harmful to the eyes, for it is said to dull the pupil of the eye, which in Greek is called korē [κόρη]. Galen left it written that it has a notable drying power and therefore dulls the sight, unless a person has moister eyes. Others have declared that the wild kind alone produces black bile, and that it is of a bad and foul-smelling juice. Some praise it with very many and remarkable commendations, especially the curled garden cabbage. For when properly prepared it suits a weak stomach, aids digestion, and gradually draws off bile and phlegm; they have also recommended the tender and delicate shoots or little stalks of cabbage for the same purpose, even more so. Grave authors testify that for six hundred years the Roman people used cabbage, and that there was no disease which they did not cure with it. The northern peoples, such as the Westphalians, among whom it grows in great abundance and of excellent quality, hold cabbage in high favour for the palate. They cook it with partridges, pigeons, fattier meats and unsalted geese; some add pepper, a healthful spice, for in this way the sharper and harsher juice becomes more wholesome and milder. In cold winters and frosts some people take delight in the pith of the stalks, and it is prepared in the same way as parsnips. Cabbage itself too becomes more delicate and sweeter in the chills and rigours of winter, as experience shows. Those who follow a more refined and elegant way of life boil the stalks lightly, place them cooked on serving dishes, and season them with salt and oil, and by this preparation they become most pleasing to the taste. That two or three raw cabbage leaves, eaten with salt and vinegar before and after a meal, keep off drunkenness and dispel the effects of excess, is established by no deceptive experience, owing to the antipathy between cabbage and vines, which do not grow well when planted near each other. The school of Erasistratus testifies that gout, paralytic nerves and tremors are greatly relieved by eating cabbage, as Pliny notes. So there is no need to seek out foreign, outlandish and costly things, since we often find help in common and very well known remedies.

units.la: De caule capitato.
units.tr: On Head Cabbage.

units.la: HVius oleris vsus in Germania nostra ita inualuit, vt vino potius aliis quàm necessa-riis ad vitam rebus quam eo carere malit. Bene enim præparatum, conditum & co-ctum longe gratius, salubriusq; est peregrinis illis, sumtuosis, eaq; longinquo accitu non nisi ad inanem prodigi luxus ostentationem, condimentis, vt olivis, capparibus, & similibus. Multis autem modis præparantur atque condiuntur caules capitati, quibus hodie culinæ principatum attribuunt: ad coctionem præcipue medullas ex bouum ossibus quærunt aut carnes pinguiores. Germania nostra caules capitatos sale condire didicit, qui postea accescunt, diuq; ita reseruantur incorrupti, ne putrescant: constat enim decoctorum aquam humi effusam fœtere, quin etiam ipsos (quod de Brassica quoque intelligendum) in hortis putrefactos intolerabilem odorem exhalare: qua ratione non immerito à prudentioribus quibusdam in cibis damnantur.
units.tr: The use of this vegetable has taken such hold in our Germany that people would rather go without wine than without it, among the other things necessary to life. For when well prepared, seasoned and cooked, it is far more pleasant and wholesome than those foreign, costly condiments brought from afar, such as olives and capers and the like, which serve only for the empty display of wasteful luxury. Head cabbages are prepared and seasoned in many ways, and cooks now give them first place in the kitchen. For cooking they especially seek marrow from ox bones, or fattier meats. Our Germany has learned to pickle head cabbage in salt, and it then ferments and is kept so for a long time without spoiling, for it is established that the water in which it has been boiled stinks when poured on the ground, and indeed that the cabbages themselves, which is to be understood of cabbage too, give off an intolerable smell when they rot in the gardens. For this reason some wiser people rightly condemn it as food.

units.la: Probè Probe itaq; conditi stomacho effuanti & latranti, sicut & fastidienti prodesse experimento quotidiano constat. Hoc velim prudentes patresfamilias meminerint, conditura adhuc ten-da esse semina anisi, fœniculi, cymini, anethi, apii, baccas unipe-rinas, & similia crasso modo contusa, hæc enim saporem conciliant & odo em cerebro gratum & ventriculo salutarem, flatus discutiunt, inflationes impediunt, vrinamq; promovent. Secus praeparatos, coctos & conditos ventriculo, quibus non affuerunt, insigniter nocuisse compertum est. Quamobrem hoc olus non protinus planeq; contemnendum est, & inscienter, meo iudicio, errant, qui indifferenter, cæco & vago iudicio, omnibus hoc cibo interdicunt.
units.tr: Head cabbage properly seasoned is known by daily experience to benefit a stomach that is sick, barking and lacking appetite. I would have prudent heads of households remember this: the seasoning should still include seeds of anise, fennel, cumin, dill and celery, juniper berries, and similar things roughly crushed; for these give it flavour and a smell pleasant to the brain and healthful to the stomach, dispel wind, prevent bloating and promote urine. It has been found that cabbage prepared, cooked and seasoned without these does notable harm to the stomach. Therefore this vegetable should not be utterly and immediately despised, and those err unwisely, in my judgement, who with a blind and wandering judgement forbid this food to everyone without distinction.

units.la: Acetaria, quæ ex caule capitato crudo, tempore, vt plurimum autumnali concinnari consueuerunt, ex oleo & aceto, (quorum vsus esq; ita apud vos frequens est, vt prima mensa, tum magnatum, tum pauperum, iis exornari multipliciter gestiant) lupini, rustici ac stupidi palati esse existimant. Videant igitur studiosi literarum, ne inter cœnam eiusmodi acetario-rum plenos bolos devorantes ex assumta quadam & pernitiosa consuetudine cruditatum copiam inglutiant.
units.tr: Salads, which are usually put together in autumn from raw head cabbage with oil and vinegar (their use is so common among you that people eagerly adorn the first course, both of great men and of the poor, with them in many ways), are thought to suit only the boorish, rustic and stupid palate. Let scholars therefore take care that, while dining, they do not swallow down great mouthfuls of such salads, devouring them, and by a fixed and harmful habit take in a store of indigestion.

units.la: De Lactuca.
units.tr: On Lettuce.

units.la: DE Lactuca diuersæ sunt autorum sententiæ. Quidam præ cæteris oleribus bene eam nutrire, purumq; generare sanguinem, scriptum reliquerunt. Alii aliter sentiunt, non admodum eam expetentes. Serapio vtilem sibi fuisse lactucam testatur, æstuantem enim choleram eâ expurgavit. Plinius quoque doctissimum medicum multam, Augusto Lactucâ vim morbi repressisse tradit. Et Galenus ipse l.2. alim. summis eam laudibus prosequitur. Et certum est, quibus assiduo os ventriculi superius bile efferuescit atque ebullit, lactuca vsum prodesse, sitim extinguere, eximieq; conciliare somnum, quam ob causam æstate feruente, morboquoque vel ætate calidiori frequentissime in cibo vbique gentium adhibetur.
units.tr: Opinions of authors on lettuce differ. Some have written that, beyond other vegetables, it nourishes well and produces pure blood. Others think otherwise and do not greatly seek it. Serapion testifies that lettuce was useful to him, for it purged his burning bile. Pliny also records that a very learned physician cured Augustus of a severe illness by means of lettuce. And Galen himself, in his second book on foods, praises it very highly. It is certain that those whose upper mouth of the stomach constantly seethes and boils with bile are helped by eating lettuce, which quenches thirst and brings sleep easily; for this reason it is most frequently eaten everywhere in the world in fervent summer, or by those of a hotter constitution or age.

units.la: Magnam in acetariis obtinuit autoritatem, sicut & præcipuam fere inter olera ei tribuunt graues scriptores. Plinius æstate gratam, stomachoque fastidium auferre, cibique appetentiam inducere memoriæ prodidit.
units.tr: It has held great authority among salads, and grave writers have given it almost the first place among vegetables. Pliny has handed down in memory that in summer it is pleasant, removes loathing from the stomach, and induces appetite for food.

units.la: Ob refrigeratricem, qua prædita est, naturam intemperatas libidines præsertim eas, quæ per somnos contingunt, coercere dudubium non est. Quamobrem videant, qui uxores duxerunt, ne vsu frequentiori ac liberaliore fequiores reddantur in venerem. Cucullatis igitur, iisque, qui castitati (fi Diis placet) vitam suam confecrarunt, largiter lactucam deuorandam relinquamus.
units.tr: That, because of its cooling nature, it restrains immoderate lusts, especially those which occur in sleep, is beyond doubt. Therefore let those who have married take care that by frequent and too free use they do not become more ardent for sexual pleasure. Let us then leave lettuce to be eaten freely by monks, and by those who (God willing) have dedicated their lives to chastity.

units.la: Ebrietatem eam arcere constat experimento, sed superingestam aliis cibis, quo etiam vtendi modo somnum promtius inducere censendum est, ad quod carmine suo Martialis non infacete lusit, cum scribit,
units.tr: It is established by experience that lettuce keeps off drunkenness, but when eaten on top of other foods; and it should be considered that this manner of eating also induces sleep more readily. Martial wittily played on this in his verse, when he writes:

units.la: Claudere qua veterum coenas lactuca solebat,
units.tr: Tell me why lettuce, which used to close the feasts of the ancients,

units.la: Dic mihi cur nostras incipit ita dapes!
units.tr: now begins our banquets!

units.la: Epulas enim antiquorum lactucam clausisse Atheneus testis est. Quod non citra rationem factitatum esse existimo: frigidae enim humentifq; naturae cum fit, a coena affumta efficacius somnum conciliat, viniq; feruorem reprimit, ebrietatique obfiftitinductâ in cerebrum humiditate. Nostra aetate coenam ab eius esu, ad appetentiam excitandam, quae ex prolixiore prandio, vel exiguo interuallo inter coenam & prandium, fofet esse fere nulla, vel exigua, auspicantur. Veterum ego morem vehementer probo, relinquens nostrae aetati suum.
units.tr: For Athenaeus is a witness that lettuce closed the feasts of the ancients. I think this was done not without reason: since it is of a cold and moist nature, when taken after dinner it brings sleep more effectively, checks the heat of wine, and resists drunkenness by inducing moisture into the brain. In our age people begin the meal by eating it, to stir up appetite, which, after a longer lunch or a short interval between lunch and dinner, is almost nil or slight. I greatly approve of the custom of the ancients, leaving our age its own.

units.la: Notandum praeterea, lactucam, quo vetustior fuerit, eo reddi amariorem, vnde, cum excaulefcere coepit cibis, non amplius est idonea, quare culinis abdicatur. Costa lactuca in pulriculam corpori deficienti bonum praebet nutrimentum, aluumq; emollit, quare edentulis inque senium vergentibus salutaris est. Galenus tamen neque multum generare sanguinem, nec tamen improbi succi esse asserit, quin medium ferre temperamentum inter ea, quae boni succi sunt, & inter ea, quae mali.
units.tr: It should further be noted that the older the lettuce, the more bitter it becomes; hence, once it has begun to run to stalk, it is no longer fit for food, and so it is rejected by cooks. Lettuce cooked in broth gives good nourishment to a weakened body and softens the bowels, so it is wholesome for those without teeth and those growing old. Yet Galen asserts that it does not produce much blood, nor is it of a bad juice, but holds a middle temperament between those things which are of good juice and those which are of bad.

units.la: Qui ficcioris sunt cerebri, vsum ejus non respuent, similiter, qui concumbendi desiderio nimis vrunt & pruriunt.
units.tr: Those of drier brains will not reject its use, and likewise those who burn and itch too much with desire for sexual intercourse.

units.la: Ad extremum mirari subit, tot laudibus celebratum olus oculorum claritati ossi-cere, spiritus visorios incrassando, humoremque crystallinum efficiendo turbidum, ab aliquibus grauibus autoribus proditum esse, cum neque Galenus, neque caeteri graeci medici, (quod quidem ego inuenerim) id annotarint.
units.tr: Finally, it is strange that some grave authors have reported that a vegetable so much praised makes the clarity of the eyes dim, by thickening the visual spirits and making the crystalline humour turbid, since neither Galen nor the other Greek physicians (as far as I have found) noted this.

units.la: Immodico ejus vsui id sine dubio scribendum est, non secus ac semen genitale immoderato ejus vsu plus satis dilutum, inefficax minusq; idoneum ad procreandos liberos efficitur.
units.tr: This must without doubt be ascribed to immoderate use of it, just as the genital seed, too much diluted by immoderate use of it, becomes ineffective and less fit for producing children.

units.la: De Endiuia, cichorio, atriplice, beta, portulaca, spinachio, &c.
units.tr: On Endive, Chicory, Orache, Beet, Purslane, Spinach, etc.

units.la: ESculenta hæc olera sunt ac culinis grata, interque hortensia solertissima cura exco- luntur. Itaque minime cibis abdicanda, quod experimento longo horum salutarem vsum vita probarit.
units.tr: These edible vegetables are pleasing to the kitchen and are grown with the most careful attention among garden plants. So they should by no means be excluded from food, since long experience of life has proved their wholesome use.

units.la: Endiuia seu Scariola hibernas hodie mensas subit, & hibernis inseruit acetariis: tantum nunc honor per frigora ei debetur & attributus est. Folia enim vbi adoleuerint exili filo, quasi in fasciculum solent colligari, & in fictilibus cooperta seruari, sic enim fit, vt & eximiè candorem, suauemque teneritudinem adipiscantur, vix enim sentitur amaritudo in candidioribus, quam diligenti olitorum cura & cultura deponunt atque amittunt.
units.tr: Endive, or scarole, now graces our winter tables and has a place among winter salads; so much honour is now given to it, and attributed to it, through the cold months. For when the leaves have grown, they are usually gathered into a small bundle with a fine thread and kept covered in earthen vessels. In this way they acquire both a remarkable whiteness and a pleasant tenderness, for bitterness is scarcely noticed in the whiter leaves, which diligent care and cultivation by gardeners remove and lose.

units.la: Quidam, si solis framentis adoperiantur putant candorem illum, gratiamque in cibis posse conciliari. Quâ de causa octobri mense vel etiam septembri seri oportet ad hiberna aceta- ria. Qui Endiuiam hiemis impatientiorem esse feribunt, vt Plinius, iis experientiam oppono, quæ in summa etiam rigoris iniuria in terris frigidioribus seruari eam testatur.
units.tr: Some think that if they are covered only with straw, that whiteness and agreeable quality can be secured in the food. For this reason it is necessary to sow in October, or even in September, for winter salads. To those who write that endive is less able to endure winter, like Pliny, I oppose experience, which testifies that in very cold lands it is preserved even amid the extreme harshness of frost.

units.la: Cichorium sativum seu hortense intene- ra adhuc ætate cibis vtiliter adhiberi cœpit con- coctii{a}coctionem enim adiuvat, epatiq ac lienis obstructiones insigniter tollit. In vsu est herba & radix. Sed Erraticum Cichorium seu Sylvestre radicem habet praclaros ad usus in medicina, ex aceto commanducata, vel etiam condita. Quidam singulariter salubrem calidiori temperatura praeditis promittunt. Abstrusas in hoc olere vires esse, flores indicant, qui Sole oriente se pandunt, quotidieq; cum eo nubilo etiam caelo circumaguntur, Eodem vero occidente se recludunt, unde & Solsequium vocitatur.
units.tr: Cultivated or garden chicory, while still young and tender, has begun to be usefully used in food; it aids digestion and notably removes obstructions of the liver and spleen. Both the herb and the root are in use. But wild chicory, or the sylvestre kind, has roots that are excellent for medicinal uses, eaten with vinegar or also preserved. Some specially promise that it is wholesome for those of a warmer constitution. That hidden powers lie in this herb, the flowers indicate: they open when the sun rises and turn daily with it even under a cloudy sky, and close again when it sets, whence it is also called sunflower (Solsequium).

units.la: Certissimum & indubitatum superiorum cum inferioribus sympathia documentum. Sed in hoc mysterio nosse oportet cichorium coeli.
units.tr: A most certain and undoubted proof of the sympathy between higher and lower things. But in this mystery one ought to know the chicory of heaven.

units.la: Atriplex, Beta & Spinachium olusculo quoq; hodie feruntur atq; excoluntur, in fculis & cibis, qui alui elicienda atque laxanda gratia, parantur, vtilia, inter quatamen Beta aluum magis ad excretionem stimulare depressa est: inter catera vero olera leuius alunt, sanguinemq; gignunt pauciorem, eumque mali succi, si non rette probeq; coquantur. Cocta enim tantum edi inueniuntur.
units.tr: Orache, beet and spinach are also now brought forward and cultivated as small vegetables, and are prepared in broths and dishes, for the sake of stirring and loosening the bowels; they are useful. Among them, however, beet is rated lower as stimulating the belly to expel. Among the other vegetables they nourish more lightly and produce less blood, and that of poor juice, unless they are cooked properly and well. For they are found to be eaten only cooked.

units.la: Hoc nota, minus ventriculo nocere, si cum sinapi aut saliem cum aceto edantur. Candida Beta magis commendatur, rubra medicamentosa est. Tenella quoque praefertur adulta.
units.tr: Note this: they harm the stomach less if eaten with mustard, or at least with vinegar. White beet is more commended; red beet is medicinal. Tender beet is also preferred to mature.

units.la: S. Spi-
units.tr: S. Spi-

units.la: Spinachium olim in re cibaria nullum habuit usum, nunc vero maximam auctoritatem assecutum solertissime excolitur. Coquitur autem aqua leniter cultello prius minutim confectum, prius tamen manibus, aut asserculis aqua, aut vligine, qua inest plurima expressa. Varios autem atque diuersos apparandi modos relinquemus cocis.
units.tr: Spinach formerly had no use as food, but now, having gained the greatest authority, it is cultivated most skilfully. It is cooked gently in water, after first being cut finely with a knife, though first squeezed with the hands or with boards, to remove the water or moisture in which it is plentiful. But we leave the various and different ways of preparing it to cooks.

units.la: Vulgo in sartagine ex oleo aut butyro frigitur, gratiaque conciliandae gratia, piperis, zinziberis, et cinnamomi polline aspergitur. Alii in olla ex largiori butyro lento igne coquunt, identidemque versant, deinde saporis gratiotia conciliandi gratia aceti momentum, et melliginem indunt, salegue condiunt.
units.tr: Commonly it is fried in a pan with oil or butter, and sprinkled with powdered pepper, ginger and cinnamon to make it agreeable. Others cook it in a pot in richer butter over a slow fire, stirring it often, then add a little vinegar and honey to give it a pleasing flavour, and season it with salt.

units.la: Certum est innocentiorem succum salubriorem que in corpus diffundere spinachium quam atriplex aut blitum. Acetarius non miscetur nisi tenellum, et parcius quidem, quia immodice sumtum promitat nauseam.
units.tr: It is certain that spinach diffuses a more innocent and wholesome juice into the body than orache or blite. It is mixed into salads only when tender, and even then sparingly, because eaten immoderately it brings on nausea.

units.la: Portulaca asitius feruoribus eximiam obtinere gratiam, nemo est qui id non norit, manditur in acetariis, nostrōque auo studiosissime in hortis magnatum feritur, quorum etiam culina cum gallinaceis pullis, aliisve lautioribus carnibus eam aegrate incoquunt.
units.tr: That purslane has an exceptional favour in the hot season, nobody is there who does not know. It is eaten in salads, and in our age is most eagerly sown in the gardens of the great, whose kitchens also cook it with chicken or other richer meats.

units.la: Quibus ventriculi os atque iecur bile aestuque efferuescunt, utilissimum iis erit cibum, alias frifrigida fumentusq; est natura, quam ob causam adjungunt cepas, ut harum acrimonia gulam irritet.
units.tr: For those whose stomach mouth and liver seethe with bile and heat, it will be most useful food; otherwise its nature is cold and moist. For this reason they add onions, so that their sharpness may stimulate the palate.

units.la: Cauliculi sale & aceto condiuntur, inque cibos hiemales astiuosq; reseruantur, aquâ deinde calidâ abluuntur aut vino, vt salsugo & acrimonia contracta ex conditura hebetetur, abluti oleo superimfuso apponuntur.
units.tr: Little stalks are seasoned with salt and vinegar and kept as food for winter and summer. Then they are washed in warm water or wine, so that the saltness and sharpness contracted from the seasoning may be blunted; washed, they are served with oil poured over them.

units.la: In horum olerum censu sunt mercurialis, asparagus, malua, rumex, buglossa, quae in cibaria non postremam dignitatem atque autoritatem reportauit, propterea quod in vinum conjecta potentibus animi hilaritatem creat melancoliamq; pellit.
units.tr: Among these herbs are counted mercury, asparagus, mallow, sorrel and bugloss, which have gained no small dignity and authority in food, because when thrown into wine they create cheerfulness in those who drink and drive away melancholy.

units.la: Verum in hac & similibus peculiariter ac priuatim naturam, ac vim singulorum considerari oportet, quatenus videl. vel sedula cura excoluntur, vel certis ac receptis experimentis salutaria & utilia hominum vita obseruata sunt.
units.tr: But in this and similar herbs one must consider the nature and power of each one particularly and individually, insofar as they are cultivated with careful attention, or their wholesome and useful qualities for human life have been observed through certain and accepted experience.

units.la: Herbarum enim in cibis alia placent caule, alia folio, alia radice, nonnulla flore, quadam cymis, hoc est, tenerioribus caulicu-lis, aliqua capite & summitatibus, &c.
units.tr: For among herbs for food, some please in the stalk, others in the leaf, others in the root, some in the flower, some in the shoots (that is, the tender little stalks), some in the head and tops, etc.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: De alimentis quæ sumuntur ex fructibus.
units.tr: On foods taken from fruits.

units.la: VArias, multiplices ac infinitas esse fructuum species atque differentias in natura rerum, ei etiam extendum est, qui à patrio solo non longe recessit: quin annus variorum fructuum feracissimus abunde id testatur.
units.tr: That fruits in nature are various, manifold and countless in kind and difference, is something that must be granted even to someone who has not strayed far from his native soil. Indeed, a year of exceptionally abundant fruit of many kinds bears ample witness to this.

units.la: Verum quoniam non omnes in cibo admittuntur, nimisque operosum foret ac prolixum de omnibus fructib. seorsim pertractare (tum quod in horum multis magnæ vitæ insidiæ subsint, tum etiam, quod major fere eorum pars voluptatis gratia magis, quam utilitatis ac salubritatis causa vsurpatur) eos hic annotabimus solum, qui salubritatem magis, quam voluptatem respiciunt. Gorgias Siculus Rhetor, Empedoclis discipulus, natus annos 109. interrogatus, quanam vitæ ratione tam optime vixisset, respondit, nihil voluptatis gratia faciendo. Hodie voluptatis gratia nihil intentatum relinquit gula in arborum fructibus, qui palatum sæpe torpidū, ventremq; cibis aliis refertissimum, alliciūt atq; inuitant magno sæpe valetudinis incommodo. Utinam ventri gulæque imperare quanquandoque possemus, ne praeter modum & intempestiue nocituris vescemur.
units.tr: Since not all fruits are admitted into the diet, and it would be too laborious and lengthy to treat each of them separately (partly because many of them carry serious dangers to life, and partly because most of them are eaten more for pleasure than for usefulness or health), I shall note here only those that have regard to health rather than pleasure. Gorgias of Sicily, a rhetorician and a pupil of Empedocles, when asked at the age of 109 by what manner of life he had lived so well, replied: by doing nothing for the sake of pleasure. Today gluttony leaves nothing untried for pleasure among the fruits of trees, which often entice and invite a palate grown dull and a stomach already crammed with other foods, often to the great detriment of health. Would that we could sometimes master our belly and our gullet, so that we did not eat things that will harm us beyond measure and at unsuitable times.

units.la: Sed quia difficile est in tanta fructuum varietate à jucundo horum aspectu blandissimisque saporibus sibi temperare, dandum est aliquid nonnunquam irritanti gulæ, pomonæque inuitanti, obseruato tamen vt dixi, modo. Plærique enim arborum fructus omnes, (vno atque altero excepto) tenue dant exiguumque nutrimentum, crudosque succos aggenerant. Itaq; nimius eorum visus cauendus.
units.tr: But since it is hard, amid such a variety of fruits, to restrain oneself from their pleasing appearance and sweetest flavours, something must sometimes be yielded to the craving appetite and to the tempting of Pomona, provided, however, that the measure I have mentioned is observed. For most tree fruits, with one or two exceptions, give thin and scanty nourishment and generate crude juices. Therefore an excessive indulgence in them is to be avoided.

units.la: Prius vero quam fructuum naturas explicare aggrediar, meminisse oportebit, quosnam ex fructibus prima mensa, & quosnam secunda apponi conueniat? Nullo enim discrimine hic fero plane modo peccatur, etiam à magnatibus, qui plus aliis valetudinem tueri studebunt. Prima mensa abdicanda sunt, nec attingenda, quæ astringendi vi pollent, nec ita promte corrumpuntur, hæc enim cum bellariis secundas mensas salubriter subeunt, cuiusmodi sunt cotonea, malorum fere omne genus, pyra, sorba, mespili, nuces, amygdalæ, pistacia, castaneæ: Prima mensa primoq; cibo apponentur, quæ facile vitiantur ac corrumpuntur, quæq; humentiora sunt, talia enim aluo molliendæ & laxandæ sunt idonea, si videl. prima sumantur, ab aliis autem escis aluum constipant, & coctionem interturbant : sicut astringendi vi prædita, vt cotonea, secunda mensa sumta, subducendæ aluo conueniunt, comprimen-do enim ac astringendo os ventriculi robo-rant, quo fit vt citius aluus deiiciat. Primam igitur mensam subibunt, cerasa, pruna, persi-ca, mora, & id genus alia fugacia & præcocia, quorum videl. gratia statim ttansuolat, mu-stea item & mellita plæraq;. Videant igitur, qui secundas mensas cerasis, prunis ac persi-cis exornant, qui tamen mos adeo in lautio-ribus mensis inualuit, principumque aulis, vt gulæ ac palato detractum putent, si non appositafuerint. Eadem ratione valetudi-nem non parum infirmant, qui primis men-sis vescuntur solidis cibis & duris, vt sunt carnes infumatæ induratæque, & quæ vel de prandio vel cœna sublatæ reseruataeque se-quenti die iterum apponuntur. Sanitatis enim tuendæ præceptum non postremum est, calida, quatenus calida, frigidis, mollia duris, humi-da siccis sunt præmittenda. Sic poma ante cotonea, hæc vero ante castaneas esitasse conuenit. Et hæc ἐν πυροδὼ & proemii loco præmonuisse placuit.
units.tr: Before I set about explaining the natures of fruits, it will be fitting to recall which fruits ought to be served at the first course and which at the second. For here people commonly go wrong without any distinction, even great men, who study most of all to guard their health. Those fruits which have a binding power and do not spoil quickly are to be kept from the first course and not touched there; they are wholesomely eaten at the second course along with the sweetmeats. Such are quinces, nearly every kind of apple, pears, sorbs, medlars, walnuts, almonds, pistachios and chestnuts. Those which spoil and rot easily, and which are more watery, are to be set at the first course and at the beginning of the meal, for such are suitable for softening and loosening the belly, provided they are eaten first; if eaten after other foods they constipate the bowels and disturb digestion. Likewise the binding fruits, such as quinces, when eaten at the second course are suited to loosening the belly, for by compressing and binding they strengthen the mouth of the stomach, which causes the bowels to move more quickly. So at the first course will come cherries, plums, peaches, mulberries, and the other fleeting and early fruits of that kind, for whose sake the appetite is at once roused, as also most of the must-like and honeyed fruits. Let those then take note who adorn their second courses with cherries, plums and peaches; yet this custom has so taken hold in more lavish tables and in princes' courts that people think their palate is cheated if these are not served. In the same way, those who eat solid and hard foods at the first course, such as smoked and hardened meats, and those things which are removed from dinner or supper, kept, and set out again the next day, weaken their health no little. For it is no minor precept for preserving health that warm things, insofar as they are warm, should be put before cold, soft before hard, and moist before dry. Thus it is fitting to eat apples before quinces, and quinces before chestnuts. These matters I have thought fit to mention by way of prelude [ἐν προοιμίῳ] and as an introduction.

units.la: Fructus igitur salubriores adq; rem ciba-riam pertinentes sunt poma, pyra, cerasa, mora, fraga, pruna, persica, melones, pepo-nes, cucumeres, cotonea, mespila, sorba, ca-stanea, nux juglans, auellana, amygdalæ, pistacia, nux pinea, malum citrium, oliuæ, ficus, vuæ, capparis. Hórum tamen quædam diuersam naturam participant, vt dicetur suo loco.
units.tr: The fruits more wholesome and relevant to the food supply are therefore apples, pears, cherries, mulberries, strawberries, plums, peaches, melons, pumpkins, cucumbers, quinces, medlars, sorbs, chestnuts, walnuts, hazelnuts, almonds, pistachios, pine nuts, citrons, olives, figs, grapes and capers. Some of these, however, share a different nature, as will be said in its proper place.

units.la: De Malis.
units.tr: On apples.

units.la: MAla hic dicuntur, quæ vulgo appellantur poma. Saporum in his multiplex differentia pro soli, cœlique natura & conditione, quæ magnas efficiunt mutationes. Pomorum in mensis secundis quoniam magna est autoritas, palmamq; sibi ante alia vendicant, ab iis quoq; exordiri nō inconueniens duxi. Verum nominatim ea persequi operosum est & parum utile, nam pro nationum & populorum libidine nomina plerumq; variant. Ordinem præcipue modumq; edendi obseruandum esse arctissime hic tenendum est. Galen. esum pomorū abdicandum censet iis, qui valetudine tueri student. Is enim quoties pomis cæterisq; fructib. immodice vesceretur, morbo tentabatur, vnde patris sui consilio (qui naturæ erat peritissimus) cautior factº, à pomis abstinuit, firmamq; sanitatem est adeptus. Sunt autem qdam prædulcia, qdam acida, austera alia & acerba. Cruda nonduq; matura ante cunċta fugienda sunt, gelidioris enim naturæ sunt, crudūq; plane succū accumulant, vnde non miru, si grauib. variisq; morbis conflictetur pueri & fœminæ, ventriculum pomis vix dū incoatæ maturitatis explentes.
units.tr: Here I mean by apples what are commonly called pomes. The differences of flavour among them are manifold, according to the nature and condition of the soil and climate, which bring about great changes. Since apples have great authority among the dessert fruits and claim the palm for themselves before others, I have thought it not out of place to begin with them. Yet to pursue them by name is laborious and of little use, for the names often vary according to the fancy of nations and peoples. The order and manner of eating must be observed most strictly here. Galen judges that the eating of apples should be forbidden to those who study to preserve their health. For whenever he ate apples and other fruits immoderately, he was attacked by sickness; and so, having taken the advice of his father, who was most skilled in nature, he became more cautious, abstained from apples, and obtained firm health. Some apples are very sweet, some sour, others astringent and bitter. Crude apples, not yet ripe, must be avoided above all, for they are of a colder nature and pile up a decidedly crude juice; hence it is no wonder that children and women, who fill their stomachs with apples barely begun to ripen, are beset by grave and varied diseases.

units.la: Qui humanioribus dant operam literis à fructuum crudorum esu plane abstinebunt, sensus enim hebetant, mentis arcem caligine replent, capita infirmiora admodum conflictant, cutimq; scabie vlceribusq; commaculant.
units.tr: Those who devote themselves to the humane letters must entirely abstain from eating raw fruit, for it dulls the senses, fills the citadel of the mind with darkness, grievously afflicts the weaker heads, and stains the skin with scabs and ulcers.

units.la: Belle matura, quæ in hiemem & æstatem seruari possunt, commendantur, salutares enim vitæ hominum præstant vsus. Cocta præterea, vel tosta ex butyro cum saccharo salubriora sunt, inque cibis magis grata. Generosa tamen quæ sunt, raro ignem experiuntur, cruda enim à magnatibus edduntur, ignobiliora, vt acerba & austera focum desiderant, coctione enim astrictionem austeritatemque amittunt.
units.tr: Apples that are fully ripe and can be kept through winter and summer are commended, for they afford wholesome use to human life. Moreover, apples that have been cooked or roasted with butter and sugar are more wholesome and more pleasing to eat. Choice apples, however, seldom undergo the fire, for great men eat them raw; the inferior sorts, such as sour and astringent ones, require the hearth, for by cooking they lose their astringency and harshness.

units.la: Quapropter perniciosum non est, vt quidam volunt, ad aluum emolliendam poma cocta primo cibo & mensa assumere, præsertim vero dulcia, quæ medium temperamentum obtinent, adque calorem nonnihil vergunt; cætera gelidioris sunt naturæ, inprimis vero fera & sylvestria, quibus ferox quoque & sapor, & succus est. Acida, austeraque stomacho robur afferunt, astringendoque aluum fluentem sistunt, stomachique vomitiones compescunt præsertim acerba, cocta ac parata. Infipida & aquofacibis plane abdicáda funt, ftomacho enim aduerfant fenfibiliter. Dul- cia quaedam & vinofa olfactu mirè, cor fami- liaritate quadam fingulari recreant, vnde in pharmacopoliis firupus de pomis celebra- tur. Vino haufto fapore & odore ingratiffi- ma cuadunt. Quae prima aeftate fere quibus- dam in locis maturefcunt Paradyfea à'qui- bufdam, aeftiua & poma S. Ioh. appellantur, parua quidem, fed odore fuaui & praedulci, odoreq; iucundo. Haec prima menfa & an- te alios cibos efiranda funt,vitiantur enim in ventriculo,fi fequantur alios cibos. Hodie in magnatum aulis fecundae menfae frequenter imponuntur,adeo praepoftere & confuse o- mnia adminiftrantur. Melimela enim o- mnia, muftea,& mellea fecundis menfis ab- dicanda esse,inter primas vero menfae volu- ptates falubriter vfurpari ratione & experi- entia conftat. Cortex pomorum odorato- rum carbonibus iniectus,fuauem fuffitum reddit, peftilentiaeque refiftere inuentus eft. Caeterum in quibufdam Germaniae locis po- ma folent(praefertim cum vberior hornm eft prouentus,aut cum vermibus teredinibusq; corroduntur, quod plurimum fieri folet,fi ante perfectam maturitatem decerpuntur) in minutas eafque oblongas partes diffecari, adq; fornacem filo appenfa,vel etiam in fur- no,vt pyra quaedam,exiccari,quae ad rei efcariæ vsus longo tempore seruantur incorrupta. Verū coćta inter alios cibos primò sunt attingenda, vt ocyus deiiciantur, post alios enim cibos sumta in ventriculo vitiantur, atq; corrumpuntur. Salubritati igitur minimè student, qui primo sumtis carnibus, tum aliis tum elixis, piscibusque poma coćta supererint. Qui mos hodie pertinaciter durat ob coquorum errorem & inscitiam. Quæstio deniq; hic prætermittenda non est, quæ sæpè in hilarioribus ac Platonicis conuiuiis controuersiam excitare solet, an vinum ab esu pomorum crudorum sit protinus superbibendum? & an meracum, an verò dilutum? Qui vinum superbibi non debere contendunt, hac se muniunt ratione, quod videlicet vinum meracius, in venas cibos incoćtos deducat, crudumque sanguinem efficiat, vnde omnis generis morbos existere necesse est, cruditates enim illæ cum sanguinea massa permixtæ malignamque qualitatem adeptæ, sanguinem ita inficiunt, vt morbi principalis causa existat. Qui in contraria sunt opinione aiunt, vinum superbibitum obtundere pernitiosos atque gelidos succos, eosq; concoquere. Experientiâ notum est, & recentiorum quorundam scriptis euulgatum, quosdam vini haustu ab esu pomorum & pyrorum intolerabiles cruciatus & dolores pertulisse, ( ab esu pyrorum quendam
units.tr: Therefore it is not harmful, as some maintain, to take cooked apples at the first course and at the beginning of the meal in order to soften the belly, especially the sweet ones, which hold a middle temperament and lean somewhat toward warmth; the rest are of a colder nature, especially the wild and woodland kinds, which have a fierce flavour and juice. Sour and astringent apples give strength to the stomach, and by binding the flowing belly they check it, and they restrain the vomiting of the stomach, especially the bitter ones, cooked and prepared. Insipid and watery apples are to be cast out of the diet entirely, for they plainly harm the stomach. Certain sweet and wine-like apples wonderfully refresh the heart by a singular affinity with it by smell, which is why a syrup of apples is celebrated in the apothecaries' shops. When wine is drunk after them, they produce a most unpleasant taste and smell. Those that ripen in early summer in some places, called Paradise apples by some and summer apples or St John's apples by others, are indeed small, but have a sweet scent and a very sweet fragrance. These are to be eaten at the first course and before other foods, for they spoil in the stomach if they follow other foods. Today in the courts of great men apples are often placed at the second course, so topsy-turvy and confused is everything they administer. It is established by reason and experience that all apples that are honeyed, must-like, and honey-sweet are to be banished from the second course, while among the first pleasures of the table they are wholesomely enjoyed. The peel of fragrant apples thrown on charcoal gives a sweet fumigation, and it has been found to resist pestilence. Moreover, in some parts of Germany, when the yield of apples is especially abundant, or when they are eaten away by worms and woodworm (which happens very often if they are plucked before full ripeness), they are customarily cut into small, elongated pieces, hung on a string over a furnace or even in an oven, like certain pears, and dried, and so kept for a long time uncorrupted for use as dried food. But cooked apples must be taken first among the other foods, so that they may be passed through more quickly, for if eaten after other foods they spoil and rot in the stomach. Therefore those who eat cooked apples after meats, both roast and boiled, and after fish, take little care for their health. This custom persists stubbornly today through the error and ignorance of cooks. Finally, a question must not be passed over here, one which often stirs debate at cheerful and Platonic banquets: must wine be drunk at once after eating raw apples? And is it to be neat or diluted? Those who contend that wine should not be drunk afterwards defend themselves by this reasoning: that undiluted wine carries undigested food into the veins and makes crude blood, and from this all kinds of disease must arise, for those crudities, mixed with the bloody mass and taking on a malignant quality, so infect the blood that they become the principal cause of the illness. Those of the opposite opinion say that wine drunk afterwards dissolves the harmful and cold juices and digests them. It is known from experience, and has been published in the writings of some more recent authors, that some men, after eating apples and pears and drinking wine, suffered intolerable torments and pains (I myself can testify that a certain man died from drinking beer after eating pears); Italy also bears witness that others died from drinking wine after eating figs, although the Italians, who seem more cautious in this matter, drink neat wine at once after apples and pumpkins, the best of wines.

units.la: plane cereuisiae potu periisse, ipse testis esse possum) alios quoque a ficuum esu, vini potu interiisse, testis est Italia, quamuis Itali, qui hac in parte cautiores videntur, vinum meracum optimum a pomis & pepo- nibus superbibunt. Hic vt certi aliquid statuatur, sequens prius quaestio, oportu- ne mihi hic occurrens, discutienda est, an poma caeterique fructus cum pane sint e- dendi?
units.tr: I myself can testify that a certain man died from drinking beer after eating pears. Italy is witness that others too have died from drinking wine after eating figs, although the Italians, who seem more careful in this matter, drink strong, pure wine after apples and melons. To settle this point, the following question, which arises here opportunely, must first be examined: should apples and other fruits be eaten with bread?

units.la: Distinctione hic opus esse video, inter fructus videlicet praecoces, qui cito mature- fcunt, & cito corrumpuntur, vt sunt cerasa, dulcia, fraga, pruna, persica, mora, & inter eos, qui per integrum feruantur annum, vt poma quaedam, castaneae, auellanae, iuglan- des. Quidam mediam naturam partici- pant, vt ficus, vuae, pyra & pomorum genera quaedam, haec enim no ita facile putrescunt, nec tam longo tempore perdurant, vt castaneae, &c. Quidam non infimae eruditionis atque grauitatis autores, primi ordinis fructus in vniuersum absque pane comedi debere existimant, quoniam sunt substantiae tenuioris aqueaeque, facilimeque putrescunt.
units.tr: Here, I see, a distinction is needed between early fruits, which ripen quickly and spoil quickly, such as cherries, sweet cherries, strawberries, plums, peaches and mulberries, and those which keep for a whole year, such as certain apples, chestnuts, hazelnuts and walnuts. Some fruits take an intermediate nature, such as figs, grapes, pears and certain kinds of apples, for these do not rot so easily nor last so long as chestnuts and the like. Some authors of no little learning and authority hold that fruits of the first order should in general be eaten without bread, since they are of a thinner and watery substance and very easily putrefy.

units.la: His vero ego regero, eo magis cum pane efitandos esse, quia panis firmiffimu esculentorum potulentorumq; vinculum, facilem eorum putredinem & corruptionem retardat &c. & impedit, tenuioremque ipsorum substantiam crassiorem reddit, quò minus in ventriculo fluctuent. Verissimum est, quicquid etiam hic statuatur, cerasa, pruna, persica, si secunda mensa apponuntur sine pane esitare insalubre prorsus esse, praesertim si multum superbibatur, id quod omnibus sanitatis conservandae studiosis diligenter observandum relinquo: cum pane enim ita commixti non adeo facile corrumpuntur, nam panis veluti refrenat iustorum malitiam. De secundi ordinis fructibus sciendum, illos à cibo edendos esse, & quidem alias cum pane, alias sine eo. Cum pane, si superbiendum est, ut in lautioribus convivii: sine pane at cum sale, si exiccare, nec multum superbibere animus est, subtantia enim eorum magis est terrea, humoribusque non redundat, tum etiam, ne, si primo sumeretur, quia grauia sunt, cibi particulam crudam ac incoctam per venas secum rapiant, unde putredines humorumque corruptiones (praesertim si in venis permanserint) generari necesse est.
units.tr: To this I reply that they should be eaten all the more with bread, because bread, the firmest bond of foods and drinks, slows their easy decay and corruption and hinders it, and makes their thinner substance denser, so that they do not float about in the stomach. It is most true, whatever else may be decided here, that if cherries, plums and peaches are served at the dessert course without bread, eating them is altogether unwholesome, especially if much wine is drunk on top of them. This I leave to all who are zealous for preserving health to observe carefully, for when they are mixed with bread in this way they do not so easily corrupt; for bread, as it were, restrains the wickedness of the juices. As for fruits of the second order, it should be known that they are to be eaten after the meal, sometimes with bread and sometimes without it. With bread, if one is going to drink freely, as at the more lavish banquets; without bread but with salt, if one intends to dry out and not to drink much. For their substance is rather earthy and does not overflow with moisture. Also, lest, if they were taken first, since they are heavy, they should carry off with them through the veins a raw and undigested particle of food, from which putrefactions and corruptions of the humours must necessarily arise, especially if they remain in the veins.

units.la: Ex medii ordinis fructibus ficus, cumprimis recentes vuaeque ante alios cibos, & quidem cum pane edantur, pyra vero pomaque fugacia & praecocia, quae videlicet cito maturescunt, secunda etiam mensa concedi possunt sine pane, si nihil superbibatur, est enim id valde noxium, cum multo sint praedita humore & corruptioni facilè obnoxia. In dysenteria omnes fructus, præsertim astrin-gentes, vt pyra, mora, sorba, cotonea, cum pa-ne edi debere recte voluit Alexander Tralli-anus. Horum enim succus cum panis sub-stantia mixtus, perque intima corporis pene-trans, aliquum sistit. Sine vero pane comesta ventrem repente & facile penetrant, parum-que aut nihil de facultate sua in intestinis re-linquunt. Experimento didici, pyrorum, cerasorum præsertim acidorum, mororum, prunorum, &c. succum post cibum degluti-tum minus noxæ inferre, quam si cum tota substantia deuorentur, succus enim ille vino exhilaratis fumos reprimit, absolutoq; prandio efficit, vt quis minus ebrietati succum-bat, mensque minus ex vapore vini debilite-tur. In hoc casu quoque præstant poma suc-culenta, citria, arantia, &c. Quidam distin-ctione vtuntur in determinanda hac quæsti-one. Fructus enim nunc medicamenti, nunc cibi rationem subeunt. Si sumuntur vt medi-camentum, absque pane esirari debent, alui sc. emolliendi corporisque alterandi gratiâ, vt refrigerandi, astringendi, humectandi, &c. Si enim cum cibis sumerentur, vis & facultas ipsorum obtunderetur, fungiqve officio suo minimè possent. Si vt cibi sumuntur, cum pa-ne, esitasse expedit, ne velociter aluum subeant, sed in ventriculo paulisper remaneant.
units.tr: Of the fruits of the middle order, figs, especially fresh ones, and grapes are to be eaten before other foods, and indeed with bread. Pears and apples that are fleeting and early, that is, which ripen quickly, may be allowed at the dessert course without bread, provided nothing is drunk on top of them, for that is very harmful, since they abound in moisture and are easily liable to corruption. In dysentery all fruits, especially the astringent ones, such as pears, mulberries, service-berries and quinces, ought rightly to be eaten with bread, as Alexander of Tralles wished. For their juice, mixed with the substance of the bread and penetrating deep into the body, checks the flux to some extent. But when eaten without bread they quickly and easily pass through to the bowel, leaving little or nothing of their power in the intestines. I have learned by experience that the juice of pears, especially sour cherries, mulberries, plums and so on, swallowed after a meal, does less harm than when they are gulped down whole, for that juice checks the vapours of those who are exhilarated by wine, and when the meal is finished it makes a man less liable to succumb to drunkenness, and his mind is less weakened by the fumes of the wine. In this case too juicy apples, citrons, oranges and the like are of service. Some make a distinction in settling this question. For fruits sometimes take the place of medicine and sometimes of food. If they are taken as medicine, they should be eaten without bread, namely for the sake of loosening the bowels and altering the body, as for cooling, astringing, moistening and so on. For if they were taken with foods, their force and power would be blunted, and they could not perform their office at all. If they are taken as food, it is advisable to eat them with bread, so that they do not pass quickly through the bowels but remain a little while in the stomach.

units.la: Vnum deniq; probè animaduertendum hic est minus malum esse, si fructibus vescentes tot diuersarum qualitatum ac virium cibos non admiscuerint, manifestum enim est, variis & diuersae naturae cibis appetitum excitari quidem, sed multo plus ingerere quam conueniat, vnde cruditates multas humorumque putredines existere necesse est, tandemque morbos. Vno igitur victus genere simus contenti.
units.tr: Finally, this one thing must be carefully noted here: it is a lesser evil if those who eat fruits do not mix with them many foods of different qualities and powers. For it is clear that appetite is stirred up by various foods of different natures, and so much more is taken in than is fitting; hence many crudities and putrefactions of the humours must necessarily arise, and at last diseases. Let us therefore be content with one kind of diet.
