units.la: Praeterea in fluxu alui & dysenteria non opus semper est astringentia ante omnes alios cibos exhibere, sed quandoque etiam post exhibita & medicamenta, & alimenta pro ventriculi scilicet corroboratione, vt ita ventriculi os corroboratu phibere possit, ne humores amplius in intestina confluant. Verû iudicio hic opus est, quàdo videl. & quomodo astringentes fructus in statu etiam sanitatis sint exhibendi. Ex hactenus igitur dictis, facile iudicare est de proposita supra quaestione, an vinum post crudorum pomorum esum statim sit superbibendum? Cesso igitur ne minima prolixitate lectorem fatigare videar. De potu ex pomis multis gentibus visato, vide cap. de potulentis.
units.tr: Moreover, in a flux of the bowels and in dysentery it is not always necessary to give astringents before all other foods; sometimes they should be given also after medicines and nourishment, namely for strengthening the stomach, so that by strengthening the mouth of the stomach it may be able to prevent the humours from flowing further into the intestines. But here judgement is needed, namely when and how astringent fruits are to be given even in a state of health. From what has been said so far, it is easy to judge the question proposed above, whether wine should be drunk immediately after eating raw fruit. I will therefore stop, lest I seem to weary the reader with excessive length. Concerning drink made from fruits, seen among many peoples, see the chapter on drinks.

units.la: De pyris.
units.tr: On pears.

units.la: GEnera pyrorum enumerare nemo poterit, & quæ de pomis sunt dicta, pariter de pyris fere intelligi possunt. Quædam ad maturitatem properant, suntque prima quæ decerpuntur, ac saporis gratissimi deprehenduntur. Sunt & alia quæ tardius ad maturitatem perveniunt, ut autumno, quæ etiam reseruata durant in hiemem, crudaque & coctissimè manduntur, sunt autem quæ mirum in modum grandescunt, ac viridiora cernuntur, à nostris hominibus vocantur Winterbirnen / quod in mensës durent hibernos. Inter muscatellina, omniaque alia quæ palato grata sunt, t rizias tenent, quæ vulgo appellantur Mandelbirnen / saporis suavissimi ac iucundissimi, vnæ præcæteris omnibus nutrire bonum corpori succum præbere creduntur: perfectè autem matura tales præstant usu, & alterâ parte rubescunt, eoque vnaslanescunt. Verum hic tenendum, pyrorum sicut & pomorum mustèorum nimio esu homines quandoque strangulari seu suffocari, saporis enim tanta est gratia, ut nec appetendi nec edendi finis fit. Itaque seruandus modus. Quidam ex pyris concinnant potum, qui tamen tanta gratia vtilitatisque non est, quam potus ex pomis, qui sæpè subiicitur pro vino inter epulas, quique sunt crassioris palato, vix fraudem deprehendunt.
units.tr: No one can list all the kinds of pears, and what has been said of apples can almost equally be applied to pears. Some ripen early, and the first ones picked are found to have the most delightful flavour. There are also others that ripen more slowly, in autumn, which keep even when stored and last into winter, and which are eaten raw and very ripe. There are also some that grow to a remarkable size and look rather green. Our people call these Winterbirnen because they last through the winter months. Among the muscatels and all the other kinds pleasing to the palate, the trizias hold the first place, commonly called Mandelbirnen . They have a most sweet and agreeable flavour, and they are believed to supply, above all others, juice that nourishes the body well. When perfectly ripe they show their effect in use: one side turns red and they become soft. Yet it must be kept in mind here that, as with must-apples, people are sometimes strangled or suffocated by eating too many pears, for their flavour is so enticing that there is no end to wanting and eating them. Moderation must therefore be observed. Some make a drink from pears, but it is not of such charm or usefulness as the drink from apples. The apple drink is often served in place of wine at feasts, and those of coarser palate hardly detect the fraud.

units.la: NB. Potus ex pomis sæpè pro vino veniit.
units.tr: Note: drink made from apples is often passed off as wine.

units.la: Occurrit mihi hic admodum lepida & facetosa historia, de perfido quodam Iudæo à pagano quodam huius loci, anno 1604. emturo vinum. Is vinariam cellam paganì ingressus, vina eius vendibilia, quæ peculiaribus in doliis seorsim reposita continebantur, degustans, inter pitíssima elegit dolium continens potum ex fele fructus pomum ohmas 4. Paganus, vix fore existimans, ut Iudæus hunc, cuius perfidia & impostura toti vicinia erat nota & pernitiosa, dolo circumuenire, consensit, cumque de pretio convenissent, Iudæus vinum ex pomis, quod ipsi inprimis vel potius stupido ipsius palato magis placuerat, latus ad suos deferri curavit, gloriari non desistens, misere simplici illum paganum à se deceptum esse, emisse se pro tolerabili pretio vinum, quo vix præstantius aliud. Verum præstanti illo vino acorem acquirente & mucorem (quod facile ex dolio vel non vsquequaque pleno, vel etiam non probè occlusó contingere potuit, vel etiam, si dolia nō exquisitè plena, alio quam ipsa continent liquore, opplentur) cum se deceptum intelligeret, paganus perfidia & malitia incusat. Venium est admodum dicem, aliud est & pronunciatum, Iudæum damnatum vinum retinere, quod ipse sibi ex multis aliis elegerat, iura coegerunt. Hactenus de Iudæo, nunc ad rem.
units.tr: A most charming and witty story comes to mind here, about a treacherous Jew who, in 1604, went to buy wine from a pagan of this place. Entering the pagan's wine cellar and tasting his saleable wines, which were kept apart in special casks, he chose from the best the cask holding a drink made from apples, four ohms of it. The pagan, scarcely thinking that the Jew could be tricked by guile, a man whose treachery and fraud were known to and harmful to the whole neighbourhood, agreed. When they had settled the price, the Jew had the apple wine, which had pleased him above all, or rather his dull palate, carried off to his people, boasting all the while that he had deceived the simple pagan: he had bought a wine at a tolerable price, hardly any better. But when that excellent wine turned sour and mouldy (which could easily happen from a cask not quite full or not well sealed, or even if casks that are not completely full are topped up with some liquid other than what they contain), the pagan, realising he had been cheated, accused the Jew of treachery and malice. The case came before a judge, and the sentence was pronounced: the condemned Jew was to keep the wine he had chosen for himself from among many others, as the laws required. So much for the Jew; now to the subject.

units.la: Pyrorum hodie quadam torrentur furno, alia cinere feruente, quædam ex butyro coquuntur cum saccharo culina, cum vino, cinnamomo & & saccharo: piflores dulciarii cinnamomo confi- gunt, & incrustata coquunt, idq; pro variis gula irritamentis. Solent etiam concidi pyra, sicut & poma ac cotonea, ficcataq; reseruari advsum ci- barium durant enim in annum & vltra. Quì- dam non leues autores omnia pyra astringere exiccareq; aperte scripserunt, quodfalsum esse (pace eorum) experientia testatur, quaedam e- nim adeo fuccofa sunt mitia & suauia, vt astrì- ctam aliam molliant, lubricamq; reddant.
units.tr: Today some pears are roasted in an oven, others in hot ashes, and some are cooked in butter with sugar in the kitchen, or with wine, cinnamon and sugar. Confectioners preserve pears with cinnamon and bake them encrusted, to tempt the palate in various ways. Pears are also commonly cut up, as are apples and quinces, dried and stored for use at table, for they keep a year or more. Some writers of no small standing have openly written that all pears are astringent and drying. This is false, with all respect to them, as experience shows: some are so juicy, mild and sweet that they soften another astringent pear and make it laxative.

units.la: De cerasis.
units.tr: On cherries.

units.la: NOminantur hæc à Ponti oppido Ce- rasunte, vnde Mithridate & Tigrane deuictis à Lucullo in Italiam sunt de- ueĉta, anno vrbis DCLXXX. teste Plinio & Atheneo, quamuis longe ante Lucullì vi- ctoria cerasa cognita fuisse Diphilus Siphni ipso Lucullo multis annorum curriculis vetu- stior, testatur, qui de iis scripsit. Distinguitur colore & sapore, quaedam enim rubent, quae- dam nigrescunt, alia albescunt simul & rube- scunt: quaedam item dulcia sunt, quaedam a- mariuscula, alia acida quae principatum obti- nuerunt, quaedam subacida, gratiqué saporis sunt. Varias autem sortiuntur appellationes, quaedam enim vocantur Macedonica, alia aproniana, nonnulla actiana, Iuliana & Du- racina. Sed de nominib° nolumus esse superstitiosi & solliciti, viribus explorandis in-cumbamus. Quæ tardius maturitatem adi-piscuntur vtacida, principatum obtinent, ci-bi enim appetentiam excitant, pituitamque incidunt, astringendiquefua viventriculum roborant, inest enim illis succus vinosus & mire gratus. Prædulcia & matura aluum e-molliunt, ocyusq; deiiciuntur, adeò quidem, vt si quis mane roscida ea deuoret, in tantum leuetur aluus, vt pedes podagrici morbo li-berentur. Omnia cerasa inprimis verò acida & rubentiora bonum generare succum te-nuiterque alere, cum peruetusto scriptore & medico Diphilo constanter affirmo. Acida quoq; insolantur, saccharoque condiuntur, quæ sitientibus ægris linguæq; ariditati ma-gnum afferunt auxilium. Siccantur etiam so-le vel furno dulcia, sicut & acida, vbi id mira-ri subit, quod illa acescant, hæc verò dulce-scant. Non probantur quæ arte fiunt præco-cia, calce sc. viua aut aqua calida arborum ra-dicibus affusa.
units.tr: Cherries take their name from the town of Cerasus in Pontus, whence Lucullus brought them to Italy after defeating Mithridates and Tigranes, in the year 680 from the founding of the city, as Pliny and Athenaeus attest. Yet Diphilus of Siphnos, who wrote about them and was many years older than Lucullus, testifies that cherries were known long before Lucullus's victory. They are distinguished by colour and taste: some are red, some blackish, others whitish and red at once; some are sweet, some slightly bitter, and others sour, which hold the first place; some are subacid and of pleasant flavour. They have various names: some are called Macedonian, others Apronian, some Actian, Julian and Duracine. But we do not want to be superstitious and anxious about names; let us set ourselves to examining their powers. Those that reach maturity later, the sour ones, hold the first place: they stimulate the appetite, cut phlegm, and strengthen the stomach by their astringency, for they contain a wine-like juice that is wonderfully pleasant. The very sweet and ripe ones soften the bowels and pass through more quickly, so that if someone eats them in the morning while they are still dewy, the bowels are so relieved that feet afflicted with gout are freed from the disease. I affirm constantly, with the very ancient writer and physician Diphilus, that all cherries, especially the sour and redder ones, generate good juice and nourish finely. Sour cherries are also dried in the sun and preserved with sugar, and they give great help to thirsty patients and to dryness of the tongue. Sweet cherries too are dried in the sun or in an oven, as are sour ones; it is a wonder to some that the former turn sour and the latter become sweet. Those forced to ripen early by artifice are not approved, namely when quicklime or warm water is poured on the roots of the trees.

units.la: Ex acidis deniq; vel solis vel etiam dulci-bus permistis, diligentes matresfamilias no-runt concinnare edulium electuarii instar, quod magni est vsus in re cibaria & familia-ri. In amplo vase æneo coquuntur luculen-to igne: semicoctacribratur nucleisabiectis, quod per cribrum traiectum est, coquitur denuò perpetuò agitando, donec iustam ele-ctuarii stuarii consistentiam adipiscatur, lautiores condiunt id zinzibere, cinnamomo, pipere, garyophyllis &c.
units.tr: Finally, from sour cherries, or from sweet ones mixed with them, careful housewives know how to prepare a food like an electuary, which is of great use in everyday household cooking. It is boiled in a large bronze vessel over a bright fire. Half-cooked, it is passed through a sieve with the stones thrown in; what has gone through the sieve is cooked again, stirred constantly, until it reaches the proper thick consistency of a stewed electuary. The more refined cooks season it with ginger, cinnamon, pepper, cloves and so on.

units.la: Dixi superstitiosum esse de nominibus alter-cari, sed potius in rebus ipsis versari atque persistere, distinguenda enim cerasa, sicut & cæteri fructus sunt non ex nominum appel-latione, in qua autores maximè dissentiunt, facilisq; lapsus est, sed ex adiunctis ipsis qua-litatibus, vt sapore, odore & colore, natura ac vires omnium fructuum inuestigantur. Quis enim Cerasorum omnium sicut & py-rorum genera, species & figuras enumerare queat, taceo appellationes & nomina, quæ cuique ferè terræ & genti sunt peculiaria. Itaq; curiosius ea distinguere superuacuum puto, cum nemini non sint notissima. Dura-cina saltè ea appellari ab autoribus animad-uerti, quæ duriori sunt callo & nucleo.
units.tr: I said it is superstitious to wrangle over names; one should rather dwell on and hold to the things themselves. For cherries, like other fruits, are to be distinguished not by their names, over which authors disagree most and where slips are easy, but by their own qualities, such as taste, smell and colour; it is from these that the nature and powers of all fruits are investigated. For who could list all the kinds, species and forms of cherries, as of pears? I say nothing of the names peculiar to almost every land and people. So I think it superfluous to distinguish them too finely, since they are known to everyone. I have only noticed that those called Duracine by the authors are the ones with a harder flesh and stone.

units.la: De morbis.
units.tr: On diseases.

units.la: IN nouissimis florent, & inter prima matu-refcunt. Arbor exasto frigore quia germinat, prudentissima dicitur. Algida loca reformi-dat, propterea quæ non vbiq; proueniit. Ex moris co-stu eclegma adoris & colli vlcera interna vti-liter adhibetur cum melle rosarū. Memorabile, quod Pytharmus apud Atheneum memoria pro-didit, l. 2. c. 20, moros in sua patria per 20. annos srustu nullu protulisse, atq; tanta podagra omnes inuasisse, vt homines nō solum pueri, item puellæ,
units.tr: In the latest season they flower, and among the first they ripen again. The tree is called most prudent because it sprouts again once the harsh cold is past. It shuns cold places, which is why it does not grow everywhere. From the juice of the mulberry an electuary is usefully applied to ulcers of the mouth and colon, with rose honey. Memorable is what Pytharmus reported in Athenaeus, book 2, chapter 20: that for twenty years the mulberries in his country bore no fruit, and gout attacked everyone so severely that not only men, boys and girls, but also eunuchs and women were afflicted by that disease, and it so infested the flocks of goats and sheep that scarcely a third part of them remained free.

units.la: T Eunuchi & mulieres, eo morbo tentarentur, sed etiam caprarum onuumq; gregem ita infestârit, vt vix tertia earum pars extaret libera.
units.tr: Eunuchs and women were attacked by that disease, but it so infested the flocks of goats and sheep that scarcely a third part of them remained free.

units.la: An vero hoc ita euenerit, quia mora podagram arcent, in controuersiam venire potest. Testatur Galenus atq; Hippocr. mora quæ satis maturue- runt, ventrem subducere, stomachumq; squalli- dum æstuantemq; consolari, præsertim frigida si sint, & paulo ante alios cibos sumantur, moxq; fiat deambulatio, unde Horatius non immerito cecinit, Ille salubres, Æstates peraget, qui nigris prandia moris Finiet, ante grauem quæ legerit arbore solem.
units.tr: Whether this happened because mulberries ward off gout is open to dispute. Galen and Hippocrates testify that mulberries which have ripened sufficiently loosen the bowels and soothe a foul, fevered stomach, especially if they are cold and are taken shortly before other food, and then a walk follows. Whence Horace not undeservedly sang: "He will spend healthy summers who ends his midday meal with black mulberries, picked before the heavy sun."

units.la: Peculiari vero facultate podagricis auxilia- ri, quo minus illi infestentur, à nemine adhuc vi- di obseruatum. Experimenti via facilis est. Ve- risimile tamen est, ac fieri potuisse credibile mo- ra frequenter Pytharini ætate ab omnib. effitata stomachis recreatis aluisq; liquatis & emollitis eorum humorum lapsum & prouentum, qui in- articulos decumbentes podagram gignere con- sueuerunt, intercipere. Id quod & Galenus con- firmat, dicens, aluos habentes astrictas podagris esse obnoxias. Verum de capris & ouibus, quæ mororum fructus non attingunt, & tamen ab ea lue immunes no exiterunt, quid sentiam, no oc- curris, nisi quod ex aeris inclementia quadam- moris moris inimica, in pedum morbos inciderint. Morus enim, teste Theophrasto, quia nouissime omnium germinat, si quando pruina laedatur vel frigoribus, quemadmodum laediprodita est, Psal. 77. & apud Plinium lib. 16. cap. 26. intemperiem caeli insignem esse constat, qua etiam ad pedes deduci ac delabi defluxiones non est a ratione alienum. Trinus inest moris color, primo candidus, mox rubens, maturis niger: rubea acerbior, funr, matura vinosa. Certum est abstrusum quid & magneticum hanc arborem, certius indicare indiciis usque externis, de qua tamen re firmiore experientia aliquid dicam amplius alibi.
units.tr: That anyone has so far observed a special power in mulberries to help those suffering from gout, so that they are less afflicted, I have not come across. The experiment is easy. Yet it is likely, and it is credible that it could have happened, that in Pytharmus' time mulberries, frequently eaten by everyone, calmed the stomachs and loosened and softened the bowels, and so intercepted the flow and outpouring of those humours which, settling in the joints, tend to produce gout. Galen also confirms this, saying that those with constipated bowels are prone to gout. But as for goats and sheep, which do not touch mulberry fruit and yet were not spared that plague, I do not see what to think, except that from some harshness of the air, hostile to mulberries, they fell into diseases of the feet. For the mulberry, according to Theophrastus, because it sprouts last of all, is easily harmed if at any time it is struck by hoarfrost or cold, as is shown in Psalm 77, and as Pliny says in book 16, chapter 26, it is well known to be a notable sign of an unsettled sky; by which it is also not unreasonable that catarrhs should drop down and flow to the feet. The mulberry has three colours: first white, then red, and when ripe black. The red is more sour, and the ripe black is wine-like. It is certain that this tree has something hidden and magnetic, which it indicates more surely than by outward signs; I shall say more about this matter elsewhere, on firmer experience.

units.la: De moris albis cur a nullo fere antiquorum mentio facta sit (excepto Ouidio, qui in fabula Pyrami & Thisbes, vbi eorum sanguine mora alba rubrum contraxisse colorem canens videtur potius vlla candida inueniri negasse) facile est illis intelligere, qui norunt, id arboris genus ex insitione super populum albam facta emanasse, quae cum in Europa ac sub Romani imperii ditione fere apparuerit, sicut complures alia insitiones, mirum non est, si pauca de ipsis ab auctoribus tradita legantur. Quam etiam causam esse puto, quod sericum ad Galeni vsque tempora rarum fuerit, qui in 13. lib. method. scribit, id in urbibus Romanorum magnis tantum opulentisque mulieribus familiare fuisse. Ea enim animalcula, quae sericam nobis diuina quadam arte laniam fundunt, quia potissimum foliis mori nutriuntur. untur, iusq; pinguefacta fœcundiora euadunt, sicut rariora tuncfuerunt, & pauciora, ita etiam mororum tenuis erat & rarus prouentus. Testatur enim in vita Iustiniani Zonaras, Imperatoris illius tempore sericam telam à Romanis texi coeptam, quæ prius à Perficis mercatoribus adducebatur, quomodo̅q; ex vermium isto-rum tela filiisq; fieret, ignorabatur. Duos enim monachos ex India Byzantium profectos originem illius declarasse, utq; ex perexiguis ouis per fatum vermes isti educerentur, edulti morifolii alerentur, post modum ipsis natura magistra filum reddentibus sericum texeretur, nō sine multis muneribus edocuisse idem auctor est. De Ægyptia moro nobis ignota, qui aliquid scire desiderat, videat Theophr. l.4.c.2.
units.tr: Why almost none of the ancients mention white mulberries (except Ovid, who, in the tale of Pyramus and Thisbe, where he sings that the white mulberry took on a red colour from their blood, seems rather to deny that any white ones are to be found) is easy to understand for those who know that this kind of tree came from grafting onto a white poplar. Since it appeared mostly in Europe and under the rule of the Roman empire, as have several other grafts, it is no wonder that little about them is handed down by authors. I think this is also the reason why silk was rare until the time of Galen, who writes in book 13 of the Method that it was customary only in the great cities of the Romans and among wealthy women. For those little creatures which spin for us silk wool by a divine art feed chiefly on mulberry leaves. As they are fattened by these and become more fruitful, so when those were rare and few, the yield of mulberries was also thin and scarce. For Zonaras, in the Life of Justinian, testifies that in that emperor's time the Romans began to weave silk cloth, which had previously been brought in by Persian merchants, and how thread and cloth were made from those worms was unknown. The same author says that two monks who had come from India to Byzantium explained its origin, and taught, not without many gifts, how these worms are hatched by fate from tiny eggs, fed on mulberry leaves, and afterwards, with nature as their teacher, yield thread from which silk is woven. On the Egyptian mulberry, which is unknown to us: whoever wishes to know more, let him see Theophrastus, book 4, chapter 2.

units.la: De fragis.
units.tr: On strawberries.

units.la: DE his parum à veteribus medicis proditum reperitur. Quidam fructum terræ nominant, & fraga terrestria, ad differentiam mororum Celsi, de quibus in præcedente cap. & mororum rubi, quæ vulgus <bl>Himbeeren vnd Brombeeren</bl> appellat. Fructus sunt pulcrè rubentes, suauisq; odoris. Reperiuntur & fraga à maturitate candida, sed rariora sunt. Fœminarum nobile genus fraga in maximis habet delitiis, edunt enim ea ex lactis cremore saccharo inspersó; sperso:aliæ vino irrigant,facchariq; pollinem adiiciunt, quædam statim lectaac decerpta vorantur. Pulticulæ quoq; ex fragis concinnantur pro delicatioribus aduersus iecoris, stomachi,renumq; æstum vtiles. Cui etiam rei mire conducit aqua destillata, calentem enim nimis sanguinem refrigerat & recreat, faciesq; plurimum rubentibus auxilio est.Hic vero errorem coarguere oportet, quod plerique omnes potissimum feré Magnates secundas suas mensas iis exornant, cum vt cerasa, mora,cæteraq; fugacia primo cibo fumi deBeant,aluum enim molliunt, refrigerant & humectant,sitimque leniunt, peractoenim prandio,autcœna in corpus admissa putrescunt,morbisq; ex putredine excitatis seminaria ministrant. Adnotasse præterea hoc in loco oportebit, fraga, vt quæ parum à terra distent,facile a serpentibus,bufonibus, & id genus venenatis animalibus calcari, arrodique,nec tamen virus accipere, aut alienum saporem assumere, quod argumento est nullam iis cum venenis esse cognationem: neq; enim scriptum aut auditum vsquam est, quenquam esu horum veneno infectum fuisse. Nihilominus tamen decerpta, antequam deuorentur, frigida pura abluantur.
units.tr: Little about these is reported by the ancient physicians. Some call it the fruit of the earth, and wild strawberries, to distinguish them from the mulberries of Celsus, discussed in the preceding chapter, and the brambleberries which the common people call Himbeeren and Brombeeren. The fruits are beautifully red and sweet-smelling. Strawberries are also found white when ripe, but these are rarer. Women of noble rank take the greatest delight in strawberries: they eat them with cream of milk sprinkled with sugar; others steep them in wine and add sugar dust; some are eaten straight away, as soon as they are picked. Pulp of strawberries is also prepared as a delicacy, useful against the heat of the liver, stomach and kidneys. Distilled water from them is also remarkably helpful for this, for it cools and refreshes blood that is too hot, and it is a great help to those with red faces. Here, however, it is right to correct an error: most people, and especially the great men, adorn their dessert with them, whereas, like cherries, mulberries and other perishable things, they should be eaten at the first course. For they loosen the bowels, cool and moisten, and soothe thirst; but when dinner or supper is over and they are taken into the body, they rot and provide seedbeds for diseases arising from putrefaction. It will also be worth noting here that strawberries, since they lie close to the ground, are easily trodden on and gnawed by snakes, toads and that kind of venomous creature, yet they do not take on poison or acquire a foreign taste. This is evidence that they have no kinship with those poisons; for it has never been written or heard anywhere that anyone was infected with poison by eating them. Nevertheless, before they are devoured, let those that have been picked be washed in clean cold water.

units.la: T
units.tr: T

units.la: Quibus deniq; eparestfrigidum, ventriculusq; eadem intemperie laborat, vel à nimio fragorum vsu abstinebunt, vel comedent ea ex vino cum saccharo & cinnamomo.
units.tr: Those whose stomach is cold, and whose stomach suffers from the same intemperance, should either abstain from excessive use of strawberries or eat them in wine with sugar and cinnamon.

units.la: De prunis.
units.tr: On Plums.

units.la: PRuna feré omnia pofi Catonem coepisse certum est. Plura sunt eorum genera, sapore, calore, figura & magnitudine diftin-cta. Principatum obtinent Damascena, quorum quædam nigra sunt, quædam rubent, quædam violacea cernuntur. Sic appellata à celeberrima vrbe Damasco, alii vocant Syriaca: deportantur sicca in omnem feré terram, inq; coquinis magnatum non postremum tenent locum. Conficitur ex his confectio, quæ diaprunum appellatur, ad febres siccas commodissimum, ob humectandi & refrigerandi vim. Recentia omnia aluum laxant, emolliuntq;, insigniter enim humectant probè matura, immatura enim acerbiora sunt, unde ob acriorem quendam qui illis inest, succu eumq; crudum, intestina vellicant, fluxumq; dysentericum excitant.
units.tr: It is certain that almost all kinds of plums began to be grown after Cato's time. There are many varieties, distinguished by flavour, warmth, shape and size. The damson holds the first place; some are black, some red, and some appear violet. It is so called from the famous city of Damascus, though others call it the Syrian plum. They are exported dried to nearly every land, and hold no small place in the kitchens of the great. From them is made a confection called diaprunum, most suitable for dry fevers because of its power to moisten and cool. All fresh plums loosen and soften the bowels, for well-ripened ones moisten notably, while unripe ones are more sour. Because of a certain sharper quality in them, their raw juice pinches the intestines and provokes dysenteric flux.

units.la: Eligenda autem quæ amplitudine, suavitate, saporisq; gratia commendantur, ea enim cæteris plura alunt, vino aut mulso incoctæ. Verum memineris, ante alios cibos horas aliquot commanducanda esse, nec cum aliis cibis miscenda. Recentium gratia quia non diu durat, siccari solent seruarique, usque ad alia nascentia, ad varios in re cibaria vsus. Succus quoque prunorum a matribus quibusdam familiás decoquitur, ad sitim febricitantium leuandam, linguaque ariditatem humectandam. Diosco-ridem mirantur multi, quod scripserit, siccata Damascena aliquam nequaquam deiicere, cum inconsessio sit ea id praestare, brodio enim seu iusculo eorum nihil fere in aluo leniter laxanda frequentius.
units.tr: Choose those commended for size, sweetness and pleasant flavour, for these nourish more than the others, especially when stewed in wine or mead. But remember that they should be eaten some hours before other foods, and not mixed with other foods. Because fresh plums do not keep long, they are usually dried and preserved until the next crop, for various culinary uses. Some housewives also boil down the juice of plums, to relieve the thirst of feverish people and moisten the dryness of the tongue. Many marvel at Dioscorides, who wrote that dried damsons by no means loosen the bowels, since it is well known that they do so; indeed nothing is more often used to gently loosen the bowels than their broth or soup.

units.la: De Perficis.
units.tr: On Peaches.

units.la: PErsica mali succi esse, vt quo deterius in cibis esse nihil possit, doctissimi quique statuunt. Plinius l. 15. c. 18. pomum Persicum innocuum esse, expetiqué vndique ab aegris aperte scripsit, Et l. 23. c. 7, Persica vtiliora esse stomacho quam pruna prodidit.
units.tr: Most learned men hold that the peach is of bad juice, so that nothing worse can be eaten. Pliny, in book 15, chapter 18, wrote that the peach fruit is harmless and is openly sought on all sides by the sick; and in book 23, chapter 7, he stated that peaches are more useful to the stomach than plums.

units.la: Sed à veritate eum aberrare, refellendumque propterea esse quidam contra scripserunt. Verum, quod pace illorum dixerim, innoxium esse malum Persicum aegris recte scripsisse Plinium sentio, in ardentibus enim febribus ob qualitatem frigidam &c humidam persica mala prodesse nemo est qui inficias iturus est.
units.tr: But some have written against him, arguing that he strays from the truth and must therefore be refuted. Yet, with due respect to them, I agree that Pliny rightly wrote that the peach is harmless to the sick. No one will deny that in burning fevers peaches help, because of their cold and moist quality.

units.la: Stomacho enim, cumprimis aestu turgido non incommodant, modo ante alios cibos sumantur, quemadmodum 1. de alim. bene monet Galenus. Et quod hic de perficis dicitur, debere ea alias escas praecedere, id de omnibus temperariis & fugacibus semel fit dictum. Immodico liquore persica luxuriare constat, unde promtissime celeriterque putrescere solent, qua de causa continuus multiplexque eorum usus improbatur; praesertim ventriculo existente humido & flatulento. Paulus Aeginetha coacescere statim in ventriculo docuit, & admodum esse improbi succi. Delicatiores ea decorticata vino madefaciunt, sic enim tolli noxam existimant. Verum videant, ne in venas succus ille crudus celerius deducatur. Mauritani remedium praeclarum esse aiunt contra animae grauitatem, quae a vitio ventriculi exhalat.
units.tr: For they do not trouble the stomach, especially when it is swollen with heat, provided they are taken before other foods, as Galen rightly advises in his first book on foods. And what is said here of peaches, that they should precede other foods, has been said once and for all of all delicate and perishable fruits. It is well known that peaches abound in watery juice, and so they quickly and readily go bad. For this reason continuous and frequent eating of them is disapproved, especially when the stomach is damp and windy. Paulus Aegineta taught that they curdle at once in the stomach and yield a very bad juice. Fastidious people peel them and soak them in wine, for they think the harm is thus removed. But let them take care that the raw juice is not conveyed more quickly into the veins. The Mauritanians say it is an excellent remedy against bad breath, which rises from a disorder of the stomach.

units.la: Armeniaca & praecocia, quae circa festum D. Joh. apparent, caeteris omnibus praestant, quia intus magis sicca spectantur, ea intra 30. annos reperta fuisse, dum historiam suam conderet, Plinius testatur, & primo singula denariis venundata, hoc est, sestertiis quaternis, postea, augescente gratia, gulaque titillante pretium ad tricenos nummos euasse sisse. Vnde mirum non est singulas arbores bina millia nummum annuo reditu meruisse, cum septem & sexaginta malaillam summam conficere potuerint, triginis nummis singula venundata. De nucleis persicorum non praetereundum est ex oleo rosaceo, & aceto temperatos capitis dolores sedare, esitatos autem tormina ventris. Flores saccharo conditi stomacho utiles sunt. Eligenda quae minus succulenta sunt persica, quorumque; fissa caro ligno minime adhaeret. Succosa enim nimis damnantur.
units.tr: Apricots and early apricots, which appear around the feast of St John, surpass all others, because they look drier inside. Pliny testifies that these were discovered within thirty years of his writing his history. At first each was sold for a denarius, that is four sesterces; afterwards, as their popularity grew and tickled the appetite, the price rose to thirty coins. Hence it is no wonder that single trees brought in two thousand coins a year, since those sixty-seven fruits could make up that sum, each being sold for thirty coins. It should not be passed over that peach kernels, steeped in rose oil and vinegar, calm headaches, and when eaten, relieve gripes of the bowels. Flowers preserved in sugar are useful for the stomach. Choose peaches that are less juicy, and whose flesh splits cleanly and does not cling to the stone, for overly juicy ones are condemned.

units.la: De cucumere, cucurbita, melone, pepone.
units.tr: On the cucumber, gourd, melon and pumpkin.

units.la: MElonum, peponum, cucumerum, cucurbitarumque varia genera nouit Italia & Gallia, quorum plaraque in Germaniam nunc quoque nostram commigrarunt. Non enim indiligenter in hortis excoluntur, expetuntur enim tum a magnatibus, tum a pauperibus, non sine valetudinis sepe incommodo. Calidioris enim temperatura hominibus, & ab ineunte aetate iis asuetis magis conueniunt, frigido humido, ventriculo incommodant. Semina vero omnium in renum vesicaque affectib. ut stranguria, calculo &c. valde commendantur.
units.tr: Italy and France know many kinds of melons, pumpkins, cucumbers and gourds, and many of them have now also migrated into our Germany. They are cultivated with care in gardens, and are sought after both by the great and by the poor, not without often harming health. For they suit people of a warmer constitution, and those accustomed to them from an early age, but they trouble those with a cold and moist stomach. The seeds of all of them are highly commended for disorders of the kidneys and bladder, such as strangury, stone and the like.

units.la: Cucurbita in cibos decoquuntur, cruda nimis non edunt, fatua siquidem & insipida sunt.
units.tr: Gourds are cooked into food. They do not eat them raw, for they are insipid and tasteless.

units.la: Apparandi modus variat. Quidam cum Sinapi efitant, alii cum Salsis eoquunt, nonnulli cum malo cydonio hodie addunt crocum & piper, sic enim humor eius immoderatus coercetur: vescentes autem cito satiat, ob redundantem humorem alimentumq; prabet humidius. Esite vero potissimum elixa cum jusculis edi debent, autumno in oleo aut butyro fixa vel asse farina prius circumlita, acerbeq; vua succo aspersa.
units.tr: The method of preparing them varies. Some eat them with mustard, others cook them with salted meats; some now add saffron and pepper along with quince, for in this way their excessive moisture is checked. Those who eat them are soon satisfied, and because of their excess moisture they supply a rather watery nourishment. They are best eaten boiled with broths; in autumn they are fried in oil or butter, or first dusted with flour, and sprinkled with sour grape juice.

units.la: Cucumeres, melones, pepones, crudiffrequenter in cibos veniunt. Itali, Galli, & Hispani liberalissime iis vescuntur & frequentissime.
units.tr: Cucumbers, melons and pumpkins, eaten raw, often come to table. Italians, French and Spaniards eat them most freely and very frequently.

units.la: Vidi in Italia multos tanta cum auiditate pepones vorasse, ut satis putarint ad justum prandium aut liberalem coenam, peponibus Saturari. Edunt autem cum pane, pipere & Saccharo, vinumq; superbibunt. Sed certum est & indubitatum, licet nonnulli recte eos coquant in ventriculo, eoq; fiji affatim iis & frequenter sese repleant, temporis tractu & progressu gelidos vitiosq; succos in venis coacerwari, qui cum in bonum sanguinem converti non possint, clam senfimq; leuissima putredine occasione arrepta, tontumaces sanasq; febres excitare consueuerunt. Id quod praeter experientiam praedicta gentes fateri coguntur, sauio-ribus frequentioribusq; morbis, quam alia obnoxia.
units.tr: I have seen many in Italy devour pumpkins with such eagerness that they thought a pumpkin feast enough for a substantial lunch or a lavish dinner. They eat them with bread, pepper and sugar, and drink wine on top. But it is certain and undoubted that although some digest them well in the stomach, and fill themselves with them abundantly and often, over time cold and bad juices gather in the veins. Since these cannot be turned into good blood, they secretly seize the chance of a slight putrefaction and are wont to excite stubborn and dangerous fevers. These peoples are forced to admit this from experience, as they suffer more grievous and frequent diseases than other nations exposed to them.

units.la: NB.
units.tr: NB.

units.la: In promtu causa est, quia vinum meracum superbibunt, quod tanquam vehiculum eruditates ingestorum fructuum secum in venas deducit atq; rapit, unde obstructiones pu-tredinesq; existere tandem verisimile est.
units.tr: The cause is ready to hand: they drink undiluted wine over them, and this, like a vehicle, carries and drags the crude juices of the fruit they have swallowed into the veins, whence obstructions and putrefactions at last are likely to arise.

units.la: Italorum tamen & Hispanorum maxima pars innoxie iis vescitur, ex consuetudine, ut ipsi putant, tum etiam, quia vinum meracum malitiam eorum obtundere vomitumq; coercere experti sunt, &c. Verum consuetudinem illis relinquamus, valeantq; qui istorum fructuum esu impensiu gaudent. In exemplis est Paulum secundum Pontificem esu pepo-nis interiisse, quin & Clementem septimum auidissimum eorum fuisse inde constat, quod in morbo, quo etiam extinctus est, aulde eos vorant-vit.
units.tr: Yet the greater part of Italians and Spaniards eat them without harm, from custom, as they themselves think, and also because they have found that undiluted wine blunts their harmfulness and checks vomiting, and so on. But let us leave the custom to them, and farewell to those who take great delight in eating these fruits. Among the examples: Pope Paul II is said to have died from eating pumpkins, and it is clear that Clement VII was also very greedy for them, since in the illness of which he also died, he devoured them eagerly.

units.la: Quare perpetuo illud cogitandum, ne ad satietatem quis eos ingerat. Diphilus apud Atheneum non vult cucumeres assumi primo cibo, propterea quod sursum ferantur, raphani infar, ultimo innocentiores concoctuq; faciliores arbitratur, quod tamen quidam non probant.
units.tr: Therefore one must always take care not to force them on anyone until he is full. Diphilus, in Athenaeus, does not want cucumbers taken as a first course, because they rise upward like radishes; he thinks they are more harmless and easier to digest when eaten last, though some do not approve of this.

units.la: Verissimum & indubitatum est, Cucumeres peponesq; copiosius sumtos, nisi probe coquantur, aq; ventriculo conficiantur, vel etiam boni succi cibis non vna assumantur, in ventriculo corrumpi atq; vitiari, succumq; parere lethalibus venenis non absimilem. Vide de hac re Galen. librum de cibis boni & mali succi. Item lib.
units.tr: It is most true and undoubted that cucumbers and pumpkins, if eaten in larger quantities, unless they are well cooked and digested in the stomach, or if they are taken together with foods of good juice, corrupt and spoil in the stomach and produce a juice not unlike deadly poisons. See Galen's book on foods of good and bad juice on this matter. Likewise...

units.la: NB. Galen. lib. de cibis boni & mali succi. lib. 2. de alimentorum facult. Paulum Ægi-netam lib. 1. c. 80. Plin. l. 19. cap. 5. vbi cucumeres esstatos in stomacho vivere scribit in posterum diem, nec perficiposse. Videant igitur aulicarum voluptatum sectatores, qui eos in taleolos dissectos ex aceto & sale pipereq; vel muria mandunt, sic enim in alienos menses condiuntur & asseruantur, hocq; modo asseruati pestilentissimi sunt in commessationibus noctypnis, sicut & in mensis secundis. Chrysippus eos in cibis damnauit. Taurus Philosophus apud Aulum Gellium cœnam obsonio instruebat ex lente confecto & cucurbita, cujus etiam caulem in cibo primum esse Plinius autor est: verum quo longior & tenerior, eo gratior, salubriorq; quæ pendendo crevit. Secantur autem cucurbitæ deraso cortice in tenuia filamenta, quæ siccata servantur.
units.tr: NB. Galen, book on foods of good and bad juice; book 2 on the powers of foods. Paulus Aegineta, book 1, chapter 80. Pliny, book 19, chapter 5, where he writes that cucumbers eaten live on in the stomach into the next day and cannot be digested. Let those who pursue courtly pleasures consider this, who eat them cut into slices and seasoned with vinegar, salt, pepper or brine. For in this way they are kept for months, and so preserved they are most harmful at night-long drinking parties, as well as at dessert. Chrysippus condemned them as food. Taurus the philosopher, in Aulus Gellius, prepared his dinner with a dish made of lentils and gourd; Pliny also says that the stalk of the gourd is first among foods, but the longer and more tender it is, the more pleasant and wholesome it is, being what grew hanging. Gourds are cut, with the rind scraped away, into thin strips, which are kept dried.

units.la: Cucumeres, si quando iis vesci, vel necessitatis, vel voluptatis gratiâ contingat, sint infantes, teneriores, parumq; adhuc ventricosi. Suaviores quoq; ac dulciores redduntur, semine eorum latte vel mulsa temperato ante sationem. Impudicis textricibus venerisq; appetentioribus cucumerem edendum Græcorum est proverbium, cucumerem enim Venereis cupiditatibus refragari Diphilus autor est.
units.tr: Cucumbers, if anyone happens to eat them out of necessity or for pleasure, should be young, more tender, and not yet very bloated. They are also made sweeter and more pleasant if their seed is steeped in milk or mead before sowing. There is a Greek proverb that cucumber should be eaten by shameless weavers and by those more eager for sex, since Diphilus is the authority that cucumber works against Venereal desires.

units.la: De Cotoneis.
units.tr: On Quinces.

units.la: NOn sunt priuanda gloriâ sua mala cotonea, ex insula Creta hujusq; oppido cydone primum aduecta, vnde cydonia mala appellantur. Præclarum quid ante cætera mala præstare Galenus aliiquę graues autores, tum quotidiana quoque experimenta testantur. Ventriculum enim debilem magis aliis malis corroborant astringendi vi, qua etiam aluus firmatur. Flauam etiam bilem coercent, atque cor spiritusquė exhilarant. Cruda in cibos non veniunt, decocta vero hieme summam fecundis in mésis autoritatem obtinuerunt. Coctura habenda est ratio: Prout enim magis vel minus ventrem firmare astringereque scopus est, pro eo magis vel minus lentè diuue coquenda sunt, certum enim est longa coctura vim constringendi amitti. Delicatior gula ea cocta saccharo aspergit, cinnamomoq; & garyophillis configit. Succus cotoneorū cum melle coctus ad præstátes vsus seruabilis est. Quin & medicamētū cotoneatū vocāt, vulgatissimi est apud magnates in nocturnis cōmeslationib. vsus, eo nāq; mores huj° sæculi venere, vt multa à medicinę leg.ad gulę ventrisq; delitias trâsierint. Vestib. interposita odoré his conciliât, susp̃ésa in cubiculis paulo ante maturitate odore suaui coloreq; aureo, parumq; virescente spiritus recreare insensibiliter deprehenduntur. Effi-
units.tr: The quince must not be deprived of its glory. It was first brought from the island of Crete and from its town Cydon, whence it is called the Cydonian apple. Galen and other weighty authors, as well as daily experience, testify that it excels all other apples. It strengthens a weak stomach more than other apples, by its astringent power, which also firms the bowels. It likewise checks yellow bile and cheers the heart and spirits. Raw, they do not come to table, but cooked they have won the highest authority at second courses in winter. Account must be taken of the cooking: since the aim is to strengthen and bind the stomach more or less, they must be cooked more or less long and slowly, for it is certain that long cooking loses the binding power. The more delicate palate sprinkles them with sugar when cooked and seasons them with cinnamon and cloves. Quince juice boiled with honey can be kept for useful purposes. They even call it quince medicine, and its use is very common among great men at nocturnal revels. The customs of this age have come to such a pass that many things have passed from the laws of medicine to the delights of the belly and gluttony. Placed among clothes, they give them a pleasant smell. Hung in bedchambers shortly before ripeness, when the odour is sweet and the colour golden with a slight greenness, they are found to refresh the spirits imperceptibly. Effi-

units.la: NB Efficacissimum antidotum, medicamentumque contra venena & toxica esse malum cotoneum praeter experientiam gravissimi autores prodiderunt. Qui de Parthorum Scytarumque toxico literis prodiderunt, (vt Plin.l.11.c.53. Ouid.1. de Ponto. Lucan.l.3. Diosc.l.6.c.20. Arist.de mirabilib. auscult.) testantur humano sanguine viperinaq; sanie constare, quo tela sagittasq; suas inficiebant inungebantque, vt leui etiam tactu mortem accelerarent. Qui hoc potarunt, his labia intumescebant, rabiosique luporum instar vociferabantur, quos cotonea mala concisa ac cum pulegio comesta juvisse compertum fuit. Aduersus Aegyptiorum Pharicum, quod potum resolutionem, convulsionemque cum delirio afferebat, efficacissimum antidotum esse malum cotoneum velinde praecipue patet, quod solus hujus odor vires Pharici virulentas obtundit atq; eneruat, ita vt si vna in risco includantur, hujus virtus illius odore debilitetur. Vnde Philarchus sexto historiarum libro ait, Cotonea mala suo odore omnium deleteriorum vim obtundere. Vide Athen. lib.3. ex Philarcho.
units.tr: NB: That the quince is a most efficacious antidote and remedy against poisons and toxins, the most weighty authors have declared, apart from experience. Those who have written about the poison of the Parthians and Scythians (as Pliny, book 11, ch. 53; Ovid, Epistles from Pontus, book 1; Lucan, book 3; Dioscorides, book 6, ch. 20; Aristotle, On Marvellous Things Heard) testify that it consists of human blood and viper's ichor, with which they smeared and anointed their weapons and arrows, so that even a slight touch hastened death. Those who drank it had their lips swollen, and they howled wildly like wolves. Quince cut up and eaten with pennyroyal was found to help them. Against the Egyptian Pharicum, which, when drunk, causes loosening, convulsion and delirium, the quince is a most efficacious antidote. This is especially clear because its smell alone blunts and weakens the poisonous power of the Pharicum, so that if both are shut in one box, the power of the poison is weakened by the odour of the quince. Hence Philarchus, in the sixth book of his Histories, says that quinces by their smell blunt the power of all deadly things. See Athenaeus, book 3, citing Philarchus.

units.la: Saepe contingit, vt, qui hesterna in coenalargius meraciusque poculis indulserunt, tantam postero die sentiant capitis grauedinem, vt in id cyclopas migrasse jurent, qui alteralternatis illud feriant ictibus. His coto-neum tostum ant: somnum vel etiam mane sumtum vapores è ventriculo in cerebrum exhalantes reprimit ac coercet, efficitque ut vina minus noceant. Quare cotonea in hunc vsum diligenter afleruanda sunt, iis, quos postera die Cepfalalgia ex crapula solet conflictare.
units.tr: It often happens that those who indulged too freely in strong wine at dinner the day before feel such a heaviness of the head the next day that they swear the Cyclopes have migrated into it and are striking it with alternate blows. Against this, roasted quince, taken fasting or even in the morning, restrains and checks the vapours that rise from the stomach into the brain, and makes wine do less harm. Quinces should therefore be carefully kept for this purpose, for those whom headache from excess usually troubles the next day.

units.la: De Sorbis & Mespilis.
units.tr: On Service-berries and Medlars.

units.la: Orba & mespila pro medicamine potius, quam pro esca edenda Galenus praecipit, stomachum enim roborant, aliunde fi-ftunt, quae de causa fecundis mensis assumenda sunt.
units.tr: Galen advises that service-berries and medlars be eaten as a medicine rather than as food. For they strengthen the stomach, and otherwise they constipate, and for this reason they should be taken at the second courses.

units.la: Mespila melle condita reseruantur. In-uento nouo in magnatum mensis madent intin-ctu quodam qui vino cinnamomite conficitur. Rustici popellum cruda, sed mollia (in his enim gratia saporis est) edunt, cocta autem falubrio-ra. De Sorbis torminalibus hoc adnotandum certissimum esse, quod Martialis scripsit, Sorba fumus molles nimium durantia ventres.
units.tr: Medlars are preserved in honey. A new invention: at the tables of great men they are steeped in a dip made with cinnamon wine. Country folk eat them raw but soft (for in these the taste is the point), while cooked they are more wholesome. About the torminal service-berries this is most certainly to be noted, what Martial wrote: service-berries harden bellies that are too soft.

units.la: Noui quosdam dysenteria grauissime tentatos deploratos, exitio opem ac medicinam superante, nullo medicamento morbum leniente, consilio fatidica cuiusdam anus sorbis crudis largiter voratis postridie vim prope tormi-talem nalem omnem depulisse, indeque firmata aluo pri-stina valetudini se restituisse. Verissimum igi-tur est Celsi dictum, temeritatem plerunque effi-cere in morbis, quod prudentia nequiverit.
units.tr: I know some who were severely afflicted with dysentery and given up for dead, when the power of death overcame all help and medicine, and no remedy eased the disease. On the advice of some prophetic old woman, they ate raw service-berries in great quantity, and the next day this drove out nearly all the torment, as it were. Their bowels being firmed, they restored themselves to their former health. Most true, then, is the saying of Celsus, that rashness often accomplishes in diseases what prudence could not.

units.la: De castaneis, nucibus iuglandibus & avellana.
units.tr: On Chestnuts, Walnuts and Hazelnuts.

units.la: CAstaneae igne tostae, juglandes item & avellanae secundis mensis gratissi-me apponuntur, cumprimis vero ca-stanea, quae praecipuam obtinuerunt dignitatem & gratiam. Quin & plebeculae multis in locis sunt solatio, quando sedanda fames animalis est. In Italiae quibusdam locis, praesertim vero Romae passim tostentur in cibis, venundanturque voce praeconis. Difficilis autem coctionis esse, crassosque humores generare, obstructionesque, ii experiuntur, qui liberalius iis & frequentius vescuntur. Quapropter citra satietatem edendae sunt praesertim calculo colicoque dolori obnoxiis: tostae velaste porcellis anserculisque infartae gratiores sunt & salubriores. Galenus arbores omnes fructus improbi succi esse, praeter castaneas attribuere non dubitavit. Arrius quoque, medicus clarissimus inter cunctos agrestes fructus sardinias glandes, sic enim appellat castaneas, alimentum praestare vescentibus insigne asserit, verum tentare caput. Peculiare autem genus esse, quod id effiefficiat, dubium non est, Galli enim genero-sissimas, amplitudine saporisque suauitate commendatissimas prædicant, quas Marrones vocant, magnatibus valde expetitas. De nostris adeo magna pollicēri non ausim, nisi ex liquore rosaceo saccharato decorticatæ, vel etiam porcellis anseribusque infarctæ assæque manducentur. Molitura earum quibusdam gentibus pulmentariorum ac panis vicem præbet, quod tamen panificii genus rusticis magis conueniens est.
units.tr: Chestnuts roasted in the fire, and likewise walnuts and hazelnuts, are most gladly set before the second courses, chestnuts especially, which have won the chief dignity and favour. Indeed the common folk in many places find them a comfort when hunger must be assuaged. In some parts of Italy, and especially at Rome, they are roasted everywhere as food and sold by the crier's voice. Those who eat them more freely and often find that they are hard to digest, generate thick humours and cause obstructions. Therefore they should be eaten without satiety, especially by those liable to stone and colic pain. Roasted or baked, or stuffed into suckling pigs and young geese, they are more pleasing and wholesome. Galen did not hesitate to ascribe bad juice to all fruit trees, except the chestnut. Arrius too, a most famous physician, asserts that among all the wild fruits the Sardinian acorns (for so he calls chestnuts) give outstanding nourishment to those who eat them, but they try the head. That there is a peculiar kind which produces this is not doubtful, for the French praise their most noble kind, commended for size and sweetness of flavour, which they call marrons, and which great men desire greatly. Of our own I would not dare promise so much, unless they are eaten peeled and sweetened with rose water, or stuffed into suckling pigs and geese and roasted. Ground into flour, they serve in some nations in place of side dishes and bread, though this kind of baking suits country folk better.

units.la: De Nucibus.
units.tr: On Nuts.

units.la: DE Nucibus strictim & absque verborum ambage. Nucis vocabulum omnibus commune est, quæ duro sunt operimento, vt castaneæ, anellanæ, nuces juglandes, quæ quia ex Perside primum allatæ perhibentur, persicæ, & Euboicæ appellantur. Nucem vero à nocendo juglandem vero, quod satis noceat, dictam volunt. Nuces juglandes à capitis gratiedine græcè καρύα appellantur, foliorum enim vires in cerebrum penetrant, ipsaque præsertim sicca vberius comesta capitis dolorem inferunt, stomachum grauant, difficulter coquuntur, tussimque excitant certissimè experientia. Itaque quo veteriores et plus oleosæ, cibis itaque abdicandæ. Recentes commendabiles sunt saporis, stomachoque cum sale innocentiores. Venenis eas repugnare certum est in cibis præsumtas, quā de re etiam Plinius l. 23. c. 8. scribit in hunc modum. In sanctuariis mithridatis maximi Regis Ponti deuicti Cn. Pompeius inuenit in peculiari commentario ipsius manu scriptam compositionem antidoti, duabus nucibus siccis, ficus totidem & rutha folijs 20. simul tritis, addito salis uno atque altero grano, quod qui ieiunus sumat, nullum venenum nociturum illo die. Hæc Plin. Porro pugnantia quaedam ut & antipathia piscium malignitati, aquosis ipsorum ac pituitosis humoribus aduersari nuces juglandes compertum est, quare a piscium esu abstinendum.
units.tr: Concerning nuts, briefly and without wordy circumlocution. The word "nut" is common to all things with a hard shell, such as chestnuts, hazelnuts and walnuts. Walnuts are called Persian or Euboean nuts because they are said to have been first brought from Persia. Some hold that "nux" comes from "nocere" (to harm), and that the walnut (juglans) is so named because it harms enough. In Greek walnuts are called karya from the heaviness of the head, for the strength of the leaves penetrates into the brain. Walnuts themselves, especially when dry and eaten in quantity, cause headache, weigh on the stomach, are hard to digest, and certainly provoke coughing, as experience shows. Therefore the older and oilier ones are to be excluded from food. Fresh nuts are pleasant in taste and less harmful to the stomach when salted. It is certain that they counter poisons when taken in food, and Pliny writes of this matter in the following manner, book 23, chapter 8. In the sanctuaries of Mithridates, the greatest king of Pontus, once conquered, Gnaeus Pompey found in a private commentary, written in the king's own hand, a recipe for an antidote: two dry walnuts, as many figs and twenty rue leaves, all ground together, with a grain or two of salt added. Whoever takes this fasting, no poison will harm him that day. So Pliny. Furthermore, it is known that walnuts oppose the malignity of fish, that is, their watery and phlegmatic humours, which are contrary to them; for this reason one should abstain from eating fish.

units.la: Virentes adhuc ligneo sc. putamine nondum duritiem adepto, garyophyllis ac cinnamomo confixæ saccharo condiuntur, seruanturque in multos annos ad varios usus, ventriculo enim refrigerato & imbecillo utiles sunt, seni-bus item & pituitosis, maritisque in venerem pigris.
units.tr: Still green in their woody husk, before they have hardened, walnuts are stuck with cloves and cinnamon, preserved in sugar, and kept for many years for various uses. For they are useful to a cold and weak stomach, likewise to the elderly and the phlegmatic, and to husbands sluggish in love.

units.la: Avellanæ nuces plus quam notæ sunt. Patri & nomine appellantur Abellinæ ab Abellino Campaniæ oppido, Græcis Ἀβελλανίδες quasi nuces exiguæ: alii Ponticas vocant, quoniam e Ponto in Græciam primo venisse rentur. Pranestinæ etiam quod Pranestini eis abundent. Largius esitata atque ac juglandeas capiti noxiæ sunt. In cibo gratissima sunt rubentem tuni-cam nactæ, exactam tamen omnino maturita-tem non adeptæ, alendi enim præstantia præpol-lent ob substantiam illarum solidam minusque pingue (centem, qua de causa juglandibus in ci-bis postponi oportere medicina prudentes asseue-rant.
units.tr: Hazelnuts are better known than most. They are called by their homeland and name Abellinae, from Abellinum, a town of Campania; the Greeks call them Abellanides, as if they were small nuts. Others call them Pontic, since they are thought to have first come into Greece from Pontus. Praenestine, too, because the Praenestines have them in abundance. Eaten in excess, they are harmful to the head like walnuts. In food they are most pleasant when they have gained the reddish skin but have not fully reached complete ripeness. For in nourishing they excel because their substance is solid and less fatty; for this reason, doctors of good judgment assert that walnuts should be placed behind them in diet.

units.la: Quæstionem hic video obrepere, qua mi-nime prætermittenda est. Cum vulgo dicitur: Unica nux prodest, nocet altera, tertia mors est,
units.tr: I see a question creeping in here, which must by no means be passed over. When it is commonly said: one nut does good, the second harms, the third is death.

units.la: Quæritur, quia triplicis hic nucis fit mentio, quanam sit innocens, quæ nocens, & quæ plane mortifera. Respondent per primam intelligunt quidam nucem moschatam, per secundam nucem juglandem, per tertiam nucem metel-lam seu vomicam, qua duarum drachmarum quantitate sumta mortem accelerat. Alii de foliis juglandibus intelligendum id esse, sic exponunt, unica prodest, mane, id est pauca, (synec-dochicos) scilicet & jejuno stomacho advers{us} venena sumta, veletiam ventris laxandi gratia: altera nocet, immodico usu: tertia mors est, continuatus enim & præter modum immodicus earum usu dysenteriam parit, sapeque mortem.
units.tr: The question is asked, since mention is made of three nuts, which of them is harmless, which harmful, and which plainly deadly. Some understand by the first the nutmeg, by the second the walnut, and by the third the nux metella, or vomica, which, taken in the quantity of two drachms, hastens death. Others say that it must be understood of walnut leaves, and explain it thus: one does good, that is, a few (by synecdoche), namely taken on an empty stomach against poisons, or even for the sake of loosening the bowels; the second harms, by immoderate use; the third is death, for continual and immoderate use of them breeds dysentery and often death.

units.la: De amygdalis & nucibus pinéis.
units.tr: On Almonds and Pine Nuts.

units.la: IN cibis ex amygdalis valent dulces, amarae enim cibis abdicantur. Naxiæ & Cypriæ priæ magis laudantur. In delitiis habentur dulces saccharo conditæ vel obductæ. Culinas amygdalas ad varios escarum vsus adhibere, nemini non constat.
units.tr: In food, the sweet almonds are wholesome, for bitter ones are excluded from food. Those of Naxos and Cyprus are most praised. Sweet almonds candied or coated with sugar are regarded as delicacies. Everyone knows that culinary almonds are used for many kinds of dishes.

units.la: Varia deniq; ex amygdalis concinnantur, quæ amygdalata nuncupantur, sicut ex pineis pignolata, & hodie vix sine amygdalis Ptisana parantur, quæ sine iis colore & sapore ingratior est, de viribus autem Ptisanæ vide supra cap. de tritico & hordeo. Lac amygdalinum in febribus quid præstet, pulmentum quoque ex iis & nucibus pineis, quam gratum sit vtileq; pthificis, experientia testatur. Menses fecundas abunde implet atq; exornant variis modis.
units.tr: Finally, various things are made from almonds, which are called almond confections, just as pignolata are made from pine nuts. Today barley-water is hardly ever prepared without almonds, and without them it is less pleasing in colour and taste. On the powers of barley-water, see above, in the chapter on wheat and barley. What almond milk does in fevers, and how pleasant and useful a pottage made of them and of pine nuts is for consumptives, experience attests. They abundantly furnish and adorn the tables in various ways.

units.la: Nolo hic omittere, vt crapulæ quoq; nonnihil consuleretur, potores quinis vel pluribus præsumtis ebrietatem non sentire. Plutarchus memoriæ prodidit, fuisse apud Drusum Tiberii Cæsaris filium medicum quendam, facile omnes potando superantem: is autem paulo ante potum quinq; vel sex amygdalas amaras præsumere solitus est, ne crapulæ cogenti deesset: existimauit enim nucum amaritudine siccari absorberiq; humorem immodicum. Verum quæritur, cur amaritudo in amygdalis ebrietatem arceat, & non etiam in absinthio, centaurio, alpe? an quia occultum dissidium est & antipathia inter amygdalas amaras & liquorem vini ? persuasum habe : non enim amaritudo id præstat quatenus amaritudo est, sed quatenus in amygdalis amaris est.
units.tr: I do not wish to omit here that, to provide some remedy also for drunkenness, drinkers who have taken five or more of them do not feel the effects of drink. Plutarch records that Drusus, the son of Tiberius Caesar, had a certain physician who easily outdrank everyone. This man used to eat five or six bitter almonds shortly before drinking, so that the compelling hangover would not catch him, for he thought that the bitterness of the nuts dries up and absorbs the excessive moisture. But the question arises why bitterness in almonds prevents drunkenness, and not also bitterness in wormwood, centaury or aloes. Is it because there is a hidden discord and antipathy between bitter almonds and the liquor of wine? Be assured of this: it is not bitterness as such that does this, but bitterness as it is found in bitter almonds.

units.la: De pistaceis & nucibus pineis non difficile est recte judicare, fi, quæ de amygdalis dicta sunt, accurate quis obseruauerit, græcis ftrobila dictæ. Grandiffimæ autem sunt nuces pineæ, nucleosque exiles inclusos in fe continent, qui probi ac crassi succi sunt, valenterque alere existimantur. Aquâ autem simplici vel rosacea macerandæ sunt, ad resinosam illam acremque vim deponendam, hocq; modo faucibus exasperatis, exulceratisque præclare medentur. Plinius ac Diofcorides sitim sedare, virilium infirmitatem roborare, renibusque vtiles esse fpodent. Diocles thoracem purgare prodit obvim resinosam. Menefitheus corpus implereait, vnde ptificis & tabidis vtiles. Saccharo incrustatæ bellariorum vicem supplent.
units.tr: Concerning pistachios and pine nuts it is not difficult to judge rightly, if one carefully observes what has been said of almonds; in Greek they are called strobili. Pine nuts are very large and enclose within them small kernels, which are of good, rich juice and are thought to nourish strongly. They must be steeped in plain water or rose water, to remove that resinous and sharp quality; so prepared they cure excellently a throat roughened and ulcerated. Pliny and Dioscorides report that they quench thirst, strengthen male weakness, and are useful for the kidneys. Diocles is said to purge the chest of resinous phlegm. Menestheus says they fill out the body, and so are useful for consumptives and the wasting. Coated with sugar, they take the place of sweetmeats.

units.la: De pistaciis, quæ ę genere quoque nucum sunt, autores variant. Ea in Italiam ex Syria Vitellium primum intulifle, & in Hispaniam Flaccum Pompeium equitem Romanum qui cum eo militabat, Plinius dilige ntiffimus naturæ scrutator, autor est lib. 15. cap. 22. Eosdem autem vsus & effectus habere cum pineis idé Plinius restatur l. 15. quæ histohistoriae cap. 8. ad quem lectorem remitto, pluribus enim ibi de amygdalis, pineis, juglandibus, castaneis disserit. Galenus non esse sibi compertum tradit, an sint stomacho amica, quod tamen Diofcorides aperte tradit.
units.tr: Authors differ about pistachios, which are also among the nuts. Pliny, the most diligent investigator of nature, is the authority for saying that Vitellius first brought them into Italy from Syria, and that Flaccus Pompeius, a Roman knight who served under him, brought them into Spain (book 15, chapter 22). Pliny likewise asserts that they have the same uses and effects as pine nuts (Natural History, book 15, chapter 8), to which I refer the reader, for there he discusses at greater length almonds, pine nuts, walnuts and chestnuts. Galen relates that he has not discovered whether they are friendly to the stomach, though Dioscorides states this plainly.

units.la: Quin etiam an aluo subducendae, an cohibenda vtilia sint, se exploratum non habere sit. Mira hominis integritas in re medica posteris tradenda, qui ne posteritati imponeret, nihil inexpertum scripto tradere voluit, sed potius in cognita sibi, assidua experientia magna cum fide explorauit. Et certe magis ingenuum est, de ignorantia confiteri, quam turpes & ridiculas causas atque rationes promere. Sacchato à seplasiariis incrustantur, gratia tamen eorum vetustate perit, rancida enim vt caeterae nuces, evadunt.
units.tr: Nor do I know for certain whether they are useful for loosening the bowels or for binding them. The remarkable honesty of this man in medical matters deserves to be handed down to posterity. Lest he deceive posterity, he wished to commit to writing nothing untested, but rather investigated with great fidelity what was known to him through constant experience. And certainly it is more ingenuous to confess ignorance than to put forward shameful and ridiculous causes and reasons. Incrusted with sugar by confectioners, they nevertheless lose their charm with age, for like other nuts they turn rancid.

units.la: De Capparibus & oliuis.
units.tr: On capers and olives.

units.la: MEnsa magnatum opulentant ad aviditatem excitandam, sed gulosorum inventum est. In iis regionibus, vbi vberrimus oliuarum est proventus, vt in Gallia Narbonensi, singulis prandiis coenisve ab incolis apponuntur. Seruantur autem sale, aceto, & oleo. Apud veteres condiebantur muria, ipsisque foeniculum admiscebatur. Ex defruto quoque & passo condirifolitas Celsus autor est, lib.2. cap.19. Ægineta oximelite conditas lau-dat. Aetius aceto & oleo conditas ad excitandum appetitum coltionem quam iucundam nobilissimas esse ait, minorique negotio a ventriculo perfici, quae iucundiores sunt. Acerba enim & virides omnes crudae, nam nemo potest, adeo certissimum est omnem acerbitatem diffi-cillime domari ac vinci. Albas oliuas (quae scilicet mediae sunt inter virides & maturas, quarum illae acerbae sunt haueno, quae & nigrae sunt, stomachum sua pinguedine relaxant) stomacho utiles esse prodiderunt Plin.lib.23.cap.3. Celsus lib.4.cap.20. Galen.5. de compos.medicamen-dic. secundum loc. nec non Oribasius libr.7. Omnes enim hi iis in stomacho astringendo vtun-tur.
units.tr: Rich men's tables offer them to stir up appetite, but they are the invention of gluttons. In those regions where olives yield most abundantly, as in Narbonese Gaul, the inhabitants serve them at every lunch and supper. They are preserved in salt, vinegar and oil. Among the ancients they were pickled in brine, with fennel added. Celsus, book 2, chapter 19, also states that they were pickled in must-syrup and raisin wine. Aegineta praises those preserved in oxymel. Aëtius says that olives pickled in vinegar and oil, to rouse the appetite, are the most pleasant and most noble of all, and that they are digested by the stomach with less effort, and these are the more agreeable. For all green and unripe olives are harsh, and it is quite certain that all harshness is very hard to tame and overcome. Pliny, book 23, chapter 3, reports that white olives (which are midway between green and ripe, the green ones being bitter, and the black ones, which relax the stomach with their oiliness) are useful to the stomach. Celsus, book 4, chapter 20, Galen, book 5, On the Composition of Drugs according to Places, and also Oribasius, book 7, say the same. For all of these use them to tighten the stomach.

units.la: Vilis enim stomachi relaxatus appetitum perditur, & ventriculus fit debilis, corroboratur eiusdem astringit. Quae igitur magis astringunt, sedundum menses adhibendae sunt, vt robora-to ore ventriculi deorsum pellantur cetera cibaria. Sed hodie eruditi pariter atque inerudsti, primo, medio & postremo cibo, vt carnibus, piscibus eas sine vllo discrimine intermiscent. Capparis fructus crudi stomacho nocent, quare coctos primum, deinde ex oleo & aceto mandere eos consuenit, sic enim appetitum excitant pitui-tam in ventriculo incidunt, atque educunt. Continuum Capparum vsus difficulter vrinam reddentibus, podagricis, splenetici, magno ad- cra sit.
units.tr: For when the stomach is relaxed, the appetite is lost and the stomach becomes weak, and it is strengthened by what binds it. Therefore those things which bind more strongly should be taken according to the courses of the meal, so that, once the mouth of the stomach is strengthened, the other foods are pushed downward. But today learned and unlearned alike mix them without any distinction into the first, middle and last course, with meats and fish. Raw caper fruits harm the stomach, which is why people are accustomed to eat them first cooked, then with oil and vinegar; for in this way they excite the appetite, and they cut through and expel phlegm in the stomach. Continuous use of capers is a burden to those who pass urine with difficulty, to the gouty, and to the splenetic.

units.la: V s iumeniumento est. Radicis vsus maioris momenti experimenti est. Germani nostri iampridem in assuefecerunt in cibis liberalibus vti, sicut & alii non sine valetudinis incommodo, licet magnum sibi inde commodum promittant, vel potius imaginentur. Galli, Hispani & Itali, quorum ventriculi acquisita per consuetudinem proprietate in corpore is alimoniam eiusmodi fructus digerunt, frequentiorem ac liberaliorem usum renunquam.
units.tr: Their root is a useful remedy. Its use is a matter of greater importance, as experience shows. Our Germans long ago accustomed themselves to use it among their delicacies, as did others, not without harm to their health, although they promise themselves, or rather imagine, great benefit from it. The French, Spanish and Italians, whose stomachs have acquired through habit the capacity to digest such food, use it more often and more freely, without any such harm.

units.la: De ficubus.
units.tr: On figs.

units.la: Ficuum naturam breuiter & vt rei veritas postulat, perstringemus. In magna autem autoritate atq; admiratione fuisse ficum indicio est, quod multi ex Græcis multa de ea memoriæ prodiderunt, eamque omnibus arboribus fructus bonitate prætulerunt. Galenus ficus in fenestute inter omnia poma minus sibi nocuisse testatus est, ab omni enim fugaci pomo abstinuit, exceptis maturis vuis & ficub*. Plato φιλόσυκος id est, ficuum amator cognominatus est. Recentes plenamque maturitatem adeptæ innocentius eduntur, aluum enim laxant, celeriterq; per eam deiiciuntur, quin & infigniter abstergunt, in cibis namque sumtæ è calculosis renibus arenularum vim magnam detrahant, valentissimumq; corpori alimentum præstant, licet id non sit vsq; adeò soli-dum. dum, sed sublaxum & tenue. Immodice efita-tæ, frequenterque devoratæ improbum sanguinem pariunt, ventremque inflationibus implent, quæ tamen cito euanescunt, modo non aliorum ciborum copia impediat. Itaq; non ignorandum est, in his quoq; non exiguas vitæ subesse insidias. Est in exemplis, quoddam blandidissimus ficuum saporibus prolectatos, vsq; adeò ab earum esu sibi temperare non potuisse, vt supra modum tumidum, turgidum, distentumque in amplitudinem vetrem adepti, prope perierint, nisi mature remedium iis fuisset adhibitum. Scio in Italia id contigisse quibusdam Germanis, nā hi auidius plerunq; cibos eiusmodi exoticos & inconsuetos expetere consueuerunt. Itaque, quibus Italiam, vel Galliam perlustrare ac peruadere animus est, me consultore fructibus vescendis paulatim assuefaciant.
units.tr: We shall briefly, and as the truth of the matter demands, describe the nature of figs. That they were held in great authority and esteem is shown by the fact that many of the Greeks related much about them in their writings, and preferred them to all trees for the goodness of their fruit. Galen testified that in his own experience figs had harmed him least of all fruits, for he abstained from every fleeting fruit except ripe grapes and figs. Plato was surnamed *philosykos*, that is, a lover of figs. Fresh figs that have reached full ripeness are eaten with less harm, for they loosen the bowels and quickly pass through them; indeed they also cleanse remarkably, for when eaten they draw out a great quantity of grit from the kidneys of those troubled with stones, and they provide a very strong nourishment for the body, though this is not very solid but loose and thin. Figs eaten immoderately and frequently produce bad blood and fill the belly with flatulence, but these effects soon pass away, provided the abundance of other foods does not hinder them. Therefore it must not be ignored that in these also lie no small dangers to life. There is an example of a certain man who, enticed by the very pleasant taste of figs, could not so restrain himself from eating them that, his belly swollen beyond measure, tumid and distended to an enormous size, he nearly died, unless a remedy had been applied to him in time. I know that this happened in Italy to some Germans, for they usually crave such exotic and unaccustomed foods rather greedily. Therefore, those who intend to travel through or to traverse Italy or Gaul should, with my advice, gradually accustom themselves to eating such fruits.

units.la: De vuis.
units.tr: On grapes.

units.la: Innumeras vuarum esse differentias, ostendunt, color, figura, sapor, amplitudo, duritiex, mollitiesque. Quin & acini, qui in quibusdam exiles & parui, in aliis grandiores, rotundi vel prælongi sunt differentiæ constituunt, quas omnes ac singulas persequi operosum est & difficile. Legatur Plin. l. 14. c. 2 & Diosc. l. 5. c. 5, qui diligentissimè vitiū vini etiam genera descripserunt. Quædam tamen, ne nihil fecifle videar, adnotabo, cum primis de vuarum in annuos vsus conditura. In vuis autem non pictura, sed natura consideranda venit. Nő enim omnia dici possunt, sed maxime vtilia & necessaria. Notandum itaque {a}dulces vuas probeque maturas corpus mediocriter alere, calidioris- que esse temperaturæ, ob idque sitim afferre pariterque alluum emollire, idque præstant eò magis quò sunt humidiores. Maximum enim beneficium commodumque in iis est, quæ celeriter alluum mouent, velociterque subsident, & quæ ventrem non inflant, quod fit, si post alios cibos sumantur, quod in primis hic obser- uandum est contra prosperæ valetudinis minus studiosos, nec non contra receptam vsuque pene sed male confirmatam in Germania consuetudinem, quâ, quæ tenuiori involuuntur cortice, vt sunt vuæ, cerasa, pruna, persica, fecundis semper mensis imponitur, more rationi probatissimorumq; medicorum placitis, quin & experientiæ ipsi aduerso. Sed de hoc errore, quo in omnib. fere Magnatū aulis nihil frequentius est, alibi festa est mentio. Porro q auctoræ sunt acidæ q; gelidioris sunt naturæ, quapropter choleram ardoremque restinguunt, mitescunt autem acidulæ diutius pendentes, auctoræ in perfecta etiam maturitate suspensæ mitiores non reddunredduntur: vtraque vero alimento parum apta deprehenditur. Galenus commendat eas uvas, quae duriori sunt callo & acino (vnde duracinae appellantur) solidioris quefubstantiae, minusque liquoris habeant, has enim valentius nutrire affirmat.
units.tr: The differences among grapes are innumerable, as their colour, shape, taste, size, hardness and softness show. Moreover, the berries, which in some kinds are small and slender, in others larger, round or very long, also make distinctions, all of which it is laborious and difficult to pursue one by one. Let the reader consult Pliny, book 14, chapter 2, and Dioscorides, book 5, chapter 5, who described very carefully even the kinds of wine. Yet, lest I seem to have done nothing, I will note some points, chiefly concerning the preserving of grapes for use throughout the year. In grapes, however, one must consider not their appearance but their nature. For not everything can be said, but only what is most useful and necessary. It must therefore be noted that sweet grapes, properly ripe, nourish the body moderately, are of a somewhat warmer temperament, and for that reason cause thirst, and at the same time loosen the bowels; and they do this the more, the juicier they are. For the greatest benefit and advantage lies in those that move the bowels quickly and pass through rapidly, and that do not inflate the belly. This happens if they are eaten after other foods, which must be observed here above all, against those who are less careful of good health, and against the custom received and nearly universal in Germany, though poorly established, by which fruits enclosed in a thin skin, such as grapes, cherries, plums and peaches, are always placed on the table after the courses. This is contrary to reason, to the judgement of the most approved physicians, and even to experience itself. But of this error, which is nowhere more frequent than in the courts of nearly all the great, I have made mention elsewhere. Furthermore, those that are sour and of a colder nature quench choler and heat; sourish grapes that hang on the vine for a long time become milder, but those that remain hanging even in full ripeness do not become milder. Both kinds are found to be little suited to nourishment.
