Galen recommends those grapes which have a harder skin and berry (whence they are called duracinae), and which have a more solid substance and less juice, for he asserts that these nourish more strongly.

units.la: Verum de conditura vuarum opere pretium est aliquid meminisse, multipliciter enim tiune vua modo in annuos reseruantur vsus. Principio condiantur notasse hic lectorem oportet, vuam fine tur ac sernoxa seruari, si luna decrescente serenoque caelo colligatur, id quod & de feminibus & fructibus intelligendum. Rationem in Cur luna promtu esse animaduertes, si considerauerits, decrescent vim alimentorum insuauem crudumque; succum, qui saepe in feminibus fructibusque de-caelo vua litescit, solis virtute castigari corrigique, humi fiminaque iusque actione inutilem humiditatem exugi, sint collisopitumque ac deperditum saporem restitui genda? atque reuocari. Caeterum Columella refert inter multos seruandarum vuarum modos huncextitisse fere praecipuum, quando in labello fictili nouo, paleis quam ficciffimis cribatis, vt fine puluere essent, impleto, vuae condebantur, deinde labellum luto paleato circumlinitum in tabulato ficciffimo paleis ficciffimis obruebatur, talesque; vuas paleales vocarunt, quae humore superuacaneo spolia-te aegris impune concedebantur. Quae autem in officinis fabrorum ferrariorum suspendebantur,
units.tr: But concerning the preserving of grapes it is worth recalling something, for grapes are kept for use throughout the year in many ways. First, the reader must here take note that grapes are preserved without spoiling or shrivelling if they are gathered while the moon is waning and the sky is clear; this is to be understood also of seeds and fruits. The reason is easy to grasp if one considers that the waning moon's influence drives out the unpleasant and raw juice, which often forms in seeds and fruits from the heavens, and that this is corrected and purged by the power of the sun and the action of the earth, and that the useless moisture is drawn out by the dryness and heat, and that the lost flavour is restored and recalled. Moreover, Columella reports that among the many methods of preserving grapes, the chief one was this: the grapes were stored in a new earthen jar filled with very dry chaff that had been sifted so as to be free of dust; then the jar was smeared around with clay mixed with chaff, and set in a very dry place, buried in very dry chaff. Such grapes they called "chaff grapes," and they were given without harm to the sick, once the superfluous moisture had been removed. Those that were hung in the workshops of iron-smiths, so that they might be kept longer, dried by fire and smoke, were called "smithy grapes."

units.la: {a} Quid vua palea les, & fa- brilla? bantur, vt igne atque fumo exiccatæ diutius possint incorruptæ seruari, fabriles appellatæ sunt. Plinius docet eas seruari in ollis fictilibus, atq; in doliis inclusas, vinaceis stipatas circumsudantibus. Quæ in ollis fictilibus asseruantur, obturato atq; etiam picato ore earum ventriculum infirmum corroborant & firmant, appetentiam torpescentem excitant, sed liberalius voratæ caput tentant, idq; ob nullam aliam causam quàm vinaceorum halitum. Aliæ multo condiuntur, quæ stomacho inimicæ censentur. Alii in granariis eas suspendunt, putantes sic pensilibus pulue-rem optimo operimento esse. Matresfamilias in quibusdam locis in alta eas cruce seruabiles faciunt, durantq; per hiemem, ac etiam in æstatem. Duracinæ sine vllis vasis sunt in vite seruabiles. Quidam solem prius passas in aqua cœlesti recondunt, quas Plinius saluberrimas dicit, sicut sapâ conditas improbat, nec non quæ in musto fuerunt. Atheneus in vino reponi scripsit. Alii denique vuas per vindemiam legunt, quas foliis vitiū implicitas atque inuolutas furno siccant, solent etiam per se in furno exiccari, ægrisque reponi.
units.tr: {a} What are palea grapes and fabrilla grapes? Pliny teaches that they are kept in earthen pots, and enclosed in casks, packed around with grape-skins that sweat. Those kept in earthen pots, with the mouth stopped and even sealed with pitch, strengthen and fortify a weak stomach and rouse a sluggish appetite; but when eaten too freely they harm the head, and this for no other reason than the vapour of the grape-skins. Others are preserved in much salt, and these are regarded as harmful to the stomach. Some hang them in granaries, thinking that dust is the best covering for hanging things. In certain places housewives keep them on high crosses, where they last through the winter and even into the summer. Duracinae can be kept on the vine without any vessels. Some put raisins first in heavenly water and store them there; Pliny calls these most wholesome, while he disapproves of those preserved in grape-syrup, and likewise those that have stayed in the must. Athenaeus wrote that they are kept in wine. Finally, others gather grapes at the vintage, wrap them in vine-leaves and dry them in an oven; they also commonly dry them by themselves in an oven and store them for the sick.

units.la: De vuis passis.
units.tr: On raisins.

units.la: Quanta vero in ciborum gloria hodie sint vuæ passæ, nemini non constat. Bonum enim prabent nutrimentum, stomachoq; optimè conueniunt, ac in cibo ficubus suauiores sunt & utilio-ës. Laudatissimæ sunt pingui tenerog; callo prædita: dulciores quoq; palato & stomacho magis arridentes: austerã ventrem firmant, alium umq; cohibent, ad vinosum enim accedunt saporem. Dulcium autem ingens est turba, adq; nos in magna copia iuncta fiscellis includuntur plurimum ex Hispania, quæ grandes mittit & suauitate præstantissimas. Minimas, quæ videlicet acinus carent, Galen. 2. de aliment. facult. scribit, in Cilicia prouenire: alias non satis constat, vbi & vt gignantur, nisi quod calida eas opus habere terra, facile potest coniici.
units.tr: How highly raisins are esteemed in the kitchen today is known to everyone. They provide good nourishment, agree very well with the stomach, and in food they are sweeter and more useful than figs. The most prized are plump, with a tender skin; they are also sweeter to the palate and more pleasing to the stomach. Their astringency strengthens the belly and checks looseness, for they have a winy flavour. Sweet raisins come in great variety, and large quantities of them are imported to us in baskets, mostly from Spain, which sends the large ones, outstanding for their sweetness. Galen, in book 2 of On the Faculties of Foods, writes that the smallest kind, which have no stones, grow in Cilicia. Where and how the others are grown is not well established, though one can easily guess that they need a warm soil.

units.la: De malis citreis & arantiis.
units.tr: On citron and orange apples.

units.la: Hæc poma colore, odore & succo insignia sunt, myropoliis magis quàm culinis nota. Distinguuntur autem amplitudine colore, figura, odore, sapore. In nostra Germania citrea malus non perinde frequens reperitur, atque in Italia & Gallia, propterea quod rigida illi apud nos obstet hiems, siquidem frigoris impatientissima est. Porro q aureo colore refulgent, odoratissimiq; sunt halitus arantia dicuntur vulgo & chrysomela: ouata specie turbinata luteoq; colore nitētia citrangula & citrea vocāt her- baceo vero colore virentia limones dicitur, quæ fi prægrandia sunt melonumquë modo orbiculata facie turgent ponceria vocantur, sed vernacula hæc specierum nomina sunt, quæ sicut & alia sollicitè disquirere luperstitiosum est. Ad facultates igitur quibus pollent, veniamus.
units.tr: These fruits are distinguished by their colour, smell and juice, and are known more to perfumers than to cooks. They differ in size, colour, shape, smell and taste. In our Germany the citron tree is not nearly as common as in Italy and France, because our harsh winter stands in its way, since it cannot endure cold at all. Those that shine with a golden colour and have the strongest scent are commonly called oranges and chrysomela. Those of oval shape, tapering and shining with a yellow colour, are called citrangula and citrea. Those of a grassy green colour are called limones. If they are very large and swell into a round shape like melons, they are called ponceria. These, however, are vernacular names of kinds, and it is superstitious to inquire carefully into them, as into other such names. Let us therefore come to the powers they possess.

units.la: Præsentissimum exhibet remedium contra deleterium pharmacum potum, si quis femina cum pomorum succo contusa cum vino biberit, per ventrem enim pharmacum exturbat. Tempore Theophrasti & Plinii pomum non edebant, sed veluti thesaurum, teste Atheneo lib.3. in scriniis cum vestimentis reponebant, iis enim interiectum tineas necat, vestesque ab illarum rufione inoffensas conseruat. Vnde Homerus & Neuius Poeta vestes citrosas nominant. Quam verò sit contra omne virus remedium efficax, ex Athenei de duobus latronibus historia conici potest, quos ad virulentas bestias condemnatos in Ægypto refert: verum cum ad supplicii theatruum, bestiis virulenta atrocitate efferatis plenum deducerentur, mulier cauponaria illis obuia horumque miserta, citriu quod manu tenebat illis edendum præbuit, quo comesto, cum illæsi & citra noxam cum Draconibus colluctarentur, accersito à præside carceris præfecto, ecquid Alexipharmaci præbibissent vel edissent, percontatus, nihil præter citrium respondit. Præses igitur de viribus citrii mali certius periculum factu-rus, alteri tantum de eo praebuit, cui item be-stiarum virus nihil nocuit, alter vero ab aspi-de morsus quamprimum in theatro concidit & expirauit. Anhelitus praeterea grauiore lentiam arcet, si decocto pomorum os colluitur. Praegnantium quoque malaciae prosunt mala citria. Sed Plinius semen tantum laudat.
units.tr: The citron offers a very effective remedy against a poison drunk, if someone crushes the juice of the fruit with a woman's aid and drinks it with wine; for it drives the poison out through the bowels. In the time of Theophrastus and Pliny people did not eat the fruit but kept it, as a treasure, in chests with their clothes, according to Athenaeus in book 3; for placed among the garments it kills moths and keeps the clothes safe from their gnawing. Hence Homer and the poet Naevius call garments "citron-scented". How truly effective it is against every kind of poison can be inferred from the story of Athenaeus about two robbers, whom he reports were condemned in Egypt to be thrown to venomous beasts. But when they were led into the arena, full of beasts raging with venomous fury, a tavern-woman who met them, pitying them, gave them a citron she held in her hand to eat. After they had eaten it, they wrestled with the dragons unharmed and without injury. When the prefect of the prison summoned by the governor was asked whether they had drunk or eaten any antidote, he answered that they had taken nothing but the citron. The governor, wishing to test more certainly the power of the citron, gave some only to another man, and the venom of the beasts did him no harm, but the other, bitten by an asp, collapsed in the theatre at once and died. Moreover, if the mouth is rinsed with a decoction of the fruit, it drives away bad breath more effectively. Citrons also help women who are pregnant against nausea. But Pliny praises only the seed.

units.la: Inter arantia quae acida sunt praeclaros intinctus cibariis praestant, durantque in maximam aestatis partem, calorem enim temperant, fastidium abigunt, auiditatemque excitant. Dulcia tuflicutolis, thoracicpulmonibus exasperatisque faucibus sunt amica. Ex acidis liquor magis experitur. Sed disseeta vinoque iniecta non paruam ei gratiam conciliant. Cortices Citriorum & arantiarum saccharo varie praeparantur, nunc incrustando, nunc integendo, nunc condiendo ad varios visus & delitias gulae. Vnum notandum carnem horum pomorum crassi succi esse ac pituitosi: succum acidum refrigerate & siccare: cortices vero odoratos quidem esse constat acres & efficaces, praesertim contra venena & ventris tormina, sed in ventre difficulter conficiuntur, quia praeduri rugosi & callosi sunt, quare conditi, vel decocti vel etiam macerati vino, ventriculum magis firmabunt. Nuclei eandem pene cum X cortice obtinent vim calefaciendi scilicet discutiendi & exiccandi. Ad extremum de liquore acido sciendum, cum saccharo coqui, seruariquead æstatis æstuantis febres, pestilentiaeque contagia certo experimento. Ipsa vero poma in Magnatum aulis in taleolas conciduntur, sacchariquepolline asperso manducantur prima mensa, acetariorum vicem supplentia, sed ita comesa difficulter in ventriculo confici extra dubium est, praedura enim caro est, pituitosa ac gelida, unde colicos excitari dolores necesse est, si immodice & frequentius esitetur.
units.tr: Among oranges, the sour ones provide excellent relishes for food, and they keep for most of the summer; for they temper heat, drive away loathing and stir up appetite. The sweet ones are good for coughs, for the lungs when they are roughened, and for a rough throat. Of the sour ones, the juice is more effective. But when they are cut up and mixed with wine they bring no small favour to the stomach. The peels of citrons and oranges are prepared in various ways with sugar, now by encrusting, now by candying, now by preserving, to suit different tastes and the delights of the palate. It should be noted that the flesh of these fruits is thick and phlegmatic, and the acid juice is cooling and drying. The peels, indeed, are known to be fragrant, sharp and effective, especially against poisons and gripes of the bowels; but they are digested with difficulty in the stomach, because they are very hard, wrinkled and tough. Therefore, preserved, boiled or even steeped in wine, they will strengthen the stomach more. The kernels have nearly the same power, namely to warm, disperse and dry. Finally, one should know from sure experience that the acid juice, when cooked with sugar and kept, is good for the fevers of the sweltering summer and for the contagion of plague. The fruits themselves, in the courts of great men, are cut into slices and eaten at the first course, sprinkled with powdered sugar, taking the place of salads. But that such fruit, eaten in this way, is digested with difficulty in the stomach is beyond doubt; for the flesh is very hard, phlegmatic and cold, so that if it is eaten immoderately and too often, it necessarily brings on colic pains.

units.la: Submonitio ad locum de citriis, &c.
units.tr: Note on the passage about citrons, etc.

units.la: Graeci & Arabes in qualitatibus citrii malirecensendis nequaquam consentiunt. Avicenna cortice citri calidum esse ait, in primo, & siccum in gradu secundo. Galenus siccum absolute in secundo, nec calidum contra aftuit. Idem Avicenna carnem dicit calidam, Galenus & Aegineta frigidam. Semen decoctum suavem ori conciliare odorem, corpus reddere pingue scribit, quorum postremum a nullo Graecorum traditum est, omnemque excedit rationem. Acidam eiusparem bonum esse nutrimentum gutturi & pulmoni contendit, quorum utrumque rationi, aliorum Serapioni etiam contra:ontrarium est, nocere pulmoni affirmanti. Veum Auicennæ sententiam confutat experientia psa, cui refragari ineptum est. De cortice aran-iarum certum est calidioris eum esse naturæ quam citriorum, frigidos enim stomachi humo-res discutit atque educit. Poma ipsa ante ma-turitatem adhuc viridia cortices habent gustu amarum & ferentem, qui recens compressus reddit oleum, attrahendi exiccandiq; vt ignē.
units.tr: The Greeks and Arabs by no means agree in describing the qualities of the citron. Avicenna says that the rind of the citron is hot in the first degree and dry in the second. Galen says it is dry absolutely in the second degree, and does not assert it to be hot in any way. The same Avicenna says the flesh is hot, while Galen and Aegineta call it cold. He writes that the decocted seed gives the mouth a sweet smell and makes the body fat; of these the last has been handed down by no Greek, and it goes beyond all reason. He maintains that the acid part of the same is good nourishment for the throat and lungs; both of these are contrary to reason and to the opinion of others, and even Serapion, affirming that it harms the lungs. Experience itself refutes the opinion of Avicenna, and it is foolish to gainsay it. It is certain that the rind of oranges is of a warmer nature than that of citrons, for it disperses and draws out the cold humours of the stomach. The fruits themselves, before ripeness, still green, have rinds bitter and astringent in taste, which, when pressed fresh, yield an oil that draws and dries like fire.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: De alimentis quæ veniunt ex floribus, vbi commodè de acetariis rite præparandis.
units.tr: On foods that come from flowers, and on the proper preparation of salads.

units.la: ACetariis nullum ab antiquis scriptoribus, Græcis præsertim, peculiare nomen impositum reperitur, quibus tamen maxima in assignandis & imponendis rerum vocabulis erat licentia. Sunt autem acetaria non tantum, vt vulgò putatur, herbæ virentes, quæ ex aceto, sale, oleoque guttatim instillato concinnantur, ad languentem scilicet appetitum excitandum, ventriculumque corroborandum, nec non humores in ore ventriculi residentes appetitum extinguentes, extergendos, verum etiam cappa-res, bulbi, oliuæ, oua indurata, carnes minu-tim concisæ & ex aceto sumtæ, suilla salita, citria saccharo conspersa, & id genus alia. Vnde videre est, acetaria non recte ab aceto nominari, cum ab accipiendo potius nomen flectatur, quoniam horti igne non indigeant, ac ligno parcant, finique res expedita & parata semper, testante Plinio l. 19. c. 4. Antiqui enim hortos suos acetaria quasi acceptaria appellabant. Acetaria autem nobis vocata veteribus mensæ frigidæ fuerunt appellata, inque vltimo mensæ apponebantur, quæ tamen tempore Plutarchi primò in mensas loco ferri cœperunt, cui Martialis, qui iisdem temporibus quibus Plutarchus vixit, adstipulatur, qui lactucam vltimo prius loco positam, sua verò ætate ante alias dapes efitatam testatur hoc disticho,
units.tr: No special name for salads is found in the ancient writers, especially the Greeks, though they had great freedom in assigning and giving names to things. Salads are not, as is commonly thought, only green herbs dressed with vinegar, salt and oil poured on drop by drop, to rouse a flagging appetite, strengthen the stomach, and wipe away the humours that settle at the mouth of the stomach and dull the appetite. They also include capers, bulbs, olives, hard-boiled eggs, meats cut small and taken with vinegar, salted pork, citrons sprinkled with sugar, and other things of that kind. From this it is clear that "acetaria" is not rightly named from vinegar (acetum), since the name is more properly derived from "accipere" (to receive), because these dishes need no fire, spare the wood, and are always ready and prepared at hand, as Pliny testifies (Book 19, chapter 4). For the ancients called their kitchen gardens "acceptaria," as it were. The dishes we call acetaria were called by the ancients "cold tables," and were placed at the end of the meal. Yet in Plutarch's time they first began to be brought in at the start of the meal. Martial, who lived in the same period as Plutarch, agrees, and in this couplet attests that the lettuce, formerly placed last, was in his own day served before other dishes:

units.la: Claudere quæ cœnas lactuca solebat auorum,
units.tr: The lettuce that used to close the dinners of our forefathers,

units.la: Dic mihi cur nostras incipit illa dapes?
units.tr: Tell me why it now opens our feasts.

units.la: Causam autem cur veteres cœnam lactucis finire sint soliti, vide loco de lactuca.
units.tr: The reason why the ancients were accustomed to end dinner with lettuces, see in the place on lettuce.

units.la: Cæterum, quia acetaria (hoc enim vocabulum neotericum ab omnibus receptum esse video) diuersi sunt temperamenti pro variarum rerum, ex quibus conflantur natura & proprietate, tum etiam, quod liberaliorem liorem eorum & frequentiorem vsum mi ius salubrem esse pro comperto habetur, modum in iis tenendum esse ante omnia me- minifle oportebit. Non enim palati tan- tum gratia ea inuenta sunt, sed & valetudinis causa, iisque non vtepulis semper & cibariis, sed & vt medicamentis vti oportet. Con- stat herbis crudis crebrius immoderatiusque vsos grauibus aegritudinibus tentari, quoni- am ex his succus, qui in corpus diffunditur, maxima ex parte crudus ac vitiosus est. Vi- rens certe ille succus, quem bilem porrace- am appellant, & plerique euomere solent, (german. die grüne Gallen) non panis aut carnis, aut alterius escae culpa gignirur, sed al- terius cuiufdam feruidioris acriorisque fuc-ci noxa, qualis est ceparum, allii, porri, raphani: & licet plurima huiusmodi modice sumta salutaria deprehenduntur, immoderata ta-men & frequentiora graues adferunt mor-bos: Quod obiter hic noto propter gentium quarundam morem, quae talia in quotidiano habent victu.
units.tr: Moreover, since acetaria (for I see this modern word is received by everyone) differ in temperament according to the nature and properties of the various things of which they are made, and since it is established that their more generous and frequent use is harmful, one must above all remember to keep moderation in them. They were devised not only for the sake of pleasure but also for health, and they should be used not always as food and nourishment, but also as medicines. It is established that people who often and immoderately eat raw herbs are attacked by serious diseases, because the juice that passes into the body from them is for the most part raw and faulty. That green juice which they call bitter bile, and which most people are accustomed to vomit (German: die grüne Galle), arises not from the fault of bread, meat, or other food, but from the harm of another, hotter and sharper juice, such as that of onions, garlic, leeks and radishes. And although many such things taken in moderation are found to be wholesome, yet taken immoderately and too often they bring serious diseases. I note this in passing, because of the custom of certain peoples who have such things in their daily diet.

units.la: Quibusdam etiam acetaria adeo sunt vsi-tata, vt in cibis aestate praesertim, vix habeant aliquid frequentius, stupido enim & bruto plane palato ea deuorant & inglutiunt nulla habita distinctione & discrimine ipsarum, quae in ea ingrediuntur, rerum. Exemplo est
units.tr: For some people acetaria are so commonly used that, especially in summer, they hardly have anything more frequent among their foods. With a plainly dull and brutish palate they gulp them down and swallow them without any distinction or discrimination among the things that go into them. An example is

units.la: X Antuerpiensium conuiuarum interitus, qui in acetariis radice lupatię seu aconiti vescentes diem suum obierunt. Ventriculo naturā frigido & imbecillo, cerebroque nimis humido acetaria frigida, vt quæ ex lactuca, acetosa, portulaca, endiuia, & similibus parantur, nocent, quare ventriculus ita affectus in vniuersum ab eiusmodi crudis abstinebit, nisi eiusmodi frigida calidis contemperentur, vt eruca, fœniculo, anisio, coriandro, mentha, hyssopo, thymo, satureia, tragopogo, & similibus, quæ commodè frigidis possunt commiscerì, hæc enim frigus lactucę calore immisto temperant. Commodissimè quoq; acetariis immiscentur flores buglossæ, borraginis, cichorii, rosarum, saluiæ, hyssopi, flores persicæ arboris, saporem enim iis conciliant gratum & salutarem. Quibus verò ventriculus immodica bile efferuescit ac ebullit, iis acetaria frigida concedVntur: bilis enim feruorem sitimque extinguunt. Conficiuntur quoque acetaria palato delicatiori non ingrata, ex asparago lupuloque, sed recentibus adhuc, cum scilicet in caulem nondum prorupuerunt, quod fit ineunte vere. Nasturtium quoque aquaticum in acetariis celebratur hieme, æstate verò hortense ad fastidium discutiendum, lienisque obstructiones aperiendas.
units.tr: the death of the Antwerp feasters, who died from eating, in their salads, the root of wolfsbane, or aconite. Cold salads, such as those made of lettuce, sorrel, purslane, endive and the like, harm a stomach that is by nature cold and weak, and a brain that is too moist. So a stomach so affected will in general abstain from such raw foods, unless these cold things are tempered with warm ones, such as rocket, fennel, anise, coriander, mint, hyssop, thyme, savory, goat's-beard, and similar herbs, which can conveniently be mixed with cold ones; for these temper the coldness of lettuce by the mixed-in warmth. Flowers of borage, of bugloss, of chicory, of roses, of sage, of hyssop, and flowers of the peach tree are also most conveniently mixed into salads, for they give them a pleasant and wholesome flavour. Cold salads are allowed to those whose stomach boils and seethes with excess bile, for they quench the heat and thirst of the bile. Salads of asparagus and hops, which are not unpleasing even to a more delicate palate, are also made, but only while the shoots are still fresh, that is, before they have pushed up into stalk, which happens at the beginning of spring. Water cress is also commonly used in salads in winter, and garden cress in summer, to dispel distaste and to open obstructions of the spleen.

units.la: NB. Quibus acetaria conueniant, & quibus noxia sint? Acetariorum recte temperandorum & concinnandi modus. Flores ex quibus conficiuntur acetaria.
units.tr: NB. For whom are salads suitable, and for whom are they harmful? The manner of rightly seasoning and preparing salads. The flowers from which salads are made.

units.la: Notandum tamen, olei non multum acetariis immitti debere, ventriculi enim os relaxat, appetentiamque restinguit magis quàm excitat. In ventriculo enim robo- rando incidentia & astringentia adhibenda sunt non relaxantia, vt sunt oleosa & vn- guinosa. Quare improbantur eiusmodi acetaria, quæ in quibusdam locis parān- tur ex immodico butyro feruefacto, olei vicem supplente ob causam iam comme-moratam. In vniuersum quoque damnan- tur acetaria, quæ multis in locis præsfer- tim circa autumnum fiunt ex caule capita- to minutum dissecto acetoque perfuso; (vulgus nominat wetlfen Salat) cuius tanta est cupido, vt in lautioribus etiam & splendidioribus conuiuiis inter primas mensarum delicias habeatur, primumque mereatur locum: eo enim venere mores luxuriaque, vt gulæ potius quam vitæ habeatur ratio. Abdicanda denique ace- taria sunt, quæ calidis herbis vel aromati- bus,vt pipere, saleque non sunt contempe- rata, quod hodie ab omnibus fere negligi animaduerto, etiam mitiorem & delica- tiorem vitam sequentibus, qui non raro pe- cudum instar ea turgidis buccis ingluti- unt, quod sæpe ad stuporem vsque miratus sum.
units.tr: It should be noted, however, that not much oil ought to be added to salads, for it relaxes the mouth of the stomach and dulls the appetite rather than sharpening it. For in strengthening the stomach, cutting and astringent things are to be used, not relaxing ones such as oily and greasy foods. For this reason those salads are disapproved which in some places are prepared with excessive melted butter standing in for oil, for the reason already mentioned. In general, too, those salads are condemned which in many places, especially about autumn, are made from cabbage finely cut up and drenched in vinegar (the common people call it wetlfen Salat). Such is the craving for them that even at more elegant and splendid feasts they are counted among the first delicacies of the table and deserve the first place. Manners and luxury have come to such a pass that regard is had to the belly rather than to life. Finally, those salads must be rejected which have not been seasoned with hot herbs or spices such as pepper and salt. I observe that today nearly everyone neglects this, even those who follow a milder and more delicate way of life, who often gulp them down with swollen cheeks like cattle; I have often wondered at this to the point of amazement.

units.la: Stulte gos. Stultè enim sibi persuadent & imaginantur, ventriculum se habere calidum, eparque calidioris esse temperaturæ, propterea à calidis abstinendum.
units.tr: Foolishly, then. For they persuade themselves and imagine that their stomach is hot, and that they are of a hotter temperament, and therefore must abstain from hot things.

units.la: Sed sciant isti facilius esse & tutius membrum nimio calore efteruescens refrigerare quam nimio algore emortuum excalfacere. Similia enim similibus sunt conseruanda & roboranda, nam destructio fit per contraria. Modus tamen seruandus præcipitur. De aceto illud non omittendum, quanto fuerit acrius, tanto minus id frigidæ naturæ esse: huiusque acorem saccharo aut vuis passis in eo decoctis mitigari: acetum igitur quo acrius, eo ad acetariorum vsum accomodatius est. Hactenus de alimentis quæ veniunt ex vegetabilibus, quib. nō inepte subiici possunt tubera & fungi quos terra vegetabilium mater sponte protrudit.
units.tr: But let those people know that it is easier and safer to cool a part that seethes from excessive heat than to warm one that is dead from excessive chill. For like things are to be preserved and strengthened by like things, since destruction comes about through contraries. Moderation must nevertheless be kept, as is prescribed. Regarding vinegar, this should not be omitted: the sharper it is, the less it is of a cold nature; and its sharpness is softened by sugar, or by raisins boiled in it. Therefore the sharper the vinegar, the better suited it is to the use of salads. So far concerning foods that come from plants, to which truffles and mushrooms, which the earth, the mother of plants, puts forth of her own accord, may not unfittingly be added.

units.la: De fungis.
units.tr: On mushrooms.

units.la: DEmirandum, eo vsque nostri feculifu-riosam & insanam deuenisse gulam, vt in cibos adhibere velit ea quæ vitæ sunt pestis. Quid enim quasi nobis esse potest commune cum pistuita illa arborum (sic enim recte nominat Plinius l.22.c.13.) & terra vitiis, inter quæ pestilens fungorum scelus? Familiae enim eos interemisse & coniugia, Anneum Serenum prafeƈtum Neronis vigilum, & tribunos, & centuriones, idem Plinius est testis. Ni- hil enim aliud esse fungos quam terra, arbo- rum, lignorum, aliarumq; putrilaginum super- sluas humiditates, inde colligi potest, quod omnes fere e tonitribus & pluuioso cœli statu frequen- tius soleant enasci absq; radice, floribus & semi- ne. Unde veteres, cum animaduerterent fun- gos absq; semine procreari, crediderunt cogna- tionem illis aliquam cum cœlo esse. Repente vero e medio iterum tolluntur, nam ortus occasiu- eorum qui humi proueniunt, septem plerunq; in- cluditur diebus, cuius ortus interitusq; causa est abundans, qua scatent, humiditas. Merito igitur a fungorum esu se deterreri sinent sanita- ti consulentes, primo quod a clarissimis scripto- ribus inter venena collocantur, & a funere a- gendo distos quidam existimant, tum etiam, quod pituitosum, gelidum, crassum, lentum, iniquiq; succi alimentum præstant, magna enim ex parte vix consiciuntur, sed cum alui excre- mentis sape reiiciuntur integri & non confecti. Caueant igitur sibi, qui funginis istis delitiis gaudent. Sed hodie sine modo vorantur etiam a magnatibus, qui singulari studio ad dubias eos cœnas exquirunt.
units.tr: It is astonishing that our people have fallen into such a mad and insane gluttony that they want to take into their food things that are a plague to life. For what fellowship can we have with that sluggish corruption of trees (for so Pliny rightly calls it, book 22, chapter 13), and with the vices of the earth, among which is the deadly wickedness of mushrooms? Pliny also testifies that they have destroyed whole households and marriages, including Annaeus Serenus, prefect of Nero's night watch, and tribunes and centurions. Indeed, it can be gathered that mushrooms are nothing but the superfluous moisture of the earth, of trees, of wood and of other rottenness, since nearly all of them tend to sprout, without root, flower or seed, most often after thunder and in rainy weather. Hence the ancients, noticing that mushrooms are produced without seed, believed they had some kinship with heaven. Yet they are soon taken away again from the middle, for the life of those that spring up on the ground is usually confined to about seven days, and the cause of their birth and death is the abundant moisture with which they teem. Therefore, those who look after their health rightly let themselves be deterred from eating mushrooms: first, because the most distinguished writers reckon them among poisons; second, because some think they are unfit for performing the functions of life; and third, because they yield a food that is phlegmatic, cold, thick, viscous and of bad juice. For they are for the most part hardly digested, but are often cast out whole and undigested with the excrements of the belly. Let those who delight in these mushroom dainties take care. Yet today they are devoured without measure even by the great men, who with particular eagerness seek them out for those doubtful feasts.

units.la: Noui, quibus pituita illa fungosa cibo- rumq; excrementis nihil delicatius est, dicunt enim non omnes fungos venenatos esse & perni- ciales, ut sunt, qui communiter tubera dicuntur, germ. Mörcheln/vernoq; potissimum tempore ab Aprili ad Majum usq; cernuntur : hos aqua feruente bullire sinunt, postmodum aromatibus & butyro conditos menses imponunt : Item amanita & boleti germani. Heiderling/ in campis & jumentorum pascuis proventes Iunio primum mense, durantq; usq; in Augustum : Hos, membranula tamen liuida prius detracta, similiter butyro aromat. bu q; condiunt : alii super ignitos carbones eos assant, saleq; asperso mandunt, sed quo fructu, ipsi experiantur.
units.tr: I know there are those for whom nothing is more delicious than that fungal phlegm and the excrements of food. For they say that not all mushrooms are poisonous and deadly as those are which are commonly called tubers (German: Mörcheln), which appear mostly in spring, from April to May. These they let boil in boiling water, and afterwards put them in the pot seasoned with spices and butter. Likewise amanita and the true boletes (German: Heiderling), which grow in fields and pastures used by cattle, first appear in June and last until August. These, after first peeling off their livid skin, they season in the same way with butter and spices. Others roast them over glowing coals and eat them sprinkled with salt, but what benefit they get from this, let them find out for themselves.

units.la: Sic inter esui aptos fungos annumerant Orbiculatos, german. Pfifferling/ ab acri & piperis gustu, fractiem laeteum fundunt succum feruentissimi saporis, ac proueniunt in altissimis & tenebrosis montibus colore prorsus candido, disco interdum lateres. Hos, quisquam Odenwald cognominatam incolunt, carbonibus ignitis assare solent, saleq; asperso mandere.
units.tr: Thus among the mushrooms fit for eating they count the round ones (German: Pfifferling), which have a sharp and peppery taste. When broken, they pour out a milky juice of very strong flavour. They grow in the highest and shadiest mountains, of a wholly white colour, sometimes with a disc. Those who live in the region called the Odenwald are accustomed to roast these over glowing coals and eat them sprinkled with salt.

units.la: Ad horum catalogum quoque referunt, quos Brotling appellant in altissimis montibus nascentes punicco colore, hi a quibusdam crudi devorantur, sed qua utilitate nescio.
units.tr: To this catalogue they also refer those called Brotling, which grow on the highest mountains with a purple colour. Some eat these raw, but to what advantage I do not know.

units.la: Hi sunt pracipui, qui hodie in delitiis habentur, inque usum cibarium trahuntur. Praeterea tamen gratiam & praestantiam obtinuerunt parte membranulis liuidis obducti, quae, antequam in cibos veniant, sunt detrahendae. runt tubera, & boleti, qui inter fungos ab antiquis semper sunt habiti optimi. Sed quis hoc spondebit in venenibus? Certum est omnes venenis esse accommodatissimos, improbique succi, quibus nominibus omnino vitari debent.
units.tr: These are the chief ones that are held in favour today and are brought into use as food. Besides these, however, the tubers and the boletes have won favour and excellence; among mushrooms these have always been held the best by the ancients. But who will vouch for them where poisons are concerned? It is certain that all of them are most suited to poisons and contain harmful juice, and for these reasons they must altogether be avoided. Some of them are covered with livid skins, which must be removed before they are taken as food.

units.la: Fungorum enim temerario esu magnas vitae strui insidias exemplo est Claudius Tiberius princeps, cui boletorum avidissimo venenum datum confat ab Agrippina conjuge, quo facto illa terris venenum alterum sibi ante omnes Neronem dedit. Verisimilius tamen videtur Claudium, non vitio boleti, sed vi medicamenti, quo imbutus fuit boletus extinctum fuisse.
units.tr: For that mushrooms are a snare laid for life by reckless eating, the example of the emperor Claudius Tiberius is proof. It is generally agreed that poison was given to him, a great lover of boletes, by his wife Agrippina; and she afterwards, having done this, gave poison to herself, before all others to Nero. Yet it seems more probable that Claudius was killed not by a fault of the bolete, but by the strength of the drug with which the bolete had been soaked.

units.la: Submonitio de fungis.
units.tr: Preliminary remark on mushrooms.

units.la: NE fungorum meauctoritatem prorsus abrogare velle quis existimet, voluptuariosque ac hydnophagos plane mihi inuisos reddam, tum etiam vt ventri ac gulae nonnihil consulatur, sciendum est, vsum quidem me minime damnare, (per me enim licebit cuique ad satietatem etiam iis vesci,) sed modum seruandum praecipere nec ita liberaliter iis vescendum esse.
units.tr: Lest anyone think I wish to abolish altogether the authority of mushrooms, or to make myself wholly hateful to pleasure-seekers and mushroom-lovers, and so that the belly and gullet may be somewhat indulged, it must be known that I by no means condemn their use (for I shall allow anyone to eat them even to the full), but I advise that moderation be observed and that one should not eat them so freely.

units.la: Gratum etiam hydnophagis me facturum rum spero, si non omnes fungos ab antiquis damnatos esse, planum fecerim. Galenus ex fungis boletos orbiculatos tantum attingendos censuit. Celsus item alios fungos vtiles, alios inutiles esse dixit, & hos cochurae genere fieri vtiles. Quod si verum est, vt certe est, etiam muscarii fungi, qui partim rubri partim albi cernuntur, coquendi modo innoxii reddi possunt, praesertim si diligenter elixentur, mox ex oleo aut butyro additis capis & pipere frigantur. Quidam addunt acetum, quod eos eximie debellat.
units.tr: I hope also to please the mushroom-lovers if I make it plain that not all mushrooms were condemned by the ancients. Galen thought that only the round boletes should be touched among mushrooms. Celsus likewise said that some mushrooms are useful and others useless, and that those of the kind called cochura are made useful in this way. If this is true, as it certainly is, then even the fly mushrooms, which appear partly red and partly white, can be made harmless by the manner of cooking, especially if they are carefully boiled, and afterwards fried with oil or butter, with capers and pepper added. Some add vinegar, which greatly tames them.

units.la: Alii vino coquunt fungos adjecto origano vel hyssopo. Qui vero eduntur expoline piperis, vel ex jure pingui cocti, omnino veneris irritamenta sunt. Dioscorides crudos edi docuit, sed qui crudis vescerentur, nemo adhuc visus est, nisi id fiat a pauperibus, & in summa rerum penuria. Aduersus pernicies radiculam antesumtam cum sale & aceto prodesse Scribonius Largus testis est. Quercum & Castaneam boletos ferre probatissimos omniumque maximos, vt vnus pluribus sufficiat conuiuis, quidam asserunt. Tutissimos existimant qui coquendo mollescant, qui enim duriores fiunt, noxii deprehenduntur. Venenis etiam accommodatissimi sunt, in quibus dilutus rubor est, rancidus aspectus, color intus liuidus, pallidum per ambitum labrum, rimosae striae. Multi etiam venenosi fiunt, si serpentis cauerna juxta fuerit, si chalybis rubigo, aut panni marcor: quæ sane nec immerito ab esu & visu fungorum aliquem deterrebunt. Ego certe caute eos attingendos existimo. Clemens VII. Pontifex tam avide expetebat fungos, qui è spinetis vere nascuntur rotunditate clusili, vocantque Spinulos Cardeolofque, vt solus iis cœnaret nullo non die. Edixerat iis in locis quæ ditioni suæ parebant, ne cui alteri demeterentur. Immatura autem illius mors indicio fuit, quantum intemperata viuendi ratio, noxiorumque sculentorum assiduus vsus hominibus ad vitam breuiandam valeat. Nam & Peponibus immoderatius vescebatur. Martialis quoque feruorem gulæ Ceciliani detestatus est carminib. suis, qui vocatus ad cœnam ab amicis solus ipse boletos vorabat, carmina hæc sunt,
units.tr: Others cook mushrooms in wine with marjoram or hyssop added. But those eaten seasoned with pepper, or cooked in rich broth, are altogether incitements to lust. Dioscorides taught that they be eaten raw, but no one has yet been seen to eat them raw, unless this is done by the poor and in extreme want. Scribonius Largus bears witness that a little root taken beforehand with salt and vinegar is a remedy against their dangers. Some assert that the boletes that grow under oak and chestnut trees are the most approved, and the largest of all, so that one of them is enough for several guests. They think those are safest which become soft in cooking; for those which grow tougher are found to be harmful. They are also most suited to poisons when they show a faded redness, a rancid look, a livid colour within, a pale lip around the edge, and cracked streaks. Many also become poisonous if a serpent's den lies near them, or if there is rust of iron, or the rot of cloth; these things will rightly deter anyone from eating or even looking at mushrooms. I for my part think they should be touched with caution. Pope Clement VII so eagerly desired the mushrooms that come up in spring from the thickets, round and compact, which they call spinuli and cardeoli, that he dined on them alone every day. In the places under his rule he had issued an edict that they should not be sold to anyone else. His untimely death was a proof of how much an intemperate way of life and the constant use of harmful foods can shorten human life. For he also ate pumpkins to excess. Martial, too, in his verses condemned the fervour of the gluttony of Cecilianus, who, when invited to dinner by friends, devoured the boletes all by himself. The verses are these:

units.la: Dic mihi quis furor est? turba spectante vocata
units.tr: Tell me, what madness is this? Summoned before a watching crowd,

units.la: Solus boletos Ceciliane vorat.
units.tr: Cecilianus, you alone devour the boletes.

units.la: Quid dignum tanto ventri, gulæque precabor?
units.tr: What worthy prayer can I offer for a belly and gullet like that?

units.la: Boletum qualem Claudius edit, edat.
units.tr: Let him eat the kind of bolete that Claudius ate.

units.la: Pestiferos denique esse fungos breuis illa vita satis indicat, terra enim eruti ocyssime putrescunt atque contabescunt, & in ipsa hærentes terra vix diem vnum atque alterum vigere animaduertuntur. Proinde, nisi probe coquantur, aromatibusque condiantur diantur, suffocationis periculum inferre praeter experientiam graves autores tradunt. Haec vis strangulandi illis ut adimatur, parari eos oportere ex aceto aut oxymelite, aut etiam ipso melle & sale, Diphilus docuit. Qui vero ex intempestiuo auidoque illorum esu strangulatus similitudinem perfentiunt, ut saepe fit in magnatum aulis, apud quos maxima fungorum est autoritas, iis vomitu ex oleo, aut potu lixiuii e sarmentis, aut pyrastri furculis succurrendum: quin & ipsa pyra mansa praeclare auxiliantur, funtq; haec remedia parabilia, ac cuique in promtu, hucque obiter apposita, quoniam ancipitis hujus escae maxima vbiuis fere locorum percipitur foecunditas ac abundantia.
units.tr: Finally, that mushrooms are deadly is sufficiently shown by their short life: for when dug from the earth they very quickly rot and decay, and while still growing in the earth they are seen to thrive scarcely a day or two. Therefore, unless they are thoroughly cooked and seasoned with spices, serious authors report, apart from experience, that they bring a danger of suffocation. To take away this strangling power from them, Diphilus taught that they should be prepared with vinegar or oxymel, or even with honey and salt. But those who feel the likeness of strangling from their untimely and greedy eating of them, as often happens in the courts of great men, among whom the authority of mushrooms is greatest, must be helped with vomiting induced by oil, or a drink of lye made from vine-cuttings, or sprigs of wild pear; indeed, the chewed pears themselves help greatly. These remedies are easily got and at hand for everyone, and I have set them down here in passing, since the great abundance of this doubtful food is found almost everywhere.

units.la: Hactenus de fungis eorumq; natura.
units.tr: Thus far on mushrooms and their nature.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: De alimentis quae veniunt ab animalibus.
units.tr: On foods that come from animals.

units.la: Commodum nunc est differere de cibariis, quae ab animantibus veniunt, ordinem vita sequendo.
units.tr: It is now fitting to discuss foods that come from living creatures, following the order of life.

units.la: Nam prima illa aetas carnis deside ia in primis damnauit, pecora agricultura tantum nasci exisitimans, ideoq; tam capitale erat bovem
units.tr: For that first age condemned the eating of flesh above all, thinking that cattle were born only for farming. For this reason killing an ox was as grave a crime as killing a citizen.

units.la: {y} Ex quadam, Cibariis, animal. vem occidisse, quam civem, primumq; pecudes interrimendi morem ac modum a vilissimis deorum & placationibus alimenti hominum gratia emanasse nonnulli diligenter observarunt: unde postea non pauci naturae rerum viri calentissimi in lucem emiserunt commentarios, quibus explicarunt, mitiores longe salubriores esca, praebere mortalibus animantia, quam olera, aut arborum poma, glandesq;.
units.tr: {y} From a certain section, foods, animal. Some careful observers have noted that the custom and manner of killing livestock for human food first arose from the humblest sacrifices and propitiations of the gods. Later, not a few men of keen insight into the nature of things published commentaries explaining that animals provide mortals with food far milder and more wholesome than vegetables, fruit of trees, or acorns.

units.la: Sed id non factum est ab omnibus pari inducтria & scientia. Numerosa enim animalium, quae in cibos hominum admittuntur genera, haud dubie omnibus non percognita, earum varietas copiaq;, coquendi parandi-q; diversitas, iporumq; animalium partes diffidentes causam, praebuerunt perplexitati. Nos, quantum nobis licet in hoc praeclaro naturae munere commemorando per exiles ingenii vires assequi, cibaria, quae ab animantibus sumuntur studiosius & methodice persequemur.
units.tr: But this was not done with equal diligence and knowledge by everyone. The many kinds of animals admitted as human food, which are doubtless not all known to everyone, their variety and abundance, the differences in cooking and preparing them, and the divisions of the animals' parts have caused confusion. We, as far as our slight mental powers allow us to pursue this excellent gift of nature, will examine more carefully and methodically the foods taken from animals.

units.la: Alimenta autem ab animalibus petita vel sunt animalium sanguineorum vel exanguium.
units.tr: Foods taken from animals are either from animals with blood or from bloodless ones.

units.la: Sanguinea vel simplicis vita sunt, vel amphibia.
units.tr: Blooded animals are either of a single kind of life, or amphibious.

units.la: Simplicis vita vel solum in aere viuunt, vel in aqua tantum.
units.tr: Those of a single kind of life live either only in air or only in water.

units.la: Ex aeris alia volucria sunt, alia gradi-entia.
units.tr: Among those of the air, some fly and others walk.

units.la: Volu-
units.tr: Fly-

units.la: Volucria, quod in aere volent, dicta sunt aves.
units.tr: Those that fly in the air are called birds.

units.la: Humi gradientia vel ambulant, ut homines & quadrupedes, vel reptant ut reptilia.
units.tr: Those that walk on the ground either go on foot, like humans and quadrupeds, or crawl, like reptiles.

units.la: Amphibia animalia dicuntur, quae ancipitis sunt naturae, inter aerea & aquea, hoc est, partim in aere, partim in aqua viuunt, ut rana, crocodilus, lutra, laxus, fiber, natrix, mergus, anas.
units.tr: Animals are called amphibious which are of two natures, between air and water, that is, they live partly in air and partly in water, such as the frog, crocodile, otter, lynx, beaver, water snake, merganser, and duck.

units.la: Huiusmodi sunt sanguinea, succedunt ex sanguia, sanguinis scilicet expertia, ut sunt polypus, sepia, loligo, crustacea item, ut cancer, locusta, squilla, & testacea, ut limaces terrestres, cochlea marina, ostrea, pectines, concha.
units.tr: Such are the blooded animals. Following these come the bloodless, that is, those lacking blood: such as the polyp, cuttlefish, and squid; likewise the crustaceans, such as the crab, lobster, and squilla; and the shelled, such as land snails, sea snails, oysters, scallops, and cockles.

units.la: Haec est compendiosa animalium familia. Nunc operaepretium erit recensere quibus animantibus, horumque partibus, tam externis, quam internis homines potissimum utantur, exordium sumendo ab avibus.
units.tr: This is the compact family of animals. Now it will be worth listing which animals, and which of their parts, both external and internal, men chiefly use, beginning with birds.

units.la: De avibus in genere, earumque differentiis in re cibaria.
units.tr: On birds in general, and their differences as regards food.

units.la: NE nihil quod vitae interfit, omittatur, utque lectorem pleniori atque vliore obsequio demereat, adnotare hic oportebit, complures in avium genere reperiri differentias, tum a tempore, aetate, victu, tum loco, coeloque, quae avium ipsarum car-
units.tr: Lest anything that bears on life be left out, and so that he may earn the reader's goodwill by fuller and more diligent service, it will be right to note here that many differences are found within the kind of birds, arising from time, age and diet, and also from place and climate, which the birds themselves

units.la: Aues sunt animal bipes pennatum, agile & leve. arnes salubriores aut infalubriores reddunt, cibisq; magis aut minus idoneas. Quo enim tempore libidine pruriunt coeuntque macrescunt praesertim sylueftres: quin etiam quando incubant pullosque excludunt, tunc enim minus comedunt, unde extenuantur.
units.tr: Birds are a two-footed, feathered animal, nimble and light. Their flesh makes them more or less wholesome, and more or less suitable as food. For at the time when they are lustful and mate, the wild ones especially grow lean; and indeed also when they sit on their eggs and hatch their young, for then they eat less, and so waste away.

units.la: Ex domesticis & villaticis, ut sunt gallinae, columbae, anseres, anates, pavones &c. nemo facile edit incubantes. Porro aliae omnino vere, aliae magis placent aestate quae scilicet frugibus vescuntur, aliae autumno, quae vuis, ficubus & caeterarum arborum pomis baccisque. Quibusdam hiemis frigora gratiam conciliant, ut turdis, merulis, aliisque seribus feris, gruibus, aquaticisq; fere omnibus. Complures quoq; hieme latent, nec omnes ad loca tepidiora abeunt, ut merula, turdus, alauda. Turtur latere incipit praepinguis, nec vspiam per hiemem videtur, & licet pennas dimittat in latibulo, pinguedinem tamen seruat. Palumborum aliqui latent, aliqui non. Sturnus latet qui per vindemias obseruat eximie. Certum est adalgores aestusque, mutationes temporum aues sentire, natura quippe iis indidit sensum, a quo mutationes frigore vel calore factas cognoscant, ideoq; loca, quae possunt, permutant, nonnullaque subsidium in locis iis sibi consuetis comperiunt: aliae peregre proproficiscuntur, vt grues ex Scythicis campis ad paludes Ægypto superiores veniunt. A victu quoque differentiae non paucae sunt.
units.tr: Among the tame and farmyard birds, such as hens, pigeons, geese, ducks, peacocks and so on, no one readily eats those that are sitting. Further, some are at their best in spring, others are more pleasing in summer, when they feed on grain, and others in autumn, when they feed on grapes, figs and the fruits and berries of other trees. For some birds the cold of winter makes them more agreeable, as with thrushes, blackbirds and other wild birds of that kind, cranes, and almost all water birds. Many also lie hidden in winter, and not all go off to warmer places, as the blackbird, thrush and lark do. The turtle-dove begins to hide when it is very fat, and is nowhere to be seen through the winter; and although it sheds its feathers in its hiding place, it keeps its fatness. Some wood-pigeons hide and some do not. The starling, which watches the vintage closely, hides. It is certain that birds perceive the changes of the seasons, the chill and the heat, for nature has implanted in them a sense by which they recognise the changes made by cold or warmth; and so they change their places where they can, and some find help in those places they are used to. Others travel abroad, as cranes come from the Scythian plains to the marshes above Egypt. There are also not a few differences in diet.

units.la: Quibus adunci vngues sunt omnes carniuorae, vt aquilae, milui, accipitres, vultures, buteo, nocturnaeque aues, bubo, noctua, vlula: quaedam frugiuorae sunt & omniuorae, vt cornices, & vt summatim dicam, omnium fere auium, aliae victum à terra petunt, aliae à fluuio, aliae à lacu, aliae à mari.
units.tr: All birds of prey with hooked talons are flesh-eaters, such as eagles, kites, hawks, vultures, buzzards, and the night birds, the owl, the screech-owl and the horned owl. Some are grain-eaters and omnivores, such as crows; and, to put it briefly, nearly all birds seek their food, some from the land, some from rivers, some from lakes, and some from the sea.

units.la: Ubi notandum, auium carnes, ipsarum quo vtuntur, alimenti semper fere referre saporem: quae enim formicis vescuntur, formicarum, quae culicibus culicum, quae vermiculis vermiculorum saporem repraesentant. Sic sylueftrium carnes prope referunt saporem pabuli. Quae aluntur piscibus, piscis olent, & quae circa aquas viuunt, lutum coenumque, quae circa mare, virus illud marinum redolent, proindeque cibis abdicandae.
units.tr: Here it should be noted that the flesh of birds almost always takes on the flavour of what they feed on: those that eat ants taste of ants, those that eat gnats of gnats, and those that eat grubs of grubs. Thus the flesh of woodland birds comes close to the taste of their pasture. Those that are fed on fish smell of fish, and those that live about waters smell of mud and filth, while those about the sea smell of that marine stench; and so they are to be rejected as food.

units.la: Ætatem quod attinet, aliae placent in infantia, aliae cum adoleuerint: Seneca semper improbatur. Pulli columbacei generis, pulli perdicum, pulli coturnicum, pulli gallinarum, vt pullastri & pullastrae parentibus semper praestant, gallinae juvencae quoque animulae veteribus anteponuntur. Sicut & capi juuenes suauitate praestant. Quid? quod & castratione gallinaceum genus suasuauius efficitur & vtilius, quin & fœminas nunc castrare gula luxusque didicit. Ad extremum non prætereundum caueis conclu-sas, altilesque redditas, inque vrbium domi-bus vagantes & saginatas gulosis ganeoni-bus, suauius quidem sapere, sed vitæ minus esse salutares, propterea quod vberiori excremento scateant, probumq; succum non gignant, nam quæ in agris versantur præstan-tiores existunt, vnde capones salubetrimi existimantur, qui circa tritici metas pingue-scunt, nec sine exercitio, discurrunt enim vl-tro citroq;. Idem judicium sit de omni gene-re animantium, tum ferorum, tum cicurum, quæ mortalibus cibaria præbent, in quib. sa-gina illa atq; adiposa obesitas carcere otioq; conciliata vitæ insidiosa deprehenditur & pestifera. Sic columbæ quæ turres incolunt salubriores sunt domesticis, & quæ in locis humilib. educantur, volatus enim salubritati gratiam adiicit. Aues item montanæ campe-stribus, & quę in locis palustrib. degunt, sicut & apri montani campestribus præferuntur. Atq; hæc de auium differentia in genere, se-quitur nunc de singulis seorsim. Immen-sam autem ac Numerosam volucrum multi-tudinem esse, testatur cœna illa Vitellio à fratre data, in qua septem avium millia ap-posita traduntur, tantus fuit istius seculi lu-xus tantaque vorago.
units.tr: As for age, some birds please in infancy, others when they have grown up; old age is always disapproved of. Young pigeons, partridges, quails and hens (as the young cockerels and pullets) always excel their parents, and young hens are also preferred to old ones. Just so, young capons excel in sweetness. What of it? Castration makes the cock tribe both sweeter and more useful, and indeed luxury and gluttony have learned to castrate the hens too. Last of all, one must not pass over birds that are shut up in cages and made fat for feasting, and that wander about in the houses of cities and are fattened by greedy gourmands; these taste sweeter indeed, but are less healthy for life, because they abound in excessive excrement and produce no good juice. For those that live in the fields are more excellent, and so capons are thought the most wholesome, since they fatten about the stacks of wheat, and they do not lack exercise, for they run hither and thither of their own accord. The same judgement holds for every kind of living creature, both wild and tame, which provide food for mortals, in which that fat and greasy obesity, brought on by confinement and idleness, is found to be treacherous and deadly to life. So pigeons that dwell in towers are more wholesome than domestic ones, and those bred in low places; for flight adds a grace to wholesomeness. Likewise mountain birds are preferred to those of the plains, and those living in marshy places, just as mountain boars are preferred to those of the plains. And this is enough on the differences of birds in general; now follows the treatment of each kind separately. That there is an immense and countless multitude of birds is attested by that dinner which Vitellius was given by his brother, at which seven thousand birds are said to have been served up; so great was the luxury and so great the gulf of that age.

units.la: Y
units.tr: Y

units.la: Aquatilium volucrum genera 177. esse, quae nominatim percognita sint, Plinius autor est, sed in terrestribus id fieri nequit, tantum enim abest, ut in consideratione omnes venire possint, ut etiam omnes Indiae, Aethiopiae, Scythiae, aut aliarum Septentrionalium occiduarumque terrarum desertorumque aues non sint notae: Omitto Taprobanae, insularumque nuper patefactarum immensam multitudinem, aliasque fabulosae magis quam vere narratas. Quare notas magis, nobiscumque degentes persequemur.
units.tr: Pliny is the authority that 177 kinds of water birds have been thoroughly examined by name; but this cannot be done for land birds, for so far are they from all being able to come under observation, that even the birds of all India, Ethiopia, Scythia, and of the other northern and western lands and deserts are not known. I say nothing of the immense number of Taprobane and of the islands lately opened up, and of others described more as fables than as truths. Therefore I shall pursue those better known and living among us.

units.la: Ex auibus autem escas hominum praecipue adjuuant, gallinacei, vrogalli, gallinae, pulli gallinacei, columbae, palumbi, anseres, anates, perdices, attagines, rusticulae, roftrulae, turdi, merulae, sturni, coturnices, cornices, picae, pici, monedulae, phasiani, alaudae, fringillae, passeres, galguli, aliaeq; complures, quae in minuto auium genere sunt, quas singulas persequi immensi effet laboris & difficultatis, praesertim cum multae inter eas sint vitae & colore ignobiles.
units.tr: Of birds, the following chiefly serve as human food: cocks, turkey-cocks, hens, chickens, pigeons, wood-pigeons, geese, ducks, partridges, woodcocks, rusticolae, rostrulae, thrushes, blackbirds, starlings, quails, crows, magpies, woodpeckers, jackdaws, pheasants, larks, finches, sparrows, ortolans, and many others among the small kinds of birds. To pursue each one would be a task of immense labour and difficulty, especially since many of them are obscure in life and colour.

units.la: Ex grandioribus vero non praetermittendi sunt struthiocameli, grues, ciconiae, cygni, gallopaui, pauones, ardeae, & id genus aliae.
units.tr: Among the larger birds, the ostrich, cranes, storks, swans, bustards, peacocks, herons and others of that kind must not be passed over.

units.la: Nec omiserim carniuorum genus, ut aquiaquilas, coruos, miluios, accipitres ambos, fringillarium & palumbarium, hirundines &c. aues item nocturnas,& falcones.
units.tr: Nor would I omit the flesh-eating kind, such as eagles, ravens, kites, both sorts of hawks, the finch-hawks and pigeon-hawks, swallows and so on; likewise the night birds, and falcons.

units.la: Atque hic est præcipuarum magisque confeflarum ac nostris terris familiarium auium catalogus, externas, peregrinas, & nouas persequi parum ad institutum nostrum attinet. Nunc in vsu mensarum quæ præcipuæ sint,dispiciendum.
units.tr: This is the catalogue of the chief and best-known birds, which are familiar in our lands; to pursue foreign, strange and newly discovered ones has little to do with our purpose. Now it must be examined which are the chief ones in use at table.

units.la: De gallis gallinaceis.
units.tr: On Cocks.

units.la: Gallinaceos ex Perfide primum in alias terras transiisse prodiderunt graci. Ex his fiunt capi, lautiorum hodie mensas plurimum opulentantes. Castrantur autem galli tum ut facilius pinguescant, tum ut suaui-ores reddantur ac delicatiores. Castrantur nonniffima parte sua alui eximendo testiculum utrumq. Quod fi enim alter relinquatur, cucurient ac canet, coitumq; repetet. Elegantiores quoq; & maiores evadunt, fi castrentur dum crescunt.
units.tr: The Greeks reported that cocks first passed from Persia into other lands. From these come capons, which today greatly enrich the tables of the wealthy. Cocks are castrated both so that they fatten more easily and so that they become more tender and delicate. They are castrated in the lowest part of the belly by removing both testicles. If one is left, they crow and sing and seek to mate again. They also turn out more elegant and larger if they are castrated while still growing.

units.la: Vetulorum gallorum carnes ingrata sunt & insuaues, sed jus in quo decoquuntur in aluo soluenda celebratur, juniorum vero gallorum & gallinarum carnes & jus eximie nutriunt.
units.tr: The flesh of old cocks is unpleasant and insipid, but the broth in which they are boiled is esteemed for loosening the bowels. The flesh and broth of young cocks and hens, however, are exceptionally nourishing.

units.la: Cerebrum gallorum gallinarumq; exi-guum gnum quidem est, sed tanto quadrupedum cerebro praestantius, quanto durius. Hodie primo elixum, deinde prunis tostum manditur a delicatioribus. Vitellius Phasianorum et Pavonum cerebella in delitiis gula habuit, ea enim appositit in patina sua, quam Minerva clypeum appellabat.
units.tr: The brain of cocks and hens is indeed small, but it is as much more excellent than the brain of quadrupeds as it is firmer. Today the more refined eat it first boiled and then roasted over embers. Vitellius counted the brains of pheasants and peacocks among the delights of his gluttony; he served them on his dish, which he called Minerva's shield.

units.la: Gallorum testes mirus laudibus extulit Galenus praesertim eorum, qui cibariis laete maceratis saginantur, veleducantur, succum enim laudabilem praebent, facile concoquuntur, valenterque nutriunt ac Venerem stimulant certo experimento.
units.tr: Galen praised the testicles of cocks greatly, especially those of birds that are fattened or reared on softened food. They yield a commendable juice, are easily digested, nourish strongly, and, as is proven by certain experience, stimulate Venus.

units.la: Incidit mihi hic historia admodum facetosa cuius meminit Amatus Lusitanus centur. 2. curationum medicinalium, de nobili quadam foemina, quae marito suo gallorum quos castrauerat testes, melle, pipere, aliisque aromatibus laute praeparatos in coena comedendos obtulit. Hic cum alacriter avideque palatum explevisset, subsequente nocte tantus concubandi appetitus, tantaque ei tentigo excitata fuit, ut vxor ex nimia continuatione coeundi plus satis delassata et fatigata, vt tandem evaserit, inque aliud cubiculum se abdiderit. Ipse vero eam infectus pruriente adhuc materia, in ancillarum dormitorium irrupit, easque similiter ad fugam usque subegit. Ex quibus patet, testes gallinaceorum inter ea, qua venerem excitant, feminisq; ac spiritum generationi sunt accommodata, non potremum obtinuisse locum.
units.tr: A rather amusing story comes to mind, which Amatus Lusitanus mentions in the second century of his medicinal cures. A certain noble woman served her husband at supper the testicles of cocks she had castrated, richly prepared with honey, pepper and other spices, for him to eat. When he had eagerly and gladly satisfied his palate, such a great appetite for lying with her arose that night, and such a lustful itch was roused in him, that his wife, exhausted and worn out by his excessive and continual coupling, at last escaped and hid herself in another bedchamber. He, still infected with the inflamed matter, burst into the maids' dormitory and drove them likewise to flight. From this it is clear that the testicles of cocks, among those things that excite venery, are suited to seed and vital spirit and do not hold the last place.

units.la: Verum tenendum, veterum gallorum testes virosos esse & effœtos, quare juniorum ad hanc rem assumendi sunt.
units.tr: Yet it must be held that the testicles of old cocks are virile and spent, so those of young ones should be taken for this purpose.

units.la: Delicatiores quoque fœmina in delitiis gula habent oropygia gallinaceorum & gallinarum, præsertim altilium & prapinguium, ac certum est ea boni succi esse, licet veterani milites oropygiorum voratores a quibusdam appellantur.
units.tr: Women who are more delicate also hold in delight the rumps of cocks and hens, especially of fattened and very plump birds, and it is certain that they are of good juice, although old soldiers are called by some devourers of rumps.

units.la: De Gallinis.
units.tr: On Hens.

units.la: GAllinaceæ carnes, ut graues testantur autores, ipsaque experientia, præstantissimæ sunt, facile enim conficiuntur, omnibusque naturis & temperamentis peridoneæ sunt, ideoq; alimenti præcipui. Quapropter in villatica pastione cum suis pullis merito obtinent primas, ex iis enim numerosissima epularum genera fiunt, infinitosque mortalibus in re cibaria vsus subministrant, nec alius cibus est, qui innocentius, tum ægris, tum sanis possit exhiberi. Nullo quoque magis cibo juuamur in re-pen-
units.tr: Hen's flesh, as serious authors attest and experience itself shows, is most excellent. It is easily digested, suits every constitution and temperament, and is therefore a chief food. For this reason, among farmyard fowl together with their chicks, hens rightly hold first place. From them come very many kinds of dishes, and they supply countless uses in food for mortals. No food can be given more harmlessly, both to the sick and to the healthy. Nor are we helped by any food more in the sudden arrival of friends and guests than by a hen.

units.la: pentino amicorum hospitumque adventu quam gallinaceo: qua de caula multa tradita reperiuntur quomodo tenerescant, sic enim repente jugulatae plerumque durae admodum sunt.
units.tr: For this reason many methods are handed down for making a hen tender, since a hen slaughtered on the spur of the moment is usually very tough.

units.la: Horatius eleganter, quomodo id fiat docuit his carminibus, Si vespertinus subito te oppresserit hospes, Nec gallina malum responset dura pa-lato, Doctus eris vivam misto mersare fa-lerno, Hoc tenera mihi faciet.
units.tr: Horace elegantly taught how this is done in these verses: If an evening guest should suddenly catch you, and no tough hen should answer your palate badly, you will be skilled at dipping a live hen in mixed Falernian wine; this will make her tender for me.

units.la: Atque hunc morem a multis obseruari constat. Caeterum in prandia elixas, in coenas vero inflatas gallinas fumere ganeae proceres jubent, inuento non insalubri, sed in paucis hodie id obseruari video mensis. Non praetereundum miraculum naturae, si auro liquescenti gallinarum membra misceantur, consumi hoc in se, ita hoc venenum auri est. Saginare gallinas primum coepere Deliaci, unde pestis exorta opimas aues & suopte corpore inunctas devorandi.
units.tr: Indeed it is agreed that many observe this custom. Otherwise, the leaders of gluttony order boiled hens at lunch and puffed-up hens at dinner. This is not an unwholesome invention, but I see it observed today at only a few tables. Not to be passed over is a wonder of nature: if the limbs of hens are mixed with liquefying gold, they are consumed in it, so great is the poison of gold. The Delians first began to fatten hens, whence a plague arose of devouring rich birds that were anointed with their own fat.

units.la: De gallinaceis non omittendum, quod circulo e sarmentis ipsorum addito collo non canunt.
units.tr: Regarding cocks it should not be omitted that when a circle of vine-twigs is placed around their necks, they do not crow.

units.la: De pullis gallinaceis.
units.tr: On Chicks.

units.la: BImestres & trimestres magis laudantur, nec non qui ante solstitium nascuntur, mense scilicet Martio, Aprili, Maio, qui enim post solstitium nascuntur tustam magnitudinem non implere creduntur, idq; tanto minus quanto serius proveniunt. Inventum est vt omni hiberno etiam tempore contingant & habeti possint. Qua calido in loco, sosita paleis igne modico fouentur, versanturq; pariter die & noƈte, statutoq; tandem die illinc erumpit sœtus: quem morem & hodie durare audio Hierolymis, & in Syria, Rhodo, & Ægypto: quin & apud nos huius rei extiterunt ingeniosi artifices præsertim in Magnatum aulis. Aristoteles præter id asserit oua in vasis quibusdam tepidis sponte pullos prompsisse. Fabulosum quibusdam videtur, (quanquam à grauibus auctoribus prodituni reperiatur) quod de quodam vini potore Syracusano reperitur, quem tamdiu potare soli-tu strauit, donec ab eo cooperta in terra sœtū ederent oua, quo etiam nomine inter bibacissimos sui temporis habitus est.
units.tr: Chicks hatched in the second and third months are more praised, as are those born before the solstice, namely in March, April and May, for those born after the solstice are believed not to reach full size, and the later they come, the less they grow. It has been devised that they can be produced at any time in winter and be had. They are placed in a warm place on chaff and kept warm by a moderate fire, and they are turned equally by day and by night. Then on the appointed day the brood bursts out from there. I hear that this practice still lasts today in Jerusalem, in Syria, at Rhodes and in Egypt; indeed among us too, skilled craftsmen of this art have appeared, especially in the courts of great lords. Aristotle further asserts that eggs in certain warm vessels spontaneously produced chicks. It seems fabulous to some (although it is reported by serious authors) what is recorded of a certain wine-drinker of Syracuse, whom the habit of drinking so long struck down that eggs covered in the earth hatched chicks. For this reason he too was counted among the most drunken men of his time.

units.la: De vsu gallinaceorum & gallinarum in medicina.
units.tr: On the use of cocks and hens in medicine.

units.la: NOn tantum in re cibaria infinitos vsus administrant, numerosissimaque epulaepularum genera suppeditant, verum etiam in re medica insigne praestant saepe auxilium & quidem facilè, idque ferè quotidianum.
units.tr: Not only do fowls serve countless purposes in food and supply the most numerous kinds of dishes, but they also often give remarkable help in medicine, and that easily and almost every day.

units.la: Gallinaceorum cerebro vino epoto, (sicut & carnibus illorum tepentibus) serpentum venenum domari tradit Plinius lib. 29. cap. 4. nec non morsum canis rabidi. Parthi gallinae cerebrum malunt, quod peculiariter etiam debili memoriae prodesse traditur.
units.tr: Pliny (book 29, chapter 4) reports that the brain of a cock, drunk in wine (as also its warm flesh), tames the poison of serpents, and also the bite of a mad dog. The Parthians prefer the brain of a hen, which is said to be especially good for those of weak memory.

units.la: Carnes gallinarum viperis, saginatarum elixarumque, elephantiasis labe infectis profuisse certò obseruatum est. In aeris veró peste maximè inter cibos commendantur.
units.tr: It has certainly been observed that the flesh of hens, fattened and boiled, has helped those infected by the bite of vipers or by the taint of elephantiasis. In times of pestilence of the air, they are especially recommended among foods.

units.la: Ius gallinaceorum & gallinarum potum praeclarè medetur venenis, praesertim si allium fuerit incoctum. Pantherae, Leonesque non attingunt eo perunctos: aluum praeterea mollit ac soluit, sed validius è veteri gallinaceo: prodest & contra longinquas febres torpentibus tremulisque membris, articulari morbo, renibus, epati, vesicae, & demum contra suspiria & cruditates. Veneficiis ex mustela sylvestri factis contrarium est ius gallinacei veteris largè haustum, sed peculiariter contra aconitum, adiecto tamen salis modico.
units.tr: Broth of cocks and hens cures poisons well, especially if garlic has been cooked in it. Panthers and lions do not touch those smeared with it. Moreover it softens and loosens the bowels, but more strongly the broth of an old cock. It also helps against long fevers, against limbs that are numb and trembling, against joint disease, kidney, liver and bladder complaints, and finally against asthma and indigestion. Against poisons made from the wild weasel, a generous draught of the broth of an old cock is the remedy, but especially against aconite, with a little salt added.

units.la: Fel gallinacei dilutum aquâ, ulcerationes & oculorum albugines, suffusiones item & calicalgationes fanat,& maximè candidi. Laudatur & gallinæ fel,præcipueque adeps contra pustulas in papillis,adiuuatq; mirifice ruptas oculor tunicas admixtro lapide hæmatite.
units.tr: The gall of a cock, diluted in water, heals ulcers and white films of the eyes, as well as suffusions and inflammations of the eyes, especially that of a white cock. The gall of a hen is also praised, and especially its fat, against pustules on the nipples; and mixed with the stone haematite it wonderfully helps torn membranes of the eyes.

units.la: Fimum gallinaceorum,sed rubrum, lufcifis illinendum suadent, morsisque à rabido cane exaceto : fimum quoque gallinarum candidum in veteri oleo corneisque pyxidibus assemuare solent ad oculorum albugines, miscetur autem cum rosacea, fœniculacea, vel oui albumine. Earundem fimum candidum hissopo aut mulso decoctum,venena fungorum astringit, inflationes it& & strangulationes,quod mirari subit,fi enim id fimû gustauerit aliud animal,torminibus afficitur & inflationibus. Verrucas quoq; pellit cum oleo & nitro fimum gallinaceorum.
units.tr: They advise smearing the red dung of cocks on bloodshot eyes, and treating the bite of a mad dog with vinegar. The white dung of hens they usually boil in old oil and in horn boxes, for white films of the eyes; it is mixed with rose water, fennel, or egg white. The white dung of the same, boiled in hyssop or mead, checks the poison of mushrooms, as well as bloating and strangulation. What is surprising is that if another animal tastes this dung, it suffers gripes and bloating. Cock's dung with oil and nitre also drives away warts.

units.la: Non omittam hic mysterium naturæ. Nam cor è viuente gallina exectum dextreq; coxæ palpitans adhuc alligatum partum difficile m accelerat.
units.tr: I shall not omit here a mystery of nature. The heart cut from a living hen, still beating, tied to the right thigh, speeds a difficult birth.

units.la: Ventriculi gallinaceorū membrana, quæ in coctionibus abiici solet, vino trita aurib* purulentis calida infunditur, sic & gallinarū adeps:eadem siccata & potioni inspersa stomachicis,pectoris destillationibus, humidæque medetur tussi. Gallinaceorum iecur assum cum prædicta ventriculi membrana admisto papaueris succo dysentericis pdeft vétrisq; malis. VidePlin. l.29.c.5.&6.&l.30.c.7.
units.tr: The membrane of a cock's gizzard, which is usually thrown away in cooking, rubbed up with wine and poured warm into purulent ears; so too the fat of hens. The same membrane, dried and sprinkled into a drink, helps stomach complaints, rheums of the chest and a moist cough. Roasted cock's liver with the said gizzard membrane, mixed with juice of poppy, helps dysentery and stomach ailments. See Pliny, book 29, chapters 5 and 6, and book 30, chapter 7.

units.la: De columbis.
units.tr: On pigeons.

units.la: A Gallinaceo genere proximum est columbaceum non minoris in re cibaria vsus quam gallinaceum. Varro columbas dicit putat, quod in summis columninibus villa nidificent.
units.tr: Next to the fowl kind is the pigeon kind, of no less use in food than the fowl. Varro says that they are called columbae, as is thought, because they nest on the tops of the columns of the country houses.

units.la: Xenophon libro expeditionis Cyri primo tradidit Syros columbas habere sacrosanctas, nefas putare eas violare. Ante bellum ciuile Pompeianum in magno fuerunt pretio. Nam L. Axius eques Rom. denarijs quadringentis singula paria vendidit. Nam magnis in rebus fuerunt internuncia, epistolas annexas earum pedibus obsidione Mutinensi in castra consulum Decimo Bruto mittente. Multa sunt illarum genera, quae omnia percensere superuacaneum est. Aristoteles prolem vernam prastantiorem asserit quam autumnalem, deterrimamque estiuam. Galli alii vernam fœturam damnant improbantque, quoniam pulli non perueniant ad volatum tempestiuum, cum sæpe propter imbres veris largiores in nidis intereant, vel etiam aqua vitientur.
units.tr: Xenophon, in the first book of the Expedition of Cyrus, reports that the Syrians hold pigeons sacred and think it wrong to harm them. Before the Pompeian civil war they were of great price: Lucius Axius, a Roman knight, sold single pairs for four hundred denarii. For in great affairs they were messengers, with letters tied to their feet, when Decimus Brutus sent them from the siege of Mutina into the consuls' camp.
