There are many kinds, and it would be superfluous to go through them all. Aristotle asserts that spring brood is better than autumn brood, and summer brood the worst. Some Gallic writers condemn and reject spring breeding, since the young do not reach flight in good time; often in the heavy spring rains the chicks perish in the nests, or are spoiled by water.

units.la: Præstantissimam ad volatum & cibos prolem existimat Iulio vel Augusto mense natam: messis enim tempore pulli maximè pingues inueniuntur propter pabuli copiam. Calor enim columbis, vt & cæteris auium generibus, vtilissimus, imbres vero inimicissimi. Delectantur mirum in modum sale, ideoq; cibaria illa salsa crebrius brius obiiciuntur. Qui domicilia sua habent in turribus carcere contabescunt, volatu enim exercitioq; exhilarantur atque pinguescunt. Domestica vero, qua intra limina solent educari prepinguata fiunt. Mauritiani columbos cibis damnā̄ unt: at Galenus eos qui in turribus degunt, commendat.
units.tr: The most excellent offspring for flight and for food is thought to be that born in July or August, for at harvest time the young are found especially plump because of the abundance of fodder. For heat is most useful to pigeons, as to the other kinds of birds, and rain most harmful. They take a wonderful delight in salt, and so salty foods are offered rather often brius obiiciuntur. Those who have their homes in towers waste away in confinement, for they are cheered and grow fat by flight and exercise. Domestic ones, which are usually reared within doors, become overfed. The Mauritanians condemn pigeons as food, but Galen commends those who live in towers.

units.la: Nec dubitandum pullos columbarum sanis atq; aegris esse maxime salutares. Damnatur autem gula qua etiam infantissimos, hoc est pluma nondum teBtos mandere inuenit, nec enim nouelli nimium nec adulti nimium probantur, acceptissimi sunt medii. Idemq; de gallinaceis, quos similiter quidam in prima infantia edunt, intelligendum. Turturum caro sapientis fenum cibus dicitur, sensus enim omnes corroborat, cogitationem acuit, memoriam quoque corroborat.
units.tr: There is no doubt that young pigeons are most wholesome for the healthy and the sick alike. Gluttony is condemned, which eats even the very tender ones, that is, those not yet feathered. For neither the very young nor the fully grown are approved; the middle-aged are most acceptable. The same should be understood of fowls, which some likewise eat in their earliest infancy. The flesh of turtle-doves is said to be food for the wise, for it strengthens all the senses, sharpens the thought, and also strengthens the memory.

units.la: De palumbis.
units.tr: On wood pigeons.

units.la: IN colubaceo genere maximi sunt palumbi, quorum captura in quibusdam locis, ut Aquitania apud Vasates, vberrima est, gloriaq; inter epulas non postrema; concordia difficiles iudicantur, succiqué non adeo boni. Torquatum vnum genus dicitur à torque, quo collum insignitur, germ Stin seltaubes/quorum caro ob glandium esum traditur, hebetare venerem, quod non ignorauit Martialis, scribens,
units.tr: Among the pigeon kind the greatest are the wood pigeons, whose catching is most abundant in certain places, as in Aquitaine among the Vasates, and is no small boast at feasts. They are judged hard to digest and not very good in juice. One kind is called torquatus, from the torque (ring) by which its neck is marked; in German it is Ringeltaube. Its flesh, because of its feeding on acorns, is said to dull lust, which Martial did not fail to know, writing,

units.la: Inguina torquati tardantque hebetantque pa-lumbi
units.tr: The ringed wood-pigeons slacken and dull the loins

units.la: Non edat hanc volucrem, qui cupit esse salax.
units.tr: Let him not eat this bird who desires to be lustful.

units.la: Porro palumborum vitam vel ad 40. annos durare, quibusdam ad 25. & ad 30. protrahi annum, Aristoteles testis est lib. 6. de hist. c. 4. & lib. 9. cap. 1. cui astipulatur Plinius lib. 10. cap. 37. Lauri se foliis purgare palumbos quotannis, idem Plinius testis est lib. 8. cap. 27. Sicut columbae, turtures & gallinacei herba helxine, anates, anseresque siderite, grues junco palustri. Venerem denique trimestres palumbi nolle incipiunt, & foetificare, quod uberrima eorum copia ostendit. Nam in agrum Volaterranum, ut & alios tractus palumborum vis ingens quotannis aduolat e mari. Pariunt vere, nec plus quam bis. Hibernis mensibus inter elegantiores epulas collocari palumbos, notum est iis, apud quos eorum magna copia est, eosque quidam cum brassica elixant, parum tamen ante inflatos.
units.tr: Aristotle is the witness that wood-pigeons live as long as forty years, some reach twenty-five or thirty years of age: Hist. an. bk. 6, ch. 4, and bk. 9, ch. 1. Pliny agrees with him, bk. 10, ch. 37. Pliny also attests, bk. 8, ch. 27, that wood-pigeons purge themselves every year with bay leaves, as do doves, turtledoves and cocks with the herb helxine; ducks and geese with siderite; and cranes with marsh rush. Lastly, wood-pigeons begin to lose their desire for sex at three months, yet they breed, as their great abundance shows. For a huge flock of wood-pigeons flies every year from the sea into the territory of Volterra and other regions. They breed in spring, and not more than twice. It is well known, among those where they are plentiful, that in winter wood-pigeons are served at the more refined feasts, and some boil them with cabbage, though not until they are somewhat swollen.

units.la: Visus columbarum & palumbium in medicina.
units.tr: The uses of doves and wood-pigeons in medicine.

units.la: Columbarum caro recens contra serpentes auxiliatur: integra vero per longitudinem viua dissecta phrenetique ticique verticiapplicata q. miraculo profuis- se sæpe animaduersum est.
units.tr: The flesh of doves, fresh, helps against snakes. Whole, and split lengthwise while still alive, and applied to the head for frenzy and for tics, it is often observed to have done good, by a kind of miracle.

units.la: Fimum columbarum ex aceto laudatur ad ægilopas, id est, tubercula circa magnum oculi angulum: priuatim vero contra viui argenti potum, præcipuè syluestrium. Pulli columbarum paraliticis & senibus conueniunt frequentius efitati cū maiorana & rorismarino: iidem elixi febrientibus vtiliter dari possunt, succo limonum vel citronum asper-so, vel corticibus cum iis incoctis. Panos denique, tumoresque sub faucibus, auribus & inguinibus fimum columbinum cum farina hordeacea discutit, clauos vero pedum ex aceto.
units.tr: Dove dung in vinegar is recommended for aegilops, that is, the swellings near the great corner of the eye; and especially against drinking quicksilver, particularly that of the wild doves. Young doves are most often suited to paralytics and the elderly, boiled with marjoram and rosemary. The same, boiled, may be given usefully to the feverish, sprinkled with lemon or citron juice, or with the peel boiled in them. Lastly, dove dung with barley meal disperses boils and swellings under the throat, the ears and the groin, and dove dung in vinegar disperses corns on the feet.

units.la: De ansere.
units.tr: On the goose.

units.la: ANseres Romanis sacrosanctos fuisse satis constat inter graues auctores, quin & ob iecur solum auium saginatos, Athenæus l. 9. diphnos. testis est, scribit enim tanto eos in pretio fuisse, vt essent apud eos, qui anseres ita alerent, vt eorum iecur mirificè angeretur. Idemque tradit Plinius lib. 10. cap. 22. iecur, inquit, faruilibus in magnam amplitudinem crescit, exemptuq; latè mulso augetur. Id quodq; Martialis signifi at, dicens, Aspice q tumeat magno iecur ansere maius Miratus dices, hoc rego creuit vbi? Inuentum autem hoc alii Scipioni Metel-lo, alii Marcello viro consulari, nonnulli Marco Seßio eadem ætate equiti Romano ascribunt. Hucitem alludit Horatius Sermonum l. 2. Satyra 8.
units.tr: It is quite well established among serious authors that geese were sacred to the Romans; and Athenaeus, bk. 9, Deipnosophists, is a witness to this too, for he writes that they were held in such high value that there were people who fed geese in such a way that their liver grew marvellously large. Pliny also reports the same, bk. 10, ch. 22: "The liver," he says, "of the stuffed birds grows to a great size, and when it is removed and soaked in honey-wine it swells greatly." Martial signifies this too, saying: "Look how the liver swells, larger than a great goose! Wondering, you will ask, where did it grow?" This discovery is ascribed by some to Scipio Metellus, by others to Marcellus, a man of consular rank, and some ascribe it to Marcus Seius, a Roman knight of the same period. Horace alludes to this in the Satires, bk. 2, satire 8.

units.la: Non sine farre,
units.tr: Not without spelt,

units.la: Pinguibus & ficis pastum iecur anseris albi,
units.tr: and the liver of the white goose fattened on rich figs,

units.la: id est, iecur saginatum & auctum pinguibus ficis. Candidorum autem in pluma vestigal maximum, unde bis vel etiam ter velluntur quibusdam in locis anno. Porro iecur anserinum valenter nutrire probiq; succi esse ab omnibus fere receptum est. Alas quoq; Galenus commendabilis facit. Sed carnem ipsorum excrementis scatere, adq; concoctionem esse peruicaciorem quidam existimant. Certissimum est ex omnibus alitibus, solis anseribus, censores magistratum inuenientes, gratiam restulisse, nihil enim agebant, quam ut eorum alimenta locarent, sacrosanctos enim eos fuisse, Capitolio seruato, vel inde costat, quod violare illos fas non erat. Immensos praeterea vsus in re cibaria & culinis prastant. Britannos quoq; anserem in honore habuisse (safar in suis commentariis testis est), eum enim gustare fas non putabant: alebant tamen animi voluptatisq; causa. Parentes rarium epulas opiparas subeunt, sed pulli & semestres frequentius. Infantissimi a Magnatibus quibusdam amide exp petuntur, sed adultiores vt trimestres, magis concommendantur, illi enim excrementis abun-dant. Optimantur loco tenebroso, & tepidò caueis conclusi. Largioribus autem cibariis opus est & largiori potu, voracitas enim in iis eximia est & bibendi desiderium ingens: atque sic bene curati, duobus ad summum mensibus altiles prapinguesq; euadut Castaneis, pyris, malis, & id genus aliis ad farcturam idoneis solent farciri veiuli & adultiores, sic enim lautiores euadunt, pulli vero oleribus herbisq; ac lardo minutim concisô. Ceruix, ala, pedes cum palmis, pipere & vino solent elixari, idq; edulii genus prima mensa solet apponi palato gratissimum & saluberrimum, ius enim contra toxica & aconita efficax esse admodum, compertum habetur.
units.tr: That is, the liver fattened and enlarged with rich figs. The white geese, however, are a very great source of revenue from their down, and in some places they are plucked two or even three times a year. Moreover, it is accepted by almost everyone that goose liver is strongly nourishing and of good juice. Galen also commends the wings. But some think the flesh is full of excrement and makes digestion more difficult. It is quite certain that of all birds, geese alone earned the gratitude of the censors, who, when they came to office, did nothing but let out the contracts for their feeding. That they were sacred, and that the Capitol was saved by them, is shown by the fact that it was not lawful to harm them. Besides, they provide immense uses in food and in the kitchen. The Britons too held the goose in honour (Safar, in his commentaries, is a witness): they did not think it lawful to eat it, yet they kept them for pleasure and delight. Parent geese are seldom served at lavish feasts, but young ones and half-grown ones more often. The very youngest are eagerly sought after by certain nobles, but the older ones, like three-month-olds, are more commended, for those are full of excrement. They are best kept in a dark, warm place, shut up in coops. They need richer feed and richer drink, for their voracity is extraordinary and their desire to drink is immense; and so, well cared for, they become fat and plump within two months at most. Older geese and young ones are usually stuffed with chestnuts, pears, apples and other such things suited to stuffing, for in this way they become more delicate; the young ones, however, are fed with vegetables, herbs and finely chopped lard. The neck, wing and feet with their webs are usually boiled with pepper and wine, and this kind of dish is usually set before the first course, most pleasing and most wholesome to the palate, for the broth is well known to be very effective against poisons and aconite.

units.la: Ad extremum adipem anserum fartilium celeberrimos vsus nobis praestare frigoribus hibernis in condienda brassica aliisque oleribus, sicut & alii obsoniis parandis, omnibus culinis pluscquam notum est, omitto nunc, quantum in re medica valeat, de quo hic meminisse nihil attinet.
units.tr: Finally, the fat of stuffed geese provides us with very famous uses in the winter cold, in preserving cabbage and other vegetables, and likewise in preparing foods, as is more than known in every kitchen. I now pass over how much it avails in medicine, about which it is not worth mentioning here.

units.la: De Feris anseribus.
units.tr: On wild geese.

units.la: FEros & syluestres quoq; esse anseres nō ignotum est: quos sedem mutare, perinde vt grues dubium non est, nam & eò ipso tempore solent ad nos redire quo grues. Hieme autem inter magnificas epulas reponuntur, inassantur enim garyophyllis confixi, seruanturque aliquot dies. Nec autem succi boni esse, nec facile confici norunt ii, qui crebrius iis vsi, licet aliis in cibis non sordeant, propter longinquiorem enim volatum aiunt, minus eos esse excrementis refertos, quod verisimile videtur.
units.tr: That wild and forest geese also exist is well known. That they change their dwelling place, just like cranes, is beyond doubt, for they tend to return to us at the same time as the cranes. In winter they are served at magnificent feasts: they are roasted, pierced with cloves, and kept for some days. Those who have often eaten them know that their juice is neither good nor easily digested, although in other dishes they are not despised. They say that, because of their longer flight, they are less full of excrement, which seems likely.

units.la: De anate.
units.tr: On ducks.

units.la: INter amphibia reponuntur anates, petunt enim tum à terra, tum ab aqua alimentum. Quæ in vrbibus versantur, liberéq; cœlo, ac aquis fluentibus non fruuntur, in cibis sunt inutiliores infalubriores q; viuunt enim cibariis abiectissimis & fœ idissimis, vt iis, quæ à culinis eiiciuntur in vicos. Cœnum item mire devorant, sicut & ranas, bufones & serpentes. Et, si assa vel elixa diutius tempore estiuo asseruentur, serpentes vermiumq; colluuiem iis innasci animadnersum est. Vnde facile colligere est, carnem earum mali esse succi excrementosamq;, ac pertinaciter confici in ventriculo. Quare qui eruditioris
units.tr: Ducks are classed among the amphibious birds, for they seek food both from land and from water. Those that live in towns, and do not enjoy the open sky and running waters, are less useful and less wholesome as food, for they live on the most abject and filthy scraps, such as what is thrown out of the kitchens into the streets. They also greedily devour mud, as do frogs, toads and snakes. And if roasted or boiled ducks are kept for longer in summer, it has been observed that snakes and a swarm of worms breed in them. Whence it is easy to gather that their flesh is of bad, excrementitious juice and is digested with difficulty in the stomach. Wherefore those of more refined palate

units.la: NB. ditioris sunt palati, facile poterunt discernere inter eas quæ in urbium lacunis ac paludibus degunt, & quæ in rivulis aquisq; fluentibus, hæ enim longè maiorem saporis habent iucunditatem. Pulli autem earum in maiori sunt gloria. Pectus vero & ceruicem delicatius sapere Martialis ganeæ peritus docuit hoc carmine, Tota tibi ponatur anas, sed pectore tantum Et ceruice sapit, cætera redde coquo.
units.tr: those of more refined palate can easily distinguish between those that live in the pools and marshes of cities and those that live in streams and running waters, for the latter have a far greater pleasantness of flavour. Their young are in greater esteem. The breast and neck, however, taste more delicate, as Martial, expert in gluttony, taught in this verse: "Let the whole duck be served to you, but only the breast and neck have flavour; give the rest to the cook."

units.la: Anserum & anatum in medicina vsus varius.
units.tr: On the varied use of geese and ducks in medicine.

units.la: Adeps anserinus celebratissimi vsus est : cum melle morsui canis rabidi occurrit : medeturque vulneribus cum foliis cucurbitæ sylvestris tritis. Sonitum auriumque grauitatem emendat cum succo ceparum. Cum pipere albo & similibus vtiliter illinitur ad perfrictiones, conuulsiones, cæcos ac subitos dolores, omniaque quæ acopis curantur. In leniendis vero & sedandis doloribus, ob partium scilicet & substantiæ tenuitatem magis penetrabilis adeps anserinus caeterarum volucrum adipibus longè praefertur, ut pluribus in locis patet ex Galeno, praesertim 2. ad glauc. vbi de scirrhis. At verò sanguinem profluentem à cerebro, fracto scilicet capite, idem vel etiam anatum cum rosaceo coctus sistit, vel etiam vtriusque infusus sanguis. Sed peculiariter sanguis anatum contusis medetur oculis cum melle.
units.tr: Goose fat is in very famous use: with honey it meets the bite of a mad dog, and it heals wounds with crushed leaves of wild gourd. With onion juice it corrects ringing and heaviness of the ears. Mixed with white pepper and similar things it is usefully smeared on chills, convulsions, blindness and sudden pains, and on all things treated with soothing remedies. For softening and calming pains, goose fat is far preferred to the fats of other birds, because of the fineness of its parts and substance, which makes it more penetrating; this is shown in many places by Galen, especially in book 2 to Glaucon, where he speaks of scirrhi. But blood flowing from the brain, when the head is broken, is stopped either by the blood of geese or of ducks boiled with rose oil, or by either blood infused. Duck blood in particular heals bruised eyes when mixed with honey.

units.la: Sanguinem anatum Ponticarum à Mithridate Rege nobilitatum inuenimus, spissatum enim miscuit antidotis felici succesu, quoniam veneno viuerent, de nostris polliceri id non ausim, nisi experimento facto.
units.tr: We find that the blood of Pontic ducks was ennobled by King Mithridates: having thickened it, he mixed it into antidotes with happy success, since they lived on poison. I would not dare promise the same for our ducks unless it were tested by experiment.

units.la: Contra lepores quoque marinos sanguis valet anserinus cum olei aequa portione: contra mala item medicamenta omnia servatur cum Lemnia terra & spinae albae succo in pastillos redactus.
units.tr: Goose blood with an equal portion of oil is also effective against sea hares. Likewise it is kept as a remedy against all bad drugs when reduced to lozenges with Lemnian earth and juice of white thorn.

units.la: Anserum trium linguas inassatas, inque cibo sumtas hydrocelicis, id est, herniā aquosa afflictis prodesse, Anaxilaus autor est.
units.tr: Anaxilaus is the authority that the tongues of three geese, eaten roasted in food, benefit those afflicted with hydrocele, that is, watery hernia.

units.la: Porro in peste aeris carnes anserinae, in peste verò aquae anatinae magis celebrantur: quae verò pestis aeriae aqueaeque sint signa, vide cap.de aere.
units.tr: Further, goose meats are more commended in pestilence of the air, and duck meats in pestilence of water. What the signs of aerial and watery pestilence are, see the chapter on air.

units.la: De
units.tr: On

units.la: De perdicibus.
units.tr: On partridges.

units.la: PErdicum carnem à coturnicum carne non longum differre constat ex Aristotele, qui de perdicibus & coturnicibus eodem capite tradidit, ut natura inter se non multum differentibus.
units.tr: It is agreed from Aristotle that partridge flesh does not differ much from quail flesh; in the same chapter he taught that they are by nature not very different from each other.

units.la: Præstantiorem tamen & succi bonitate & concoctionis facilitate esse carnem perdicum norunt proceres & magnates. Infantes enim pulli regum sunt epulæ, adultiores facti, & qui peruolare possunt, non in minori sunt pretio & gloria.
units.tr: Nevertheless nobles and magnates know partridge flesh to be superior both in goodness of juice and ease of digestion. The chicks of partridges are the food of kings. Once grown and able to fly, they are no less prized and esteemed.

units.la: Annicula perdices in cibos quoque admittuntur, ultra vero displicent. Vetulæ & adultæ non nisi per frigora mensas subeunt, tunc enim parum inassatæ lardo transfixæ incoquuntur eum brassica, vel solum inassantur.
units.tr: Yearling partridges are also admitted to food, but beyond that they displease. Old and mature ones come to tables only in cold weather; then, lightly roasted, pierced with lard, they are cooked with cabbage, or simply roasted.

units.la: Libidinosissimas autem esse perdices, sicut & coturnices, inde palam euadit, quod crebrius eas efitantes, aduenerem proritent potenter, cumprimis externis saporibus magis inunctæ vinoq; delibutæ. Gula eas hodie cicurari & mirè opinari docuit.
units.tr: That partridges, like quails, are very lustful is plain from this: when they are often made to fly about, they powerfully stir up desire, especially when anointed with foreign spices and steeped in wine. Gluttony has taught that they are nowadays domesticated and marvellously prized.

units.la: Non omnibus præterea terris eas esse datas planum est, in Attica enim non transuolant uis terra Boeotiæ fines, nec in Anaphi insula fuerunt, priusquam eo delatæ. Superiorum seculorum memoriâ notum est legatos Regis Anglorum caneis conclusas perdices in Britanniam deportasse, {a}s, quoniam illic nulla essent, non tamen potuisse vivere. Germania nostra, ut est omnium bonarum rerum ita & perdicum fertilissima, quas inter primarias etiam escas reponit: quæ rostro pedibusque sunt rubentibus, palmam in cibis obtinuerunt apud gentes quasdam: griseas, quibus neque pedes neque rostrum rubent, pretiosissimi sunt saporis: rubras quibusdam in locis, præsertim Francia, sordescunt: candidas, quæ in Alpibus Allobrogicis nascuntur, satuo sunt gustatu, ut & nigræ, hæc enim inueniri literis proditum est.
units.tr: Moreover, it is clear that they have not been given to all lands. In Attica, for instance, they do not fly beyond the borders of Boeotia, nor were they on the island of Anaphe before they were brought there. It is known from the memory of earlier centuries that envoys of the King of the English carried partridges shut in cages into Britain, but since there were none there, they could not live. Our Germany, as it is fertile in all good things, is also most fertile in partridges, which it counts among its chief foods. Those with red beaks and feet have won the palm in eating among certain peoples; the grey ones, whose feet and beak are not red, are of the most precious flavour. Red ones are cheapened in some places, especially in France; white ones, which are born in the Allobrogian Alps, are of sweet taste, as are the black ones, for these are reported in writings to be found.

units.la: In Paphlagonia bina perdicibus corda esse, prodidit Plinius lib. II. cap. 37. Porro annuum fastidium lauri folio eas purgare, idem testis est. Fel earum cum melle aquo pandere mixtum oculis claritatem conciliat. Oua vero illarum cum melle cocta oculorum vlceribus medentur. Sanguis vero perdicum, ut & columbarum, turturum, palumbium, oculis cruore suffusis eximiè prodest, teste Plin. lib. 29 cap. 6. Ius illarum vel ventriculus contritus ex vino nigro dysenterias ventrisq; mala sanat. Quorum putamen ceræ mixtum stantes mammas sernare, & à partu custodire, oua vero sorpta fœcunditatem facere laćtisq; copiam, testatur idem lib. 30. cap. 14. Carnes in peste aeris commendantur, quæ vero pestis aeris signa sint, & quomodo discernatur à peste terræ, aquæ, ignisque, vide principio huius tractatus de aere.
units.tr: Pliny, book 2, chapter 37, says that in Paphlagonia partridges have two hearts. Further, the same authority says that laurel leaf purges them of their yearly disgust. Their gall mixed with honey and water, spread on the eyes, brings clarity. Their eggs cooked with honey heal ulcers of the eyes. The blood of partridges, as also of doves, turtledoves and wood pigeons, is especially beneficial to eyes suffused with blood, witness Pliny, book 29, chapter 6. Their broth, or their crushed gizzard with black wine, cures dysentery and disorders of the bowels. Their shells mixed with wax keep standing breasts firm and guard them from childbirth, while eggs swallowed make women fertile and increase the flow of milk; the same author testifies to this in book 30, chapter 14. Their meats are commended in pestilence of the air. What the signs of pestilence of the air are, and how it is distinguished from the pestilence of earth, water and fire, see the beginning of this treatise on air.

units.la: De attagena, turdo, merula, sturno, rusticula, roftrula.
units.tr: On the attagen, the thrush, the blackbird, the starling, the woodcock, and the rostrula.

units.la: ABantiquis attagena, vulgo gallina corylorum, maximè celebrata fuit, præstertim Ionica, ob succum quem parit bonum, tum etiam quod facilimè in ventre eam perfici optimeq; nutrire, nullum est dubium, ob quam causam Martialis carmine suo laudes eius non omisit, lib.13. Epigr.60.
units.tr: The ancients held the attagen, commonly called the hazel-hen, in the highest esteem, especially the Ionian kind, because it yields good juice. That it is easily digested in the stomach and nourishes well there is beyond doubt, and for this reason Martial did not omit to praise it in his poem, Book 13, Epigram 60.

units.la: Inter sapores fertur altum primum Ionicarum gustus attagenarum.
units.tr: It is said that among flavours the Ionian attagens have the highest taste.

units.la: Cæterum nō abs re addo, tum etiam, quia si res quædam est boni succi, non statim sequitur, quod sit bonus cibus, qui multa desiderat: Bonus enim cibus est, qui facile à naturæ robore edomatur, in calorem ventricu-li non reagit, tempestiuè in eo perficitur, in corporis cedit nutrimentum, putredinisque labem non subit. Eiusmodi verò cibum leuem esse oportere atque friabilem, succoque laudabili præstantem, extra controuersiam est: nā cibi crassi & duri crassum concoctuq; difficilè succum generant, vt ex leguminibus sunt fabae, lentes, lupini &c. & fructus quidā arborei, piscesitem saliti, carnesq; nimium infumatæ & duræ, crassum enim hæc succum generant, & in calorem natiuum reagentem:
units.tr: I add, not without reason, that if a food has good juice, it does not follow at once that it is good food, since a good food needs many other qualities. A good food is one that is easily overcome by the strength of nature, does not resist the heat of the stomach, is perfected in it at the right time, yields its nourishment to the body, and does not fall into putrefaction. It is beyond dispute that such food ought to be light and crumbly and excellent in its praiseworthy juice. Thick and hard foods produce thick juice that is hard to digest: among pulses, beans, lentils and lupins are examples, and certain tree fruits, salted fish, and meats that are too much smoked and hard. These produce thick juice, and it acts upon the natural heat.

units.la: Z 4 & & licet quædam ex his succum habeant gra- tum & bonum, non tamen protinus bo- nus cibus sunt, cum possint & obstructione, & qualitate, & coctionis etiam duritie, aliaue ratione multifariam obesse. Ex quibus in- telligitur, multa licet existant inter alimenta boni quidem succi, exinde tamen non sequi, bonum etiam esse cibum, qui, vt dictum, multa requirit, quorum vnum si desit, bonus esse nequit. Et si succus alicuius rei nulla alia ratione peccat vel obest, certa sola quali- tate noxius deprehenditur, corpusque hu- manum alterat immutatque, vel exiccando, id est, humores valide absumendo, vt acetum forte, muria, lixiuium, alumen, calx, petrole- um, succique rerum valide purgantium, nec non nimius calidorum ac resoluentium v- sus, vt balnei, vini, veneris, vel incrassando, hoc est, humores fluxiles reddendo confi- stentiores, vt sunt omnium crassarum, terre- narumque, ac citra acrimoniam amarorem- que frigidarum rerum succi liquoresque, vt hypociftidis, acaciæ, sorborum, gallarum, cupressi, mororum immaturorum, balau- stiorum, malicorii, mespilorum, corti- cis & foliorum quercus, myrthi, coto- neorum, &c. vel acrimonia nimia, qua in- situs calor vel extinguitur abfumiturq;, vel etiam mutatur in igneu, hoc est, intenditur ad maiomajorem gradum, secundum hujus enim intentionem & augmentum generatur morbi calidi: hujus generis sunt piper, zinziber, & similia linguam acriter vellicantia.
units.tr: Although some of these have a pleasant and good juice, they are not at once good food, since they can do harm in many ways: by obstruction, by their quality, or by the hardness of their digestion, or in other ways. From these things it is understood that although many foods have a good juice, it does not follow that they are good food, since, as I have said, good food requires many qualities, and if one of them is lacking, it cannot be good. And if the juice of some thing harms or hinders in no other way, but is detected as harmful by its quality alone, and alters and changes the human body, it does so either by drying, that is, by vigorously consuming the humours (such as perhaps vinegar, brine, lye, alum, lime, petroleum, and juices of strongly purging things, and also the excessive use of hot and dissolving things, such as the bath, wine, and sex); or by thickening, that is, by making the flowing humours more solid (such as the juices and liquors of all thick and earthy things that are cold without sharpness or bitterness, for example hypocistis, acacia, sorb-apples, galls, cypress, unripe mulberries, pomegranate flowers, medlars, pomegranate rind, medlars, the bark and leaves of the oak, myrtle, quinces, and so on); or by excessive sharpness, by which the innate heat is extinguished or consumed, or even changed into fire, that is, pushed up to a greater degree. For it is from this intensifying and increase that hot diseases are generated. Of this kind are pepper, ginger, and similar things that sharply sting the tongue.

units.la: Vel humectando & emolliendo, vt Spinachium, Beta, Malua, Mercurialis, caulis capitatus & id genus alia culinis nota.
units.tr: Or by moistening and softening, as spinach, beet, mallow, dog's mercury, cabbage, and other kinds known in the kitchen.

units.la: Vel detergendo, viscosofque humores viscetibus adhaerentes eluendo, vt succus absinthii, aristolochiae, centaurii minoris, fubinae, gentianae, agrimoniae, dracunculi, hellebori, ari, falisq; liquor.
units.tr: Or by cleansing, washing away the viscous humours that cling to the viscera, as the juice of wormwood, birthwort, lesser centaury, fumitory, gentian, agrimony, dragonwort, hellebore, arum, and brine.

units.la: Vel astringendo, hoc est, meatus, venarumq; arteriarum ora coarctando, vt succus tormentillae, cotoneorum, prunorum fyli ueftrium, pyrorum fyli ueftrium, malorum granatorum, citriorum, aurantiorum acidorum, aliaque plura quorum facta est mentio interincraffantia: & certum est magnas hic strui vitae insidias: difficile enim est a blandissimis suavissimisque malorum quorundam noftratium & exoticorum, vt citriorum & arantiorum, succis sibi temperare, quibus multi porcorum more saginam explent, vnde postea insignem corporis alterationem sustinere & perpeti coguntur: alii enim succi sunt praedulces, alii acidi, alii austeri, acerbi alii, quidam vero ex horum multis vel duobus temperati sentiuntur. Hic vero meminisse oportebit, rectam cuiuis hominis natu-
units.tr: Or by astringing, that is, by constricting the passages and the mouths of the veins and arteries, as the juice of tormentil, quinces, the sloes of the wild plum, the sloes of the wild pear, pomegranates, citrons, sour oranges, and many others already mentioned among the thickening things. And it is certain that great snares of life are laid here. For it is hard to restrain oneself from the very sweet juices of certain fruits of ours and of foreign lands, such as citrons and oranges, with which many fill themselves like pigs, and afterwards they are forced to undergo and endure a marked alteration of the body. Some juices are very sweet, others sour, others austere, others bitter, and some are felt to be tempered by two or more of these. Here it will be fitting to remember that nature has given every person a right reason, so that he may avoid what would harm and embrace what would benefit,

units.la: NB. natura tributam esse rationem, vt nocitura declinet, profutura vero amplectatur, vtriqueacgulæ constanter imperet, ne præter modum & intempestiue iis vescatur, in quibus plus voluptatis, quam vtilitatis infle deprehenditur. Vitam enim salubriter prorogare cupienti, duo inprimis considerandafunt, primum: præseruare corpus à præpostera siccitate, deinde vitare nimium ac immodicum, intempestiuumq; rarefactionem, hoc est, solidam compactam q; materiam disiungentium ac relaxantium vsum, hæc enim quia plurimum calida sunt tenuis- que substantiæ, alte penetrant, humoresque per resolutionem & euaporationem tenuiū partium à crassioribus & terrestribus absumunt, vnde tandem corpus exiccari ac contabescere necessario contingit.
units.tr: NB. and so that he may constantly govern both appetites, lest he eat beyond measure and unseasonably of those things in which more pleasure than usefulness is found. For one who wishes to prolong life in health must consider two things above all: first, to preserve the body from unnatural dryness; second, to avoid excessive and immoderate and untimely rarefaction, that is, the use of things that loosen and relax solid and compact matter. For since these are mostly hot and of thin substance, they penetrate deeply, and by dissolution and evaporation of the thin parts they consume the humours from the thicker and earthy parts, so that the body necessarily ends by being dried out and wasting away.

units.la: Pessime igitur sanitati consulunt, qui ventriculo relaxato, debili & imbecillo adhibent relaxantia, vt maluaticum, piper, napi, theriacam, mitridaticum, & similia, iisque vires prostratas vel languidas recuperare studeant & corroborare, cum potius astringentia & austera, quæ sc. corrugando vniendoq; ventriculi villos, calorem congregent, ejalq; dissolutionem impediant, appetituq; excitent, sint vsurpanda. Atq; hæc monuisse hic & meminisse (quoniam inter meditandum occurrebant) studiose volui, vt lector delectatus recedat, & fideliter monitus ad reliqua quoq; perlegenda reuertatur.
units.tr: Those therefore consult health very badly who, for a relaxed, weak and feeble stomach, apply relaxing things such as mallow, pepper, mustard, theriac, mithridate, and the like, and strive to restore and strengthen the prostrate or languid powers with them, whereas astringent and austere things should rather be used: these, by wrinkling and drawing together the villi of the stomach, gather the heat and prevent its dissolution, and they excite the appetite. I have wished to note these things here, and to remember them (since they came to mind while I was thinking), so that the reader may depart delighted and, faithfully warned, return to read through the rest.

units.la: De turdis inter autores non conuenit. Multi mirantur, quod Horatius scripserit, Nil melius turdo, vulua nil dulcius ampla,
units.tr: Authors do not agree about thrushes. Many marvel that Horace wrote, Nothing is better than a thrush, nothing sweeter than a plump sow's belly,

units.la: Et Martialis, Inter aues turdus si quis me judice certet, Inter quadrupedes gloria prima lepus:
units.tr: and Martial, If a thrush should contend among birds by my judgment, the first glory among four-footed creatures is the hare.

units.la: inque eam venerunt sententiam, vt veteres tanquam rei alimentariæ indoctos damnârint.
units.tr: And they came to the opinion that the ancients condemned them as men ignorant of foodstuffs.

units.la: Sed & illud non parua admiratione dignum est, quod Gal.3. de alim. facult. scripsit, turdos & passerculos, perdicibus, attagenis, columbis, gallis, phasianis & gallinis concoctu esse duriores, & posset hunc locum mento scatere quis suspicari, nisi eadem verba apud Oribasium & Ætium notata haberetur.
units.tr: But it is also worthy of no small wonder that Galen, in Book 3 of On the Faculties of Foods, wrote that thrushes and sparrows are harder to digest than partridges, attagens, pigeons, cocks, pheasants, and hens. One might suspect this passage to be corrupt, were it not that the same words are found noted in Oribasius and Aëtius.

units.la: Cur autem in admirationem hoc veniat, potissimum in causa est, quod idem 7. methodi nutrit & alibi scriptum reliquit, quæcunque magis entia dif- nutriunt, difficilius a calore naturali confici. ficilius a
units.tr: The reason this causes wonder is chiefly that the same author, in Book 7 of the Method and elsewhere, left it written that whatever foods nourish more are digested with more difficulty by the natural heat.

units.la: Vnde si turdis & passerib. perdices, gallinæ, & calore ve- phasiani magis nutriunt, suntque, vt loquitur triculi ca Celsus, firmioris materiæ, par quoque est diffi- ficienda cili concoq. At vero phasianos, quo, quatu sunt. ad concoctionis nutriendique vim attinet, gallinis Phasiani pares, edendi vero suauitate superiores facit solis va- Galen, solis vaporib. a culinaru pfc ctis magi-poribus ftrifq; maiore ob gulæ jucunditate coq cofue- costi. uisseD. Hier. testis est, in epist. n. ad Oceanum. 83.
units.tr: Hence, if partridges, hens, and pheasants nourish more than thrushes and sparrows, and are, as Celsus says, of firmer matter, then they too are equally hard to digest. But pheasants, as far as the power of digestion and of nourishment is concerned, are equal to hens, yet superior in pleasantness of eating, since they are cooked with the vapours of the kitchen more thoroughly and with greater delight to the palate. Jerome bears witness to this in his letter 83 to Oceanus.

units.la: Sacerdotis munera typice enarrans sic eum depingit, debere esse domum suam bene regentem, non vt opes augeat, non vt regias paret epulas, non vt caelatas struat patinas, non vt phasidas aues lentis vaporibus coquat, qui ad ossa perveniant, superficiemque carnis non dissoluant artificii temperamento: atque hoc pacto quoque fructus coqui solitum pro valetudinariis meminit Galenus 2. de compos. medicament. & Alexander Trallianus l.12.cap. de tertiana. Verum enimvero exactius re considerata apparebit veteres non male judicasse: quantam enim nutriendis saginandisque turdis majores impenderint operam M Varro 3. de re rust. l.i. & Columell, testatum fecerunt. Agrippina Claudii Caesaris conjunx turdum habuit imitantem sermones hominum, quod nunquam ante visum, teste Plin. l.10. c.42. Certum est tantam fuisse Romae turdorum auiaria, tamque breui in tantam multitudinem excreuisse, vt ex eorum fimo agri stercorarentur, teste Varrone qui principatum turdorum fimo ex auiariis tribuit: quamobrem non immerito exclamauit Plinius apud Varronem id legens, Bene ait sperandum est de moribus nostris, si tanta fuerunt apud majores auiaria, vt ex iis stercorarentur agri. In tanta tamen copia stupendum, tam memorabilia fuisse turdorum pretia, singulos enim Ro-
units.tr: Explaining allegorically the duties of a priest, Jerome depicts him thus: his house must be well governed, not to increase its wealth, not to prepare royal banquets, not to set out carved dishes, not to cook pheasant birds with thin vapours that reach the bones and do not dissolve the surface of the flesh by the temperate art of cooking. Galen also mentions this kind of cooking for invalids in Book 2 of On Compound Medicines, and Alexander of Tralles in Book 12, in the chapter on tertian fever. Yet if the matter is considered more exactly, it will appear that the ancients did not judge badly. For how great an effort the elders spent on feeding and fattening thrushes, M. Varro in Book 3 of On Agriculture and Columella have attested. Agrippina, wife of Claudius Caesar, had a thrush that imitated human speech, something never seen before, as Pliny attests in Book 10, chapter 42. It is certain that there were such great thrush aviaries at Rome, which grew so quickly into such a multitude, that fields were manured with their dung, as Varro attests, who gives the chief place among thrush dung to that from the aviaries. Hence Pliny, reading this in Varro, not undeservedly exclaimed: "We ought to hope well of our morals, if the aviaries of our ancestors were so great that fields were manured with them." Yet amid such abundance it is astonishing that the prices of thrushes were so remarkable, for single ones were sold at Ro-

units.la: Romæ denariis ternis, hoc est, duodecim nummis venditatos constat, vt ita turdorum quinque millia tali pretio diuendita sexaginta nummorum millia faciant, hoc est, æstimatione nostra coronatos 1500. Vnde constat mira & immensa auium fuisse pretia apud Romanos, vrbemque Romam quasi arcem quandam expilatorum totius orbis fuisse. Hodie turdorum saginandorum nulla geritur cura, sed quales capiuntur, mittuntur in culinas, vnde manducandi in illis tanta suauitas non percipitur, enutriti enim & saginati jucundissimi euadunt, cum macri ignobiliores ciboque minus commendabiles sint. De his enim verum est, quod Galenus scripsit, perdicibus, gallinis & phasianis eos esse duriores in cibatu, proptereaq; difficilius concoqui ac perfici. Non enim abso- lute accipiendum est, quod scribit, quæcunque magis nutrire debent, difficilius ea à calore naturali perfici oportere, verum id est, datis cæteris paribus. Vox difficilius limitanda est & secundum quid aliud intelligenda, vt sensus fit, quæcunque magis debent nutrire, necesse est, vt diutius in ventriculo & intestinis (nam & hæc habere vim chylum conficiendi, qui scil. in ventriculo πλεόνασμα acquirere non potuit, ostendunt heluones, quibus ob ventriculum nimis distentum alimentum in intestina prolabitur) com-
units.tr: It is recorded that at Rome they were sold for three denarii each, that is, twelve coins, so that five thousand thrushes sold at that price would come to sixty thousand coins, that is, by our reckoning, 1,500 crowns. From this it is clear that the prices of birds among the Romans were remarkable and immense, and that the city of Rome was, as it were, a citadel of plunderers of the whole world. Today no care is taken to fatten thrushes, but whatever kind are caught are sent to the kitchens. Hence the great sweetness in eating them is not perceived, for the well-fed and fattened ones turn out most delightful, while the lean ones are of lower quality and less esteemed as food. What Galen wrote is true of these: that they are tougher to eat than partridges, hens and pheasants, and so are digested and completed with more difficulty. But what he writes should not be taken absolutely, that whatever ought to nourish more must be perfected with more difficulty by natural heat. It is true only when other things are equal. The word "more difficult" must be limited and understood in some other respect, so that the sense is: whatever ought to nourish more must of necessity remain longer in the stomach and intestines (for these too have the power of completing the chyle, which, namely, could not acquire excess [πλεόνασμα] in the stomach, as gluttons show, whose food slips into the intestines because the stomach is overstretched), so that

units.la: Galenus explicatur. commorentur, vt alimentum penitus confi-ciatur : venis enim mefaraicis necessarius succus interciperetur, si chylus cito & cum impetu, debitam moram non præstans, dilaberetur.
units.tr: Galen is explained. they may remain there until the food is thoroughly digested. For the necessary juice would be taken up by the mesaraic veins if the chyle were to flow away quickly and with force, not remaining the due time.

units.la: Cæterum turdorum carnes probitate succi insignes sunt, cumprimis qui apud nos capiuntur per hiemem, quo tempore maxime cernuntur, illaqueanturque in dumetis juniperinis, baccis enim juniperi victitant, qua de causa in peste aeris insignes sunt, hydropicis quoque, calculosis & colica confl-ctatis frequens esus prodest : cum myrthi vero baccis & cydoniis turdus inflatus, dy-sentericis.
units.tr: Moreover, the flesh of thrushes is distinguished by the excellence of its juice, especially that of those caught among us in winter, when they are most easily seen and snared in the juniper thickets, for they live on juniper berries. For this reason they are excellent in a plague-laden air. Frequent eating of them also benefits dropsical, stone-afflicted and colic patients, while a thrush stuffed with myrtle berries and quinces benefits dysenteric patients.

units.la: Merularum & turdorum amicitia est. Dicta merula quod sola volet, & solitaria pascatur, quasi mera volans. Merularum genus alterum undiquaque nigrum est, rostro etiam nigro, alterum rostro croceo, quod canorum magis est. Cantu enim maxime vocales hujus generis in auiariis passim hodie cernuntur, nam docentur secreto, & vbi nulla alia vox miscetur auditurque, assiduenter qui crebro præcinat, cibisque abblandiat. Tertium genus candidum est, idque nusquam reperiri, quam circa Cyllenen Arcadiæ montem vult Plinius. Sed & in Norvegia aliisque locis septentrionem versus albicant, nec non in Helvetia albas metulas rulas captas esse, rostro tamen flauente, Gesnerus testatur. Carnes merularum bonitate succi quidam turdis pares esse volunt, sed quo inuento, vel fundamento, nondum mihi adhuc constat. Alii succum melancolicum & paucum generare asserunt pari dubio. In confesso est, succi praestantia merularum carnes turdis non posse esse pares, ob victus, quem partim in sepibus & vepribus, partim circa loca palustria quaerunt, dissimilitudinem & improbitatem. Sunt enim quaedam, quae vermiculos quaerunt in fimo equino, quaedam vescuntur vermiculis aquaticis, unde & riuales & aquaticae nuncupantur.
units.tr: There is a friendship between blackbirds and thrushes. The blackbird (merula) is so named because it flies alone (sola volet) and feeds solitary, as if it were a pure flyer (mera volans). One kind of blackbird is entirely black, even with a black beak; another has a saffron beak and is more tuneful. For the singers of this kind are commonly seen today in aviaries everywhere, since they are taught in private, where no other voice is mixed in and they are heard, and one that sings often and sweetly is kept in constant practice and coaxes its food. A third kind is white, and Pliny says it is found nowhere except near Cyllene, the mountain of Arcadia. But also in Norway and other places farther toward the north they are whitish, and Gesner testifies that white blackbirds have been caught in Switzerland, though with yellow beaks. Some hold that blackbird flesh is equal to that of thrushes in the goodness of its juice, but on what discovery or ground this rests is not yet clear to me. Others assert with equal doubt that it produces a melancholy and scanty juice. It is agreed that blackbird flesh cannot be equal to thrush flesh in the excellence of its juice, because of the difference and inferiority of their diet, since they seek their food partly in hedges and brambles, partly near marshy places. For some seek small worms in horse dung, and some feed on aquatic worms, whence they are also called ousel and water-blackbirds.

units.la: Optimae tamen esse creduntur tor- quatae, sic dictae ab alba linea totum earum collum ambiente, vulgo merulæ fyluaticæ, & montanae, quod in fyluis & circa montes degant: nec non fuscae saxa circa & fruticeta degentes, magnitudine paulo minores. Ubi magna harum frequentia est, capiuntur noctu ad ignis splendorem retibus extensis: alibi vero visco, quibusdam & pluribus in locis laqueis aut tendiculis, vt turdi, & sturni, estque haec captura, infimae etiam hodie plebi ruricolis, equisonibus, & agasonibus notissima, qui captos in vrbes, magnatumque ac delicatorum culinas vendunt.
units.tr: The best, however, are thought to be the ring ousels, so called from the white line encircling their whole neck. In common speech they are the wood and mountain blackbirds, because they dwell in woods and around mountains. Also the dusky ones that live among rocks and thickets, a little smaller in size. Where these are very plentiful they are caught at night, by the glow of a fire, with nets spread out; elsewhere they are caught with birdlime, and in some and many places with snares or traps, as thrushes and starlings are. This method of catching them is well known even today to the lowest common people, to country folk, horsemen and carters, who sell the captured birds in towns and in the kitchens of great men and the pampered.

units.la: Ca. Galenus l.6.de sanit.tuend. esum sturnorum concedit iis, qui gracili, attenuato, siccatoque sunt habitu, carnes enim eorum ab attagenarum carnibus proximas collocat. Alii illaudabilis eos nutrimenti esse contendunt decepti errore Arabum, qui flurnos aconito vesci tradiderunt, cum non aconito, sed cicuta flurnos nutriri apud certos auctores & praesertim apud Galenum notatum reperiatur. Verum an propterea mensis cibisque sint abdicandi, non inconuenienter hic quaeritur. Hujus quaestionis explicationem invenient aequus lector titulo de coturnicibus, ibi enim fusius eam tractandi occasio erit. Unum hic adiicere libuit vuas matu-rescentes eos mirifice appetere, quo etiam tempore pinguiores capiuntur, & meliores seipsis jucundioresque, vuarum enim pretiosus ille succus carnis ipsorum improbum succum abolet ac emendat. Apud Romanos fuisse flurnos (item lusciniasj latino sermone graecoque doctiles, praeterea quae meditatos in diem assiduo, nova locutos esse longiori etiam contextu memoriae proditum est. Quod minus mirabile est, cum vbique fere in Galliarum amplis vrbibus gallicum sermonem longiori etiam contextu explanent atque exprimant: foeminas autem ad id ineptas existimant.
units.tr: Galen, in book 6 of On Preserving Health, allows the eating of starlings to those of slender, thin and dry constitution, for he places their flesh nearest to the flesh of the great bustards. Others maintain that they are a poor food, deceived by the error of the Arabs, who handed down that starlings feed on aconite, whereas it is noted in certain authors, and especially in Galen, that starlings are nourished not by aconite but by hemlock. Whether, for that reason, they should be rejected from tables and foods is discussed here not out of place. The fair reader will find an explanation of this question under the title on quails, for there will be occasion to treat it more fully there. It is only worth adding here that the birds eagerly seek ripening grapes, and at that season they are caught fattest and best and most pleasant in themselves, for the precious juice of the grapes corrects and removes the bad juice of their flesh. It is recorded that among the Romans starlings (as well as nightingales) were docile in Latin and Greek speech, and that they were known to rehearse daily and speak new things in a longer passage. This is less wonderful, since almost everywhere in the great cities of Gaul people speak and pronounce French even in longer passages, though they think women unfit for this.

units.la: Ad gallinarum fyluestrium, quarum permulta sunt genera, figurâ magnitudine, locisque in quibus degunt, diffidentia, classem, qui volet, rusticulas, gallinagines & rostrulas seu roftratulas referre poterit. Estautem rusticula perdix rustica {sic} Schneepfhun/ adque differentiam minoris dicitur rusticula major.
units.tr: For the wild hens, of which there are very many kinds, differing in shape, size, the places where they live and their wariness, whoever wishes may refer them to the class of rusticulas, gallinagines and little snipes (rostrulae, or roftratulae). The rusticula is a rustic partridge, called in German "Schneehuhn", and to distinguish it from the smaller one it is called the greater rusticula.

units.la: Rostrulæ vero à rostro cognominatæ sunt, quod in quibusdam porrectius ac longius, in quibusdam breuius est. Natura omnium circa cibos exploranda est à locis, vt plurimum in quibus degunt, & tempore, quo visuntur. Quædam enim syluaticæ sunt gallinam fere æquantes: quædam turmatim iuxta sepes decurrunt celeriter, humiq; nidulantur: quædam locis humidis gaudent & palustribus: quædam circa æquinoctium vernum adueniunt, à lacuum & stagnorum marginibus quoquam vix discedentes: aliæ vere & æstate non visuntur, sed sub autumni fere finem totaq; hieme spectantur, degunt- que in dumetis & genistis, vbi laqueis capi constat: has vermibus viuere, terræ intestinis excrementisque, aliisque bestiolis plenum est, quædam inter gramina latent: aliæ in agris nouaiibus & quiescentibus: In deli- tiis autem mensarum & gulæ celebrantur omnes. Quæ tamen amplitudine sunt perdicis, ejusdemque prope coloris, rostriq; Aa parui, vel eadem cum rusticula majori, forma rostri, capitis, corporisque, (nisi quod longe minores sint) aulicarum delitiarum Proceres quidam perdicibus non dubitant anteponere. Sed cettum est, sæpe subesse fraudem. Itaque notandum, quarum carnes sunt candidiores, teneriores, suauioris̛que saporis, eas probum quoque generare succum & facilius concoqui, quarum vero carnes nigræ sunt & duræ, gustatuq; referunt aliquid auium palustrium, difficilius quoq; confici.
units.tr: The rostrulae are named from their beak (rostrum), since in some it is longer and more extended, in others shorter. The nature of all of them as food should be judged from the places where they mostly live and from the season when they are seen. For some wild kinds are nearly the size of a hen; some run quickly in flocks along the hedges and nest on the ground; some delight in wet and marshy places; some arrive around the spring equinox and scarcely leave the edges of lakes and ponds; others are not seen in spring and summer, but are observed towards the end of autumn and through the whole winter, living in thickets and broom, where they are known to be caught in snares. These feed on worms, the entrails of the earth, excrement and other small creatures; some hide among the grasses, others in newly ploughed and fallow fields. All of them, however, are celebrated for the delights of the table and the palate. Some of these are of the size of the partridge and nearly the same colour, with a short beak like the partridge, or the same beak shape, head and body as the greater rusticula (except that they are much smaller). Certain leaders in courtly delights do not hesitate to prefer them to partridges. But it is certain that deceit often lies beneath this. Therefore it should be noted that those whose flesh is whiter, more tender and of pleasanter flavour produce good juice too and are more easily digested, while those whose flesh is black and hard, and which taste somewhat of marsh birds, are also more difficult to digest.

units.la: Quæ tota spectantur hieme, inter hiemales cibos non postremum obtinent locum: Sed bruti ac rustici plane palati sunt, qui eas inassatas, interaneis non repurgatis, hoc est, vna cum fimo suauissime deuorant, vt in Suecia & Norvegia, vbi magna illarum copia est.
units.tr: These, which are seen all through the winter, hold no mean place among winter foods. But coarse and rustic people, who have quite uncultivated palates, devour them most sweetly ungutted and unroasted, that is, along with their dung, as in Sweden and Norway, where there is a great abundance of them.

units.la: De Coturnicibus scitu digna.
units.tr: On Quails, Worth Knowing

units.la: DE Coturnice veteres & recentiores differentiae reperiuntur. Plinius lib. 10. cap. 23. antiquorum Romanorum cibis damnatas scribit, quod veratro vescerentur, eoque pinguescerent, simulque ob comitialem morbum, quem sola animalium sentiant, praeter hominem. Hæc Plinius, Galenus lib. sext. epidem. comm. 5. ait, in Deride, Beotia
units.tr: Early and later writers differ about the quail. Pliny, book 10, chapter 23, writes that the ancient Romans condemned quails as food because they fed on hellebore and so grew fat on it, and because they suffer from the falling sickness, which, apart from man, only animals of this kind are thought to suffer. So far Pliny. Galen, in the sixth book of his commentary on the Epidemics, says that in Deris, in Boeotia and in Thessaly, many people became ill with spasms from eating quails, since they feed on hellebore, and that the same thing happened to some Athenians who had gorged themselves on quails.

units.la: Thessalia, plurimos ex esu coturnicum mus-corum dissentionibus correptos, quoniam scilicet vescantur veratro, atque idem quibusdam Atheniensis accidisse, qui coturnicibus largius se impleverant. Plinii sententiam, quod attinet dubitandi illa occasionem praebet, solas videlicet coturnices inter animalia, praeter hominem morbum pati comitialem, cum & alia sint animalia, quae hoc malo conflictantur, ut cati, capri, landae, equi, sciuri, quod vidi ipse, pica & suēs: nisi quis dubitationem hanc tolli posse pro Plinio dicat, coturnices animalium solas praeter homines, talem potissimum sentire morbum, quemadmodum etiam de canibus scripsit Aristoteles, nam & mulos, aliaque animantia rabie corripi videmus.
units.tr: As for Pliny's opinion, it gives occasion for doubt: he says that among animals only quails, apart from man, suffer from the falling sickness, yet there are other animals afflicted by this disease, such as cats, goats, hares, horses, squirrels (which I have seen myself), magpies and swine. Unless someone wishes to defend Pliny by saying that quails alone among animals, apart from men, suffer this kind of illness in particular, just as Aristotle wrote of dogs; for we see that mules and other living creatures also are seized by madness.

units.la: Verum his missis, inquirendum, cujus succi & nutrimenti sit coturnix, seu qualea, sic enim a voce quidam nominant? Quidam in cibo eas reformidant, ob causas antea a Galeno commemoratas, alii menses minime abdicandas censent, ob bonum quem praebent succum quamvis carnes earum tuturum carnibus aequiparant, quae sapientum senum cibus habentur, sensus enim roborare, cogitationem acuere, & memoriam confortare creduntur. Aristoteles de perdicibus & coturnicibus tradit in eodem capite, quasi natura non multum inter se differant, sed eiusdem sint generis. Unde non ita, ut vulgus putat, prauisucci coturnices esse credendum est,
units.tr: But setting these aside, we must inquire what juice and nourishment the quail provides, or what kind of food it is, for so some call it, by its name. Some shrink from it as food for the reasons Galen mentioned earlier. Others think it should by no means be rejected, because the good juice it yields is comparable to that of its flesh, which is regarded as food for wise old men; for they are believed to strengthen the senses, sharpen thought and fortify the memory. Aristotle, in the same chapter, teaches that partridges and quails do not differ greatly in nature but belong to the same kind. Hence we must not believe, as the common people think, that quails produce bad juice,

units.la: Aa sed potius tenendum, conveniens ac inculpatum prabere eas nutrimentum. Nec propterea etiam ab illarum esu abstinendum omnino, quod morbo comitiali corripiantur, venenoq; pascantur, cum nonnulla sint animalia, qua licet venenis quandoque nutriantur, quemadmodum de sturnis dictum, qui ex cuta pastu pinguescunt, inter boni tamen succi cibos connumerantur, quo Galenus etiam stur- nos 6. de tuenda sanitat. lib. refert. Sic coturnici veratrum est alimentum, homini medicamentum, liquidem coturnicis natura est in substantiam suam veratrum convertere. Sic anati bufo alimentum est, ciconia serpens, homini vero venenum. Sic veratrum purgat hominem, non etiam coturnicem. Cicuta refrigerat hominem, non etiam turdum, vel sturnum. Licet igitur veneno vescantur coturnices, nec ipsis tamen, nec aliis animalibus aut hominibus, qui horum esui assueverunt, sunt venenum.
units.tr: but rather hold that they provide a suitable and blameless nourishment. Nor on that account should one abstain altogether from eating them, because they are seized by the falling sickness and fed on poison, since there are some animals which, although sometimes nourished on poisons, are nevertheless counted among foods of good juice, as was said of starlings, which grow fat on hemlock; Galen also reports this of starlings in the sixth book of his work on preserving health. Thus hellebore is food for the quail but medicine for man, for it is the quail's nature to convert hellebore into its own substance. Thus the toad is food for the duck, the serpent for the stork, but poison for man. Thus hellebore purges man but not the quail; hemlock cools man but not the thrush or the starling. Therefore, although quails feed on poison, it is not poison to them, nor to other animals or to men who have become accustomed to eating them.

units.la: Nam teste Theophrasto, omnium Pharmacorum vires debiliores deprehenduntur in assuetis, in nonnullis etiam plane inertes.
units.tr: For, according to Theophrastus, the powers of all drugs are found weaker in those who are used to them, and in some cases quite inert.

units.la: Quicquid enim a natura acceptatur, devincitur, conficitur, caloreq;, aut congenita, vel ex consuetudine acquisita, corporis proprietate alteratum in corporis alimoniam digeritur, id alito venenum esse non potest. Hoc modo puella illa Indica, & anus illa attica, a momento cicuta quod
units.tr: For whatever is received by nature, overcome, digested, and, by the warmth and the bodily property either inborn or acquired by habit, altered and distributed into the nourishment of the body, cannot be poison to the one who feeds on it. In this way that Indian girl, and that old woman of Attica, had become so accustomed to hemlock that, from the moment it could be overcome and digested by nature, they harmlessly got used to devouring whole handfuls.

units.la: Quarat. 1. de Veneno. quod natura evincere ac concoquere posset, integros assuevere manipulos devorare innoxie. Sic venena quotidie, praesumtis tamen remediis, hausit Mithridates, & a tali consuetudine ei fuerunt innoxia, adeo, ut captus a Pompeio magno, in carceribus veneno interimere sese non potuerit. Succum vero cicutae non assuetis, & puluerem quoque, esse lethale & soporiferum venenum, Athenien(s)ium supplicia indicant, qui morte condemnatos sorbitione cicuta interemerunt, quam & Socrates impietatis condemnatus in carcere hausisse fertur, ut ita plurimum hic valere consuetudinem naturasque acquisitias fatendum sit.
units.tr: Quarat. 1. de Veneno. In this way Mithridates swallowed poisons every day, though with remedies taken beforehand, and by such habit they were harmless to him; so much so that, when captured by Pompey the Great, he could not kill himself with poison in prison. That the juice of hemlock, and its powder too, is a deadly and soporific poison to those not accustomed to it, the executions of the Athenians show, who put condemned men to death by having them drink hemlock; and Socrates, condemned for impiety, is said to have drunk it in prison. So it must be admitted that habit and acquired natures count for very much here.

units.la: Porro & illud meminisse hic lectorem oportebit, quod alibi etiam monuimus, veneni seminaria calore concitata in vivorum corporibus energia longe esse vegetiora & efficaciora, in defunctorum corporibus, calore extincto fere consopita. Unde in veneris cum muliere, Spiritus morbo gallico infecta, conflictu, quo corpus & veneni spiritus, veneni vehicula, incalescunt, contagii vehicula seminaria fiunt nocentiora, qua in feris ac volucribus toxico interemtis, praecipue si in veru Ignis cer torreantur, vel in lebete elixentur, ignis feruore dissipata diffiantur ac evanescunt. Fera igitur volucresve veneno pasta, vel capta optimis carbonibus tosta, vel etiam elixata menses minime sunt abdicanda. Et ut ad coturnices rium. redeamus, Auicennas earum esum non improbat, propterea quod vescantur elleboro, convulsionesque excitent, ait enim talem generandi spasmum facultatem inesse ipsarum substantia, seu ut alii exprimunt, prodire ab abdita quadam & latente causa, non ab ellebori male-ficio tantum. Averrhoes in 5. collect. cap. 32, mirifice coturnicum carnem laudat, tanquam bonum generantem succum.
units.tr: Further, the reader will also need to remember what we have noted elsewhere: the seeds of poison, when stirred by heat, act far more vigorously and effectively in the bodies of the living than in the bodies of the dead, where they are almost lulled to sleep once the heat has gone out. Hence in intercourse with a woman infected with the French pox, as the bodies and the spirits of the poison, the vehicles of poison, grow hot in the struggle, the vehicles of contagion become more harmful seeds; whereas in wild animals and birds killed by poison, especially if they are roasted on a spit over a fire, or boiled in a pot, the seeds are dissipated and vanish in the heat of the fire. Therefore wild animals or birds fed on poison, or caught and roasted over the best charcoal, or even boiled, are by no means to be rejected for food. And to return to quails: Avicenna does not condemn eating them, because they feed on hellebore and cause convulsions; for he says that such a power of producing spasm inheres in their substance, or, as others put it, that it comes from some hidden and latent cause, and not from the mere malign action of hellebore. Averroes, in the fifth book of his Collections, chapter 32, praises quail flesh wonderfully, as producing good juice.

units.la: Et certum est pullos messium tempore suavissimos esse, inque lautiorum ciborum haberi censu. Adultiores a superiori parte pissa, de ratio adipe, sale condiuntur, adipem vero liquant, servantque in alabastris condiendus epulis jucundissimum, idque condimenti genus veteres ignorarunt. Pinguescunt autem ocyssime, opimantur que maxime frugi-bus, femine canabis & milio. Iusto diutius in aviario reservat adipositam illam, propter molem emori exploratum habetur, nec tamen ob id in cibo reformidantur. Ex quibus manifestum evadit, helleboro illis magis, quam coturnicibus opus esse, qui coturnices in cibis damnant, ob nullam aliam causam, quam quod vescantur elleboro, quasi helleborus nascatur omnibus locis, ubi sunt coturnices, tum etiam, quod veteres eas improbarint, tanquam ventriculo ob nimiam pinguedinem infestas, nauseamque parientes & fastidium. Galenum de simplicit. medicam. vbi docet discernere, facileque cognoscere alimenta bona & mala, si quis diligentius inspexerit, intelliget cotur-nicem praesertim assam boni gratique odoris esse & saporis, ac boni etiam nutrimenti. Illud quoque non omiserim, DEVM Israelis populum, quem ardentissime diligebat, dum-per deserta illa transfiret loca, ad satietatem- usque coturnicibus pastum non fuisse, nisi probati illa fuissent alimenti & salutaris. Quid multa? Coturnices bene in ven-triculo confici, inque corporis alimoniam- verti probae temperaturae & substantiae indi-cium est, Nam in omnibus cibis ad boni suc-ci generationem tantum requiritur, ut probe in ventriculo concoquantur, quicquid enim- venter concoxerit, adjecur transit, ab hoc vero ad nutriendum partes transmittitur.
units.tr: It is certain that the young quails of the harvest season are most delicious and are counted among the more refined foods. The older ones are seasoned from the upper part with pepper, spice and salt; they render their fat and keep it in alabaster jars, to season the most pleasant dishes, a kind of seasoning the ancients did not know. They grow fat very quickly and are fattened especially on grains, hemp seed and millet. If they are kept too long in the aviary, they are known to die from their great bulk, yet they are not on that account rejected as food. From these facts it is plain that those who condemn quails as food have more need of hellebore than the quails do, and they condemn them for no other reason than that they feed on hellebore, as if hellebore grew in every place where quails are; and also because the ancients rejected them as troublesome to the stomach on account of their excessive fatness, and as causing nausea and loathing. If anyone looks more carefully at Galen's work on simple medicines, where he teaches how to discern and easily recognise good and bad foods, he will understand that the quail, especially when roasted, is of good and pleasant smell and taste, and also of good nourishment. I should not omit this either: that God did not give the people of Israel, whom he loved most ardently, quails to satiety while they passed through those deserts, unless those birds were proved to be wholesome and healthful food. What more is there to say? That quails are digested well in the stomach and turned into the nourishment of the body is a sign of good temperament and substance. For in all foods, to produce good juice it is required only that they be well digested in the stomach; for whatever the stomach has digested passes on to the liver, and from there is sent on to nourish the parts.

units.la: Ubi interim hoc adnotandum a praui ventre succi eduliis, licet a nonnullis interdum probe probe- conficiantur, abstinendum esse, clam enim- ac sensim longa dierum serie pravum in venis bonum succum, humoresque exius coacervari, qui vel creat leuissima putredinis arrepta occasione febres succum- contumaces accendant, quotidiana docet experi-entia.
units.tr: Here meanwhile it should be noted that foods which produce bad juice should be avoided, even though some of them are sometimes well digested by certain people; for the bad juice gradually and secretly accumulates in the veins over a long series of days, and it mixes with the good juice and the humours. Daily experience shows that this bad juice, once any slight occasion of putrefaction seizes it, kindles fevers that resist the juices.

units.la: Verum, quia deleetissimorum ciborum- copia non semper, & ad voluntatem nobis suppe-tit, vnice studendum, vt, quicunque etiam & qualescunque fuerint, proba eorum fiat concoctio, tum etiam, quia nullum magis aptius adminiculum, ad sanitatem tuendam succorum bonitate inveniri potest, ut, quoad fieri potest, bona sint temperatura & substantia. Nam pravi succi cibi, licet concoquantur, si tamen vel minimam putredinis occasionem fuerint adepti, morbos excitant, quamvis Galenus 2. aphor. 28. cibum cum voluptate sumtum, licet deterior paulo sit, aut non modo, non manere deteriorem, sed quandoque reddi meliorem. Idem confirmat 2. de alimentorum facult. & in consilio pueri epileptici.
units.tr: But since the abundance of the most delightful foods is not always at hand for us, nor at our will, we must strive above all that, whatever foods they are and of whatever kind, they be well digested; then also, since no more apt aid ... for preserving health can be found than the goodness of the juices, that, as far as can be done, they have good temperament and substance. For foods that produce bad juice, even if they are digested, if they have obtained even the slightest occasion of putrefaction, cause diseases; although Galen, in the second book of his Aphorisms, aphorism 28, says that food taken with pleasure, although it may be somewhat worse, does not remain worse, but is sometimes made better. He confirms the same in the second book of On the Powers of Foods, and in his consultation on an epileptic boy.

units.la: Hoc coronidis loco addo, modice coturnicibus vesci posse, qui convulsionibus obnoxios se sentiunt: plane vero ab illarum esu abstinere, vanum est & insanum.
units.tr: As a closing note to this, I add that one may eat quail in moderation if one feels prone to convulsions; but to abstain from them altogether is vain and foolish.

units.la: Non me latet Psellum inter illa, qua boni succi non sunt, coturnicem etiam connumerasse, sed quoniam nullis idrationibus probat, non multum in prasens, testimonium ipsius magnificiendum existimo, ut qui turturem etiam damnarit, qua tamen a Galeno et aliis plurimum laudatur.
units.tr: I am not unaware that Psellus counted the quail among those foods that do not yield good juice, but since he proves this by no arguments, I do not think his testimony deserves much weight for now, especially as he also condemned the turtle-dove, which Galen and many others greatly praise.

units.la: Isti namque autores graeci, qui longe post Galeni seculum sunt secuti, quique Arabum doctrinam degustarunt, in plerisque a praecepto-re Galeno declinarunt, ut exempli gratia, in sectione vena, extrema manus venam magis eligentes, quam curuatura brachii, & in nonnullis aliis nunc non recensendis: fendis:quia tamen pauca admodum ipsi memo-ria mandarunt, quae Galenus ipse non scripserit aut animadverterit, magis etiam ipsorum monimenta imitanda sunt & amplexanda, ut quae Galeni Hippocratique doctrinam magis redoleant, quam barbarorum istorum. Galenus quidem 1. ad glaucon. lib. sectionis venae in manu facit mentionem, vbi passione existente in dextra locorum parte, a dextra manu aut crure eodem sanguinem mitti praecepit.
units.tr: For those Greek authors who followed long after Galen's age, and who tasted the doctrine of the Arabs, often departed from their teacher Galen: for example, in venesection they prefer a vein at the end of the hand to one at the bend of the arm, and in several other points that I will not list now. Yet since they committed to memory very few things that Galen himself did not write or observe, their writings are all the more to be imitated and embraced, as they savour more of Galen and Hippocrates than of those barbarians. Galen indeed, in his first book to Glaucon on venesection, mentions the hand, where, when the affliction lies in the right part of the body, he orders blood to be taken from the right hand or the right leg.

units.la: Verum sciendum Galenum ibi manus vocabulo synecdochicos pro brachio Graecorum mo-refuisse vsum, vt saepius confuenit alibi, & ipse etiam explicauit in libello de motu musculorum, manum in tres partes dividens: brachium, vlnam, & summam extremamque manum.
units.tr: But it should be known that Galen there used the word "hand" synecdochically for the Greek "arm", as he often does elsewhere. He himself explained this in his little book on the motion of the muscles, where he divides the hand into three parts: the arm, the forearm, and the extreme hand.

units.la: Rationes igitur, cur coturnix non sit laudabilis succi nutrimentique, quia a Pfello afferuntur nullae, aut certe exigua, coturnicem inter boni probique succi ac nutrimenti aues retinebimus tantisper, donec contrarium quis probauerit.
units.tr: Therefore, since the reasons Psellus gives for saying that the quail is not praiseworthy as a source of juice and nourishment are none, or certainly slight, we will for the time being keep the quail among the birds of good and sound juice and nourishment, until someone proves the contrary.

units.la: De aue alauda, caeterisque minutis.
units.tr: On the lark and other small birds.

units.la: Vulgatissimus alaudarum cibus est apud gentes quasdam, vbi etiam captura earum largissima praesertim hibernis mensibus, quo tempore obesae admodum spectantur.
units.tr: The most common food of larks is among certain peoples, where they are also caught in very large numbers, especially in the winter months, when they look quite fat.

units.la: Quibusdam in regionibus senas aut duodenas denas ligneo transfixas bacillo, cum saluia lardoque inaffant. Elixantur etiam, pipereque, garyophyllis, & id genus aliis condiuntur. Quin & piftorio opere includuntur madentes cinnamomi condimento. Verum locupletum & ditiorum ventriqueac gulæ obedientium is cibus est. Cristatæ, quas corydalos & galeritas à crista appellant, licet rarius in cibis expetantur, experimento tamen certo inter graues autores conuenit, elixas, aflasque in cibo sumtas-assiduè, colicos debellare dolores. Alii cineres galeritæ adustæ commendant ad eosdem vsus. Est in exemplis, quosdam corde huius in armilla aurea inclusò gestatoque à colicis doloribus ex antipathia quadam liberatos fuisse: quod ideo hic meminisse volui, quia morbo isto nunc nihil fere frequentius, tum quod Democritus de vna hac aue priuatim commemorarit.
units.tr: In some regions they thread six or twelve on a small wooden skewer and baste them with sage and lard. They are also boiled and seasoned with pepper, cloves and the like. Indeed they are enclosed in pastry with a cinnamon seasoning. But this food belongs to the wealthy and rich, who obey their belly and gullet. Crested larks, which they call corydali and galeritae from their crest, are less often sought as food; yet it is agreed by weighty authors, on certain experience, that when eaten boiled or roasted they constantly relieve colic pains. Others recommend the ashes of burnt galerita for the same uses. There is an example of some who wore the heart of this bird enclosed in a gold bracelet and were freed from colic pains by a certain antipathy. I wished to mention this here because nothing is now more frequent than this disease, and because Democritus singled out this one bird for particular mention.

units.la: Et Plinius lib. 30. cap. 7. de hac aue sic scribit, Coli vitium efficacissimè sanatur aue galerita asta & in cibo sumta: quidam in vase nouo cum plumis iubent exuri, conteriq; in cinerem, bibiqué ex aqua cochlearibus ternis per quatriduum: quidam cor eius adalligare femori, alii recens tepensq; dequo-rari. Hæc Plinius.
units.tr: And Pliny, book 30, chapter 7, writes thus about this bird: "The vice of the bowels is most effectively cured by the crested lark, roasted and eaten. Some order it to be burnt with its feathers in a new vessel and ground to ash, and drunk in water, three spoonfuls for four days; some tie its heart to the thigh; others have it swallowed fresh and warm." Thus Pliny.

units.la: Galeno quoque experimento compertam esse auis huius aduersus colicos dolores vim literis traditur, bonum praeterea largi-s-s(s) succum, coliqueque doloribus subuenire praeter connumeratos autores, etiam Dioscorides testatur, sed cuique experimenti via facilis est, praesertim qui isto morbo frequentius & acerbius conflictantur.
units.tr: It is recorded that Galen, by experience, found this bird to have power against colic pains. Besides the authors already listed, Dioscorides also testifies that it yields good, rich juice and helps colic pains. But the way of testing it is easy for anyone, especially for those who suffer from that disease more often and more severely.

units.la: De Lúscinia.
units.tr: On the Nightingale.

units.la: LVsciniam,fringillam, passerem, & in summa, minuta auitia persequi im-mensi & laboris esset & difficultatis, praesertim cum maior pars cantus magis, voluptatisque quam mensarum causa alatur, complures namque earum Latino, Graeco, Germanico, Italico, Gallicoque sermone dociles spectantur. Memorabilia pretia harum fuisse olim Romae, testatur impendiosa ista coena Æsopi, qui multas luscinias in patina sua apposuit. Non sumuntur in cibo ab elegantioribus, vt & caeterae pleraeque huius generis, quae caueis includuntur, cantu tantum oblectant.
