units.tr: To pursue the nightingale, the finch, the sparrow, and in short all the little songbirds would be an immense labour and difficulty, especially since most of them are kept for their song and pleasure rather than for the table. Many of them are seen to be taught to speak Latin, Greek, German, Italian and French. That these birds were once highly priced at Rome is attested by the extravagant dinner of Aesop, who served many nightingales on his platter. Among the more refined, they are not eaten, nor are most others of this kind that are shut up in cages and delight us only with their song.

units.la: Dignissima autem Luscinia miratu auis, inquit Plinius, lib.10. cap.28. cuius in tam paruo corpusculo tanta vox, tamque pertinax, tam paruulis in faucibus spiritus, vt in vna perfecta Musicae scientia modulatus edatur sonus, qui nunc
units.tr: The nightingale is a most remarkable bird to wonder at, says Pliny (book 10, chapter 28), whose tiny body produces such a great and persistent voice, with such a little throat, that in that one bird the perfect science of music is performed, a sound which now

units.la: continuo spiritu trahitur in longum, nunc variatur inflexo, nunc distingnitur concisio, copulatur intorto, promittitur reuocato, infuscatur ex inopinato: interdum & secum ipse murmurat, plenus, grauis, acutus, creber, extentus, vbi visum est, vibrans, summus, medius, imus: breuiterque omnia in paruulis tam faucibus, quae tot exquisitis tibiarum tormentis ars hominum excogitauit, vt non sit dubium hanc suauitatem praemonstratam efficaci auspicio cum in ore Stefichori cecinit infantis.
units.tr: is drawn out in one long unbroken breath, now varied by a turn, now broken into distinct pauses, now joined by a twisted run, now held back, now suddenly darkened; sometimes it even murmurs to itself, full, deep, sharp, rapid, sustained, trilling where it pleases, high, middle and low. In short, everything that human art has devised with so many exquisite pipe-tricks is found in that tiny throat, so that there is no doubt that this sweetness was foreshadowed by the powerful omen when the infant Stesichorus sang in the mouth of the nightingale.

units.la: Ac ne quis dubitet artis esse, plures singulis sunt cantus, nec iidem omnibus, sed fui cuique. Certant inter se, palamque animosa contentio est. Victa, morte saepe vitam finit, spiritu prius deficiente quam cantu. Meditantur aliae iuniores, versusque quos imitentur, accipiunt. Audit discipula intentione magna, & reddit vicibus cantum. Intelligitur emendatae correctio, & in docente quaedam reprehensio. Ergo feruorum illis pretia sunt, & quidem ampliora, quam quibus armigeri olim parabantur. Scio candidam sestertiis sex (hoc est, 1500 coronatis) aliquin, quod est prope inusitatum, veniisse, quae Agrippinae Claudii Caesaris coniugi dono daretur &c. Hactenus Plinius. Idem cap. 42. Caesares iuuenes habuisse lusciniras, sturnosque graeco & latino semone dociles, praetereaq; tereaq; meditantes in diem, & assiduè noua loquentes longiori etiam contextu. Docentur autem secreto, & vbi nulla alia vox misceatur, assidente qui crebrò dicat ea quę códita velit, ac cibis blandiente. Memorabile est & admirabile, de lusciniis duabus homi- num sermones imitatis Ratisbonæ in Comitiis, an. 1546. de quibus Gesnerus ipse sic scribit : Ego profecto nunquam Plinio nostro credidissem, multa adeo miranda de auicula hac scribenti, nisi ipse has bestiolas talia promentes & oculis vidisem, & auribus hisce audiuissem. Hæc Gesnerus. Placuit huc reponere in gratiam Lectoris Carmen T. Vespasiani Strozæ in philomelam, lib. 6. Erotičon: Æmula diuini suauissima carminis ales Quæ virides vmbras & loca sacra tenes. Mollibus & variis quæ tot discrimina vocum, Flexibus humana dulcius arte refers. Munere pro tali tibi quid philomela rependam? Premia quæ tanto digna labore putem? Dum vagus huc illuc hortis genialibus erro, Miror & artifici culta vireta manu, Hospitis officio tu protinus, vsa benigni, Fingis in aduentu carmina mille meo. Nec procul hinc densis canis abdita frodib^, alta Ilicis in ramo, populeisue comis, Verù hic Iuniperi insides mihi proxima trunco, Non imitabilibus me venerata modis.
units.tr: And lest anyone doubt that this is art, each bird has several songs, and not the same ones for all, but each its own. They compete with one another, and there is open, spirited rivalry. The loser often ends its life by dying, its breath failing before its song does. Younger birds practise, and take up verses to imitate. The pupil listens with great attention and gives back the song in turns. The correction of the improved phrase is recognised, and there is a certain rebuke in the teacher. Therefore these singers fetch prices, and indeed higher than those for which armed slaves were once bought. I know that a white nightingale was once sold for six sestertii (that is, 1500 crowns), which is almost unheard of, and was given as a gift to Agrippina, wife of the emperor Claudius, and so on. So far Pliny. The same author, chapter 42: the young Caesars had nightingales and starlings that were taught to speak Greek and Latin, and that practised daily and constantly spoke new things in longer passages too. They are taught in private, where no other voice is mixed in, with someone sitting beside them who often repeats the words they are to learn and coaxes them with food. It is a memorable and wonderful thing that at Regensburg, at the Diet of 1546, two nightingales imitated the speech of men, concerning which Gesner himself writes thus: "Truly, I would never have believed our Pliny, who wrote so many marvellous things about this little bird, had I not myself seen these little creatures producing such sounds with my own eyes and heard them with my own ears." So Gesner. It has pleased me to set down here, for the reader's delight, the poem of T. Vespasiano Strozza on the nightingale, from book 6 of the Erotica: O sweetest bird, rival of the divine song, you who dwell among the green shadows and sacred groves, with soft and varied notes, through so many changes of voice, you render things more sweetly than human art. What reward shall I, a nightingale, give you for such a gift? What prize do I think worthy of such labour? While I wander here and there through the pleasant gardens, marvelling at the groves cultivated by a skilled hand, you, kindly host, at once, at my arrival, make up a thousand songs. Hidden in the dense thickets, you sing from a high branch of holm oak or a poplar's crown, but here you sit on a juniper trunk near me, honoured by me with inimitable tunes.

units.la: Et licet hæc præstem tibi tam vicinus in umbra, Deq; tua suauis garrulitate loquar. Nil tamen ipsa times, nec gutturis ista canori, Sedulitas ideo dulce remittit opus. Grata sed in longum luco resonante querela Ducitur argutis continuata modis. Nos vero tali quoniam dignaris honore Dicimus in laudis hæc tibi pauca tuas. Humanas animum quæ mulcent cantibus aures, Cedere carminibus carmina cuncta tuis. Vive diu simili quoq; tui generata propago, Finiat extremum non nisi fera diem.
units.tr: And although you offer these things to me, so close in the shade, and I speak of your sweet chatter, yet you fear nothing, nor does your sweet-voiced throat relax its diligence in its work. Rather, a pleasing lament, continued in clear modulations, is carried on at length through the resounding grove. But since you deign to honour us with such a gift, we speak these few words in your praise: you, whose songs soothe the ears of men, all songs yield to your songs. Live long, offspring born like yourself, and may only a wild beast end your last day.

units.la: De luscinia quoque autor Philomelæ sic canit:
units.tr: The author also sings about the nightingale, under the name Philomela:

units.la: Scribere me voces animum Philomela coegit, Quæ canis cunctas exuperat volucres Dulcis amica veni noctis solatia præstans, Inter aues etenim nulla tibi similis. Tu Philomela potes vocum discrimina mille, Mille potes varios ipsa referre modos. Nam quamuis aliæ volucres modulamine tentent, Nulla potest modulis æquiualere tuis. Insuper est animum spatiis garrire diurnis, Tu cantare simul nocte diegi potes.
units.tr: Philomela, the bird that surpasses all the singing birds, has driven me to write of voices. Sweet friend, come, bringing comfort of the night; among birds there is none like you. You, Philomela, can render a thousand distinctions of voice, a thousand varied modes. For although other birds try with their modulation, none can match your melodies. Moreover, you can sing through the long days, and you can sing at night as well.

units.la: Extat & Philippi cuiusdam carmen inter Epigrammata græca de luscinia, quæ boream fugiés cum per mare volaret, delphini dorso suscepta sit vectaque, illumque natantem carminibus suis delectarit, vt ita hoc Arionis historiæ fidem faciat, qui cum Tarentho Corinthum rinthum peteret, ac videret sibi a nautis insidias struí, petiit ab iisdem, ut cythara paulum canere liceret, ad cuius sonum cum delphini conuenissent, excussit se supra vnum, atq; ita imminens periculum effugit. Seruius in Vergilii Eclog. 8.
units.tr: There is also a poem of a certain Philip, among the Greek Epigrams, about the nightingale, which, fleeing the north wind as it flew over the sea, was taken up and carried on the back of a dolphin, and delighted the swimming dolphin with its songs. Thus it lends credibility to the story of Arion, who, when he was making from Tarentum to Corinth and saw that the sailors were plotting against him, asked them to allow him to play a little on the lyre; when the dolphins gathered at its sound, he threw himself upon one of them and so escaped the impending peril. Servius, on Vergil's Eclogue 8.

units.la: De passeribus.
units.tr: On sparrows.

units.la: Passeris nomen licet ad omnes fere aues minutas extendatur, priuatim tamen certam significat speciem, vt Graecis ςρηϑος, quod sc. cum furore quodam ad libidinem feratur, vnde hominem salacem, & supra modum libidinosum ςρηϑον dicimus, & quae stridunt potius quam canunt, ςρηϑιζειν graece dicuntur, ex passerum voce. Memoranda autem falacitatis & libidinis sunt passeres, & propterea vita breuissima: ob quam etiam causam Mauritanorum medicina cibis in totum abdicandos eos censuit: Venerem in cibatu sumti excitant, unde mariti in venerem pigri solent id genus auitis crebro & large mandere.
units.tr: Although the name sparrow is extended to almost all small birds, it properly denotes one particular species. The Greeks call it στρῆθος [strēthos], because it is driven with a certain frenzy towards lust. Hence we call a lecherous man, and one excessively lustful, a στρῆθος [strēthos]. Those birds that screech rather than sing are said in Greek to στρηθίζειν [strēthizein], from the voice of sparrows. Sparrows are notable for their lechery and lust, and for that reason their life is very short. For this reason the Mauritanian physicians judged that they should be avoided altogether as food: when eaten they stir up lust, so that husbands who are sluggish in love are accustomed to eat this kind of bird often and in large quantities.

units.la: Galenus natura peritissimus Pyrgitas, id est, eos qui in turribus habitant, paruos item merularum carnibus habere carnes proximas, praeipue autumno esse commendabilissimas asserit, quoniam per messes & vindemias mire pinguescunt, succis acquirunt probitatem. Qui propterea in cibis ius abstinent, quod temperatura sint vulgi iudicio, calidioris & siccioris, nimis superstitiose vita prorogandae cupidi sunt atque solliciti, vulgi se opinionibus magis quam rationi subiicientes. Passerculi minimi troglodytae dicti, sapes iuxta ac muros victu quaeritantes, miram, Aetio teste, contra calculos renum & vesicae vim habere dicuntur a natura. Sale conditi seuantur. Porro cinerem passerum iuniorum sarmentis crematorum ex aceto infricatum aurium dolores minuere Plinius testis est, cap. 3. lib. 30. vbi quoque idem laudatur passerum fimus cum oleo calfacto infusus, &c. Qui renum vel vesicae calculo conflictantur, passeres & motacillas in cibos assumere frequentius debent, modo assas, modo elixas cum iusculo, adiectis anisi & foeniculi feminibus, vel etiam petroselino.
units.tr: Galen, most skilled in natural science, says that the sparrows called pyrgitae (that is, those that live in towers), and likewise the small birds closest to them in flesh, the blackbirds, are most commendable especially in autumn, since they grow wonderfully fat during the harvests and vintages and gain goodness from their juices. Those who therefore abstain from these foods because they are judged by popular opinion to be of hotter and drier temperament are too superstitiously eager and anxious to prolong life, subjecting themselves more to popular opinions than to reason. The very small sparrows called troglodytes, which seek their food both among the bushes and along the walls, are said by Aëtius to have a wonderful power by nature against stones of the kidneys and bladder. They are preserved by salting. Moreover, Pliny bears witness that the ash of young sparrows burned in vine-twigs and rubbed in with vinegar lessens pains of the ears (book 30, chapter 3), where the same author also praises sparrow dung infused in warmed oil, and so on. Those troubled by a stone of the kidneys or bladder ought more often to take sparrows and wagtails as food, sometimes roasted, sometimes boiled with broth, with seeds of anise and fennel added, or even parsley.

units.la: De phasianis.
units.tr: On pheasants.

units.la: APhasi amne, (ad cuius ostia phasianorum multitudinem cibi gratiaconuenire tradiderunt graeci) qui Colchorum arua facit ditissima, primum in Graeciam ab argonautis inuectas esse, testatur Martialis, Argiua primum fuit asportata carina, Ante mihi notum nil nisi Phasis erat.
units.tr: From the river Phasis, at whose mouths the Greeks report a great multitude of pheasants gathers for food, and which makes the fields of the Colchians very rich, the bird was first brought into Greece by the Argonauts, as Martial testifies: "The Argive keel first carried it away; before this, nothing was known to me but the Phasis."

units.la: Auis nobilissima, nunc Germanis quoque nota, Regum tantum & Magnatum mensas exorexornans atque opulentans. Galenus quan-tum ad coctionis nutriendiqúe vim spectat gallinis Phasianos pares, edendi verò suaui-tate facit superiores. Carnis enim succiqúe bonitatem, concoctionisque facilitatem prę-dicant omnes. Solonem ad Croesum Re-gem in regali solio, diademate & purpura auroque superbum, interrogantemq; nun-quid speciosius quicquam spectasset, dixisse fuerunt, phasianos & pauones, venustiores sibi videri, quoniam ornamento naturali de-coratæ, non asscititio fuco spectabiles essent. Plutarch.
units.tr: A most noble bird, now known also to the Germans, which adorns and enriches the tables of kings and magnates alone. Galen, as far as the power of digestion and nourishment is concerned, rates pheasants equal to hens, but superior in pleasantness of eating. For all men praise the goodness of their flesh and juice and the ease of their digestion. They say that Solon, when Croesus the king, sitting on his royal throne, proud in diadem, purple and gold, asked him whether he had ever seen anything more beautiful, replied that peacocks and pheasants seemed to him more lovely, since they were adorned with natural ornament and were conspicuous not by borrowed paint. Plutarch.

units.la: De cornice, pica, monedula, psyttaco, coruo, cæterisq; carniuoris & ad-uncis.
units.tr: On the crow, magpie, jackdaw, psittacus, raven, and other carnivorous and hooked birds.

units.la: OBstupescere fere solet nostra ætas, si quem miluum, aut picam, aut cornicem, aut ancipitrem edisse conspexerit, cum antiquis ciconiæ & Struthiocameli auium grandissimæ, peneq; bestiarum feri-niq; generis in delitiis fuerint. Eduntur psit-taci ab incolis nouæ Indiæ, nam apud eos vo-lant gregatim. Et certum est, monstrifica animalia quædam, hominis gulam euadere non posse. Nam quis non admiretur admira-bilem aquatilium, vt balenarum, delphino-rum, rum, vitulorum marinorum, canum, &c. in recentibus vsum?
units.tr: Our age is usually astonished if it sees anyone eating a kite, or a magpie, or a crow, or a hawk, although among the ancients storks and ostriches, the largest of birds, and almost of the wild and beastly kind, were delicacies. Parrots are eaten by the inhabitants of New India, for among them they fly in flocks. And it is certain that some monstrous animals cannot escape the gullet of man. For who would not marvel at the admirable use of aquatic creatures in fresh form, such as whales, dolphins, sea calves, sea dogs, and so on?

units.la: Cornices coloris ex cinereo albicantis à non paucis septentrionis gentibus mandun-tur, frigoribus enim pinguescunt, & gratissimi in cibo sunt, nutrimentum nam q; firmum præbent, & non facile fluens. Quidam tostas parum cum brassica coquunt eodem modo quo palumbes. Sunt omniuorae, vescuntur enim carnae, nucibus, pomis, quin & in littoribus animalia ab vnda electa, petunt. Carnes earum in morbis diuturnis esse vtilissimas, clari quidam auctores tradiderunt, Plin. lib. 30. cap. 11. Quidam, vt inauspicatae sunt garrulitatis, ita & inauspicati alimenti esse volunt, sed nulla probabili ratione. Potro prodigiosam huic aui viuacitatem tribuunt. Hesiodus, qui primus de spatiis vitae longissimis quaedam prodidit, multaque de hominum aeuo retulit, cornici nouem noctras attribuit aetates, quadruplum eius ceruis, id triplicatum coruis, sed fabulosè magis quàm verè, vt nouem videatur accipiendum pro multis per synecdoch. quasi sit πολυγηρας, vt interpretatur Theon. Centum autem viuit iuxta Aegyptiorum morem computatis annis, annus Aegyptiacus verò constat quatuor visitatis & communibus. Verum de vera & certa aetate adhuc inter autores non conuenit. Hoc adnotasse non inconueniens hic est, cornu-
units.tr: The crows of an ashen, whitish colour are eaten by not a few northern peoples, for they grow fat with the cold, are most pleasant to eat, and provide firm nourishment that does not easily flow away. Some cook them lightly roasted with cabbage, in the same way as wood pigeons. They are omnivorous, for they feed on flesh, nuts and fruits, and even seek out creatures cast up by the waves on the shores. Certain famous authors have handed down that their flesh is most useful in long-lasting diseases (Pliny, book 30, chapter 11). Some hold that, as the bird is of ill omen for its chattering, so too is its flesh of ill omen as food, but on no probable ground. Moreover, they attribute to this bird a prodigious vitality. Hesiod, who first set forth something about the longest spans of life and related much concerning the age of men, assigned nine ages to the crow, four times that to the stag, and three times that again to the raven; but this is more fabulous than true, so that "nine" must be understood as "many" by synecdoche, as if it were πολυγηρας [polygēras], "many-aged", as Theon interprets it. Moreover, it lives a hundred years if the years are reckoned by the Egyptian custom, and an Egyptian year consists of four ordinary seasons. But authors have not yet agreed on the true and certain age. It is not out of place to note here that the crow...

units.la: NB. Optimè nutrimentum quod non facile diffluit.
units.tr: NB. The best nourishment is that which does not easily dissolve away.

units.la: Natura comicum. cornices temperamenti esse firmioris & ficiotis, obque id longæuas, gaudereque pluriū thuris frigidis atq; humectantib». Tempestates præsentiunt, vt & corui, quod Virgilius expressit carmine suo; Tum cornix plena pluuiam voce improba vocet, Et sola in sicca secum spatiatur arena.
units.tr: The nature of the crow: crows are of a firmer and drier temperament, and for that reason long-lived, and they delight more in cold and moist places. They foretell storms, as do ravens, which Virgil expressed in his poem: "Then the crow, full of rain, calls with a shameless voice, and alone walks about in the dry sand."

units.la: Et Horatius 3. carm. Ante sequam stantes repetit paludes, Imbrium diuina (præscia) auis (cornix) imminentium;
units.tr: And Horace, Odes book 3: "Standing before the stream, it seeks the marshes again: the divine (far-seeing) bird, the crow, of the coming showers."

units.la: Nec non Lucretius; Mutant cum tempestatibus vnā; Raucisonos cantus cornicum secla vetursta Coruorumq; greges, vbi aquā dicuntur stimbrā Poscere, & interdum ventos aurasq; vocare.
units.tr: And Lucretius likewise: "They change along with the weather: the raucous songs of crows and the flocks of ravens of old ages, which are said to demand water and to summon the winds and breezes."

units.la: Nec præterea eundum, in pluuiarum denuntiatione cornicem contra naturam suam cro- & corui citare voce crassa & rauca, coruos verò non in pluuiis rauca voce, sed purissima contra naturam denunciatam, non solitarios, sed plures, pluuiæ dare and qua signum. voce v-
units.tr: Nor should it be passed over that in foretelling rain the crow, contrary to its nature, cries with a thick and hoarse voice, whereas ravens do not cry hoarsely in rain but with a very pure voice; and contrary to the announced nature, they cry out not singly but in several, as a sign of rain.

units.la: Ad extremum carnes earum aeriæ pestis anitur tempore conferre plurimum creditur, quia Carnes venenis putredinique obsistunt, qualitate coruorū tum manifesta, tum etiam antipathetica venena Manifesta est in sicco, & ad frigiditatem ver- aduer- gente temperamento tale enim putredinem fantur. prohibet. Galenus & Philosophi ac Medici omnes.
units.tr: Finally, their flesh is believed to contribute much at a time of aerial pestilence, because meat resists poisons and putrefaction. The quality of the raven is both manifest and also antipathetic to poisons: manifest in its dryness, and in a temperament tending towards coldness, for such a temperament prevents putrefaction. So say Galen and all philosophers and physicians.

units.la: Bb
units.tr: Bb

units.la: Experientiæ quoque testimonium hîc illustre est in vento Borea natură frigido & sicco,quo omnia quàm diutissimè imputria durant. Sic carnes & alia, quæcunque aseruari ab hominibus assólent, sale, muria, aceto, vel alio quopiam ex iis, quæ siccandi naturam habent, commodè præparantur. Galenus 1. de temper. & passim alibi. Calida autem & humida facilimè putrescere, nisi refrigerari ac exiccari contigerit, idé 2. de febr. differentiis fusius explicat. Qua de causa etiam Hippocrates siccitates imbribus salubriores multo existere non sine ratione scripsit 3. lib. aphor. 15. In siccitatibus enim superfluæ humiditates dissoluuntur & absorbentur, perimbres autem in corpore collectæ putresiunt, nisi quis singulis diebus collectas exercitiis expurget, vel purgantib* pharmacis exturbet, vel etiam per balnea euacuet, vbi tamen diætæ & consuetudinis ratio, commoda ac incommoda exactè cognoscenda sunt.
units.tr: Experience also gives illustrious testimony in the north wind, which is cold and dry by nature, and in which all things last longest without rotting. Thus meats and other things that men customarily keep are suitably prepared with salt, brine, vinegar, or some other of those things that have a drying nature. Galen, On the Temperaments, book 1, and passim elsewhere. Moreover, hot and moist things putrefy most easily, unless they happen to be cooled and dried, which he explains more fully in his book On the Differences of Fevers, book 2. For this reason Hippocrates also wrote, not without reason, that dry seasons are much more healthful than rainy ones (Aphorisms, book 3, aphorism 15). For in dry seasons superfluous humours are dissolved and absorbed, but rains collected in the body putrefy, unless someone purges them daily by exercise, or drives them out with purgative drugs, or evacuates them through baths; but here the account of diet and habit, with their advantages and disadvantages, must be exactly known.

units.la: Corui cibis omninò abdicantur ob pabulum, quod magna ex parte ex hominum, aliorumque animantium cadaueribus assumunt: si quis tamen horum esui sensim assueuerit, comperiet, solidi eos esse & firmi nutrimenti, licet non ita suauis sint succi. Sed quid tum? quasi omne, quod gustui ac palato suaue est ac gratum, protinus etiam nutriendi vim
units.tr: Crows are wholly excluded from food on account of their diet, which they take in large part from the corpses of men and other animals. If anyone, however, gradually grows accustomed to eating them, he will find them solid and of firm nourishment, although their juice is not so pleasant. But what then? As if whatever is sweet and pleasing to the taste and palate at once also has the power to nourish?

units.la: * Vide. vim habeat? Non certè, si quippiam est boni succi, sequitur, quod idem sit bonus cibus, qui plura desiderat, vt supra demonstratum est: In coruo quædam sunt partes, quæ sum- tæ bonum alimentum præbent, iis præsertim partibus, quæ substantiæ quadam familiaritate cum illis concordant, licet eæ non sint adeò probi succi, quod forsan aliquibus vi- debitur paradoxon. Nec abs re: quia in- quiunt, si res quædam sit boni succi, sequitur, quod sit etiam bonus cibus: falsum autem id esse, inque nutritionis operæ ac mysterio rem aliter longè se habere ex hactenus dictis facile quis intellexerit.
units.tr: * See. Certainly not. If something has good juice, it does not follow that it is good food, which is more than is demanded by what was shown above. In the crow there are certain parts which, when taken, give good nourishment, especially those parts that agree with our substance by some natural affinity, even though they are not of so good a juice. This may perhaps seem a paradox to some, and yet not without reason: for, they say, if a thing has good juice, it follows that it is also good food. But that this is false, and that the matter stands quite differently in the work and mystery of nutrition, anyone may easily understand from what has been said so far.

units.la: Cibi boni virtus est esse bene alterabilem ad coctionem, ab virtute instrumentis, quibus coctionis munus est à natura demandatum: facile coctibilem, totâ substantia nobis amicum & familiarem, facile denique assimilari, cumque corpore quod nutritur, naturæ beneficio coalescere seu coadunari aptum.
units.tr: The virtue of good food is that it is readily alterable for digestion by virtue of the organs to which nature has assigned the task of concoction; that it is easily digestible; that it is wholly friendly and familiar to us in its substance; and, in short, that it is easily assimilated and fit to be united and joined, by nature's benefit, with the body it nourishes.

units.la: In coruis, & id genus aliis quibusdam cariorum niuoris aduncisq; auibus quasdam esse partes, quæ substantiæ occulta quadam familiaritate cum corporis nostri certis partibus cō- spirent, inque cibis sumtæ eas nutriant, visq; bra nobis assimilentur, si quis negauerit, is in toto anti-pathias & sympathias mysterio plane cæcutit, alimentorumque ac ciborum naturam via.
units.tr: In ravens, and in other kinds of birds with black plumage and hooked beaks, some parts have a hidden familiarity of substance with certain parts of our body, so that when eaten they nourish those parts and are assimilated to our strength. Whoever denies this is completely blind in the whole mystery of antipathies and sympathies, and has too little knowledge of the nature and power of foods and aliments.

units.la: Bb viresque parum habet cognitas. Non e- nim intelligunt, coctionem fieri ab ea sub-stantia, cum qua inest similitudo, non à solis elementorum qualitatibus. Simile enim nu-trit similiter, eodemque nutritur, cor corde, e-parepate, pulmo pulmone, &c. Quapropter non simpliciter verum est, quod Plutarchus aliorum Philosophorum opinioni reclamat, prodens, animalia stomacho & calore valen-tia serpentes & scorpiones digerere posse. Nam struthiocamelus non digerit ferrum solius caloris ventriculi ratione, sed quia in-ter hunc & illud inest, vel potius intercedit substantia quaedam latens & abdita similitu-do. Quod si solo calore concoctio absol-ueretur, leo, struthione longe calidior, aurū, ferrum, & aes quoque digeret, quae quam-uis ignis calore sint inexpugnabilia, struthio-nes tamen ex his conflata numismata deglu-tire & concoquere tam experientia clarum est, vt in horto ducis Ferrariae id se vidisse Lā-gius in Epistolis aperte testetur. Quin & mu-res, quia metallorum scobem adeo appe-tunt, metalla concoquere, iisque nutriri ve-risimile est: Et Theophrastus in Syaro In-sula, expulsis incolis, ferrum arrosisse eos tradit, quos etiam arrosis Lauinii argenteis clypeis Marsicū portendisse bellū, magnāq; ad chalybas, in ferrariis officinis fecisse ia-quam.
units.tr: For they do not understand that digestion is effected by a substance with which there is likeness, not by the qualities of the elements alone. Like nourishes like in a like manner, and is nourished by it: heart by heart, liver by liver, lung by lung, and so on. Therefore it is not simply true what Plutarch says, against the opinion of other philosophers, when he reports that animals with a strong stomach and heat can digest serpents and scorpions. For the ostrich does not digest iron by the heat of the stomach alone, but because some hidden and concealed likeness lies, or rather intervenes, between the one and the other. If digestion were completed by heat alone, the lion, far hotter than the ostrich, would also digest gold, iron and bronze; yet these, though invulnerable to the heat of fire, are swallowed and digested by ostriches, when they are melted into coins. Experience makes this so clear that Lagus openly testifies in his Letters that he saw it in the garden of the Duke of Ferrara. Indeed, mice, because they so eagerly seek the filings of metals, probably digest metals and are nourished by them. And Theophrastus relates that on the island of Syaros, when the inhabitants were driven out, they gnawed iron; and that those who gnawed the silver shields of Lavinium foretold the Marsian war; and that a great deal of iron was made to drip into the forges of the smiths.

units.la: {y} calorībus ... sensum: text partly illegible. {a}turam, constat ex Plinio lib. I cap. 37. Sed quis haec solo calore, quae vix igne domari possunt, in corporibus animalium confici posse putabit? Vix id, opinor, quispiam crediderit, nisi congenitae totius membrorum subsistantiae coquendi istam virtutem ac proprietatem attribuerit.
units.tr: {y} ... (text partly illegible) ... It is established from Pliny, book 1, chapter 37. But who would think that these things, which can hardly be subdued by fire, can be digested in the bodies of animals by heat alone? I think hardly anyone would believe it, unless he attributed this power and property of digesting to the innate substance of all the members.

units.la: Verum, vt ad coruos nostros reuerta- mur, sciendum, carnes eorum mirè conducere iis, qui naturâ temperamentum compaginemque corporis habent laxiorem, hoc est, minus solidam firmamque ac compactam, hu- midumque radicale nimis fluxile: obsuc- cum inquam increscantem ac consolidan- tem, qui coruorum carnibus inest, prodest coruis vesci, iis, qui se naturâ sentiunt minus vegetos, viriumque dissolutarum. Unde eui- dentissimè vitae longioris breuiorisque causam innotescere diligens lector facilè per- spexerit.
units.tr: But, to return to our ravens: it should be known that their flesh is remarkably beneficial to those who by nature have a looser constitution and build of body, that is, a body less solid, firm and compact, and a radical moisture too liquid. For the dark, growing and consolidating substance that is in raven flesh benefits those who feel by nature that they are less vigorous and have dissolved strength. From this the diligent reader will easily discern the most evident cause of a longer or shorter life.

units.la: Assi autem in cibis praestant elixis, & hieme quoque quam aestate salubriores sunt, per aestatem enim in autumnum morbo cor- pos conflictari Plinius autor est, lib. 29, cap. 3.
units.tr: Roasted ravens are better as food than boiled, and they are also healthier in winter than in summer, for Pliny is the authority that in summer the body is afflicted by disease until autumn (book 29, chapter 3).

units.la: Caeterum insufpicatissimos eos esse omnium consensu traditur, sed tum maximè cum vocem glutiunt, velut strangulati, tunc enim pessima eorum significatio est. De coruorum intelligentia mira refert Plinius lib.10. cap.43. Soli enim in auspiciis videntur habere intellectum significationum suarum, nam cum Medię hospites occisi sunt, omnes, è Peloponneso & Attica regione volauerunt. Ab ortu accinentes clara voce præsentem felicitatem, ab occasu vero vel læua clamantes, exitium denunciasse observatum est. Hominum voces sermonemq; imitantur. Augusto ex Actiaca victoria redeunti occurrit inter gratulantes quidam tenens coruum, quem instituerat proferre hæc verba, aue Cæsar Victor Imperator. Miratus Cæsar tam officiosam auem viginti millibus eam emit, hoc est, quingentis aureis solatis, multasque præterea similes comparauit. Quo exemplo commotus pauper sutor, instituere ipse quoque aggressus est coruum ad parem salutationem, sed impendio exhaustus ad auem non respondentem de cere solebat, opera & impensa periit. Coepit tamen aliquando coruus optatam salutationem exprimere, ac forte audita, dum transiret Cæsar, respondisset, satis taliū salutatorū habeo domi, superfuit coruo memoria, ut & illa, quibus Dominū querente solebat audire, verba subiungerer, opera & impensa periit: ad quod subridens Cæsar emi auem iussit, quanti nullam aliam emerat. Perotus. Vide Macrob. lib.2. Saturn.cap.4.
units.tr: Moreover, by universal agreement they are said to be most suspicious birds, but chiefly when they gulp down their voice, as if strangled; for then their omen is at its worst. Pliny, book 10, chapter 43, reports the remarkable intelligence of ravens. For they alone seem to have understanding of the meaning of their omens: when the Median guests were killed, all the ravens flew out from the Peloponnese and the region of Attica. It was observed that, singing from the east, they announced present happiness with a clear voice, and that, crying from the west or on the left, they announced ruin. They imitate human voices and speech. When Augustus was returning from the Actian victory, among the people congratulating him there met him a certain man holding a raven that he had trained to utter these words: "Hail, Caesar, victorious commander." Caesar, amazed at so dutiful a bird, bought it for twenty thousand sesterces, that is, five hundred gold solidi, and acquired many other similar ones besides. Moved by this example, a poor cobbler also set about training a raven to give a similar greeting; but, drained by the expense, and because the bird did not answer, he lost both his labour and his money, and was used to complain about it. Yet at last the raven began to utter the desired greeting, and by chance, when Caesar was passing by, it heard and answered, "I have enough greeters of that kind at home." The raven still had the memory to add also those words which it used to hear from its master complaining, "I have lost my labour and my money." At this Caesar smiled and ordered the bird to be bought at whatever price he had paid for none other. (Perotti.) See Macrobius, book 2, Saturnalia, chapter 4.

units.la: Plinius
units.tr: Pliny.

units.la: {y} Coruus loquax quingentis aureis emptus.
units.tr: A chattering raven, bought for five hundred gold pieces.

units.la: Plinius loco citato refert, sutorem quendam coruum pullum religione sibi ab officinæ Domino commendatum educasse, maturequae sermoni assuefactum, omnibus matutinis euolasse in rostra, in forum versus Tiberium principem, dein Germanicum & Drusum Cæsares, nominatimque eos salutasse, moxtransiisse populum Romanum, postea ad tabernam remeasse plurimorum annorum, assiduo officio mirum. Hunc siue æmulat e incitatus manceps sutrinæ proximæ, liveiracundia subita, vt videri voluit, ab excrementis eius aspersa calceis maculâ, examinauit, tanta plebei consternatione, vt primo pulsus ex ea regione, mox & interemtus sit, funusque innumeris aliti celebratum exequiis, constratus lectus fuit super æthiopum duorum humeros, præcedente tibicine, & coronis omnium generum, ad rogum vsque, constructum dextrâ via Appia ad secundum lapidem in campo Rediculi appellato. Tanta fuit coruis gratia apud Pop. Romanum indignatione testata & conscientia.
units.tr: Pliny, in the place cited, relates that a certain cobbler had reared a young raven, which his shop-master had entrusted to him as a sacred charge; that, being accustomed early to speech, it used to fly out every morning to the rostra in the Forum, first greeting Tiberius, the emperor, then Germanicus and Drusus, the Caesars, by name; then it greeted the Roman people, and afterwards returned to the shop, year after year, a marvel for its constant duty. Then a neighbouring cobbler, either out of envy or from sudden anger, as he wished it to seem, having had his shoes spattered with its droppings, killed it. Such was the uproar of the common people that he was first driven out of that district and soon himself killed. The raven was honoured with countless birds at its funeral rites: a bier was carried on the shoulders of two Ethiopians, with a flute-player going before, and garlands of every kind, all the way to the pyre, built on the Appian Way at the second milestone, in the field called Rediculus. Such was the favour that ravens enjoyed with the Roman people, as shown by their indignation and their conscience.

units.la: Non prætereundum denique, quod Plinius l.10.cap.12. prodidit, grauidas, si ederint corvinum ovum per os partum reddere, atque in totum difficulter parere, & lib 8.c. 49. corvum, occiso chamæleonte, qui etiam victori nocet, lauro infestum virus extinguere. Hactenus de corvis.
units.tr: Finally, it should not be passed over what Pliny, book 10, chapter 12, reported: that pregnant women, if they eat a raven's egg, bring forth the child through the mouth and in general give birth with difficulty; and (book 8, chapter 49) that a raven, having killed a chameleon, which also harms the victor, extinguishes the poison by means of the laurel, which it hates. So much concerning ravens.

units.la: Coruini generis sunt graculi seu monedulæ, sic dicti quod gregatim volent, vel à sono oris, quasi garruli, sunt enim clamosi: vel vt alii putant à gerendo, quod jacta semi-na segetum legant, monedulæ vero à mone-ta, quasi monetulæ, solis enim his micam auri, argentique furacitatem inesse tradit Plinius lib. 10. cap. 29. Vnde Cicer. in orat. pro Flacc. non plus aurum tibi, quam mo-nedulæ committebatur. Insitionis tene-ræque inferendi emplastrationis causam & inuentionem monedulis tribui, condenti-bus femina in cauernarum thesauros, idem lib. 17. capit. 13. testis est. Quibusdam in locis habentur in cibatu, & tonstrinæ ibidem eas educant in caveis, docentque humanas exprimere voces. Mira autem his in vino lasciuia, à cuius potu evadunt loquaciores. Quidam existimant monedulas, vt & picas comitiali morbo tentari, quoniam plerunque velut extinctæ ex arborum tectorumque culminibus decidere in terram conspiciuntur, ob eamque causam à vulgo mensis etiam abdicantur.
units.tr: Jackdaws are of the raven kind; these are called graculi or monedulae. They are so called because they fly in flocks, or from the sound of their mouths, as if garrulous, for they are noisy; or, as others think, from carrying, because they gather the seeds sown in the crops; but monedulae are so called from money, as if little money-birds, for Pliny, book 10, chapter 29, reports that only these have a greed for crumbs of gold and silver. Hence Cicero, in the speech for Flaccus: "More gold was not entrusted to you than to jackdaws." That jackdaws are credited with the invention of grafting and of the plastering of the nest, and that they carry the seed into the treasure-stores of caves, the same author attests in book 17, chapter 13. In some places they are kept in cages and reared by barbers, and taught to imitate human voices. Their playfulness in wine is remarkable: from drinking it they become more talkative. Some think that jackdaws, like magpies, are afflicted with epilepsy, since they are often seen falling to the ground from the tops of trees and roofs as if dead; and for this reason they are also abhorred by the common people as ominous.

units.la: Linguam reliquis animantibus habet latiorem, vnde loquacissima & humanæ vocis magis æmula est. Expressior loquacitas certo generi picarum est, ait Plinius lib. 10. cap. 42. adamant verba quæ loquantur, nec dilcunt tantum, sed diligunt, medimeditantesque intra semet, cura atque cogitatione intentionem non occultant.
units.tr: Jackdaws have a broader tongue than other animals, whence they are very talkative and most imitative of the human voice. Pliny says, book 10, chapter 42, that a certain kind of magpie has a more distinct talkativeness: they love the words they speak, not only learn them, and, meditating on them within themselves, do not hide their attention, which is fixed by care and thought.

units.la: Constat etiam vietas difficultate verbi, ac nisi subinde eadem audiant, memoria falli, quaerentes mirum in modum hilarari, si interim audierint id verbum: nec vulgaris iis forma, quamvis non spectanda: sat illis decoris in specie sermonis humani est. Verum addiscere alias posse negant, quam, quae ex genere earum sunt, quae glandibus vescuntur, & interea facilius, quibus quinque sunt digiti in pedibus, ac ne eas quidem ipsas, nisi primis duobus vitae annis. Haec Plinius. Altus quoque earum insignis in eo cernitur, quod, cum diligentius, visum ab homine nidum sensere, ova alio transferant. Pulli mire in cibis a quibusdam expetuntur, magnaque cum voluptate manducantur, licet a nitidiorem splendidiorem quae vitam statutibus damnati, quos cibis minime abdicarent, si carnem eorum visui acuendo conducere, facilisque coctionis esse animaduertissent.
units.tr: It is also agreed that they are slow to learn a word, and that unless they hear the same thing again and again they forget it; and they rejoice wonderfully when they hear that word in the meantime. Their form is not common, though it is not to be prized; they have enough beauty in the appearance of human speech. But, Pliny says, they cannot learn any other things than those which belong to the kind of birds that feed on acorns, and even these only with more difficulty, and not at all, except in the first two years of life. Their notable habit is also seen in this: when they have perceived with careful watching that a man has seen their nest, they carry their eggs to another place. The young are eagerly sought as food by some and eaten with great pleasure, though those who condemned them to the bright and splendid life, whose flesh they would not at all refuse, have noticed that it sharpens the sight and is easy to digest.

units.la: Aduncas aves & carnivoras fere omnes, urbaniores atque liberaliores hominibus in cibos non admittunt, ut sunt aquilae, vultures, milvi, accipitres ambo, fringillarius & palumbari, multo inter se magnitudine differentes, & buteo, magnitudine miluum aequans, quem graeci aetalona vocant, solus enim.
units.tr: Hooked and almost all carnivorous birds, which the more refined and well-bred do not admit to their tables: eagles, vultures, kites, both kinds of hawk, the sparrowhawk and the woodpigeon-hawk, differing greatly in size from one another, and the buzzard, equal in size to the kite, which the Greeks call aetalon, since it alone...

units.la: Quana expicus facilius humana vocem a- mulentur?
units.tr: Which of them imitate the human voice more easily?

units.la: Picarum pulli viacuendo conferunt.
units.tr: The chicks of magpies help to sharpen the sight.

units.la: Aduncae carnivorae. enim omni tempore apparet, caeteri hiemè abeunt: triorchis etiam à testium numero dicitur, principatumque ei in auguriis Phoenonoë dedit: buteonem appellarunt Romani, familiaque ex eo cognominata, cum prosperò auspicio in ducis nauì sedisset. In mensarum autem honore hic fuisse inueniture, sicut & accipitrum pullos suaues admodum esse, pinguesque reddi Aristoteles testis est l. 9. hist. anim. Palumbarios quoq; accipitres cibis omnino abdicare inhumani & insipidi palati est, quod tamen lautiorum mensarum venia dictum volo. Plura autem eorum genera, quae ex auiditate distinguì possunt. Alii enim non nisi ex terra auerunt rapiunt, alii non nisi circa arbores volitantem, alii sedentem in sublimi, alii volantem in aperto: unde columbae nouere ex iis periculum, visque eo confidunt, vel subvolant, contra naturam ejus sibi auxiliantes. Caeterum non praetereundum, accipitres scalpendo lactucam, quae hieracium dicitur, succoque oculos tingendo obscuritatem, cum sensere, discutere. Et certissimi experimenti est, oculorum vitiis, hunc succum apprime mederi.
units.tr: ...it appears at all times, while the others leave in winter. The triorchis is also so named from the number of its testicles, and Phoenonoë gave it first place in augury. The Romans called the buzzard buteo, and a family took its surname from it, when a bird of good omen settled on the flagship of a commander. That it was also found at the tables of the rich is shown, as Aristotle testifies in book 9 of the History of Animals, by the fact that the young of hawks are very tender and grow fat. To reject the woodpigeon-hawks altogether as food is the mark of an inhuman and insipid palate, though I would say this with the indulgence of more refined tables. There are several kinds, which can be distinguished by their rapacity. Some seize prey only from the ground, others only while flying about trees, others while perched on high, others while flying in the open. Hence doves recognise danger from them and trust their own strength, or fly up beneath them, helping themselves against the hawk's nature. But it must not be passed over that hawks, when they perceive dimness in their eyes, scrape at lettuce, which is called hieracium, and moisten their eyes with its juice to dispel it. It is most certainly proven by experiment that this juice is especially good for defects of the eyes.

units.la: De Vulturis, inexplebilis scilicet edacitatis alitis pelle seu plumoso tegmine Lemnius l. 4. de occ. naturae miraculi scribit, foris admotum robur ventriculo debili afferre, co-
units.tr: Concerning the vulture: Lemnius, in book 4 of On the Hidden Miracles of Nature, writes that the skin, or feathered covering, of this bird, that insatiable glutton, applied externally, brings strength to a weak stomach, and helps digestion

units.la: Diffin-ctio accipitrum ex auiditate.
units.tr: The distinction of hawks according to their rapacity.

units.la: NB.
units.tr: N.B.

units.la: Vultur. coctionique adminiculari, cibique auidita-tem efficacius excitare, quam zinziber con-ditum. Est autem caeterarum pellium modo arte pellicea subigenda ac concussione co-plananda. Cum enim omnia haec auis, & quidem avide appetat, inoffenseque consu-mat, tegmini ejus ea est vis infusa, vt ventri-culum humanum roboret, naufeantiq; sto-macho vires apperendi concoquendiq; cibi conferat: qua de causa etiam carnes ejus ci- bo sumtas ventriculo debili, appetentiaeque dejectae ac poftratae prodesse, extra omnem dubitationem affirmo ex fympathetico in- fluxu & operatione. Plinius l.29.c.4. fcri- bit, cor hujus alitis habentes, tutos non fo-lum a serpentum impetu esse,sed etiam fe-rarum,latronumque insidiis & Regum ira.
units.tr: Vulture. ...and it stirs the appetite for food more effectively than preserved ginger. It is to be prepared, as with other skins, by the art of tanning and smoothed by beating. For since this bird eats all these things eagerly and devours them without harm, this power is infused into its covering: that it strengthens the human stomach and gives strength to a queasy stomach for taking in and digesting food. For this reason I affirm beyond all doubt that its flesh, eaten as food, benefits a weak stomach and an appetite that has been depressed and prostrated, by sympathetic influence and operation. Pliny, book 29, chapter 4, writes that those who have the heart of this bird are safe not only from the attack of serpents, but also from the snares of wild beasts and robbers, and from the anger of kings.

units.la: Sed haec Magiae Studiosis vlterius per-scrutanda relinquimus, parum enim ad no-ftrum institutum.
units.tr: But we leave these matters to be examined further by students of magic, since they bear little on our present purpose.

units.la: Ex noctreturn auibus vnum aflonum genus affert Ariftoteles corpulentia pingui, autumno quandoque apparens, ac vno tan-tum atque alrero die immorans,esui est val-deque probatur, perennes vero omnibusque anni temporibus apparentes esui non esse asseuerat ob carnis vitium, malum succum, coctionisque contumaciam. Pullinihilo-minus nocturnarum auium, a quibusdam non infalubriter appetuntur. Carnes no-ctua{*}ƈuarum membris paralyticis auxiliari compertum habetur, cerebrumque vino coctum capitis doloribus. Porro bubones funebres & maxime abominatos publicis præcipue auspiciis, defertaincolere, nec tantum desolata, sed dira etiam & inaccessa, nodis monstrum, nec cahtu aliquo vocales esse, sed gemitu potius, nemo fere est, qui non norit. De bubonis augurio historia memoratu dignissima est apud Nicolaum Clemangium Bajocensis Ecclesiae in Gallia olim Archidiaconum, qui Pisani concilii improbitate offensus, in quandam de conciliis disputationem incidit. Agens autem de concilio Romano, quod Johannes XXIIII. Pontifex, in Esquilino monte aede D. Martini celebrauit, sequens narrat prodigium. Convocauerat, inquit, ante 4. annos Romę Concilium, maxima quorundam impulsus contentione, Balthasar Cosla perfidissimus, nuper è Petri sede, quam turpissime foedabat, ejectus in quo paucissimis præsentibus, ex aliquibus, qui aderant, Italis & aulicis suis, sessiones aliquot tenuit de rebus superuacaneis, nihilq; ad ecclesiæ vtilitatem pertinentibus. Cum autem ante primam concilii congressionem pro invocatione Spiritus S. sacra de more fuisset facta, Patres assederunt; & Balthasar sublimi in loco præsedit, ecce dirus ac feralis bubo, funeris aut alterius calamitatis mitatis fere semper nuncius, è latebris pro-rumpens, voce sua illa horrifica, continuo aduolat, superque trabem templi mediam, oculis in Balthasarem intentis, astitit. Universis mirantibus, quod nocturna avis & lucifuga, in turbam diurna luce aduolasset, malumq; ex prodigio ominantibus, Balthasar, in quem fixa acie oculos intendebat, angi, sudare, atque intra semetipsum coepit astuare, & dimissis patribus, solutoque convento discesserit. Aliqui prodigium vertentes in risum, dicentes, specie bubonis in congregationem improborum advenisse Spiritum S. Secuta altera deinceps sessio, in quam eodem modo rursus bubo aduenit, versó semper in Balthasarem contuitu, qui majore pudore, quam prius perturbatus, avem ominosam clamoribus abigi & manuum supplosione terreri praecepit, sed illa non prius amota fuit, quam fustium ictibus pulsata in conspectu omnium examinis deciderit. Hic autem bubonis adventus augurio suo non caruit: nam & concilium cum dedecore Pontificis dissolutum, & Balthasar paulo post Constantiae exauctoratus est, Monheimiique in oppido Principis Palatini in vinculis fuit detentus. Refert Haithonus in libro de tartaris, Chaungium Can Imperatorem tartarorum victum ab hostibus interarbusta latitasse, inter quas, cum forte buboinsideret, victores dum perquirunt victos passim occultatos neminem latere putarunt, quasi avem illic minime mansura, si hominum quisquam adesset. Itaque factum est, ut silentio noctis secutae Imperator ad suos evaserit, & salutis suae causam exposuerit.
units.tr: Of nocturnal birds, Aristotle mentions one kind of owl, plump and fat, which appears sometimes in autumn and lingers only one or two days; it is eaten and is well esteemed. But he asserts that the owls which are present all year round, at every season, are not eaten, because of the poor quality of their flesh, their bad juice, and their stubbornness in digestion. Nevertheless, the young of nocturnal birds are eaten by some, not without benefit to health. The flesh of owls is held to help paralysed limbs, and the brain boiled in wine helps headaches. Further, that funereal owls, and especially those most abhorred, bring public omens above all, that they haunt deserted places, and not only deserted but also dreadful and inaccessible ones, a portent of knots, and that they are not vocal with any song but rather with a moan, almost everyone knows. A most memorable story about the owl's augury is found in Nicolas Clamanges, once archdeacon of the Church of Bayeux in France, who, offended by the wickedness of the Council of Pisa, fell into a discussion about councils. Speaking of the Roman council which Pope John XXIII held in the church of St Martin on the Esquiline hill, he relates the following portent. Four years earlier, he says, a council had been convened at Rome, driven by the great contention of certain men, by Balthasar Cossa, most perfidious, lately ejected from the seat of Peter, which he had most shamefully defiled. With very few present, among those who were there, Italians and his courtiers, he held several sessions on superfluous matters, nothing pertaining to the good of the Church. But before the first meeting of the council, when the sacred rite for invoking the Holy Spirit had been performed as usual, the Fathers took their seats, and Balthasar presided in a high place. Behold, a dire and deadly owl, almost always the messenger of death or of some other calamity, burst out of its hiding place with its horrid cry, flew straight in and stood above the middle beam of the church, its eyes fixed on Balthasar. While all marvelled that a nocturnal bird which shuns the light had flown into the crowd in daylight, and took it as an omen of evil, Balthasar, on whom it kept its gaze fixed, began to be troubled, to sweat, and to seethe inwardly; and dismissing the Fathers, the assembly was broken up and he departed. Some turned the portent into a joke, saying that the Holy Spirit had come to the gathering of the wicked in the form of an owl. Then a second session followed, into which the owl came again in the same way, always turning its gaze upon Balthasar, who, more disturbed than before and with greater shame, ordered the ominous bird to be driven off with shouts and frightened away by clapping of hands. But it was not removed until, struck by blows of clubs, it fell in the sight of all. Now this arrival of the owl did not lack its omen: for the council was dissolved with dishonour to the Pope, and shortly afterwards Balthasar was deposed at Constance and was held in chains at Monheim, in a town of the Count Palatine. Haithonus, in his book on the Tartars, reports that Chaungius Can, emperor of the Tartars, defeated by his enemies, hid among trees, among which, by chance, an owl was sitting. The victors, searching everywhere for the vanquished who were hidden, thought that no one lay concealed there, since the bird would certainly not have remained there had any man been present. And so it happened that in the silence of night the emperor escaped to his men and explained the cause of his safety.

units.la: A quo tempore Tartari bubonem seu avem felicem, auspicatam & sacram reverentur, plumasque ejus ceu amuletum & prosperitatis causam in capitibus gestant, ac felices se praedicant, quicunque eas habere possunt.
units.tr: From that time the Tartars revere the owl as a lucky, auspicious and sacred bird. They wear its feathers on their heads as an amulet and a cause of prosperity, and count themselves fortunate whoever is able to have them.

units.la: De grandioribus alitibus.
units.tr: On the larger birds.

units.la: AVium grandissimi & pene bestiarum generis sunt Struthocameli. In Africa & Aethiopia altitudinem equitis insidentis equo exceedunt, celeritate vincunt, nec tamen sunt volucres, nec a terra tolluntur. Xenophon expeditionis Cyri lib. 1. tradit in Arabia repertos Struthocamelos, quos nemo ex toto exercitu capere potuerit. Athenaeus Arabicos Regum Persarum mensis epulis adhiberi solitos scripsit. Galenus quoque in ciborum censu eos reposuit, horum alas deteriores caterarum volucrum alis non esse promittit, carnes tamen excrementis abundare refertas concoctioneque esse pertinaces. Concoquendi sine delectu devoratas miram in iis naturae est, nam ipsum ferrum perfi-cere certo dicuntur, quod absurde & inepte quidam ventriculi calori vehementiori crassi-tudinique ejus attribuunt, ut supra quoque anno-tatum est. Ex ovis ipsorum caput infantis mag-nitudine referentibus olim vasa siebant potoria ex transfuerso secta, teste Plin. l. 10. cap. 1. Mira vero sit id idem autor est in tanta enim corporis altitudine, cum colla frutice occulta-verint, toto se latere corpore exist imant.
units.tr: The largest of birds, and almost of the beasts, are the ostriches (struthocameli). In Africa and Ethiopia they stand taller than a horseman sitting on his horse, and they outrun it. Yet they are not birds, and they cannot be lifted from the ground. Xenophon, in the first book of the Expedition of Cyrus, reports that ostriches were found in Arabia, and that no one in the whole army could catch one. Athenaeus wrote that Arabian ostriches were customarily served at the feasts of the kings of Persia. Galen too placed them among foods, and he says that their wings are inferior to the wings of other birds, while their flesh is full of excrement and hard to digest. Digesting whatever they have swallowed without discrimination is a marvel of their nature, for they are said to digest iron itself. Some foolishly and absurdly attribute this to the greater heat and thickness of their stomach, as has been noted above. Their eggs, which are as large as a child's head, were once cut across and made into drinking vessels, according to Pliny, book 10, chapter 1. That this is wondrous, the same author says: for with such a great height of body, when they have hidden their necks in the bushes, they imagine that their whole body is hidden.

units.la: De Gruibus.
units.tr: On cranes.

units.la: Altitudine carnisque duritie succe-dunt, frugilegae grues, Augusti Prin-cipatu in cibis gratae, teste Nepote Cornelio: Plinii vero aetate inter primas expetebantur: hodie hibernos cibos nobi-litant, & praesertim in claris amplisque fa-miliis.
units.tr: Next in height and toughness of flesh come the grain-gleaning cranes, which were pleasing as food under the principate of Augustus, according to Cornelius Nepos. In Pliny's time they were sought after among the finest dishes. Today they lend distinction to winter food, especially in famous and wealthy families.

units.la: Inastantur autem, garyophyllisq; per-fodiuntur & pipere, solidaeque postea appo-nuntur. Quibusdam repositae & infrigi-datae placent magis quam calentes, & sic pa-ratae durant in multos dies.
units.tr: They are basted, pierced with cloves and pepper, and then served whole. Some people prefer them cold and chilled rather than hot, and so prepared they keep for many days.

units.la: Caeterum, quia fibrosae ac praedurae carnes ipsarum sunt, tenerescere eas sinunt tes carne pendendo, si scil. grave aliquod pondus pe-quarati-dibus alligetur. Inuenitur quoque aues pŗ-duras teneritudinem adipisci, si e ficu pen-deant, deant, tantam enim arbori huic inesse vim dicunt. Minores grues vipiones appellatæ in maximo quondam mensarum honore fuerunt Balearicis. Extremos fluuii Gangis accolas spithamæos, pygmæos, ternos spithamas longitudine, hoc est, ternos dodrantes non excedentes à gruibus infestari Homerus prodidit. Quin & Plinius l.4.c.11. ex Gerania, Thraciæ regione, eos ab illis fugatos, autor est.
units.tr: Moreover, since their flesh is fibrous and very hard, they make it tender by hanging the bird by its feet with some heavy weight attached. It is also found that birds become tender if they hang from a fig tree, for they say this tree has such a power. The smaller cranes, called vipiones, were once in the greatest esteem at Balearic tables. Homer reported that the Pygmies, the people living on the far banks of the river Ganges, who are three spans tall, that is, not exceeding three dodrantes (quarter-feet) in length, are harassed by the cranes. Indeed, Pliny, book 4, chapter 11, is the authority that they were driven off by them from Gerania, a region of Thrace.

units.la: Cæterum de volatu & migratione gruum mira sunt, quæ apud Aristot. Æliānum, Plinium, Plutarchum, Isidorum, & Gillium scripta reperiuntur. Thraciam in quas-cuntur, vt patriam amore prosequuntur, in eaque æstiuo tempore patriæ sedis amore & studio captæ, ætatem ducunt, medio autumno, salutis ergo frigoris vim non sustinentes, tanquam cœli mutationem temporumque varietatem scientia & cognitione, comprehenderint, frequentes in Ægyptum, Libyam ac Æthiopiam proficiscuntur. Septembri autem discedere incipiunt, ac more Regis Persarum æstiua & hiberna conficiunt. Inducias autem habet Pygmæorum gens abscessu gruum cum iis dimicantium. Cum verò jam proximum est, vt auolent hiberni, circa Nilum victus desiderio incensi, grus quæ inter alias extremo ætatis tempore affectafuerit, ter circa vniuersum gregem volans,
units.tr: Concerning the flight and migration of cranes there are marvellous things, which are found written by Aristotle, Aelian, Pliny, Plutarch, Isidore and Gellius. They are said to seek Thrace, and to pursue it as their homeland with love. There, in summer, seized by love and zeal for their native seat, they spend their life. In mid-autumn, for the sake of safety, not enduring the force of the cold, as if they had grasped by knowledge and understanding the change of the sky and the variety of the seasons, they set out in great numbers for Egypt, Libya and Ethiopia. They begin to depart in September, and, like the kings of the Persians, they make their summer and winter residences. The race of Pygmies has a truce when the cranes leave, since they fight with them. When it is now near the time for the wintering birds to fly away, burning with a desire for food around the Nile, the crane which among the others has grown old at the end of its life flies three times around the whole flock,

units.la: Notatu digna de gruum volatu. Volans, supremum vitæ diem conficit: Hanc primo sepultura reliquæ afficiunt, rectaque deinde in Ægyptum iter faciunt, neq; imensa pelagi spatia alarum robore transmittentes. vsquam interquiescunt: Volant autem alte, vt procul possint prospicere, & si nubes tempestatemq; viderint, conferunt se in terram humiq; quiescunt. Volantes triangăli figurā formant; vt facilius hac forma aerem aduersum secent, & extriquetra figura quandoq; edunt sexangulum. Proue&ctiores ætate in primum ordinem volando collocant, ne se fatigent nimium sequendo, si juniores præcederent, clamorem etiam edunt, ne seperentur nimium ab aliis. Siq; quam sensere defessam, aliæ duæ utrinq; eam alis subleuant, aut etiam super dorsis aut pedibus ferunt; retrorsum enim sereno cælo pedes solent extendere, secundos ventos & retro flantes obseruare norunt. Ducem habet etiam, & eos qui clamant dispositos in extremo agmine, vt vox percipi possit. Cū confiltūt, cæterę dormiunt, capite subter alā condito, alternis pedib. insistentes. Dux nudo capite spicit, & quod senserit, voce significat. Cū in terrā defcederint cibi gratiā, dux earū caput in altum erigit in custodiam omnium, cæteris securę pascentib. In tergo præuolantium colla & capita reponūt; quod quia duxipse facere nō potest, nō habes quo nitat, reuolat, vtipse quiescat quoq; in ejus vero loco succedit alia. ex sequentibus, eaque vicissitudo in omni cursu ab iis obseruatur. Custodes semper ac duces circumeunt, & siue homo, siue fera accedat, exclamant, altaque voce insidias indicant, vt de fuga reliquae in tempore sibi consulant. Vigiles etiam constituunt, & decima quaeque excubias custodit. Quae noctu excubant in terra crurum altera utrici corpore innituntur, alteroque addu-cto prehensum tenent lapillum. Quae in retinendo jugitas obrepere diutius somnum non finit, sed statim vt remisere, decidens calculus excitat, arguitque negligentem. Igitur non est, cur istud Herculis quisquam admiretur, quod alique subdens arcum haerentem brachio, & dextra clauam regens manu quiescerit. Certum deniq; est pontum transuolaturas, primum omnium angustias petere inter duo promontoria Criumetopum & Carambin, mox saburra stabiliri, cum medium transfierint, abiici lapillos e pedibus, cum attigerint continentem & e gutture arenam. Lapidibus vero non omnes inter volandum, sed quaedam se onerant, quae aliis leuiores sunt & velocires, ne reliquas celeritate volandi praeueniant, & defessae posteriores aciem deferant. Lapides abeis proiici a nautis obseruatum est, in quorum aliquando naues inciderunt, quos ideo etiam ferunt, vt ex eorum casu percipiant supra mare ne an terram volent, si enim ad mare lapides deferantur, iter susceptum facere pergunt, sin ad terram decidant, à volando requiescunt. Fessis aliquibus ad terram omnes descendunt, vt se inuicem expectent.
units.tr: Notable things about the flight of cranes. Flying, it completes the last day of its life. The others first give it burial, and then they make their way straight to Egypt, not resting anywhere, carrying themselves across the vast spaces of the sea by the strength of their wings. They fly high, so that they can see far, and if they see clouds and storms, they betake themselves to the earth and rest on the ground. In flight they form a triangular figure, so that they can cut the opposing air more easily in this shape; and sometimes they form a hexagon from the triangular figure. The older ones they place at the front of the flight, lest they tire themselves by following if the younger ones led. They also make a clamour, lest they be separated too far from the others. If they perceive that any one of them is tired, two others on either side lift her with their wings, or even carry her on their backs or feet; for in clear skies they are accustomed to stretch their feet backwards, and they know how to watch for favourable winds and those blowing against them. They also have a leader, and those who cry out are placed in the rear of the column, so that the voice can be heard. When they settle, the rest sleep with the head tucked under the wing, standing on alternate feet. The leader keeps watch with bare head, and signals with its voice whatever it has perceived. When they have come down to earth for food, their leader raises its head high as a guard over all, while the others feed without care. They rest their necks and heads on the backs of those flying ahead. Since the leader cannot do this itself, having nothing to lean on, it flies back so that it too may rest, and another from the following ranks takes its place; this alternation is observed by them in every journey. The guards and leaders always go round, and whether a man or a beast approaches, they cry out and point out the danger with a loud voice, so that the rest may take thought in time for flight. They also appoint sentinels, and every tenth one keeps watch. Those who keep watch at night stand on the ground, resting the body on one leg; with the other leg drawn up they hold a small stone grasped. Whoever is overcome by sleep and lets the grip slacken for too long is roused when the stone falls, which rebukes the negligent one. Therefore there is no reason for anyone to marvel at that feat of Hercules, that he rested with his bow resting on his arm and his club in his right hand. It is certain, finally, that when they are about to fly across the sea, they first seek the narrows between the two promontories, Criumetopon and Carambis. Then they steady themselves with ballast: when they have crossed the middle, they throw the pebbles from their feet, and when they have reached the mainland, the sand from their throat. Not all of them load themselves with stones while flying, but some do, those that are lighter and swifter than the others, lest they outstrip the rest in speed of flight, and the weaker ones behind lose heart. Sailors have observed that stones are dropped from them, and sometimes ships have fallen in with them. They also carry the stones so that, from their fall, they may perceive whether they are to fly over the sea or over land: if the stones are carried over the sea, they continue the journey they have undertaken; but if they fall to land, they rest from flying. When some are tired, all come down to the ground, so that they may wait for one another.

units.la: Hæc de volatu gruum, quæ licet ad propositum nostrum nihil faciant, vtilem tamen commonefactionem ob oculos ponunt de societate & amicitia fideliter colenda, nec temere dirimenda. Rara auis in terris, mihi crede, est fidus amicus.
units.tr: These things about the flight of cranes, although they contribute nothing to our purpose, nevertheless set before our eyes a useful reminder that friendship and fellowship are to be faithfully cultivated and not rashly broken. A faithful friend is, believe me, a rare bird on earth.

units.la: De Cygnis.
units.tr: On Swans.

units.la: INter epulas lautiorum quoq; spectantur oléres, & præcipue pulli, qui laudabilis succi sunt. Inaffantur autem et solidi apponuntur. Elixi insuaues sunt. Temperamenti, quidam ajunt, eos esse cholerici, quibus non assentiør, contrarium probante experientiâ. Corporis quippe amplitudo victusq; ratio naturam ipsorum satis indicant non absimilem cateris palustribus alitibus. Degunt in aquis, Proceresq; ac Magnates eos alunt in aquis perennib. & reuu-lis, qui domos arcesq; alluunt. Aquilam fi pugnam coperit, vincunt, nunquam enim nisi lacessiti dimicant. Socrates apud Platonem Apollini cygnos consecrates asserit, ob diuinationem quandam, quâ prouidentes, quid in morte boni sit, cum cantu moriuntur. Cantant autem, ait Plato, non ex tristitia, sed potius latitia, propinCc s quante fato, quod immortales se sentiant, & ad Apollinem suum remigraturos. Itaq; allegorice cygnus anima boni viri comparari potest, qui laetus mortem obit. Caelius tamen cygnum canentem, ait, paucissimos audiisse, etiamsi vulgatior fama tenet, ingruente fatali momento. Et Aelianus l. i. hist. var. inquit, nunquam se audivisse cygnum canere, & fortasse neq; alium. Alexander Mindius apud Athenaeum complures se cygnos morientes secutum affirmit, nec unquam eorum cantum audivisse. Mea sententia est tunc canturos cygnos, sum gracili tacuerint.
units.tr: Among the dishes of the wealthy, roasted birds are also served, especially chicks, which are prized for their juicy flesh. They are basted and served whole. Boiled, they are insipid. Some say their temperament is choleric, but I do not agree, since experience proves the contrary. The bulk of their bodies and their manner of feeding indicate a nature not unlike that of other marsh birds. They live in the water, and great lords keep them in perennial, flowing streams that wash their houses and castles. If an eagle attacks, they win, for they never fight unless provoked. Socrates in Plato asserts that swans are sacred to Apollo, because of a certain prophetic power by which, foreseeing what is good in death, they die singing. They sing, says Plato, not from sadness but rather from joy, because they feel they are immortal and are going back to their Apollo. Thus allegorically the swan may be compared to the soul of a good man who meets death joyfully. Celius, however, says that very few have heard a swan sing, though the more popular report holds that it sings as the fatal moment approaches. Aelian, in book 1 of his Varia Historia, says he never heard a swan sing, and perhaps no one else has either. Alexander Mindius, cited by Athenaeus, affirms that he followed many dying swans and never heard their song. My opinion is that swans will sing when they die, though in life they have kept silent through their slender throats.

units.la: De Ciconia.
units.tr: On the Stork.

units.la: Augusti principatu gruibus in cibis ciconias praelatas Cornelius Nepos auctor est, postea vero nemo attigisse voluit: unde inuentorum auctoritatem pretiosiores res facere dubium non est, idecque Si quis nunc mergos suaues edixerit asos, Parebit pravi docilis Romana juventus.
units.tr: Cornelius Nepos records that under the principate of Augustus storks were preferred to cranes as food, but afterwards no one wished to touch them. There is no doubt that such authority of discoverers makes things more valuable, and so: "If anyone now should declare seagulls sweet to eat, / the docile Roman youth will obey the perverse command."

units.la: Hodie magnatum mensae nullum iis honorem tribuunt, cum tamen carnes ipsarum oculis lippientibus venenisq; aduersari in experimentis fit, tum etiam comitiales adjuvare. Verum de ciconiarum esu pluribus à me supra est annotatum, ut & in tractatu meo de peste. Caeterum admirandae naturae dotes, ut ingenium, prudentia, justitia, & gratitudo tudo in hoc alite historiarum monumentis celebrantur. Magna cura exacta aetate parentes alunt, etsi humanis hoc facere legibus nullis jubeantur, sed sola naturae bonitate ad id impelluntur. Quantum enim curę in sobolis curam & educationem conferunt, tantum senio cofectis rependitur, quod vere ἀντιπελαργεῖν est, hoc est, mutuum beneficium & gratitudinem iis, a quibus vel enutritus, vel institutus fueris, exhibere. Unde ab Aristophane νόμῳ πελαργικός dicitur, quâ liberi parentes alere jubentur. Æliani historiam de ciconiarum gratitudine, & Oppiani in Ixeuticis Paraphrastes sic expressit. Mirabilis omnino & solertis ingenii ciconię sunt, sue iniuria causa, siue gratitudinis aliquod edendum signum fuerit. Nam & hoc accidisse fertur. Cum quidam ciconiae crus lapide confregisset, eaq; in nidum, ut poterat, se reciperet, à mulieribus, quae claudicantem viderant, restitutam est, & cum ceteris auolauit. Sequentis deinde anni vere cum ad eundem locum rediisset (agnoscebatur autem ex claudicationis signo) & mulieres conspecta sui, ceu quae libenter apud ipsas diuerteret, exhilarasset, mox è rostro oblongo egregiam & pretiosam gemmam ad pedes mulierum evomuit, quod quidem illae gratitudinis ergo sibi intellexerunt.
units.tr: Today the tables of the great pay them no honour, yet in experiments their flesh has been found to be useful against dim eyes and poisons, and also to help those who suffer from epilepsy. I have already noted at length above the eating of storks, as also in my treatise on the plague. Moreover, the admirable endowments of nature, such as intelligence, prudence, justice and gratitude, are celebrated in the records of history concerning this bird. Parents feed their young with great care when they are grown, though no human laws order them to do so; they are impelled to it by nature's goodness alone. For as much care as they give to the rearing and education of their offspring, so much is repaid to them in old age, which is truly antipelargein, that is, to return a mutual kindness and gratitude to those by whom you were nourished or taught. Hence Aristophanes calls it the pelargic law, by which children are ordered to feed their parents. The Paraphrast of Aelian's history of the stork's gratitude, and of Oppian in the Ixeutica, expresses it thus: "The storks are truly wonderful birds of remarkable intelligence, whether they show a sign of resentment for an injury or of gratitude. For this is reported to have happened. When someone broke a stork's leg with a stone, and it retreated as best it could to its nest, the women who had seen it limping took it in and cared for it, and when it had recovered it flew off with the others. Then in the spring of the following year it returned to the same place (it was recognised by the sign of its limp), and the women, seeing it, were delighted as if it gladly lodged with them. Soon it dropped from its long beak a remarkable and precious gem at the women's feet, which they understood to be a sign of gratitude."

units.la: Justinus Goblerus J. C. ab avis & majoribus suis saepe commemoratam scripsit se audiuisse, contigisse vidêl. non procul ab ipsius patria (Sanctogoarinum appellant) in civitate quondam imperii libera Wesalia superiore, vt ciconia nidum in cujusdam ciuis tecto haberet, in quo per multos annos ova exmere excluderet, & pullos nutricaret. Tanto autem tempore eadem avis benigni hospitis clementiam experta, vt, quae à nemine domesticorum, (pio patrefamiliâs ita cavente) infestaretur, quotannis suo tempore reauolare & redire, eundemq; nidum repetere solebat. Habuit autem in more praeter caeteras sui generis aues haec bestia, hospitis frugi modestia & humanitate ducta, siue commoditate loci aediumq;, siue, quod verisimilius est, natura ad hoc ipsum irritante, vt bis, nimirum sub veris & autumni tempus pridie fere antequam auolaret, & postridie cum rediret, circum limen ac porticum dom.[?] hospitis sui volitaret, & stridenti rostro se praesentâ velut indicaret, semp lætabundo acceu applaudente gestu vocēq; à patrefamiliâs acceptaac rursus dimissa. Haec cū jā multis annis inter aue & hospitē consuetudo fuisset, tādealiquando ex more sub autumnū auolatura ante ad porticum dom.[?] obstrepo impetu ferē, ac crepitanti rostro, ceu hospiti valedictura insolentius aliquato gestire visa est, cui
units.tr: Justinus Goblerus, a doctor of law, wrote that he had often heard it recounted by his grandfathers and ancestors, and that he had seen it happen not far from his own homeland (they call it Sanctogoarinum), in the free imperial city of Upper Wesel. A stork had its nest on the roof of a certain citizen's house, where for many years it laid eggs, hatched them and reared its young. For so long a time this bird, having experienced the kindness of a generous host, and being protected by the pious householder, so that no one of the household harassed it, used to return each year at its proper season and revisit that same nest. Moreover, this creature, led by the thrifty modesty and courtesy of its host, had a custom peculiar to it among birds of its kind. Whether from the convenience of the place and the buildings, or, more likely, because nature prompted it for this very purpose, it would twice, namely at the spring and autumn seasons, just before it flew off and on the day after it returned, fly about the threshold and porch of its host's house, showing itself with a clattering beak as if announcing its presence. Always joyfully, with a gesture as if applauding, it was received with voice and gesture by the householder and then let go again. When this friendship between bird and host had continued for many years, at last, when it was about to fly off in autumn as was its custom, it seemed to rush rather insolently at the porch, almost with violent impulse, and with a rattling beak, as if about to take leave of its host in some unusual way, which

units.la: bene precatus herus amico ore auem quasi alloquens, iubet vt salua & incolumis redeat. Sub verigitur postmodum reuerta ex more hospitem in foribus aedium rostri crepitu salutat, ac mox ante pedes viri, radicem magnæ recentis zinziberis e gutture exerens tanquam gratulabunda collocat, rostro vtplurimum obstrepero, in symbolum hospitalitatis. Admiratus hospes, peregrinum & informe quodammodo munus accipit, vicinisque videndum præbet, certo cognoscentibus gustando veram ac viridem zinziberis esse radicem.
