Et quandoquidem hactenus apud multos fuit dubium, & quodammodo incompertum, (inter quos etiam Plinius est) quonam e loco veniant, aut quo se referant ciconiæ, vel ex hoc facto constabit, calidas eas terras & vltramarinas, vbi zinziber hodie nasci dicitur, cum a nobis auolant, petere. Verum & hoc exemplo qualicunque, si non aliud, certe admoneri nos arbitrarer, inter homines cum pietatem, tum hospitalitatem plurimi fieri oportere. Extat & aliud luculentum super ciconiarum mirifica gratitudine exemplum in Ixeuticis oppiani. In Italia, inquit, vt fertur, cum serpens quidam ad nidum prorepens ciconiarum pullos devoraret, & alteram deinde sequetis anni fœturam similiter perdidisset, ciconiæ tertio demum anno reuersæ, nouam quandam auem Cc 5 & & prius non visam, (quæ breuior quidem coniis erat, sed rostrum magnum & acutum instar ensis è capite exerebat) secum adduxere, indicata nimirum ei fœtus sui calamitate, vt opem ferret inuitatam, siue pollicitationibus vllis siue verbis. Nam vtrum aues & animantes aliæ, suum inter se colloquium nobis ignotum misceant, in dubium vocari potest. Auis hæc nondum absoluto coniarum fœtu, coniuncta eis non erat, pullis vero iam exclusis, cum parentes ad comparandum pullis auiq; custodi victum longius auolarent, ipsa nidum non deserunt, vt serpenti obsisteret. Serpens igitur paulò post progressus è latibulo, pullos aggreditur, & licet ab aue custode roitro impeteretur, non tamen statim recessit, sed erectus corpore, caudæque innitens se opposuit, & secundò iam ictus spiris inuoluere custodem frustra molitus est, vtcunq; pluribus se flexibus insinuaret, nam facile euasit auis in sublime se recipiens, sic dum ille perdere, hæc seruare pullos annituntur, pluribus tandem ille vulneribus confossus iacuit, at non impune, auem enim in conflictu dentibus venenatis adeò læsit, vt omnes ei pennæ defluerent. Cum vero reuertendi tempus appetiisset ac reliquæ ciconiæ iam auolassent, parentes eum pullis feruatis, vt beneficii se memores declararent, tamen mansere, donec nouis ei pennis renatis simul auolarent. Hæc Oppianus.
units.tr: the master, kindly addressing the bird as a friend, bade it return safe and sound. Afterwards, in spring, it came back as usual and greeted its host at the doors of the house with a clatter of its beak. Soon, before the man's feet, it set down, as if rejoicing, a root of large fresh ginger that it brought out from its throat, beaking often as a token of hospitality. The host, amazed, received this strange and somewhat shapeless gift and showed it to his neighbours to be seen; those who tasted it recognised with certainty that it was a true and green root of ginger. And since until now there has been doubt among many, and some uncertainty (among whom is even Pliny), as to whence storks come or whither they go, this deed will establish that when they fly away from us they make for warm and distant lands, where ginger is said to grow today. Yet even by this example, whatever it is worth, if nothing else, I think we are reminded that among men both piety and hospitality ought to be practised very much. There is another splendid example of the storks' remarkable gratitude in the Ixeutica of Oppian. In Italy, he says, as it is reported, when a certain serpent crept up to a stork's nest and devoured the young, and then in the following year likewise destroyed the brood, the storks, returning in the third year, brought with them a new bird not seen before. It was indeed smaller than storks, but carried a large, sharp beak like a sword from its head; they had clearly told it of their misfortune, so that it might come to help, invited by promises or words of some kind. For whether birds and other animals exchange conversation among themselves unknown to us can be called in doubt. This bird, while the storks' young were not yet fully grown, was not joined to them; but when the young had already hatched, while the parents flew farther off to gather food for the chicks and for the guardian bird, it did not desert the nest, in order to resist the serpent. The serpent, therefore, crept out a little later from its hiding-place and attacked the chicks. Although the guardian bird struck it with its beak, it did not withdraw at once, but, raising its body and leaning on its tail, set itself against the bird. When struck a second time it tried in vain to coil its rings around the guardian, though it insinuated itself with many twists, for the bird easily escaped by rising aloft. So while the one strove to destroy and the other to save the chicks, the serpent at last lay pierced by many wounds, but not without cost, for in the struggle it had wounded the bird with its poisonous teeth so badly that all its feathers fell out. When the time for returning came and the other storks had already flown off, the parents, with their chicks saved, nevertheless stayed on, so that they might show themselves mindful of the kindness, until the bird's feathers had grown back and it could fly off with them. Thus Oppian.

units.la: Riuali quoque inuidia laborare ciconias Ælianus testatur. Nam cum in Cranone Thessaliæ eximia forma mulier, cui nomen Alcinoe, à coniuge peregrè profecto domi relicta stupri consuetudine fecisset, hoc quidem ipsum ciconia intelligens, seruiles iniurias in Dominum non sustinuit, quo minus mox facto impetu eum oculorum sensu orbans, iniuriam in Dominum illaram vlcisceretur. Sed hæc virtus potius castitatis quam rivalis inuidia in hac aue appellanda. Nam, vt autor libri de natura rerum scribit, non dubium est ciconias castitatis sectatrices esse, fœdusq; coniugii inuicè seruare. Fertur enim quod in eminentiori loco domus cuiusdam par ciconiarum habitarit: unde mare ad pastum recedente, frequenter alius mas aduenieris fœminam adulterina coniunctione polluebat. At illa statim eminus in fonte se mergebat, sic scelus adulterii per aquæ lauacrum delens, marem proprium deludebat. Huiusmodi factum dominus habitationis frequenter aduertit, & quodam post adulterium die eam à fonte, ne lauaretur, prohibuit: nec mora masculus è pastu rediens in fœmina sua scelus adulterii deprehendit, & in præsentia dissimulans abiit. Reuersusque secunda die maximam multitudinem secum adduxit, quas quæ singulæ adulteram aggressæ miseram crudeli morte dilaniarunt. Auentinus id factum esse scripsit sub duce Bauariæ Humberto, in pago quodam Bauarico nomine <bl>Thengen</bl>, in quo frequentia fuerint adulteria: adduxque hanc ciconiam adulteram coactam fuisse solam educare & pascere pullos exclusos, mare operam ipsi suam negante, hunc vero sub illud tempus, quo à nobis in alias migrare terras ciconiæ solent, venisse comitatum agmine ciconiarum, à quibus adultera confixa & dicerpta fit.
units.tr: Storks also, Aelian testifies, suffer from the jealousy of a rival. For when a woman of outstanding beauty, named Alcinoe, at Cranon in Thessaly, committed adultery at home while her husband was away abroad, the stork, understanding this very thing, would not tolerate the servile wrong done to its master. Without delay it attacked the man with a sudden assault, depriving him of his eyesight, and so avenged the injury done to its master. But in this bird this quality should be called chastity rather than the jealousy of a rival. For, as the author of the book On the Nature of Things writes, there is no doubt that storks are followers of chastity and keep the bond of marriage faithfully with one another. It is reported that a pair of storks lived in a rather high place on a certain house. Whenever the male went off to feed, another male who came along often defiled the female with an adulterous union. But she at once dived into a fountain at a distance, washing away the guilt of adultery in the water, and so deceived her own mate. The owner of the house often noticed this happening, and on one day after an adultery he kept her from the fountain so that she could not wash. Without delay the male, returning from feeding, caught his mate in the crime of adultery, and, pretending not to notice in the moment, went away. Returning on the second day, he brought with him a very great crowd, and they all attacked the adulteress and tore the wretched bird apart with a cruel death. Aventinus wrote that this happened under the Duke of Bavaria, Humbert, in a certain Bavarian village called Thengen, where adulteries were frequent. He adds that this adulterous stork had been forced to rear and feed the chicks that hatched by herself, the male refusing to help her; but at the time when storks are accustomed to migrate from us to other lands, he came with a crowd of storks, and by their flock the adulteress was pierced and torn to pieces.

units.la: Ad extremum honos ciconiis in Theffa-lia tantus, vt capitale sit occidisse, eademque legibus pœna, quæ in homicidam, teste Plin. lib.10.cap.23. In ea namque regione tantam aiunt serpentum prouenire vim, vt, nisi à ciconiis conficerentur, incolas pellerent.
units.tr: Finally, storks are held in such honour in Thessaly that killing one is a capital crime, and the penalty under the law is the same as for a homicide, as Pliny witnesses (book 10, chapter 23). For they say that in that region such a multitude of serpents arises that, unless they were destroyed by storks, they would drive the inhabitants out.

units.la: Præsensionum quoque quandam vim inesse ciconiis testatur Alexander ab Alexandria, Anno enim à Christi natiuitate 454. cum Atila Aquileiam obsideret, ciconias animadvertit, quæ in turribus ciuitatis nidificauerant, vno impetu ex urbe migrare, atque suos fœtus exportare, unde milites hoc auspicio exhortatus tanquam urbem interitui proximam ciconiæ deserere rent, urbem cepit. Prudentia denique ciconiarum ex eo apparet, quod ante abitum vno in loco congregentur, consilia quasi publica de abitione ineuntes &c. & commurmurátes, tum verò maximè, quod abituræ aquilonis secundum flatum prudenter expectent, in calidas & meridionales terras se recipientes, ex his enim illas ad nos redire multorum non incerta persuadet opinio. Hæc de ciconiis.
units.tr: Alexander of Alexandria also testifies that storks have a certain power of foreknowledge. In the year 454 after the birth of Christ, when Attila was besieging Aquileia, he noticed storks which had nested in the towers of the city, all at once leaving the city and carrying away their young. Encouraged by this omen, he urged the soldiers, as if the storks were deserting a city close to its ruin, and so he took the city. Finally, the prudence of storks appears from this: before departing they gather in one place, holding what are almost public deliberations about their departure and murmuring together; and especially in that, when about to leave, they prudently wait for the north wind to blow favourably, and then retreat to warm and southern lands. For from these lands, the not uncertain opinion of many persuades us that they return to us. These things concerning storks.

units.la: De ardea.
units.tr: On the heron.

units.la: Ardeam quasi arduam, quod alte volet, diētam putant. Circa aquas & in aquis victum quaerit. Quæ coloris cinerei est, in maximo apud gentes quasdam nunc honore est, non ob cibos tantum, sed ob voluptatem, quam Magnates hodie in venatu eius per falcones, qui ad eius captuam mansuefiunt &, cicurantur, impetuoso volatu eam prosternentes capiunt, quo quidem in Magnatum aulis nihil admirabilius fere incundius cernitur. Hieme autem potissimum potentiorum subit mensas, vere enim asparagos fœtificat, quo tempore pulli magis expetuntur. Pectore vero tantum placere in cibatu gulæ norunt artifices. Porro spectabilis & plane nobilis est ardearum cum accipitribus dimicatio, quibus podicem obuertentes pennas earum conspurcant, quæ postea computrescunt. Optimum augurium aiunt esse, cum ad austrum volant vel Septentrionem, solui enim periculâ & metus, Plinius l. II. cap. 37. In medio arenis tristis futuram tempestatem sentire. tire atque prefagire animaduersum est, quod tamen deleucis seu albis intelligendum Plinius vult.
units.tr: The heron is thought to be named as if arduea, from arduus, because it flies high. It seeks its food around and in the waters. Ash-coloured, it is now held in the highest honour among certain peoples, not only for its food but for the pleasure which the magnates today take in hunting it with falcons, which are tamed and trained for its capture, and which seize it by swooping on it in impetuous flight; nothing more admirable or pleasant is almost to be seen in the courts of the magnates. In winter especially it comes to the tables of the powerful, for in spring it fattens the asparagus, when the young birds are most sought after. But cooks know how to please only the palate with their food. A notable and quite noble spectacle is the fight of herons with hawks, in which the herons turn their rear ends and foul their feathers, which afterwards rot. They say the best omen is when they fly toward the south or the north wind, for then dangers and fears are released (Pliny, book 11, chapter 37). It has been observed that they feel and foretell a coming storm while standing among the sands, though Pliny wants this understood of the white or pale herons.

units.la: Submonitio de aquaticis alitibus.
units.tr: A note on water-birds.

units.la: TRactus Oceano vicinos aquaticarum auium omni genere abundare coftat, quarum captura hibernis praecipue mensibus fit ingens. Vere enim appetente abeunt gregatim, cateruatim q; volant, capi-unturq; in pratibus retibus protentis: earum autem quaedam in cibis ob carnium suauitatem magnam obtinuerunt auctoritatem, quaedam etiam rariores func, ideoq; pretiosiores epulisq; commendabiliores.
units.tr: The coast near the ocean is known to abound in water-birds of every kind, and their catching is especially great in the winter months. For when spring approaches they depart in flocks and fly in troops, and they are caught in meadows with nets stretched out. Some of them have won great authority as food because of the high sweetness of their flesh, and some are also rarer, and therefore more prized and more recommended at banquets.

units.la: Hoc obferuatu hic dignum, omnium aquaticarum carnes pro corporis magnitudine duras esse, concoctionisq; sua natura diffi-cilis, ac excrementis abundantes: quasdam etiam algę odorem, limiq; ac piscium fubolere, vnde stomacho nausea faftidiumq; prouocatur, quasdam sapore suaui abblandiri, quarum assiduo vsu graues sensim accersuntur morbi. Itaq; vt concoctu euadant facilio-res, ventriculoq; minus noxae inferant, tenuitudine easadipisci oportet, postmodum q; culinis comendentur & coquis. Vide locum de gruibus, vbi haec fufius explicantur. Assas deniq;, cuiuscunq; generis etiam sint inter aquaticas, bonitate ac suauitate elixis salubriores esse, longo experimento comprobatu habet.
units.tr: It is worth observing here that the flesh of all water-birds is, for the size of their bodies, tough, difficult to digest by its nature, and full of excrement. Some also smell of seaweed, mud and fish, whence nausea and loathing are provoked in the stomach; others flatter the palate with a pleasant flavour, yet by constant use they gradually bring on serious diseases. Therefore, so that they may pass through digestion more easily and do less harm to the stomach, they should be made lean, and afterwards they are recommended to cooks and kitchens. See the place on cranes, where these matters are explained at greater length. Finally, it has been proved by long experience that roasted birds, of whatever kind they are among the water-birds, are more wholesome than boiled ones, both in goodness and in sweetness.

units.la: De cuculo.
units.tr: On the cuckoo.

units.la: Avium, quae in humanos vsus & cibos admittuntur, agmen claudet cuculus, cuius carnes omnium esse suavissimas, gratissimus Philosophus, locupletissima, velut alterum copia cornu, veterum autorum bibliotheca, Plinius lib.10. cap.9. prodidit. Nec mirum, quod in alienis pariat nidis, maxime palumbium, alauda & curruca atque etiam luteola; singula quoque ponat ova, bona raro quod nulla alia avis; pullus item eius subdatur & educetur, avidumque is ex natura cibos reliquis pullis praeripiat, indeque pinguescat, nitidumque nutriticem in se convertat ac demoret, ut nullam ita avium suavitate carnes comparari cum cuculi carne posse verisimile sit quidem, dubium tamen, an nutriendi vi succique probitate cum aliis sit aequiparanda. Ego quod hic statuam, non habeo, nec scio, gulae proceribus experimentum relinquo. De pullis cuculi, minus certi aliquid licet affirmare, quos Aristoteles ait, neminem vidisse, nam in lib.6.& 9.historia. cuculum non facere nidum constantem asserit. Et hac de cuculo. Hactenus de alimentis quae veniunt a volucribus, seu volatilibus, sequuntur humi gradientia.
units.tr: The cuckoo closes the list of birds that are admitted to human use and food. Pliny, the most agreeable philosopher, the storehouse of ancient authors and, as it were, a second cornucopia of plenty, reports in book 10, chapter 9, that its flesh is of all the most delicious. Nor is it surprising that it lays its eggs in the nests of others, especially those of the wood pigeon, the lark, the whitethroat and even the yellow wagtail. It lays a single egg at a time, which is rare for any other bird. Its chick is likewise placed under and reared by these foster parents. Being greedy by nature, it snatches food from the other chicks, grows fat, and so wins over and holds its nursing bird. Thus it is indeed likely that no bird's flesh can be compared with the flesh of the cuckoo for sweetness, though it is doubtful whether it can be equalled by others in nourishing power and the goodness of its juices. What I should decide on this I do not have, and I do not know; I leave the experiment to the leaders of the gourmets. About the chicks of the cuckoo one may affirm something less certain, since Aristotle says that no one has seen them, for in books 6 and 9 of the History of Animals he asserts that the cuckoo does not make a constant nest. And so much on the cuckoo. Thus far on foods that come from birds or flying creatures; what follows are those that come from creatures that walk on the ground.

units.la: De
units.tr: On

units.la: CAP. XIV. De alimentis, quae veniunt ab animalibus humi gradientibus.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV. Of foods that come from animals that move on the ground.

units.la: Hominis gradientia vel ambulant, ut homo, & quadrupes vel reptant, ut reptilia.
units.tr: Creatures that move on the ground either walk upright or on their feet, as man does, or crawl, as reptiles do. Walking creatures include man and the quadrupeds.

units.la: De carne humana.
units.tr: Of human flesh.

units.la: Cytharum multa genera esse, qui corporibus humanis vescerentur, olim fuisse, & esse nostro seculo in nova India Cannibalos vocatos, historiarum monumentis proditum legimus. Quin & in remediis ac deliciis summis quidam habuerunt, viscera offaq; humana vorare, in epulis praesertim funebribus & parentalibus.
units.tr: We read in the records of history that there were once many kinds of people who fed on human bodies, and that in our own century, in the New India, a people called Cannibals has been reported. Indeed, some have regarded the viscera and bones of men as the greatest delicacy and remedy, especially at funeral and ancestral feasts.

units.la: Effedones Scythiae populi parentum suorum funera cantibus laeti prosequi fuerunt soliti, conuocatisque propinquorum caetibus, cadauera ipsa dentibus laniarunt, pecorumque visceribus mixta, conuiuis inter epulas appositerunt: cranio autem poculi loco sunt vsi, quod & auro circum ornarunt, teste Solino cap. 20.
units.tr: The peoples of Scythia called the Effedones were accustomed to follow the funerals of their parents with joyful songs. Having summoned the gatherings of their kinsfolk, they tore the corpses themselves with their teeth, mixed them with the flesh of cattle, and served them to the guests at the feast. They used the skull as a drinking cup and even decorated it with gold, as Solinus reports in chapter 20.

units.la: De Padaeis Indica gente, scribit Herodotus, aegrotantes eos interimere, ac epulari, mulieresque mulieribus idem officii praestare, re,etiamsi se negent ægrotare, qua de causa, inquit, pauci apud eos ad senectutem perue-nire dicuntur, etsi perueniant, mactati itidé comeduntur. Sic Massagethæ quoque Scythiæ gens, eos miserrimos ac infelicissimos putabant, qui infirmitate ac morbo decum-bentes morerentur, talesque feris beluisque devorandos proiiciebant. Vnde cum parentes ac propinqui in senium vergerent, iugulabant, eosque in frusta concisos, & ouiū pecudumque carne permixtos in mensa appositos absumebat, latius rati à se illos, quam a vermibus consumi. Herodot. l. 1.
units.tr: Herodotus writes that among the Padaei, an Indian people, they kill their sick and feast on them, and women perform the same service for women, even when the women deny that they are ill. For this reason, he says, few of them are said to reach old age; and if they do reach it, they are likewise slaughtered and eaten. Similarly, the Massagetae, a Scythian nation, thought those most wretched and unfortunate who died lying ill of sickness, and they threw such people to be devoured by wild beasts. So when parents and kinsfolk grew old, they slaughtered them, cut them into pieces, and mixed them with the flesh of sheep and cattle, serving them at table and eating them, thinking it more honourable that they be consumed by themselves than by worms. Herodotus, book 1.

units.la: Idem Ponticis quoque gentibus adscribit Tertullianus in libris aduersus Marcionem. Parentum, inquit, cadauera cum pecudibus cæsa conuiuio conuorant, qui non ita decef-ferat, vt efcatilis esset, maledicta mors exis-timabatur.
units.tr: Tertullian, in his books against Marcion, ascribes the same custom to the peoples of Pontus. He says that they devour the corpses of their parents, slaughtered together with cattle, at a feast; and that a death was regarded as accursed if it did not end with the body becoming food.

units.la: Indorum, ac eorum inprimis qui Calati nominantur, parentes suos, priusquam annis aut morbo aliquo in maciem Senium, abirent, velut Deorum hostias mactare, cæsu-rumque visceribus epulari mos fuit, idque maxime pium iudicabant. Quare Darius accitos, qui in sua ditione erant, græcos, per-conctatus est, quanta pecunia vellent defun-ctis parentibus vesci. Illis negantibus, vlla se pecunia hoc esse facturos, Darius deinde græcis præsentibus, & quæ dicebantur per
units.tr: Among the Indians, and especially those called Calatians, it was the custom to kill their parents, before they wasted away with old age or some sickness, as if sacrificing them as victims to the gods, and to feast on their flesh; and they judged this to be especially pious. Hence Darius, having summoned the Greeks who were in his dominion, asked them for how much money they would be willing to eat their dead parents. When they refused, saying that they would not do this for any sum of money, Darius then, with the Greeks present and learning through an interpreter what was being said, asked those Indians for how much money they would be willing to burn their dead fathers. The Indians, protesting vehemently, bade him keep his mouth to better things; and Herodotus, a witness of all these matters, adds that Pindar had spoken rightly when he said that custom is king of all.

units.la: D¢ interinterpretem discentibus, interrogauit illos Indos, quantum accipere pecuniarum vellent, vt patres defunctos comburerent, Indi vehementer reclamantes, meliora illum omnari iubebant, vnde Herodotus horum omnium testis addit, recte Pindarum dixisse, morem omnium esse regem.
units.tr: Likewise the Derbices, a Scythian people neighbouring Hyrcania, used to slaughter those who had already passed their sixtieth year, and they served them at their feasts, inviting their kinsmen and relatives to the banquet. They abstained, however, from the flesh of old women, as unwholesome, and merely strangled them and buried them. But if anyone had died by fate before that age, they did not eat him but buried him in the earth. These things are told of those ancient man-eaters, and of their most savage and monstrous feasts, in which the choicest dishes were the flesh of the dead.

units.la: Derbices similiter gens Scythica, Hircaniae proximi, eos qui sexagesimum annum iam excessissent, iugulabant, & in conuiuis appositos, necessarios & propinquos ad epulas conuocabant, abstinebant vero vetularum carnibus, vt virosis, eas enim tantum praefocatas condebant. Atqui si anteid temporis spatium fato aliquis cessisset, non esse, sed terra condere solebant. Atq; haec de antiquis illis anthropophagis, feriissimisq; ac immanissimis eorundem epulis, in quibus potiora fercula demortuorum fuerunt carnes.
units.tr: Such as these are the Americans and other man-eaters of our own age, who are accustomed to devour, with great joy, wantonness and dancing, the bodies of their enemies, especially those they have taken in war, roasted after they have first been fattened for some days, as the most delicious delicacies; as John Léry, a French eyewitness, reports.

units.la: His persimiles sunt Americenses, aliique nostri aeui anthropophagi, qui hostiu suorum, quos praesertim in bello ceperunt, per dies aliquot prius bene saginatorum cadauera assata, ceu suauissimas delicias magna cum laetitia, lasciuia, atque tripudiis deuorare consueuerunt, prodente Ioh. Leryenfi Gallo oculato teste, in sua illa nauigationis historia, gallico sermone in lucem edita. Verum ferinum illum morem anthropophagis istis relinquamus, ac Christiano homine indignum existiexistimentius hominis viscera persequi, quæ aspicere horret animus, quantò magis man-dere. In confesso quidem est, etiam à Chri-stianis cadauera hominum in morborum & vulnerum auxilia adhibeti, mumiam appellant: ipsumq; sanguinem humanum destillatum & præparatum comitiali morbo vexatis pro-pinari, verum ex homine ipso illum adhuc calidum, & quidem vena secta sorbere, vt quidam literis prodiderunt; horror est. Gale-nus alias carnes humanas gustatu dulces, pa-rumq; à bubula differre, à quibusdam, qui ea-rum periculum fecerant, se acccepisse tradit. Etapud Græcos fuerunt, qui scrupulosè ho-minis viscera sunt persecuti, eorumque sapo-res. Nos anthropophagis valere iussis, ad ci-bos, qui ex quadrupedibus homini veniunt, progrediemur.
units.tr: Like these are the Americans and other man-eaters of our own age, who, having prepared the corpses of their enemies, especially those they took in war, fattened for some days beforehand, have been accustomed to devour them roasted with great joy, wantonness and dancing, as the most delicious delicacy. This is reported by Jean de Léry, a Frenchman and eyewitness, in his account of his voyage, published in French. But let us leave that savage custom to these man-eaters, and consider it unworthy of a Christian to pursue human viscera, which the mind shudders to look at, let alone to eat. It is certainly known that even Christians use human corpses as remedies for diseases and wounds, which they call mummy; and that human blood itself, distilled and prepared, is given to drink to those suffering from epilepsy. But to drink it from the man himself while it is still warm, and indeed with the vein opened, as some have written, is horrible. Galen, moreover, relates that he had heard from some who had tried them that human flesh is sweet to taste and differs a little from beef. And among the Greeks there were some who carefully investigated the viscera of men and their flavours. Having bid farewell to the man-eaters, we now proceed to those foods that come to humans from quadrupeds.

units.la: De alimentis ex quadrupedibus.
units.tr: Of foods from quadrupeds.

units.la: Ordinem vitæ materiaq; tractandæ se-quendo vt nullum prætermittatur na-turæ & artis munus, commodum nunc est differere de cibariis, quæ sumuntur ex qua-drupedibus, cum primis vero pecoribus. Experi-mento enim compertum est, ac quotidianum vi-sus id comprobat, mitiores longè salubriorésque escas præbere mortalibus animantia, quam ole-ra, arborum poma, aut glandes. Vnde non pau-ci etiam rerum naturæ callentissimi certis-simis commentariis in lucem emissis docuerunt explicarunt, quam multiplicitér hominibus pecora præstent alimenta, quam quam eleganter tum lautiorum tum rusticorum mensas instruant, exornent, ac opulentent. Prima quidem illa ac innocens vita atque carnis imprimis desideria damnauit, pecora agriculturæ tantum nasci existimans, idcoque tam capitale erat bovem occidisse, quam ciuem, primumque morem alimenti hominum grauia pecudum interimendi a victimis & placationibus Deorum, quæ ex iis laudatissima erant, emanasse quidam statuunt, sicque ad posteros transfisse.
units.tr: Following the order of life and the matter to be treated, so that no gift of nature or art is passed over, it is now fitting to discuss the foods taken from quadrupeds, and chiefly from cattle. For it has been established by experience, and daily observation confirms it, that animals provide mortals with food far milder and more wholesome than vegetables, tree fruits, or acorns. Hence not a few men most skilled in the nature of things have, in very accurate commentaries published to the light, explained how many ways livestock supply men with nourishment, and how elegantly they furnish, adorn and enrich the tables of both the more refined and the rustic. That first innocent life condemned the eating of flesh above all, thinking that cattle were born only for agriculture, and therefore killing an ox was as grave a crime as killing a citizen. Some hold that the first custom of using animals as food, of slaying cattle, arose from sacrifices and the propitiation of the gods, which were most praised among them, and so passed down to posterity.

units.la: Caterum ex quadrupedibus animalibus in cibum veniunt, mensisque adhiberi possunt, leo, elephantus, panthera, vrsus, camelus, equus, asinus, canis, felis, mustela, mus, mele, sciurus, erinaceus, vulpes, cuniculus, lepus, cervus, hircus, capra, pecus, ouilla, bubulum, suillum. Quæ vero ex hominis natura & temperatura magis sint familiaria ac amica, vel longiùs ab ea, vitaque humaniore discedant, suo dicetur loco, ad quem remitto. Hoc ἐν παραδοχῇ hic, & obiter addo, esse gentem aliquam quæ lupinis vixerit, adhuc me legisse vel audiisse non memini-nisse.
units.tr: Here, by way of concession [ἐν παραδοχῇ], I add in passing that there is some people who have lived on lupins; so far I do not remember having read or heard of it. Among quadrupeds that come to food and can be served at table are the lion, elephant, panther, bear, camel, horse, ass, dog, cat, weasel, mouse, marten, dormouse, squirrel, hedgehog, fox, rabbit, hare, stag, buck, goat, sheep, lamb, beef and pork. Which of these are more familiar and friendly to human nature and temperament, or further removed from it and from a more humane way of life, will be said in its own place, to which I refer the reader.

units.la: De carne generatim, notatu digna.
units.tr: On meat in general, worthy of note.

units.la: Arnes, inquit Aristoteles, & quicquid iis, simile est, in genere sanguineo sunt, cui aßtipulatur Galenus 2. de temper. Carnis abundantiam, dicens, à sanguinis copia nasci, vbi mediocri corporis habitu præditos eu sarcos nominat, vt quibus humidum non abundat. Idem in fine lib. 1. carnem dicit multi sanguinis esse & calidum, vt ita caliditatem humiditatemq; quam continet, à sanguine acceperit, aq; boni sanguinis copia corpulentiam augeri in confesso sit. Vnde pro confesso etiam & confirmato tenendum, carnem fere talem esse, qualis sanguis, ex quo tota cōstat, colorem etiam à sanguinis bonitate, cuius index est, dependere. Cæterum, plus alimenti inesse carnibus quam in vllo cibo alio, ob affinitatem scilicet quam habent cum natura nostra, copiosum etiam, quod suppeditant, nutrimentum, & sanguinem, præsertim si sint animantium boni succi, nemo est qui non norit. Verum differentias carnis in re alimentaria corporis salubritatem desideranti ad vnguem explo-ratas habere vtilissimum erit.
units.tr: Lambs, says Aristotle, and whatever is like them, belong to the sanguine kind. Galen agrees in book 2 of On the Temperaments, where he says that abundance of flesh arises from abundance of blood, and calls those of moderate bodily habit "eusarcous" (well-fleshed), since moisture does not abound in them. At the end of book 1 he says that flesh is full of blood and warm, so that it takes its heat and moisture from the blood, and it is agreed that an abundance of good blood increases bulk. Hence it should be held as agreed and confirmed that flesh is for the most part like the blood from which the whole body is made, and that its colour too depends on the goodness of the blood, of which it is the sign. Moreover, that meats contain more nourishment than any other food, because of their affinity with our nature, and that they supply abundant nourishment and blood, especially if the animals are of good juice, no one is unaware. Yet it will be very useful for one who desires bodily health in matters of food to have examined the differences between meats with precision.

units.la: Ab animalium enim ætate, à pabulo, à se-xu, à castratione, parandi ratione, & vt vno dicam multa, pro proportione & temperatura eorundem multifaria. In genere quidem primò sciendum omnem carnem natura esse calidam & humidam, aliam tamen plus, alia minus, pro ætatis & nuttrimenti ratione.
units.tr: For meats differ in many ways according to the age of the animals, their fodder, sex, castration, method of preparation, and, to say many things in one, their proportion and temperament. In general, one must first know that all flesh is by nature warm and moist, though some more and some less, according to the age of the animal and its nourishment.

units.la: 2. Non omnes quemuis hominem nutrire, sed quasdam quibusdam esse lethales.
units.tr: 2. Not every meat nourishes every man, but some meats are deadly to some people.

units.la: Dd
units.tr: Dd

units.la: 3. Sicut extenuatorū nimis & macrorum, ita obesorum & nimis saginatorum carnes improbantur, illic ob nimiam si-citatem, probiq; succi carentiam, hic ob contrarium.
units.tr: 3. Just as the flesh of the overly thin and lean is disapproved, so too is that of the very fat and overfed: the former because of excessive dryness and lack of good juice, the latter for the opposite reason.

units.la: 4. Vetulorum quoq; & nuper natorum deteriores sunt, illorum enim aridæ sunt & præduræ, concoctuque contumaces, horum verò immodicè madescunt, excrementisque abundant, præsertim verò quæ humidioris sunt naturæ, vt oues, sues.
units.tr: 4. The flesh of the old and of the newly born is also worse. For the former is dry and tough and resists digestion, while the latter are excessively wet and abound in excrements, especially those of a moister nature, such as sheep and pigs.

units.la: 5. Et certè standum hic iudicio, quod longo experimento innititur, standum ab antiquorum obseruatione præsertim rationibus consentientibus, inter quas plurimum valet quæ ab ipsius, carnis sumitur substantia: durities enim in carne facit, vt sero & paulatim nutriat, teste Gal. in expositione aph.ıı.l.2. Quemadmodu enim, inquit idem, in sin.l.ȝ.de temper. quod facilè concoquitur & citò nutrit, respectu nostri calidum est, ita è contrario, cp tardè & paulatim, frigidum: facilè n. in substantiam nostram couertitur, quod cum ea habet maiore similitudinem, difficilius id quod magis dissimile. Præterea eadem duritiēs euidens indicium sicci- tatis est, teste Gal. l.2.de temper. Licet enim nō omne durum sit siccum, idtamen durum, ƈp neq; à vehementi calido indurarum est, neq; à frigore vehementi congelatū, siccū procul- dubio censebitur. Tantam auré caliditate in quiquibusdam carnibus esse non posse constat, vt ab ea indurantur, nec tantâ etiam frigiditate, vt congelet. Quare cum sint nihilominus duræ, siccæ siccas etiam esse oportebit, ob idq; enumero bonarum carnium excludendæ.
units.tr: 5. And certainly one must abide by a judgement that rests on long experience, and abide by the observation of the ancients, especially where reasons agree; among these the most powerful is that drawn from the very substance of the flesh. For toughness in flesh makes it nourish late and slowly, as Galen testifies in his commentary on the Aphorisms, book 2. For as the same author says at the end of book 3 On the Temperaments, what is easily digested and quickly nourishes is hot relative to us, and conversely what is digested slowly and gradually is cold. For what has greater similarity to us is easily converted into our substance, and what is more unlike us with more difficulty. Moreover, the same toughness is a clear sign of dryness, as Galen testifies in book 2 On the Temperaments. For although not everything hard is dry, yet what is hard, being neither hardened by vehement heat nor congealed by vehement cold, will undoubtedly be judged dry. Indeed it is established that in some meats there cannot be so much heat that they are hardened by it, nor so much cold that they freeze. Therefore, since they are nonetheless hard, they must also be dry, and on this account they are to be excluded from the number of good meats.

units.la: 6. Animalium quoq; non exercitatorum carnes Galen. damnat, ob nimium illorum humorem excrementitium, contra verò montanorum, sylustrium & exercitatorū, quæq; idoneis vescuntur pabulis, liberamq; agunt vitâ, laudat. Certissimū enim est, quod in plenum dixisse sufficiat, pro temporum, pascuorumq; ac pabuli ratione pecora macrescere, aut obesari, succiq; melioris aut peioris fieri,
units.tr: 6. Galen also condemns the flesh of animals that are not exercised, on account of their excessive excrementitious moisture; on the contrary he praises that of mountain, wild and exercised animals, which feed on suitable pasture and lead a free life. For it is most certain (enough to say in full) that according to the season, the pasture and the kind of fodder, cattle grow lean or fat, and their juice becomes better or worse.

units.la: 7. Quæ domi aluntur, vt sues &c. aut frumentorū farina, aut rapis, aut alio huiusmodi, lardi quidem plus obtinebunt, verum non perinde vtilis in cibis censetur caro.
units.tr: 7. Those raised at home, such as pigs and so on, fed on flour of grain, or on turnips, or other such things, will indeed have more lard, but their flesh is not considered equally useful as food.

units.la: 8. Recenter edita animalia & adhuc lactentia plurimum lentoris & viuidi humoris obtinere obscurū non est: ac veterib. maximè in cibis commendata testatur Plin. l. 29. c. 4, tantoque magis sicca efficiuntur, quanto absunt à partu longius, ætateque processerint.
units.tr: 8. It is not unclear that recently born animals, and those still suckling, have a great deal of viscosity and lively moisture. Pliny, book 29, chapter 4, testifies that the ancients especially commended them as food, and that they become drier the further they are from birth and the more advanced in age.

units.la: 9. Dulce ac delicatissimū sanguine habētia, quemadmodū de sanguine leporino scripsit Gal. 3. de alim. fac. bonitatis alimōia stare creditu difficile non est. Sed de lepore suo loco.
units.tr: 9. That meats with sweet and most delicate blood, as Galen wrote about hare's blood in book 3 On the Properties of Foods, are good for nourishment, is not hard to believe. But of the hare in its place.

units.la: 10. Assas & in sartagine frixas sicciores esse, in aqua v. dulci exlixas humidius corpori alimentū sbere, testat Gal. 3. de alim. fac. & idipsum comprobat quotidiana experientia. Vnde illæ naturis humidioribus, hæ vero ficcioribus temperaturis magis conueniunt.
units.tr: 10. Galen testifies in book 3 On the Properties of Foods that meats roasted or fried in a pan are drier, while those boiled in water or sweet wine yield food that is moister for the body; daily experience confirms the same. Hence the former suit moister natures, the latter drier temperaments.

units.la: II. Ad extremum in ouillo pecore mares præstare fœminis, & in bubalo quoq;, quod calidiores sint, minusque excrementis abundent: castratorum vero etiam quadrupedum carnes plurimum suauitatis ac salubritatis afferre immo plus quam non castratorum præter experientiam multorum cofenfu traditur, rationem hanc quidam assignant, quod ipsa qualitas carnium in non castratis simile quid testium qualitati præ se ferat graue, & virosum ad odorem vsq; similitudine porrecta:tum etiam quod castrata nullo à calido & sicco morbo subiecta sint. Hoc inuento castrantur gallinæ cæteris gratissimæ. Galenus l.1. de femine, sues fœminas castrari in Asia, & in superioribus nationibus Cappadociam vsque docet, quæ castratis maribus similes euadunt. Obseruantur enim admodum, carnisque suauitate aliis præstant fœminis, quemadmodum & castrati mares non castratis. Error deniq; quorundam detegendus hic est, qui carnes quomodolibet teneras recentibus semper præferunt, haud cogitantes teneritudinem illam velut putredine quandam, aut saltem ad putredinem, quandam præparationem esse, q cibū dentib9 quidé fscilioré reddat & grationé, sed q postea in venis deteriores succos, &
units.tr: 11. Finally, among sheep the rams are better than the ewes, and among oxen likewise, because they are warmer and abound less in excrements. The flesh of castrated quadrupeds is also said, by the general agreement of many and beyond experience, to bring much more sweetness and healthfulness than that of uncastrated animals. Some assign this reason: the very quality of the flesh of uncastrated animals displays something like the quality of the testicles, heavy and rank, even to the point of smell by resemblance; and also, castrated animals are not subject to any hot and dry disease. From this discovery capons are castrated, being most pleasing of all. Galen, in book 1 On Semen, teaches that sows are castrated in Asia, and in the upper nations as far as Cappadocia, and that they become like castrated males. For they are greatly esteemed and surpass other females in sweetness of flesh, just as castrated males surpass uncastrated ones. Finally, the error of certain people must be exposed here: they always prefer tender meats, however tender, to fresh ones, not considering that this tenderness is a kind of putrefaction, or at least a preparation towards putrefaction, which makes the food somewhat easier for the teeth to chew and more pleasing, but afterwards produces worse juices in the veins, and

units.la: Censura. & longo tépore prauas affeƈtiones ꝓgignat. Recentes enim carnes plus roboris afferre corporibus præter Hippocr. rationem 2. de diæta ( vbi recentia omnia plus virium aliis præbere dicit, eo quod viuenti sint proximiora, vieta vero & marcida recentibus excernantur magis, quod ad putredinem proximè accedant) bruta omnia carniuora demonstrant, quæ carnes recentissimas, immo calentes & quasi viuentes comedentia omnium aliorum sunt robustissima. Verum aliquam hic rationem habendam, tum hominum edentium, tum carnium edendarum etiam, patescet ex speciali singulorum tractatione : in generalibus hisce non sine ratione præmissis, haud pigebit nec pœnitebit paululum immorari lectorem.
units.tr: Censure. and over a long time produces bad affections. For fresh meats give more strength to the body, against the reasoning of Hippocrates in book 2 On Diet (where he says that all fresh things give more strength than others, because they are closer to the living, while stale and withered things are cast off more, since they approach putrefaction). All carnivorous brutes demonstrate this: those eating the freshest meats, even warm and almost living, are the most robust of all. But that some reasoning must be had here, both of the men who eat and of the meats to be eaten, will become clear from the special treatment of each. In these general matters, premised not without reason, it will not irk or displease the reader to linger a little.

units.la: De Leonina, Elephantina, Camelina, Pantherina, Vrsina, & Lupina carne.
units.tr: On the flesh of the lion, elephant, camel, panther, bear and wolf.

units.la: AGriophagos Æthiopia gentem, Pantherarum carnibus atq; Leonum victitasse, sicut & orientis populos quosdam Africaq; leonina, vera historia prodiium est. Solinus c. 33. Plin. l. 6. c. 30 Elephantos similiter in victu quorundam Nomadum frequentes fuisse idem testis est.
units.tr: Historical accounts report that the Agriophagi, a people of Ethiopia, lived on the flesh of panthers and lions, as did certain peoples of the East and of Africa. Solinus, ch. 33; Pliny, book 6, ch. 30. The same witness says that elephants were likewise a common food among certain nomads.

units.la: Verum ab hominis temperatura horum. animalium carnes alienas esse, praesertim pa- therarum & leonum, arbitrandum est, nam Leonis tradunt tantum esse virus, ut halitus suo odorem cibis foedum relinquat, eoque proscisse interiora ejus gravissime olent: flatus preterea emittit acerrimos, virinamque graviter olentem, quemadmodum testantur, qui in Magnorum Principum aulis Leonum domitores fuerunt & custodes.
units.tr: But it must be judged that the flesh of these animals is foreign to the human constitution, especially that of panthers and lions. For they report that the lion's poison is so strong that its breath leaves a foul odour on food, and its entrails, when cut open, smell very badly. Moreover it gives off the sharpest breath, and urine with a strong stench, as those testify who were lion-tamers and keepers in the courts of great princes.

units.la: Orientis gentes quasdam, ut Bactros, Camelorum carnibus vesci certum est. Aristoteles lac ac carnes camelorum omnium suavissimae esse testatus est, qui tamen locum eruditioribus quibusdam suspectum est, ut Hieron. Mercuriali variar. lect. l. 2. putat enim τὸ χρέα ab aliquo ex marginibus interserta, tum etiam quod Plinius l. 28. solum lac & non carnes Camelarum ab hominum lacte facit dulcissimum. Ac de lacte convenit inter omnes. Galenus 3. de aliment. carnes camelinas valde damnat. Solinus c. 32. scribit lutulentas aquas Camelos capture, refugere puras, & nisi coenosior fuerit liquor, assidua conculcatione limum excitare, ut turbetur, quod vel maxime ab illorum esu aliquem deterreri debeat. Antiphanes Comoediarum scriptor apud Athenaeum tradit, Graecos aliquando solitos Camelum solidum assam apponere etiam regibus. Qui de situ novi orbis posteris monumentum reliquerunt, quae-
units.tr: It is certain that some peoples of the East, such as the Bactrians, eat camel flesh. Aristotle testified that camel milk and flesh are the most pleasant of all, though this passage seems suspect to some more learned men. Hieronymus Mercurialis, in Variae lectiones, book 2, thinks the word for flesh was inserted by someone from the margins, and also because Pliny, book 28, says that only camel milk, and not their flesh, is sweeter than human milk. All agree about the milk. Galen, in book 3 On Foods, strongly condemns camel flesh. Solinus, ch. 32, writes that camels seek muddy waters and shun clear ones, and that unless the liquid is rather thick with mud, they stir up silt by constant trampling until it is troubled; this alone ought especially to deter anyone from eating them. Antiphanes, a writer of comedies, relates in Athenaeus that the Greeks once used to set a whole roasted camel before even kings. Those who have left posterity an account of the situation of the New World

units.la: Ioan. 3. quasdam esse Insulas affirmant, quarum incola camelina vescantur, illicq; esse armenta camelorum ingentia, quin etiam Ægyptii, dum Sultano parebant, Camelos in cibatu habuerunt, vt ita non plane extra humanos mores sit Camelis vesci.
units.tr: Joan. 3. affirm that there are certain islands whose inhabitants eat camel flesh, and that there are huge herds of camels there. Indeed the Egyptians too, while they obeyed the Sultan, kept camels for food, so that eating camels is not altogether outside human custom.

units.la: Sed vrsinum plane videbitur vrsos in cibos vocare, quorum tamen catulos, seu vrsulos conditos tanta esse suauitatis quidam prodiderunt, vt non minorem saporis gratiam habeant, quam alia ferina. Helvetios quosdam & Allobroges, necnon Septentrionis gentes plurimas vrsorum venatui deditas, horumque carnibus vesci, dubium non est. Omnivorum animal est, & carnivorum etiam, non solum enim cervos, sed & feros sues invadit. Cerebro eius inesse veneficium Hispanias existimasse Plinius testatum reliquit l.8.c.36. ideoq; occisorum capita in spectaculis cremasse, exploratum enim, potum in vrsinam rabiem egisse.
units.tr: But it will seem quite absurd to call bears food. Yet some have reported that their cubs, preserved in pickle, are of such sweetness that they have no less pleasant a flavour than other game. That the Helvetians and Allobroges, and most of the peoples of the North who are devoted to hunting bears, eat their flesh, is beyond doubt. It is an omnivorous animal, and a carnivorous one too, for it attacks not only deer but also wild boars. Pliny, book 8, ch. 36, left the testimony that Spain believed there was poison in the bear's brain, and therefore burned the heads of those killed in the shows, since it is well known that drink drove men into a bear-like madness.

units.la: Unde illiberalem plane esse carnem, & insalubrem vrsinam carnem esse quidam arbitrantur, vt qua iniquum creet succum & atrabilarium, stomachoque vt difficilis concoctu adversetur, praesertim vero genitorum catulorum tolerabilior foret. Adipes vrsorum multis remediis nobilitantur. Animam ferunt iis adeo virosam esse, vt contacta ea nulla fera attingat, cuius rei causam nullam video aliam producì, quam quod omnivorum animal vrsus est, vescitur namq; fructibus arborum, leguminibus, apibus formicis & carnibus præmaceratis ac pene putridis, tum etiam, quod veterno in antris recondití pinguescant.
units.tr: Hence some think bear flesh is quite ignoble and unwholesome, since it produces bad juices and black bile and is hard for the stomach to digest, though the flesh of young cubs would be more tolerable. Bear fat is valued for many remedies. They say its breath is so foul that no wild beast touches what it has touched. I see no other cause given for this than that the bear is an omnivorous animal, for it eats the fruits of trees, pulses, bees, ants and flesh half-rotten; and also because, hidden away in caves during its winter sleep, it grows fat.

units.la: Lupinam vllam gentem in cibata habuisse, nec me legisse, nec audiisse memini, cum tamen cetera animantia asperrima & ferocissima in cibatum venerint. Quidam non minus maleficii in carne esse credunt, quam in eorum visu. Pastores oves à lupis jugulatas, bones, sues, ceterasq; pecudes plurimum in cibis reformidant, credentes aliquod inesse iis venefi-cium. Epar eorum, si vescatur, epaticu prodesse, eparq; vitiatum recreare medicorum docent, placita, sicut & cor eorundem terræ factum asservatumq; benum de se odorem prebere, Comitialibus quoq; tritum in potu auxiliari. Dentem lupi caninum dextrum in magnis haberi operibus Plinius autor est l. 11. c. 37. Tantamq; inesse huic animali vim, ut vestigia eius calcata equis torporem afferant, ac rostrum eius venefici ressat, ob id q; villarum pertu prefigatur eundem effectum præstare & pellem, è cervice solida idem testis est l. 28.
units.tr: I do not remember having read or heard that any people has eaten wolves, although other very rough and fierce animals have been used for food. Some believe there is no less harm in the flesh than in the sight of them. Shepherds greatly dread eating sheep, oxen, pigs and other cattle killed by wolves, believing there is some poison in them. Physicians teach that their liver, if eaten, is good for liver complaints and restores a diseased liver; likewise their heart, dried and kept, gives off a pleasant smell, and taken in drink it helps those with epilepsy. Pliny, book 11, ch. 37, is the authority that the right canine tooth of the wolf is held in great esteem for important works. And such great power resides in this animal that horses are numbed by treading on its footprints, and that its snout is fastened to the doors of farmhouses to produce the same effect; the same witness, in book 28, says the same of its skin taken from the solid neck.

units.la: De equina, asinina, canina.
units.tr: On the horse, the ass, and the dog.

units.la: EQuinam, asininam, caninamque obsessos etiam homines durasse cum aliis, tum nostra memoria compertum habetur. Et vrgente fame foediora etiam animalia, vt feles, glires, ac mures, in dura obsidione cinctis vrbibus homines attingere coguntur.
units.tr: That men beset by hunger have endured on horse flesh, ass flesh and dog flesh, both among other peoples and within our own memory, is a matter of record. And when famine presses, men are forced to touch even more foul creatures, such as cats, dormice and mice, in towns cut off by a harsh siege.

units.la: Pullos equarum alpini quidam populi epulari dicuntur. Turcas quoqua in bello equinam siccatam, inque farinam molitam cibis adhibere ferunt: olim barbaris quibusdam gentibus in visu fuit, lac cum sanguine equino potare, & hoc quoque aeuo lac vel sanguis milio commixtus à Sarmatis & Asianis pultis instaraditur. Improbi autem omnino succi putatur equina, ideoque nisi summa vrgeat necessitas, ea abstinendum. Lac equi fœminæ potum matricis dolores sedare, comitialesque subuenire quidam in secretis habent.
units.tr: It is said that some Alpine peoples eat the foals of mares. The Turks too are reported to use dried horse flesh, ground into flour, as food in war. Among certain barbarian nations it was once customary to drink milk mixed with horse blood, and in our own age milk or blood mixed with millet is made into porridge by Sarmatians and Asians. Horse flesh is thought to be altogether of bad juice, so it should be avoided unless great necessity compels. Some keep it as a secret that a mare's milk, drunk, relieves pains of the womb and helps against epilepsy.

units.la: In asinorum numero à quibusdam censentur, qui eorum carnes edunt. Sapore enim esse insuaui, succumque improbum parere, crassum & atrabiliarium, stomachoque aduersari à quibusdam notatum est.
units.tr: Some count among the asses those who eat their flesh. For some have observed that it is insipid in taste, that it produces a bad juice, thick and black-bile-forming, and that it is harmful to the stomach.

units.la: Verum asinorum carnes in cibatu fuisse quibusdam familiares Galenus autor est. Et pullos præcipue expetitos, tanquam suauiores & graciores epulas subministrantes, memoriæ proditum reperitur. Mecoenas apud Romanos epulari eos primus instituit, eoq; tempore magnam autoritatem iis faciebant vescentes. Erat autem Mecoenas Augusto Imp. mire carus, suo pene nutu Remp. gubernans, post eum tamen autoritas saporis interiit. Nostro ævo Galliarum & Hispaniarum proceres quidam ( inter quos Ant. Pratensis Gall. Cancellarius )avidissimi Mecoenatis extitere in eo escæ genere imitatores, sed cum ipsis, carnis quoque illius gratia sepulta est.
units.tr: Galen is the authority that the flesh of asses was a familiar food to some people. Foals especially are recorded as having been sought after, since they provided more pleasant and choice dishes. Maecenas was the first to make it the custom among the Romans to dine on them, and at that time those who ate them enjoyed great prestige. Maecenas was wonderfully dear to the Emperor Augustus, almost governing the state by his nod; after him, however, the reputation of this taste died out. In our own age some nobles of France and Spain (among them Antoine Prat, Chancellor of France) became the most eager imitators of Maecenas in this kind of food, but with them that fashion for the meat was buried too.

units.la: Certum autem est priscis illis temporibus Mecoenatem greges asinarum generosissimarum habuisse ex agro Rheatino, vbi amplitudinis dignitate præstabant. Popea, Neronis conjunx, asinarum greges secum duxisse fertur, propter lacțis gratiam ad cutem conciliandum, quoties enim è balneo exiret, lacte asinino corpus abluisse legimus.
units.tr: It is certain that in those ancient times Maecenas kept herds of very noble she-asses from the Rietine district, where they were distinguished by their size and worth. Poppaea, the wife of Nero, is said to have led herds of she-asses with her, to win a smooth complexion by their milk; for we read that whenever she came out of the bath she washed her body in asses' milk.

units.la: Unde facile conjectare licet, tunc temporis hujus animalis pretium admodum fuisse adauctum. Meminit Plinius asinam Rheatinam suo ævo diuenditam quadringentis millibus nummum, quæ summa intra idem stabit, si quis æstimationem ejus ad calculum retulerit, lib. 8. c. 43. Porro de asinarum lacte eiusque viribus dicetur seorsim. cap. de Lacte. In medicinis praecipue commendantur splen, pulmo, lingua, jecur, vngulae. Tradit Plin. ex vngulis & ossibus asini confectum annulum, non tamen nigri coloris à comitiali morbo praeseruare.
units.tr: From this one can easily conjecture that at that time the price of this animal had risen greatly. Pliny records that in his day a Rietine she-ass was sold for four hundred thousand sesterces, a sum which would come to the same if anyone reckoned up its value, book 8, chapter 43. Moreover, the asses' milk and its powers will be discussed separately, in the chapter on milk. In medicines the spleen, lung, tongue, liver and hooves are especially recommended. Pliny relates that a ring made from the hooves and bones of an ass protects against epilepsy, though not one of black colour.

units.la: Gulae infantiam aliquando apud Romanos experti sunt, & canes fidelissimi ante omnia homini: lactentes enim catulos adeo puros existimarunt ad cibum, vt placandis etiam numinibus hostiarum vice iis vtercntur, teste Plin. l. 29. c. 4. Hippocrates quoque gravissimus autor pluribus in locis non parum eos in variis aegritudinibus commendauit, sicut etiam Oribasius in primo collect. ex sententia Mnesithei Atheniensis. Galenus catulos praepingues similiter videtur commendare, quos tamen nolter orbis in epulis non admittit. Qui in aedibus educantur ad custodiam, aliisque animalib. non infidi antur, in cibis non damnari possunt, ob victu non plane ferinum. Africae gentes quasdam, vt Ptoembaros & Sambtris proximos, canè pro rege habere, motuque ejus imperia augurari Solinus autor est c. 33. Genito mane catulo re apud Prisicos fieri diuinam, Plin. testis est, ca. 4. l. 29. & in coenis Deum etiamnum poni catalinam. Plautinę quoq; fabulę indicio sunt, adiicialib. in epulis coenisque catulinam fuisse celebre. Praeclarus hujus animalis est in medicinis vsus. Sanguine enim eius contra toxicanihil praestantius putatur.
units.tr: The Romans once tried the delicacy of infants, and dogs, most faithful of all creatures to man. For they thought suckling puppies so pure as food that they used them in place of victims to placate the gods, as Pliny testifies, book 29, chapter 4. Hippocrates too, a most weighty author, in several places commended them highly for various illnesses, as did Oribasius in the first book of his Collections, on the opinion of Mnesitheus of Athens. Galen seems similarly to commend very fat puppies, which, however, our part of the world does not admit to its feasts. Those raised in houses to guard them, and not hostile to other animals, cannot be condemned as food, since their diet is not wholly savage. Solinus is the authority that some African peoples, such as the Ptoembari and those near the Sambtri, keep a dog as king and foretell commands from its movements, chapter 33. Pliny is witness that among the Prisici a sacrifice is made on the morning after a puppy is born, and that even now the goddess Catulina is set up at feasts. The fables of Plautus are also evidence that puppy meat was a well-known dish at dinners and banquets. This animal has a distinguished use in medicine, for its blood is thought to be the most effective of all against poison.

units.la: Canum celebre, in medicina vsu, Vo notabile.
units.tr: The famous use of dogs in medicine is worth noting.

units.la: Vomitiones quoque homini canis monstrasse videtur, aliosque ex eo maxime laudatos vsus,hic referre operae pretium erit, quia hoc animali nullum fere familiarius homini. In canis rabidi morsu tuetur ab hydrophobia seu pauore aquae,capitis canini cinis illitus vulneri. Oportet autem,inquit Plinius l.29.c.5.omnia comburi in vase fictili nouo argilla circumlito atque in furnum indito.Idem & in potione proficit. Quidam ob id edendum dederunt: alii vermem e cadauere canino adalligauere, menstruaue in panno subdidere calici,aut intus ipsius caudae pilos combustos infuere vulneri. Cor canimum habentes fugiunt canes. Non latrant vero lingua canina in calceamento subdita pollici. Jecur caninum vtilissime in rabie morsis datur, si possit fieri,crudum mandendum, si minus, quoque modo coctum, aut jus coctis carnibus. Saliuntur & carnes eorum qui rabidi fuerunt ad eadem remedia in cibo dandae. Quin & catuli statim necantur in aqua, ad sexum ejus qui momorderit, vt jecur crudum ex iis deuoretur. Caninus dens sinister maximus, circumscarificato eo, qui doleat, dolorem tollit. Idem praestat collutio caninis dentibus decoctis in vino ad dimidias,nec non cinis eorum, qui rabie perierunt, capitum crematorum sine carnibus. Lien caninus viuenti exemtus inque cibo sumtus à lienis vitio liberat. Alii recentem superalligant. Alii duorum dierum catuli lienem exaceto scillitico dant ignoranti. Laterum doloribus rabiosi canis caluariæ cinis medetur potioni inspersus. Sedis vitiis canini capitis cinis efficacissimus est, nec non fimi canini candidi cinis cum rosaceo, feruntq; inuentum Æsculapii esse, eodemq; verrucas efficacissime tolli. Ac verrucas quidem omnium generum vrinam canis recentem cum suo luto illitam auerruncare Plin. l.30.c.8.&9.testis est. Nigri canis masculi fel amuletum esse domus totius suffitæque purificatæue, contra omnia mala medicamenta Magia naturalis docet. Sanguine item canis respersis parietibus, genitalique ejus sub limine januæ defosso. Minus autem mirandum hoc, cum fœdissimum animalium ricinum, vermiculum seu pediculum canum, (cui vni,inquit Plinius, nullus est exitus saginæ diutius in fame viuenti) in tantum magnificent: hunc enim ex aure sinistra canis, adalligatum omnes dolores sedare ajunt. Eundemque in augurio vitalium habent, nam si æger ei respondeat qui intulerit, à Pedibus stanti interrogantiq; de morbo, spem vitæ certam esse, morituram respondere nihil, voluntque evellendum ex aure læua canis, cui non sit alius, quam niger color. Lac porro canis primi partus cum cinere per se mixtum depilatorium est, evulsis prius pilis quos renasci nolumus.
units.tr: The dog seems to have shown man even the use of emetics, and other much-praised uses from this animal. It will be worth recording them here, since scarcely anything is more familiar to man than this animal. For the bite of a mad dog, the ash of a dog's head rubbed on the wound guards against hydrophobia, or fear of water. "All of it," says Pliny, book 29, chapter 5, "must be burned in a new earthen vessel smeared with clay and put into the oven." It helps also when taken in a drink. Some therefore have given it to be eaten; others have tied on a worm from a dog's carcass, or placed menstrual cloth under the cup, or infused the burnt hairs of the tail itself into the wound. Dogs flee from a dog's heart. Dogs do not bark if a dog's tongue is placed under the big toe in a shoe. The liver of a dog is given most usefully to those bitten in rabies: raw, to be chewed if possible, or otherwise cooked in any way, or as broth of boiled meat. The flesh of those who have been mad is also said to be given in food for the same remedies. Indeed puppies are drowned at once in water, of the same sex as the one who bit, so that their raw liver may be eaten. The great left dog's tooth, after scarifying the part that hurts around it, removes the pain. A rinse made from dog's teeth boiled in wine down to half is equally effective, and so is the ash of those who died of rabies, the heads burnt without the flesh. The spleen of a dog taken alive and eaten in food frees one from diseases of the spleen; others apply a fresh one over it. Others give the spleen of a puppy two days old, with squill vinegar, to someone who does not know. For pains in the sides, the ash of a rabid dog's skull, sprinkled into a drink, is a cure. The ash of a dog's head is most effective for ailments of the seat, and so is the ash of white dog dung with rose water; they say this was discovered by Aesculapius, and that warts are most effectively removed by it. Pliny indeed testifies, book 30, chapters 8 and 9, that the fresh urine of a dog, smeared on with its own mud, removes warts of every kind. Natural magic teaches that the gall of a black male dog is an amulet for the whole house, and for a house that has been fumigated and purified, against all harmful drugs. Likewise dog's blood sprinkled on the walls, and its genitals buried under the threshold of the door. This is less to be wondered at, since they magnify so greatly the most foul of animal vermin, the dog's louse (of which alone, says Pliny, there is no end to fatness for one that lives long in hunger). For they say that this louse, tied on from a dog's left ear, allays all pains. They also hold it as an omen of life: if a sick man, standing at his feet, asks the one who brought it about of the disease, and it answers nothing, hope of life is certain, but if it answers that he will die, then it is doomed. They want the left ear of the dog to be plucked out, which has no other colour than black. Furthermore, the milk of a dog's first litter, mixed by itself with its ash, is a depilatory, once the hairs we do not want to grow back have first been plucked out.

units.la: Ad extremum, anginae, dysenteriae, vlceribusque inueteratis, stercus canis, solis ossibus per biduum nutriti, durum, candidum, minimeque foetens exiccatum, inque pollinem redactum, aliis conuenientibus his affectibus medicinis admixtum, mederi ac opitulari, multis documentis manifestatum est. Addy senteriam lacti decocto, aut quod filices candentes extinxerit, iniciendum. Felle denique canino cum melle suffusiones & albugines oculorum curauit Apollonius.
units.tr: Finally, for quinsy, dysentery and long-standing ulcers, dog dung is shown by many proofs to heal and help, when the dog has been fed for two days on bones alone, the dung being hard, white, least foul-smelling, dried and reduced to powder, and mixed with other medicines suited to these conditions. Add it for dysentery, to be injected into a decoction of milk, or into the water in which red-hot irons have been quenched. Finally, Apollonius treated suffusions and films of the eyes with dog's gall mixed with honey.

units.la: De murium acerrimo hoste, fele.
units.tr: On the Cat, the Bitterest Enemy of Mice.

units.la: Gula insidias & feles effugere non potuerunt. Sunt enim qui pro delicatissimis epulis vtantur, tantum potestatis habet venter pro cibo porrigendi quicquid velit. Hodie in confessa damnatione relinquuntur. Cerebrum namque veneficio infamatur, animamque illorum adeo esse ajunt pestiferam hominI, ut tabem afferat, qua de causa etiam minus eos quidam contrectant. Excrementa felis cum digito bubonis adalligata quartanis febribus aduer-sari tradit Plin. l. 28. c. 15. & ne recidant, tenu- remoueri septeno circuitu quidam jubent. Quis hac
units.tr: Gluttony has not been able to escape the snares of the cat either. Some people use it for the most exquisite delicacies, so much power does the belly have to serve up whatever it wants as food. Today it is left under open condemnation. Its brain is branded with poisoning, and they say its soul is so pestilential to man that it brings a plague; for this reason some people even handle cats less. Pliny, book 28, chapter 15, hands down that the excrement of a cat, tied up with the toe of an owl, counters quartan fevers, and that, to keep them from returning, some order it to be moved around in a sevenfold circuit. Who could have discovered this

units.la: {NB} hac quaso inuenire potuit? quæve est ista mistu-ra, & cur digitus potissimum bubonis electus est? antipathias certe misterium hic admiran-dum fatendum q; concordiam istam rerum, aut repugnantiam medicinas gignere & genuisse. Alii jecur felis decrescente Luna occisi sale in-veteratum, bibendum ex vino ante accessiones quartanarum mandant.
units.tr: Who, I ask, could have discovered this? What is this mixture, and why was the owl's toe chosen above all others? Here one must surely acknowledge a wonderful mystery of antipathies, and that such a concord or repugnance of things both produces and has produced remedies. Others order the liver of a cat, killed when the moon is waning, salted and left to age, to be drunk in wine before the attacks of quartan fevers.

units.la: De Mustelina.
units.tr: On the Weasel.

units.la: MAgna autorum asseueratione commendantur multæ mustelæ partes aduersus comitialem morbum, vt cerebrum, jecur, (quod peculiariter etiam jecinoriis vitiis medetur) testes, ventriculus, vulva. Et quidem Comitiales tota in cibo sumta liberare dicitur: quod tamen catulus præstat efficacius. Syluestrem Plinius totam in cibis prædicat. Vetustate non corrumpi, & à muribus non attingi caseos, affirmant, si coagulo misceatur mustelæ cerebrum. Cæterum Italos mustelas inter cupedias ponere ac comedere non est ignotum.
units.tr: Many parts of the weasel are commended, on the great assurance of authors, against epilepsy: the brain, the liver (which also cures diseases of the liver in particular), the testicles, the stomach, and the womb. Indeed the whole animal, taken in food, is said to free from epilepsy, though a whelp does this more effectively. Pliny praises the wild weasel, taken whole in food. They affirm that cheese is not spoiled by age and is not touched by mice if the brain of a weasel is mixed in with the rennet. Moreover, it is not unknown that the Italians count weasels among their delicacies and eat them.

units.la: De Muribus.
units.tr: On Mice.

units.la: Qui portenta terrarum verterunt in ga-neam, torpidique palati extiterunt, in-delitiis gulæ quoque habuerunt mures, quos quos omnes quadrupedes conscia refugiunt, sole fele excepto : ex putredine enim maxima ex parte ortum eos habere constat, ingentemq; eorum vim navibus innasci. Pontici duntaxat albi sunt. In annalibus reperitur venisse murem ducentis nummis Casilinū obsidente Hannibale, eumq; qui vendiderat, fame interiisse, emtorem vixisse. In Hispania murium copiam pestilentem strabo auctor est.
units.tr: Those who have turned the monsters of the lands into their throats and grown torpid in the palate have also counted mice among the delights of gluttony, though every four-footed creature, aware of them, shuns them, except the cat. For it is established that they arise for the most part from putrefaction, and that a huge swarm of them is bred in ships. Only the Pontic mice are white. In the annals it is recorded that a mouse was sold for two hundred coins while Hannibal was besieging Casilinum, and that the seller died of hunger while the buyer lived. Strabo the author says that in Spain the abundance of mice is a plague.

units.la: Pulmonum vitiis detractā cute, exenterato saleq; oleoq; decoctos, & in cibo sumtos, mederi Plinius auctor est. Vrinam quoq; non continentes, vt pueri, elixatis sistitisq; praeclare juvantur. Dissesti & impositi serpentum scitibus efficaciter medentur, verrucasq; exedunt, estq; eorum natura hic nonsperneda, praesertim insiderum assensu, cum Luna lumine fibrarum numero crescente ac decrescente, quod de epate pœculiariter quidam intelligendum asserunt. Capitum caudarumq; murinarum cinerem ex melle inunctum claritatem visus restituere gravēs autores prodiderunt, Commendantur autem magis sylvestres, aut glires. Sed in hoc spectatur vel maxime natura potentia, si verum est, quod alvum laxare muscerdam potu sumtam, quidam se expertos ajunt. Experimentum cuiq; relinquitur liberum.
units.tr: Pliny the author says that for diseases of the lungs, mice with the skin removed, gutted, and boiled with salt and oil, and taken in food, bring a cure. Those who cannot hold their urine, like children, are wonderfully helped by them boiled and administered. Dissected and applied to the scales of serpents, they cure effectively and eat away warts, and their nature here is not to be scorned, especially with the agreement of the stars, since the number of fibres in the liver increases and decreases with the light of the moon, which some assert is to be understood particularly of the liver. Grave authors have related that the ash of mouse heads and tails, anointed with honey, restores clarity of sight. Field mice and dormice are commended more highly. But in this the power of nature is especially to be observed, if it is true what some say they have tried: that mouse dung taken in drink loosens the bowels. The experiment is left free to each person.

units.la: De
units.tr: Of

units.la: De Gliribus.
units.tr: On Dormice.

units.la: TAnta fuit vorago, tantusque gurges, tam insanus gulæ ventrisque luxus prisci illius seculi, vt cognata muribus animalia, glires, in epulis lautioribus Romanorum gloriam non obscuram obtinuerint. Nam qui apris vivaria primus instituit Fulvius Hirpinus, gliribus quoque in doliis instituisse fertur. Et glirarium quo pacto construendum sit Varro docuit. Sed in cœnis censoriâ tandem lege prohibiti, non alio modo, quam conchilia aut aves peregrinæ quædam. Pinguia glirium soricumque decoctorum paralysin timentibus utilissima esse graves autores tradunt. Quin & deplorata aurium vitia fanari gliribus, detracta pelle, intestinis exemtis, melle in vase novo decoctis, vel è nardo, vt malunt alii, vsque ad tertias, atque ita aliservatis, cumque opus sit, tepide infusis, Plinius testis est l.29. c.vlt. Estq; hoc remedii genus in secretis.
units.tr: Such was the abyss and such the whirlpool, so mad was the extravagance of gullet and belly in that ancient age, that animals akin to mice, dormice, won no small glory at the more lavish feasts of the Romans. For Fulvius Hirpinus, who first established boar-preserves, is said also to have kept dormice in jars. And Varro taught how a dormouse-enclosure is to be built. But they were at last banned from dinners by the censors' law, no differently from certain foreign shellfish or birds. Serious authors tell us that the fat of dormice and of boiled mice is most useful for those who fear paralysis. Indeed, Pliny is a witness (book 29, last chapter) that deplorable ear diseases are cured by dormice: the skin is removed, the entrails taken out, and they are boiled in honey in a new vessel, or in nard, as others prefer, down to a third, and so preserved; when needed, they are poured in warm. This kind of remedy belongs among the secret remedies.

units.la: De Melina.
units.tr: On the Badger.

units.la: MEllis hoc animal auidissimum, alveariisque infestum semper perhibetur. Carnes ejus ferum gustatu saporem redolere, ac virosum quid exhalare tradunt, potissimumq; cum canibus exagitatum tatum capitur, ideoque liberaliorem ac humaniorem sectantibus vitam in epulis eo abstinendum. Septentrionis tamen gentibus quibusdam in cibis melés non sordere sicio. Adeps huius animalis ad multa millia remediorum utilis est, inprimis vero renum junctura-rumque doloribus commodat. Sanguis ejus distillatus in canicularibus ad ƺii sumtus pestifero veneno aduer-satur.
units.tr: The badger is said to be a most greedy creature, always hostile to beehives. They report that its flesh gives off a wild taste and exhales something foul, especially when it is caught after being hunted down by dogs; therefore those who pursue a freer and more civilised life should abstain from it at feasts. Yet I think some northern peoples do not scorn badger meat in their food. The fat of this animal is useful for many thousands of remedies, and above all it helps with pains of the kidneys and joints. Its blood, distilled in the dog days, at a dose of two drachms, counters deadly poison.

units.la: De Sciuro.
units.tr: On the Squirrel.

units.la: QVi aridius & atrabiliarium alimentum Sciuros praestare scripserunt, meo quidem judicio, quod tamen pace illorum dixerim animalculi huius naturam plene non habuerunt cognitam. Dulci enim gaudet cibo, quem in recentibus, tum fructibus, tum omnis generis nucibus studiose exquirit, has etiam in cavernas suas comportat, ad futuram sibi prospiciens hiemem. Quare inter delicatiores suaveque succi cibos non immerito quidam Sciuros reponunt: & fuisse olim Martialis testatur. Ad ipsos mire gratos ipse sum expertus in Suecia & Dania, ut verisimile sit, qui cibis eos abdicarunt, nunquam degustasse. Summa in eorum venatu voluptas est, quippe ex arbore in arborem transiliunt, cursu ac recursu pernici, quo libuerit, exultant. Porro amnem aliquem transiturus. Sciurus lignum leve cui insidet, aqua imponit, cauda veli vice, vento flante, vtens. Vulgus comitiá-litentari existimat fabulose magis, quam vere.
units.tr: Those who have written that the squirrel provides a dry food that produces black bile have, in my judgement (though with all respect to them I say so), not fully understood the nature of this little animal. For it delights in sweet food, which it eagerly seeks among fresh fruits and nuts of every kind, and it carries these even into its dens, looking ahead to the coming winter. Hence, among the more delicate and sweet-juiced foods, some not unjustly rank the squirrel; and Martial testifies that it was once so esteemed. I myself have found squirrels wonderfully pleasant in Sweden and Denmark, so it is likely that those who reject them as food have never tasted them. The greatest pleasure lies in hunting them, for they leap from tree to tree and exult in swift running to and fro wherever they please. When about to cross some river, the squirrel sets a light piece of wood on which it sits upon the water, using its tail as a sail when the wind blows. The common people think this is more a fable than a truth.

units.la: De Erinaceo.
units.tr: On the Hedgehog.

units.la: ET hoc animal ventribus humanis na-sci portentosæ culinarum artes ganeæ-que artifices docuerunt: licet alii vitæ hominum supervacuum esse dicere non dubitârunt.
units.tr: That this animal was born for human bellies, the ingenious arts of cooks and the craft of gluttons have taught us with monstrous inventiveness; although others have not hesitated to say that it is superfluous for human life.

units.la: Certum est carnes eius ventrem soluendi, ventriculumque corroborandi, nec non vrinas exinaniendi vi pollere, iisq; prodesse in cibis, quorum natura ad lepram vergit & malignas pustulas. Tergum viuis detrahitur, postea curatur, interaneis abjectis, & inflatur. Urinam in extrema spe, seu desperatione tergori suo spinisque noxiam & tabificam reddere Plinius testatur, l. 8. c. 37. quo maleficio non potest fieri, quin & caro perfundatur, vnde plus periculi timendum, quam suauitatis sperandum, quamobrem exinanita prius vrina venari, ars est. Capite autem percusso, si vno ictu perimatur, minus periculi est.
units.tr: It is certain that its flesh has power to loosen the bowels, strengthen the stomach, and expel urine, and it is beneficial in foods whose nature tends toward leprosy and malignant pustules. The hide is stripped from the living animal, afterwards treated, the entrails thrown away, and it is inflated. Pliny testifies (book 8, chapter 37) that in extreme hope or despair the hedgehog makes its urine harmful and poisonous to its own back and spines.
