Because of this mischief it cannot be that the flesh is not also tainted, so more danger is to be feared than pleasure hoped for; therefore it is an art to hunt it only after its urine has first been emptied out. If, however, its head is struck and it is killed with a single blow, there is less danger.

units.la: Ee
units.tr: Ee

units.la: De Vulpina.
units.tr: On the Fox.

units.la: AVtumno, quo tempore maxime vulpes pinguescunt, esufc.vuarum, palato gratissimas esse iccircoq; Venatores apud Gracos tunc ipsas esitasse conjuevisse, Galenus 4. de vict.acut.comment. & 3. de alim. facult. scripsit. Seipsis enim circa id tempus meliores evadunt. Rura in multis locis diligenter eas venantur, captasq; elixant & inassant, suavissimeq; mandunt. Nitidior vita eas damnavit. In Magnatum tamen aulis non raro degustantur. Sed fraudem detexit virosum quasi quiddam & in carne agreste. Pulmo vulpis ad pulmonis vitia insignis est, sumitur enim in cibis a lautioribus etiam, qui pulmonis tabem reformidant. Adeps ad podagras & convulsiones nobilitatur. Pellis humidioribus naturis prodest, calida enim est, & confortat humidum, frigidumque ventriculum foris admotu.
units.tr: In autumn, when foxes grow especially fat, they are most pleasing to the palate with their eating of grapes; for this reason the Greek hunters were accustomed to eat them at that time, as Galen wrote in book 4 of his commentary on the Acute Diseases and in book 3 of On the Properties of Foods. For they themselves become better at that season. In many places the countryside hunts them diligently, and having caught them, they boil and roast them and eat them with great relish. A more refined way of life has condemned them. Yet in the courts of the great they are not infrequently tasted. But their fraud reveals something rank and somewhat rustic in the flesh. The fox's lung is remarkable for curing diseases of the lungs, for it is taken in food even by the more refined, who dread wasting of the lungs. The fat is celebrated for gout and convulsions. The skin benefits moist constitutions, for it is warm and, applied externally, strengthens a moist and cold stomach.

units.la: De Cuniculis.
units.tr: On Rabbits.

units.la: Fertur in occultis habitare cuniculus antris, Monstrauit tacitas hostibus ille vias.
units.tr: They say the rabbit lives in hidden caves and showed the enemy secret ways.

units.la: Quo carmine Martialis cuniculorum in bello inuentionem huic animali ascribere visus est. Innumerae autem foecunditatis animal est cuniculus, urbib. quandoq; oppidisq; fodiendo parans exitiu, vt M. Varro autor est.
units.tr: With these verses Martial seems to credit this animal with the invention of mining in war. The rabbit is an animal of boundless fecundity, and, as M. Varro reports, it digs out destruction for cities and towns.

units.la: Balearicis insulis famem frugibus populatis attulisse, Balearicosque auxilium militare per legatos ab Augusto petiisse aduersus eorum prouentum, Strabo, qui sub Augusto vixit, & Plinius certò prodiderunt. Satis autem patet veteres Romanos horum fecisse mentionem. Obtinent verò in opiparis epulis summam gratiam, præsertim verò infantibus pullis habetur honor. Fœtus ventre exectos vel uberibus ablatos non repurgatis interaneis, gratissimo in cibatu esse Plinius testatur, lib.8. cap.57.
units.tr: Strabo, who lived under Augustus, and Pliny state with certainty that the Balearic Islands were stripped of their crops and brought to famine by these animals, and that the Balearians sent envoys to Augustus asking for military help against the pest. It is clear enough that the older Romans mentioned them. They are highly prized at lavish banquets, and young ones especially are considered a delicacy. Pliny testifies that the unborn young, taken from the womb or from the udders without their innards being cleaned out, are a most welcome dish, Book 8, chapter 57.

units.la: Certum est, carnem eorum capacem esse alterius odoris saporisque. Itaque cuniculi, quo in loco alantur, plurimum interesse arbitrantur, pabuli enim, sicut & perdices, gratiam referunt, aut vitiū: à leporario genistis confito genistā referent, si iuniperis iuniperum, si pinastris pinastrū, aut aliud huiusmodi odoratius vibrans, quod in leporibus contingere non deprehenditur. Porro inalsantur omnes, & nunquam aut rarissimè elixantur, sunt enim humentioris naturæ. Non pinguescere, vt & leporem Plinius lib. 11. cap.37. affirmat, & sensusid confirmat. Venantur multis modis cuniculos, sed maximè viuerris, ad hoc gratia est, quas in speculis iniiciunt, in quos subeuntes mirabili pernicitate cuniculos inuadunt, qui perterriti ab iis vel iugulantur, vel foras prorumpunt inque cassis prætensis incidentes capiuntur. E cuniculorum quoq; genere videntur esse, quos porcellos Indicos nominant, passim nunc ali educariq; coepti.
units.tr: It is certain that their flesh takes on different smells and flavours. So people who rear rabbits think it matters a great deal where they are fed, for like partridges they reflect the quality or fault of their fodder. Fed on broom in a hare-warren, they taste of broom; on juniper, of juniper; on pine, of pine; or of some other strongly scented plant, which is not observed in hares. Moreover, all rabbits are roasted, and only very rarely boiled, since their nature is moister. Pliny, Book 11, chapter 37, affirms that they do not grow fat, as with hares, and experience confirms this. Rabbits are hunted in many ways, but chiefly with ferrets, which are employed for this purpose. They are sent into the burrows, and the rabbits, terrified, rush out with astonishing speed and attack them; some are killed by them, while others break out and, running into the nets spread before them, are caught. Some think those called Indian guinea pigs belong to the same kind; they have only lately begun to be bred and reared everywhere.

units.la: De leporina scitu digna, & ad vitam prorogandam necessaria.
units.tr: On the flesh of the hare, worth knowing, and necessary for prolonging life.

units.la: VEnatio huius animalis peculiaris est nobilitati & Magnatibus, & nisi natura benignitas tantam lepori fœcunditatem tribuisset, genus iamdudum desiisset, nam omnium fere prædæ nasci videtur, aliarum sc. ferarum, volucrum & hominum. Superfœtare lepores, aliud educantes, aliud in utero pilis vestitum, aliud implume, aliud incoato partu gerentes, & vtramq; vim singulas habere, sineq; mare concipere posse, Herodotus auctor est. Quare desinat illi mirari, qui nihil mirabile se videre aiunt, quod quotidianis epulis matres atq; infantes absumantur, & tamen gulæ populationi tam constanter resistere atque sufficere. Caeterum de animalis huius natura & temperatura inter eruditos non conuenit. Quidam carnem eius faciunt boni succi, facilis concoctionis, eamq; ab omni melancholica sece abesse aiunt, adductli auctoritate Galeni, qui 3. de alim. leporum sanguinem bonitatis & alimonia præstantia, aliis omnibus præfert ob suauitatem & dulcedinem, qua de causa plurimq; consuetudo est, illum cum epate caterisque leporis visceribus decoquere ac comedere. Indeq; concludunt, leporinam carnē melancholicum non esse, quia sanguis talis non est, tum etiam, quod grauissimi autores, (inter quos est Plinius) qui rerum naturalium historiam conscripserunt, & Poeta tradunt, (inter quos Martialis) esse leporis venustatis decorem in 7. aut 9. vsq; diem prorogari. Alii leporinas, vt omnium oblongas aures habentium animalium carnes, melancholicum succum parere, proindeque ex leporum esu puellarum genas rosarum rubore efflorere non posse contra stattuunt, pro se adducentes venerandam antiquitatem, & per totam secula inculcatam mordicusque recepiam sententiam, quam ab Hippocrate vetustissimo coepit autore. Scribitur enim in lib. 2. de diaet. qui Hippocrati ab omnibus ascribitur, in hunc modum, Leporina caro sicca & astringens, lotium aliquantisper movet. Post hunc Galenus, vel quisquis ille fuerit, lib. 2 de effectis ait, leporum caro sanguinem grauem generat crassiorem: & in comment. de attenuante vitio, vtilem eam esse ait in vitio exiccante, non autem attenuante, quia crassum sanguinem generat. Et lib. 3. de locis aff. magnam eam habere vim dicit in melancholici sanguinis generatione. Pfellus & Paulus eodem fere verbis subscribunt Galeno, & post hos omnes Simeon Seth lib. de esculentis inter cibaria atra bile gignentia leporinam connumerauit, Carnes inquiens, leporis hic connumerandae, quibus exiccare corpus animum est, minime veroficiori temperatura praeditis, sanguinem enim crassarum partium gignunt & melancholicum.
units.tr: The hunting of this animal is a special pleasure of the nobility and great men, and if nature's kindness had not given the hare such fecundity, the species would have died out long ago, for it seems almost everything's prey, namely of wild beasts, birds and men. Herodotus records that hares superfetate, carrying in the womb some young that are furred, others unfeathered, others at an unfinished stage of birth, and that each kind has both powers, and can conceive without a male. So let those cease to wonder who say they see nothing marvellous, when mothers and infants are consumed in daily feasts, and yet the belly's gluttony is so constantly resisted and satisfied. Apart from this, learned men do not agree about the nature and temperament of this animal. Some say its flesh is of good juice, easy to digest, and free from all melancholy, relying on the authority of Galen, who in the third book On Foods prefers the blood of the hare to all others for its goodness and nourishing quality, on account of its sweetness and pleasant taste; for this reason it is very common to cook it with the liver and the other entrails of the hare and eat them. From this they conclude that hare's flesh is not melancholic, since such blood is not, and also because the most weighty authors, among them Pliny, who wrote accounts of natural things, and the poets, among them Martial, hand down that the beauty of the hare's freshness lasts until the seventh or ninth day. Others maintain that hare's flesh, like that of all animals with long ears, produces melancholic juice, and that therefore girls who eat hare cannot make their cheeks blossom with the red of roses. They cite in support the venerable antiquity and the opinion, handed down through all the ages and clung to stubbornly, which began with the most ancient author Hippocrates. For in the second book On Diet, which everyone ascribes to Hippocrates, it is written in this way: "Hare's flesh is dry and astringent, and somewhat moves the urine." After him Galen, or whoever he was, says in the second book On Effects that hare's flesh generates thick, heavy blood; and in the commentary on the attenuating defect he says it is useful in a drying defect, but not in an attenuating one, because it generates thick blood. And in the third book On Places Affected he says it has great power in generating melancholic blood. Psellus and Paulus agree with Galen in almost the same words, and after all these, Simeon Seth in his book On Edibles counts hare's flesh among foods that generate black bile, saying: "Hare's flesh is to be counted here, which tends to dry up the body, and is by no means of the most correct temperament, for it generates thick and melancholic blood."

units.la: Circa hanc opinionum diuersitatem primo lectorem haud dubito meminisse, quod in vere philosophantium scholis receptum est, sc. rationibus disputandum esse non autoritate, nec a pura autoritate standum, sed rationum pondera ac momenta consideranda esse. Quod & nos in praesenti velitatione conabimur. Sciendum vero, si certi quid concludatur, Medicos, cum de temperatura alicuius rei loquuntur, non de ea loquuntur, si quaelibet res per se considerata adepta est, (ad philosophum enim spectat haec consideratio) sed hominis respectu, vt calidum, humidum, frigidum vel siccum dicatur, quod humanum corpus calefacere vel frigefacere potest. Non igitur ciborum natura, vt & leporina, carnis temperatura exterina cuiusdam rei consideratione vel comparatione metienda est, sed relatione ad corpus humanum iudicium formandum, ex eo enim, quid homini cibus sit, an talem habeat cum homine similitudinem, vt conuerti in eius substantiam possit, dignoscitur, atque hoc est & non aliud, quod facit aliquam rem, & dici & esse efficam homi-nis. Si quis igitur recte iudicare voluerit leporinam carnis temperaturam, vt esca est, cognoscere eam inprimis oportet, in quos humores a calore humano vertatur, quod certe longam requirit experientiam, teste Hipp. in Epidem. Cibi & potus experientia egent. Hoc ergo iudicio standum, huicque innitendum, quod experientia ac obser-uatione, nec non rationibus consentientibus est suffultum. Inter has validior aliis omnibus est, quæ carnium substantia sumitur, quæ in lepo-refatu dura est: quæcunque autem dura carne constant, ait Galenus in expositione aphorif. 18. lib. 2 c. f. de san. tuen. tardius & paulatim nutriunt, idq; non leve frigiditatis & siccitatis argumentu exi-stimant, exanguis enim & veluti vita vaporeq; omni atque hu-more fere desti uta leporina videtur, quin & friabilis fibrisq; abun-dans, quæ omnia siccam, duram, difficilem conco-ctu leporinam ostendunt. An vero omne durum sit siccum, supra, vbi de carnium differentiis, annotatum reperitur. De altero, dura, quaq; tardius & paulatim nutriunt, frigida, vt vult Manardus, ea vero quæ celeriter concoquuntur & nutriunt, esse calida, qui affirmant, vehementer mihi videntur errare. Multa enim sunt dura substantia cibaria, quæ quidem longe post assumtionem tempore atque paulatim nutriunt, vt sunt cafei duri, carnes infumatæ & sali a, nec non ova ad indurationem elixata: nam & hæc inter duras esas Galenus connumerat loco citato: Quis autem hæc frigida dixerit, propterea quod duriores sint substantia, tardiusq; conficiantur, ac tardiorem habeant excretionem? (Nam quæ velociter nutriunt, veloces habent deiectiones, inquit Hipp. aph. citato.) Et econtra multa velociter concoquuntur, veloceq; habent deiectiones, quæ tamen calida omnia nemo sanus recte dixerit, nisi qui velociter, leniter ac infirmis
units.tr: On this difference of opinion, I have no doubt the reader first remembers what is accepted in the schools of those who truly philosophise: that one should dispute by reasons, not by authority, and should not simply stand by authority, but weigh the force and weight of the arguments. This we shall also try to do in the present skirmish. It must be understood, however, that if anything certain is to be concluded, physicians, when they speak of the temperament of some thing, do not speak of it as it is considered in itself (for that consideration belongs to the philosopher), but with respect to man, so that it is called warm, moist, cold or dry according to whether it can warm or cool the human body. Therefore the nature of foods, and so the temperament of hare's flesh, is not to be measured by the consideration or comparison of some external thing, but judgement must be formed in relation to the human body. For it is known from this what food is to a man, whether it has such a likeness to man that it can be turned into his substance; and this, and nothing else, is what makes a thing both be called and be truly suitable for man. If anyone therefore wishes to judge rightly the temperament of hare's flesh as food, he must first know into what humours it is turned by the human heat, which certainly requires long experience, as Hippocrates witnesses in the Epidemics: "Food and drink need experience." So we must stand by this judgement and rest upon it, which is supported by experience and observation, and also by agreeing reasons. Among these the most weighty is the substance of the flesh that is taken, which in hare's flesh is hard; and whatever foods consist of hard flesh, says Galen in the exposition of aphorism 18 of the second book on preserving health, nourish more slowly and gradually, and this they consider no slight evidence of coldness and dryness, for hare's flesh seems bloodless and, as it were, almost destitute of life, vapour and every moisture, and moreover crumbly and abounding in fibres, all of which show hare's flesh to be dry, hard and hard to digest. Whether all hard things are dry is noted above, where the differences of flesh are discussed. As to the other point, that hard things which nourish more slowly and gradually are cold, as Manardus holds, and that those which are quickly digested and nourish are warm, those who assert this seem to me to be greatly mistaken. For there are many foods of hard substance which nourish only long after eating and gradually, such as hard cheeses, smoked and salted meats, and eggs boiled hard; and Galen counts these among hard foods in the passage cited. But who would call these cold because they are harder in substance and digested more slowly, and have a slower excretion? (For those which nourish quickly have quick evacuations, says Hippocrates in the aphorism cited.) And conversely, many things are quickly digested and have quick evacuations, which yet no sane man would rightly call warm, unless he wishes to nourish quickly, gently and without weakening, and something cold.

units.la: & frigidum mius nutriri cupit. Quin potius contrarium, affirmat optima ratione posse exist imo, quo facilius quicquam solidum est ac durius, co firmius humi- dum & calidum innatum id asserere & continere, & econtra quo quia tenerius est ac tenuius, eo citius & facilius etiam calidum innatum exhalare & diffl are. Firmius igitur nutriuntur efficere duriores, licet tardius & concoquantur & deiciantur. Fundamentum huius assertionis rationibus, experientia & auctoritate niti-tur. Galenus namque ipse testis est, in fine expositi aphor. ea, quæ cunque tenuem habent humorem, distribuendum, celeritate quidem distributionis atque appositionis exuperare, stabilem vero naturam non habere, sed facile diffluere: quæ vero crassiores habent humores & tenaciores, tardius quidem distribuuntur, sed stabilius adhærent partibus alendis. Qua de causa vere & recte Aristoteles ait elixis humidiora statuit, congenita videl. humiditatis ratione, quæ in assatione asseruatur, elixatione deperditur, nam elixa admentitio, assa proprio humore abundant. Intelligendum vero Aristotelem modice assis est, alias in confesso est igne assantem, si immodicus sit, exteriora & interiora plus nimio exiccare, imo non rarum exurere. Ex his ita se habentibus (ita autem se habere, certis documentis patefactum est) facile est pronunciare, auritiam in leporina (ut & in cerusina, de qua in sequentibus) frigiditatis indicium certum non esse, nec unquam esse posse, argumento inter alia, quod sanguis eius fluoris ac dulcedinis suavitate praestet, nec dilutus tenuisque nimis nec crassus nimis sit, sed consistentia mediocris: carnem autem sanguinis sequi temperaturam & dispositionem, praeter alia color, qui a sanguinis bonitate vel vitio dependet, ostendit. In hypoferca enim, menstruum suppressione, febribus & splenetic is, quibus lien vel epar, alterum vel utrumque procreandi aut depurandi sanguinis organum, induratum vel obstructum, aut quovis modo affectum esse, liquore vultus pallescere animadvertimus, qui melancholicus peculiaris color est. At Alexandrum Severum Imper. quotidiano leporum esu venustatem ruboremque vultus adeptum esse testatur notum illud, & non illepidum hendecasyllabum,
units.tr: Rather, the contrary is true, and it can be asserted with the best reason: the more solid and harder something is, the more firmly it holds and contains the moisture and the innate heat; and conversely, the more tender and fine it is, the more quickly and easily the innate heat is exhaled and dissipated. Harder foods therefore nourish more firmly, even though they are digested and evacuated more slowly. The foundation of this assertion rests on reasons, experience and authority. For Galen himself is a witness, at the end of the exposition of the aphorism, that those things which have a thin humour are distributed, indeed exceeding in speed of distribution and apposition, but do not have a stable nature, and easily flow away; whereas those which have thicker and more tenacious humours are distributed more slowly, but cling more steadily to the parts to be nourished. For this reason Aristotle rightly and truly says that boiled foods are moister: namely, because of the innate moisture, which is kept in roasting and lost in boiling; for boiled foods are watery, roasted foods abound in their own juice. It must be understood, however, that Aristotle means moderately roasted; otherwise it is agreed that roasting over an immoderate fire dries the outside and inside far too much, and indeed often burns them. From these things being so (and that they are so has been shown by certain proofs), it is easy to pronounce that the dryness of hare's flesh (as also of the wild boar's, of which below) is not, and never can be, a certain sign of coldness, the argument being, among other things, that its blood is excellent in flow and sweetness, neither too diluted and thin nor too thick, but of moderate consistency; and that the flesh follows the temperament and disposition of the blood, as colour, which depends on the goodness or fault of the blood, shows, among other things. For in hypochondria, in suppression of the menses, in fevers and in spleen troubles, when the spleen or liver, whichever of them is the organ for producing or purifying the blood, is hardened, obstructed or affected in any way, we notice that the face grows pale with a liquid that is a peculiarly melancholic colour. But that well-known and not unwitty hendecasyllable attests that the Emperor Alexander Severus obtained beauty and a ruddy face from daily eating hares:

units.la: Pulcrum quod vides esse nostrum regem, Quem Syrum sua detulit propago, Venatus facit, & lepus comesus.
units.tr: The king you see is handsome, our king, whom his Syrian stock produced: he is made handsome by hunting, and by eating hare.

units.la: Ex quo continuum capit leporem.
units.tr: Ever since, he takes a hare every day.

units.la: Et Plinius l. 28. c. 19. gratiam corpori conciliare leporem esum in 7. diebus, vel etiam 9. venustatis decore prorogare scribit, ac in tanta persuasione addit causam aliquam subesse debere.
units.tr: Pliny, book 28, chapter 19, also writes that eating hare gives grace to the body, and that eating it for seven or even nine days extends the bloom of beauty; in such strong persuasion he adds that some cause must lie behind it.

units.la: Quapropter leporina, licet melancholica sit temperatura (tales autem efficacius firmius apponunt mementum, ut alibi demonstratum est) sicca, dura, non tamen ideo frigida, dura, siccaque procreabit sanguinem in corporis officina. Veterum omnium liberis & memoria celebratum & prodita est omne alimentum in calidum in frigidum, cum in sanguinem abierit, nutrit. abierit, calefacere, non quidem sanguinis & ca-lidi innati qualitatem caloris q; gradum, vt Fer-nelius quoq; annotauit lib. 1. de morb. causis, c. 14. sed horum substantiam: laticem enim aeque calidum sanguinem, atque vinum, aut piper vel allium gignere qui censuerit, omnium efficientium causarum vires & naturas tueriet. Ergo etiam leporina sanguinem humoresq; sua natura consentaneos proferet, hoc est, consistentia crassiores, firmiores & tenaciores, sanguinemq; talem, qui spiritus contentos, calidumq; innatum non facile patitur exhalare ac difflare, & quoties externo occursu erroreq; dissipari, in quo vno vel maxime vita nostra prorogande ars consistit. Ad extremum, quod quidam leporinae carnis frigiditatem ex animalis timiditate offendere mordicus contendunt, eamq; ex sanguinis crassitie nigroreq;, vel etiam tenuitate & aquositate aut manere, sciendum, hoc obiectum non magni momenti esse. Quemadmodum enim crassities aterq; sanguinis color non semper sunt frigiditatis indicium (tauri enim sanguis, Aristoteles etiam teste, crassissimus est & nigerrimus, ipsumq; animal calidum valde est) sic etiam ex sanguine dilutiori, tenuiori & aquosiori quocunq; frigiditas, & ex hac timor tanquam illius signum, non semper & protinus est arguenda. In leone quidem siccitati coniuncta calidi tas facit audaciam & magnanimitatem, in lepore vero non item. Itaq; omni prorsus ratione caret, & comi- ferendum ferendum potius quam ulterius refutandum est illorum obiectum, quo leporina frigiditatem defensant. Calidi as inquiunt, & siccitas in leone faciunt audaciam, ergo etiam in lepore, si talis effet, eam excitarent.
units.tr: Therefore hare meat, although its temperament is melancholic (such foods, as I have shown elsewhere, impose their influence more powerfully and firmly), is dry and hard, yet it does not for that reason produce blood that is cold, hard and dry in the workshop of the body. It has been celebrated and handed down by the memory of all the ancients that every food, once it has turned into blood, nourishes whatever it is, warm or cold, by warming it. Not indeed the quality or degree of heat of the blood and the innate heat, as Fernelius also noted in book 1 On the Causes of Diseases, chapter 14, but its substance. For whoever thought that milk makes blood as warm as wine, or pepper, or garlic, would be overturning the powers and natures of all efficient causes. So hare meat too will produce blood and humours consonant with its own nature, that is, thicker in consistency, firmer and more tenacious, and such blood as does not easily let the contained spirits and innate heat breathe out and dissipate, and as often as it is scattered by external encounter and error. In this one thing above all the art of prolonging our life consists. Finally, as to the claim which some stubbornly maintain, that the coldness of hare flesh arises from the timidity of the animal, and that it remains from the thickness and blackness of its blood, or even from its thinness and wateriness, one should know that this objection is of little importance. For just as thickness and either colour of blood are not always a sign of coldness (for bull's blood, as Aristotle also testifies, is very thick and very black, and the animal itself is very hot), so too from thinner, more watery blood of whatever kind, coldness, and from it fear as its sign, is not always and at once to be inferred. In the lion, indeed, heat joined with dryness produces boldness and magnanimity; in the hare, not so. So that objection of theirs, by which they defend the coldness of the hare, is wholly without reason, and should be borne with courtesy rather than refuted further. They say: heat and dryness in the lion produce boldness, therefore in the hare too, if it were such, they would arouse it.

units.la: Amygdala amara resistunt ebrietati, ergo omnia amara resistunt ebrietati. Logicis arrib. vel leniter initiari vitium agnoscent. Caliditas enim & siccitas in leone excitant audaciam, non qua tales, sed quatenus in leone excellunt, est enim sic amara et calida & siccus. Sic amygdalina amaritudo, non etiam alia quaevis, ebrietatem arcet, ex indiuiduitica enim & specifica totius substantiae familiaritate ac proprietate potentiam illam promanare occultior philosophia docet. Hactenus de lepore, cuius in cibatu gratia, succi bonitas ac praestantia paulo diutius me detinuit, immorata est, fecundi namque lepo-ris armos sapienti fellandos Horatium docuit, gaudia non imperitus. Sunt qui clunes fellentur adiuvitissime. Vetulorum armi totaque anterior pars aculeus elixatur, ex aqua & vino addito pipere, postrema vel inassantur, vel panificio incrustantur, siccique durant in multos dies, potissimum hiberno tempore. Pulli & iuvenes inter lautissimas dapes apponuntur, bimestres, & trimestres pretiosiores sunt & suaviores, optimestres quoque commendantur, nec non semestres. Anniculi iam sordescere incipiunt, ultra in confessa damnatione sunt apud quosdam. Vulgata enim paromia
units.tr: Bitter almonds resist drunkenness, therefore all bitter things resist drunkenness. Those trained in logic will recognise the fault, or at least will be lightly initiated into it. For heat and dryness in the lion arouse boldness not as such, but insofar as they excel in the lion; for it is bitter, hot and dry in this way. Thus it is the bitterness of almonds, and not any other whatever, that keeps off drunkenness, for a more hidden philosophy teaches that this power flows from the individual and specific familiarity and property of the whole substance. So far concerning the hare, whose flavour and excellence in eating has kept me a little longer than I intended. For Horace, not unversed in pleasures, taught that the shoulders of a fat hare are to be sucked by the wise. There are those who suck the haunches most eagerly. The shoulders and the whole front part of old hares are boiled in water and wine with pepper added; the hindquarters are either roasted or baked in a pastry crust, and they keep dry for many days, especially in winter. Young hares and juveniles are served among the most lavish feasts; those of two months and three months are more valued and sweeter, the very youngest are also commended, and so are those of six months. Yearlings begin to lose their savour, and beyond that they are condemned by common agreement among some. For the common proverb has it that old hares are food for geese and for bad teeth.

units.la: Ff paræmia dicitur, veteres lepores anserœ malorum dentium escam ess: Certissimum est, tanto deteriores reddi, quam o magis a as processerit. Antiqui loco clauso faciebant pinguès è lepo- rius exceptos, (veteres enim Romani lepores non neglexerunt) quod hodie non obseruatur, passim enim omnis e tempore capiuntur, nā sic clausi virus quoddam redolere deprehenduntur. Le- porum fœcundissimam esse insulam Astyaleam Hesiz_ander Delphicus scripsit, idq; euenisse: ope- ra cuiusdam Anaphæi, qui in insulam istam perdicibus refer am, duos lepores intulit, indeq; tanta exorta mul i udo est, vt quotannis capeꝛentur multa millia, an ea vero non fuisse id a- nimalin infula illa, sed perdices. Sale ass ruasi ac comesi insalubres censentur, perinde ac mustelasalsa.
units.tr: It is most certain that they grow the worse the older they become. The ancients made fat hares caught in an enclosed place (for the old Romans did not neglect hares), which is not practised today, for everywhere they are taken at any time; for hares thus enclosed are found to smell of some poison. Hesiander of Delphi wrote that the island of Astypalaea is most fertile in hares, and that this came about through the work of a certain Anaphaean, who, having brought partridges to that island, introduced two hares, and from these arose so great a multitude that many thousands were caught each year. Yet it may rather have been partridges, not hares, that were on that island. Salted and preserved, they are judged unwholesome to eat, just like salted weasel. ## On the deer.

units.la: De cernina.

Vlæ delitiis & ceruinam seruire in- primis, notum est, Magnatum enim Procerumque mensas opulentant. Est in exemplis fœminas quasdam Principes om- nibus diebus matutinis, carnem ceruinam degustare solitas, longoque æuo caruisse fe- bribus, quoniam id animal febrium morbos non sentire Plinius tradit l.8.c.32. quin potius huic timori mederi. Verum ita demum id ra- tum existimatur, si vulnere vno interierit. Libidinis tempore caro ceruorum vitiatur; foetet enim perinde ac hircorum, quare cibis omninò tunc abdicanda, sicut & æstatis tempore, quo viperis rescuntur & serpentibus, vnde striculosi fiunt, sitim tamen tolerant, eaque incenduntur, ipsi enim norunt, quod, si aquam ante illorum coctionem hauserint, interea tamen per hiemem tutius sumuntur, meliusque concoquuntur. Ex hinnulis verò generosæ principibus ac potentibus epulæ coquinantur, eorum enim carnes salubres, sapo-res; mirè suaues sententiuntur. Porro vita ceruis in confesso longa, post 100 annos aliquos captos cum torquibus aureis, quos Alexander Magnus addiderat, adopertis iam cute in magna obesitate, Plin. l. 8. c. 32. testis est. Aristoteles tamen videtur dubitare, cum nec gestatio nec incrementum hinnuli ita eueniat, quasi vita esset præ longa. Certum est, si ad tantam senectutem pertingerent, carnes eorum omnis succi esse expertes, cibisq; hominum penitus abdicandas. Singulis annis Aprili mense cornua amittere dicuntur, quo tempore etiamnù occultantur interdiu, noctuq; palcuntur, donec cornua recipiant, quæ primum quasi cute vestita, & molli lanugine plumata emittunt, quibus portentosa etiam gula non pepercit, elixata enim in frustula postea friguntur, Regumq; is cibus habetur, de cuius natura dici aliud nihil potest, quam sunt.
units.tr: It is well known that deer meat is especially served among the delicacies of the table, for it enriches the tables of magnates and nobles. There is an example of certain noblewomen of princely rank who used to taste deer flesh every morning, and for a long life were free from fevers, since Pliny records that this animal does not suffer the diseases of fever, and rather cures that fear. But this is thought valid only if the deer died from a single wound. In the mating season the flesh of deer is spoiled, for it smells just like that of goats; therefore it must then be entirely excluded from food, as also in summer, when they shed their skins and cast off vipers and serpents, whence they become scabby. Yet they endure thirst, and are inflamed by it, for they themselves know that if they drink water before it is cooked, it is safer and digests better, though in winter it may be eaten at any time. From young stags, however, the tables of noble princes and the powerful are prepared, for their flesh is judged wholesome and of wonderfully sweet flavour. Moreover, it is admitted that deer live long; Pliny, book 8, chapter 32, bears witness that some were captured after a hundred years or so, wearing golden collars which Alexander the Great had put on them, their hide now covered in great fatness. Aristotle, however, seems to doubt this, since neither the gestation nor the growth of the fawn proceeds as it would if their life were so very long. It is certain that if they reached such great age, their flesh would be entirely devoid of juice and wholly to be excluded from human food. Each year, in the month of April, they are said to lose their horns, at which time they hide by day and graze by night until they grow new horns; these at first come out as if clothed in skin and feathered with soft down. Even prodigious gluttony has not spared them, for they are boiled into little pieces and afterwards fried, and this food is counted among the foods of kings, of whose nature nothing more can be said than that they are what they are.

units.la: Cerui cornua tu nerui scu-tam in cibo rum etiam gloria quam quod vires habere fit existimandum, quales ceruorum cornua, quę millibus remediorum nobilitantur, præcipuè verò aduersantur venenis, suffituque eorum abiguntur serpentes. Ad multos quoq; vsus celebrantur adeps, medulla & sanguis.
units.tr: The horns, sinews and hide of deer are esteemed as food no less than for their strength. Their horns, which are celebrated for thousands of remedies, are especially opposed to poisons, and serpents are driven away by their fumes. Their fat, marrow and blood are also celebrated for many uses.

units.la: De caprilla, hœdina, hircina.
units.tr: Of the she-goat, the kid and the he-goat.

units.la: CApris sacerdotem adeo abstinere voluerunt prisci, vt non modo attingere, sed ne nominare quidem aut appellare liceret, siue quod id animal luxuriosum & olidū abhorrerent, siue ⁊ tanquā morbidū timerent. Comitiali enim morbo laborare capras, nec non febribus graues autores tradūt, ideoq; animam forsan iis quam ouibus ardentiorem, concubitusq; calidiores esse. Flatus ructusq; ciere, choleramq; morbum parere, Hippocr. auctor est, quod tamen de nimis tenellis, nimisq; adultis, & non probè coctis vel præparatis accipiendum esse quidam existimant. Suauiorem caprinam esse, minusque malam, cum syluæ primum noua frequentiq; fronde germinant, virgultaque turgescunt, experientia docuit. Est in exemplis, athletam quendam Thebanum cunctos alios robore præcelluisse, quod sc. caprilla carne vescerentur, quam valentissimi esse alimēti, ob firmū, lentumq; succum, nec facilè dissipabilem apud Atheneum reperitur.
units.tr: The ancients were so careful to keep away from the goat in connection with the priest that it was not lawful to touch it, or even to name or mention it. Either they abhorred the animal as lustful and foul-smelling, or they feared it as diseased. Serious authors report that goats suffer from the falling sickness and also from fevers, and so perhaps their spirit is more fiery than that of sheep and their mating hotter. Hippocrates is the authority that goat meat produces wind and belching and causes cholera. Some think this should be understood of very tender or overgrown goats, and of those not properly cooked or prepared. Experience has shown that kid meat is sweeter and less harmful when the woods first put forth fresh, thick foliage and the shoots swell. There is an example of a certain Theban athlete who surpassed all others in strength because they ate goat meat. According to Athenaeus, it is found to be a most powerful food because of its firm and tenacious juice, which is not easily dissipated.

units.la: Sed hœdina inter eximias & præcipuè sa-lubres lubres epulas perpetuò adnumerata est, ficciorem enim agnina, esuiquè aptiorem esse communi consensu traditur, qnin & cætero-rum quadrupedum carnibus anteponitur: Hesiodus l.2. &c. hœdorum pri-mogenitorum carnem maximè commendat, vt boni succi, facilisque coctionis. Gedeone hœdum caprarium coxisse, angeloq;, quem inuitarat, in conuiuio apposuisse, sacra mo-nimenta testantur. Sapiunt autem tunc ma-ximè hœdi cum herbarum sunt expertes, bi-mestres, atque etiam trimestres, si mater la-ctea abundet, adultiores enim & ab vbere de-pulsi saporis suauitatisq; gratiam amittunt. Nullam autem aliam magis idoneam à mor-bo se recolligentibus quidam promittunt, quin etiam otio deditis, & non laborantibus salubriter editur, grauiores verò operas ex-ercentibus insalubriter, facile enim alimen-tum eius dissipatur atque euanescit. Galenus 7.de San.tuen. Senibus non incommodam spondet. Manditur elixa pariter atque tosta, & quidem recens. Cocta, quæ refrixerit, ca-lente cefetur vtilior Mauritanorum opinio-ne. Galenus frigidam esse edendam voluit in commentario l.4.de rat.vict.in acutis. Quod Plutarchus prodidit de caprina, qui eam gu-starint aut attigerint, comitiali morbo afflici, auditur verius quam creditur.
units.tr: But kid meat has always been counted among the outstanding and especially wholesome dishes. By common consent it is said to be drier than lamb and better suited to those who fast, and it is even preferred to the flesh of other quadrupeds. Hesiod, in book 2 and elsewhere, especially commends the flesh of the firstborn kids, as having good juice and easy digestion. The sacred records attest that Gideon cooked a kid of the goats and set it before the angel whom he had invited to dine. Kids taste best when they have not yet eaten grass, at two or even three months old, provided the mother's milk is plentiful. Older kids, weaned from the udder, lose the grace of their flavour and sweetness. Some promise that no other meat is more suitable for those recovering from illness, and that it is eaten healthfully by those given to leisure and not labouring, but unhealthily by those who do heavier work, for its nourishment is easily dissipated and vanishes. Galen, in book 7 of On Hygiene, promises that it is not unsuitable for the old. It is eaten boiled as well as roasted, and fresh. Cooked meat is more useful when it has been allowed to cool than when it is eaten warm, according to the opinion of the Mauritanians. Galen wished it to be eaten cold, in his commentary on book 4 of On Diet in Acute Diseases. What Plutarch reported about goat meat, that those who have tasted or touched it are afflicted with the falling sickness, is heard rather than believed.

units.la: Cæterum præclaram in medicinis laudem ad varios vsus obtinuerunt, caprinū lac, sanguis, fel, adeps, pilus, fimus, vrina, cornu, ie-cur, femina, caput. De lacte eiusq; inprimis fero suo loco, vbi de lactis differentiis. Sanguis cum medulla coctus cōtra toxica vene-na sumitur, nec non dysenteriam & hydropisin, arefactus verò calculi medicamentis vtiliter adhibetur. Iecur caprinum efficatum vespertinam aciem restituere dicitur his, quos lusciosos & nyctalopas vocant. Fel plurimis modis ad oculorum caligines, cicatrices, albugines, pterygia, rupturas tunicularū, celebratur cum melle vel mulieris lacte, aut alio cōueniente liquore diftemperatu. Adeps in sorbitione aliqua sumptus intestina laesa & corrosa mirè sarcit, ita tamē vt protinus hauriatur frigida: hœdi verò feminū cineré rupta intestina efficaciter resarcire à grauib. autoribus proditū reperio. Cornuū pilorūq; fumo fugari serpentes prisce autoritatis est. Pilorū verò cinis calculos pellit. Cornu ipso suffiri vuluam vtilissimū putatur. Vrina apostemata & suppurationes lanari, cum melle permixta, quidam certo promittunt. Caprini capitis cū suis pilis decocti succu laudatissimū aiunt in intestinis ruptis. Sed caprarū fimus, cuius cerberrimus vsus est, Galeno teste, digerentis & acris facultatis est, vt induratis scirrhorum in modu tumorib. etiam congruat. Ad aquā intercute, splenis affectus, calculos pellendos, dolo-
units.tr: Goat products have otherwise won a notable reputation in medicine for various uses: goat's milk, blood, gall, fat, hair, dung, urine, horn, liver, womb and head. Of the milk, and especially its whey, I shall speak in its proper place, where I discuss the differences of milk. Blood boiled with marrow is taken against poisons, and also against dysentery and dropsy; when dried, it is usefully applied in remedies for stones. The goat's liver, dried, is said to restore the evening sight of those whom they call purblind or night-blind. Gall is celebrated in many ways for clouds on the eyes, scars, whiteness, pterygia and ruptures of the tunics, mixed with honey or a woman's milk, or another suitable liquid. Fat taken in some broth wonderfully mends injured and corroded intestines, provided it is swallowed at once while cold. I find it reported by serious authors that the ashes of kid testicles effectively repair ruptured intestines. The smoke of horns and hair is, by ancient authority, a means of driving away serpents. The ash of the hair expels stones. Horn itself used as a fumigation of the womb is thought most useful. Some confidently promise that urine mixed with honey heals abscesses and suppurations. A decoction of the goat's head with its hair is said to be most praised for ruptured intestines. But goat's dung, whose most excellent use, according to Galen's testimony, has a digesting and sharp quality, is suitable, in the manner of hardened scirrhous tumours, for dropsy, disorders of the spleen, expelling stones, and the pains

units.la: dolores podagricos & Ischiadicos mitigan- dos varius eius vsus est, nec non in extergen- dis psoricis humiditatib, digerendi sq; paro- tidib, ac diuturniorib bubonibus. Hœdorū deniq; sanguinem recentem cum aceto cal- factum vtilissimè dysentericis propinari cer- tis documētis patefactū est. Superest hircina, q omniū animal ūab omnib fœdissima ha- bita est, sicut ipsum animal fœdissimū esse in conststo est, ideoq; in cibo damnarū. Castra- tos tamen eximiè obseruari ac pinguescere, gu- statuq; non ingratos esse quidā experti sunt.
units.tr: of gout and sciatica that need to be relieved. Its use is varied: it is also applied to cleanse moist psoric eruptions, to disperse parotid swellings, and to treat long-lasting buboes. Finally, it has been shown by certain proofs that fresh kid's blood, warmed with vinegar, is most usefully given to those suffering from dysentery. There remains the he-goat, which has been regarded as the most foul of all animals, just as the animal itself is agreed to be most foul, and so it is condemned as food. Yet some who have tried it have found that castrated he-goats are remarkably well kept and fatten, and their flesh is not unpleasant to the taste.

units.la: Sanguiné hircorū præsentissimū ac validum lithontribon esse experimenta docuerunt. lecoris eorū dissectisanies efficaciter sangui- nè sistere dicitur. Hircinus verò adeps cū ca- præ simo & croco, sinapiq; podagricis non inutiliter illinitur. Carnes deniq; hircinas e- pilepticis auxiliari Clem. Alexandrinus tra- dit, quod equidē mirum, cū de capris contra- rium sit proditū, quod tamen de ouib. verisi- milius videri quidā non vulgaris literatu æ existimant, nempe, quoniā capite ferè semper in terrā inclinato, halitus prauos, humiditate sq; sæpe maligná in caput trahunt, subinde q; ob id in sacrū morbū incurrant: caprae verò, q alto capite vtplurimū pascunt, siccęq; sunt, ac febrire magis dicunt, quomodo ouibus epilepsię magis, vt q à larga pituita oriatur, subiiciant, nā admodū le intelligere fatetur. nisi cæteris animalib.comitiali morbo magis capras tentari quis dixerit ob meatuu densitatem & anguistiam, quam arguit vocis tenuitas. Arist.in probl. quærens, cur homines soli vel maxime inter animalia oculis peruertantur, inter alia hanc affert causam, quod sc. foli in animalium genere fiant epileptici, epilepsia aute oculorum peruerfione inducat. Quam sententia falsam omnino esse quidam arbitrantur moti duobus: vnu est, quod ipse Arist.l.de animalib. nonnulla recenset, quæ iisdem morbis, quib. homines tentari scribit, vt oues: alteru, quod in lib.de sacro morbo, qui vt Hipp. à Galeno in t.progn.text.4.& lib.de sanguis in arteriis continentur, nec non à Cælio Aureliano l.1.pass.chron.c.4. citatur, scriptum est, oues & maxime capras epileptico morbo nō parū obnoxias esse. Qui certè Hippocratis locus Aristoteli repugnat, cuius sententia sic moderanda est. Mercurialis l.4.variar.left. docet, quod homo vel maxime oculis peruertitur, quoniam vel solus vel maxime in infantia epilepticus fit. Vnde in l.de somno & vigil præceptu dedit, vt non solum pueri verum etiam nutrices à vino, præsertim nigro abstinerent, tanquam id magis quam album ad caput euaporet. Pueros autem & infantiam epilepsia maxime tentari experientia notum est, tum quia superfluitatibus abundant, tum quia neruosas partes non habet validas, tete Galen in expositione aphor. 25.l.3.
units.tr: Experiments have shown that the blood of he-goats is a very ready and powerful lithontriptic. Their liver, cut up, is said to stop bleeding effectively. Hircine fat, mixed with goat's dung, saffron and mustard, is applied not unprofitably to the gouty. Finally, Clement of Alexandria teaches that the flesh of he-goats helps epileptics. This is indeed surprising, since the opposite has been reported of goats; yet some scholars of no common learning think it is more likely true of sheep. Their heads are nearly always bent towards the ground, so they draw foul vapours and often harmful moisture into the head, and so they sometimes fall into the sacred disease. Goats, however, which mostly feed with their heads held high, and are dry, are said to be more prone to fever, just as sheep are more subject to epilepsy, which arises from abundant phlegm. For he himself admits he understands very little of this. Unless someone should say that goats are more troubled by the falling sickness than other animals, because of the density and narrowness of their passages, which the thinness of their voice proves. Aristotle, in the Problems, asks why men alone, or most of all among animals, are perverted in their eyes, and among other causes he gives this: that men alone among the kind of animals become epileptic, and epilepsy induces a perversion of the eyes. Some think this opinion wholly false, moved by two things. The first is that Aristotle himself, in his book On Animals, lists several animals which he writes are subject to the same diseases as men, such as sheep. The second is that in the book On the Sacred Disease, which is cited by Galen in his commentary on Hippocrates' Prognostics, text 4, and in On the Blood Contained in the Arteries, and by Caelius Aurelianus in Chronic Passions, book 1, chapter 4, it is written that sheep, and especially goats, are not a little liable to the epileptic disease. This passage of Hippocrates certainly conflicts with Aristotle, and Aristotle's opinion must be moderated accordingly. Mercurialis, in book 4 of Various Lessons, teaches that man is most of all perverted in the eyes, since he alone, or most of all, becomes epileptic in infancy. Hence in On Sleep and Waking he gave the precept that not only boys but also nurses should abstain from wine, especially black wine, as it rises to the head more than white. That boys and infants are most often affected by epilepsy is known from experience, both because they abound in superfluous humours and because they do not have strong nervous parts, as Galen says in his exposition of aphorism 25 of book 3.

units.la: De caprilla ferina.
units.tr: On the wild goat.

units.la: NUmerosissimum ferarum caprarum ef-fegenus conflat, inq; plurimas fimilitu-dines reperire est transfiguratas. Sunt, caprea, sunt rupicapra, sunt ibices velocitatis admiranda, & dama seu caprea platycornes à cornuum latitudine. Inter agrestia autem animalia posterior & moderna medicina jucundi-oris saporis carnes capreas & capreolos obtinere, facile concoqui, probumq; præstare alimentum, experimento vult, eaq; omnia pernicitati, cursi-bus recurfibusq; accepta refert. Elixas vero quam aßas salubriores quidam putant, sic enim siccitatem ajunt temperari. Hodie magnatum ac potentiorum mensas exornant, sed inaf-fata magis quam elixa. De caprarum porro Amblyferarum jecore spectabiliore potentia in medicina opia, est, quam villicarum, tostum enim id & commanducatum aciem oculorum recreare, obtufamq; clariorem reddere locupletissimis autoribus est proditum. Caprarum meminit Martialis, cum inquit, Pendentem summâ capream de rupe videbis, Casuram speres, decipit illa canes,
units.tr: The genus of wild goats is very numerous and is found to take on very many forms. There are the roe deer, the chamois, and the ibex of remarkable swiftness, and the fallow deer, or the broad-horned roe deer, so called from the breadth of its horns. Among wild animals, later and modern medicine holds that the flesh of roe deer and young roe deer has a pleasant taste, is easily digested, and provides a good nourishment, as experience shows, and it attributes all of this to their nimbleness and their running to and fro. Some think boiled meat is more wholesome than roast, for they say boiling tempers its dryness. Today they adorn the tables of magnates and the powerful, though they serve it raw rather than boiled. Moreover, the liver of wild goats has a more notable power in medicine than that of domestic goats; for it is reported by the most authoritative authors that when it is roasted and chewed, it refreshes the sharpness of the eyes and makes dull sight clearer. Martial mentions goats when he says: "You will see a roe hanging from the top of a rock; you would expect it to fall, but it deceives the dogs."

units.la: quod tamen de rupicapris, quæ cursu atq; recursu pernici per petras & montes, quo libuerit, exultant, intelligendum est.
units.tr: This, however, must be understood of the rock goats, which by their swift running and leaping exult over rocks and mountains wherever they please.

units.la: De agnina, vervecina, arietina, ovilla.
units.tr: On Lamb, Mutton, Ram and Sheep Meat

units.la: PEcus ovillum mille in re alimentaria praestat vsus: quanta enim gloria est in lanificio pro corporis tutela, tanta est carni, lactis, caseoque ad idem cibandum. Exordiri autem prius placuit ab infantibus, qui a parentibus.
units.tr: Sheep serve human food in a thousand ways. For as great as the glory of their wool is in protecting the body, so great is the value of their flesh, milk and cheese in feeding it. I have decided to begin with the young, the lambs, which come from their parents.

units.la: Agninam in antiquorum epulis praecipuam fuisse Graecorum Latinorumque monumenta testantur. Frequentius hodie manditur hieme assa magis quam elixa, sunt enim agni humidioris & vividioris naturae, qua de causa ficcioris temperaturae naturis, tabidis item & extenuatis praestant. Summam nobilitatem & gloriam obtinuerunt in elegantioribus mensis, qui a binis ouibus diuius aluntur, nec herbarum nouerunt pabula, tum enim suauiores, salubrioresque deprehenduntur, quanto enim junior agnus, tanto pituitosior concoctuque difficilior. Ut autem suaues, salubrioresque evadant agni, requiritur ouium plenus nutricatus, hae enim si bene alantur, bonos praestabunt fœtus, a parentibus enim male enutritis morbidisve, fieri qui potest, vt fœtus vitiatum temperamentum non contrahat? Apud Homerum in epulis agnina celebrata reperitur, quam tamen Samaritanis & Hierosolymi lymitanis Amos cap. 6. exprobrat, vt qui comederent agnos de grege, hoc est, egregias, pingues, & ex toto ouium grege lectissimas. Tenellas oues, quod omittere hic noluerim, ante maturum tempus venere prudentes futurae pestis indicium esse quidam affirmant, quod quidem ego quotidiane observatione relinquo.
units.tr: The monuments of the Greeks and Latins testify that lamb was the chief dish at the banquets of the ancients. Today it is eaten most often roasted rather than boiled, in winter. Lambs have a moist and lively nature, and for that reason they are better for those of drier temperament, and for the wasted and emaciated. They have gained the highest reputation at the more elegant tables, where they are fed for two months on milk and have not yet tasted grass, for then they are found to be sweeter and more wholesome. The younger the lamb, the more phlegmatic it is and the harder to digest. For lambs to turn out sweet and wholesome, a full nursing is required, for if the ewes are well fed they will produce good offspring. For how can offspring avoid a faulty constitution if their parents were poorly nourished or diseased? In Homer lamb is found at feasts. Yet Amos, chapter 6, rebukes the Samaritans and the people of Jerusalem for eating lambs from the flock, that is, the choicest, fattest and most select of the whole flock. Some maintain that tender sheep brought to market before their proper time are a sign of coming pestilence. I will not omit this here, though I leave it to daily observation to decide.

units.la: Ouillam, sicut & arietinam, elegantiorum quidem in epulis damnari inuenio, propterea, quod illa excrementosior sit succique pariter iniquioris, haec vero odorem & saporem virosum referat, succi bonitate careat, vixque conficiatur, & ab hircina determinima habeatur. Verum multorum mensas ovillam opulentare, nec infimam gratiam retinere notum est. Pabula ovium sale respersa efficaciora sentiuntur, magisque eas opimant, carnesque reddunt salubriores. Anniculae non improbantur, sed quo plus vltra, eo difficilioris censentur coctionis. Vere porro primo ac medio ouillum pecus praestantius haberi, sicut omnia animantia, quae humili vescuntur herba, Galenus voluit. Iuuenibus etiam ovillam non malum cibum esse, senibus vero eandem minus commodare, atque hac multo minus agnam idem 5.de sanitat. tuenda scriptum reliquit.
units.tr: I find that ewe mutton, like ram meat, is condemned at the tables of the more refined, because it is more full of waste and its juice is correspondingly poorer, while ram meat has a rank smell and taste, lacks the goodness of juice, is hardly digested, and is regarded as little different from goat meat. Yet it is well known that ewe mutton furnishes the tables of many and holds no lowly favour. Sheep fed on pasture sprinkled with salt are found to be more effective, and they fatten them more, and make their flesh more wholesome. Yearlings are not disapproved of, but the older the sheep, the harder they are judged to be to digest. Galen held that in spring, early and mid-spring, sheep are better than other animals that feed on low grass. He also wrote in his fifth book On Preserving Health that mutton is not a bad food for the young, but less suitable for the old, and still less so for lamb.

units.la: Mirabilis hujus animalis merito ducitur
units.tr: Its marvellous fruitfulness is rightly considered

units.la: fœcunditas, vt quæ quotidianæ populationi gulæ sufficere queat, quippe locupletes, plebs media, pariterqj infima vervecinam vorant: & paucos reperias,qui eam fastidiant. Mauritanam autem Medicinam auctoritatem illam,quam in cibis tenet,vervecinæ tribuisse reperitur,antiquior non inuenitur. Verueces porro appellant arietes catratos,quibus sc.tesiculi exemti sunt, habitioris acquirendi corporis gratiâ, qui enim ad prolem generandam tenetur, dicitur aries. Anniculos verueces, bimos etiam trimosve,inprimis commendari certum est, quos & altiles facere inuentum est. Constat Ludoicum Borbonium Cardinalem in Belgica Gallia, nec non plures alios, nostris vulgaribus proceriores amplioresque vervecesaluisse, quos obesitare insignes aulicis proceribus ostentabat, dabatque epulandos. Generosissimos & suauissimos ad cibos educant Germania & Gallia. Italia non vsq; adeo his nobilitatur. Piftorienses tamen in gloria esse compertum est. Castrari denique agnos, nisi quinquemestres, præmaturum tradunt.
units.tr: fecundity, so that it can suffice for the daily gluttony of the appetite. Rich and middling folk and the lowest of the common people alike devour mutton, and you will find few who turn up their noses at it. No older source is found that gives mutton the authority in food which Mauritanian medicine holds. Moreover, they call castrated rams wethers, those whose testicles have been removed in order to acquire a fatter body, for the ram kept for breeding is the one called a ram. It is certain that yearling wethers, and also those of two or three years, are especially recommended, and it has been found that they fatten well. It is well known that Cardinal Louis of Bourbon in Belgian Gaul, and several others, raised wethers taller and larger than our common ones, and displayed them fattened to distinguished courtiers and gave them to be eaten. Germany and Gaul breed the finest and sweetest wethers for the table. Italy is not so renowned for them, though the people of Pistoia are known to be famous for them. Finally, they say it is too early to castrate lambs unless they are five months old.

units.la: De bubula, bubalina, vaccina, vitulina, taurina, iuuencorum & iuuencarum carnibus.
units.tr: On beef, buffalo, veal, calf, bull, and steer and heifer flesh.

units.la: POsteritati minime probro dandum est, quod ad vita vsu bubulum pecus, in tanta praesertim fecunditate transtulerit:
units.tr: It is least of all to be cast as a reproach upon posterity that it has put the cattle herd to use as food, especially given such great fecundity.

units.la: Licet enim apud maiores olim bubulis visceribus vesci, scelus haberetur, maxima tamen & innumera mortalibus praestare cibaria expertum & compertum habetur.
units.tr: For although among our ancestors eating beef was once thought a crime, it is nevertheless known from experience and observation that it provides mortals with very great and countless food.

units.la: Bubulam summo olim apud Graecos in honore fuisse, satis testatur Heroum vitus apud Homerum, conviviorumq; & nuptialium epularum structura: Constat enim non solum bubulam, sed quorumuis animalium carnes, assas semper fere fuisse appositas. Agamemnon Rex convivio excipiens Ajacem aut Nestorem, cosas boum assas posuit: Menelaus Telemacho, Ulyssis filio, hospitio comiter accepto, costam bubulam appositam, ac in summa, bubula esum Homeri temporibus vsitatum fuisse Atheneus quoque probat i.lib.cap.4. Nullo autem non tempore epulas prabet bubula. Verum hieme magis placet & frequentior est: Elixatur pariter atque inassatur, & vtraq; coctura gratissima est, praesertim opima & prapinguis. Aulicis culinis ampla & pinguedine refertiora vocantur frusta regia, regia, quasi regia mensa digna, folentq; prima fere mensa apponi elixa, eque sinapis intinctu eduntur magna gula aviditate & irritamento: rarius assumantur, preter enim costas ex toto bove verubus nihil torreri solet, qua inter elegantiores esas hiemis reponuntur a quibusdam, salviaque confixa expetuntur: crebritu eduntur ex condimento atro, vini acetiq; momento, sale ac pipere concinnato. Lautiores piperatum condimentum vocant. Caterum laniariorum fraus & dolus hic detegenda morbos sæpe boues maffantium, quos tamen macellare in amplioribus urbibus lege cautum est. Cognoscuntur autem morbosi, cum fœno aut pabulo objecto abstinent, quo negletto certum est magnas sæpe clades vescentibus accidisse, præsertim cum deprehensum sit, tabe pulmonis, morbisq; aliis pene confectos jugulatos esse, inq; cibos admissos, carnibus scilicet sale alendo familiis asservatis. Quâ avaritia quid quasi pestilentius? vitiatam enim carnem vitiosos humores ac sanguinem generare non verisimile, sed verissimum est. Idem qui scilicet ad cultrum boves emunt, non considerant, quæ rei rustica & pastoritia periti examinant, attentem scilicet calorem & nutricatum, tantum si pingues sint & habitiori corpore, pragrandibus enim amplisq; dignitas, & laus maxima, cuiusmodi nobilissima graminosissimaq; regiones alunt, perq; vniuersum fere Germania orbem aliialtius pleneque saginatos mittunt. Sed & bodie in plerisque Germaniae locis saginati amplitudiniśque dignitate spectabiles atque insignes cernuntur. Est vero certa bovos saginandi ars, quae ad tantam pinguitudinis molem eos extumescere facit. Galenus herba adulta & proceriore facta, jamque ad semen properante bovis optime oris, crassiores bonoque succo pleniores fieri censet. Multi herba antumnali & post prata secta proveniente, eleganter saginari boves existimant, quem morem multi Germaniae populí ubique observant, in isto enim pabulo multum emolumenti esse compererunt. Quidam bubulae ad mentum in sanitate prorogandae improbant, atramentum bilem, crassiorem quoque genere sanguinem affirmant, propterea quoque largum crebriusque ea vescentes, si obnoxii fuerint alicui aegritudini splenicae, ut quartanae, scabiei, lepra, cibo esuque eius opportuniores reddi, facilius quoque tentari. Verum de sale condita & jusspensa adaccipiendum. In amplis enim familiis boves ma us simul ac faemina condiuntur ad cibaria annua famulorum operarumque, deinde muria exemta pensilis servatur caro, quae adeo induratur ut longiori etiam coctura postea pertinacissime dometur, gustatuque interdum suavitatem referat nullam. Potores hac commendata sibi habent tanquam acerrimum sitis stimulum, eque ac pernas sullas. Ego otiosis et sedentariis, literarumque studiosis parcum hanc attingendam pramoneo, utpote
units.tr: That beef was once held in the highest honour among the Greeks is sufficiently attested by the feasts of heroes in Homer and by the arrangement of banquets and wedding feasts. For it is established that not only beef but the flesh of every animal was almost always set before guests roasted. King Agamemnon, receiving Ajax or Nestor at dinner, set out roasted ox ribs; Menelaus, courteously receiving Telemachus, son of Ulysses, as a guest, set before him a beef rib. In sum, that beef was eaten in Homer's times Athenaeus also proves, in book 1, chapter 4. Beef provides food at every season. But in winter it pleases more and is more frequent. It is boiled as well as roasted, and both methods of cooking are very pleasing, especially when the meat is fat and well covered with fat. In court kitchens the thick, fattier pieces are called "royal morsels", regia, as if worthy of a royal table. Boiled meat is usually served as the first course, and is eaten dipped in mustard with great greed and appetite. Roast meat is taken less often; for apart from the ribs, nothing from a whole ox is usually roasted on the spit. Among the more refined, these roasted ribs are put aside by some for winter meals, and are sought out when pierced with sage. They are commonly eaten with a black seasoning, a dash of vinegar and wine, prepared with salt and pepper; the more luxurious call it the peppered seasoning. Moreover, here the fraud and trickery of the butchers must be exposed: they often slaughter oxen that are diseased, though the law in the larger cities forbids this in the butchers' shops. The sick ones are recognised when they refuse the hay or fodder offered them. When this is neglected, it is certain that great disasters have often befallen those who eat them, especially since it has been discovered that animals almost worn out by wasting of the lungs and other diseases are slaughtered and admitted to food, the meat being salted and kept to feed households. What is more pestilential than such greed? For it is not merely likely but most certain that spoiled flesh generates corrupt humours and blood. Those who buy oxen for the knife do not consider what those skilled in farming and herding examine: namely the innate heat and the nourishment, provided only that the animals are fat and of a fuller body. For the very large and ample ones have dignity and the greatest praise, such as the most noble and grassy regions nourish; and throughout almost the whole of Germany others send them, higher and more fully fattened. But even today in most places in Germany they are seen as fattened and remarkable for their size and dignity. There is indeed a sure art of fattening oxen, which makes them swell to such a mass of fat. Galen thinks that the ox's mouth is best when the herb is grown tall and mature and is hastening towards seed, and that the oxen become thicker and fuller of good juice. Many think oxen are fattened elegantly on the autumn grass that comes up after the meadows are mown; this custom many peoples of Germany observe everywhere, for they have found much profit in that fodder. Some disapprove of beef for maintaining health, saying that it produces black bile and a rather thick blood; for this reason they say that those who eat it largely and often, if they are subject to any splenic illness, such as quartan fever, scabies, or leprosy, are made more liable to it by eating it, and more easily attacked. But this must be understood of meat preserved in salt and hung up. For in large households the castrated bulls and cows are salted together for the year's food of servants and labourers; then the meat, taken out of the brine, is kept hanging, and it becomes so hardened that afterwards it is subdued only by very long cooking, and sometimes it has no pleasant taste at all. Drinkers value this meat as a very sharp goad to thirst, as they do salted tongues. I advise that this meat be touched sparingly by those who are idle and sedentary, and by students of letters, inasmuch as

units.la: Bubula quibusdam cur improbata? vtpote parum vel nihil alentem, diutissimeque in stomacho morantem, concoctuque difficilimam, & coctam licet vel confectam, peßimum tamen crassumque succum in corpus distribuentem, dissecta enim rubet & insigniter dura est. Interim negari non potest, appetentiam quandoque momento eius assumto excitari atque recreari praesertim in vini avidioribus.
units.tr: Why is beef disapproved by some? Because it nourishes little or nothing, stays a very long time in the stomach, is very hard to digest, and even when cooked or thoroughly done, distributes a very bad and thick juice into the body; for when cut it is red and remarkably tough. Meanwhile it cannot be denied that the appetite is sometimes stirred and refreshed by taking it in, especially in those more eager for wine.

units.la: Ad extremum non praetereundum, Galenum 2. de simplic. medicam. referre, coquos, antequam velpisces, vel carnes assarent, oleo inungere solitos, credit ideo hoc ab ipsis factitatum esse, ne exteriores partes vi ignis exusta consumerentur, interiorumque coctionem impedirent.
units.tr: Finally, it should not be passed over that Galen, in book 2 of On Simple Medicines, reports that cooks, before roasting fish or meat, were accustomed to anoint them with oil. He thinks this was done so that the outer parts would not be consumed by the force of the fire and the cooking of the inner parts impeded.

units.la: Mercurialis l. 1. variar. lect. id facium potius esse existimat, ne carnium intestinum & proprium humor extra flueret, sed intus cohibitus coctusque iucundiorem cibum palato redderet. Oleum enim occludere extimos corporum meatus, quo minus quicquam effluere queat, & Galenum fassus est, & Alexander, qui in probl. ea ratione animalia infecta ab oleo enecari disputat, prohibita ex olei obstipatione nativa eorum spiratione: & hoc passo assata intellexisse Aristotelem verisimile est, quando in 4 de mixtorum affectibus lib. ea elixatis humidiora facit. Quanquam assata etiam intus humidiora evadunt, cum multo igne statim extimis crusta ceu lorica inducitur, qua induta humor intraneus non ita promite valet exorbere atque foras. forat erumpere, quod in assandus cumprimis observandum, in pluribus enim humor ille nutrimentalis vitignis, elicitur atq; consumitur, nihilq; generatini humoris retinetur, unde minus etiam nutrimenti vescentium corporibus accedere in confesso est.
units.tr: Mercurialis, in book 1 of Variae Lectiones, thinks this was rather done so that the meat's inner moisture and proper juice would not flow out, but being held within and cooked, would make the food more pleasing to the palate. For oil closes the outer pores of bodies, so that nothing can flow out; Galen has admitted this, and so has Alexander, who in the Problems argues that animals killed by oil are destroyed in this way, their breathing being prevented by the natural obstruction of the oil. And it is likely that Aristotle understood roasted meat in this sense, since in the fourth book On the Affections of Mixed Bodies he makes boiled meat moister. Yet roasted meat also becomes moister inside, when a crust is at once drawn over the outside by a strong fire, like a breastplate; once this is put on, the inner moisture cannot so easily force its way out and burst forth. This must be especially observed in roasting, for in most cases that nutritive moisture is drawn out and consumed by the force of the fire, and no moisture is retained to generate; whence it is admitted that less nourishment also reaches the bodies of those who eat it.

units.la: Boves foeminas notum est plerunq; vetulas lanio tradi, cum aut seneßute sterilescunt, aut alia de causa inutiles evadunt. Sed sic effoetae ad elegantiores cibos damnantur, pauperumque praecipue vulgi mensas subeunt, magis enim insalubris earum caro, quam vetulorum bovum censetur.
units.tr: It is well known that female cows, being old, are commonly handed over to the butcher when they become barren through age, or otherwise become useless. But being thus worn out they are condemned to less fine foods, and go especially to the tables of the poor common people; for their flesh is considered more unwholesome than that of old oxen.

units.la: Veteribus bubalum seu bufalum (quo nomine bouem ferum & sylvestrem significari inuenio) non fuisse incognitum (ut quidam putarunt) probari potest ex Flavio Josepho l. 8. antiquit. vbi quotidianos sumtus mensae regiae Salomonis enumerans etiam feros bubalos una cum cervis refert. Quin & Amos horum mentionem facit, Numquid, inquit, currere queunt in petris equi, aut arari potest in bubalis? vbi Bened. Arius Montanus stupidius, quam boui bubalo ingenium esse & indocilius. Armenta horum in Italia circa Pisas videntur, & in Romanorum agris, nam Roma carnem eorum non venalem tantum esse, Iudaeis in gratissimo cibatu, verum etiam ex lacte eius animalis caseos conficiebat Roma aliuq; in locis in pretio, maximi etiam cibi, sed qui sumti difficilius transeant. Gg Columella scribit. Phil. Camerarius in meditation. hujus cent. 2. testatur de caseo hac vera esse, enumq; cum nausea id expertum, atq; bubalinam carnem insuetis dura esse coctionis, dulcoreq; suo insipidam. Alii tanto lentore praeditam eam afferunt, ut in parietem adaelta tenacissime adhaereat, qua de causa mensis nitidioribus abdicandam censent, idq; juratissimis affirmant verbis. Sed forsan ventriculo illi non usq; adeo fuerunt robusto.
units.tr: That the buffalo, or bubalus (a name which I find to mean a wild and savage ox), was not unknown to the ancients, as some have thought, can be proved from Flavius Josephus, book 8 of the Antiquities, where, listing the daily expenses of King Solomon's table, he mentions wild buffaloes along with deer. Indeed Amos also makes mention of them: "Can horses run upon rocks, or can one plough with buffaloes?" where Benedictus Arias Montanus says, rather stupidly, that the buffalo has a nature more dull and less teachable than an ox. Herds of them are seen in Italy around Pisa and in the fields of the Romans; for Rome not only sold their flesh, a most welcome food to the Jews, but also made cheeses from the milk of that animal, which were valued in Rome and elsewhere, a very great food, though they pass through the body with difficulty when eaten. Columella writes this. Philip Camerarius, in his Meditations, century 2, testifies that these things about the cheese are true, and that he himself experienced it with nausea, and that buffalo flesh is hard to digest for those unaccustomed to it, and insipid despite its sweetness. Others say it has such a stickiness that when thrown against a wall it adheres most tenaciously; for which reason they think it should be excluded from elegant tables, and they affirm this with the most sworn words. But perhaps those men did not have stomachs so robust.

units.la: Boves adulti nondum castrati, quiq; admissura fervantur, tauri vocantur. Horum carnem omnium fere sententiis proscriptam reperio atq; damnatam. Castrati autem ante bimatum (postea enim non debent, nam duri sunt, Varrone teste) nondum laborib fracti, mediaq; atatis, utiliores habentur, vehementer enim alunt, alimentumq; quod subministrant, non facile dissipatur. Raro tamen macellum intrant, nisi arure fracto, aut alia causa inutiles ad agricul-turam fuerint. Laudem taurorum siluisse hic naturalium rerum periti vitio vertent, qui eo-feruarunt, licet hoc animal in libidinem admo-dum effœratum sit & concitatum, non tamen fa-pius quam bus in die inscendere, a conceptu vera ipsius vacca, modestum castumq; ulterius nihil moliri, unde taur in hieroglyphicis Ægyptiorum temperantia & continentia fuit symbolum. Quo libidinosi monentur, ut ab hoc bruto exemplum sumentes in conjugio alienos amores non sectentur.
units.tr: Adult oxen not yet castrated, kept for breeding, are called bulls. I find the flesh of these almost universally rejected and condemned by all opinions. Castrated ones before two years old (for afterwards they should not be eaten, for they are tough, as Varro testifies), not yet broken by labours and of middle age, are considered more useful; for they nourish greatly, and the food they supply is not easily dissipated. Yet they rarely enter the butcher's shop, unless their strength for the plough has broken down, or they have otherwise become useless for agriculture. Those skilled in natural things will take it amiss that I have passed over in silence here the praise of bulls, though they have kept it: although this animal is very wild and inflamed with lust, yet it does not mount more than twice a day; after conceiving with the cow itself it attempts nothing further, being modest and chaste. Whence among the Egyptians' hieroglyphics the bull was a symbol of temperance and continence. By this the lustful are warned that, taking an example from this brute beast, they should not pursue other men's loves within marriage.

units.la: VtukiVitulinam, suavitatem qz saporis ac odo-ris in ea fragrantiam celebrat Mauritanorum omnium acerrimi ingenii Averrhoes, quam etiam gallinaceā anteponit. Quare intrepide tutoque à se semper agris datam constanter asserit. Secuta medicina ex hujus sententia in praecipuam salubritatis admirationem eam evexit. Verum commendatio illa examinatione indiget, Certum est recenter editos plurimum & lentoris, & vividi humoris obtinere, tantoque esse ficciores, minus autem humentiores, quanto a partu longum recesserunt. Multi Germania tractus vitulos & vitulas, mensem unum & quandoque eo minus natos, aut etiam sesquimensem lanie tradunt. Sunt alii tractus, in quibus macellum non subeunt propter majorem utilitatis spem. Sunt qui plane in cibis iis abstinent, oletum citius, quam vitulinam expectentes, ut septentrionales quidam, quibus ferum plane & insipidum palatum est. Romani Italorumque complures semestri, aut etiam anno toto a lacte eos non depellunt, cavent qz, ut herbarum expertes aliorumque pabulorum, per id tempus degant, sic enim jucundiores, pretiosiores, & saluberiores ipsorum fieri carnes experimento didicerunt, proindeque Cardinalitias, Pontificias, nec non Regias mensas lautissimas esse persuasum habent, si vitulina apponatur. Hoc cibo mire delectatus dicitur Franciscus Galliarum Rex huius nominis primus: nec no hodie in splendidis amplis
units.tr: Averrhoes, the sharpest mind of all the Moors, praises veal for its sweetness, and for the fragrance of its taste and smell, and he even ranks it above chicken. For this reason he confidently and safely affirms that it is always to be given to the sick. Medicine, following his opinion, has raised it to a position of special regard for its wholesomeness. Yet that commendation needs examination. It is certain that freshly slaughtered calves are very slimy and full of raw moisture, and that they become drier and less moist the longer they are removed from their birth. Many in the regions of Germany sell calves, both males and females, a month old, sometimes even younger, or a month and a half old, from the butcher's stall. There are other regions where they are not sent to the slaughter at all, because of a greater hope of profit. Some people abstain from these foods altogether, preferring to wait for mutton rather than veal, as certain northerners do, whose palate is quite savage and insipid. The Romans and many Italians do not wean them from milk for six months, or even for a whole year, and they take care that during that time they live without grass and other fodder, for they have learned by experience that the flesh becomes in this way more pleasant, more costly and more wholesome. Hence they hold that the most sumptuous tables of cardinals, popes and kings are those where veal is served. Francis, the first of that name, King of France, is said to have been wonderfully delighted with this food; and today, in splendid and large cities, veal is the most common of foods, easily holding first place among the flesh of larger animals, whether it is boiled or roasted. Hence country folk manage their stock so that they always have some to sell, from which they gain both profit and advantage.

units.la: Quidam vitulinā plane ab ominantur. amplisq; urbibus vulgatissimi cibi est vitulina, inter grandiorum animalium carnes facile tenens primas, sive elixetur, sive assetur: unde rustici ita rem suam dispensant, ut nullo non tempore supersint, ex quo commodum percipiant & lucrum. Caeterum vitulinam jurulentam magis alere quam assam, assamque magis quam frixam, seu butyro tostam, experiuntur, qui crebrius ac largius ea vescuntur. Magiricum etiam artificium hic jure requiritur, ut exquisite sciil. vitulina probeq, vel elixetur, vel inassetur, ita quidem, ne humiditas illa nutrimentalis plane exorbeat, ut supra quoq; anaotatum est.
units.tr: Some utterly abhor veal.
