Yet in large and splendid cities veal is the most common food, easily holding first place among the flesh of larger animals, whether it is boiled or roasted; hence country folk so arrange their affairs that they have stock at every time of year, from which they derive advantage and profit. Moreover, those who eat it more often and in larger quantities find that veal boiled in broth nourishes more than roasted, and roasted more than fried, or browned in butter. Here a skilled technique is rightly required, so that veal is carefully and properly either boiled or roasted, in such a way that its nourishing moisture is not wholly lost, as has also been noted above.

units.la: De juvencorum porro, & juvencarum carnibus, non adeo difficile est aliquid asseruere, vel judicare, si modo dicta ad memoriam revocentur. Aetatem duriiem & siccitatem parerein confesso est. Vitulinis quoq; auctoritate inferiores esse ex praecedentibus & antediclis patere arbitror. Semestres & annicula, bima, trimaq; in cibis a quibusdam mire expetuntur, valenter enim nutrire experimentis multis patefactum est. Iuvenci tamen rarius a quibusdam mactantur. Iuvenca venerem non experta laudabiliores existimantur, ampliusq; eo augentur, quo plus temporis venereorum expertes degunt, recentiores autem, quam anniculas venerem non pati aiunt.
units.tr: As for the flesh of young bullocks and heifers, it is not very difficult to state something, or to form a judgement, if only what has been said is recalled to mind. It is agreed that their age produces hardness and dryness. I think it is clear from what has gone before and from what was said earlier that they are also inferior to veal. Six-month-old animals, yearlings, two-year-olds and three-year-olds are eagerly sought after as food by some, for many experiments have shown that they nourish powerfully. Bullocks, however, are slaughtered less often by some. Heifers that have not known sexual intercourse are considered more commendable, and they grow larger the longer they live without venereal experience; but the younger ones, they say, do not suffer the male before they are a year old.

units.la: De Suilla memoratu digna.
units.tr: On pork, things worth recording.

units.la: EX nullo animali numerosiores ganeæ dapes præparari, suesque nihil habere præter escam, tantumq; donatas à natura ad epulandum, antiquissimi pariter ac prudentissimi Philosophi prodiderunt.
units.tr: Philosophers, both the most ancient and the most prudent, have handed down that no animal provides more numerous gluttonous banquets than the pig, and that the pig has nothing but food, and was given by nature only for feasting.

units.la: Itaq; iis animam pro sale datam, ne caro viuenti putresceret, Chryfippus ait. Nihil enim fere in hac pecude reperias, quod edendo non fit, suamq; propriam suauitatem repræsentet. Hinc abdomina prisci celebrata, glandia, testiculi, vulvæ, jecinora, verrina, & nostra memoria maxime nobilitantur latera, coxæ tam priores, quam posteriores sale macerata & suffitæ pernæ dictæ & petasones, aures, pedes, costæ, spina, sanguis & intestina ipsa, & operosum esset singula recensere cibaria, quæ ex illis parantur. Titus Quintius ante tribunatum & prœturam consul designatus, in Chalcide apud hospitem cœnans miratus esse traditur carnium copiam varietatem q;, hospite vero affirmasse, illas omnes suillas esse, condimentis saltem & præparationib. differentes. Conuenit autem inter omnes percelebres medicos, suillam boni succi esse, valentissimeq; omnium escarum nutrire : testantur id fossores, meflores, huiusmodi q; alii grauiorum operarum, hos enim, salio cibo pascere velis, imbecilliores reddes. Nam etsi parem alterius obsonii molem pridie assumserint, postridie si aeq; laborauerint, infirmiores erunt minusque validi, & ad opera promti. Qui igitur suillam frequenter comedunt, plene se nutriri deprehendent, celerrimeq; excrementorum copia abundabunt, & arctissime meminisse velim literarum studiosos, & qui domi sedent otiosi: congesta illa excrementa laborib. & vehementiorib. frictionib. dissipanda sunt ac discutienda. Caeterum teterrima antiqui porci caro censetur vt q aegre concoquatur, concoctaq; sanguine atra bile contaminet: optima vero & ad gulę illecebras & ad corporis alimoniā est porcorum mediae aetatis caro, non obesa nimis, nec macra nimis, porcorum inq, qui veteris victimae, vel non excesserint, vel nondum annos assecuti sint, hi enim facile concoquuntur, sanguinemq; probum generant, & ad bonos gignendos succos carnem habent aptissimi, & probatissimam. teste Gal. l. 4. reg. acut. Et in l. i. ad Glauc. exquisita tertiana affectis, praeter tesiculos & alas gallorum, vitellaq; quorum sorbilia, porcorum pedes & cerebra, porcelorum q; carnes in jure albo liquefactas praebet, effoetafq; à morbo conualescentiū vires illarum esu reficere praecipit his verbis: Suillas ait, carnes edere à pedib. in Ptisana elixis incipient, post vero etiam imum crus recte sumptus ab hoc etiam reliquas partes primum quiquidem porcelli juvenis, qui, si hiems fit, etiam pridie mactetur nam hesternus, quare- cens mactatus facilius concoquitur: aestate sat fuerit, si mane immolatus porcellus fit, ac circa solis occasum comedatur. Gal. 7. meth. Necabs re hoc pcepiffe videtur, omnium n. esculentorum, quota sunt, caro porcina valentissime nutrit, si modo concocta fuerit, (nihil enim nutrit, nisi naturae viribus concoctum) adeoque magna habet cum humana affinitatem & similitudinem, ut non modo nostro aevo in Gallia, sed & Galeni tempore Romae, scelerati quidam Pandochei & caupones, carnem humanam cum aromatib. in pastillis coctam pro suilla magni vendiderint, nec comestores alteram ab altera sapore, odore aut colore dilcernere poterant, donec humanus digitus per negligentiam cum sua vngue coctus & repertus atrox mox coci facinus ꝓ-didit, q & meritas supplicio in furca pepedit poenas. Porro recente suillam, h.e. nuper ma-statae suis, faleq; non aspersam, stomacho efle grauem, difficulter concoqui, aluiqua quan-doq; ꝓfluuium liberali vefcentib. ciere quotidiano experimento constat. Mucofa n. & praehumida est, qua de causa pituitosis & frigidis naturis crebrior illius vsus noxius est. Porcellos seu lacteos porcos opipara convi- via admittit, mefaeq; elegatiores, sed magno errore prandius potius, q coenis hodie edunt.
units.tr: Therefore Chrysippus says that the soul was given to it in place of salt, so that its flesh would not rot while it was alive. For you will find almost nothing in this creature that is not eaten and does not present its own proper sweetness. Hence the ancients celebrated its belly, its glands, testicles, udders and liver, and in our own time the sides, the hams both front and back, the salted and smoked hams called pernae and petasones, the ears, feet, ribs, spine, blood and the intestines themselves; and it would be tedious to list each of the foods that are prepared from them. Titus Quintius, before he became tribune and praetor, while he was consul-designate, is reported to have dined at Chalcis with a host, and to have marvelled at the abundance and variety of the meats; but the host assured him that all of them were pork, differing only in seasonings and methods of preparation. Moreover, all the most celebrated physicians agree that pork is of good juice and nourishes more powerfully than any other food. Diggers, reapers and others of this kind who undertake heavier labours bear witness to this; for if you wish to feed them on other food, you will make them weaker. For even if they have consumed the same bulk of another dish the day before, if on the next day they have laboured as hard, they will be weaker and less strong and less ready for work. Therefore those who often eat pork will find that they are fully nourished, and they will abound very quickly in an abundance of excrements. And I would very much have students of letters, and those who sit idle at home, remember this: those accumulated excrements must be dispersed and dispelled by labours and by vigorous rubbing. Moreover, the flesh of an old pig is judged most foul, so that it is digested with difficulty, and once digested it contaminates the blood with black bile. But the best flesh, both for the allurements of the palate and for nourishment of the body, is that of pigs of middle age, neither too fat nor too lean, and of those which have either not yet passed the age of the old sacrificial victim or have not yet reached a year; for these are easily digested, generate good blood, and their flesh is most suitable and most approved for producing good juices. So Galen, book 4 of the Method for Acute Diseases; and in book 1 of the work to Glaucon, for patients who suffer from an exquisite tertian fever, besides the testicles and wings of cocks, and the yolks whose sorbile preparations he gives, he provides pigs' feet and brains and the flesh of sucking pigs melted in white broth, and he orders that the strength of convalescents, worn out by disease, be restored by eating these, in these words: he says that they should begin to eat pork boiled in barley-water, and afterwards also the lower part of the leg, rightly taken from the same animal, first indeed from a young sucking pig, which, if it is winter, should be slaughtered even the day before, for yesterday's slaughtered pig is more easily digested; in summer it is enough if the little pig is killed in the morning and eaten about sunset. Galen, book 7 of the Method. Nor does he seem to have been mistaken in this, for of all edible things, however many there are, pork nourishes most powerfully, provided it is well digested (for nothing nourishes unless it has been digested by the strength of nature). And it has such great affinity and likeness to human flesh that not only in our own age in France, but also in Galen's time at Rome, certain wicked innkeepers and taverners sold human flesh cooked with spices in little pastries as pork at a high price, and the diners could not distinguish the one from the other by taste, smell or colour, until a human finger, cooked with its nail through carelessness, was found and at once revealed the cook's atrocious crime, and he paid the penalty he deserved on the gallows. Moreover, that fresh pork, that is, the flesh of pigs lately slaughtered and not sprinkled with salt, is heavy in the stomach and hard to digest, and that it sometimes provokes a flux of the bowels in those who eat it liberally, is established by daily experience. For it is slimy and very moist, and for this reason its frequent use is harmful to phlegmatic and cold constitutions. Suckling pigs, or milk-fed pigs, admit of sumptuous banquets, and they are more elegant as food; but by a great mistake people today eat them at lunch rather than at dinner.

units.la: Gg in quibus valentiora & vtiliora alimenta plæriq; promittunt. Aliiautem frequentissime menías subeunt, elixi raro: calidiqué e- deadi potius quam frigidi, & absque cute, quamtamen igne retorridam jucundissime quidam vorant. Olim quoq;in pretio eos fuisse testatur Martialis l.13.
units.tr: Many promise more powerful and more useful nourishment in those [parts]. Others, however, very often come to the table, rarely boiled; and they prefer to eat them hot rather than cold, and without the skin, which some devour with great delight even though it has been dried by fire. That they were also highly prized in former times is attested by Martial, book 13:

units.la: Lacte mero pastum pigra mihi matris alumnu Ponat, & Ætolo de sue dinas edat.
units.tr: Let my lazy foster-child be fed on pure milk, and let him eat the Aetolian sow's dainties.

units.la: Sed de Suillæ carnis alimonia omnia hactenus dicta, neminí non perspecta esse arbitror. Unus Hippocrates l.4. de Ptisana, & 4. regimin. acut. de suillæ carnis differentia multorum ingenia torsit, vbi carnes porcinas vituperat, suillas vero commendat: Porcinæ carnes, inquit, siue ambustæ, siue subcrudæ, malæ, nam & bilem pariunt, & turbationem: Suillis nullæ aliæ meliores sunt, idq; si non admodum pingues, neque etiam pertenues sunt, ac neque veteris victimæ æstem sint assecutæ: at vero reiecta pelle, & subfrigidæ edendæ sunt. Ubi sciendum, vetères græcos porcellos lactentes & adhuc subrumes χοίρας appellasse, horumq; esum ob viscidos & crudos humores carnis, Hippocrates improbasse, cui subscribit Gal. 3. de alim. & 2. de temper. merito, inquiens porcelli tanto magis excrementitiam prębent nobis alimoniam, quanto sunt magnis suib. humidiores, & minus quoq; nutriunt. Nupn. editi quouis animali. mali terrestri, quo homo vescitur, carnem habent humidiorem, sanguinis & phlegmate viscosi comitem. Differentiam hinc apud Homerum Eumæus Subulcus Vlyssis, quem ex bello Troiano & naufragio sibi tum ignotum, reducem hospitio excepit, obseruat dicens, Ede ō hospes, nam hæc choerea, porcellorum carnes, debentur & supersunt famulis, proci vero Penelopes obesos, & spumantes sues adultos edunt, qui delphaces dicebantur, sic enim nominabant sues corpus robore compactum habentes, & qui adoleuerant. Vt autem carnes suauitatem adipiscantur & iucunditatem, adq; pinguedinem sues adolescant, glande maximè aluntur, faba, hordeo, cæterisque frumentis, facile enim ad quoduis pabulum assuescunt. Vrbium pistores frugum farina & furfuribus saginant ad tantam sæpe pinguitudinem, vt vix loco se mouere queant, & si alio quis transferre velit, plaustro id faciendum esse. Pinguedo & adeps horum, aptissimum aliarum escarum condimentum est. Carnes pro glandium natura variare certum est: sagineam enim su- em hilarem facere, carnem coctibilem, leue, & stomachoque vtilem: ilignam suem nitidam, angustam, ponderosam: quernam diffusam, grauissimam, certi autores tradunt. Monta-norum quoque caro domesticarum carni præferetur, grata enim his in lato volutatio. Gg locisque obscœnis. Quare, qui sues domi alunt, curabunt, vt cubile semper sit mundū, crebroque suilia verrantur, hæc enim cura ad carnis suauitatem, salubritatemque plurimum facit. Quoad tempora, præstantiores quæ sub hiemis initium nascuntur, deterrimæ, quæaestate, plærunque enim grandini reddūtur obnoxiæ, præsertim autem grandinofi fiunt, Aristotele teste, quorum crura, collum & armi carne constant, quibus partibus vel plures grandines innasci conspiciuntur. Dulcior autem caro est, cum pauciores sunt grandines, sio multas habet, humida valde & insipida est. Certum est non parum dotibus, & gloriæ suillæ detrahere grandinē, vt & pretio. Qui grandent probantur ante emtionem, facileque cognoscuntur, parte e-nim linguæ inferiore habentur grandines, & si setam dorso euellas, cruorem in radice pili euulsi videris, cum lactent, grandine carent. Morbosas igitur, viscerasque habentes vitiata non attingent sanitatis vitæque prorogandæ studiosi, sunt etenim, quibus lien in tumorem attollitur atque induratur, quod non accidit, nisi à corporis temperamento vitiato.
units.tr: But I think that all that has been said so far about the nourishment of pork is known to everyone. Hippocrates alone, in book 4 On Barley-Water and in the fourth book of the Regimen in Acute Diseases, on the difference between kinds of pork, has tormented the minds of many; there he finds fault with the flesh of pigs but commends the flesh of sows. "The flesh of pigs," he says, "whether burnt or underdone, is bad, for it produces bile and disturbance. Of all others, sow flesh is the best, provided it is neither very fat nor very thin, and that the sow has not passed the age of an old sacrificial victim. But it must be eaten with the skin removed, and somewhat cool." Here it should be known that the ancient Greeks called suckling pigs and those still tender [χοίρας], and that Hippocrates disapproved of eating them because of their viscid and raw humours; Galen agrees with him in book 3 On Nutrition and book 2 On Temperaments, rightly saying that young pigs provide us with more excrementitious nourishment the more moist they are compared with full-grown pigs, and that they also nourish less. Animals recently born, of any kind of earthly creature on which man feeds, have flesh that is more moist and accompanied by viscous blood and phlegm. Homer's difference in this matter is noted by Eumaeus the swineherd of Ulysses, who received him kindly into his hut when he returned from the Trojan war and from shipwreck, though at that time he was unknown to him. He says: "Eat, O guest, for these young porkers' flesh is owed to and remains for the servants; but the suitors of Penelope eat the fat and foaming full-grown swine, which were called delphaces, for so they named swine that had a body compact with strength and had grown up." Now, so that the flesh may acquire sweetness and agreeableness, and that the swine may grow fat, they are fed chiefly on acorns, beans, barley and other grains, for they easily become accustomed to any kind of fodder. Bakers in cities fatten them with flour of grain and with bran, often to such a fatness that they can scarcely move from their place, and if anyone wishes to move one elsewhere, it must be done by a wagon. The fat and lard of these is a most suitable seasoning for other foods. It is certain that the flesh varies according to the nature of the acorns: writers report that a swine fed on beech-mast makes flesh that is cooked easily, light, and useful for the stomach; one fed on holm-oak is shining, narrow and heavy; one fed on oak is loose, very heavy. The flesh of mountain swine is also preferred to that of domestic ones, for they delight in wallowing in the wide and obscene places. Therefore those who keep pigs at home will take care that the bed is always clean, and that the pigsties are often swept; for this care contributes greatly to the sweetness and wholesomeness of the flesh. As for seasons, those born at the beginning of winter are best, and the worst are those born in summer; for they are mostly liable to hail-stones, and especially they become hail-stoned, as Aristotle testifies, whose legs, neck and shoulders consist of flesh in which many hailstones are seen to be produced. The flesh is sweeter when there are fewer hailstones, but if it has many, it is very moist and insipid. It is certain that the hailstones take no little from the qualities and reputation of pork, as well as from its price. Hail-stoned pigs are tested before purchase and are easily recognised: for hailstones are found in the lower part of the tongue, and if you pull a bristle from the back you will see blood at the root of the pulled hair; when they are free of hail, they are not affected. Therefore those who are zealous for preserving health and prolonging life will not touch diseased pigs, and those having diseased viscera; for in them the spleen is raised up into a swelling and becomes hardened, which does not happen unless the temperament of the body has been corrupted.

units.la: Ad extremum perfida Iudæorum gens e-sum suillæ temerè infamauit. Nam, prodente Iustino lib. 36. & Cornelio Tacito lib. 5. cum hæc gens in Ægypto Diis hominibusque busque inuisa, fœda scabiei porrigine & tabe laboraret, eiusque contagium totam Ægyptum inficeret, Iuppiter Hammonius de remedio per Bochorim Ægypti Regem, consultus, Iudæos Ægypto repudientes arcendos, quorum exulum dux designatus Moses, memor quàm fœda scabies & vitiligo ipsorum corpora deturparet, simulque quod porci grandine & scabie eadem infestarentur, iudæis suillæ carnis esui interdixit, nec verò quod insalubris sit suillæ eius, vetuit, sed, ut hoc Moses decretum rectius intellexit Eusebius de præpar. Evan. l. 8. c. 3. cum sus sit amica luto, locisque vliginosis, in quibus se voluntate, ut ea quæ externè corpus, intus verò animam coinquinarent, sedulo cauerent, & sobriè non ut fuces in crapula & sagina viuerét. Meminit huius quoq; Plutarch in 4. Sympos. problem. 5. vbi rationem reddit, cur Iudæi carnibus suillis abstineant.
units.tr: Lastly, the treacherous Jewish people have rashly slandered the flesh of the pig. For, as Justin reports in book 36 and Cornelius Tacitus in book 5, when this people, hated by gods and men in Egypt, was suffering from a foul scabby eruption and a rot whose contagion was infecting all of Egypt, Jupiter Hammon, consulted about a remedy through Bochoris, king of Egypt, ordered that the Jews, who were to be expelled from Egypt, be kept away. Their exiled leader was Moses. Mindful of how foul scab and vitiligo disfigured their bodies, and that pigs were likewise afflicted by scab and scurf, he forbade the Jews to eat pork. Yet he did not forbid it because its flesh is unwholesome. As Eusebius understood this decree more correctly (Praep. Evang. book 8, ch. 3), the pig is fond of mud and marshy places, and so the Jews were to take care, in their own will, to avoid what defiles the body from outside and the soul from within, and to live soberly, not like drones in gluttony and fattening. Plutarch also mentions this in the fourth book of the Symposiacs, problem 5, where he gives the reason why the Jews abstain from pork.

units.la: De feris suibus.
units.tr: De feris suibus.

units.la: A Prugnam Magna: es & Potentes studiosissime hodie venantur, non sine vita periculo, tantaque est gula insania apud quosdam, ut mori satius existiment, quam ea cibo carere. Romani solidos apros epulis apponere solití sunt, huiusce luxuria auctor fuit P. Serrilius Rullus, qui enim Romanorum primus integrum aprum apposuit, ut testantur annales. In huiusmodi mores clamat Satyricus,
units.tr: Great men and the powerful today hunt wild boars most eagerly, not without danger to life, and among some the madness of gluttony is so great that they think it better to die than to go without such food. The Romans used to set whole wild boars on their banquet tables. The originator of this luxury was P. Serrilius Rullus, who, as the annals attest, was the first of the Romans to serve a whole boar. Against such customs the satirist cries out:

units.la: Quanta est gula, quæ sibi totos Ponit apros, animal propter convivia natum.
units.tr: How great is gluttony, which sets out whole boars for itself alone, an animal born for feasts.

units.la: Et sub finem,
units.tr: And near the end:

units.la: Semesum leporem atq; aliquid de clunibus apri.
units.tr: A half-eaten hare and something from the haunches of a boar.

units.la: Huius autem lumbus, omnibus aliis partibus præponebatur; quem Plautus & Cato aprugnū vocarunt. Sedidem Martialis vix unquam cœnas aut nobiles escas memorat, quin inter ipsas apro nobiliorem prope locum tradat, quem sicut hodie variis iuribus ac delicatis liquoribus condiunt, exquisitissimeq; apparare consueuerunt coqui, ut eius sylvestrem odorem occul ent, ita quoque maiores nostros facilitasse intelliget, quicunque Apitii illius opsodedali varias condituras examinauerit. Obseruatum quippe a ganea proceribus est, aprugnam meliorem esse carne suum domesticorum, propterea quod tantas non habeat superfluitates, nec glutinosum adeo tenacemq;prosreet succum. Caput vero aprinum inter nobiliores cibos hodie prædicatur, optimiq; ac grati saporis est, præsertim eorum aprorum qui libere vaganter, non qui in viua-rius nati ciconres, aut feri capti includuntur, hi enim non perinde gratam ac iucundam carnem salubrem q; obtinent. Montanos enim gula proceres præferunt, ut & medici, minus enim excrementis abundant. Hastenus de suibus.
units.tr: The loin of this animal was placed before all other parts; Plautus and Cato called it aprugnum. Martial, indeed, hardly ever mentions a dinner or noble dishes without placing the boar's loin almost in the most noble position among them. Today cooks seasoned it with various broths and delicate sauces, and they were accustomed to prepare it most carefully so as to hide its wild odour. Anyone who examines the various seasonings of that Apicius of old will understand that our ancestors also made it agreeable in this way. It has indeed been observed by the glutted nobles that the loin of a boar is better than the flesh of domestic pigs, because it does not have such excess of fat, nor does it yield a glutinous and tenacious juice. The boar's head is today praised among the more noble foods, and it has an excellent and pleasing flavour, especially that of boars which roam freely, not of those born in enclosures or taken wild and shut up. For these do not yield flesh as pleasant, agreeable and wholesome. Indeed the nobles, and physicians too, prefer mountain boars out of gluttony, for they abound less in excrements. Thus far concerning pigs.

units.la: Adhuc de alimentis, quæ veniunt ab animalibus hibus humi gradientibus, sequuntur reptilia, ut serpens, vipera, omnisq; generis vermes & insecta, vt formicae, scorpius, aranei, cimices, pediculi, pinorum eruca : nec non pennata quaedam, vt musca, papiliones, apes, vespae, scarabaei.
units.tr: Hitherto concerning foods that come from animals walking on the ground, there follow reptiles, such as the serpent, the viper, and all kinds of worms and insects, such as ants, scorpions, spiders, bugs, lice, and the caterpillar of the pine; and also certain winged creatures, such as the fly, butterflies, bees, wasps and beetles.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: De serpentina & viperina.
units.tr: Of serpent and viper flesh.

units.la: ESse ophiophagos, serpentibus vesci afffuctos, Candeos vocatos, à grauissimis auctoribus proditum reperitur. Solin. c.36. Plin. l.6. c.29. Et fuisse in Africa Marsos, & Psyllos, nec non Ophiogenes in Cypro, quorum illis exitiale virus serpentibus ingenitum erat, vt odore solo eas sopirent, his veròserpentum ictus solo cotactu leuare, manuque impolita venenum corpori extrahere, huiusque experimenti causa ex Ophiogenarum familia legatus Exagon nomine, à Consulibus Romae in dolium serpentum coniectus circumnulcentibus linguis miraculum praebuit : Signumque eius familiae est, si adhuc durat, vernis temporibus odoris virus. Plin. l.28. c.3. Qui Athon montem incolunt viperinis carnibus vescuntur, itaqj nec capiti nec vestibus eorum noxia corpori innasci animalia, certi autores tradunt. Certissimis experimentis patefactum est, viperina nam valide siccare & digerere, proindeque insanabilia eam persanare ulcera, cacochymiae mederi & elephantiafi, prurititbus cutisq; foeditati, nec non pediculos expellere toto corpore, in cibis sumtam, Plinio & Galeno restibus, meminitq; Galenus harum beneficio & vsu, duos integrae sanitati restitutos elephantiasis contagione contaminatos. Cauda autem & ceruice abscissis viperae vino pri' fustocandae, vel vt Plinius tradit l.29. c.6. primum occisis sal in os addunt, donec liquescat humor, utrinque postea praecisas exemtisq; interaneis diluoquunt cum aqua, vel vino, quod melius est, oleo, sale & anetho, omnibusq; aut statim vescuntur, aut pane colligunt vt saepius vtantur. Diosc orides viperinas carnes claritatem oculis afferre, neruorumq; vitiis auxiliari autor est, coctas ac esitatas. Antonius Musa quoq; insanabilia & maligna ulcera, vsu vini viperini persanata esse certis experimentis testatus est: eligendas vero esse foetas & iuxta mare degentes praecipiunt. Venenis deniq; vinum viperinum potenter resistere clari autores promittunt. Caetera reptilia & infecta, quibus nihil praeter luridum, fuscum, crassumq; lentore, quia terrae, aerisq; vtplurimum inquinamenta sunt & purgamenta, cibariorum albo excluduntur. Vnum meminisse tamen non indignum, quod praegrandes arborum vermes, cossi appellati, pellati, in delicatiori ciboRomanis olim fuerint, quos farina saginatos altiles fecerunt, tanta fuit seculi istius prodigiosa & vesana luxuria, vt ventris irritamenta & delitias in foedis etiam infectis quaesiuerit, saporesq; ex caulis & putridis arborum corticibus.
units.tr: It is recorded by very weighty authors that there were ophiophagi, people who fed on serpents and were called Candaei. Solinus ch. 36; Pliny bk. 6 ch. 29. There were also the Marsi and the Psylli in Africa, and the Ophiogenes in Cyprus. The deadly poison was innate in the serpents of the first two peoples, so that by smell alone they lulled them to sleep, while the Ophiogenes could relieve the bites of serpents by touch alone and draw the poison out of the body with an unanointed hand. To test this, an envoy of the Ophiogenes family named Exagon was thrown by the consuls at Rome into a tub of serpents, and as they licked him with their circling tongues he provided a wonder. The sign of this family is, if it still endures, that in spring its members give off a poisonous smell. Pliny bk. 28 ch. 3. Those who live on Mount Athos feed on viper flesh, and so, certain authors relate, no animals harmful to the body breed in their heads or clothes. It has been shown by very certain experiments that viper flesh strongly dries and digests, and therefore cures ulcers that are otherwise incurable, heals cachexia, elephantiasis, itching and foulness of the skin, and, taken as food, expels lice from the whole body. Pliny and Galen bear witness to this, and Galen recalls that by its benefit and use two men infected with the contagion of elephantiasis were restored to full health. To prepare the viper, the tail and head are cut off and it is singed with wine beforehand; or, as Pliny reports book 29, ch. 6, after it is killed they put salt into its mouth until the moisture liquefies, then cut it open on both sides, remove the entrails, and wash it with water or wine (better still, oil), with salt and dill. Then they either eat the whole of it at once or preserve it in bread so that they may use it more often. Dioscorides is the authority that viper flesh, boiled or roasted, brings clarity to the eyes and helps defects of the nerves. Antonius Musa too attested by certain experiments that incurable and malignant ulcers were cured by the use of viper wine; he directs that pregnant vipers living near the sea should be chosen. Finally, famous authors promise that viper wine powerfully resists poisons. The other reptiles and insects are excluded from the list of foods, since they contain nothing but a lurid, dusky, thick sliminess; for they are for the most part the filth and refuse of earth and air. It is worth remembering one thing, however: the very large worms of trees, called cossi and pellati, were once a delicacy among the Romans, who fattened them on flour until they were plump dainties. So prodigious and insane was the luxury of that age that it sought stimulants for the belly and delights even in foul, unclean things, and flavours from cabbages and the rotten bark of trees.

units.la: Hactenus de alimentis quae homini in cibos veniunt ex animalibus in aere degentibus, sequuntur, quae in aqua viuunt, vt pisces.
units.tr: So far on foods that come to people as meat from animals living in the air. Next come those that live in water, such as fish.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: TAm apud Graecos antiquos quam Romanos etiam summo semper in mensarum pretio atq; honore fuisse pisces, tot eorundem conscripti de iis libri satis superq; testantur. Alexander ille Macedo Orientis dominator maximus & potentissimus cupidine animalium naturas noscendi inflammatus Aristotelem praeceptorem incitauit, vt studiosissimè ac prolixissimè animalium, aquatilium verò potissimum naturas & partes fuerit persecutus, proque tam praeclaro & mirabili opere fertur accepisse ab Alexandro octingenta talenta quam summam immodicam nemo existimare debet, si huius Regis opulentiam immensam, diuinamque erga omnium bonarum artium Magistros liberalitatem consideraverit.
units.tr: That fish were always held in the highest regard at the tables of both the ancient Greeks and the Romans is sufficiently attested by the many books written about them. Alexander the Macedonian, the greatest and most powerful lord of the East, was so inflamed with a desire to learn the natures of animals that he urged his tutor Aristotle to study animals, and aquatic animals above all, most diligently and at great length. For this admirable and remarkable work, Aristotle is said to have received eight hundred talents from Alexander. No one should think this sum excessive if he considers the king's immense wealth and his divine generosity towards the masters of all the liberal arts.

units.la: Obtrectatoribus autem non caruit Aristoteles maxime vero in iis quae de piscibus disputauit, in quibus eum plus iusto curiosiorem fuisse & scrupulosiorem prodiderunt, vix enim sciri posse affirmarunt, quae de generatione & coitu aquatilium tradidit. Constanter hoc asserendum, omnia fere, quae de piscibus cognita sunt, Aristotelì debere accepta referri, & q aliorum libros, quos de piscib. exararunt, (vt sunt Oppian, Aelianus, Seleucus Tarsensis) euoluerit, comperiet ab Aristotele tanquam limpidissimo & abundantissimo fonte riuulos eorum defluxisse. Apud latinos pauci admodum ex antiquis rem piscariam attigerunt. Solus Plinius in hac materia videtur latinos adiuuisse, in arctum enim fatetur ipse collegisse, quae Aristoteles de animalibus prodidit, quo nobis labore latine loquitur Aristoteles. Mirari subit à Romanis tam ofcitanter rem piscariam fuisse praetermissam, cum conster statim ab vrbe condita pisces marinos in vsu fuisse, postea vero orbe deuicto luxuriaque vrbem inundante, coeperunt Proceres Romani piscinas instituere, in quibus pretiosissimos pisces alerent educarentque, ex quibus etiam magnos reditus capiebant. Claudebant autem dulcibus aquis piscesmarinos, eosque gula maxime probabat, quia in suburbanis litoribus inueniretur, quod ab ipsis Gadibus aut mari
units.tr: Aristotle was not spared critics, especially for his work on fish, in which they declared that he was more curious and scrupulous than was right. They claimed that what he taught about the generation and mating of aquatic creatures could scarcely be known. It must be affirmed firmly that nearly everything known about fish should be credited to Aristotle. Anyone who reads through the books others wrote on fish (such as Oppian, Aelian and Seleucus of Tarsus) will find that their small streams flowed down from Aristotle as from a very clear and abundant spring. Among the Latins, very few of the ancients touched on the subject of fishing. Pliny alone seems to have helped the Latins in this matter. He admits that he gathered into a short compass what Aristotle had written about animals, so that by his labour Aristotle speaks to us in Latin. It is surprising that the Romans so carelessly neglected the subject of fishing, since it is clear that sea fish were in use from the founding of the city. Later, however, once the world had been conquered and luxury had flooded the city, the Roman nobles began to build fish ponds in which they kept and raised the most prized fish, from which they also drew large incomes. They kept sea fish in fresh water, and the gourmands especially approved of them if they were found on the suburban shores, since otherwise they had to be fetched from Gades or the far end of the sea.

units.la: Solus Aristoteles accuratissime piscatilia describit. mari aliâs extremo peteretur. Inprimis verò Luculli Euripus, (quo excisô monte maria admittebat) fuit admirabilis. Reliquorum piscium viuaria inuenit Licinius Murena, quem postea nobilitas secuta est. Philippum & Hortensium Cicero non sine mordaci ceto piscinarios appellasse prædicatur, quod scilicet piscinas, piscibus ad gulæ incendia idoneis refertissimas possiderent. Sergius Orata primus omnium ostrearum viuaria in Baiano instituit, non gulæ gratiâ tantum, sed auaritiæ etiam, magna enim ex iis vectigalia percipiebat. Constat quoq; nonnullos ex mari externo in freta Italica deuectos, estque in exemplis Optatus Tyberii Cæsaris libertus classisque præfectus, qui Scarum vndis Italicis ignotum nomine q; vacantem latino, inter Ostiam & Campaniæ littus in mare sparsum disseminauit, & nouo exemplo nouum Italis dedit incolam. Verum tanta impensa, tantiquefumtus & studium ventris gulæque causa magis fiebant, quam valetudinis prorogandę. Nam quos Magnatum Principumque libido in cibos admittebat, statim alii in pretio atque auctoritate habebant, vt ita indubitatum fit, nullam valetudinis eos rationem habuisse, vt nec rerum naturæ cognitionis. Cæterum pisces à maioribus etiam non-stris non fuisse neglectos Mosis, libri & sacri vates testatum faciunt. Nam & ipsa aquatilia ...
units.tr: Only Aristotle describes fish with the greatest accuracy. Above all, the Euripus of Lucullus was admirable, into which he let the sea in by cutting through a mountain. Licinius Murena discovered fish-tanks for the rest of the fish, and afterwards nobility followed him. Cicero is reported to have called Philippus and Hortensius "fish-pond men," not without a biting jest, since they possessed fish ponds crammed with fish suited to kindle the fires of gluttony. Sergius Orata was the first of all to set up oyster beds at Baiae, and he did so not only for the sake of gluttony but also for greed, since he drew great revenues from them. It is also established that some fish were brought from the outer sea into the Italian straits. Optatus, a freedman of Tiberius Caesar and prefect of the fleet, is an example. He scattered the scarus, a fish unknown to Italian waters and without a Latin name, into the sea between Ostia and the Campanian shore, and by this new venture he gave Italy a new inhabitant. Yet such great expense, such great outlay and such zeal were undertaken for the sake of the belly and the throat rather than for prolonging health. For whatever fish the lust of the magnates and princes admitted to their tables at once became valued and esteemed by others. So it is beyond doubt that they paid no heed to health, nor to knowledge of the nature of things. Moreover, that fish were not neglected by our forefathers either, the books of Moses and the sacred prophets bear witness. For they write that the aquatic creatures themselves were first created by God, the Best and Greatest, and they believe...

units.la: H h pri-
units.tr: H h pri-

units.la: primum à Deo Opt. Max. creata scribit & credit Christo quin ipsi piscium esum fuisse familiarissimum legimus, & post resurrectionem piscem allatum degustasse, Lucas testis est. Merito igitur mirari subit nostri seculi sationes quorundam, qui piscium esum non damnant tantum, sed etiam ex Christianorum mensis penitus abdicare annituntur, cum patres nostros mille quingentis annis in eo vitu perdurasse inveniantur. Et certè, (si historiis fides adhibeatur, aliisque scriptoribus antiquis) in cibis omnibus fere, nationibus placuisse reperiuntur. Alexandro potentissimo atque opulentissimo regi in deliciis fuerunt, ad amicos enim pro summo munere piscículos misisse proditum est.
units.tr: ...and we read that Christ himself was very familiar with eating fish, and Luke bears witness that after the resurrection he ate a piece of fish that was offered him. It is therefore right to wonder at the opinions of some in our own age, who not only condemn eating fish but strive to banish it entirely from Christian tables, when our fathers are found to have kept to that diet for fifteen hundred years. And indeed, if histories and other ancient writers are to be trusted, fish are found to have pleased almost all nations in their food. They were a delight to Alexander, the most powerful and wealthy king, for it is recorded that he sent small fish to his friends as a great gift.

units.la: Agrigentini Geloni tyranno gulæ & luxui dedito piscinam extruxerunt magnificentissimam, 7. stadiatum longitudinis, tum latitudinis, altitudinis verò continentem cubitos viginti. Nostris in tertis passim adalendos piscés, lacustres visuntur, omnibus ferè in tractatibus piscinæ, quibus non quidem ad luxum semper omnes, sed ad necessitatem utuntur & voluptatem, educantur verò tantum in iis aut lucii, percæ, anguillæ, cyprini, tincæ & alii quidam, quorum apud antiquos Romanos nullum fuisse in mensis visum, sicut necaliorum fluviatilium & lacustrium, in confesso est.
units.tr: The people of Agrigentum built a most magnificent fish pond for Gelon the tyrant, who was given over to gluttony and luxury. It was seven stadia long, and its breadth and depth were twenty cubits. In our lands, freshwater fish which are fed in ponds are found almost everywhere in most estates, and all men use them not always for luxury but for need and pleasure. In these ponds only pike, perch, eels, carp, tench and certain others are raised. It is agreed that none of these, nor any other river or lake fish, was ever seen on the tables of the ancient Romans.

units.la: Piscium differentiae variae: quinam & quando in cibis praestantiores?
units.tr: Varieties of fish: which are the more excellent for food, and when?

units.la: Piscium discrimina & species enumerare omnes, immensi foret laboris, & extra infinitum. Quis enim marinos seu in mari degentes vasto[q;] Oceano, totaque fretis ac fluviis generatos numero explicare queat, cum qui in nostris fluminibus, amnibus, lacubus ac stagnis agentes vix exploratos habeamus & compertos.
units.tr: To enumerate all the kinds and species of fish would be an immense labour, and an endless one. For who could count those that live in the sea, in the vast Ocean, or those born in straits and rivers throughout the world, when we have hardly explored and known those that live in our own rivers, streams, lakes and ponds?

units.la: Differentias tamen piscium praebet generatio & victus eorundem. Sunt enim qui ex coitu prome-niant, sunt alii qui in limo vel arena, vel spuma maris, imbribus excitati; alii carne vivitant, alii alga & caeno, alii humore dulci & potulento, alii lentore quodam suo, omnes autem generatione constitutionis sua talem materiam participant, qualem in pastu sibi assumunt, ut ita in cor-sessio sit, innumeră piscium genera, variaque loca varia esse & diversa, difficile propterea cunctos describere. Sufficiat hic nosse ac de piscibus prodere, quae ad sanorum aegrotantiumque commoditatem facere videntur, maxime ve o quinam vitae sanitatis prorogandae conducant, nec non boni mali, succi existant. Cestat inter omnes Medicina scientia claros ac peritos, qui de piscium alimento & natura sagacissime ac prudentissime pariter historiam posteris reliquerunt, eorum piscium carnem, qui in aquis degunt coenosis, sordidis, stagnis tranquillis, & à ventis silentibus, fluctibusq; minime commotis, amnesq; praeterea grandes non admittentibus, fontes non habentibus, neque largum effluxum, deterrimam esse malisq; succi. Nam stagna, quae nullas emittunt aquas, sedpigra & immota tantum permanent, Galenus testimonio, l. de malis boni q; succi cibis, necnon iis qua de alimentis facuit scripsit: voluminibus sunt in confessa damnatione, omnino q; carnem improbissimam obtinent, qui in lacubus ac paludibus aquis q; stantibus aluntur. Minus enim natant exercentur q;, ac eq; vtuntur & vitiu deteriori, maxime vero si in earum lacum aqua ex magnis cuitatibus, latrinas, balnea, maxilla, ac culinas, fullonum q; qui vestes & linteas eluunt, sordes expurgans, effundit, pessima enim tam faeculenta aqua degentibus caro nascitur, quae commestae corporis nostri alimoniam facile conspurcare apta est. Et e contra, quem admodum piscis marini saxatiles, in alto aequore degentes, sunt salubriores, sic quo q; fluviatiles, qui adversus torrentium impetu exercentur ac fatigantur, atq; occurrentibus abruptis vadorum petris illiduntur, his qui in stagnis limosis q; lacubus tranquille degunt & torpent, castigatiora habere sumina, inq; salubri vitius ratione praeferendos esse existimandum est. In aquis rapidis & currentibus nati probam carnem habent & succum, sed praepreferuntur his marini, quia salsus aquoris liquor & fluxus inter saxa collisio, visciduum illorum liquorem vel potius mucorum attenuat & digerit. Unde Cornelius Celsus l. 2. c. 17. inquit, leuior pisces est inter saxa editus quam in arena, leuior in arena quam in limo, quo fit, ut ex stagno vel lacu eadem piscium genera graviora sint, leuiorque qui in alto, quam qui in vado vixit.
units.tr: Yet the generation and diet of fish supply differences among them. For some come forth from mating, some arise from mud or sand, or from sea-foam stirred up by rains; some live on flesh, some on seaweed and slime, some on sweet and liquid moisture, some on their own viscous humour; and all, by their generation and constitution, take on the nature of the matter they take in as food. Since therefore the kinds of fish are innumerable and their places various and different, it is difficult to describe them all. It is enough here to know and set forth about fish what seems useful for the convenience of the healthy and the sick, especially which of them help to preserve health, and which are good or bad in juice. All agree that the authors famous and expert in medicine, who wrote most wisely and prudently on the food and nature of fish, have left to posterity the history that the flesh of fish living in foul, muddy, still ponds, untouched by winds, not stirred by waves, not admitting large rivers, having no springs and no free outflow, is the very worst and of the worst juice. For ponds that send out no water but remain stagnant and motionless are condemned, as Galen testifies in his book on good and bad juice foods and in the volumes he wrote on foods. And those fish fed in lakes and marshes with standing water have the most wretched flesh. For they swim less, take less exercise, and have a poorer and more vicious quality, especially if into their lake flows water from great cities, carrying away the filth of latrines, baths, sewers and kitchens, and of the launderers who wash clothes and linen. For the fish living in such foul water produce the most wretched flesh, which, when eaten, is apt easily to defile the nourishment of our body. And conversely, just as sea fish that live among rocks and in deep water are healthier, so river fish that are tested and worn out by fighting the force of torrents, and dashed against the jagged rocks of the shallows, should be thought to have more refined juices and to be preferred for a healthy diet over those that lie sluggish and dull in muddy ponds or quiet lakes. Fish born in swift and running waters have good flesh and juice, but sea fish are preferred to these, because the salt liquid of the sea and the collision of the current among rocks thin and digest their viscous liquid, or rather their mucus. Hence Cornelius Celsus, book 2, chapter 17, says: "A fish taken among rocks is lighter than one from sand, and lighter from sand than from mud. So it comes about that the same kinds of fish are heavier from a pond or lake, and the one that lived in deep water is lighter than the one that lived in shallows."

units.la: Saxatiles omnium iudicio celebrantur, qui amnibus puris, limpidis, saxeisque aquis littoribus que eduntur ac degunt, proinde horum esu febricitantibus nonnunquam conceditur, ut sunt dulcorum, auratarum, luciorum, barbatulorum, percarum, quia qualitates habent febricitantibus contrarias, frigiditatem sc. & humiditatem, tum etiam quia excrementis, ut ceteri, non adeo abundant, interque scopulos & saxa, seu in saxosis locis sese exercent, haec enim fluxus inter saxa, scopulosque collisio mucum illorum absorbet atque abstergit. Unde arbitror facile pisces vere saxatiles dici, fernipossunt ab iis qui in lentibus, arenosis aut terreis littoribus aquaque natant, qui improprie & perperam a quibusdam saxatiles nominantur, cum potius ita appellari a graecis autoribus inveniantur, qui in saxosis locis ac circa promontoria scopulosque maris delitescunt, fasciaque exercent.
units.tr: Rock fish are celebrated by the judgment of all, those that are born and live in clear, limpid, rocky waters and along the shores. Therefore their eating is sometimes allowed to the feverish, such as dace, gilt-head, pike, barbel and perch, because they have qualities contrary to fever, namely coldness and moisture; also because they do not abound in excrements as others do, and they exercise themselves among reefs and rocks, or in rocky places, for the flow and collision among rocks and reefs absorbs and wipes away their mucus. Hence I think that those may rightly be called truly rock fish, which cannot be said of those that swim in sandy, muddy or earthy shores and waters. These are improperly and wrongly called rock fish by some, whereas Greek authors are found to have so named those that hide among rocky places and around promontories and reefs of the sea, and exercise there.

units.la: Porro alimentorum, quibus vtuntur pisces, habenda ratio est, nam alimenta carnis bonitatem vel malignitatem faciunt, succique probitatem
units.tr: Moreover, the food that fish eat must be considered, for food makes the goodness or badness of the flesh, and the soundness of the juice.

units.la: Leues pisces sunt qui mollem tenerarumque, non glutinosam habent carnem.
units.tr: Light fish are those that have soft and tender, not glutinous, flesh.

units.la: Qui pisces aegris conceßi? & ob quam causam? Pisces saxatiles quinam vere dicantur?
units.tr: Which fish are allowed to the sick, and for what reason? Which fish are truly to be called rock fish?

units.la: Alimenta piscium notanda. tem vel improbitatem. Certum est, vbi herba-rum radicumq; copia nascitur, excellentiores in cibis fieri & salubriores piscer. Qui limosas herbas malique succi radices attingunt, improbantur. Qui in amnibus, magnas & populosas urbes praeterfluentibus hominum stercoribus, aliisque id genus sordidissimis efficiunt nutriuntur, omnino cibis sunt abdicandi, pestilentes n. succi tales esse inde patet, quod paucô tempore, si extincti seruentur, putredinem concipiant & factorem, quod Ausonius de coruo dixit,
units.tr: The food of fish is to be noted. Goodness or badness. It is certain that where herbs and roots abound, fish become more excellent as food and more wholesome. Those that feed on muddy herbs and roots of bad juice are disapproved. Those that are nourished in rivers flowing past great and populous cities, on the dung of men and other most filthy things of that kind, must altogether be rejected as food, for their juices are plainly pestilential. This is shown by the fact that, if kept dead for only a short time, they quickly conceive putrefaction and stench, as Ausonius said of the crow:

units.la: Nec duraturi post bina trichoria corui.
units.tr: Nor will the crow last after two or three hours.

units.la: Quin & lucium a vitiu damnare visus est a loco in quo versatur, ait enim, Lucius obscuras vlua, coenoque lacunas Obsidet hic nullos menfarū lectus ad visus Feruet fumosis olido nidore popinis.
units.tr: Indeed he seems to have condemned the pike for the place in which it lives. For he says: "The pike besieges the dusky sedge and the muddy pools; no couch of tables is seen here; it seethes in smoky kitchens with a foul stench."

units.la: Sic Mosellam idem Poeta a puritate commen-dat, inquiens, Tu neque limigeris ripam praetexeris vluis, Nec piger immundo perfundis littore coeno: Sicca sed in primas spargis vestigia lym-
units.tr: So the same poet commends the Moselle for its purity, saying: "You neither cover your bank with muddy sedge, nor lazily soak your shore in filthy mud, but you scatter dry footprints over the first pebbles."

units.la: Et paulo post: Spectaris vitreo per lenia terga profundo, Secreti nihil amnis habens, atque almus aperto Pandatur intuitu liquidis obtutibus aer; Nec placidi prohibent oculos per inania venti. Sic demersa procul durante per inania visu Cernimus, arcaniq; patet penetrale fluenti.
units.tr: And a little later: "You are seen through glassy depths gliding gently, having nothing hidden, and the nourishing air is spread open to the clear gaze; nor do gentle winds hinder the eyes through the empty space. Thus we see things sunken far off through the empty clear sight, and the secret inner part of the flowing stream lies open."

units.la: Ex quibus Ausonii verbis pisces Mosellae mirè salubres esse facile est colligere, ut ita certum sit, & in consistendo, vitae sua adferre detrimentum nō poenitendum, sanitatique parum consulere, qui piscibus vescuntur malo pabulo pastis & enutriti.
units.tr: From Ausonius's words it is easy to gather that the fish of the Moselle are wonderfully healthful. So it is certain that those who eat fish fed on bad food, and nourished on it, do not hesitate to harm their own life and take little care of their health.

units.la: Sed & locorum, in quibus educantur pisces, delectus habendus, à quibus magna exurgunt differentia, tum quo ad habitum vegetiorem ac vigentiorem magnitudinem, teste Aristotele, sicut in animantibus caeteris, spirituque sces, contra regionibus plurima spectantur discrimina. Sunt enim quaedam loca piscibus singulis propria, in quibus rectius valent, commodiora sunt quidem, sunt ea, quae algarum copia scatent, pinguiores enim iis in locis solent pabulari. Nam quibus alga pabulum est, affatim pascuntur, plurimi ibi pisces reperiuntur. Pontum gregatim petunt cibi gratia, qui uberior & commodior illic est propter dulcium aquarum admixtionem, nam humor dulcior & potulentior ad partum & foetum educandum commodior. Apud Creta insulam gobiones, genusque omne saxatile satis pinguescunt. Qui in Eurypo Pyraeo sunt, feras omnes per hiemem enatant, excepto uno gorgone, sed veris circa principium eo redeunt.
units.tr: But the choice of the places in which fish are bred must also be considered, for great differences arise from them, both as to a more vigorous and lively habit and size, as Aristotle attests, and as in other animals, and in breath. Moreover, very many differences are seen according to regions. For there are some places proper to particular fish, in which they thrive better and are more suitable; those are the ones that abound in seaweed, for fish usually feed more fatly in such places. Where seaweed is their food, they are fed abundantly, and very many fish are found there. They seek the Pontus in flocks for food, which is richer and more convenient there because of the admixture of sweet waters; for sweeter and more liquid moisture is more suitable for bringing forth and rearing offspring. At Crete the gobies and all the rock-dwelling kinds grow fat enough. Those in the Euripus at Piraeus all swim away through the winter, except one gorgon, but return about the beginning of spring.

units.la: Locorum in quibus educantur pisces
units.tr: Of the places in which fish are bred.

units.la: Qui in purissimo mari degunt cateris perpetuo praestant, maxime vbi lit ora, quae aquam in orbem ambiunt, terra non abundant, nec lenia, sed aut arenosa sunt aut aspera. Quod si praeterea ad boream vergat, longe erunt excellentiores, puritas enim aquilonis, qui aquae commiscetur, subsistantia ipsorum praebitatem adauget. Aristoteles plurimum interesse voluit aquilonia sint loca an austrina. Lacus aut piscina sic posita, ut infrequens vel maris vnda, vel fluuii aut perennis fontis vel torrentis priorem submoueat, nec intra confinium veterem sinat remanere, pisces alunt commendabiliores, similes enim sunt pelago eiusmodi lacus, quod ventis consuessum assidue renouatur, vel flumini perpetuo decurrenti at labenti. Ab austro perflante lacus ingratos praebent pisces. Galenus perspicuum esse ait, mare alterum alteri praestare, quod aut maxime purum est, aut fluuios multos & grandes admittit, vt Pontus.
units.tr: Those that live in the purest sea always surpass the others, especially where the shores that encircle the water are not rich in land, and are neither gentle but either sandy or rough. If moreover the place leans toward the north, they will be far more excellent, for the purity of the north wind mingling with the water increases the wholesomeness of their substance. Aristotle held that it matters greatly whether places lie to the north or to the south. A lake or fishpond so placed that the wave of the sea, or of a river, or of a perennial spring or torrent, now and then sweeps away the former water and does not let it remain within the old boundary, nourishes more commendable fish; for such a lake resembles that sea, since it is constantly renewed by the winds, or by a river flowing and gliding on perpetually. Lakes exposed to the blowing south wind give disagreeable fish. Galen says it is plain that one sea excels another, namely the one that is either most pure or admits many large rivers, as the Pontus does.

units.la: Purissimi maris pisces praeferuntur omnibus. Stagnales Pontici bonitate quidem vincunt, sed sunt illis inferiores, eodem ipso propter aquarum dulcium ingentem abundantiam. Itaque multum interest, hoc an illo educentur loco. Nun enim, vt Varro ait, si murena optima sint in Sicilia, & helops Rhodi, continuo hi pisces omni mari tales exstiunt: annium enim & aquarum mirabilis vires, pisces, in iis degentes sentire, nemo nemo dubitauerit: quin & earundem benitate aut pravitate discrimina memoranda oriri ne-cesse est, talis quippe sunt aquae, qualis terra per quam fluunt; qualesque herbarum, quas lavant, succi: & iidem amnes reperiuntur parte quadam salubres, alia insalubres. Ctesias tradit in Armenia esse fontem nigris piscibus abundantem, qui in cibis sumti afferant mortem. Theophrastus pr' terea in fonte quodam Arcadiae lethales tradidit. Borysthenes amnis suavissimos fert piscēs, qui tamen aliate ex rivis influentibus saporemque eius mutantibus deteriores efficiantur, influentes enim alias aquas saporem immutare in ponto perspicuum est, in quem multitudo fluminum influit. Tigris a celeritate sic dictus in lacum influit Rhetusfam, omnia illa pondera sustinentem, & nitrum nebulis exhalantem, cui unum genus est piscium, quod a- quae transcurrentis alveo non miscetur: exsistunt autem pisces illi e lacu Rhetusfa hominum piscilentes, Tigris vero utiles, nam hi e Tigri in lacum Rhetusfam non transnatant, utriusque autem lacus pisces non nominatos hactenus a quo- quam inueni, quod equidem mirum, cum aliarum aquarum piscibus suis nominibus, utpluri-mum appellati reperiantur. Nilum, auctor est Strabo in libris de situ orbis, permultos diversque educare pisces, proprium quandam & suam habentes formam, omnino quae gratissimi saporis esse praedicantur, praecipue vero qui coracini dicuntur: cuntur : latum quoq; piscem pragrandem ad 20. ultraq; libras in eodem crescentem, omni apparatu ratione suavissimum & gratum alimentum esse Athenaeus testis est. Non tamen desunt, qui Nilotici piscis minus salubres existimant, forsan quoniam ventis Nilus non agitetur, Gargis anguilla ad tricenos pedes longa sunt mensa abiles Boryfthenis piscium nomina non inveniuntur, tantum laudantur saporis suavitate, praedicanturq; sine ossibus spinisq;. In India amnibus piscium genus est in terram exeuntium, ac deinde reflientium. In Eloro amne lupi, anguillaq; magnitudine insignes. Ptolomaeus Aegypti Rex apud Athenaeum testatur, circa Berenicen Libyae fluvium esse luporum, murenarum, anguillarumq; copia refertissimum. In Aorno vocales reperiri pisces, turdis similes certi autores tradunt, quos varios appellant. In Syria, Xenophonte in expeditione Cyri narrante, est Achelois, in quo sunt pisces pragrandes & manuetissimi, quos violare nefas erat. Salmo fluviatilis in Aquitania marinis omnibus praefertur. Ticinus in Insubria peculiariter alit thynnum piscem odoris suavissimi, teste D. Ambrosio. In Lario Italia lacu perca suaves alluntur & ampla, trutta etiam grandissima, quae ad 100. quandoq; libras pervenisse testatur Paulus Iovius. Mintium Benacus, qui est in agro Veronensi, mirabilis anguillarum captura mensa Octobri nobilitatur. Be- tur. Be tur. Et quas flumina illa grandia Italia, Gallia, fluviolos item rivos & torrentes piscibus scatentes enumerare queat? non opera pretium duco, cum Paulus Iovius aliique Itali, qui de piscium esu monumenta posteris reliquerunt, abunde eorum meminerint, Qui porro peregrinationes sponte suscepérunt, aut legationibus functi terras septentrionales adierunt, testantur lacus illic esse ingentes, omniumque generum piscibus mire abundantes, sponte enim illic nascuntur, & felicissime proveniunt Moscovia, Suecia, atque etiam vicini tractus lacubus huiusmodi abundant.
units.tr: The fish of the purest sea are preferred to all others. Pontic pond fish surpass them in goodness, but they are inferior to these, precisely because of the huge abundance of fresh water. So it matters a great deal in which place they are raised. For, as Varro says, if moray eels are best in Sicily, and the helops at Rhodes, these fish immediately become such in every sea. No one will doubt that rivers and waters have wonderful powers, which the fish living in them feel. Indeed, the differences in their goodness or badness must necessarily arise from the waters themselves, for the waters are such as the land through which they flow, and such too are the juices of the herbs they wash over. The same rivers are found partly healthful and partly unhealthful. Ctesias relates that in Armenia there is a spring abounding in black fish, which bring death when eaten. Theophrastus further reported deadly fish in a certain spring of Arcadia. The river Borysthenes bears very sweet fish, yet they are made worse by tributary rivers flowing into it and changing its flavour, for it is clear that the waters flowing in alter the taste in the Pontus, into which a multitude of rivers flows. The Tigris, so called from its swiftness, flows into the lake Rhetusfa, which bears all those weights and exhales nitre in mists. In it there is one kind of fish which does not mix with the water of the rushing stream. The fish from lake Rhetusfa are foul-smelling to men, while those of the Tigris are useful, for these do not swim across from the Tigris into lake Rhetusfa. I have found that the fish of neither lake have so far been named by anyone, which is surprising, since the fish of other waters are mostly found with their own names. Strabo, in his books on the geography of the world, is the authority that the Nile rears very many and varied fish, having a peculiar form of their own, which are declared to be of the most pleasant flavour, especially those called coracini; and Athenaeus is witness that a broad fish, very large, growing in the same river to twenty pounds and more, is in every preparation a most pleasant and agreeable food. Yet there are not wanting those who think Nile fish less wholesome, perhaps because the Nile is not stirred by winds. Gargis eels, thirty feet long, are fit for the table. The names of Borysthenes fish are not found; they are praised only for the sweetness of their flavour, and are said to be without bones and spines. In India there is a kind of fish in the rivers which comes out onto the land and then returns to the water. In the river Eloros there are wolf-fish and eels remarkable for their size. Ptolemy, king of Egypt, reports in Athenaeus that near Berenice in Libya there is a river very full of wolf-fish, moray eels and eels. Certain authors relate that in the Aornos there are singing fish, like thrushes, which they call "various." In Syria, as Xenophon recounts in the expedition of Cyrus, there is the Achelois, in which there are very large and tame fish, which it was unlawful to harm. The river salmon in Aquitaine is preferred to all sea fish. The Ticinus in Insubria particularly nourishes the tunny, a fish of very sweet odour, as Saint Ambrose testifies. In the Lario lake in Italy there are sweet and large perch, and trout of the greatest size, which Paulus Iovius testifies have sometimes reached one hundred pounds. The Benacus, which lies in the Veronese territory, is made famous by the remarkable catch of eels in the month of October. And what could anyone list of those great rivers of Italy and Gaul, and likewise the small streams and torrents teeming with fish? I do not think it worth the effort, since Paulus Iovius and other Italians, who left monuments to posterity on the eating of fish, have abundantly recorded them. Those who of their own accord have undertaken journeys, or who have travelled to the northern lands on embassies, testify that there are huge lakes there, wonderfully abounding in fish of every kind; for they grow there naturally and thrive most happily. Muscovy, Sweden, and indeed the neighbouring regions abound in lakes of this kind.

units.la: Caeterum ex aquarum pisculentarum cibis in frequentiori apud nos esu sunt, mensarumque delitiis habentur ut plurimum, delphinus, balena, lucius, cyprinus, seu carpio, accipenser, salmo, trutta, anguilla, prasinus, barbus, perca, mullus, scarus, scombrus, tinca, murena, lampetra, salpa, raja, platessa seu pectines, harengi, gobii, alburnus, aliique complures maritimis populis magis cogniti. Horum autem alii sunt pelagii, altum tenentes mare, inque eius penetralibus profundo degentes, terram litoraque fugientes, cuiusmodi sunt congri, asselli, thynni, rajae, &c. alii litorales, qui in vado degunt, ac in litoribus & circa ea versantur, ut mulli, gobii, mugiles, cantharí, oculati: alii saxatiles, qui scilicet in mari inter saxa degunt, quos ante cunctos Medicina magnificat. Optime inquit Cohl. 9, c. 16. saxosum mare.
units.tr: Moreover, among the fish-water foods, the following are most commonly eaten among us and are usually regarded as the delicacies of our tables: dolphin, whale, pike, carp, sturgeon, salmon, trout, eel, prasinus, barbel, perch, mullet, parrotfish, mackerel, tench, moray, lamprey, salpa, skate, plaice or flounder, herring, gobies, bleak, and several others better known to maritime peoples. Of these, some are pelagic, keeping to the open sea and living deep in its recesses, shunning the land and shores, such as conger eels, hake, tunny, skates, etc. Others are littoral, living in shallows and moving about the shores and their vicinity, such as mullet, gobies, grey mullet, cantharus, and oculate fish. Others are saxatile, that is, living in the sea among rocks, and these above all are praised by medicine. "Best," he says (Cohl. 9, c. 16), "the rocky sea."

units.la: Piscium tres praecipuae differentiae. mare nominis sui pisces alit, qui quod in petrU stabulentur, saxatiles dicti sunt, ut merula, turdi, melanuri, quos Galenus l. 3. de alimento. facult. recenset, & perspicue, scares, cottyphos, juliadas, phycidas, percas, petraos nominat pisces, a locis in quibus inveniuntur & diuersantur, non enim in lubricis, arenosis, aut terrestribus aquoris littoribus, sed ubi petra & saxosa sunt littora, sese illatebrant & parturiunt. Alimonia ex his non modo concoctu facilis, sed humanis quoque corporibus saluberrima est, sanguinem enim substantia mediocrem generant: unde Galenus in esculento piscium jure albo elixatos, marasmo aut sincope ex spirituum inopia languentibus, & lassitudine ulcerosa defessis salutaris eos esse statuit, quibus vires effectas reficere nouit, nec illorum efficam febri aut pleuritide laborantibus a morbi statu denegauit.
units.tr: Three principal differences of fish. The sea feeds fish that take their name from the sea itself. Those which dwell among rocks are called saxatile, as the blackbird, thrush and melanurus, which Galen lists in book 3 of On the Faculties of Foods. Clearly he also names scares, cottyphos, juliadas, phycidas, perca and petraos as fish named from the places where they are found and live. For they do not hide and breed on slippery, sandy or earthy shores, but where the shore is rocky and stony. Food from these is not only easy to digest but also most wholesome for human bodies, for they produce blood of moderate substance. Hence Galen, in the edible broth of fish boiled in white, judged them healthful for those wasted by atrophy or fainting from lack of spirits, and for those weary from ulcerous weakness; he knew they restore strength that has been spent, and he did not deny their efficacy to those suffering from fever or pleurisy in the course of the disease.

units.la: De Delphino.
units.tr: On the Dolphin.

units.la: CElsus inter eos cibos, qui plurimum praebent alimenti retulit omnes bestias marinas. Galenus omnes cetaceos pisces duram prauiqueque fricci, excrementisque plenam carnem obtinere constanter affirmat, proinde sale eos condiendos esse, qua conditura alimentum exipsis proveniens, promtius faciliusque in corpus distribuitur faciliusque concoquitur. Delphinum phinum, certum est, in cibos venire, nec ferinum ejus gulam fastidire saporem. Ex mari mediterraneo adfertur in Galliam, Italiamque, habeturque in pretio. Maritimis tamen gentibus raro editur, imo nec plebs infima eum attingit. Porro epar commendari video & linguam, ipsam vero carnem, quia præpinguis est, nauseam excitare, ventriculumq; relaxare verisimile est. Adeps eius ad eosdem vsus, ad quos græci oleum, in testis repositus inuentus est à Græcis apud Mofynœcos, sicut & ex carne ejus salsamenta, teste Xenoph. in expeditionis Cyri L.f.
units.tr: Celsus, among the foods that furnish the most nourishment, listed all sea creatures. Galen constantly affirms that all cetacean fish have hard, rather tough flesh, full of excrement, so they should be seasoned with salt. By this seasoning the nourishment arising from them is distributed into the body more readily and easily, and is digested more easily. It is certain that dolphin is eaten, and the wild palate does not disdain its taste. It is brought from the Mediterranean Sea into France and Italy and is held in high esteem. Yet among maritime peoples it is rarely eaten, and not even the lowest common people touch it. Moreover, I see that the liver and the tongue are commended, but the flesh itself, because it is very fatty, probably causes nausea and relaxes the stomach. Its fat, put to the same uses to which the Greeks put oil, was found by the Greeks stored in jars among the Mosynoeci, and salted meats were made from its flesh too, as Xenophon testifies in the Expedition of Cyrus, book 5.

units.la: De Balena.
units.tr: On the Whale.

units.la: HUjus caro vilissima habetur. Sed lingua in præcipua auctoritate est præsertim diebus quadragenarii jejunii apud Pontificios. Caro pinguis est & dura, coquitur cum pisis, vicemq; non raro supplet siilla: quidam verubus eam figunt, torrentq;: admodum autem noxia recens deprehensa est, falsa innocentior: qui colico dolori sunt obnoxii, ab illius esu sibi omnino temperent: otiosis quoq; infalu-berrima est, graves vero laboresque subeuntibus aut vehementer exercitatis non adeo inutilis.
units.tr: Its flesh is considered very cheap. But the tongue is in especial favour, particularly on the days of the forty-day fast among the Papists. The flesh is fatty and tough; it is cooked with peas and often takes the place of herring. Some skewer it on spits and roast it. It has recently been found to be very harmful when fresh, but less harmful when salted. Those subject to colic should abstain from it altogether. To the idle it is not at all wholesome, but to those undertaking heavy labours or vigorous exercise it is not much harmful.

units.la: De
units.tr: Of

units.la: ON leuem inter celebres autores diglatiationem concitauit lucius, fere enim omnes lupum appellandum censuerunt non lucium, propterea quod in pisces non secus ac lupus in oues grassetur. Verum hic error docte pariterac diligenter à Paulo Jouio explosus est. Porro Aulonius in Mosella de lucio ita canit.
units.tr: Over the pike, a slight dispute has been stirred up among famous authors, for almost all of them have judged that it should be called the wolf (lupus) rather than the lucius, because it attacks fish just as a wolf attacks sheep. But this error has been learnedly and diligently exploded by Paulus Jovius. Moreover, Ausonius in the Moselle sings thus of the pike:

units.la: Hic etiam Latio risus prænomine cultor Stagnorum, querulus vis infestissima ranis Lucius, obscuras vlua cœnoq; latitnas Obsidet, hic nullos mensarum lectus ad vsus, Fervet fumosis olido nidore popinis.
units.tr: "Here too the pike, which in Latium goes by the name of Laughter (Risus), a dweller in the pools, a querulous and most hostile enemy of frogs, lurks in dim sedge and mud. No table's couch claims him for its uses; he seethes in smoky cookshops with a foul stench."

units.la: Ex quibus intelligere facile est, olim nullo in honore mensarum fuisse.
units.tr: From these lines it is easy to understand that formerly it held no honour at the table.

units.la: Nunc passim inter lautissimos pisces amnicos annumeratur. Certum autem est quasdam gentes parum luciis delectari ob aliorum marinorum præsertim abundantiam. Et Itali parua in gloria eos habent, ob saporem insuauem ac pene fastidiosum. Gulosissimus enim est & voracissimus, præcipueque carniuorus, suique generis piscibus vescitur gratissime, sicut & raniis. Quia tanta est gula huius piscis, vt anserculos anaticulasque in aquis natantes deglutiat. Qui in fluuiis rapidis ac puris aluntur magis commendantur, limosum virus gustatu referenserenfetentes, cibis vt inutiles, abdicandi. Porro in coquendo elixandoq; artificium adhibetur non paruum, vt durior evadat, dura enim piscium caro gratior est, mollis insalubris. Apparatum hunc culinae germanorum primum videntur docuisse alios, nam condimenta, quae hodie luciis adhibentur, lautiora, à populis quibusdam germanica appellantur. Fit autem id genus condimenti ex fi-vapi & butyro prunis liquato. Alii edunt ex aceto piperato: alii & quidem lautiores frigunt, exque liquore mali aurantii affumunt: alii craticula, praesertim vero lucios, torrent, prius tamen vtrinque scarificationibus cute aperta, vt butyrum, quo li- quato in cratícula humectatur, penitus subeat.
units.tr: Now it is everywhere counted among the most choice river fish. It is certain, however, that some peoples take little pleasure in pike, chiefly because of the abundance of other sea fish. And Italians hold them in low esteem, on account of their insipid and almost loathsome flavour. For it is very greedy and voracious, especially carnivorous, and feeds most eagerly on fish of its own kind, and on frogs as well. The gullet of this fish is so great that it swallows goslings and ducklings swimming on the water. Those raised in swift, clear rivers are more commended; those that taste of muddy filth and stink are to be rejected as useless for food. Moreover, in cooking and boiling, no small skill is applied so that it becomes firmer, for hard fish flesh is more pleasant and soft flesh unwholesome. The German kitchen seems first to have taught this preparation to others, for the seasonings used today with pike, the more refined ones, are called German by certain peoples. This kind of seasoning is made from a certain mixture and butter melted over coals. Others eat it with peppered vinegar. Others, the more refined, fry it and add the juice of bitter orange. Others grill it on a gridiron, especially pike; but first the skin is cut with incisions on both sides, so that the melted butter moistens the gridiron and penetrates thoroughly.

units.la: Anglia praecipuae nobilitatis lucios o- stentar, ventribusque eorum cultro apertis, fenum pingueque, vendentes ementibus ostendunt, & si non emantur, (mirum dicto) in aquas eos rursum coniiciunt, nec intereunt, sed vulnus celerrime coalescit, quod quidam contactu tincarum ascribunt, tinca enim glutinosa admodum est, alii rectius eam vim iis inesse à natura affirmant, inveneum enim est interaneis lucii coagulari lac, ac glaciari aeque ac coagulo.
units.tr: In England, pike of the highest quality are displayed. Their bellies are cut open with a knife, and they show the fat and the roe to those who would buy. If they are not bought, (wonderful to say) they are thrown back into the water, and they do not die; the wound heals very quickly. Some ascribe this to contact with the tench, for the tench is very glutinous. Others more correctly affirm that this power is in them by nature, for it is found that in the entrails of the pike the milk coagulates and sets, just as with rennet.

units.la: De
units.tr: Of

units.la: De Cyprino.
units.tr: On the Carp.

units.la: Cyprinum piscem eruditi existimant esse, qui a nostris Carpio, Carpus & Carpena vocatur, quem Aristoteles inter lacus stres & amnicos retulit. Linguam eius seu palatum, lautissimos inter cibus reponunt ganeae periti, de quo Aristoteles 2. de animalium partibus sic prodidit compluribus piscibus carnosum est palatum, & quidem inter fluviatiles cyprinis admodum carnosum & molle. Est in exemplis Lurco quidam Borbonensis Verdeletus nomine, qui in vivariis aut piscinis Illustrissimi familia Borbonia ad duo triave millia Cyprinorum cepit, iisque singulis linguam seu palatum detraxit, ut quid in gloria palati, palatum possit, experiretur, gulam quasi suam, quae postea ob insaniam tantum a carnifice laqueo et fracta est, expleret. Carne autem constant molli & phlegmatica, seu aquea, non glutinosa. Qui educantur stercoribus & sordibus urbium, cibus omnino abdicandos censent eruditiores. Nec enim ullum dubium est, quin propiscinarum ac vivariorum situ ac natura magnas alimenti sortiantur differentias, cum alibi pinguiores, alibi graciliores, alibi glutinosiores, & lentulentiores, qui omnium pessimi sunt, esse deprehendantur. Itaque, quo loco piscina instituenda ac ponenda sint, diligenter considerandum. Pabulum namque gratia & salubritati addit vel detrahit. Porro multifariam coquuntur apud Germanos adeo. adq; varios vsus in re cibaria adhibentur. Mo-dos coquendi relinquemus coquis. Vt vero in multos dies coctus duret, fumenda sunt vini & aquae partes aequales, quibus aceti, aut omphacii nonnihil adaitur ad acorem conciliandum, deinde piperis, garyophyllorum, zinziberis & nucis moschata pollinem liberalius adiicere oportet, adq; colorem elegantem inducendum, crocum, qua postea cum cyprino diutius sunt coquenda.
units.tr: Learned men think that the cyprinus is the fish that among us is called carp, carpus, or carpena, which Aristotle counted among the lake and river fish. Gourmets place its tongue or palate among the most refined foods. Aristotle wrote about this in book 2 of On the Parts of Animals thus: "In many fish the palate is fleshy, and among river fish the cyprinus has a very fleshy and soft palate." There is an example: a certain glutton of Bourbon named Verdelet, who caught two or three thousand carp in the fishponds or tanks of the most illustrious house of Bourbon, and took the tongue or palate from each of them, so that he might test what the palate could do for the glory of taste, and so that he might fill a throat that was, as it were, his own. Later, for madness alone, he was broken by the executioner's noose. The flesh is soft, phlegmatic, watery, not glutinous. The learned consider that carp raised on the dung and filth of cities should be wholly rejected as food. For there is no doubt that from the situation and nature of ponds and fishtanks they receive great differences in nourishment: elsewhere they are found fatter, elsewhere slenderer, elsewhere more glutinous and sluggish, which are the worst of all. Thus, the place where a fishpond is to be established and sited must be carefully considered, for the food adds to or takes away from both flavour and healthfulness. Moreover, they are cooked in many ways among the Germans and put to various culinary uses. We shall leave the methods of cooking to the cooks. But so that they keep for many days when cooked, equal parts of wine and water are to be taken, to which a little vinegar or verjuice is added to give sharpness. Then pepper, cloves, ginger and powdered nutmeg should be added more generously, and saffron to give an elegant colour, with which the carp must afterwards be cooked for a longer time.

units.la: Cum squamis quoqve elixare eos expedit, sic enim sapidum illum pinguemq; succum intus servari, qui desquamatis aliàs deperiret, constat, Aristoteles miram cyprino fertilitatem tribuit, quinquies aut sexies anno parere affirmans. Plinius marinum tantum nominat, eumq; canicula exortu siderari, tonitruq; sopiri in mari ab aliquibus existimari, prodidit, quod in fluviatilibus nondum accidisse observatum est.
