units.tr: It is also useful to boil them with their scales on, for it is agreed that this keeps inside the savoury, rich juice which would otherwise be lost if they were scaled. Aristotle attributes a remarkable fertility to the carp, affirming that it spawns five or six times a year. Pliny names only the sea fish, and reported that some think it is struck by the rising of the Dog Star and lulled by thunder in the sea, which has not been observed to happen in river fish.

units.la: De Accipensere.
units.tr: On the Sturgeon.

units.la: Piscium apud antiquos nobilissimum fuisse accipenserem Plin. l. 9. c. 17. autor est, hodieque in summo mensarum honore habetur apud eos, in quorum fluminibus capitur, subit enim e mari flumina. Rhodanum delicatissimos & suauissimos, amplissimosq; praebere constat, vt & Albim, prope Hamburgum inprimis, vbi vasto ore in Oceanum germanicum exoluitur.
units.tr: The sturgeon was the most prized of fish among the ancients, as Pliny witnesses (bk. 9, ch. 17). Even today it holds the highest place at table among those in whose rivers it is caught, since it comes up from the sea into the rivers. It is agreed that the Rhone yields the most delicate and sweetest sturgeon, and very large ones, and so does the Elbe, especially near Hamburg, where it empties into the German Ocean through a wide mouth.

units.la: De nomine inter eruditos non conuenit, alio atq; alio eum appellantes. Paulus Iouius Silurum Aufonii existimauit : Hermolaus Hiccam apud Athen. alii Tursionem Plinii esse crediderunt, cuius etiam opinionis fuisse Christoph. Longolium inuenio. Rondeletus his omnibus scriptor recentior Accipenserem Romanorum literis nobilitatum s. Sturionem esse putauit, & Dorionis ἰνίσκον, siue Galeni galaxian lib. 5. aliment. Sturio igitur mire ingenia doctorum torsi-gulam interim suauiter demulcens, boni enim suauisque succi est, carnisque durae & candidae, adultioris vitulae carnibus haud absimilis: unde nutriendi vi Sturionem pollere certum est, modo bene in ventre perficiatur, secus enim negotium facessit ventriculo. Coctus in aceto seruatur ad aliquot dies. Praefertur mas in cibo: Sed fœmina ouis grauida autoritatem quoque retinuit. Quidam succum crassum & glutinosum eum obtinere ajunt, quod de crudo, vel etiam non probe cocto ac praeparato concessero. Porro in magna fuisse autoritate & honore in mensis Ro- manorum accipenserem testatur Horatius l.1. serm. satyra 2. sic scribens,
units.tr: Scholars do not agree on its name, and they call it by different names. Paulus Iovius thought it was the Silurus of Ausonius. Hermolaus held that it was the hikka mentioned by Athenaeus. Others believed it was the Tursio of Pliny, and I find that Christopher Longolius also held this view. Rondelet, a more recent writer than all of these, thought that the sturgeon, which the Romans made famous in their writings, is the sturio, and also Dorion's inisko [ἰνίσκον], or Galen's galaxias (bk. 5 on foods). The sturgeon is wonderfully pleasing to the palate of scholars, and it soothes the throat meanwhile with its sweetness. For it has good and sweet juice, and its flesh is firm and white, not unlike the flesh of a well-grown calf. It is certain that the sturgeon is strong in nourishing, provided it is well digested in the stomach; otherwise it causes trouble for the stomach. Cooked in vinegar, it keeps for several days. The male is preferred as food, but the female, when full of roe, has also kept its reputation. Some say that it has thick and gluey juice, but I would concede this only of raw fish or fish not properly cooked and prepared. Further, that the sturgeon was held in great esteem and honour at the tables of the Romans is attested by Horace (bk. 1, Satires, satire 2), who writes thus:

units.la: — haud ita pridem. Galloni praeconis erat accipere mensa infamis.
units.tr: — not so long ago, a sturgeon was a disgrace at the table of Gallonius the auctioneer.

units.la: Et Lucilius apud Cic. l. 2. de finib. O Publi, inquit, o gurges Galloni, es homo miser, coenaisti in vita nunquam bene, cum omnia in ista consumis aquilla atque accipe-fere cum decumano. Unde appparet hunc Gallonium obsoniorum gurgitem, accipenseere, ut carissimo & suauissimo pisce ornasse instruxisseque conuiuium. Archestratus apud Athen. lib. 8. existimat ψαλίον eundem piscem esse, atque eum qui apud Accipen- Romanos cum tibiis & coronis ad coenas ser cum cum pompa quadam circumferrut, corona- tibiis & tis etiam iis qui eum ferunt, & appellatur coronis accipenser. De eodem quoque Ciceronis conuiuii illa verba ex lib. de fato leguntur apud Macrob. l. 13. Nam cum esset apud se ad Lauer-nium Scipio, vnaque Pontius, allatus est forte Scipioni accipenser, qui admodum raro capitur, sed est piscis, ut ferunt, inprimis nobilis. Cum autem Scipio vnum & alterum ex iis, qui ipsum salutatum venerant, invitaffet, plurefq; etiam inuitatur videretur, in aure pontius, Scipio inquit, vide quid agas, accipenser iste paucorum hominum est. Comendatur quoq; a Martiali hoc disticho,
units.tr: And Lucilius, quoted by Cicero (bk. 2, On Ends): "O Publius," he says, "O glutton Gallonius, you are a wretched man; you have never dined well in your life, since you spend everything on that eel and sturgeon, along with the tithe-collector." From this it appears that Gallonius, that gulf of delicacies, furnished and equipped his banquet with the sturgeon as the most costly and sweetest fish. Archestratus, cited by Athenaeus (bk. 8), thinks that the psalion [ψαλίον] is the same fish as the one that the Romans, with flutes and garlands, carried around at their dinners with some ceremony; the bearers were also garlanded, and the fish is called the sturgeon. The same passage of Cicero about the banquet is also read in Macrobius (bk. 13), from his book On Fate: "For when Scipio was at his house at Lavernium, together with Pontius, a sturgeon was brought to Scipio by chance. It is a fish rarely caught, but, as they say, a particularly noble one. When Scipio had invited one or two of those who had come to greet him, and seemed about to invite more, Pontius whispered in his ear: 'Scipio,' he said, 'see what you are doing; that sturgeon belongs to a few people.'" It is also commended by Martial in this couplet:

units.la: Ad palatinas accipenseras mittite mensas
units.tr: Send the sturgeons to the tables of the Palatine.

units.la: Ex ouis ejus nigris conditis paratur edulium lium Venetiis laudatissimum, quod Caniaco appellatur, inassuetisque mouet nauseam, assuefactis vero gratissimum. Salsamenta quoq; parantur ex eius dorsi spina, reliqua caro sale fumoq; asseruatur.
units.tr: From its black roe, preserved in salt, a dish is prepared at Venice, most highly praised, which is called caviar. It turns the stomach of those who are not used to it, but it is most pleasing to those who are. Salted meats are also prepared from the backbone of the fish, and the rest of the flesh is kept with salt and smoke.

units.la: De Salmone.
units.tr: On the Salmon.

units.la: Nec te puniceo rutilantem viscere Salmo Transierim lata cuius vaga verbera cauda, Gurgite de sofummas referuntur in vndas, Occultus placido cum prodit ur aquore pulsu, Tu loricato squamosus pectore frontem Lubricus, & dubia faturus fercula cœna, Tempora longarum fers incorrupte morarum Prasignis maculis capitis, cui prodiga nutat Aluus, opimatoq; fluens abdomine venter.
units.tr: Nor shall I pass over you, the salmon, glowing with purple flesh, whose wandering tail beats the waters wide; from the deep you rush up into the surface waves, hidden until you appear, with a gentle splash on the calm water. You, scaly and slippery, with armoured breast, a doubtful dish for a late dinner, endure the seasons of long delays without decay, marked with bright spots on your head, and your belly flows out, loose and fat, with a swelling paunch.

units.la: Ex his Ausonii carminibus facile est elicere Salmonis dotes in re cibaria.
units.tr: From these verses of Ausonius it is easy to draw out the qualities of the salmon as food.

units.la: Intelligit autem Aquitanicum fluviatilem, quem Plinius marinis omnibus praeferri affirmat, lib. 9. cap. 18. Massarius omnibus, tam marinis, quam fluviatilibus anteponere videtur, in quo tamen ab aliis non immerito reprehenditur, cum esu Salmonis colica passione plures correptos esse constet, ob crassum & flatuosum succum, quo abundat. Verum probe praeparatus, hoc est, elixatus in vino cum garyophyllis, pipere, cinnamomo, zinzibere, vel etiam craticraticula tostus in assulas dissectus, & garyophyllis confixus, tum, quod præcipue spectandum, perfectè in ventre coctus confectusq;, alit egregie, extraq; noxam est, quod Rheni, Albis, Rhodaniq̄ue accolæ, Salmonenamque clarent isti fluuii, contestantur. Venter adiposus in præcipua ciborum gloriaest: quin caput etiam magnificatur à ganeæ peritis. Recens suauissimus est: sale quoque conditus atque, vt cæteri grandiores pisces, asseruatus, gratus est, nec insalubris, mutatoque nomine dicitur esox. E mariflumina subeuntes meliores euadunt, marinum illud virus exuentes, vel ad minimum emendantes. Constat tamen non semper è mari in flumina ascendisse, sed pluribus in locis natos & educatos. Rhodanicos & Ligerinos præcipue commendatos apud certos autores inuenio. Mirum vero nullam à græcis Salmonis mentionem factam esse, & à Latinorum, præter Plinium & Aufonium, nullo: quidam trottam fluuiatilem volunt esse Salmonem, quam opinionem relinquo ego in medio.
units.tr: He means the river fish of Aquitaine, which Pliny (bk. 9, ch. 18) says is preferred to all sea fish. Massarius seems to prefer it to all fish, both sea and river, and he is not unjustly reproved by others on this point, since it is well known that many have been seized with colic from eating salmon, because of its thick and windy juice, of which it has plenty. But when it is properly prepared, that is, boiled in wine with cloves, pepper, cinnamon and ginger, or roasted on a gridiron, cut into little strips and studded with cloves, and then, which is chiefly to be looked for, thoroughly digested in the stomach, it nourishes excellently and is free from harm. The people who live along the Rhine, the Elbe and the Rhone, and those rivers famous for their salmon, bear witness to this. The fatty belly is the chief glory of the dish; indeed the head too is extolled by those skilled in gluttony. Fresh, it is most delicious; salted and kept, like the other larger fish, it is pleasant and not unwholesome, and when its name is changed it is called the esox. Fish that come up from the sea into rivers become better, casting off, or at least lessening, the marine taint. It is agreed, however, that they do not always ascend from the sea into rivers, but are born and raised in many places. I find that the salmon of the Rhone and the Loire are especially commended by certain authors. It is strange, however, that the Greeks make no mention of the salmon, and among the Latins none except Pliny and Ausonius. Some want the river trout to be the salmon, but I leave that opinion undecided.

units.la: De trutta, aurata & variola.
units.tr: On the trout, the aurata and the variola.

units.la: NEC tu, trutta, silentio damnanda es adeo in mensarum aulicarum gloria prae aliis nobilitata, saporeq; suaui celebrata, vt etiam Ausonius in sua Mosella te non conticuerit, sic canens, Teque inter geminas species, neutrumq; & vtrumque, Qui necdum Salamo, nec tam Salar ambiguusque Amborum medio sario intercepte sub aeuo
units.tr: Nor are you, trout, to be passed over in silence. You are so renowned above other fish for the glory of the courtly table, and so celebrated for your savour, that even Ausonius did not fail to sing of you in his Mosella: "And you, between the twin kinds, neither one nor the other but both, who are not yet a salmo, nor yet a salar, and ambiguous between both, caught in the middle age."

units.la: Ex quibus versibus colligitur, farionem, variolam seu forellam, salarem & salmonem eundem esse piscem, dicitq; salarem forellam adhuc teneram, farionem media aetate, jam vero grandem forellam Salmonem, seu truttam Salmoneam, cujusmodi plurimi Germania amnes, rivi, rivuli, torrentes, fertilissimi sunt. Celebratur imprimis, quae in fluminibus fontium scaturiginibus abundantibus capiuntur. Porro elixa assis praestant, eduntur q; ex aceto, rarius friguntur, nec alia condimenta patiuntur, suo enim sapore satis placent.
units.tr: From these verses it is gathered that the fario, the variola or forella, the salar and the salmo are the same fish. He says the salar is a forella still tender, the fario is one of middle age, and the salmo, or salmon trout, is a large forella. Germany's many rivers, streams, brooks and torrents are very fertile in such fish. The ones especially praised are those caught in rivers fed by abundant springs. Moreover, boiled they are better than roasted. They are eaten with vinegar, more rarely fried, and they do not need other seasonings, since their own flavour pleases well enough.

units.la: Sale quoq; conduntur, laquearibusq; adium appensa aservantur. Caeterum nobiliores semper habentur & pretiosiores purpureis aureisq; maculis variegatae, & quibus caro rutilescens, & dura est: candida, & quibus est caro alro al-
units.tr: They are also preserved in salt and hung up to keep in the panelled ceilings of houses. The more noble and more precious are always those variegated with purple and golden spots, and whose flesh is reddish and firm. The white ones, whose flesh is

units.la: Quaenam forellae optimae? ro albida mollisq; insipida sunt, & minus pretio-sa. Illa nobiliores culina commendant pracipue vt sapidissimas. Attamen,
units.tr: whitish, soft and insipid, are less precious. The kitchen especially commends the nobler ones as the most savoury. Nevertheless,

units.la: Non omnis laudem pretium: q; aurata meretur, canente Martiali.
units.tr: not every fish deserves its price, but the gilthead does, as Martial sings.

units.la: De Prasmo, Barbo, Perca.
units.tr: On the prasmus, the barbel and the perch.

units.la: IN ciborum quoque gloria, palatique delitiis sunt Prasmus seu Erythrophthalmus (sic dictus à rubro oculorum colore) barbus seu barbatus (sic cognominatus à barbula utrinque in inferiori labro pendente) & Perca (per antiphrasin sic appellata, quod nemini parcat, iratus namque pisces alios pinnis suis vulnerat.) De hoc pisce Ausonius in Mosella elegante carmine ita cecinit, quem etiam pretiosissimis mullis non veritus est comparare,
units.tr: Among the glories of food and the delights of the palate are the prasmus, also called the erythrophthalmus (so named from the red colour of its eyes), the barbus or barbatus (so named from the little barbel hanging on each side of its lower lip), and the perch (called by antiphrasis, since it spares no one; when angry it wounds other fish with its fins). Ausonius sang of this fish in his elegant Mosella poem, not hesitating to compare it even with the most precious mullets:

units.la: Nec te delitias mensarum Perca silebo, Amnigeros inter pisces dignande, marinis Solus puniceis facilis contendere mullis, Namq; & guslus iners, solidoq; in corpore partes Segmentis coeunt, sed dissociantur aristis.
units.tr: Nor will I pass over you, perch, delight of tables, worthy to be honoured among the river-fish, you alone who can easily vie with the purple mullets of the sea. For even your taste is sluggish, and in your solid body the parts hold together in segments but are divided by spines.

units.la: Et hodie certe nobilitatem illam atq; praestantiam pertinacissime retinuit, nec de ejus in cibis salubritate ac suavitate etiam dubitandum est, ob carnem candidam, duram, parumque obtinentem lentoris: amnicatamen & fluviatilis lacustris. semper prae-fertur. fertur, tum enim bene valentibus, tum etiam ægrotantibus præsertim febricitantibus, in cibatu posterior medicina vtilem eam esse prodidit.
units.tr: And certainly today it has most stubbornly kept that nobility and excellence. Nor need one doubt its wholesomeness and pleasantness as food, though its flesh is white, firm, and not very soft. The river and lake fish is always preferred to the sea fish. It is useful, the later medical writers have declared, both for those in good health and for the sick, especially the feverish, as food.

units.la: De barbo præterea, nullum Latinorum, præter Aufonium, mentionem fecisse inuenio, cuius elegantissima carmina huc asscribere placuit, graphice enim barbum ita pingit, Tuq; per obliqui fauces vexate Satani, Qua bis terna fremunt scapulosis ostia pilis, Cum defluxisti fama majoris in amnem Liberior, laxos exercet barbe natatus, Tu melior pejore uno, tibi contigit uni Spirantum ex numero non illaudata senectus.
units.tr: Moreover, I find that none of the Latins, except Ausonius, has mentioned the barbel. I am pleased to add his most elegant verses here, for he paints the barbel vividly: "You, tormented through the jaws of oblique Satan, whose mouths bristle with twice three bristly hairs, when you have flowed down into the greater river more free, the barbel's loose swimming exercises you. You are better than the worse one, and you alone among breathing things have been granted an unblamed old age."

units.la: Hæc Aufonius. Adultiores autem & seniores inter lautiores habentur, præsertim æstatis temporibus, cibos, tunc enim cum vino & aqua elixantur, ac eduntur. Barbulones hoc est, minores & juniores in cibos quoq; veniunt, sed non adeo lauti sunt. Porro rostrum barbi, quam sit gulæ proceribus gratum, quamq; auidè expetatur, nemini nō est notum. Vnde Germanorum vulgatum jactatur & joculare prouerbium, Deß Hechts Zungen/ Deß Karpffen Siten/ Deß Barben Mäulchen / brachten mich vmb mein Apffelgrawes Säulchen.
units.tr: So Ausonius. Older and full-grown barbels are counted among the more luxurious foods, especially in summer, when they are boiled and eaten with wine and water. Young barbels, the little ones, also come to the table, but they are not so luxurious. Moreover, how pleasing the barbel's snout is to the lords of the palate, and how eagerly it is sought, is known to everyone. Hence the common German saying, joked about: "The pike's tongue, the carp's sides, the barbel's little mouth, have brought me to ruin, along with my apple-grey little horse."

units.la: Ad extremum infamantur barbi ouorum malitia & vitio, esitata enim intolerabiles alui cruciatus concitasse expertum est, tum ipsam etiam aluum immodice soluisse, quod obiter hic memoriae causa adiicio.
units.tr: Finally, barbels are discredited for the harm and fault of their roe. It has been found that when eaten they provoke intolerable pains in the bowels, and also cause violent purging. I add this here in passing, for the sake of memory.

units.la: De anguilla.
units.tr: On the eel.

units.la: AB anguium similitudine videtur nomen sortita, unde Iuuenalis in sua Satyra, Vos anguilla manet, longae cognata colubrae.
units.tr: The eel seems to have taken its name from its resemblance to the snake, whence Juvenal in his Satire: "There remains for you the eel, a close relation of the long serpent."

units.la: Sed vulgus falso coire eas cum serpentibus credit, hocq; modo veneficiis impleri, unde estiuo tempore mensis plane abdicant. De ortu anguillarum inter autores nonconuenit. Aristoteles naturarum callentissimus, sine coitu, sine ouo, anguillas procreari, inq; iis nec masculinum nec fœmininum genus esse constanter affirmat. Prio-ris rationem videtur afferre hanc, quod scilicet in nonnullis fœculentis stagnis, aqua omnino ex-hausta, limoq; detracto, anguillae denuo generentur, vbi aqua accesserit pluuia. Plinius aiterere se scopulis, eaq; strigmenta reuiuiscere, nec esse aliam earum procreationem asserit. Oppianus lib. 1. aliter sentit, cuius carmina, Lippio vertente, subnectere, non erit incongruum,
units.tr: But the common people falsely believe that eels mate with serpents, and that in this way they are filled with poison; hence they clearly abstain from them in the summer months. Authors do not agree about the origin of eels. Aristotle, most skilled in natural things, affirms that eels are produced without mating and without eggs, and that in them there is constantly neither a male nor a female sex. He seems to give this reason for the former view: that in some muddy pools, when the water has been entirely drained off and the mud removed, eels are generated again when rain water has come in. Pliny says that he has seen them revive from scrapings on rocks, and asserts that there is no other way they are produced. Oppian, in book 1, thinks otherwise. It will not be out of place to add his verses, in the translation of Lippius:

units.la: Anguillae spiris, multoq; volumine nexae Concubunt, lentor destillat corpore toto, Qui spumae similis, bibula caelatur arena,
units.tr: The eels, bound in coils and many folds, lie together; slime drips from their whole body,

units.la: Ii
units.tr: Ii

units.la: Accipit hunc cœnum, quid enim fœcundius illo?
units.tr: It takes in this mud, for what is more fruitful than that?

units.la: Concipit accepto, nascuntur lubrica turba. Sic coeunt congri, sic lubrica membra resoluuntur.
units.tr: It conceives when it has received, and the slippery crowd is born. So the conger-eels mate, so their slippery limbs are loosened.

units.la: Sed nobis perinde est, sive ex cœno, sive ex fœno, sive ex limo, sive ex fimo procreentur. Quid in gloria œsophagi valeant, inquiramus. Certum est anguillarum carnem medicos plerosque omnes damnasse, tum in sanorum tum in ægrorum cibis, sed nulla probabili ratione, quod tamen pace illorum dictum volo. Lenta enim illa et glutinosa pituita, quam vescentibus pestem, imo larguis crebrius sumtam, mortem afferre dicunt, elixatione, vel assatione sudando facile extillat, nullo relicto vel alieni saporis, vel lenti illius glutini pigmento. Parandi igitur ratio hic, quae varia est, non ignoranda. In confesso est, uberioris alimenti esse anguillas ob carnem molem dulcem, adeoque suavem, ut ad largius edendum diuturno morbo confectos et extenuatos non alliciat modo, verum etiam cito reficiat, virescque restaurat. Non ea inficias, uberius in cibis, crebriusque sumtam, perniciosam esse, vitaque periculum afferre non asseveratio. Itaque dentes in iis locis, ubi anguillarum abundantia est, (sic Homerus Pheacas appellat) quasi anguillis abundantissimos. Et propterea in quotidiano sunt usu, paulatim iis edendis assuescent, assuefacti impune postea iis vescentur. Ubi memi-
units.tr: But for us it makes no difference whether they are produced from mud, from hay, from slime, or from dung. Let us inquire what they are worth for the pleasure of the gullet. It is certain that most physicians have condemned eel flesh, both in the food of the healthy and of the sick, but on no sound reasoning, which I say with their leave. For that sticky and gluey phlegm, which they say is a poison to those who eat it, or even death if taken too often in large amounts, easily drips away when they are boiled or roasted, the sweating removing it, and no trace of foreign flavour or of that gluey stickiness is left behind. The method of preparing them is therefore varied and should not be ignored. It is agreed that eels are a richer food, because their flesh is so sweet and pleasant that it not only attracts those worn down and wasted by long illness to eat more of it, but also quickly restores them and renews their strength. I do not deny that eaten too richly and too often they are harmful and do not fail to bring danger to life. Thus, in those places where eels are abundant, people are called teeth (as Homer calls the Phaeacians), as if they were most abundant in eels. And because they are in daily use, they gradually grow accustomed to eating them, and once accustomed they eat them afterwards without harm. Where it should be remembered

units.la: meminisse quoque vita prorogandæ studiosum vel-lim, crebro anguillarum cibo calculos gigni in re-nibus & vesica, glutinoso lento non probè ab-sterso: tum quoque nigra illa venula per spinæ me-dium porrecta, non exempta, antequam coquatur, veneni enim particeps esse creditur. Diphilus apud Athenaeum lacustrem anguillam marinam quidem insuaviorem asserit esse, verum vberioris alimenti.
units.tr: by one who is eager to prolong life, that eating eels often produces stones in the kidneys and bladder, when the sticky slime has not been properly wiped away. Also that black little vein running along the middle of the backbone, if not removed before cooking, is believed to share in the poison. Diphilus, quoted by Athenaeus, says that the sea eel is indeed less pleasant than the lake eel, but more nourishing.

units.la: Qua ex fluminibus in mare descendunt, (falsa enim delectantur) salubriores effici aqua maris & nutrimento, omnium consensu traditur, exuere enim illas lentum illud glutinum, periculosamque illam pinguedinem, hacque ratione mirè agiles effici, minusque lubricas, atque esui salubriores, teffantur maritimi piscatores, qui circa catarrhactas (Schlüsen vocant, claudendo) qua apertis valuis aquam, quæ hibernis mensibus agri opprimuntur, violento impetu in mare profundunt, inusitata magnitudinis anguillas nassis ac sagenis eximunt.
units.tr: It is agreed by all that those which descend from rivers into the sea (for they delight in fresh water) become healthier through the sea water and food. Maritime fishermen bear witness to this. Near the sluices, which they call Schlüsen from closing, through which the water that the fields hold in winter is released with violent force into the sea when the gates are opened, they take out eels of unusual size with traps and nets.

units.la: Porrò coctura rationem quod attinet, Ratio coelixantur ex aqua & vino detracto corio, quendi adiectis pipere, cinnamomo, zinzibere & croco, anguillas. Alii, & quidem salubriori inuento eas torrenti craticula, & quae sunt ampliores, verubus. Sale quoq; condiuntur, quibus vulgus suauissime vescitur per illos praesertim dies quibus carnibus abstinet. In vino suffocata abstemios reddere homines, si ex eo bibant, qui plus satis mero indulgent, & hinc offenduntur, atq; delinquunt. Mizaldus prodidit, caius quoq; commeminit Plinius l. 32. c. 10. Ad extremum non praetereundum, singularem anguillis etiam extra aquam vivacitatem esse, aquilone quoq; flante plures viuere dies, austro pauciores. Turbidam aquam omnino reformidant, profundam & puram appetentes, non leue salubrioris alimenti indicium. De alimento ipsorum nihil certi proditum inuenio, nisi quod quibusdam in locis vescantur limo, atq; aliis eduliis si quis apposuerit. Atheneus se vidisse ait in Arethusa circa Chalcidem anguillas mansuetas, inaureasq; aureas & argenteas habentes, & capientes ab offerentibus cibos. Cuius quoq; rei Plinius meminit lib. 32. cap. 2. Idem in amne Gange ad tricenos pedes longas reperiri lib. 6. c. 3. autor est. Lacustres carniuoras esse certo constat, piscciculos enim ranasq; persequuntur. Vitium indubitatè manifestant odor & gustatus: inculpatae nihil virosum sapiunt aut redolent. Examinees, piscium solas non fluitare Aristoteles & Plinius prodiderunt, quod mirum quidem, ratione tamen non plane carens. Capiuntur vt plurimum rimum circa Virgilias, fluminibus fc. tum præ- cipuè in bidis.
units.tr: As for the method of cooking, eels are boiled in water and wine, with the skin removed, and with pepper, cinnamon, ginger and saffron added. Others, and indeed by a healthier invention, roast them on a gridiron, and the larger ones on spits. They are also seasoned with salt, and the common people eat them with the greatest relish, especially on those days when they abstain from meat. Eels stewed in wine are said to make men sober if they drink of it, though they have drunk more than enough wine and so are offended and sin. Mizaldus has written this, and Pliny also mentions it, book 32, chapter 10. Finally, it should not be passed over that eels have an extraordinary liveliness even out of the water; when the north wind blows, more of them live for several days, and fewer when the south wind blows. They utterly dread turbid water, seeking deep and clear water, which is no slight sign of more wholesome food. I find nothing certain recorded about their food, except that in some places they eat mud, and other things if anyone sets them before them. Athenaeus says he saw, in the Arethusa near Chalcis, tame eels with golden and silver ornaments in their ears, which took food from those who offered it. Pliny also mentions this thing, book 32, chapter 2. The same author states that in the river Ganges they are found thirty feet long, book 6, chapter 3. It is quite certain that lake eels are carnivorous, for they pursue little fish and frogs. Their faults are plainly shown by smell and taste: the blameless ones have no rank flavour or smell. Aristotle and Pliny have recorded that eels alone of fish do not float when examined dead, which is indeed remarkable, yet not wholly without reason. They are mostly caught near Virgilias, in the rivers, especially in the traps.

units.la: De Mullo, Scaro, Scombro.
units.tr: On the Mullet, the Scarus, and the Mackerel.

units.la: QVanta fuerit imperii Romani in a-lendis piscibus luxuria, quamque insana & portentosa eorundem pretia extiterit, docet vel vnus mullus tantoperè iactatus ac nominatus à Plinio, Iuuenale, Macrobio. Hunc octo millibus ab Afinio ce-lere viro consulari, Clodio Principe, emtum, Plinius tradidit, id est, æstimatione Budæi, ducentis aureis. Iuuenalis verò quasi dubitans ait,
units.tr: How great the luxury of the Roman empire was in feeding fish, and how mad and monstrous their prices became, is shown by the mullet alone, which Pliny, Juvenal and Macrobius praise and mention so often. Pliny reports that it was bought by Afinius, a former consul, under the emperor Clodius for eight thousand sesterces, that is, by Budaeus's reckoning, two hundred gold pieces.

units.la: Mullum sex millibus emit Æquantem sane paribus sextertia libris. Vt perhibent qui de magnis maiora loquuntur.
units.tr: Juvenal, however, speaks as if he doubted it: "He bought a mullet for six thousand, a fish that truly weighed as many pounds as it cost in sesterces, as those who speak of great things speak of them in greater terms."

units.la: Macrobius septem millibus emtum meminit, vt ita duo millia, teste Budeo, maneant in controuersia. Ex quibus satis superque videre est, in admirabili honore mensarum fuisse mullum, magnopere que gulæ placuisse, adeò quidem, vt nec accipenseris apud antiquos pretiosissimi gustus, nec scari, nec lupi celebratissimorum piscium pretium tantopere fit decantatum. Galenus lib. de facult. alment. multi in cibis sua ætate autoritatem non tacuit, ait enim, magnificari ab hominibus, ac si cunctos alios sapiditate præcelleret.
units.tr: Macrobius records that it was bought for seven thousand, so that two thousand, by Budaeus's account, remain in dispute. From these things it is more than enough to see that the mullet was held in remarkable honour at tables and greatly pleased the palate. Indeed, among the ancients neither the sturgeon, the most costly fish for taste, nor the scarus, nor the bass, the most celebrated of fish, had its price sung so loudly. Galen, in his book on the powers of foods, did not pass over the judgement of many in his own day, for he says that men extol it as if it surpassed all other fish in flavour.

units.la: At causas cur tantopere gulæ placéret, capere non potuit, quippe nec saporis gratiam, nec pariter salubritatis in eo fe reperire fatetur. Refert idem, cum aliquando quendam rogaffet, cur tam immani pretio multos prægrandes esset mercatus, respondisse, propter iecur inprimis, deinde propter caput tantam impendisse pecuniam. Horatius 1. fetin. Satyra 2. epar, caput, & denique ipsas carnes vocat pulmenta. Et epar in delitiis popinalibus fuisse Galenus testis est, qui carne multi durissima esse dicit, admodum mq; friabilem hoc est, lentoris omnis atque pinguedinis expertem, ideoque, fi probe conficiatur, valentius & vberius alere quam caeterorum piscium. Idem tamen priusquam iis coctis vescamur, ventres esse referandos præcipit, quod scilicet in ventre crebro alimenta reperiantur venenata, quæ ab ipsis deuorantur, vt nos sæpissime in luciis spectamus. Qui enim in coenosis obfcoenisque littoribus versantur, grauiter olent, gustatuque sunt insuaues, maliqueque succi. Sed adhuc peiores, qui lepore matino venenatissimo vescuntur: multos autem eo vesci elari autores tradunt. Ideoque & mullorum auctoritas in tanto gulæ desiderio ac pretio, vitæ insidias struit. Sale allerati mille remedia præstant, verum tibis minus idonei. Coêti panificioque incrustati crustati diutius durant, alias facile compu- trefcunt. Optimos Galenus censet, qui in puro versantur pelago, quaeque bona alimenta pascuntur. Oceanus Britannicus fert amplißimos. LXXX. librarum mullum in mari rubro captum Licinius Murianus prodidit, referente Plinio. Bilibres alias, trilibres, atque etiam quadrilibres vsitati sunt: Certum est, ætatem amplitudinem & ponderaus augere.
units.tr: Yet he could not grasp the reason why it pleased the palate so much, since he admits that it has neither a pleasing flavour nor an equal healthfulness. The same writer reports that once, when he asked someone why he had bought several very large mullets at such an immense price, the man replied that he had spent so much money chiefly for the liver, and then for the head. Horace, in Satires, book 1, satire 2, likewise calls the liver, the head and finally the flesh itself delicacies. Galen also testifies that the liver was among the dainties of the banquet. He says that the flesh is very hard for many and yet quite crumbly, free of all sliminess and fat, and therefore, if properly cooked, nourishes more strongly and richly than the flesh of other fish. Yet the same writer orders that, before we eat them cooked, their stomachs should be removed, because poisonous foods are often found inside them, which they have devoured, as we very often see in pike. For those who live on muddy and foul shores smell strongly, taste unpleasant, and have bad juices. Worse still are those which feed on the most poisonous sea hare, and many famous authors report that many people died from eating them. So the reputation of the mullet, in such great greed and at such a price, sets snares for life. Salted, they provide a thousand remedies, but for the table they are less suitable. Boiled and encrusted with bread-crumbs, they last longer; otherwise they easily putrefy. Galen judges the best to be those that live in the open sea and feed on good foods. The British Ocean produces very large ones. Licinius Murianus reported, as Pliny relates, a mullet of eighty pounds caught in the Red Sea. Otherwise, mullets of two, three and even four pounds have been in use. It is certain that age, size and weight all increase.

units.la: Non omittendum hic, Apitium ad omne luxus ingenium mirum, in associorum garo, (quæ quoque res cognomen inuenit) necarieos præcellens putasse, atque ieqote eorum halecé excogitare protiocasse. Quod quidem facilius est dixisse, quam quis vicerit, Plinio l. 9. c. 7. teste. Ex quibus omnibus conspicuum euadit, mullum (ficdictum à mollitie, quod seruitutis sit impatientissimus, & viuariorum claustrorumque indignantissimus à barbo nostro fluuiatili longè diuersum esse, licet imperite à quibusdam confundantur, germani. nominari potest, Seeꝛ barbel/mullus marinus, qui si barbatulus est, inque alto alitur mari, præstantissimus est, & hic in tam mirabili priscis Romanis fuit hodie & pretio: barbæ expertes inglorii habentur, german. glatte Meerbarbeln. Solus mullus terparit, Plin. & Aristotele prodenti- bus, unde τρίγλα dicitur græcis.
units.tr: Nor should it be omitted here that Apicius, a man of marvellous genius for every kind of luxury, thought the mullet surpassed all others for his garum (a sauce which also gave its name to the thing), and he tried to devise a fish-sauce from them. This is easier to say than to say who surpassed him, as Pliny testifies in book 9, chapter 7. From all these things it becomes plain that the mullet, so named from its softness (mollitia), because it is most impatient of servitude and most indignant at tanks and enclosures, is far different from our river barbel, although some unskilfully confuse the two. In German it can be called Seeꝛ barbel or marine mullet. If it is bearded and nourished in the deep sea, it is most excellent, and this is why it was held in such marvellous esteem by the ancient Romans, and why it is so highly priced today. Those without beards are considered inglorious, in German glatte Meerbarbeln. The mullet alone is bearded, as Pliny and Aristotle report, whence the Greeks call it trigla [τρίγλα].

units.la: Scatura
units.tr: Scarus

units.la: Scarum quoque in luxus patina principa-tum olim tenuisse non leues autores memo-riæ prodiderunt. Solus piscium ruminare dicitur, (vnde à quibusdam ruminalis dici-tur) herbisque vesci, mari Carpathio maxi-mè frequens. Optatus Tiberii Cæsaris clas-sis præfectus scarum piscem nouum incolam mari Italico dedit, aduectumè promontorio Troadis Lecto, quod sponte nunquâ transit. Adeò gula ex piscibus sapores sibi admouit. De eius alimento minimè dubitandum, cum omnium eruditorum consensu primatum gerat inter saxatiles. Carnem habet, teste Atheneo, facile coctibilem, & quæ celeriter distribuitur, aluoque molliendæ non inuti-lem: assari autem solet in craticula aut sarta-gine, quin & elixari. Intestina eius ac iecur inter popinales delitias à ganeæ peritis repo-sita inuenio. Martialis de scaro cecinit, Visceribus bonus est: cætera bile sapit.
units.tr: The scarus, too, not slight authors have recorded, once held the chief place in the luxury of the dish. It alone among fish is said to ruminate (whence some call it ruminalis), and it feeds on herbs; it is most frequent in the Carpathian sea. Optatus, prefect of the fleet of the emperor Tiberius, introduced the scarus as a new inhabitant of the Italian sea, carried from the Lectum promontory of the Troad, which it never passes of its own accord. So far did gluttony add flavours to fish. There is no doubt about its nourishment, since by the agreement of all learned men it holds the first place among rock fish. According to Athenaeus, its flesh is easily cooked, is quickly digested, and is not useless for softening the bowels. It is usually roasted on a gridiron or in a frying pan, and also boiled. I find that its guts and liver were stored away among the dainties of the banquet by those skilled in gluttony. Martial wrote of the scarus: "It is good in the innards; otherwise it tastes of bile."

units.la: Mirum, quod piscium omnibus ferrati sunt dentes, vni aquatilium scaro plani. Sed nec conticendus astus scarorum est, nassis enim inclusi non fronte erumpunt, nec infestis viminibus caput inserunt, sed auersum cau-dæ ictibus crebris fores laxant, atque ita re-trosum erumpunt. Quem eorum luctatum, si forsan alius scarus extrinsecus videat, ap-prehensa mordicus cauda adiuuat erumpen-tis nixus. Germ. appellari audio, ein Deuer/
units.tr: It is remarkable that all fish have toothed jaws, but among water creatures the scarus alone has flat ones. Nor must the cunning of the scari be passed over. When they are shut in wicker traps, they do not burst out through the front, nor thrust their heads against the hostile twigs. Instead, turning their backs, they loosen the doors with repeated blows of the tail, and so they force their way out backwards. If another scarus outside sees their struggle, it helps the one trying to escape by seizing its tail in its teeth and pulling with it. I hear that in German it is called ein Deuer/

units.la: Deuwer/ Heuwer/ oder Keuwbraffen/ &c. Vsum multi, recentisq; eius e capite cineris in medicinis, aduersus omnia venena & venenata animalia insignem esse Plinius grauiter prodidit lib.32. cap.5. Sumitur autem in cibo, vel allinitur.
units.tr: Deuwer/ Heuwer/ oder Keuwbraffen/ &c. Pliny, a most serious writer, reports in book 32, chapter 5, that its ash, made from the fresh head, is a notable remedy in medicines against all poisons and venomous animals, and that many have used it. It is taken in food or smeared on the body.

units.la: Ex laudatissimorum quoque piscium marinorum & gregalium genere est Scomber, Mafrell/ vel Mafrill/ qui recenter captus melior est, mensisq; lautioribus primis diebus gratior, sed gratia breui perit ob faftidiū, quod ex diuturniori afferu* e parit. Olim ex Scombris, Plinio teste, praestantissimum conficiebatur garum, cuius Atheneus quoq; meminit lib.3. Torrentur autem in craticula, viridi inuoluta foeniculo & butyro: quibusdam in locis irrorantur ex butyro vel oleo. Sale etiam condiuntur, & asseruantur. Bene autem alere, bonique succi esse non est dubium. Scombros in aceto putrefactos vulua strangulatu opprefias excitari Plinius grauis- simus scriptor autor est. Sumendus autem est adeps linamentaq; eo sunt accendenda.
units.tr: The scomber, called Mafrell/ or Mafrill/, also belongs to the kind of the most praised sea fish that go in shoals. When freshly caught it is best, and at the first days of more elegant tables it is more pleasing; but its pleasure soon perishes through loathing, which comes from its being kept longer. Formerly, according to Pliny, the most excellent garum was made from mackerels, which Athenaeus also mentions in book 3. They are roasted on a gridiron, wrapped in green fennel and butter; in some places they are basted with butter or oil. They are also seasoned with salt and preserved. That they nourish well and have good juice is beyond doubt. Pliny, a most serious writer, reports that mackerels putrefied in vinegar will rouse a womb that is oppressed by strangulation. The fat is to be taken, and wicks are to be lit with it.

units.la: De Tinca.
units.tr: On the Tench.

units.la: HOdie in lautioribus mensis exiguam obtinet autoritatem tinca seu tencha, perfuasissimum enim habent, infalubberrimam. mam esse, propterea quod coenosis & limosis locis sponte vel proveniat, vel quod lutô & cæno gaudeat & alatur, unde germanis Schleyen appellatur, vel à lubricitate, vel à muco, quem German Schleim nominant. De lacustribus seu palustribus non tamen inficiat glutinosi eas esse & difficilis succi- dæ aquatilibus non item, has enim elixas, frixas, vel craticula tostas, oleribus odoratis vel aromatis farctas, commendatas à gratiis auctoribus reperio. Popi-nalis lautitiæ & ganeæ studiosissimum quendam, alio laridoq; eas contritas, additis odoratis oleribus & multo aromate, ad vaporem tepidorum furno felicissimè percoxisse, Paulus Iovius p-odidit. Difficilis per dorsi longitudinem plantisq; pedum appositas, febrium ardentium flammas sedare Medici quidam experti sunt.
units.tr: Today the tench, or tencha, holds only a small reputation at well-appointed tables, since people are firmly convinced that it is very unwholesome, because it either breeds spontaneously in muddy and slimy places or delights in mud and ooze and feeds on it. For this reason the Germans call it <bl>Schleyen</bl>, either from its slipperiness or from the slime which the Germans call <bl>Schleim</bl>. I do not deny that the tench of lakes or marshes is somewhat glutinous and of difficult juice, but the tench of running water is not so. I find that these, when boiled, fried, or grilled on a gridiron and stuffed with fragrant herbs and spices, are commended by reliable authors. Paulus Iovius reports that a certain man very devoted to luxury and gluttony at the tavern, after crushing them with lard, adding fragrant herbs and much spice, very successfully cooked them in an oven until they were warm and steaming. Some physicians have found by experience that the tench, laid along the length of the back and against the soles of the feet, calms the flames of burning fevers.

units.la: De Muraena, lampetra, asellis, raia, platessis, harengis, gobio, alburno, &c.
units.tr: On the Moray, the Lamprey, the Asellus, the Ray, the Plaice, the Herring, the Gudgeon, the Bleak, etc.

units.la: TAnta fuit prisco sapud Romanos huius pisces gratia, tantoperequeabiis honoratus, vt etiam nobiles ab eo familiæ fuerint denominatæ. Plurimum autem inter se differre muraenas Galenus vult, pessimamque earum carnem asserit, qui in ostiis fluminum degunt latrinas cloacasque expurgantium, aut culinas aut balnea, aut vestium, ftium, aut linteolorum sordes, aut fi quæ alia sunt in vrbibus, per quas medias fluunt, expurganda, potissimum si populosæ fuerint. Itaq; murænis non semper contingit esse optimas.
units.tr: The moray was so esteemed among the ancient Romans, and so honoured above other fish, that even noble families were named after it. Galen maintains that morays differ greatly among themselves, and he declares that the flesh of the worst ones is found in those which live at the mouths of rivers, where people clean out latrines and sewers, kitchens or baths, or the dirt of clothes and linen, or whatever else must be washed away in cities through which the rivers flow, especially if they are populous. Therefore morays are not always the best.

units.la: Traduntur & alia, quæ murænas abdicandas cibis suadeant, concipere enim eas ex serpentibus autores non dilutæ fidei affirmarunt. Prodidit id Plinius l.9. c.23. & l.32. c.2. autoritate Licinii Macri, cuius etiam opinionem secutus est Oppianus, murænam scil. & serpentem mutuo amore ardere, ac serpente veneno mortifero in saxis depositio è littore sibilo murænam evocare, quem si audiat muræna, ex aquis confestim proruat, expletoq; Veneris desiderio serpentem venenum depositum repetere, quod si non inveniat, dolore emoriatur. Aristoteles tamen videtur negare cum serpentibus eas misceri ac generare, marem enim proprium vocat myrum, qui generat. Potrò fuisse in delitiis & hore mensarum Poetæ multi latini aliique scriptores prodiderunt. D. Ambrosius l.9. sui hexameti ait, Muræna, quam ferunt aliquid habere noxium, esca pretiosior est: Siculæ pretiosiores erant, testante Iuuenale,
units.tr: There are also other reports which advise that morays be excluded from food, for certain writers of no unreliable faith have affirmed that they are conceived from serpents. Pliny relates this in book 9, chapter 23, and book 32, chapter 2, on the authority of Licinius Macer, whose opinion Oppian also followed: namely, that the moray and the serpent burn with mutual love, and that when the serpent has laid down its deadly poison on the rocks, it summons the moray from the shore with a hiss; if the moray hears it, it immediately rushes out of the waters, and when its desire for love is satisfied, it seeks again the poison which the serpent has laid down; but if it does not find it, it dies of grief. Aristotle, however, seems to deny that they mix with serpents and produce offspring, for he calls the male of their kind the myrus, which generates. That the moray was a delicacy and a dish at the tables of the great, many Latin poets and other writers have reported. Saint Ambrose, in book 9 of his Hexameron, says: "The moray, which is said to have something harmful in it, is a more precious food." The Sicilian morays were more precious still, as Juvenal testifies:

units.la: Virroni murena datur, qua maxima vet-nit
units.tr: To Virro a moray is given, the largest that the whirlpool of Sicily has produced.

units.la: Gurgite de Siculo.
units.tr: On the Whirlpool of Sicily.

units.la: Horatius Sat. vlt. 1. 2. Serm. grauidam commendat his versibus,
units.tr: Horace, Satires, book 2, satire 8, commends the pregnant moray in these verses:

units.la: Affertur squillas inter murena natantes, In patina porrecta sub hoc herus, hæc grauida, inquit, Capta est, deterior post partum carnefutura.
units.tr: A moray is brought in among the swimming prawns; the master, placing it on a dish under his guest's gaze, says: "This one was caught pregnant; it would have been worse after giving birth."

units.la: Venenatam vim inesse dentibus ipsarum piscatores certò sibi persuasum habent, viuam enim manibus non attinguntfed forcipe. Lactes earum mirè commendatur. Refert Ælius Lampridius Heliogabalum aulam omnem & rusticos aliquando iis pauisse. Viuarium murænarum primus instituit & excogitauit C. Hirius ante alios, Plinio l. 9. c. 55. teste. Cœnis is triumphalibus Cœsaris Dictatoris sex millia numero murænarum mutuo appendit, nam permutare quidem pretio noluit aliaue mercede.
units.tr: Fishermen are firmly convinced that there is a venomous power in their teeth, so they do not touch them alive with their hands, but with pincers. Their milt is greatly commended. Aelius Lampridius reports that Heliogabalus once fed the whole court and even the country folk with them. C. Hirius was the first, before all others, to establish and devise a fishpond of morays, as Pliny attests in book 9, chapter 55. At the triumphal feasts of the dictator Caesar, he weighed out six thousand morays in number, for he was not willing to exchange them for money or any other reward.

units.la: Crassus cognomento diues, murænam altilem adeo adamauit, vt fato fundam aliquando luxerit. Cumque à L. Domitio admodum ob id rideretur, respondit, mirum quidem esse quod extinctum piscem lacrymis prosequeretur, sed multo admirabilius, quod ipse tres à se elatas vxores non lugeret. Tres enim è medio sustulerat, vt dotibus potiretur.
units.tr: Crassus, surnamed the Rich, so loved the fattened moray that once he is said to have wept at its death. When Lucius Domitius mocked him greatly for this, he replied that it was indeed strange that he should mourn a dead fish with tears, but far more remarkable that he did not mourn the three wives he had buried. For he had removed three from the midst so that he might obtain their dowries.

units.la: Cinerem murænarum cum melle Lichenas & lepras sanare proditum est.
units.tr: It is reported that the ash of morays mixed with honey cures lichens and leprosy.

units.la: Non est mirandum, si cibo plures pereant quam gladio, quia nulla extat lex, quæ vefa-nam gulam puniat, solisque culinis homines perimentibus non impunitas solum promit-titur, sed & in summa gloria habetur. Lampetrociolis enim, hoc est, lampetris exiguis, hædos configere atq; assare quandoque, gulæ insanæ inuentum est, quin & capos iis in spiras detortis implicare, verubusque torrere, quo tamen cibo omnes postridie cõuiuæ fe grauiter narrarunt conflictatos, stomacho enim negotium facessérat. Porro Illustria ingenia torsit lampetra, dum quisque pro eruditionis suæ ostentatione nomen eius antiquum docere contendit. Nos de nomine parum contendentes, quæ ad propositum nostrum pertinere videbuntur attingemus. A lambendis autem & fugendis petris lampetram nominatam reperio, murenæ simi-lem, longam, lubricam, sine pinnis, septem foraminibus læua parte distinctam, quibus murænæ caret. Fertur autem primo vere praetiosissimus esse cibus, cum scilicet cartilago illa quæ pro vertebris & spina illi inest, non-dum induruit, illa enim indurata insuauio-res esse incipiunt, gratiamque ac pretium amittere. Cæterum apparatus culinarum circa eas varius & operosus magnique impendii est, & verissimum est condimentum multo pretiosius esse & carius quam ipsam lampetram.
units.tr: It is no wonder if more people perish by food than by the sword, because there is no law that punishes gluttony, and those who kill people only with the kitchen not only go unpunished but are held in the highest glory. For to pierce young lampreys, that is, small lampreys, and roast them, is an invention of insane gluttony; and sometimes they wrap them in coils and roast them on spits, yet all the guests reported the next day that they had been grievously troubled by this food, for it had caused trouble for the stomach. Furthermore, the lamprey has tormented illustrious minds, since each man, to display his learning, strives to teach its ancient name. We shall not contend much about the name, but touch on those points which seem relevant to our purpose. I find that the lamprey was named from licking and fleeing stones; it is like a moray, long and slippery, without fins, marked on the left side with seven holes, which the moray lacks. It is said that it is the most excellent food in early spring, when the cartilage which lies in place of the vertebrae and spine has not yet hardened; for once hardened, they begin to be less pleasant, and lose their grace and value. Otherwise the preparation of the kitchen for them is varied, laborious, and very costly, and it is quite true that the seasoning is much more precious and dear than the lamprey itself.

units.la: Kk
units.tr: Kk

units.la: Vnde facile quis potest coniicere,non admo- dum suaves salubresque esse escas, quae tot adulteriis & pigmentis placere coguntur: nam lora & coria ipsa eo modo apparata & condita placere possent veru tosta. Magnates ex liquore arantii suauiter mandunt: elixan- tur quoque & incrustantur panificio à pisto- ribus dulciariis. Ad extremum lampetram mustelam esse Aufonii Plinii que inter erudi- tos plerosque conuenit, à maculati huius nominis quadrupedis tegmini simillitudine, hoc est, longitudine candoreque ventris, aqui tergoris superioris subluteo colore.
units.tr: Hence one can easily conjecture that foods which must be made to please by so many adulterations and spices are not very pleasant or wholesome; for thongs and hides themselves, prepared and seasoned in that way, might please when roasted on a spit. The great men savour them sweetly with orange juice; they are also boiled and encrusted with pastry by confectioners. Finally, it is agreed among most learned men, both of Ausonius and of Pliny, that the lamprey is a weasel, from the resemblance of the spotted quadruped of this name in its covering, that is, in the length and whiteness of its belly and the somewhat yellowish colour of its upper back.

units.la: Huius generis est Enneopthalmus, lampreta fluuiatilis, <bl>Neunauge</bl> / alias lumbricus aquatilis: item lampreta longior, <bl>Bricke</bl>. Fluuiatilis quoque mustelae genus est piscis, qui vulgo vocatur <bl>Aalrupp</bl> propter similitudinem quam habet cum anguilla, cuius piscis epar cum conueniente succo oculis obscuris & caligantibus tenebrico- sq; miraculo mederi expertum est.
units.tr: Of this kind is the Enneophthalmus, the river lamprey, <bl>Neunauge</bl>, otherwise called the water earthworm; likewise the longer lamprey, <bl>Bricke</bl>. The river eel-pout is also a kind of weasel-fish, commonly called <bl>Aalrupp</bl> because of its resemblance to the eel; experience has shown that its liver, with a suitable juice, heals dim and misty eyes and a marvellous kind of darkness.

units.la: Asellorum permultae sunt species, quae distinguendae sunt. Prima est marlucius, hoc est, lucius marinus a similitudine lucii fluuiatilis: huic magnam fuisse olim auctoritatem Plinius scribit ex Cornelii Nepotis & Labe- rii Poetae testimonio. 2. Merlanus pleb- eis in frequentissimo cibo, quem lautiores etiam quandoque mensae, rarius tamen, ad- mitmittunt, voluptatis magis quam vtilitatis gratia. 3. Tertius asellus capiteest magno, oris scissura magna, oculis magnis. 4. Species aselli maris Oceani est, qui ex terræ partenuper reperta salitus aduehitur. 5. Species est asellus varius, seu molua maior. Est quoque de asellorum genere Anglorum <bl>Golffsch/</bl> à nigredine forsan sic dictus. Nomen germanicum <bl>Stocffsch/</bl> (sic appella-tus à trunco, cui aridus hic piscis tundendus imponitur) diuersas asellorum species comprehendit. A quo longe alius est piscis, qui Salpa dicitur, <bl>Golbstriemer/</bl> à striis seu lineis aureis. Aselli partes circa ventrem & pinnas resectæ & seorsim salitæ, doliisque includuntur variis nominibus appellantur. Alii <bl>Stockfisch</bl> & <bl>Dorsch/ Stauchfisch/ Fiachfisch</bl> vocitant: cuius quoque generis est Capellarius vulgò dictus, <bl>Bolch/ Kal</bl>, quamuis <bl>Kabeljau</bl> vocetur piscis vi-uus aut recens, <bl>Bolch</bl> verò capite iam mutilatus & salsus. Huius quoque census est, quem piscem Rhenanum nuncupant, & calarium <bl>Schellfisch/</bl> à scabra cute ac squa-mata, vnde cum elixandus est, torreri enim recusat, cultro deradendus est ac desquamandus) vel à fluuio <bl>Schell/</bl> quod in Oceani ostiis, in quæ flumen hoc se exonerat, vel hamo vel retibus subducatur. Cæterum Galen, in re cibaria tale profert. de asellis iudicium, quod, si inculpato alantur nutrimento, inque puro versentur mari, carnis succiqúe probitatem adipiscantur, adque saxatilium carnes proxime accedant.
units.tr: There are very many kinds of asellus, which must be distinguished. The first is the marlucius, that is, the sea pike, named from its likeness to the river pike; Pliny writes that this once had great authority, on the testimony of Cornelius Nepos and the poet Laberius. 2. The merlan is a very common food for the common people, which the more refined tables also sometimes admit, though more rarely, for pleasure rather than for use. 3. The third asellus has a large head, a large mouth-cleft, and large eyes. 4. There is a species of asellus of the Ocean sea, which is brought in salted from a part of the land recently discovered. 5. There is a species called the spotted asellus, or the greater mola. There is also among the English of the asellus kind the <bl>Golffsch</bl>, perhaps so named from its blackness. The German name <bl>Stockfisch</bl>, so called from the trunk on which this dried fish is pounded, embraces various kinds of asellus. Quite different from this is the fish called salpa, <bl>Goldstriemer</bl>, from its golden streaks or lines. The parts of the asellus around the belly and fins, cut away and salted separately and enclosed in casks, are called by various names. Some call them <bl>Stockfisch</bl>, <bl>Dorsch</bl>, <bl>Stauchfisch</bl> and <bl>Fiachfisch</bl>. Of this kind also is the fish commonly called the capellarius, <bl>Bolch</bl> or <bl>Kal</bl>, although the living or fresh fish is called <bl>Kabeljau</bl>, while the <bl>Bolch</bl> is the fish already beheaded and salted. Of this class too is the fish which they call the Rhenish fish, and the haddock, <bl>Schellfisch</bl>, from its scaly and rough skin, whence when it is to be boiled it refuses to be roasted, and must be scraped with a knife and descaled; or from the river <bl>Schell</bl>, at whose mouths in the ocean this river discharges itself; or because it is drawn up by hook or nets. Moreover, Galen, concerning food, gives this judgement about the asellus: if they are fed on blameless nourishment and live in clean sea water, they acquire a good quality of flesh and juice, and they come very near to the flesh of rock fish.

units.la: Idem in methodo medendi boni succi & concoctu faciles tradit, minimeque glutinosos: & alio in loco, molli esse carne, nec minus laudandos quam saxatiles, atque ex iure albo febricitantibus esse adponendos. In libello de boni maliq; succi cibis, molles quidem esse carnis asellos asserit, sed non æquè ac saxatilium friabilem. Iecur in popinalibus delitiis haberi reperio. Eduntur autem aselli, inprimis verò truncus cum suis speciebus, ex butyro bono & synapi, adiectis pipere, cinnamomo vel zinzibere; quin & frixus ex synapi cum pipere: vel ex arantii succo. Sale condiuntur & asseruatur aselli in Anglia, Scotia, Dania, Norvegia indeque in alias regiones deportantur. Sic autem sale conditi pessimi esse nutrimenti vel inde constat, quod septentrionis & maritimæ gentes frequentiori vberiorique asellorum salitorum esu pessimo conducto in corporibus inquilino scorbuto, conflictentur, huiusque mali causam crebriori salitorum esui assignatam reperio.
units.tr: The same author, in his Methodus medendi, says that the flesh of the donkey fish (asellus) yields good juice that is easily digested and not very glutinous. Elsewhere he says it is soft-fleshed and no less praiseworthy than rock fish, and that it should be given to feverish patients in white broth. In his little book on good and bad juices he says the flesh of the asellus is soft, though not as crumbly as that of rock fish. I find that the liver is counted among the delicacies of the cookshops. Donkey fish are eaten especially the body with its seasonings, cooked in good butter and mustard, with pepper, cinnamon or ginger added; also fried with mustard and pepper, or with orange juice. In England, Scotland, Denmark and Norway they are salted and preserved, and then shipped to other regions. That salted fish is very poor food is clear from the fact that the people of the north and of the seacoasts, who eat salted donkey fish often and in large amounts, suffer from scurvy, which lodges in their bodies; and I find that the frequent eating of salted fish is assigned as the cause of this disease.

units.la: De hac engis sale coditis idem esto iudicii.
units.tr: The same judgement applies to the salted eel (engis).

units.la: Melso.
units.tr: Melso.

units.la: {y} Catus scorbuti Messorum, fossorum, bajulorum, & helcia-riorum palato magis sapiunt.
units.tr: The catfish is more to the taste of reapers, diggers, porters and bargemen who suffer from scurvy.

units.la: Lapillos ex asello pisce plena luna inuentos in capite linteolo alligatos febrium circuitus tollere Plinius autor est.
units.tr: Pliny is the authority that small stones found in the donkey fish under a full moon, tied in a little cloth on the head, relieve the recurring fevers.

units.la: Piscis est planus, cartilagineus totus, aculeis praecipue circa caudam asper, foecundissimus, maximeque varius, gustatu jucundus teste Atheneo, tenerioris & probi succi, praesertim qui asterias dicitur, <bl>ein Stein-Roch</bl>. Lejobatus hoc est, laevis raja, <bl>ein glatter Roch</bl>/difficulter ventrem subit, viruisque redolet. Galenus de nutrimento cartilagineorum differens rajam paistinaca (cui similis est, unde Paistinacam, rajam quidam appellant) duriorem asseruit, difficulterque in ventriculo perficii. Certum est abundanter alere, quod nautae, qui eam in deliciis habent, testantur. Subit quoque lautiorum mensas elixata, quandoque frixaque. Jecur gratissime edi ajunt ex aceto piperato. Archestratus apud Atheneum, hibernum esse cibum voluit. Dorion dixisse fertur. rajam perinde bonam esse escam atque pallium elixatum, quod jocose magis, quam vere eum dixisse autumo. Ad Venerem denique incitare rajam largius comesam saepius me audiuisse memini ab iis, qui piscis hujus naturam longo usu probe cognoverant.
units.tr: It is a flat fish, wholly cartilaginous, rough with prickles chiefly around the tail, very prolific and most varied in kind; it is pleasant to taste, according to Athenaeus, of tender and good juice, especially the kind called asterias, ein Stein-Roch (a stone ray). The smooth ray, that is, the laevis raja, ein glatter Roch, enters the stomach with difficulty and smells of its stench. Galen, discussing the nourishment of cartilaginous fish, says the ray called paistinaca (which resembles a parsnip, whence some call it Paistinaca or ray) is harder and is digested with difficulty in the stomach. It is certain that it nourishes abundantly, as sailors, who take it as a delicacy, attest. It also appears on the tables of the wealthy, boiled and sometimes fried. People say the liver is eaten with great pleasure in peppered vinegar. Archestratus, cited by Athenaeus, wanted it to be a winter food. It is said that Dorion remarked that the ray is as good a food as a boiled cloak, which I think he said more as a joke than in earnest. I remember having often heard from those who had come to know the nature of this fish through long experience that eating plenty of ray stirs up desire for love.

units.la: Vsus in medic.
units.tr: Use in medicine.

units.la: E planorum piscium genere sunt passeres, quos Aufonius Plateffas nominat, Lethalisq; Trygon, molleisq; Plateffa.
units.tr: Among the flat fish are the plaice, which Ausonius calls plateffae: "and the deadly sting-ray, and the soft plaice."

units.la: Hodie in lautiorum quidem ciborum albo non habentur, sunt tamen nutrimenti non malipraesertim recentes, & quae in arenosis gurgitibus aluntur. Marinos autem fluuiatilibus & stagnalibus praeferri aequum est. Passeres quoque & planos omnes in limosis locis bene educari Columella testis est. Certum est, aquas quasdam passeres alere saporis miram obtinentes gratiam. Ligerinas mirè audio commendari. Aridae, quae ad nos exportantur, quia duriores sunt, diligentem probamq; apparandi coquedique requirunt rationem. Suauiter eduntur ex jure piscorum adjecto zinzibere, mace & croci momento, vel etiam ex butyro & lacte, adjectis petroselini foliis. Muldandi sunt, qui calce maceratas, ut teneriores fiant & mollescant e is vendunt, ac debet magistratus officii sui memor in has insidias animadvertere. Injurato mihi aequus lector credat, magna inde incommoda concitari, ut torsiones & rosiones in ventriculo, quod expertus ipse sum.
units.tr: Today they are not counted among the dishes of the rich, yet they are not bad food, especially when fresh and when they are reared in sandy waters. It is fitting to prefer sea plaice to river and pond plaice. Columella bears witness that plaice and all flat fish are well reared in muddy places. It is certain that some waters breed plaice of wonderful flavour. I hear that the Loire plaice is highly recommended. Dried plaice, which are exported to us, are harder and so require a careful and proper method of preparing and cooking. They are eaten pleasantly in fish broth with ginger, mace and a pinch of saffron, or also in butter and milk, with parsley leaves added. Those who sell plaice that have been soaked in lime, to make them more tender and soft, should be beaten; and the magistrate, mindful of his duty, should take action against these tricks. Let the fair reader believe me when I say that great troubles arise from this, such as twisting and gnawing pains in the stomach, which I have experienced myself.

units.la: Suauissimi saporis sunt recentes cocti. Sed incautius ac largius esitati facile febres generant, quod mihi contigit Hafniae. Saporis enim suavitas ad vberius vescendum allicit. Itaque ex jure bene piperato & butyro salito edendi sunt. Torrentur etiam in craticula, butyroque irrorantur salubri invento. Magnatum quoque mensas subeunt, exornantque. Saliti & muriati pessimi nutrimenti sunt, cibisque omninoabdicandi. Macerati minus mali, infumati plane difficilis coctionis sunt, nisi aliorum ciborum beneficio vna conficiantur. Quieruditioris sunt palati, abstineant.
units.tr: Freshly cooked plaice have the sweetest flavour. But eaten too carelessly and in large quantities, they easily produce fevers, as happened to me at Copenhagen. For the sweetness of the flavour tempts one to eat more. They should therefore be eaten in well-peppered broth with salted butter. They are also roasted on a gridiron and basted with a healthy butter sauce. They also grace and adorn the tables of the great. Salted and pickled plaice are the worst food, and should be avoided altogether. Pickled ones are less harmful, while smoked ones are plainly hard to digest, unless they are eaten together with other food. Those of more refined taste should abstain.

units.la: Harengulus, paruus Harengus Sardina & Trichis dicitur ob spinarum copiam. Porro sciendum alecem non esse harengum. Significat enim alec piscciculum omnem vilem, vel muria conditum, vel etiam liquam ex intestinis piscium: vnde Horatius,
units.tr: The harengulus, a little herring, is called sardine or trichis because of its many spines. Moreover, it should be known that alec is not the herring. For alec means any cheap little fish, or one preserved in brine, or even the liquid from fish guts. Hence Horace:

units.la: Ego fœcem, inquit, primus & alec, Primus & invenit piper album.
units.tr: "I, he says, was the first to discover the lees and the alec, the first to discover white pepper."

units.la: Et Hermolaus piscem omnem vilem halecularium dixit. Harengus vero piscis est ex thriffarum genere, qui in Oceano tantum reperitur, minoribus thriffis, & sardinis majoribus plane similis. Spinosissimus autem est, adeo vt vescentibus infestissimæ sint pinnæ, æque ac alofarum & thriffarum, deglutitæ enim grauissimam adferunt molestiam & pene strangulant, si gulæ hæreant infixæ.
units.tr: And Hermolaus called every cheap fish a halecularium. The herring is a fish of the shad family, found only in the ocean, quite like the smaller shad and the larger sardines. It is very full of bones, so that its fins are very troublesome to those who eat it, as are those of the shad and the twaite shad; for if swallowed they cause very grave discomfort, and nearly choke a person if they stick fast in the throat.

units.la: Tu quoq; flumineas inter memorande cohortes Gobio, non major geminis sine pollice palmis,
units.tr: "You too, worthy of mention among the river troops, the gudgeon, no bigger than hands without a thumb,"

units.la: Prapinguis, teres, ovipara congestior alvo, Propexi jubas imitatus gobio barbi.
units.tr: "very fat, round, more full of eggs in the belly, imitating the bearded gudgeon with its outspread barbels."

units.la: Haec Aufoniusin Mofella. Eundem quoque Martialis laudauit in Xeniis,
units.tr: Ausonius praised these in his Mosella. Martial also praised the same fish in his Xenia:

units.la: In venetis sint lauta licet conuiuia terra, Principium coena gobius esse solet.
units.tr: "Though the Venetian land may have lavish banquets, the gudgeon is usually the first course of the dinner."

units.la: Sunt autem gobii pisces vix excedentes duorum pollicum crassitiem aut palmi longitudinem, lubrici, & tamen squamis tecti: marini sunt & fluuiatiles: fluuiatilis a nostris dicitur, Creffio, <bl>Kreßling/Grun-delen</bl> forsan quod circa fundum leu vadum aquae degere solent, limpidis enim aquis gaudent, unde fundulos alii appellitant. Hujus generis est Cottus, qui inter fundulos capitur, & etiam venditur, alias capito <bl>Keuling</bl> & papa a capitis mole mitram referente papalem. Marini gobii appellantur <bl>Meergoben/Meergroppen</bl>: Suntque albi & nigri. Caeterum gobiones in arenosis littoribus, limpidisque aquis degentes optimi sunt, suaues & jucundi, ad coctionem & distributionem faciles, probique nutrimenti & succi: quiin coenosis aluntur locis, aquisque vrbes expurgantibus a Galeno pro damnatissimis habentur. Candidos ait Diphilus teneros esse, probi succi, concoctuque faciles, deterrimi virides, licet grandes sint. Atheneus quoque lib. 7. gobiones plurimi esse nutrimenti scribit, facilesque excretu:
units.tr: Gudgeons are fish scarcely more than two thumbs thick or a palm long, slippery yet covered with scales. They are both sea and freshwater fish. The freshwater kind is called by our people Kreffio, Kreßling or Grundeln, perhaps because they usually live near the bottom or in shallow water, for they delight in clear waters; hence some call them fundulus. Of this kind is the bullhead, which is caught among the gudgeons and also sold, otherwise called capito, Keuling, and papa, from the bulk of its head which resembles a papal mitre. Sea gudgeons are called Meergoben or Meergroppen; they are white and black. Moreover, gudgeons living on sandy shores in clear waters are the best, pleasant and agreeable, easy to digest and distribute, and of good and wholesome nourishment; but those that live in muddy places and in waters that cleanse cities are counted by Galen among the most condemned. Diphilus says that white ones are tender, of good juice and easy to digest, while green ones are the worst, even if large. Athenaeus also, in book 7, writes that gudgeons are of great nourishment and easily excreted:

units.la: differre autem albos abatris: viridium vero carnem macriorem, atidiorem, tenuiorisq; succi esse, & pinguitudinis expertes. Diocles saxatiles gobios mollioris esse carnis dixit, quod tamen Galenus mullorum re-spectu vult esse verum, ait enim, gobionum caro saxatilium carne durior est, & mollior, quam mullorum.
units.tr: but that white ones differ from the green: the flesh of the green is leaner, drier and of thinner juice, and lacks fatness. Diocles said that rock gudgeons have softer flesh; but Galen holds this to be true in comparison with the mullet, for he says the flesh of the gudgeon is harder than the flesh of rock fish, yet softer than that of the mullet.

units.la: Pisces candidi, Leucisci, Alburni, german. dicuntur Weißfisch / Bleiling à Zwibelfisch, quasi quaedam splendore, quod nimirum cum coepis coquantur, Rotfeder Augenlein, ab oculis rubicundis, & a vilitate Schneiderfisch Breitling, item a corporis latitudine. Meminit horum Ausonius, cum inquit,
units.tr: The white fish, called leuciscus, alburnus and in German Weißfisch or Bleiling, from Zwibelfisch, as if of some splendour, because they are cooked with onions; Rotfeder, Augenlein, from their reddish eyes; and Schneiderfisch, Breitling from their cheapness, and also from the breadth of their body. Ausonius mentions these when he says:

units.la: Et alburnos pradam puerilibus hamis.
units.tr: "And the bleak, the prey of boyish hooks."

units.la: Porro carnes eorum molles sint & pituitosae. Certum est aquis exemtos diutiusq; seruatos cito corrumpi, virus enim quoddam redolent, id quod odore facile cognoscitur ventre refecto interaneisque exemtis. Ex jure autem piperato non inutiliter edun-tur.
units.tr: Further, their flesh is soft and phlegmatic. It is certain that when taken from the water and kept too long they quickly spoil, for they give off a certain stench, which is easily recognised by the smell once the belly is opened and the entrails removed. They are not unprofitably eaten in peppered broth.

units.la: Adhuc de alimentis quae veniunt ab animalibus sanguineis simplicis vitae, sequuntur amphibia, quae ancipitis sunt naturae, ut ranae, lutra, fiber.
units.tr: Next, after foods from blooded animals of simple life, come the amphibians, which are of doubtful nature, such as frogs, the otter and the beaver.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CAP. I.

units.la: CAP. XVII. De ranis memorabilia & scitu digna.
units.tr: CHAP. XVII. Concerning frogs, things worth recording and worth knowing.

units.la: Ranarum in re alimentaria visus non est proscribendus, licet rustici & ineruditi palati homines eas averseantur. D. Ambrosius in suo hexamero omnibus fere alimentis praestare asserit. Et licet Romanorum ganea de iis tacuerit, hac tamen tempestate velut delicatissima guttantur a multis nationibus, praesertim Italis, quos hoc nomine batrachophagos appellari animadverti.
units.tr: The use of frogs as food should not be rejected, although rustic people and those of uncultivated palate shun them. St Ambrose, in his Hexameron, asserts that they surpass almost all other foods. And although the Roman feasts say nothing of them, in these times many nations eat them as a most delicate dish, especially the Italians, whom I have noticed are called batrachophagi on this account.

units.la: Certe vivaria Romani instituissent, ut ranarum delitias habuissent exploratas, namque fossas arborumque vermes in rem cibariam verterunt. Commendantur autem, edulesque sunt, ac valenter alunt, si probe perficiantur, fluviatiles, in aqua pura, fluviis, fontibusque dentes ac rivulis, palustres & cænosis in locis natantes pernitiosa & venenata sunt. Refert Alvisius Mundella Epist. 8. Se ranas sale oleoque conditas, partim ex jure albo cœlas, partim frixas in cœna sumptisse, paulo post tribus fere diebus continuis tanta sensisse symptomata, ut in veneni assumti suspicionem venerit, postea ait se comperisse ranas illas stagnantis cujusdam & palustris loci fuisse incolas, longoque ex itinere alatas continuo calore & agitatione semicorrupta. ptassnijsse. Itaq; recenter capienda sunt, & qui-dem ex aquis puris, diligenterq; denudanda, tum abjectis capite elixanda, inq; sartagine fri-genda, aspersa farina, & tandem apio. Gula generosior piperis pollinè salubriores & delica-tiores reddit. Cibum non sentientibus, quos græci ἀτρόφως appellant, nec non tabidis vtilissimè sumuntur. Antiquitas adversus venena eas magnificauit. Ætius l.2. c.162. & l.13.c.s. Item Ægineta l.7. prodiderunt, ranarum jus cum sale oleoq; haustum mirifice illis prodesse, quia venenatis reptilibus essent pertussi. Plinius hissuffragaturl.32.c.5. vbi legiuntur sequentia. Fluviatilis rana, si carnes earum edantur, jusq; vel decoctum sorbeatur, prosunt contra leporem marinum & contra serpentes. Item ranarum mainarum ex vino & aceto decoctarum suc-cus contra venena bibitur & contra rubeta ve-nenum. Est autem rubeta in vepribus tan-tum viventi rana plena veneficii.
units.tr: Certainly the Romans set up fishponds so that they might have the delights of frogs well tested; for they also turned ditches and worms of trees into food. River frogs are commended and are good to eat and nourish vigorously, if they are properly prepared; those taken in clean water, in rivers, springs and streams. Marsh frogs, swimming in muddy places, are harmful and poisonous. Alvisius Mundella, in Epistle 8, reports that he ate frogs preserved in salt and oil, some boiled in white broth and some fried, at dinner. A little after, for almost three days in a row, he felt such symptoms that he suspected poison. Afterwards he learned that those frogs had come from some stagnant and marshy place, and that, having been carried on a long journey, they had been semi-spoiled by constant heat and agitation. Therefore they should be caught fresh, from clean waters, and carefully skinned; then their heads are cut off, they are boiled, fried in a pan sprinkled with flour, and finally seasoned with parsley. A more generous palate makes them more wholesome and delicate with powdered pepper. They are most usefully taken by those who cannot digest food, whom the Greeks call atrophic, and also by the wasting sick. Antiquity extolled them against poisons: Aetius, book 2, chapter 162, and book 13; likewise Aegineta, book 7, have recorded that frog broth drunk with salt and oil does them wonderful good, because they have been pierced through by venomous reptiles. Pliny supports this in book 32, chapter 5, where the following is read: "A river frog, if its flesh is eaten, and its broth or decoction is sipped, helps against the sea hare and against serpents. Likewise the juice of such frogs boiled in wine and vinegar is drunk against poisons and against the venom of the rubeta. The rubeta, however, lives only among brambles, and is full of poison."

units.la: Mirafunt, qua Plinius certatim a scri-ptoribus tradita de rubeta prodidit. Illatas sc.in populum silentium fieri. Officuto quod sit in dex-tro latere, in aquam ferventem dejecto, refrige-rari vas, nec postea ferverre, nisi exemto. Inveni-ri autem idobjectâ rana formicis carnibus q; e-rosis. Etiam si esse in sinistro latere, quo dejecto fervere videatur, apocynum vocari: eo cohiberi tantum impetus, amore concitari, et jurgia addi-to in potionem: venerem adaillgatum stimulare. Rursus dextro adalligato in pellicula agnina recenti quartanas sanari aliasq; febres: amorem item inhiberi eo. Lienem quoq; ex his ranis contra ipsarum valere venena, & cor etiam efficacius esse. Hac Plinius de rubeta. Caterum rana oculum dextrum dextro, sinistrum lavo suspensos e collo natiui coloris panno, lippitudines sanare idem c. 7 refert: & si per coitum rana eruantur, albuginem quoq; adalligatas similiter in putamine ovi, reliquas carnes impositas suggillationem rapere. Tussim quoq; sanare ranas expertum est piscium modo e jure decoctas, pedibus autem suspensas, destillante in patinam saliua earum, exenterandas, abjectisq; interaneis condiendas esse idem c. 8. retulit. Ranam praeterea esse parvam arboresque candentem, exq; ea vociferantem, in cujus ossi quis expuat, ipsamq; dimittat, tussi liberari narratur, experimentum cuiq; liberum.
