units.tr: Wonders are told, which Pliny handed down, vying with other writers, about the rubeta. When it is brought in, silence falls upon the people. If the one that is on the right side is thrown into boiling water, the vessel cools and does not boil again unless it is removed. It is found that a frog thrown in with its flesh eaten away by ants does the same. Even if it is on the left side, which when thrown in makes the water seem to boil, it is called apocynum; by it only the impulse is checked, while love is aroused, and quarrels are added to the drink; bound to the body it stirs desire. Again, with the right one bound in fresh lambskin, quartan fevers and other fevers are cured; likewise love is restrained by it. The spleen of these frogs is also effective against their poisons, and the heart is even more powerful. So Pliny on the rubeta. Moreover, Pliny in the same chapter 7 reports that a frog's right eye, hung from the neck on the right side, and its left eye on the left, in cloth of natural colour, cures inflamed eyes; and if frogs are dug out during mating, the white of the eye, likewise bound in an eggshell, and the remaining flesh laid on, take away bruises. It has also been tested that frogs cure coughs; they are boiled in broth like fish, but hung up by their feet, so that their saliva drips into a pan; then they are gutted, and the entrails being thrown away, they are seasoned. This is in chapter 8. Moreover, a small frog that sits in a tree and croaks loudly is said to free a person from cough if he spits into its mouth and lets it go; the experiment is open to anyone.

units.la: Ranarum adipe aurium dolores tolli, arthriticos affectus sedari, tabida membra corroborari ac refoveri, multis experimentis patefactum est. Nec contemnendum, singulas ranas in aceto decoctas, ut dentes colluantur, dolorem sedare. Siq; fastidium obstaret, Salustius Dionysius suspendebat plures ranas pedibus posterioribus, ut flueret ex ore virus in acetum ferunt, quo maxillares sanari praecipue dentes putant, mobiles vero stabiliri. Alii ad idem binarum ranarum corpora praecisis pedibus in vino macerant. rant, colluiq; eo labentes dentes jubent: alii totas adalligant maxillis: alii 36. ranarum cor da in olla vetere sub area tesla disfoxere, ut infundeant per aurem dolentis maxillae: alii jecur ranae decoctum & cum melle tritum dentibus imponunt. Ad extremum parvam illam ranam in herbis & arundinetis maxime viventem, mutam & sine voce, viridem, boum ventres distendentem oculis tenebricosis, nebulosisq; mede-ri quidam abstruxorum natura periti in arcanis habent. Præcipue autem id præstare dicitur corporis humor specillis derasus inunctus, ipsa vero carnes doloribus oculorum superponuntur.
units.tr: The fat of frogs is shown by many experiments to relieve ear pains, calm arthritic complaints, and strengthen and warm wasted limbs. It is not to be despised that single frogs boiled in vinegar, used to rinse the teeth, relieve pain. If disgust stands in the way, Salustius Dionysius hung several frogs by their hind feet, so that the poison flowed from their mouths into the vinegar; they think this cures especially the teeth of the jaw, and makes loose teeth firm. Others steep the bodies of two frogs, with their feet cut off, in wine for the same purpose, and bid those with slipping teeth rinse their mouths with it. Others bind whole frogs to the jaws. Others have the hearts of 36 frogs boiled in an old pot under a tile, so that the broth may be poured into the ear of the one with the aching jaw. Others rub the frog's liver, boiled and ground with honey, onto the teeth. Finally, some men learned in the secrets of nature have, for eye disorders, dark and clouded, a remedy from that small frog which lives mostly among herbs and reeds: it is mute and voiceless, green, and it swells the bellies of cattle. Especially, it is said, the humour of the body, scraped off with a spatula and anointed, does this; the flesh itself is applied over eye pains.

units.la: De Lutra, & Fibro.
units.tr: On the Otter and the Beaver

units.la: EJusdem fere sunt generis lutra & fiber, nisi quod cauda differant, quam fiber habet piscibus similem, cætera lutræ species. Utrumq; animal horrendi est mor-sus, & lutra non desistit, nisi fracti ossis, ut ajunt, crepitum senserit. Lutram autem in cibos venire notum est, præsertim autem manditur à rusticis circa piscolentos lacus fyluis aut nemorosis locis proximos, habitantibus. Pisces hujus carnem olere certum est, ideoque de natura ejus non difficile est judicare: quidam lenti eam, crassi & pituitosi succi esse affirmant, difficulterque con-coquii. coqui. In fibro, priori parte pro carne, posteriori vero pro pisce vescuntur nationes quaedam: de vlteriori in re alimentaria potentia nihil aut parum constat. Caeterum castorii, h.e. Castoris seu fibri testium exectorum, milleni in medicina vsus, Vide Plin. l. 32. c. 3. Diofcor. l. 2. c. 22.
units.tr: The otter and the beaver are of almost the same kind, except that they differ in their tails: the beaver's tail is like a fish's, while the rest of its form matches the otter's. Each animal has a horrible bite, and the otter does not let go unless it feels, as they say, the crack of a broken bone. It is well known that otters are eaten, especially by country folk who live near fish-stinking lakes and in woody or forested places. It is certain that the flesh of this animal smells of fish, so it is not hard to judge its nature: some affirm that it is sluggish, of thick and phlegmatic juice, and hard to digest. Some peoples eat the beaver, the front part as meat and the hinder part as fish, but little or nothing is known for certain about its further nutritional value. Meanwhile, castoreum, that is, the testicles of the castor or beaver when cut out, is used in medicine by thousands. See Pliny, book 32, chapter 3; Dioscorides, book 2, chapter 22.

units.la: Adhuc de alimentis quae veniunt ab animalibus sanguineis, sequuntur sanguinis expertia.
units.tr: Next, after the foods that come from animals with blood, we come to those from creatures without blood.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: HUjusmodi sunt sepia, loligo, polypus: item crustacea, hoc est, crustis cotecta, graecè μαλακόστρακα, vt cancer, squilla, locusta: &c. necnon testacea testis inclusa, graeci ὀστρακόδερμα, vt limaces terrestres, cochleae, marinae, ostreae, pectines, concha.
units.tr: Of this kind are the cuttlefish, the squid and the octopus; likewise the crustaceans, that is, those covered with a crust, called malakostraka in Greek, such as the crab, the squill and the lobster; and also the testaceans, which have their bodies enclosed in a shell, called ostrakoderma in Greek, such as land slugs, snails, sea snails, oysters, scallops and the conch.

units.la: De Sepia, Loligine, & Polypo.
units.tr: On the Cuttlefish, Squid and Octopus.

units.la: SEpias, Polypos & Loligines germani vno nomine vocant Tintenfisch / angli Kuttel/Kuttelfisch: sa tamen vt à differtinguuntur. Is oligo major sit, ein groffer langer Blackfisch, ad differentiam loliginis minoris, sepia generatim Blackfisch nominatur: Polypus vero sit ein Blackfisch mit einem kleinen Leibe / vnnd langen Füssen/ darauff er gehen kan/ quib. etiam à priuribus dignoscitur, qui pedes habent breuiores, ampliusque. pliufq; corpus. Sepia & loligo cruore tan- tum differunt, qui in sepia ater, in loligine ruber effunditur. Nutrimentum horum pi- scium quod attinet, graves autores testantur valenter alere polypum, fi probe conficia- tur, veneremq; ciere vehementer. Unde a- cetabula & extremitates cirrorum a senibus expetuntur ad parandam sobolem. In aqua & atramento suo fi elixetur melior euadit. Venetias adferuntur ex Illyrico & Dalmatia sale inueterati. Loliginem sepia concoctu ef- fe faciliorem, verum insuauiorem graeci au- tores quidam tradiderunt. Parua, quam Cas- feronem quidam vocant, inter lautas epulas habetur. Diphilus apud Atheneum de sepia ait, teneram eam esse, ori suauem, concoctu facilem, quin etiam succum ejus sanguinem extenuare, excretioneq; per hemorrhoidas concitare. Celsus quoq; sepiae atramentum aluum mollire scribit. Recentes fastidium statim pariunt. De atramento sepiae scribit Plinius, tantam ei inesse vim, vt in lucerna addito aethiopas videri ablato priori lumine, Anaxilaus tradat. Porro sepias & loligines bifium & quinum cubitorum captas, polypum vero pendentem pondo 700 inauditae magnitudinis monstrum, Lucullo pro- consule Boeticae, Plinius refert, prodente Trebio Nigro Luculli Comite, cujus etiam polypi reliquiae miraculi loco asseruatae. Plin. lib. 9. c. 30.
units.tr: The Germans call cuttlefish, squid and octopus all by one name, Tintenfisch, and the English call them Kuttel or Kuttelfisch, though they are to be distinguished. The squid is the larger, a big long Blackfisch; to distinguish it from the smaller squid, the cuttlefish is generally called Blackfisch. The octopus is a Blackfisch with a small body and long legs on which it can walk, and it is also told apart from the others, which have shorter legs and a fuller, broader body. The cuttlefish and the squid differ only in their blood: in the cuttlefish it is black, in the squid red. As for the nourishment of these fish, grave authors testify that the octopus nourishes strongly if it is properly prepared, and greatly stirs venereal desire. Hence old men seek its suckers and the tips of its tentacles to produce offspring. If it is boiled in its own water and ink it turns out better. They are brought to Venice from Illyria and Dalmatia, preserved in salt. Some Greek authors have reported that the squid is easier to digest than the cuttlefish, but less pleasant. The small one, which some call casserone, is counted among elegant dishes. Diphilus, cited by Athenaeus, says of the cuttlefish that it is tender, pleasant to the mouth and easy to digest, and that its juice thins the blood and promotes discharge through the haemorrhoids. Celsus also writes that the ink of the cuttlefish softens the bowels. Fresh ones at once cause loathing. Pliny writes of cuttlefish ink that it has such power that, when it is added to a lamp and the former light removed, it makes Ethiopians appear, as Anaxilaus relates. Further, Pliny reports, on the authority of Trebius Niger, companion of Lucullus, that cuttlefish and squid of two and five cubits were caught, and an octopus weighing 700 pounds, a monster of unheard-of size, while Lucullus was proconsul of Baetica; its remains were also kept as a marvel. Pliny, book 9, chapter 30.

units.la: De Ostracodermis.
units.tr: Concerning Shellfish.

units.la: Omnibus Ostracodermis hoc est, testa intestinis commune est, vt salsum in carne succum contineant, qui alvum soluit. Vnicuiq; vero is inest proprius secundum majus & minus, pro quantitatis & qualitatis ratione.
units.tr: All shellfish, that is, creatures with a shell, share this trait with respect to the intestines: their flesh contains a salty juice that loosens the bowels. Each kind has its own amount of this juice, greater or less according to the quantity and quality of the flesh.

units.la: Hic salsus succus in ostreis magis abundat, ideoq; ad emolliendum alvum utiles magis, quam catera dura carnis testacea. Romanos diligentes admodum circa ostreas sustineo-nibusq; earum esca am aruisse in confesso est. Nam viuaria ostreis institutae inueniuntur, quas primus inuenisse legitur Sergius Orata, primusq; optimum saporem lucrinis adjudicaunt, hi enim suauiores & meliores habebantur. Cochlearum viuaria instituisse Hirpinum, easq; altiles adeo grandes factas, vt singularum calices 80. quadrantes caperent, Plinius autor est. Verum, qui absq; vita sua infidus & noxa testaceis quibuscunq; vesci gaudet, vnice ventriculi sui constitutionem ac naturam exploratam habebit. Quae molliissima constant carne, vt ostrea, hu-moreq; foetifico abundant (quemadmodum in ostrearijs compertum est humorem ita foetifi-cum laetis modo effluere) exhibenda sunt ventriculo a vitiatis succis vacuo ac expurgato: quae vero duriores sunt carnis, vt testacea cate-ra, iis danda sunt, quibus facile cibi vitiantur inveniri.
units.tr: This salty juice is more abundant in oysters, so they are more useful than other hard-fleshed shellfish for softening the bowels. It is well established that the Romans were very diligent about oysters and that they were fond of eating them. Indeed, oyster beds are known to have been established, and Sergius Orata is said to have been the first to invent them. The Romans also judged the Lucrine oysters to have the best flavour, since these were thought the sweetest and finest. Plinius reports that Hirpinus established snail beds, and that the snails grew so large that eighty of them filled a pint measure. But whoever delights in eating any shellfish without harm to his health must first know the constitution and nature of his own stomach. Those kinds whose flesh is very soft, like oysters, and which abound in a fermenting humour (as has been observed in oyster beds, where this humour flows out like milk), should be given only to a stomach that is empty and cleansed of corrupt juices. Those whose flesh is harder, like the other shellfish, should be given to people whose food is not easily spoiled.

units.la: { } Hic textus in margine: Praecepti aur. Oftracodermophagis inprimis obseruandum in vitę prorogatione. in ventriculo ob improbos succos vel ex epate in ipsum confluentes, vel tunicis ipsius infixos atq; contentos. Sicut igitur ostrea magis alvum emolliunt, alunt vero levius, ita carnem habentes duriorem difficilius quidem conficiuntur, at valentius nutriunt. Ut autem ostrea difficilius corrumpantur, alvum reprimant, nutriantq; valentius, succum illum salsum, quo abundare ostreas dictum est, eas deponere necesse est. Mirandum, (deplorandum volebam) dicere,) eo gula insaniam rediisse, ut salutaribus escis negleciis, veneficia in cibos vertat. Ostracoderma enim omnia & inp imu ostreas humidam nimis mucosamq; obtinere carnem, in confesso est, testante id Galen. quoq; 2.de temper. & per consequens malum generare alimentum cruda illa pituita in ventriculo non probe confecta. Gulosissimi igitur phagones sunt, qui ostreas crudas devorant, & quidem cum pituita sua integras. Sunt, qui quinquagenas, sunt, qui centenas devorant prima mensa. Persuasum habent quidem gula illi ganeaq; oslentatores, humidum autem illam pituitam, cruda, vino forti largius superbibito confici atq; edomari, ut ita haud facile ventriculo officere possit. Non attendunt vero quam promte & incaute vinum cruditatem illam mucumque ostrearum secum rapiens in corpus omnes distribuat, venas repleat, corpusq; reddat cacochymum. Qui nitidioris sunt palati, vitaq; falusalubrioris curiosi, nec non ventriculi imbecil-lioris, ostreas in ollis elixant, adiiciuntq; piper, cinnamomum & garyophyllos alii reclusas salis momento addito, prunis imponunt, parumq; concalefactas vorant. Galenus in farragine coqui a quibusdam docet. Ganeones ad Venerem stimulandam experimento iis vescuntur. Plinius lib. 32. cap. 6. stomachum unice reficere indistincte affirit, fastidiumq; mederi, alvumq; quoque leniter mollire, aitq; omnia testacea modice in cibis oportere collui, quia saporis gratia perit.
units.tr: { } Marginal note in this text: The precept to be observed above all by those who eat shellfish, for the prolonging of life: in the stomach, because of bad juices, either flowing into it from the liver or lodged and held in its coats. Just as oysters loosen the bowels more, but nourish more lightly, so flesh that is harder is indeed digested with more difficulty, but nourishes more strongly. In order that oysters may be less easily corrupted, may bind the bowels and nourish more strongly, it is necessary to remove that salty juice, of which oysters were said to have an abundance. It is astonishing (I was going to say deplorable) to say that gluttony has come to such madness that, neglecting wholesome foods, it turns poisons into food. For it is generally agreed that all shellfish, and especially oysters, have a moist and slimy flesh, as Galen also testifies in book 2 of On Temperaments; and consequently that this raw phlegm, not properly digested in the stomach, produces bad nourishment. Those most gluttonous are therefore the gorgers who devour raw oysters, and indeed whole, with their phlegm. Some devour fifty, some a hundred, at the first course. Those gluttonous and greedy show-offs are convinced that this moist phlegm and raw matter is overcome and tamed by drinking plenty of strong wine, so that it can hardly harm the stomach. But they do not consider how quickly and carelessly the wine, carrying off that crudity and slime of the oysters, spreads it through the whole body, fills the veins, and makes the body cacochymic. Those of more refined palate, and more anxious about a healthy life, and also of weaker stomach, boil oysters in pots, adding pepper, cinnamon and cloves; others open them, add salt for a moment, place them on hot coals, and eat them only slightly warmed. Galen teaches this method of cookery in his Farrago. Debauchees eat them by way of experiment to stimulate lust. Plinius, book 32, chapter 6, affirms that shellfish restore the stomach indiscriminately, cure loss of appetite, and also gently soften the bowels; and he says that all shellfish should be moderately washed before being put in food, because the flavour is lost.

units.la: Celsus Cornelius lib. 2. eo capite, quo res stomacho idoneas explicat, pisces ex media materia ponit ostreas, pectines, cochleas. Idem tenerosque pisces & ostrea in his cibis numerat, quæ facile corrumpuntur, muricesq; & purpuras inter ea, quæ intus minus vitiantur. Præterea alvum moventibus contribuit ostrea, omnesq; ferè conchulas maxime ejus earum. Veteres in principio cœna ostreas præbere consueVisse. Plutarchus innuit 8. Symposi. 9. hodie mos invaluit apud quosdam extrinsecus, ostreas post alios cibos ingluttire, cum primis si præcesserint cibi duriores & astringentes, quæ difficulter corrumpuntur: cœstionem enim sic devorata impediunt, caloremque nativum ventriculi, cœstionem jam aggressurum interturbant. Non parum enim interest, quo ordine fercula aut cibi ingerantur. Galenus lib. 3. de symt. caus. cap. 1. inquit, Cibus parum conveniente ordine aut intempestive sumtus concoctionem vitiat. Et eod. in libr. cap. eod. Ciborum incoveniens ordo est, cum fructus primo, deinde alia emollientia, ut oleum ex garo sumuntur. Idem lib. 2. de alimen. facultat. de sycaminis. Ex cibis qui subducuntur, posteriores quidem sumendi, qui tarde permeant, omnium autem primi, qui celeriter pervadunt, ut sunt ostrea. Celsus lib. 1. cap. 2. inquit, cibus a salsamentis, oleribus similibus quæ rebus melius incipit, tum caro assumenda, quæ assa optima aut elixa est. Secunda mensa stomacho nihil nocet, in imbecillo coacescit, Si quis itaque hoc parum valet, palmulas pomaque similia melius primo assumit cibo. Valeriola l. 2. loc. comm. cap. 6. hunc esse debere ordinem ait, ut quæ levia sunt, alvumque subducentia prius, posterius vero, quæ plenius alunt, ingerantur, nec dura mollibus, nec astringentia subducentibus, nec crassiora tenuibus, nec concoctu gravia facilibus præmittantur. Eoigitur ordine alimenta ingerenda esse omnes præcipere videntur, ut æquo tempore omnia coquantur, ne sc. crudum misceatur cocto, vel coctum crudo: quod sit, si ea, quæ liquida sunt, lubrica, vitiosique succi pra aliis obsoniis comedantur, im enim & ipsa facile egerantur, & cateris iterparant.
units.tr: Celsus Cornelius, book 2, in the chapter where he explains foods suitable for the stomach, places among the middling foods fish, oysters, scallops and snails. He also counts among those foods that are easily spoiled the tender fish and oysters, while among those less liable to corruption inside he lists murex and purple shells. Moreover, he says that oysters, and almost all small shellfish, are especially helpful to those who wish to move the bowels. The ancients used to serve oysters at the beginning of the meal. Plutarch hints at this in book 8 of the Symposiacs, chapter 9. Today a custom has taken hold among some people of swallowing oysters from outside after other foods, especially when harder and astringent foods have come first, which are digested with difficulty. For oysters so swallowed hinder the digestion, and disturb the natural heat of the stomach that is just about to begin digesting. For it makes no small difference in what order the dishes or foods are taken. Galen, in book 3 of On the Causes of Symptoms, chapter 1, says: Food taken in an unsuitable order or at the wrong time spoils digestion. And in the same book and chapter: The order of food is improper when fruits are taken first, and then other softening things such as oil with fish sauce. The same, in book 2 of On the Faculties of Foods, concerning figs: Of the foods that are set out, the later ones are to be taken, those which pass through slowly; but the first ones are those which pass through quickly, such as oysters. Celsus, book 1, chapter 2, says: The meal should begin with salted foods and vegetables of the same kind, which are better for the first course; then meat should be taken, roasted or boiled being best. A second course does no harm to a strong stomach, but in a weak one it turns sour. So if someone is somewhat weak, he should take date-palm fruits and similar fruits first, before the meal. Valeriola, book 2 of the Common Places, chapter 6, says that this should be the order: light foods that loosen the bowels should be given first, and afterwards those that nourish more fully; neither hard foods before soft, nor astringent before laxative, nor coarse before delicate, nor heavy to digest before easy ones. Almost all writers seem to prescribe this order of taking food, so that everything is cooked in the same time, lest the raw be mixed with the cooked, or the cooked with the raw. This happens if things that are liquid, slippery and of bad juice are eaten before other dishes, for these pass out easily themselves and hinder the rest.

units.la: Ex quibus perspicuum evadit, & ostrea secundo cibo assumta concoctionem vitiare, tum quia a natura superata coctaq; descendere non possunt ob cibos praemissos nondum coctos, in ima ventriculi parte adhuc existentes, & sic retenta, quasi iam concocta sunt, corrumpuntur: tum quod hoc modo coctum crudo miscebitur. Expediet igitur praecedere ea, quae facilius coquuntur, ut cocta citius statim descendant, neq; ab aliis impediantur, aut eisdem admisceantur & confundantur. Quaedam pro evidenti veritatis affectione & clariori doctrina gratia vtuntur hac distinctione. Alimentorum quaedam habent liquidam, quaedam solidam substantiam.
units.tr: From these things it becomes clear that shellfish taken with the second course also spoil digestion: first, because, overcome and cooked by nature, they cannot pass down on account of the foods taken before them, which are not yet cooked and remain in the lowest part of the stomach, and so, held back as if already digested, they rot; second, because in this way the cooked will be mixed with the raw. It will therefore be advantageous to take first those foods that are more easily digested, so that the cooked may pass down quickly at once, and not be hindered by others, or mixed and confused with them. Some, for the sake of a clearer teaching and the plain affection for truth, use this distinction: Some foods have a liquid substance, others a solid one.

units.la: Ex solidis quaedam citius, quaedam tardius superantur a ventriculo. Ventriculus autem non habet in partibus suprema & infima parem calorem, siquidem infima crassior est & carnosior, iecoris propior. Vbi alimenta eandem habent differentiam, ut quaedam sint liquida, tenuisque substantia, quaedam solida, nihil omnino refert, siue in simul, sive praecedant liquida, sive sequantur. Exemplo est ius carnis & caroipsa, si quis enim haec duo eadem mensa assumere debeat, nihil refert ius antecedere, vel subsequi: si enim antecedat, adveniente carne, facile invicem miscentur, inq; unam deducuntur substantiam mastic ata ac comminuta prius carne. Si vero caro praecedat ius, sequatur totam carnis substantiam ius pervadet, cui exacte commiscemiscebitur. Et hac ratio est, ob quam sine manifesta noxa quidam ante, quidam post ius ingerunt, potumque cum & post cibos assumimus.
units.tr: Among solid foods, some are overcome by the stomach more quickly, some more slowly. The stomach, however, does not have the same heat in its upper and lower parts, since the lower part is thicker and fleshier and nearer the liver. Where foods have the same difference, some being liquid and thin in substance, others solid, it makes no difference at all whether they are taken together, or the liquids come first or follow. An example is broth and meat itself: if someone must take these two at the same meal, it makes no difference whether the broth comes before or after. For if it comes first, when the meat arrives they are easily mixed together and led into one substance, the meat having first been chewed and minced. But if the meat comes first and the broth follows, the broth will pervade the whole substance of the meat, with which it is thoroughly mixed. And this is the reason why some people take broth before and some after the meat without any clear harm, and why we drink both with and after our food.

units.la: Quod si vero solida fuerint alimenta, sed natura dispar, aut liquida, sed crassa, subtilia, fercula, quae sunt faciliora concoctu praeire debent, subsequi vero reliqua, docente Gal. 2. de alimento. fac. c. de piscib. ubi inquit, omnia cibaria praeunt cum humiditate succum habentia, ex facili descendere, eaque prima mensa esse assumenda. Et l. 3. de rat. vict. in acut. comm. 22. inquit, Nam perpetuo prius ingerenda sunt, quae & facilius concoquuntur, & quae subducuntur magis. Quin & valida ratione comprobatur haec sententia. Cum enim alimentum, quod facile coquitur, praeassumitur, prius coquitur, ac descendit, deinde aliud sequitur, quod eo diuti immoratur, quo longiori tempore eget ad coctionem. Non enim coctum alimentum in ventre momento temporis descendit, sed quod in superiori parte continetur, tardius: decet igitur id tardius coqui, uti tardius descendit, ut diu retentum perficiatur, & tam id quod facile quam id quod difficile coquitur, parum a completa coctione descendat. Ubi vero unum alimentum tantum assumatur, quemadmodum pars superior tardius coquetur, ita magis immorabitur, donec perficiatur.
units.tr: But if the foods are solid yet of different natures, or liquid but thick and thin, the dishes that are easier to digest ought to come first, and the rest to follow, as Galen teaches in book 2 of On the Faculties of Foods, in the chapter on fish, where he says: all foods that have juice and moisture pass down easily, and these should be taken as the first course. And in book 3 of On the Regimen in Acute Diseases, commentary 22, he says: Foods which are both more easily digested and which pass through more quickly must always be taken first. This opinion is also confirmed by a sound argument. For when a food that is easily cooked is taken first, it is cooked first and passes down; then another follows, which stays longer the longer it needs time for digestion. For cooked food does not pass down from the belly in a moment, but what is held in the upper part lingers more slowly; it is fitting, therefore, that it be cooked more slowly, just as it descends more slowly, so that, being retained for a long time, it is completed, and both what is easily digested and what is digested with difficulty pass down only a little short of complete digestion. But where only one food is taken, just as the upper part is cooked more slowly, so it remains longer until it is completed.

units.la: Excluditur igitur hic illorum placitum, qui dixerunt, alimenta tardioris difficilioris coctionis antecedere debere ea quae facile coquuntur tur, quoniam, inquiunt, venter magis calidus est in fundo ea scilicet parte, qua carnosior est, & iecori propior: ideoque tali ordine alimenta essingerenda, vt aequo tempore coquantur omnia, nec crudum coctu miscEatur, quod tum fieri aiunt, vbi, quod difficilius coquitur, antecedat, imam ventris partem, quae calidior est, praeoccupet, quod vero facilius coquitur, superiorem & minus calidam. Exploditur quoque illorum opinio, qui statuunt, quod si pars intervallo distent ciborum natura cum calore partium ventris, eam antecedere debere, qui coctioni magis reluctatur, vt vno tempore omnino coquantur: inde enim fieret, vt totum alimentum in brevissimo tempore descenderet, aut superior pars corrumperetur. Primum autem non fit, quoniam quinis facile intelligetur, plus quam duarum horarum tempore ventrem onus in intestina deponere, quo tempore tenuior sensim redditur venter. Secundum igitur, id est, alimentum in ventre corrumpi, accidet, si duarum horarum spatio coctum retineatur in ventre. Vide infra Praeceptum 3, capitis 3. Ad extremum, vt ad ostreas redeamus, non ignorandum, mensarum palmam tribui Oceanicis, damnari vero fluvialibus, quae putrescente limo, aut faecespumosa circa navigia diutius stante, defixosque palos adnascuntur. Sic autem generari ostreas Aristoteles & Plinius prodiderunt. Et verissimum id esse nostro seculo comprobavit Franciscus Gall. Rex, qui, cum adfoffam Mariana Carolum V. Imper, excepturus, navigasset, sermoq; de ostreis inci- disse, ac cives illius loci nautaq; constanter affir- marent, mare illud ostreas non alere, statim iuf- sit, vt navigiorum carinas & inferiora foris scru- tarentur diligenter, ipsoq; praesente ostrea inuen- ta sunt tenuem saporem, pelagis & Oceanicis longe ignobiliorem referentes. Nec praetereun- dum hic, ostrearum, conchatumq; corpora, quin & Cancrarium genus vnius sum, lunari pote- state grandescere, augeri, minuiq;, praesertim vero plenilunii restitui, plenioraq; fieri, magisq; in cibis placere, Aristoteles & Plinius graves auctores testantur. Id autem non euenit ab vberiore pabulo, vt alii existimant, sed obtepidiores noctes, quia plenior lux est, calorem enim desiderant frigoris patientes. Praecipue vero ait Plinius l. 32. c. 6. circa estatis initia multo lacte pragnantes spe- stantur, atq; vbi sol penetret in vada. Hacq; videtur causa, cur minora alibi in locis reperian- tur: Opacitas enim incrementum prohibet & amplitudinem, adeo rebus omnibus vitali suo lumine sol prodest, etiam in profundo mersis ma- ri. Venenis ostreas aduersari, viuasq; pestilentes bubones loco transferre, virusq; omne ad se tra- here non leues autores tradunt, sunt autem bra- chio agglutinanda, ea parte qua axillaris de- currit, si bubo in alis est, si vero in- guen obsederit, femo- ribus,
units.tr: Here, then, the opinion of those is refuted who said that foods which are harder to digest should precede those which are digested easily. They argue that the belly is hottest at its bottom, the part that is fleshier and nearer the liver, and that foods must therefore be put in such an order that all are digested at the same time, and the raw is not mixed with the cooked. They say this happens when the harder-to-digest food goes first and occupies the lowest part of the belly, which is the warmer, while the easier-to-digest food stays above, in the cooler part. Also refuted is the view of those who hold that if the natures of the foods are at odds with the heat of the parts of the belly, the food that resists digestion should be placed ahead, so that all are digested together. For then the whole meal would pass down in a very short time, or the upper part would rot. The first does not happen, since it is easily understood that the belly takes more than two hours to empty its load into the intestines, during which time it gradually becomes thinner. So the second, that the food would decay in the belly, would follow only if cooked food were kept in the belly for two hours. See below, Precept 3, chapter 3. Finally, to return to oysters: it should not be overlooked that the palm for table quality is given to sea oysters and denied to river ones, which grow on rotting mud or on foul froth, and on stakes driven in and left standing too long beside boats. Aristotle and Pliny have recorded that oysters are generated in this way. And Francis I, King of France, proved this to be most true in our own age: when he had sailed to the Fossa Mariana to receive Charles V, the Emperor, and the talk turned to oysters, and the citizens of that place and the sailors firmly asserted that the sea there did not feed oysters, he at once ordered the keels and undersides of the ships to be searched carefully. With him present, oysters were found, giving a thin flavour, far less esteemed than those of the open sea and the ocean. Nor should it be passed over here that Aristotle and Pliny, reliable authorities, testify that the bodies of oysters and shellfish, and indeed one kind of crab, grow, increase and shrink under the power of the moon, and are restored especially at full moon, becoming fuller and more pleasing as food. This does not come from richer feeding, as some think, but from the warmer nights, since there is more light; for those that endure cold desire warmth. Pliny, book 32, chapter 6, says especially that they are found full of milk near the beginning of summer, when the sun penetrates to the shallows. This seems to be the reason why smaller ones are found in other places: darkness prevents growth and size, so much does the sun benefit all things by its vital light, even those sunk in the deep sea. Not slight authorities also hold that oysters counteract poisons and draw pestilential buboes, living ones, to another place, and that they take up all the venom to themselves. They are to be applied to the arm, along the part where the armpit runs, if the bubo is in the armpit; but if it has settled in the groin, to the thighs,

units.la: Submonitio de oftracodermis.
units.tr: Preliminary note on the ostracoderms

units.la: NE in cæteris oftracodermis & testaceis describendis, enumerandisque diutius immorer, ostrearum natura & conditionem aliquanto prolixius persecutus sum, aliis, quibus plenior est de his cognitio, quiq; diu multumq; in locis illis maritimis versati sunt, pleniorem scribendi occasionem relinquens. Quæ igitur de ostreis huc sunt inserta, de cæteris testaceis quoque intelligantur: In specie vero cochleas, conchasque fluviatiles virosas esse, vepribus vero adhærentes ventrem turbare, vomitumque cière. Testudines autem, quas Græcorum pariter atque latinorum auctoritas in vsu cibario reposuit, carnes habere à vitulina non multum discrepantes, tum odoris suavitate, tum odoris gratia, graves autores affirmant. Sanguinem earum contra venena præclare auxiliari uno ore prædicant omnes. Terrestres, quæ formosiores sunt, inque nemoribus & sylvis degentes gracilibus & tabidis ab orco revocandis mire commendat posterior medicina, caliditati enim habituali in membris resistunt. Marinæ circa cimoplatas posteriorasque cruta suaves ac delicatæ prædicantur. Certissimum aiunt, probe in ventre confectas valenter alere: elixantur prius exquisitè, deinde in frusta dissectæ friguntur.
units.tr: So that I do not linger too long over describing and listing the other ostracoderms and shellfish, I have followed the nature and condition of oysters at some length, leaving the occasion for fuller writing to others who have a richer knowledge of these creatures and who have spent long and much time in those maritime places. What has been inserted here about oysters should also be understood of the other shellfish. In particular, snails and river shells are said to be foul, and when they cling to brambles they disturb the stomach and cause vomiting. Tortoises, however, which the authority of both Greeks and Latins has placed among foods, are said by reliable writers to have flesh not much different from veal, both in the pleasantness of their smell and in their taste. All authorities agree that their blood is an excellent remedy against poisons. Later medicine especially commends the land tortoises, which are the more handsome and live in groves and woods, as wonderfully effective for calling back from the threshold of death the thin and wasting, since they resist the habitual heat in the limbs. The sea tortoises are described as sweet and delicate about the neck and the back flesh. They say it is most certain that, when properly digested in the stomach, they nourish strongly. They are first boiled very carefully, then cut into pieces and fried.

units.la: {*} De testudinibus & cochleis. NB. guntur. Mare Indicum tantæ amplitudinis testudines mittere, Plinius lib. 9. cap 10. autor est, vt singularum superficies habitabiles casas integant, atque inter insulas rubri maris præcipuè his navigent, velut cymbis. Qui de novæ Indiæ rebus monitmenta tradiderunt, testudines illic reperiri aiunt ex quarum tegumento magni fiant clypei. Unde à scuti seu peltæ figura <bl>Schildkroten</bl> appellantur à Germanis. Hactenus de Oftracodermis.
units.tr: {*} On tortoises and snails. N.B. are fried. Pliny, book 9, chapter 10, is the authority that the Indian Sea sends forth tortoises of such size that the surface of each one covers a habitable hut, and that men sail among the islands of the Red Sea, especially in them, as in boats. Those who have handed down reports on the affairs of New India say that tortoises are found there from whose shell great shields are made. Hence the Germans call them <bl>Schildkroten</bl>, from the shape of a shield or small round shield. So far on the ostracoderms.

units.la: De Malacostracis, hoc est, crustis intectis, seu crustaceis.
units.tr: On the Malacostraca, that is, the shell-covered or crustacean animals.

units.la: Crustatorum nomina tam apud Latinos quam Græcos confundi certum est. Aristoteles quatuor eorum fecit genera, locustas, astacos, squillas, cancros, 4. de animal. lib. Et cancros appellasse visus est, quibus corpus est rotundum, & cauda deest. Capite enim secundo ait, Cancris ex crustaceis solis cauda deest, & corpus rotundum est, cum locustis squillisque longum fit. Plinius summus alioquin Aristotelis imitator, omnes qui crusta teguntur, tam caudatos, quam non caudatos sub cancri appellatione complectitur. Porro cancrorum genus multiplex esse Aristoteles scribit, nec facilè enumerandum, ob nominum multitudinem. Generatim, quæ de his constant, leguntúrque, depromam. Duritate autem ostracodermis similia esse, sed minus quam illa salsi liquoris continere, Galenus lib. de alimento 3. scripsit. Confirmat hoc Simeon Sethi de vsu cancrorum prodens, Cancri, inquit, salsum quendam succum habent, minusque tamen quam testacea: ventrem nihilo minus sistunt, nec leuiter alunt, in aqua potulenta prius elixati, qua ratione salsum succum amittunt. Cæterum nomina malacostracorum sic distinguenda sunt, vt cancer sit ein Krabbe/cancer marinus, ein Meerkrab/ aliud vero, ein Krebs/ altacus marinus, gammarus, ein Meerkrebs/ astacus fluviatilis, ein süsser Wasserkrebs/ cancer locustrarius, ein langer Krebs. Cancri maiores, omnium cancrorum maximi, grosse Meerspinnen/ squillæ, kleine Meerkrebs oder kleine Krabben/ locustis similes fere, nisi quod forcipe carent. Vt autem nominibus malacostraca distinguuntur, ita etiam viribus & facultatibus, pro aquæ, loci, aeris ac pabuli natura ac conditione diuersa.
units.tr: It is certain that the names of crustaceans were confused both among the Latins and among the Greeks. Aristotle made four kinds of them: locusts, astacus, squillae and crabs (cancri), in book 4 of De animalibus. He seems to have called cancri those with a round body and no tail, for in the second chapter he says: "Among the crustaceans, only the crabs lack a tail and have a round body, whereas locusts and squillae are long." Pliny, otherwise a great imitator of Aristotle, includes under the name cancer all crusted animals, both tailed and tailless. Aristotle writes that the kinds of crabs are many and not easy to enumerate, because of the multitude of names. I shall set out in general what is agreed and read about them. Galen, in book 3 of On Food, wrote that the malacostraca are similar in hardness to the ostracoderms, but contain less salty liquid than they do. Symeon Seth confirms this in his work on the use of crabs: "Crabs," he says, "have a certain salty juice, yet less than the shelled animals. Still, they fill the stomach and nourish only lightly, unless they are first boiled in fresh water, which removes the salty juice." Moreover, the names of the malacostraca must be distinguished as follows: cancer is a crab (German Krabbe, Meerkrab), a sea-crab; astacus is the crayfish (Krebs), the sea-crayfish or gammarus (Meerkrebs), and the river-crayfish (süsser Wasserkrebs); cancer locustarius is the spiny lobster (langer Krebs). The larger cancri, the greatest of all crabs, are the squillae (grosse Meerspinnen); small sea-crayfish or small crabs (kleine Meerkrebs oder kleine Krabben) are nearly like locusts, except that they lack the claw. Just as the malacostraca are distinguished by their names, so they also differ in their powers and properties, according to the nature and condition of the water, the place, the air and the food.

units.la: Omnia crustacea esse tabidis, extenuatis ac macilentis salubria, feruidos aduersosque humores refrigerare ac diluere omnium pe-ne consensu traditur: verum fluuiatilia marinis efficaciora existere, quoniam his salsugi-nis nis aliquid admixtum reperitur, qua quidem appetentiam excitant, ac palato gratificantur, sed magis exiccant, quocirca sanis mariti- mi cancri aptiores sunt, nec non iis qui infa- lubri corporis sunt habitu, vitiosq; humo- ribus scatent, humorum enim putredini ob- stant, superuacuaque excrementa exiccant atque absumunt: fluuiatiles vero humectant ac nutriunt magis, natiuumque humorem, quo corpus subsistit ac nutritur, adaugent, adhibito vino dulci & calorifico, cuius adiumento concoctio perficitur. Efficacius omnia praestant in aqua hordei loti, inque carnium vel capi iure cocti. Salis quoque & aromatum vsum non incofulto hic adhibent, qui ad aquilonios tractus vergunt, hac enim ratione minus pituitosi efficiuntur, minusq; computrescunt, liquescit enim salsis adeps, vt videre est in limacibus, quae asperso sale, minus sunt opimae ac moftrose obesae. Squillas praeterea astacos & locutas in eo quod hecticis aque morbo extenuatis eximie prosint, vincere reperio, carnisque dulcedine superare, easdemque non in vilibus apud Romanos fuisse cibis, Satyrographorum carmina fatis testantur, de qua re luuenalis, Aspice quam magno distentat pectore lancem, Quae ferunt Domino Squillas. Et Horatius, Adfertur Squillas inter murena natantes In patina porrecta.
units.tr: It is almost universally taught that all crustaceans are wholesome for those who are wasting away, thin and emaciated, and that they cool and dilute hot and harmful humours. But river crustaceans are said to be more effective than sea ones, since a certain saltiness is found mixed in the latter, which stimulates appetite and pleases the palate, but dries more. For this reason sea crabs are better suited to healthy people, and also to those of unwholesome bodily habit who abound in morbid humours, for they resist the putrefaction of humours and dry up and consume superfluous excrements. River crustaceans, on the other hand, moisten and nourish more, and increase the natural moisture by which the body subsists and is nourished, especially when taken with sweet and warming wine, by whose help digestion is completed. All of them work best when cooked in the water of washed barley, or in the broth of meat or of capons. People in northern regions also use salt and spices with them, and not without reason, for in this way they become less phlegmatic and decay less; salt melts their fat, as one sees in snails, which, sprinkled with salt, are less plump and less bloated with obesity. I also find that squillae, crayfish and locusts are particularly helpful for those thinned by hectic fever, and that they surpass others in sweetness of flesh. The verses of the satirists bear witness that these were not uncommon foods among the Romans. Juvenal speaks of this: "Look how proudly he holds up the platter with its great bulk, the squillae which they say are served to the master." And Horace: "Squillae swimming among the eels are brought in on an outstretched dish."

units.la: Non conticendum hîc remedium cancrorum fluuiatilium cauda catentium, in patella crematorum ac deustorum, quorum puluis cinisque singulari pollet virtute, in expugnando exitiali canis rabidi veneno. Exhibetur cum gentianæ radice thurisque momento cochleari mensura, frequentius iterando, quo rabies aquæque pauor propulsetur.
units.tr: I must not pass over here the remedy from river crabs that have their tails removed, roasted and burnt in a small pan. Their powder and ash have a singular power in overcoming the deadly poison of a mad dog. It is given with root of gentian and a spoonful of frankincense, repeated frequently, so that the madness and the fear of water may be driven off.

units.la: Stillatitium quoq; cancrorum liquorem, plenilunii tempore in balneo Mariæ elicitu, sicut & ius eorundem accuratè prius abluto- rum, aftmaticis & tabescentibus, nec non apoplecticis bis in die potam, prodesse compertum est.
units.tr: It is also known that the liquid that drips from crabs, drawn off in a bain-marie at the time of full moon, as well as the broth of the same animals, carefully washed first, helps asthmatics, consumptives and those with apoplexy, when drunk twice a day.

units.la: Oleo coctos aurium dolores calidos sana- re, si iniftilletur id, si vero hauriatur, venena- tam potionem, aut venenatum morsum dif- ficultur ferentibus succurrere, apud doctissi- mos autores reperio.
units.tr: I find in the most learned authors that crabs cooked in oil heal pains of the ears if dripped in, and that, if swallowed, they help those who with difficulty bear a poisoned drink or a poisonous bite.

units.la: De oculis cancrorum sciptum inuenio, collo adalligatos lippitudini mederi: tusos- que eosdem aduersus laterum puncturas bi- bi & calculum, necnon venena, & febres.
units.tr: I find it written about the eyes of crabs that, tied around the neck, they cure inflammation of the eyes; and that, pounded, they are good against stings in the sides, against the stone, and also against poisons and fevers.

units.la: Non omiserim, quod Plinius de fluuiatilibus cancris scribit, eos tritos in oleo & aqua ante accessiones inundtis febricitantibus prodesse: alii decoctos ad quartas in vino è balneis egressis bibere suadent in quartanis: alii sinistrum oculum deuorari iubent:
units.tr: I should not omit what Pliny writes about river crabs: that when rubbed in oil and water before the attacks, they help those suffering from fevers. Others advise that, boiled to the fourth part in wine, they be drunk by those coming out of the baths for quartan fevers; others order that the left eye be eaten.

units.la: alii oculos eorum ante solis ortum aegro adalligari mandant, ita vt caecae dimittantur in aquas, sicque tertianas abigi promittunt. Mirabile, & in naturae maiestate plane recondi-tum atque abstrusum, febricitanti, si vngues in pedibus & manibus resecentur, viuique cancri dorso adalligentur, cancerque in aquam fluentem viuus coniiciatur, febrim remissuram, cuius experimenti, possem, si opus esset, producere testes, qui id non semel documento comprobarunt. Et tantum etiam de animalibus exanguibus, eorumque in re cibaria visu dixisse sufficiat.
units.tr: Others direct that their eyes be tied to the patient before sunrise, and then they be let go alive into the water, and so they promise that tertian fevers will be driven away. It is a marvel, and quite hidden and concealed in the majesty of nature: for a feverish person, if the nails of the feet and hands are cut off and a living crab is tied to the back, and the crab is then thrown alive into flowing water, the fever will withdraw. If it were necessary, I could produce witnesses of this experiment, who more than once have confirmed it by proof. Let it suffice to have said so much about exsanguine animals and their use as food.

units.la: Hactenus de esculentis vitae prorogandae conducentibus ex animalibus sanguineis & exanguibus : Sequuntur nunc ordine partes animalium quorundam, quae sunt edendo.
units.tr: So far concerning the edible animals, both sanguineous and exsanguineous, that serve to prolong life. Now, in order, follow the parts of certain animals that are eaten.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: IN animalibus partes reperiuntur tum carnosae, & sanguineae, tum carnes, sanguinis expertes, adipose item ac pinguet, suaque naturâ humida ac fluida.
units.tr: Among animals there are parts that are fleshy and bloody, parts that are flesh without blood, and likewise fatty and oily parts, which by their nature are moist and fluid.

units.la: Primi generis sunt lingua, glandia, testes, vulua, renes, iecur, lien, pulmo, cor, ventres.
units.tr: Of the first kind are the tongue, the glands, the testicles, the womb, the kidneys, the liver, the spleen, the lungs, the heart, and the stomachs.

units.la: Secundi, pedes, aures, rostra.
units.tr: Of the second kind are the feet, the ears, and the snouts.

units.la: Tertii, ossium medulla, cerebrum, sanguis, adeps.
units.tr: Of the third kind are the marrow of the bones, the brain, the blood, and the fat.

units.la: De Lingua.
units.tr: On the Tongue.

units.la: ESse animalia, & homines lingua carentes. Plinius lib. 8. & c. testatur esse quoque miram linguarum diuersitatem idem eleganter ostendit libro naturalis historia 11. Itaque quae in cibis magis placeant, inquirendum. Inuenio autem suillam & bubulam a culinis magis commendari, vtramque quidem quandoque elixam, sepius tamen assam, gariophyllisque confixam. In multis Germaniae locis bubulae sale condiuntur, pensilesque asseruantur in annuos vsus. Hac zythi meriq; seu vini potores ad excitandam sitim nihil praeclarius habent, vinum liquidé iucundioris gustus fieri huius esu affirmant. Veruecinae elixae ex aceto febricitantibus, & a valetudine sese colligentibus exhibentur. Caeterum, probum pariunt succum, carnium succo similem, si commodé praeparentur, & in ventre conficiantur. Cinnamomo, garyophyllis, piperéque gaueae artifices eas praeparare inuenerunt: ex auibus nullam linguam in mensarum olim honore fuisse reperio, praeterquam phoenicopteri, & anserum, quam libidinem mouere quidam tradernt.
units.tr: There are animals, and men too, that have no tongue. Pliny, in book 8, etc., attests this, and he elegantly shows in the eleventh book of the Natural History that there is also a remarkable variety of tongues. So we must inquire which are more pleasing as food. I find that pork and beef are more commended by cooks, both sometimes boiled but more often roasted and studded with cloves. In many parts of Germany beef is seasoned with salt and hung up to be kept for the year's use. Drinkers of beer or of undiluted wine find nothing more excellent for stirring thirst than this; they affirm that wine becomes clearly more pleasant to taste by eating it. Boiled sheep's tongues in vinegar are given to the feverish and to those recovering their health. Moreover, if they are properly prepared and digested in the stomach, they yield a good juice, similar to the juice of meat. Cooks have found ways to prepare them with cinnamon, cloves, and pepper. Among birds, I find that no tongue was once held in honour at tables except that of the flamingo and of the goose, which some write stirs lust.

units.la: De glandiis,& glandulis.
units.tr: On the Glands and Glandules.

units.la: GLandia ipsas esse ceruices quidam vo-lunt, quod in his glandulæ sint : Plinio parsilla apri, in qua sunt glandulæ:quibusdam sunt vbera. Censorius olim legibus cœnas interdiciafuisse Plinius narrat. Ceterum glandulas inter salubres animalium partes, quæ in cibos veniunt, repositas reperio, alimentum q̃; si probè conficiantur, præbere vescentibus carnis naturæ proximum. Si exactè non concoquantur, duriores quæ sunt, crudum, humidiores pituitosum aggenerant succum. Præcipua autem inter hodiernas gulæ ganeaq;, cibaria mammillares glandulas laȼte refertas, præcipuam auctoritatem obtinuisse, & etiamnum obtinere video suillæ & bubulæ, vbera gulæ proceres inprimis magnificant. Assa autem elixis præstant.
units.tr: Some want the glands themselves to be the necks, because there are glandules in them; Pliny calls them the little parts of a boar in which the glands are, and for some they are udders. Pliny relates that the censor once by law forbade such dishes at dinners. Moreover, I find that the glands are placed among the wholesome parts of animals that come into food, and that, if they are properly digested, they supply nourishment close to the nature of flesh for those who eat them. If they are not thoroughly digested, the harder ones generate crude juice and the moister ones a phlegmatic juice. I see, however, that among the appetites of the present-day gluttons and banqueters, the mammary glands, filled with milk, have held and still hold the chief authority, and the nobles of the gullet especially magnify the udders of sows and cows. Roasted, moreover, they excel boiled.

units.la: De testibus.
units.tr: On the Testicles.

units.la: TEstes nitidiores in cibos raro admittunt, seminis enim virosum odorem redolent. Insalubres autem plane esse taurorum, arietum & hircorum inde constat, quod nemo elegantioris vitæ eos vnquam attigerit. De testiculis vulpis, & gallinaceis, experimento quidam compererunt, venerem languinam & desidiosam eos mirè excitare, in cibis adhibitos, Quin gallinaceos probitate alimenti præstare graves autores tradūt. Suum testiculos censoriis legibus interdictos cœnis Plin.lib.s.c.51. autor est.
units.tr: Testicles rarely admit of being more elegant as food, for they give off the rank smell of semen. That they are plainly unwholesome in bulls, rams, and he-goats is clear from the fact that no one of refined life has ever touched them. Some have discovered by experiment that the testicles of foxes and of chickens, when used as food, wonderfully arouse sluggish and languid lust. Indeed, grave authors report that the testicles of chickens are excellent for the goodness of their nourishment. Pliny, book 8, chapter 51, is the authority that the testicles of boars were forbidden at dinners by the censorian laws.

units.la: De vulua.
units.tr: On the Womb.

units.la: VLuam in animalibus interiorem fœtus conceptaculi cavitatem appellant eruditiores, quæ in homine uterus dicitur & matrix. Porro ex omnibus, suillam Romanæ gulæ proceribus in cibo placuisse, à granibus auctoribus reperitur proditum, ferculum enim ex ea conficiebant ab Apitio & Horatio celebratū, Cum sit obesō Nil melius turdo, vulua nil dulcius ampla. Tres autem erant eius differentiæ, cuius delectum Plinius indicat lib.11.c.36.his verbis. Vlua suis electo partu melior, quam edito, electitia vocatur illa, hæc porcaria. Primipara suis optima, contra effœtis. A partu, præterquam eodem die suis occisa, liuida & macra. Nec nouellarum præterquam primiperarum laudatur, potiusque veterum, dum ne effœtarum, nec biduo ante partum, aut post partum, aut quo ciecerint die. Proxima electitiæ est occiso vno die post partum, huius & sumen optimum, si modo fœtus non- hambauserit, sicitia deterrimum. Vulua vero de virgine, porca sterilis dicta, lasire Cyrenaico pipere, mentha sicca foliis, addito liquamine, mel-le & aceti modico, condita, in muria tamè prius cocta, ca eris praeferebatur, de qua Martialis,
units.tr: The more learned call the inner cavity of an animal's womb, where the foetus is held, what in a human is called the uterus or matrix. Among all foods, it is reported by serious authors that the sow's womb pleased the leaders of Roman gluttony. They made a dish of it, celebrated by Apicius and Horace: Since nothing is better than a fat thrush, nothing is sweeter than a plump womb. There were three kinds of it, and Pliny indicates the choice of them in book 11, chapter 36, in these words: "The womb of a sow is better when chosen after giving birth than when it has just been delivered. The chosen one is called electitia, the other porcaria. The first-bearing sow is the best, the barren ones the opposite. Apart from a sow killed on the day of giving birth, the womb is livid and thin. Nor are the wombs of newly-bearing sows praised, except those of first-bearers; older sows are preferred, provided they are not barren, and not two days before birth, nor after birth, nor on the day they conceived. The one nearest to electitia is that of a sow killed one day after giving birth; its udder is also very good, if only it has not suckled the young, while a dry one is the worst." But the womb of a virgin sow, called sterilis, seasoned with Cyrenaic laserwort pepper, dried mint leaves, added brine, a little honey and vinegar, and first boiled in brine, was preferred to other meats, as Martial says:

units.la: Te fortasse magis capiet de virgine porca, Me materna grauì de sue vulua capit.
units.tr: Perhaps the virgin sow's womb will please you more; but me the womb of the mother sow, heavy with young, delights.

units.la: Languidum autem ventriculum sterilem vuluam Hippitii conditurá praeparatam reficere producitum est. Celsus Cornelius lib.2.cap.14. de sue scribit, stomacho prosunt vngulae, rostra, aures, vuluae, sterilis. Vuluas quoque proincundissimo edulio olim habitas Plutarchus 8. Symp. problem. 9. inflatur. Qui nostro saeculo in mensas eas recipiant, nulli sunt aut pauci, nisi libidinis proritanda, vel etiam conceptionis iniuriandae, &c.
units.tr: It is reported that a sterile sow's womb, prepared with the seasoning of Hippitius, restores a weak stomach. Cornelius Celsus, book 2, chapter 14, writes about the pig: the trotters, snout, ears and sterile wombs are good for the stomach. Plutarch, in the eighth book of the Table Talk, problem 9, says that wombs were once esteemed a most pleasant dish, and that they were also inflated. Those who in our age admit such dishes to their tables are none or few, unless it is to arouse lust or even to hinder conception, etc.

units.la: De renibus.
units.tr: On the kidneys.

units.la: IN Brileto & Tharne Asiae regionibus cerruis quaternos renes esse Plinius commemorat lib.11.cap. 27. Vitulini aliorumque quadrupedum iuniorum, quibusdam in cibis arridemt: alias difficulter in ventriculo confici verisimile est, iniquoque & improbos succos generare, quia vrinae naturam quandam iu se receperunt, id quod foedus etiam odor manifestat, quem renes omnium aliorum viscerum maximè reddunt, corporis enim humores per eos colantur. Quare rusticis relinquantur & messoribus.
units.tr: In the regions of Brileta and Tharne in Asia, Pliny records, deer have four kidneys (book 11, chapter 27). The veal and the flesh of other young quadrupeds please some as food; otherwise it is likely that they are hard to digest in the stomach and generate bad and unwholesome juices, because they have taken on a certain nature of urine, which the foul odour also reveals, a smell that the kidneys give off more than any other viscera, since the humours of the body are strained through them. Therefore let them be left to peasants and reapers.

units.la: De iecore & liene.
units.tr: On the liver and the spleen.

units.la: TEcur cibis lautioribus non est abdicandum, habito tamen respectu animalium, quorum est proprium, natura, etatis, pabuli. Multum enim refert horum notitia. Est autem epatis caro sanguini proxima, quare optimum epar est, quod puro & sanguineo colore rubet. Porro multorum animalium iecinora medicinae potius quam culinae praestant opem, adpraeclara enim remedia magnificantur epar caprarum, aprinum, hircinum, item pisces, qui dicitur Allruppe/ huius enim epar oculis obscuris, & ex imminuta visione imbecillis miraculo mederi expertum est, ut & epar caprarum aciem oculorum restituere dicitur vespertinam kis, quos nyctalopas vocant.
units.tr: Why one should not give up the richer foods, though regard must be had to the nature, age and fodder of the animals, since each has its own. For knowledge of these matters counts for much. The flesh of the liver is closest to blood, so the best liver is the one that is reddened with a pure, bloody colour. Moreover, the livers of many animals offer medicine rather than cookery: the liver of goats, of the wild boar and of the he-goat is extolled as a notable remedy, as are fish called Allruppe. For the liver of the last is known by experience to cure those with dim eyes and weak sight from failing vision, as if by a miracle. And the liver of goats is said to restore keenness of sight in the evening to those whom they call nyctalopes.

units.la: In cibis vero sapore salubritateque commendari reperio apud autores non proletarias epar gallinarum & gallinaceorum, anserum, suum, vitulorum, raia, piscium, qui dicitur Allruppe. Suillum tum graecis, tum Romanis in laudibus ciborum fuit.
units.tr: In food, however, I find in authors that the liver of hens and cocks, of geese, pigs, calves, skate and the fish called Allruppe is commended for flavour and wholesomeness, and is not vulgar. Pig's liver was praised as a food by both Greeks and Romans.

units.la: Inuper
units.tr: Moreover.

units.la: Inuentum Apitii esse Plinius voluit caricâ saginare sues fœminas, eâsque a satietate necare repente potius mulsi dato. Galenus hac fagina configit, multo iucundius iecur esse, aliisque dotibus ac virtutibus ceteris præferri debere. Inseruerum iecoribus quantam curam veteres Romani adhibuerint, infra, vbi de anseribus dictum est, annotauimus.
units.tr: Pliny holds that the invention belongs to Apicius: to fatten sows with figs and to kill them suddenly from surfeit by giving them mulled wine. Galen, who condemns this gluttony, says that the liver is much more pleasant and ought to be preferred to others for its other qualities and virtues. How much care the ancient Romans gave to livers we have noted below, where we spoke of geese.

units.la: Fartilibus enim in magnam crescere amplitudinem, exemptaque latte augeri & mulso, Scipio, Metellus vir consularis, & Seffius eques Romanus inuenisse dicuntur. Non obscurum enim esse oportuit huius ganeæ inuentionem. Vitulinum in cibis, multis gratissimum est, garyophyllis id confixum assant, eduntque ex intinctu quodam nigro & pradulci, quod vino, aceto, pipere, saccharoque, velin defectu huius, melle, temperatur.
units.tr: For Scipio, Metellus, a consular man, and Seius, a Roman knight, are said to have invented the fattening of sows to a great size, by taking them from milk and enlarging them with mulsum. For the invention of this gluttony ought not to be obscure. Veal is very pleasing to many as food. They roast it pierced with cloves and eat it with a black and very sweet dip, which is seasoned with wine, vinegar, pepper and sugar, or, if there is none of these, with honey.

units.la: Eodemque modo & pulmones, lienesque præparari possunt, eparitem veruecinum, bubalum & ouillum, quæ tamen vulgo peculiariter edunter in sartagine fixa, vel etiam elixa frustulatimque concisa, cum pipere & butyro, esuque hoc edulium non insuave, nec insalubre.
units.tr: In the same way lungs and spleens can be prepared, and the liver of the ram, the buffalo and the sheep. These are commonly eaten in a particular way, fried in a pan, or boiled and cut into small pieces, with pepper and butter. This dish is not unpleasant, nor unwholesome.

units.la: Raia epar ganeæ artifices in summo honore habent, elixum id ex aceto piperato editur plerunque, communiter frigitur in sartagine. Aliorum animalium iecinora crassi esse succi concoctuque pertinacia, ac difficulter permapermeare ventrem, dubium nullum est. Qui indistinctè hæc de omnibus pronunciant, errant, naturæ rerum causarumq; imperiti. Nobile apud quosdam prouerbium est, iecinora suita: a vescentium iecinora exhilarare, similia enim si-milibus delectari, conseruariq;. Tabe nam q pulmonis laborantes pulmo humanus, tabe re-num, renes humani ob substantiam similitudinem, restituunt. Atrophia igitur perire malle, vel pla-ne contabescere, quam appropriatum remedium adhibere, est vitam sibi ipsi abbreuiare. Multis paradoxon videbitur, hominis pulmones tabidi auxiliari, caliditatemq; habitualem & hesti-am prepedire. Sed expedimentum cuiq; libe-rum est.
units.tr: Cooks hold the liver of skate in the highest esteem; it is usually eaten boiled in peppered vinegar, or commonly fried in a pan. There is no doubt that the livers of other animals are thick in juice, slow to digest, and pass with difficulty through the bowel. Those who pronounce this of all such livers without distinction are wrong, being ignorant of the nature of things and their causes. Among some there is a well-known proverb that pig's livers cheer those who eat the livers, since like delights in like and is preserved by it. For those suffering from wasting of the lungs, the human lung restores; for those wasting in the kidneys, human kidneys do so, because of the likeness of their substance. So to prefer to die of atrophy, or to waste away altogether, rather than apply the appropriate remedy, is to shorten one's own life. To many it will seem a paradox that the lungs of a man should help the consumptive and prevent the habitual heat and the hectic fever. But each is free to make his own trial.

units.la: Experiantur tabidi, senes, & marasmo seu marcore aridi, comperient natiuam sibi hu-miditatem iis reparari ac restitui, quod anno-tasse hic opera pretium duxi.
units.tr: Let the consumptive, the old, and those dried up by marasmus or decay try it; they will find that their natural moisture is repaired and restored by these, which I thought worth noting here.

units.la: Lienis carnes rariores, suauiores, leuio-resq; esse quam epatis constat, sanguis tamen minus rubicundus, melancholico enim succo nutritur, unde ad carnis huius speciem ad por-tionem alentis se habebit succi.
units.tr: It is agreed that the flesh of the spleen is looser, sweeter and lighter than that of the liver. Yet its blood is less red, for it is nourished by melancholy juice, so that in the appearance of this flesh it will correspond to the nature of the juice that nourishes it.

units.la: Itaque quo is improbior est, faeculentior & crassior, tanto carnem ipsam deteriorem esse ve-risimile est. Porro liene vitulì, sicut & bubalum recentem assum velelixum in cibo ad splenis dolores praesentaneum esse remedium quidam tradiderunt. Vrsorum, Luporum, Leonum, Pantherarum, & similium lienes esculentos non esse inde confiat, quod, qui horum animalium carnibus vescuntur homines, iis abstineant.
units.tr: So the more wicked it is, the murkier and thicker, the more likely it is that the flesh itself is worse. Moreover, some have taught that the spleen of a calf, like that of a buffalo, fresh, roasted or boiled, is an immediate remedy for pains of the spleen when eaten. That the spleens of bears, wolves, lions, panthers and similar animals are not fit to eat is clear from this: men who eat the flesh of these animals abstain from those parts.

units.la: De Pulmone.
units.tr: On the lung.

units.la: DIfferentiae Pulmonum variae sunt, pro sanguinis, quo pulmo alitur, diuersa constitutione; Carnem habet laxissimam & levissimam, quasi ex spuma quadam coagulatam, alitur enim sanguine ad vnguem elaborato, flavo, tenui, puro, spiritali, ad alentis igitur succi naturam se accommodat. In cibis certum est, tanto facilius jecore & splene perfici, quanto utroque est rarior, tantoque magis vires reficere & spiritus reparare, quanto puriore & tenuiore sanguine. Suilli autem pulmones magis commendantur, habenturque in delitiis: bubali & vervecini inter populares cibos referuntur. Assi quoque & a jejunis praesumpti, eo die ebrietatem arcere dicuntur. Sed hoc miratu & cognitu dignum, quod a Plutarcho de ficubus scribitur, qui in caulis naturalibus tradit Mnesitheum medicum a Galeno in Proemio libri ad Mm ʃ glauc.commendatum narrasse, eos qui in principio pulmonariæ morbi cepas appetunt seruari, qui vero ficus, interire, ideo, quia appetitus temperaturas, temperaturæ autem morbos consequuntur. Galenus 7.de alim. facult. ait, pulmone jecorem conco-ctu esse faciliorem, minus nutrire, pituito-sumque magis succum facere. At 6.de vsu partium cap.10,tradit,pulmonem tenui,levi & vaporoso nutriri sanguine, jecur vero li-moso & crasso.
units.tr: The lungs differ, according to the different constitution of the blood by which the lung is nourished. Its flesh is very loose and light, as if coagulated from a kind of foam, for it is fed by blood worked to a nicety, yellow, thin, pure and spirituous; it therefore adapts itself to the nature of the juice that nourishes it. As food it is certain that it is digested more easily than liver or spleen, in proportion as it is lighter than either, and it restores strength and repairs the spirits the more, the purer and thinner the blood. Pigs' lungs are more highly commended and are held in delight; buffalo and sheep lungs are counted among common foods. Roasted, and eaten by those who are fasting, they are said to ward off drunkenness on that day. But this is worthy of wonder and of knowledge: Plutarch, in his Natural Questions, on figs, writes that the physician Mnesitheus, commended by Galen in the preface to his book to Glaucon, related that those who in the beginning of a pulmonary disease crave onions are saved, but those who crave figs perish, because appetites follow temperaments, and temperaments in turn follow diseases. Galen, in book 7 of On the Powers of Foods, says that the liver is easier to digest than the lung, nourishes less, and makes more phlegmatic juice. But in book 6 of On the Use of the Parts, chapter 10, he teaches that the lung is nourished by thin, light and vaporous blood, and the liver by muddy and thick blood.

units.la: Unde si tale est nutrimentum, qualis est substantia nutrientis, videtur substantia pulmonis, vt est jecore tenuior, sic succum tenuiorem parere non pituitosiorem. Ætius lib.c.127. hanc dubitationem tollit, dicens pulmonis nutrimentum esse magis pituito-sum ob cartilagineum, sc. asperæ arteriæ pul-moni inexistenti corpus perpetuo madore scatens.
units.tr: Hence, if the nourishment is of the same kind as the substance that nourishes, it seems that the substance of the lung, being thinner than that of the liver, should produce a thinner juice, not a more phlegmatic one. Aetius, in book 1, chapter 127, removes this doubt, saying that the nourishment of the lung is more phlegmatic because of its cartilaginous nature, namely the body of the windpipe, which is in the lung and is always swimming in moisture.

units.la: Ad extremum monitum vitæ prorogandæ studiosum hic velim, epata, lienes & pulmones in pecudibus macatis non raro vitiata & infecta videri, quæ postea mandu-cata non leue vitæ periculum attulisse experientia satis comprobauit, & etiamnunc co-probat. Itaque vitæ ejusmodi insidiæ caute euitentur.
units.tr: Finally, I would here advise those who are eager to prolong life that livers, spleens and lungs of lean beasts are often seen to be diseased and tainted. Experience has sufficiently proved, and still proves, that when these are eaten afterwards they have brought no small danger to life. Such snares against life should therefore be carefully avoided.

units.la: De Corde.
units.tr: On the Heart.

units.la: SYmbolo Pythagorico iubebatur, cor non edendum. Et elegantioris vitae homines raro in cibos corda admittunt, quia ex fibris multiplicibus contexta sunt, carnemq; habent duram, spissam, agreq; alterabilem. Exaëtè tamen elaboratu alimentum validum praestare, minimeq; iniquum succi nullum est dubium. Caterum ventriculum frigidum & flaccidum, cibosq; retinere non valentem, animalium quorundam corda, ut vituli, leporis, cervi, suumq;, ex avibus vero, cornicis gallinarum, phasianorum, turdorum, & similium, leviter ex butyro modicoq; aceti assa garyophyllisq; confixa, corroborare ac fovere novis experimentis parefactum est, quod reticere hic nolui. Neq; enim decet posterorum commodis consulturum, in scribendo velpratermittere necessaria scitu & utilia, vel ad caligine involutam doctrinam, inextricabilisq; perplexitatem lectorem in vitare.
units.tr: By the Pythagorean maxim, the heart was not to be eaten. Also, people of more refined habits rarely admit hearts into their food, because they are woven from many fibres, have a hard, dense flesh, and are difficult to digest. Yet it is beyond doubt that, prepared with care, they provide a strong nourishment and no unpleasant juice at all. For a cold and flabby stomach that cannot hold food, the hearts of certain animals, such as calves, hares, deer and pigs, and among birds of hens, crows, pheasants, thrushes and the like, have been shown by new experiments to strengthen and warm it when lightly fried in butter with a little vinegar and pierced with cloves. I did not wish to pass this over in silence. For it is not fitting for one who writes for the benefit of posterity either to omit what is necessary and useful to know, or to leave the reader entangled in a doctrine wrapped in darkness and inextricable confusion.

units.la: De Ventribus,
units.tr: On Stomachs.

units.la: VEntres animalium, qui in cibos honorum veniunt, nec magnitudine ventrib. nec specie inter se similes sunt & vide io. quibusdam sunt multiplices, vt cornigeris, Bruer. de quibusdam, vt in auium genere gallinae re cibat. sunt, l. 12. 9. 2. sunt, anseres &c. validum, praedurum & carnosum quid vice illius partis, quae cibum recipit, obtinuerunt, quin & ingluviem quandam habent, in quam cibum recentem & inconfectum recondunt, sed in cibos non venit. Porro si exacte ventres perficiuntur, quod longiori fit tempore, succum pariunt, nec sanguineum, nec inculpatum, gelidum tamen & pituitosum. Qui validos habent ventriculos, laborosque validos aggressuri sunt, minus noxie iis vescuntur. De intestinis idem sit judicium, hoc tamen interest, quod citius conficiantur, & cum pinguedine sua plus nutriant, sine tamen pane, saleq; sufficiente deglutita insigniter noxia deprehenduntur, cogitur enim & concrescit pinguedo in ventriculo, tunicisque ejus adhaerescit.
units.tr: The stomachs of animals that come to the table are not alike in size or appearance, and see John. Some are many-chambered, as in horned animals, Bruer [?] ... on some, as among birds the hen ... [l. 12. 9. 2.] ... geese, etc. They have taken on the role of that part which receives food a strong, very hard and fleshy substance, and indeed some have a kind of crop, in which they store fresh and undigested food, but this does not go into food. Moreover, if stomachs are cooked thoroughly, which takes a longer time, they yield a juice that is neither bloody nor blameless, but cold and phlegmatic. Those who have strong stomachs and are about to undertake hard labour eat them with less harm. The same judgement holds for intestines, except that they are digested more quickly and, with their fat, nourish more. Yet if they are swallowed without bread and sufficient salt, they are found to be remarkably harmful, for the fat gathers and congeals in the stomach and clings to its coats.

units.la: De pedibus, auribus, rostro.
units.tr: On feet, ears and snout.

units.la: Ubalos, vitulinos, vervecinos, haedinos, ovillos, pedes & suillos, in cibis frequentius vsurpari video, multiplici ratione a cuiuspraeparari, sed interdum non sine noxa. In pedibus ovillis anterioribus & posterioribus, parte quaterra calcant vermiculos inhaerere sub rotunda forma, lanuginosa intus & crinita contingere implicitos, experientia & observatio testis est, qui, si ex incuria huius rei ignorantia, cum cum concretione illa, exemti nonfuerint, edenti ovillos illos pedes confestim nauseam stomachiq; cruciatum excitabunt cum ructu & vomitione. Verisimile enim est venenosum quiddam subesse capillata huic congeriei, quod cottioni obsit. Vide Lemn. l. 3. cap. 5. Caeterum aures suilla, rostrum, & pedes in summo honore mensarum sunt, hi tamen illo praestant, hoc vero cruribus. Vervecinos quidam aqua incoctos ex alceto mandunt, apio virente asperso. quandoq; frigunt, prunisq; torrent: bubalos elixos exacte quidam frigunt: sed male, quia humiditatem nutrimentalem plane eliciunt.
units.tr: I see that buffalo, calves', sheep's, kids', lambs' and pigs' feet are more often used as food, prepared in many ways by various cooks, but sometimes not without harm. Experience and observation bear witness that in the forefeet and hindfeet of sheep, in the part where they tread, small worms cling in a round form, woolly and hairy within, and become entangled in the flesh; if these are not removed through carelessness or ignorance of this matter, together with that clotted mass, those who eat such sheep's feet will at once be seized with nausea, stomach pain, belching and vomiting. For it is likely that some poisonous matter lies in this hairy mass, which harms the digestion. See Lemnius, book 3, chapter 5. Moreover, pigs' ears, snouts and feet are held in the highest honour at table, though the ears excel the others, and the feet excel in the legs. Some boil sheep's feet in water and eat them with vinegar, sprinkled with fresh celery; sometimes they fry them or roast them over embers. Some fry buffalo boiled thoroughly, but badly, because they draw out all the nourishing moisture.

units.la: Commendant etiam vitulinos elixos piperis & croci condimento addito: suilli cratitula assantur, & ex coepis concisis aceto, aspersis sumuntur. Aures suillas ex garo, veteres aceto, & sinapi edendas voluerunt, vel ex garo oleoq; affuso vino. Hodie culina ganeaq; artifices pro variis praeparationis principatu certant. Anserini pedes, omniumq; fere Planipedum, quod omittere nefas fere duxerim, succi suavitate, elixi praestant multis aliis, cumprimis vero in palati delitiis est membrana illa, quā interveniente, vngues conjunguntur.
units.tr: Calves' feet boiled with the addition of pepper and saffron are also commended. Pigs' trotters are roasted on the gridiron, and taken sprinkled with chopped onions and vinegar. The ancients preferred pigs' ears to be eaten with brine, vinegar and mustard, or with brine and oil poured over wine. Today cooks and gluttons compete for the first place in various preparations. The feet of geese, and of nearly all web-footed birds, which I would almost count it wrong to omit, are excellent boiled, for the sweetness of their juice surpasses many others; and especially among the delights of the palate is that membrane by which the toes are joined together.

units.la: De
units.tr: On

units.la: De cerebro, adipe, ossium medul-la, sanguine.
units.tr: On the brain, fat, marrow of the bones, and blood.

units.la: EX medullarum genere existere cerebrum Galenus 2. de temperamentis, & 2. de vsu part. scripsit. Cujus quoque sententiae videtur fuisse Plato in Timaeo, vbi medullae morbum omnium periculosissimum esse scriptum reliquit, sub medullae nomine cerebrum intelligens, non spinalem medullam, vt aliqui putant, vel alias medullas, quod verba Platonis ostendunt. Vide Mercurial. variar. lect. lib. 1. c. 9. Caeterum cerebra animalium, tempore Plutarchi mandari coepisse, quae tamen antiquitas abominata projecerit, idem affirmat f. Symp. probl. 9. Hodie inter praecipuas epulas quaedam reponi video, praecipue vero vitulorum, haedorum, leporum, suum, quin & auium multarum atque piscium. Inter damnatos autem cibos a grauibus autoribus cerebra collocari reperio, ob naturam pituitosiorem, difficilemque concoctionem, tum etiam, quod stomacho aduersentur, fastidiumque afferant. Unde Galenus postremo cibo cerebrum pinguiter conditum vomitu indigentibus exhibendum suadet, sic enim faciliorem fore vomitionem.
