Coquuntur multis modis, elixantur interdum, quandoque friguntur, vel carbonibus assantur. Suillum marasmo tabefcentibus vtile esse Galenus affirmat, sed vel diligenter aflum, vel in albo jure legiti-me elixum, porro & anetho injectis. Crudum devoratum laedit summopere, vt & omnium aliorum animantium. Leporis ad tremores membrorum magnificari video, sicut cuniculorum in confessa damnatione reperio, quoniam memoriae, officere creditur: Cerebrum cerebro, epar epate recrea-ri Averrhoiftarum procul dubio placitum fuit.
units.tr: Galen wrote in his 2. de temperamentis and 2. de vsu part. that the brain comes from the kind of marrow. Plato also seems to have held this view in the Timaeus, where he left it written that a disease of the marrow is the most dangerous of all, understanding by "marrow" the brain, not the spinal marrow, as some think, or other marrows; Plato's own words show this. See Mercurialis, variar. lect. lib. 1. c. 9. Plutarch, moreover, affirms that in his time the brains of animals had begun to be served at table, though antiquity had abhorred them and cast them away; see f. Symp. probl. 9. Today I see that certain brains are set out among the chief delicacies, especially those of calves, kids, hares and pigs, and indeed of many birds and fish. But I find that serious authors place brains among the foods to be condemned, because of their phlegmy nature and difficult digestion, and also because they are opposed to the stomach and cause loathing. Hence Galen, as a last resort, advises that brain, seasoned richly, be given to those in need of vomiting, for in this way vomiting will be easier. They are cooked in many ways: boiled at times, sometimes fried, or roasted over coals. Galen states that pig's brain is useful for those wasting away with marasmus, provided it is carefully boiled, either in white broth properly seasoned, or with dill added. Eaten raw, it harms greatly, as does that of all other animals. I see hare's brain praised for trembling of the limbs, and I find rabbit's brain in the recognised list of condemned foods, since it is believed to impair the memory. That brain restores brain, and liver restores liver, was without doubt the opinion of the Averroists.

units.la: Avium cerebrum tanto quadrupedum praestantius est, quanto durius. Vitellius cerebella phasianorum & pauonum apposuit, in passim illa sua ab autoribus celebrata patina.
units.tr: The brain of birds is as much more excellent than that of quadrupeds as it is harder. Vitellius put pheasant and peacock brains on his dishes, those famous dishes of his celebrated by many authors.

units.la: Concretis quosdam ossibus, ac fine medullis viuere Plinius autor est, signumque eorum esse, nec sitim sentire, nec fodorem emittere. Caeterum, quoniam medulla aliment est sanguinei in offa spinamque dorsi distributi, dulcis, pinguis, mollis, & humida, extra dubium est, eam probe ac valenter alequin & tabidis membris foris & intus auxiliari, quod multis documentis patefactum est: In exemplis nostris est paupercula, quaedam mulier, fi recte memini, Lipfica, cui integrum & ultra annum bacillo innixae & ex cruribus tabescentibus claudicanti, Medici illius loci, publicam tunc anatomen exerexercentes, portrexerunt tibiam, vt hujus medulla ad ignem crura tabida inungeret: Illa protinus, certa fiducia ducta, accenso igne, medullam liquefactam & extillantem vasculo excipiens, partim cruribus perunxit, partim, quod tamen Medici non praecepe-rant, in ventrem absumpsit: vnde postridie ejus diei, recuperato & integrato gradu, Medicis, gratias actura, quaerentibus, quanam ratione tibiae medullam adhibuisset, omnia exposuit, sicque quasi miraculo fuit restituta.
units.tr: Pliny is the authority that some men live on solid bones without marrow, and that the sign of this is that they feel neither thirst nor hunger. But since marrow, sweet, fatty, soft and moist, is the nourishment of the blood distributed into the bones and the spine of the back, it is beyond doubt that it helps weak limbs, both outwardly and inwardly, as has been shown by many proofs. In our own examples there is a poor woman, from Leipzig, if I remember rightly, who had walked for more than a year leaning on a stick, limping on wasting legs. The doctors of that place, then conducting a public dissection, brought out a shin-bone so that its marrow might be rubbed by the fire onto her wasting legs. At once, led by sure confidence, she kindled a fire, caught the melted and dripping marrow in a little vessel, and anointed her legs with part of it, and part, which the doctors had not prescribed, she swallowed. Therefore the next day, having recovered and regained her gait, she came to thank the doctors, who asked by what means she had used the shin-marrow; she explained everything, and so she was restored, as if by a miracle.

units.la: Caeterum bubalorum medullam suauissimum condimentum esse ad olera pinguefacienda, quin & tosti panis frustis eam cum sale illinere, procerum & delicatorum gula experta est. Laudatissima tamen medullarum Plinio teste, est cervina, mox vitulina, hircina & caprina. emolliunt omnes ac excalfaciunt, explentq;.
units.tr: Moreover, the taste of the great and the refined has found that buffalo marrow is a most pleasant seasoning for fattening vegetables, and that it is spread with salt on pieces of toasted bread. Yet, according to Pliny, the most praised marrows are those of the deer, then of the calf, the goat and the kid. All of them soften and warm, and they fill.

units.la: Adeps, & pinguedo licet inter se differant, confundi tamen vtramque quandoq;, alterumque pro altero poni testatur Galen. 11. de simplicibus medicamen. Idem tamen ibidem distinguit, quod pinguedo humidioribus animantibus, vt suibus, proveniat, celeriterque ad ignem colliquescat, nec semel liquata, rursus facile concrescat: Adeps vero crassior fit, non facile fundatur & liquescat, liquatus celerrime congeletur. A renibus autem detractus adeps omnis laudatissimus est, antiqui enim medici eum maxime probarunt, Plinio teste l. 20. cap. 9. Caeterum ex Aristotelis sententia dicentis, adipem & pinguedinem esse sanguinem concoctum, item ex sanguinis percoctione adipem gigni, facile explodituri illorum placitum, qui volunt, omnem pinguedinem absolute esse malam, piscium vero peffimam, pinguedinemque ex alimentorum censu proscribunt. Alimenti enim, & condimenti simul, vt & medicamenti vicem praestant pinguedo, & adeps. Pinguedo quo oleosior & humidior, eo sa- lubrior, quo crassior & ficcior, eo insalubri- or praesertim largius si fumatur: Illa enim igneam, aeriamque naturam participat, intraque corpus sumta, corpus ab occursu malorum vaporum venenatorumque praesertim vt immune, permeare enim illos non finit in intimos corporis meatus, praesertim vero hoc praestat jus capi pingue, huic enim pinguedo supernatans inducit pelliculam, quae noxiis halitibus, vna cum cibo vel potu in ventrem exceptis, fortiter resistit, quod pinguia crassior & ficcior praestare nequit. Unum hic occurrit, quod memoria dignissimum vinilar est, videl. pinguia, vini vel zythi liberalius hausti vapores reprimere, eorumque evapo-ratione in cerebrum prohibere, quod iis, qui facile ex vini potu inebriantur, capiteq; rare non N a postea sinunt. postea vexantur, obseruandum prꝳcipitur: & hoc ita se habere vel inde patet,quod ole-um vino aut aquis odoratis affusum exhala-re eorum odores non finit, humori enim subjecto pelliculam inducit, per quam sub-ditus humor evaporare non potest : Sic raphanus cum oleo commestus, eructatio-nes ventriculi, quas alias solet, ciere non potest. Probè igitur faciunt Westphaliæ populi, dum cerevsiam tepide cum butyro, vel oleo affuso jejuno stomacho bibunt, sic enim eo die à veneno se reddunt saluos.
units.tr: Fat (adeps) and suet (pinguedo), though they differ from each other, are sometimes confused, and one is put for the other, as Galen testifies in his 11. de simplicibus medicamen. Yet he distinguishes in the same place that suet arises in moister animals, such as pigs, and quickly melts at the fire, and once melted does not easily set again; fat, however, becomes thicker, does not readily pour out and liquefy, and when melted congeals very quickly. Moreover, fat drawn from the kidneys is wholly the most praised, for the ancient physicians especially approved it, as Pliny testifies in l. 20. cap. 9. Furthermore, the opinion of those who want all suet to be absolutely bad, and fish-suet worst of all, and who banish suet from the category of foods, I would readily refute from the saying of Aristotle that fat and suet are blood concocted, and that fat is produced by the boiling of blood. For suet and fat serve as food and seasoning together, and also as a kind of medicine. The more oily and moist the suet, the more wholesome it is; the thicker and drier, the less wholesome, especially if eaten in larger quantity. For the former shares a fiery and airy nature, and once taken into the body it protects the body especially from the onslaught of harmful vapours and poisons, for it does not allow them to pass into the innermost passages of the body. Especially this benefit comes from fat broth, for the fat floating on top forms a thin film which strongly resists the noxious exhalations taken into the stomach with food or drink, something that thicker and drier fat cannot do. One point here seems worth remembering: fats restrain the vapours of wine or beer drunk too freely, and prevent their evaporation into the brain; this should be observed by those who are easily made drunk by drinking wine and who are afterwards troubled with headaches. That this is so is clear from the fact that oil poured on wine or scented waters does not let their odours escape, for it spreads a film over the liquid beneath, through which the liquid below cannot evaporate. Thus radish eaten with oil cannot produce the belchings of the stomach that it usually causes. The peoples of Westphalia therefore act wisely when they drink beer lukewarm, with butter or oil poured in, on an empty stomach; for in this way they keep themselves safe from poison on that day.

units.la: Esse hæmapotas, qui sanguinem & quidem humanum exipso homine calidum adhuc sorbeant cap.14. ostensum est. Anigi-tur & qualis in cibum sit assumendus, nunc inquirendum. Sanguinem (de humano lo-quar) omnibus humoribus natura esse tem-peratiorem, humanæqué temperaturæ sami-liariorem, nutrimenti totius corporis auto-rem, humorem benignum, dilestum filium naturæ, succum naturæ familiarissimum, quem natura semper in superpurgationibus ad extremum tanquam pretiosissimum thea-saurum conseruet atque custodiat, omnes quotquot aut sunt aut extiterunt Philoso-phi & Medici, vno ore professi sunt. Proin de recte Marsilius Ficinus l. 1. c. 2. è Medico templationem, qualis est sensus, talisq; se-
units.tr: That there are blood-drinkers, who swallow blood, and human blood indeed, still warm from the man himself, has been shown in chapter 14. Now it must be inquired what sort of blood is to be taken as food. Concerning human blood, I speak thus: all who are or have been philosophers and physicians have professed with one voice that blood is by nature the most tempered of all humours, most akin to the human temperament, the author of all the nourishment of the body, a gentle humour, the beloved son of nature, the juice most familiar to nature, which nature always keeps and guards, as her most precious treasure, to the last, through all the superpurgations. Hence Marsilio Ficino rightly says in book 1, chapter 2, that from the physician's point of view, such as the blood is, such is the sense perception.

units.la: {a} Super-purgatio hyper-eatharti-ca sanguinis violenter per-gantia. sus, qualis sanguis: quæ sententia hanc habet rationem, quia ex cibo fit sanguis, talis igitur fuerit sanguis, qualis cibus fuit, necesse est, & quia sanguis in ferui t spiritui, spiritus sen- sibus, sensus rationi & intellectui, requiritur sanguine existente impuro, spiritum turbari, sensus obtundi, rationemque stupe- fieri. Ratio evidentiæ. Sanguinis enim tenuissima pars in cordis fluit fontem, ubi facultas viget vitalis, indeque generati spiritus in cerebri arcem ascendunt, in qui- bus sententiæ mouendique virtus dominatur. Nam vigente spiritu viget motus & sensus. Cacochyma igitur, difficilisque concoctionis alimenta in sublimium rerum contemplatione versatur, iuncta vitanda, crassum enim & prauum sanguinem, unde spiritus turbidi & tenebricosi generant. Qui labo- riosum & negotiosum vitæ genus, sufcepe- runt, peregrinationesque; subito coguntur, du- rioribus cibis uti interdum non inconsultum est. Sed ad rem.
units.tr: {a} Hyper-cathartic superpurgation of the blood, violently overflowing. This opinion has the following reasoning: since blood comes from food, the blood must necessarily be of the kind the food was; and since spirit is kindled by the blood, the senses by the spirit, and reason and intellect by the senses, if the blood is impure, the spirit is disturbed, the senses dulled, and reason stupefied. The reasoning is evident. For the finest part of the blood flows to the fountain of the heart, where the vital faculty flourishes, and from there the generated spirits rise to the citadel of the brain, where the power of thought and of motion rules. For when the spirit is vigorous, motion and sense are vigorous. Therefore foods that are cacochymous, hard to digest, should be avoided by those who are engaged in the contemplation of lofty things, for they produce thick and bad blood, whence the spirits become turbid and gloomy. Those who have undertaken a laborious and busy way of life, and are suddenly forced into travel, it is not unwise sometimes to use harder foods. But to the matter.

units.la: Cæterum in cibos lautiorum sanguinem præcipue leporinum, qui Galeni judicio de alimentis facultatibus, quauis fit us- que, quia ad farcimina expetitur, hædorum, item vervecū & agnorum admitti, notū est: cæterorum animalium raro aut nunquam elegantioris vitæ homines attingunt, nisi sanguinem hirci, caprarū, vel cerui in tartagine nutrimento torquent.
units.tr: Moreover, it is well known that the blood of the hare is especially admitted into the food of the more refined, which, in Galen's judgement on the faculties of foods, is wholesome, however it is prepared, because it is sought for stuffings; likewise that of kids, sheep and lambs. Men of more elegant life seldom or never touch the blood of other animals, except that they twist the blood of the he-goat, she-goat or stag into a tart-like nourishment.

units.la: Na tostum aduersus calculum, dysenteriam & toxica.
units.tr: For roasted blood is good against the stone, dysentery and poisons.

units.la: Taurorum & aprorum fibris refertior est, & quia taurorum sanguis celerrime coit, & durefcit, inter pstifera recens, præsertim habitus est potus. Hircorū tanta vis prædicatur, vt ferramentorum subtilitas non aliter acrius induretur, scabritia tollatur vehementius, quam lima. Quin & inuicta illa vis adamantis, rerum violentissimarum ferri & ignis contemtrix, hircino sanguine rumpitur calido ac recenti. Unde remediis aduersus calculum recte admiscent medici.
units.tr: Bulls' and boars' blood is richer in fibrous matter, and because bulls' blood clots very quickly and hardens, it is considered most suitable when taken fresh as a drink. Goats' blood is said to have such power that the edge of iron tools is hardened no more sharply, and their roughness is removed no more vigorously, than by a file. Indeed, adamant, that invincible substance which defies the most violent forces of iron and fire, is broken by warm, fresh goat's blood. For this reason physicians rightly mix it into remedies against the stone.

units.la: Caprinum celebrauit Homerus: gallinarum quoque & columbarum, & potissimum saginatarum à quibusdam edi compe- rio, qui tum suauitate, tum coctionis facilitate eum commendant: Leporinus cum iecore caeterisque visceribus elixatur. Quocumque autem modo præparaueris sanguinem, inuenies eam vtplurimū concoctioni contumacem esse & excrementosum. Turturum sanguinis tribus guttis puero exhibitis, epileptico auxiliari, experimentis indubitatis præfactum est: Vulnerandus autem leuiter alter pes est, sanguisque excipiendus. Non conticendum, Hippocratem negare sanguinem esse calidum contra omnium opinionem, rationem affert hanc, quod in animali mortuo calorem non reti-neat, neat,calidum vero euadere, quod calorem à corde tanquam fonte & foco caloris mutuetur, spirituumque beneficio, qui calorem communione quadam sanguini impertit. Graui ssimi autoris grauis sententia,& vera, qua quidem omnis sanguis cibo abdicandus venit, præcipuè vero, ex quo farcimina concinnantur, probatur. Constat san- guinem extra sua vasa effusum atque emis- sum coagulari & putrescere,quod indubita- tum est: Si igitur aliena tantum & non propria etiam caliditate calet, vt Hippocra- tes vult, extra vero vasa emissus statim putre- scit, quid quæso aliud est, ex quo hodie far- cimina conflantur, quam quoddam cadauer, sanguisque putridus spiritu & calore desti- tutus: is verò in alimoniam corporis nostri magna cum auiditate expetitur, animalis, magis famis sedandæ, quam naturalis gratiâ, quâ quodlibet membrum sibi amicum ac familiare ad se trahit alimentum, inimicum vero aversatur, verum, qua salubritate, iis judicandum relinquo, qui sanguineis istis farciminibus solis, ventrem probe expleve-runt. Quid alimoniæ sit in his, nitidiores ventres nondum experiri potuerunt. Sed plura de hoc paradoxo alio loco.
units.tr: Homer praised goat's blood. Some also eat the blood of hens and pigeons, especially of fattened birds, and commend it for both its sweetness and its ease of digestion. Hare's blood is boiled together with the liver and other entrails. However you prepare blood, you will find it for the most part resistant to digestion and full of excrement. It has been established by undoubted experiments that three drops of turtle-dove blood given to a boy help an epileptic. The other foot, however, is to be lightly wounded and the blood collected. We must not pass over the fact that Hippocrates, contrary to everyone's opinion, denies that blood is warm. His reason is that in a dead animal blood does not retain its heat, but becomes warm because it borrows heat from the heart, as from the source and hearth of heat, and through the agency of the spirits, which impart heat to the blood by a certain communion. The weighty opinion of so grave an author is true, and it proves that all blood should be excluded from food, especially that from which sausages are made. It is established that blood poured out and discharged from its vessels coagulates and putrefies, which is beyond doubt. If, then, blood is warm only by an alien heat and not by its own, as Hippocrates maintains, and once it is discharged from the vessels it putrefies at once, then what, I ask, is that from which sausages are made today, other than a kind of corpse, and putrid blood destitute of spirit and heat? Yet this is sought with great eagerness as nourishment for our body, more to appease hunger as an animal would, than by that natural grace by which each member draws to itself the nourishment that is friendly and familiar, and turns away from what is hostile. As to how wholesome it is, I leave that to those who have filled their bellies well on these blood sausages alone. Cleaner bellies have not yet been able to experience what nourishment there is in them. But more on this paradox elsewhere.

units.la: Adhuc de alimentis, quæ veniunt in cibos humanos ex partibus animalium quorundam: sequuntur ordine alimenta earum rerum, quae ab animalibus proveniunt, ut sunt, lac, ova, mel.
units.tr: Next, concerning foods that come into human diet from the parts of certain animals. In order, follow the foods derived from animals themselves, such as milk, eggs and honey.

units.la: CAP. XX. De Lacte memorabilia.
units.tr: CAP. XX. On the Memorable Properties of Milk.

units.la: Lacte plurasq; vixisse gentes, & hodie quoq; viuere, in confessio est. Gethas, Scythas, Nomadas, omnesq; eius tractus, galactophagos, hoc est, lac edentes, alios galactopotas, hoe est, lactis potores, vocatos, Homerus retulit. Nomadas cynocephalorum lacte viuere Plinius l. 6. cap. 30. prodidit. Nostra memoria satis constat, Belgas, & non paucas septentrionis gentes lactiitiniis nihil fere habere in cibis frequentius, ac multa praclara opera lactaria conficere. Et certe mitis, humana nitidaque vita, abfq; operis lacteis vsu, nulla dicenda est. Quis ignorat, lac, caseum, & butyrum non rura solum saturare, sed etiam urbium, & nobilitatis elegantiores mensas jucundis & numerosis dapibus exornare. Quare bruti prorsus stupidi scio didicq; palati sunt, qui lactis vsum interdicunt. Verum, quoniam varia sunt pro diuersorum animantium temperatura & natura, tum etiam pabuli alimentiq; varietate, lactis differentia, diligenter inquirendum, quodnam lac optimum, maxime nutriat, tum quibus prosit, vel obsit, & quo tempore magis conueniat.
units.tr: It is agreed that many peoples have lived on milk, and still live on it today. Homer reported that the Getae, the Scythians, the Nomads and all that region were called galactophagi, that is, milk-eaters, and others galactopotae, that is, milk-drinkers. Pliny reported in book 6, chapter 30, that the Nomads who are dog-headed live on milk. In our own memory it is well established that the Belgians and not a few northern peoples have almost nothing more common in their diet than dairy foods, and that they make many excellent dairy products. And certainly a gentle, humane and pleasant way of life cannot be called such without the use of dairy foods. Who does not know that milk, cheese and butter not only satisfy the countryside, but also adorn the more refined tables of cities and of the nobility with pleasant and plentiful dishes? So those who forbid the use of milk are utterly dull and lacking in taste. But since the temperament and nature of living creatures vary, and so does their pasture and feed, the differences between milks must be carefully examined: which milk is best and most nourishing, to whom it is beneficial or harmful, and at what time it is more suitable.

units.la: Variae la-ctis differentiae obseruandae. Sciendum itaq;, praestantissimum omni-um, quae eduntur succum esse lac, Galeno & Aëtio tefiibus, modo secundum naturam se habeat, minuq; morbidum fit, vitiosum vel viro-sum, tunc enim saniora, quam sanguis, symptomata inducit. Constat namq; lac ex sanguine Lac vitiosissime colto in colorem album beneficio osum mammillarum & glandularum generari, imo cur sanguinem exactiore, elaboratione, quam sanguinem, cum guine coqui, omnem quoq; mutationem in contrariam malo pe-um abire, omnesq; eius optimas qualitates mutas jus?lactis rum pessimas, & quae naturaliter optima sunt, generacontraria ratione praeternaturaliter lapsapessi-tio:lactis mafieri. Ergo & babiliorem ad corruptionem boni & & putredinem subsantiam sanguine ipso ac-vitiati no quisivit lac, ob exactiorem scilicet & exquisitas: lactis tiorem elaborationem & concoctionem, quia fit bonę vel ex sanguine in venis prius elaborato. Lactis malae co-autem naturali terse habentis & optimi signa & coctionote sunt color candidus, vel secundum Aristi. nis signa, ad livorem vergens, odor suavis, sapor dulcis, non salsus, acidus vel amarus, est enim dulcedo lactis peculiaris, subsistantia mediocri & omni ex parte aequali, in vngue haerens, non defluens, non foetidum quid aut putrilaginem redolente, tum cum probe in ventriculo concoquitur, cujus indicium est, fi neq; rutus acidos aut fumidos concitat, praecordiaque & ventriculum gravat, hac enim signa, fi adfuerint, dicia, lacte in ventriculo non probe concoqui arguunt.
units.tr: The differences of milk that must be observed. So it must be known that milk is the most excellent of all the foods that are eaten, as Galen and Aëtius bear witness, provided it is in its natural state and not diseased or corrupt; for then it produces healthier effects than blood. For milk is indeed made from blood, through the working of the breasts and glands, which turns it white; and milk is cooked with a more exact process than blood itself. Every change of milk into its opposite, through a faulty process, turns its best qualities into the worst, and what is naturally best becomes, by an unnatural lapse, the most harmful. Therefore milk, because of its more exact working and cooking, is more prone to corruption and putrefaction than the substance of the blood from which it comes, since it is made well only from blood that has been previously worked in the veins. The signs of good and natural milk, well cooked, are a white colour (or, according to Aristotle, one tending to bluish), a sweet smell, a sweet taste (not salty, sour or bitter, for milk's sweetness is its own), a moderate thickness, even in every part, clinging to the fingernail and not running off, and no foul or rotten odour. It is also well digested in the stomach when it does not cause belching of sour or smoky vapours and does not weigh down the praecordia and stomach. For if these signs are present, they show that the milk is being digested well in the stomach; if not, that it is not.

units.la: Huic sententiæ patrocinatur Galenus lib. i. de sanit. tuen, vbi de lacte nutricis ait, debere id esse bene temperatum, quale certe erit, si sanguis eius, quam optimus sit. Is autem talis est, qui nec flava, nec atra bile, nec serosa aut aquosa abundat substantia. Et paulo post ibidem: Optimum lac est, quod gustanti olfacienti, plane suave aspicienti seu intuenti candidum, et æquale, liquidum & crassi medium apparebit, quod vitiosum est, aut crassum, aut caseosum, aut liquidum, aut serosum ac lividum, tum consistentia coloreque ipso inæquale videbitur, gustantibus amarorem, aut salsedinem, aut qualitatem saltem exhibebit extraneam. Idem l. 7. de morb. curandis bonum lac appellat, quod nullam externam qualitatem odore, vel gustu præsefert, sed quam dulcissimum est, liquipsi continuum, & prout lacti convenit, splendens, & super omnia, similes habet partes. Hæc Galenus. Caterum cum probatissimum lac insigni vi nutriendi polleat, perhelleq; alat, vsus tamen eius non omnibus æque sit salubris, videndum vlterius, quibus sumpsisse ex vsu sit, quibus non. Certum est, si bene concoquatur, nutrire, probosq; humores generare, & dum concoquitur illa attollit & inflat, petitq; caput etiam in sanis, teste Galeno in expositione aphorismi 64. l. 5. Hipp. Unde, si hoc sanis accidit, quanto magis capite dolentibus, vel illa habentibus fusipensa. In quibusdam etiam acescit, in aliis
units.tr: Galen supports this view in book 1 of De sanitate tuenda, where, speaking of a nurse's milk, he says: it ought to be well tempered, as it certainly will be if her blood is as good as possible. Her blood is of this sort if it has no excess of yellow bile, black bile, or watery and serous substance. And a little later in the same place: the best milk is that which, to the taste and smell, is plainly sweet, and to the eye appears white and even, liquid yet of medium thickness; milk that is faulty is either thick, or cheesy, or watery, or serous and bluish, and its consistency and colour will look uneven, and it will show to tasters a bitterness, or saltiness, or at least some foreign quality. The same Galen, in book 7 of De morborum curatione, calls good milk that which has no external quality in smell or taste, but is sweetest, continuous with itself in its liquid state, shining as milk should, and above all has its parts alike. So far Galen. But since the most approved milk has a remarkable power to nourish and nourishes very well, its use is not equally wholesome for everyone, and it must be considered further to whom it is suitable and to whom not. It is certain that if it is well digested, it nourishes and generates good humours; and while it is being digested it swells and inflates, and, as Galen notes in his commentary on Hippocrates' aphorism 64 of book 5, it even causes headache in healthy people. Hence, if this happens to healthy people, how much more to those suffering from the head or having such complaints. In some people it turns sour, in others it evaporates. In a colder stomach it turns sour and distends the praecordia with wind; in a warmer bodily temperament it is burnt, sends up fumes, and brings heaviness to the head.

units.la: Lac quibus prosit, vel obsit. aliis evaporat: in ventriculo frigidiore acescit, precordia aq; flatibus distendit: in calidiori corporis temperamento aduritur, inq; nidorosos halitus effumat, capitiq; affert gravedinem. Ergo, cum eius natura sit lac, ut calore densescat ac spisse-tur frigore vero liquescat, fit ut in æstuanti stomacho promptius coaguletur, coagulatum & in grumos conversum periculosa saepe accidentia excitet, praesertim in foeminis, coagulatio illa nulla re efficacius inhiberi potest, quam melle vel tum pes-saccharo salisq; momento: Confirmat id Galenus lib. 5. de morbis curandis, his verbis, porro hoc & quid tibi de lactis usu pro maximo praecepto sit, ut ii coagulationem quibus eo opus est, omnino id astante animali tionem stationem multum bibant etiam melle iniecto, si cui prohibeatur in ventriculo sistet, & si ipsum descendere ad aluum citius cupis, etiam sale. Quapropter de-testandus nobilium quarundam foeminarum adolescentularum mos est, quae inter coenam & prandii tempus, vel etiam statim a prandio coloris ac lactis cremore, aliisq; lactariis se infarciunt, vinoq; postea affatim ea perfundere non verentur maximo valetudinis detrimento. Notum est, plurimos ex lacte sic coagulato, ecq; in grumos cocreto strangulari, spirandiq; difficultate, oborto vomitu, opprimi. Vinum enim coagulescere facit lac, atque in casei consistentiam conglobari, quo cum offenditur stomachus, ac inter se repugnantia elaborare nequeat, omnia ad putredinem vergere necesse est, gravium ... morborum
units.tr: Which people milk benefits or harms. Therefore, since it is the nature of milk to thicken with heat and to become thin with cold, it comes about that in a heated stomach it more readily curdles, and once curdled and turned into clots it often provokes dangerous symptoms, especially in women. This curdling can be prevented by nothing more effectively than honey or sugar, or at times salt. Galen confirms this in book 5 of De morborum curatione, in these words: Moreover, the greatest rule concerning the use of milk for you is this: those who need to stop the curdling should drink plenty of milk, even with honey added, if they are to have it kept in the stomach; and if you wish it to pass quickly to the bowels, add salt as well. Hence there is a custom to be condemned among certain young noblewomen, who, between dinner and the midday meal, or even straight after lunch, stuff themselves with cream of milk and other dairy dishes, and then do not hesitate to drench them with wine, to their great harm to health. It is well known that many have been strangled by milk so curdled and congealed into clots, or overwhelmed by difficulty of breathing when vomiting begins. For wine makes milk curdle and bind together into the consistency of cheese; when the stomach is burdened with this, and cannot digest the mixed and conflicting substances, everything must tend toward putrefaction, and the seeds of grave diseases gather together.

units.la: Nn borum seminaria coacernari. Sic pisces & lac, omniaq; acida lactis admixta, vinoq; pfusa scabiem generant & lepram. Sic enim impro-micue ingesta computrescunt, ac corruptioni efficiuntur obnoxia.
units.tr: Thus fish and milk, and all sour things mixed with milk and drenched in wine, produce scabies and leprosy, for things eaten in such a way rot and become prone to corruption.

units.la: Colostra fœtante enixaq; boue quidam gu-la ganeaq; proceres, in delitijs habent, sed nocen-tissime, adeo vt infantibus etiam triduo a partu lac deguftasse maternum pernitiosum sit, coit enim & crassescit in ventre, venasq; ac sanguinis rivos obstruit, vt minus commode alimenta pos-sint permeare ac distribui. Qua vero lac coagu-latum dissoluant, multa sunt, præcipua tamen cyminum, angelica, oximel, & acetum scyllitium.
units.tr: Some gluttonous and greedy nobles delight in the colostrum of a cow that has just calved, but it is very harmful; so much so that it is pernicious even for infants to have tasted their mother's milk within three days of birth, since it coagulates and thickens in the belly and blocks the veins and streams of blood, so that the nourishment cannot pass through and be distributed properly. Many remedies dissolve milk that has curdled, but the chief ones are cumin, angelica, oxymel, and squill vinegar.

units.la: Lactis porrò differentiae ab animalibus sumtas vel ortu opera pretium est hic considerare. Plinius quodcunque humanum maximè & valentissime alere prodidit. Verba eius lib. 28. c. 9. placuit subnectere. Maximè autem, inquit, quodcunque humanum alit, mox caprinum, vnde fortassis fabula locum ita nutritum dixere; dulcissimum ab humano Camelinum, efficacissimum ex asinis. Ignorum animalium & corporum facilius reddit. Stomacho accommodatissimum caprinum, quoniam fronde magis quam herba vescuntur.
units.tr: It is worth considering here the differences of milk according to the animal it comes from, and its origin. Pliny reported which milk nourishes humans most and most strongly. I thought it fitting to quote his words from book 28, chapter 9. Most of all, he says, the milk of whatever animal nourishes a human most and most powerfully: next is goat's milk, which is perhaps why fables say that a certain place was nourished in this way; the sweetest is that of the camel compared with humans, the most effective is from asses; it makes the bodies of the sick easier to heal. Goat's milk is most suited to the stomach, since goats feed more on leaves than on grass.

units.la: Bubulum medicatum, omne autem vernum aquatum, aestate, & de nonnulli. nouellis: Probatissimum vero quod in vngue haret, nec dissuit: Innocentius decoctum praecipue cum calculis marinis: alvus maxime soluitur bubulo minus inflat quodcunque decoctum. Hæc Plinius.
units.tr: Cow's milk that has been medicated; all spring milk, watered in summer, and that of some newly calved animals. The most approved is that which clings to the fingernail and does not separate. Innocentius recommends it boiled, especially with sea pebbles; it loosens the bowels most, and any boiled milk is less inflating. So says Pliny.

units.la: Alii bubulum lac crassissimum & pinguissimum esse volunt, quapropter etiam ocyus in stomacho concrescere ac glaciari, minusque aluo soluendæ utile, valentius tamen nutriri, omnium caprillo crassius habetur, caprillum vero medio se habet loco, teste Galeno lib. de bono & malo succo, utrumque tamen pinguitudinis obtinet exiguum, unde & paucum ex iis colligitur buty-rum.
units.tr: Others want cow's milk to be the thickest and fattest, and for this reason it also curdles and freezes more quickly in the stomach, and is less useful for loosening the bowels, though it nourishes more strongly. Of all, the milk of goats is considered thicker, while sheep's milk holds a middle place, according to Galen in his book On Good and Bad Juice. Both, however, have only a small amount of fat, so little butter is made from them.

units.la: Alii aliter sentiunt, non certè experti vi-ræ & naturam veri & boni laetis. Lubet huc subiicere versus Baptistæ Fieræ de lacte, qui sunt eiusmodi, Dulce sapit, subitò cur lac putrescit? aquosum est. (uis, Quod præstat? caprae. post? ouis. inde boCui nocuum? capiti, putridis & febribus, ora Inficit & neruos, sed bene pectus alit. Quando bibam? primum cum fugis ab vbere. Somnus Huic (moneo) & motus, mixtaque mensa nocent. Tot petis? vnum oro, cur in contraria fertur, Et modo lac referat, & modo fluxa tenet.
units.tr: Others think differently, not having truly experienced the power and nature of milk, whether good or bad. It is worth adding here the verses of Baptista Fiera on milk, which run as follows: "Why does milk turn sour so suddenly when it tastes sweet? Because it is watery. What is its best kind? Goat's. And next? Sheep's. Then cow's. What harms? The head, putrid fevers and the mouth; it infects the nerves, but nourishes the chest well. When should I drink it? First, when you have just left the breast. Sleep and exercise harm the one who drinks it, and so does mixing it with a meal. You ask so much? I ask only one thing: why does it turn into its opposite, sometimes restoring the body and sometimes remaining thin and watery?"

units.la: Hæc ille. Certum est & inconcussum, optimum lac illud esse, quod in florenti ætate ab animali fano emulgetur, suauibus odoratisq; pascuis cnu- trito, cum scilicet succus turgent herbæ, vt in ve- re, medicantur q; vbera pascuis, vt loquitur Pli- nius l. 25. c. 8. Cum autem omniuora fere in her- bis sint boues, frondeq; & herba vescantur simul, sequitur bubulum lac tempore verno præcipue tamen Maio, in terris vero septentrionem ver- sus sitis, Iunio optimum esse. Cuius sententia ve- ritatem ratio ipsa & experientia comprobat, ac nemo, opinor, erit, nisi plane ἀλόγος & ratione carens, qui contradicturus sit. Caprarum lac aliàs salubrius. Affinium pthisicis commo- diffimum prædicant, sed protinus bibendum est nulla interposita mora: unde Galenus lib. 10. de morb. curand. induci in ipsum cubiculum asi- num iubet. Et lib. 7. vbi de siccitatum diffe- rentiis agit in corpore humano, celeriter, exicca- tum & tabidum sanari scribit, si ipse asinam fugeret, idsi graudaretur, expedire vt quam mi- nimo tempore in aere lac moretur, propterea quod celerrime mutari sit aptum. Et paulo post ibidem. Acsanè vtilissimum lac est, cum ex ipsis mammillis quis hauserit, veluti Eurybion, Herodotus & Prodicus censent, qui tantam in eo ad corpora reficienda fiduciam habuerunt, vt etiam qui pthoe tabescerent, ex ipsa mulieris pa- pilla lac fugere iubaret: quod cum plurisq; displi- ceat, ceat, aliminum ipsis dari conueniet. Hac Galen. Conferre quoque aliquid & candori mulierum cuti existimatur. Poppaea Domitii Neronis coniux quingentas secum per omnia trahens asi-nas foetas aliminum nobilitauit, balneorum etiam folio totum corpus illo lacte macerauit, sic candefieri cute extendique existimans. Sed longe alimino inpthifi, humanum praestantius est, nam pecu-liariter extenuatis plurimum & frugi alimen-tum confert, corporisque robur restituit. In expe-rimentis sunt, qui iam tabe & atrophia cofumti solo lacte ex vegeta & florentis mulieris vberibus fuftio sunt restituti. Sic Dauid septuagenarius cum senili torpore frigeret, nec pellib. cooperitus inca-lescere t, infpeftati decoris puella amplexib caste condormiuit, vt eius calore robur stomachi foue retur. Equino septentrionis gentes quaedam in cibis & potu vtuntur, quod hic meminisse leftore volo, sicut & illud, quod in Ponto fluuius Aflaces ri-gat campos, in quibus pastae nigro lacte equae gen-tem alant. Lactaria pulticula, (quae fiunt ex lactefimilagini misto, inq; sartagine decocto, fre-quentiusque cum spatula versato in lenta pruna, lae lacta-nefartigini adhaerescat, vsq; ad modicam crassi-tudinem, & donec crusta tenui obducatur, apud noftrates quasdam foeminas Principes in summis delitiis habentur, sunt enim suauissimi saporis, & odoris, si addatur crocus, optimiq; ac firmi nutrimenti. Sofistratum nullo cibo & potu alio quam lacte toto vitae sua curriculo vsum fuisse.
units.tr: These are his words. It is certain and beyond dispute that the best milk is that which is drawn in the flower of life from a healthy animal fed on sweet, fragrant pastures, when the herbs are full of juice, as in spring; and the udders are made better by the pasture, as Pliny says in book 25, chapter 8. Since cattle are almost all omnivores and feed on both leaves and grass together, it follows that cow's milk is best in spring, especially in May, and in lands lying towards the north, in June. Reason itself and experience confirm the truth of this opinion, and I think no one will contradict it unless he is wholly ἄλογος and lacking reason. Goat's milk is otherwise more wholesome. They commend it most highly for those who are consumptive, but it must be drunk at once, with no delay. Hence Galen in book 10 of On the Curing of Diseases orders that the ass be brought into the very bedroom. And in book 7, where he treats of the differences of dryness in the human body, he writes that a person who is wasted and dried out is quickly cured if he drinks ass's milk, and if that is not available, it is useful for the milk to stand in the air for as short a time as possible, because it very quickly becomes altered. And a little later in the same place: "Truly, milk is most useful when someone drinks it straight from the teats themselves," as Eurybion, Herodotus and Prodicus thought, who had such confidence in it for restoring bodies that they ordered even those wasting with phthisis to drink milk straight from a woman's nipple. Since this displeases many, it will be fitting to give them milk from the breast of another animal. Thus far Galen. It is also thought that it contributes something to the complexion of women's skin. Poppaea, wife of Domitius Nero, made the ass's milk famous, bringing five hundred pregnant she-asses with her wherever she went, and bathing her whole body in that milk in the bath, believing that in this way her skin would become whiter and smoother. But for the consumptive, human milk is far better than ass's milk, for it nourishes especially those who are wasted, providing a very wholesome food and restoring the strength of the body. There are those in experience who, already worn down by wasting and atrophy, were restored by milk alone from the breasts of a vigorous and blooming woman. So David, an old man of seventy, when he was chilled by senile torpor and could not be warmed even with blankets, lay chastely asleep in the arms of a girl of remarkable beauty, so that her warmth might strengthen the strength of his stomach. Some of the peoples of the north use mare's milk for food and drink, which I want the reader to remember here, as also that in Pontus the river Asaces waters fields on which mares, pastured there, nourish their people with black milk. Milk porridge (made by mixing milk with flour, cooking it in a frying pan, and stirring it often with a spatula over a slow plum-wood fire, until it thickens to a moderate consistency and is covered with a thin crust, so that it does not stick to the pan) is held in the highest delight by certain noblewomen among us; for it has a most pleasant taste and smell, especially if saffron is added, and it is of the best and firmest nourishment. Sophistratus is said to have used no other food or drink than milk during his whole life.

units.la: De lacte humano memorabilia. ijs ePlutarchus lib. 4. Symposiacorum scriptum reliquit.
units.tr: Memorable things about human milk. Plutarch has written about these in book 4 of his Symposiacs.

units.la: De tribus diuersis lactis partibus, serosa, caseosa, & butyrosa:
units.tr: On the three different parts of milk: serous, caseous and butyrous

units.la: TRes in lacte substantias contineri, & praeter has nullam esse quartam, quae lactis nomine designetur, sed totum, quod ex iis tribus legitime temperatis constitit, lactis nomen sibi assumere, in confesso est.
units.tr: It is agreed that milk contains three substances, and that there is no fourth, apart from these, which is designated by the name of milk; rather, the whole that is made up of these three properly blended together takes the name of milk for itself.

units.la: Serum vnumquodq; lactis genus continet, estq; aquosior & tenuior lactis substantia, a qua caseus, hoc est, crassior & densior pars est separata: graecis ὀρὸς dicitur, quasi separatum a ὀρίζω, id est, findo, separo, germ.
units.tr: Each kind of milk contains whey, which is the more watery and thinner substance of milk, from which the cheese, that is, the thicker and denser part, has been separated. In Greek it is called ὀρὸς [oros], as if "separated" from ὀρίζω [horizō], that is, to split or separate, says Germanus.

units.la: Molcten. Porro antiquitati celebratissimum semper fuit, obq; vim abstergendi, attenuandi, aluumq; abluendae ac soluendae nobilitatum, hodie caprinum in laude magis habet. Estq; serum ipsum tanto melius ac praestantius, quanto lac ipsum melius fuerit. Porro de temperatura seri autores, & inter se & Galeno dissentire videntur: alii enim calidū alii frigidum esse contendunt. Galenus lib. 4. simpl. medicam. frigidum, libro vero 10. sicut & libro 3. alimentor. calidum id esse affirmat. Qui serum simpliciter & absolute idiotarum tarum more, frigidum pronunciant, crasse hallucinantur. Exploranda enim lactis hic natura est, quae in variis eius generibus & differentiis non est vniusmodi, alterum enim altero frigidius est vel calidius pro temporis sc. pabuli ac soli diuersa constitutione. Si itaq; lac & serum eius dicuntur frigida, non ita ac- cipiendum est, ac si caliditatis omnino sint expertia, sed quod frigiditas calori praevaleat, vel quod eum prae frigiditate habeat imbecillitorem. Ioan. Manardus Epist. f. l. 16. lacte-rumq; eius absolute frigidum statuit, & tamē idem ibidem fero acrimoniam tribuit, atte- nuandiq; ac detergendi facultatem: quas vi- res inquit, quia lactis tota subsantia a ferofis potissimum partibus nanciscitur, minime mirandum est, si illis deperditis, simul & vires illae a lacte in totum submoueantur. Quare, pergit, cui serum ademtum est, ventrem potius abstinet quam subducit, & in quantum-uis calido ventriculo ad nidorem non ampliius conuertitur, resolutis sc. non solum serosis partibus, in quibus calor aliquis supra temperamentum inueniebatur, sed & pingui-bus, quae temperatam habent caliditatem, non autem tantam vt butyrum reddant absolute calidum: Haec Manardus: ex quibus euidenter perspicitur, in fero lactis frigiditatem non praepollere, sed calorem potius cum frigiditate temperatum. Haec de fero.
units.tr: Molcten. Moreover, whey has always been most celebrated among the ancients, and has been prized for its power to cleanse, thin and wash out the bowels and to loosen them; today it is held in greater esteem when made from goat's milk. And whey is the better and more excellent the better the milk itself has been. Furthermore, the authors seem to disagree both among themselves and with Galen about the temperature of whey: some maintain that it is hot, others that it is cold. Galen in book 4 of On Simple Medicines affirms that it is cold, but in book 10, and likewise in book 3 of On Foods, that it is hot. Those who pronounce whey simply and absolutely cold, in the manner of laymen, are grossly mistaken. For the nature of milk must be examined here, which in its various kinds and differences is not of one sort, since one kind is colder or hotter than another, according to the differing constitution of the season, the pasture and the soil. If, therefore, milk and its whey are called cold, this should not be understood as if they were entirely without heat, but that their coldness prevails over their heat, or that they have too little heat in comparison with their coldness. Giovanni Manardo, in Epistle f. l. 16, also declares milk and its whey absolutely cold, and yet in the same place he ascribes to whey sharpness and the power of thinning and cleansing. He says that since the whole substance of milk derives these powers chiefly from its watery parts, it is least of all surprising that, when those are lost, those powers too are wholly removed from the milk. Therefore, he goes on, whey that has been taken away makes the bowels rather constipated than loosened, and in a very hot stomach it is no longer converted into nourishment, since not only the watery parts, in which some heat above the temperate was found, have been dissolved, but also the fatty parts, which have a temperate warmth, though not so great as to make butter absolutely hot. Thus far Manardo. From these words it is clearly seen that in whey the coldness is not predominant, but rather the heat is tempered with coldness. So much for whey.

units.la: Calcum
units.tr: Cheese.

units.la: Cafeum omnem ægre confici, succosque improbos subministrare, ventriculum flatibus replere, multorum erronea opinio est. Recentes enim laxiores & molliores, ex dulci, bono, laudabilique lacte, butyro non separato, confectos, ac puriores, aliis videlicet succis aut rebus non commixtis, induratis ac veteribus in cibis præferri debere omnium pene consensu traditur. Immodico quoque sale imbuti casei improbantur, & qui nullo pacto noxii sunt: humore destituti vetustateque corrupti, putres quoque vermibusq; scatentes pernitiosissimi sunt: acriores & calidiores certum est difficulter concoqui. Veteres, si in frequentiorem cibatum admissi fuerint, animæ grauitatem afferre, complu-ribus experimentis percognitum est. Verum facile ex iis, quæ de lacte fuerunt prodita, iudicare est, quinam præstantiores, & qui ignobiliores sint. Operosissimum enim est omnium regionum & tractuum dotes persequi. Nominatissimi sunt hodie, quos mittit Hollandia, Helvetica, Mediolanum, quos placentinos appellant, nec non Westphalia. Suecia & suos miris effert laudibus, & certe est Parmensibus parum cedere. In septentrionis quibusdam tractibus certum est caseos in tantam ab incolis molem cogi atque densari, vt vni ferendo vix quatuor robustissimi baiuli sufficiant. Soli autem ratio pluri-mum mum hic confert.Solum enim graminosisi- mum & restibule, pascuaque generosissi-macaseorum copiam bonitatemq; prębent.
units.tr: The common belief that all cheese is hard to digest, supplies bad juices, and fills the stomach with wind, is an erroneous opinion. For almost everyone agrees that fresh cheeses, which are softer and more tender, made from sweet, good and wholesome milk from which the butter has not been separated, and which are purer, that is, not mixed with other juices or substances, are to be preferred in food to hardened and old ones. Cheeses steeped in excessive salt are disapproved, and those that are harmless in no way; cheeses that lack moisture and are spoiled by age, and those that are rotten and swarm with worms, are most pernicious. It is certain that sharper and hotter cheeses are digested with difficulty. Many experiments have shown that old cheeses, if admitted into a more frequent diet, bring heaviness to the spirit. Yet from what has been handed down about milk it is easy to judge which cheeses are the finer and which the more ordinary. For it would be most laborious to pursue the special qualities of every region and district. The most famous today are those sent from Holland, Switzerland and Milan, which they call Piacenza cheeses, and also those from Westphalia. Sweden also praises its own cheeses with marvellous commendations, and certainly it is not much inferior to Parma. In some northern districts it is certain that the inhabitants press and compact cheeses into such a mass that scarcely four very strong porters are enough to carry one. Yet here the nature of the soil contributes most. For a very grassy and rich ground, and generous pastures, provide an abundance and goodness of cheese.

units.la: Galenus scribit caseum dignosci substantia & gustu,nempe molli vel dura, densa vel la- xa, lenta vel friabili: unde mollem duro, ra- rum & laxum denso praestare ait: gustus quoque certissimus testis est, qui suavitatem nullamq; vehementem & peregrinam qua- litatem in caseo solet deprehendere. Casei quoq; dotes sequenti vetustas comprehen-dit distico,
units.tr: Galen writes that cheese is judged by its substance and its taste: whether it is soft or hard, dense or loose, tough or crumbly. Hence he says that soft is better than hard, and loose better than dense. Taste is also a most certain witness, since it usually detects in cheese a pleasant flavour and no strong or foreign quality. Antiquity also sums up the qualities of cheese in a couplet:

units.la: Non Argus, largus, non Magdalena, Matuslem,
units.tr: Not Argus, not Largus, not Magdalen, not Matuslem,

units.la: Non Abacuc, Lazarus, caseus iste bonus.
units.tr: Not Abacuc, not Lazarus: that is a good cheese.

units.la: hoc est, si non multis oculis luceat, si non nimium fuerit salsus, si non capillis intrinsecus sordeat, si non nimis vetustus, si non nimis durus, & non fætens. Ad extremum mirum ait esse Plinius lib.11.c.41. barbaras gentes, quæ lacte viuant, spreuisse aut ignorasse tot seculis casei dotem. Tradit idem Zoroastrem in desertis caseo victitasse annis 20. ita temperato ut vetustatem non sentiret. Sapientes quoque à quibusdam vocari reperio, qui à caseo abstinent. Verum extremis epulis parce sumtus parum aut nihil negotii facesset, ventriculum enim sic roborat, cibumque unâ digerit.
units.tr: That is, the cheese must have plenty of holes to let light through, it must not be too salty, it must not be foul with hair-like mould inside, it must not be too old, it must not be too hard, and it must not stink. Finally, Pliny says in book 11, chapter 41 that it is remarkable that barbarian peoples, who live on milk, have for so many ages either scorned or been ignorant of the virtue of cheese. The same writer relates that Zoroaster lived for twenty years in the desert on cheese, kept in such a condition that it did not become stale. I also find that some call those wise who abstain from cheese. Yet if it is eaten sparingly at the end of a meal, it causes little or no trouble, for it strengthens the stomach and helps it digest the food.

units.la: Lactis pinguedinem interpretatur butyrum Rabbi Salomon Prouer.30. Qui exprimit lac, educet butyrum & mel comedet, Deuteron. 32. butyro boum & lacte ouium. Esaiae 7. butyrum & mel comedet. Hebr. dicitur haemach à chamam calere, quia semper calet, & nunquam frigescit seu congelatur. Lacti autem demitur pinguedo illa, tunditurque donec in massam coeat. Plinius lactis spumam appellat: quantos in re cibaria & medica praestet visus, nemini non est notum. Est autem butyrum modice calidum, digerit, nutrit, emollit, laxat & purgat. Editur crudum, adque omnis generis cibos addit ur. Belgarum & Septentrionis gentium quarundam laudatissima consuetudo est, mane & ieiuno stomacho butyrum cum panem efficare, omnibusque aliis cibis id praemandere. Econtra perniciose faciunt, qui, postquam impromisque variis cibis ventre probe infarserunt, tandem butyro quoque eundem aggrauant. Causam huius rei inuenit aequus lector infra cap. 18. vbi de ordine ciborum ingerendorum prolixius dictum est.
units.tr: Rabbi Solomon interprets the fatness of milk as butter, citing Proverbs 30: "Whoever presses milk will bring forth butter, and whoever eats honey" (Prov. 30); Deuteronomy 32: "butter of kine and milk of sheep" (Deut. 32); Isaiah 7: "he shall eat butter and honey" (Isa. 7). In Hebrew it is called haemach [חמאה] from chamam [חמם], to be warm, because it is always warm and never grows cold or congeals. The fatness is taken from the milk and beaten until it coheres into a mass. Pliny calls it the foam of milk. How greatly it is esteemed as food and medicine is known to everyone. Butter is moderately warm; it digests, nourishes, softens, loosens and cleanses. It is eaten raw and added to all kinds of food. It is a most praised custom of the Dutch and of certain northern peoples to spread butter on bread in the morning on an empty stomach, and to take it before all other foods. On the other hand, those act foolishly who, after stuffing their belly with all sorts of food, then weigh it down further with butter. The fair reader will find the reason for this below, in chapter 18, where the order of eating foods is discussed at greater length.

units.la: Hic vnum meminisse lectore volo, veteres habuisse varia butyri genera, sed pharmaci potius loco quam cibi illis in visu fuisse, vt non immerito Plinius butyrum gentium barbararum laudatissimum cibum, quique diuites à plebe discerneret, appellaret. pellarit , Et Athenæus, qui in suo conuiuio nullum cibi genus præteriit, butyri nunquam mentionem fecerit. Porro ruffescens & maiale magnificatur , candidum & rancidum virusque redolens damnatur.
units.tr: Here I want the reader to remember that the ancients had various kinds of butter, but in their eyes it was more a medicine than a food. So Pliny not unreasonably called butter the most praised food of barbarous peoples, and one that distinguished the rich from the common people. Athenaeus, who in his banquet omitted no kind of food, never mentions butter. Moreover, butter that is reddish and smells of fat is praised, while white and rancid butter that gives off a foul smell is condemned.

units.la: Westphaliæ populi potibus suis butyrum indunt , ac ieiuno bibunt stomacho salubri inuento : alii cum allii capite vno aut altero viridi, veletiam ruthæ foliis mane aduersus venenorum suspiciones pestilentisque aeris contagia mandunt , nec non ventris animalia. Vires quoque corporis per se cum pane tosto mane comesum conseruat, sed salitum, sic enim in annuos durat vius.
units.tr: The people of Westphalia put butter into their drinks and drink it on an empty stomach, a wholesome discovery. Others eat it in the morning with one or two green heads of garlic, or even with rue leaves, as a defence against suspicions of poison and the contagion of pestilential air, and also against worms in the belly. Eaten in the morning with toasted bread, it also preserves the strength of the body by itself; but it must be salted, for so it lasts for a year.

units.la: Placentarum quoque innumera genera concinnare norunt pistores dulciarii & matresfamilias, quæ butyro condiuntur uberrime, suntque suauissima & saluberrima gulæ irritamenta probè confecta , alendi enim corporisque vires roborandi vim habent insignem. Liquefactum butyrum atque epotum quidam ad intestinorum exulcerationes commendant, alii in clysteres addunt successu non infelici.
units.tr: Confectioners and housewives also know how to make countless kinds of cakes and tarts, which are richly seasoned with butter. They are very sweet and wholesome, well made to tempt the appetite, and they have a remarkable power to nourish and strengthen the body. Some recommend melted butter drunk down for ulcers of the bowels, and others add it to enemas, with no unhappy result.

units.la: Qo
units.tr: Qo

units.la: Contra sanguisugas potas butyrum reme-dio esse cum aceto ferro calefacto, Plin. au-tor est l.28.c.16. vbi quoq; acetum calefactu per fe venenis aduersari tradit.
units.tr: Butter drunk against the bites of leeches is a remedy when it is taken with vinegar heated in an iron vessel. Pliny is the authority, Book 28, chapter 16, where he also says that vinegar heated by itself counters poisons.

units.la: De butyro Scytharum confecto ex lacte equino digna lectu inueniuntur apud Mer-curialem lib.1. variar. lect. vbi de variis eius generibus apud veteres, vsuque tum in cibo, tum in vngendis corporibus post balneum, olei loco, fit mentio.
units.tr: Matters worth reading about butter made from mares' milk of the Scythians are found in Mercuriale, book 1 of the Variae lectiones, where mention is made of the various kinds of butter among the ancients, and of its use both in food and for anointing the body after the bath, in place of oil.

units.la: Tenuior a butyro separata substantia, dum videlicet lactis pinguedo tufione in massam cogitur, ferum butyri dicitur, germ. Molcken/q. ferum, quod ex tufione fit, rura vocant Buttermilch/eftiuisq; temporibus haud infalubriter aduersus sitim febriumq; ardores eo vtuntur.
units.tr: The thinner substance separated from the butter, that is, what remains once the fat of the milk has been churned into a mass, is called buttermilk (ferum butyri), in German Molcken, though country people call it Buttermilch. In summer it is used, not unhelpfully, against thirst and the heat of fevers.

units.la: Sed oxygala, hoc est, lac acidum, plurimi apud veteres aestimatum fuisse reperio. Et Plin. l.11. c.41. scribens, consueuisse barbaras gentes lac in iucundum acorem condensare, & butyrum pingue quod spuma lactis effet, nihil aliud intelligit quam oxygala & aphrogala apud Romanos niue refrigerati foli-tum, testante Galen. 7. meth. Et aphrogala hodie apud multos inter suauissima edulia reputatur. Porro confectionem oxygalae do-cet Columella l.12.c.8. cum scribit recipe olam nouam, eamque fundum iuxta terebrato, deinde surculo cauum obturato, lacteq; ouillo
units.tr: But I find that oxygala, that is, sour milk, was greatly esteemed by the ancients. Pliny, writing in book 11, chapter 41, says that barbarian peoples were accustomed to thicken milk into a pleasant sourness, and that the fatty butter which was the foam of milk. He means nothing other than oxygala and aphrogala, which the Romans were accustomed to take cooled with snow, as Galen attests in book 7 of the Method. Today aphrogala is still counted among the most delicious foods by many people. Further, Columella, book 12, chapter 8, teaches how to make oxygala, when he writes: "Take a new jar, pierce it near the bottom, then close the hollow with a small peg, and fill it with the freshest sheep's milk (for this makes the best).

units.la: Oxygala. Aphrogala. Oxygala confectio. ouillo (ex hoc enim optimum fit) quam re-centiffimo vas repleto, adiicitoque viridium codimentorum fasciculos, origani, menthę, cepæ, coriandri. Has herbas in lacte demitto, vt ligamenta earum extent. Post diem quintum, quo cauum obturaueras furculum eximito ferumq; emittito. Cum deinde lac coeperit manare, eodem surculo cauum obturato, intermissoque triduo, ferum iterum emittito, & fafculos condimentorum exemtos adiicito. Deinde exiguum aridi thymi & cunilæ aridæ super lac distringito concisique sectiui porri quantum fatis videbitur adiicito & permisceтo; mox intermisso biduo rursus ferum emittito, cauumque obturato, acsalis triti quantum satis erit, adiicito & misceтo. Operculo deinde imposito & oblito non ante aperueris quam vsus exegerit. Plinius l. 28. c. 9. oxygalæ mentionem faciens, scribit, fieri ex acido lacte in recens quod acescere velit, addito, stomachoque id vtilissimum esse: Et cap. eod. quod maximè coactum est, in summo fluitat, id exemtum sale addito appellatur oxygala, reliqua decoquunt in ollis, ibi quod supernatat, butyrum est oleosum naturâ. Hæc Plinius.
units.tr: Oxygala. Aphrogala. The preparation of oxygala. Fill the vessel and add bundles of green herbs: marjoram, mint, onion and coriander. I put these herbs into the milk so that their stalks hang out. After the fifth day, when you have closed the hollow with the peg, take out the peg and let the whey run off. When the milk then begins to flow, close the hollow again with the same peg, and after an interval of three days let the whey run off again, and add the bundles of herbs you took out. Then scatter a little dried thyme and dried savory over the milk, add finely chopped leek as much as seems enough, and mix it in. Then, after an interval of two days, let the whey run off again, close the hollow, add as much finely ground salt as will be enough, and mix. Then put on the lid, seal it, and do not open it before use requires." Pliny, book 28, chapter 9, in mentioning oxygala, writes that it is made by adding to sour milk, when it is about to turn sour, that the stomach finds this most useful; and in the same chapter: "the part that is most thickened floats on top; this, removed and salted, is called oxygala; the rest they boil in pots, and what floats on top there is naturally oily butter." So far Pliny.

units.la: Magno autem oxygala esse auxilio in caloribus ad temperandos internos æstus febriumque ardores pestilentes, indubitatis experimentis recentior medicina compro-bauit. bauit. Aphrogala verò, flos, cremor seu spuma lactis, quantam æstate inprimis gratiam Pomeridianis epulis, atque etiam in cœnis secunda mensa obtinuerit, miscentibus huic nobilibus fœminis humi nascentia fraga saccharique; pollinem (Sic enim innocentiorem esse vsum eius compererunt) nemini non est notum, nisi omnium salubrium rerum ignaro.
units.tr: That oxygala is of great help in heat, for cooling the inner burnings and the pestilential fevers, recent medicine has proved by undoubted experiments. As for aphrogala, the froth, cream or foam of milk, how much favour it gained especially in summer at afternoon meals, and even at the dessert course, when noble women mixed with it wild strawberries growing on the ground together with sugar and fine flour (for they found this use to be harmless), is known to everyone except those ignorant of all wholesome things.

units.la: De ouis.
units.tr: On eggs.

units.la: NVllum esse alimentum, quod æquè in ægritudine alat, neque oneret, similiterque vim ac cibi vsum habeat, quam ouum, Plinius lib. 29. cap. 3. prodidit. Quemadmodum enim lac quadrupedum sanguis est percoctus, sic ouum est sanguis avium feminæ confersus, nutritioni vberrimè accommodatus. Verum Hippocrates lib. de diæta ob nutrimenti dissimilitudinem ouum admodum videtur improbare. Naturam enim vitellus & albumen habent contrariam, non colore tantum, sed virtute etiam. Vitellus enim temperatus est, facilius concoquitur, magis humet, frigoreque spissatur, album contra frigidius est, & crassius ac igne spissatur, cum vitellus mollis perfiatur, magisque in aqua feruente quam adignem coquatur atq; induretur. Sed hoc incommodum facile tollitur, fi reiiciatur, vel cocturæ, in qua summa differentia est, diligens habeatur ratio. Infinitis enim modis culinæ oua parant, sed apparatus non rarò euadunt pestilentes ob aliorum societatem & mixturam, vt alibi quoque notatum est. Modice cocta, seu mediocrem consistentiã per cocturam adepta, qualia sunt tremula & mollia, græc. τρομηπώ, eademque recentia, quemadmodum omnium consensu excellentissimè alunt, cæterisq; in virium restauratione præstant, ita econtra ἐφθα dicta, id est, ad indurationem cocta, difficulter perfi-ciuntur, crassumq; præbent nutrimentum: q vero in vniuersum cocta sunt, ἀψοῦς λικα græc. cibis abdicata sunt, quamuis sordidi quibusdam palati hominibus ea in æstiuis acetariis maximè placere sciam non fine valetudinis iactura, & bruto plane appetitu. Sorbilia & ψυφῆσα vix parantur calida, vtiliterque in faucium gutturisque morbis sorbentur, aluu quoq; probè molliunt, sed propter celerem descensum minus nutriunt: in ventre vero calidiore impuriore-q; iusto diutius retenta facilimè alteratur inq; nocentiffima vertitur bile, quare in his deglutiendis cautio obseruanda est, facilimè enim febrim accendunt, q> ipse voluptatis magis q vtilitatis gratiâ aliquado bina sic absorbes expt° sum,
units.tr: Pliny (book 29, chapter 3) has recorded that there is no food which nourishes the sick equally well, without burdening them, and which has the same strength and use as food, as the egg. For just as milk is the blood of quadrupeds, cooked down, so the egg is the blood of birds, gathered together and most abundantly suited to nourishment. Yet Hippocrates, in his book on diet, seems to disapprove of eggs greatly because of the unlikeness of their nourishment. For the yolk and the white have opposite natures, not only in colour but in power too. The yolk is temperate, is digested more easily, moistens more, and is thickened by cold; the white, on the contrary, is colder and thicker, and is thickened by fire. The soft yolk is also more easily cooked in boiling water than over the fire, and hardens there. But this inconvenience is easily avoided if careful attention is paid to the reheating or cooking, in which the difference is very great. For cooks prepare eggs in endless ways, but the preparations often turn out harmful because of the mixing and combining with other things, as is noted elsewhere. Eggs cooked lightly, or cooked to a moderate consistency, such as the tremulous and soft ones [τρομηπώ], and fresh ones, as all agree, nourish most excellently and excel in restoring strength. On the other hand, eggs called hard [ἐφθα], that is, cooked until they harden, are digested with difficulty and provide a thick nourishment. Those which are cooked thoroughly [ἀψοῦς λικα] have been rejected by the Greeks as food, although I know that some men of dirty palate are very fond of them in summer salads, not without loss of health and with a plainly brutish appetite. Soft-boiled eggs and those beaten up [ψυφῆσα] are hardly ever prepared hot, and are usefully taken in diseases of the throat and gullet; they also gently loosen the bowels, but because they pass down quickly they nourish less. Yet if they are kept too long in a warmer and more impure stomach, they are very easily altered and turn into the most harmful bile. So care must be taken in swallowing them, for they very easily kindle fever. I myself, indeed, have sometimes swallowed two of them in this way, for the sake of pleasure rather than usefulness.

units.la: idque idq; nullam ob aliam euenire causam veri‑simile est, quam ex duabus repugnantibus naturis per coctuiram non vnitis & contem‑peratis,sed maximam adhuc partem crudis. Vnde celebriores quidam Practici qua fe‑bricitantibus,vt omnino pernitiofa interdi‑cunt, ilouum enim inde febri fomentum suppeditari recte sibi persuasum habent.
units.tr: It is likely that this happens for no other cause than that two opposing natures, not united and tempered by cooking, but still for the most part raw, are present. Hence certain well-known practitioners forbid feverish people to eat them at all, being firmly persuaded that eggs supply fuel to the fever.

units.la: In cineribus praeterea aflà, frixa,velin far‑tagine costa & rotundata improbantur.Suf‑focata à veteribus celebrata reperio, graec. ψυκτρ, quae fc. rupto putamine in patinam, in qua butyrum fit liquatum, coniecta co‑quuntur prunis subditis,igne molli & conti‑nente,donec vitelli in medio coeant, albu‑mina aute circudent, feq; in oras constituat.
units.tr: Moreover, eggs fried in ashes, roasted, or baked in a pan with a crust are disapproved of. I find that the ancients praised the so-called "suffocated" eggs [ψυκτρ], which are cooked by breaking the shell, putting the egg into a pan in which butter has been melted, and heating it over a gentle, steady fire of coals, until the yolks come together in the middle and the white collects round them and settles at the edges.

units.la: Haec Graecos Medicos oleo garoq; & vi‑no conspergenda esse,censuisse reperio, fri‑xisq; assis ac elixis vtiliora promisisse,sed a‑liter tamen praeparaffe. vbi notandum, per‑petuò moderatam in iis coctionem obser‑uandam esse. Vetustate vel incubatu magna ex parte deprauata virosa sunt & pessima, nec fine magna edentis ruina edi pollunt.
units.tr: I find that the Greek physicians thought these should be sprinkled with oil, garum and wine, and they promised more useful results from fried, roasted and boiled eggs, but prepared them otherwise. Here it should be noted that a moderate cooking must always be observed in these preparations. Eggs that are old or have been left to incubate are for the most part spoilt, poisonous and very bad, and they cannot be eaten without great harm to the eater.

units.la: Ad extremum, licet multarum, imò fere omnium auium oua sint esculenta, nulla ta‑men magis frequentiusq; rem cibariam ad‑iuuant quam gallinarum, hodieq; gallinarū Indicarum oua mirifice commendari coepe‑runt,caetera vix à vita lautiori attinguntur, nisi
units.tr: Finally, although the eggs of many, indeed almost all, birds are edible, none of them more frequently or more usefully supports the food supply than those of hens; and today the eggs of Indian hens have begun to be wonderfully recommended. Other eggs are scarcely taken up except in a more luxurious way of life,

units.la: Oua fe-bricitan-tibus ma-la,&c. nisi vel voluptatis gratia vel in aliorum penuria, vt anserina, anatumque, quae, licet minus probe nutriant, quam gallinacea, naturam tamen confortant, Veneremque proritant experimento.
units.tr: Eggs are bad for those with fevers, etc. except either for the sake of pleasure or in the lack of others, such as goose eggs and duck eggs, which, although they nourish less well than hen eggs, nevertheless strengthen the body and, as experience shows, stir up sexual desire.

units.la: De melle apum minorem notatu digna.
units.tr: Concerning the honey of bees, some things worth noting.

units.la: NOn minorem esse mellis in esculentis auctoritatem atque praestantiam quam sacchari, ex multis omniq; ex parte homini vtiliffimis viribus atque dotibus, quas a natura obtinuit, manifestum est. Quin & veteribus in maximis fuisse delitiis, vt qui innumera escarum genera melle condiebant, multaque ex eo panificia ac potus concinnabant, in confesso est. Id quod hodie quoq; Septentrionis Sarmatiaeque populi in Moscouia, Lithuania, terrisque vicinis faciunt, vberrimus enim laudatissimi mellis apud eos prouentus est, quod apum mellificio ex floribus myricae, thymi, aliarumque arborum ac herbarum succo in alueariibus elaboratur, nec non in fyluis in arborum cauis atque petris etiam copiosissime colligitur, quod mel fylueftre propterea vocant. Laudatissimum autem ac optimum, praeter quod Hymettus Atticae regionis mons profert, in nominatis Sarmatiae regionibus prouenire testatur nobile illud ac celeberrimum,
units.tr: That honey has no less authority and excellence among foods than sugar is plain from the many and most useful powers and qualities which it has from nature, useful to man in every respect. Indeed it is agreed that it was among the greatest delights of the ancients as well, who seasoned countless kinds of food with honey and prepared many breads and drinks from it. The peoples of the North and of Sarmatia do the same today, in Muscovy, Lithuania and the neighbouring lands, for there is a very rich yield of their most praised honey. It is made by bees in hives from the juice of flowers of the tamarisk, thyme and other trees and herbs, and it is gathered most abundantly in the woods, in hollows of trees and in rocks too; for this reason they call it wild honey. The most praised and best honey, besides that which Mount Hymettus in the region of Attica produces, is said to come from those regions of Sarmatia, namely that noble and most famous

units.la: Qo 5 celebratissimum hydromel, quod tantopere ab omnibus expetitur, indeque in alia loca exportatur. Nam in tanto apud Moscoviae, vicinarumque terrarum Proceres honore est, vt generosis vinis etiam praeferre non vereantur, peregreque aduentantibus missisque legatis etiamnunc felicis ominis aduentusque ergo plenis id propinent cyathis, & quidem prima statim mensa.
units.tr: very famous hydromel, which is so greatly sought after by all and exported from there to other places. For it is held in such honour among the nobles of Muscovy and the neighbouring lands that they do not hesitate to prefer it even to fine wines; and when foreigners arrive or envoys are sent, they still pour it out in full cups for the sake of a happy omen and welcome, and indeed at the very first course.

units.la: Porro mel ψοφιμον esse, corporisque acanimi viribus reficiendis accommodatissimum, praeter experientiam grauissimi autores prodiderunt, cumprimis vero senibus & pituitosis naturis saluberrime estur, calidioribus vero, adolescentibus, aetateque florentibus & biliosis non aeque conuenit, facile enim iis in bilem vertitur. Gal. 2. de nat. facult. ex sententia Hipp. Unde Galenus in febribus hecticis à melli s vsu abstinendum suadet l. 10. de morbis cur. propterea quod protinus vertatur in bilem, & ficciores acriorisq; caloris reddat febres. Plin. l. 11. c. 12. 13. & seq. multa de melle scitu digna prodidit. Etl. 22. ca. 24. inquit, mellis natura talis est vt putrescere corpora non sinat, iucundo sapore atque non aspero, alia quam salis natura. Faucibus, tonsillis, anginae, omnibusque oris desideriis vtilissimum, atescentiq; in febrib. linguae &c. Haec Plin.
units.tr: Moreover, grave authors have written, besides their experience, that honey is [ψοφιμον] and most suitable for restoring the strength of body and mind. It is eaten most healthfully especially by the old and by phlegmatic natures, but it does not suit the hotter natures, the young, those in the flower of age, and the bilious, for it is easily turned into bile in them. Galen, On the natural faculties, book 2, follows Hippocrates. Hence Galen advises abstaining from honey in hectic fevers, in On the Cure of Diseases, book 10, because it is immediately turned into bile and makes the fevers drier and of sharper heat. Pliny, book 11, chapters 12 and 13 and following, has recorded many things about honey worth knowing. And in book 22, chapter 24, he says: the nature of honey is such that it does not allow bodies to rot, and it has a pleasant, not harsh, taste, unlike the nature of salt. It is most useful for the throat, the tonsils, quinsy, and all desires of the mouth, and in fevers when the tongue is dry, etc. Thus Pliny.

units.la: Columell. l. 11. scribit, exanimum corpus hominis per annos plurimos inoxium con-seruare. Et Plin. refert, Principatu Claudii se vidisse Hippocentaurum in Thessalia natu, ex Ægypto ad Imperatorem in melle allatū. Ante vero Plin. Xenophon in S. rerum grec. morem quandoque sepeliendi mortuos in melle, vt conseruarentur, extitisse tradidit, quod in 3. Lucret. intellexisse putatur, cum scribit,
units.tr: Columella, book 11, writes that honey preserves a dead human body harmlessly for many years. And Pliny reports that in the principate of Claudius he saw a Hippocentaur, born in Thessaly, brought from Egypt to the Emperor preserved in honey. Before Pliny, Xenophon, in his Greek history, handed down that at times the custom arose of burying the dead in honey so that they might be preserved; and Lucretius is thought to have understood this when he writes:

units.la: Aut in melle situm suffocari atq; rigere Frigore, cum in summo gelidi cubat aquore saxi.
units.tr: Or lying buried in honey, to be smothered and stiffened by cold, when it lies on the top of a cold rock in the sea.

units.la: Insigne quoque exemplum est 1. Sam. 14. quo probatur mellis vtilitas in viribus reficiendis & restaurandis. Cum enim Saul in bello, quod gessit contra Palæstinos graui edicto prohibuisset militibus ante vesperam & partam victoriam cibum vllum capere, Jonathan edicti illius ignarus fame impulsus mel quod in sylua quadam decurrebat, caeteris ab eo abstinentibus, degustauit, cuius esu oculi eius fuerunt illuminati, hoc est totius corporis vires inediâ fractæ ac debilitate fuerunt instauratæ. Nam vt inediâ oculi exiccantur atque excæcantur & caligant, ita cibo reficiuntur ac q. illuminantur. Est in exemplis Pollio Romulus, qui excedes annū centesimū, cū ab Aug. Imp. interrogaret, quanâ ratione maxime vigore illū animi corporisq; coseruassef, respodit, intus mulso, foris oleo, De-
units.tr: There is also a notable example in 1 Samuel 14, which proves the usefulness of honey in restoring and renewing strength. For when Saul, in the war he waged against the Philistines, had by a severe edict forbidden the soldiers to take any food before evening and until the victory was won, Jonathan, ignorant of that edict and driven by hunger, tasted honey which was flowing in a certain wood, while the others abstained from it. By eating it his eyes were enlightened; that is, the strength of his whole body, broken by fasting, was restored. For as fasting dries up and blinds the eyes and makes them dim, so food refreshes them and makes them bright again. Among the examples is Pollio Romulus, who passed the hundredth year. When the Emperor Augustus asked him by what method he had preserved the vigour of his mind and body so well, he replied: "Inwardly with mead, outwardly with oil."
