units.la: Democritus quoque Abderides senex, inʼ terrogatus, quanam ratione quispiam sane degeret, respondit, si interiora melle, exteriora oleo madefierent, melle enim ipsum plurimum delectatum tradunt, sicut & Pythagoram, qui cum frugalissime viueret, solo lepe melle fuit contentus.
units.tr: Democritus of Abdera, too, when asked as an old man by what method one might live in good health, replied: "If the inner parts are moistened with honey and the outer with oil." For they say that Democritus took the greatest delight in honey, just as Pythagoras did, who, though he lived most frugally, was content with only a little honey.

units.la: Cyrnios Sardiniam incolentes ideo diutius viuere quidam tradiderunt, quod ipsis mel perpetuum erat escarium. Vallerriola in locis suis comm. L. 3. melle, ob detergendi calefaciendiq; potestatem insignem, lenibus plurimo vtendum consulit, si modo illaesam senectam in multum aeui producere velint, idque probat Antiochi Medici & Telephi Grammatici exemplo, qui senes annosi, attico melle & pane plurimum vtebantur, Gal. f. de san. tuenda teste. Quin & ipse Saluator Christus à melli s vsu non abstinuit, testatur enim Lucas spectantibus post resurrectionem discipulis ipsum de mellis fauo comedisse, non quidem φυσικῶς, vt inquit Theophylactus, cibo enim non amplius indigebat, sed οἰκονομικῶς, nempe resurrectionis, & veri sui corporis confirmandi gratia. Non omittendum autem in hac de melle historia, Eudoxum Cindium apud Apollonium referre, in Aphrica quandam gentem esse, quae supra Syrtes & Chartaginem
units.tr: Some have written that the Cyrnians, who inhabit Sardinia, live longer because honey was their constant food. Valleriola, in his commentary on the places of Galen, book 3, advises that honey, because of its power to cleanse and warm, should be used plentifully by old people, if they wish to reach a great age with their old age unharmed. He proves this by the example of Antiochus the physician and Telephus the grammarian, who, being aged old men, used a great deal of Attic honey and bread, as Galen testifies in On the Preservation of Health. Indeed the Saviour Christ himself did not abstain from honey: Luke testifies that, in the sight of the disciples after the resurrection, he ate of a honeycomb, not indeed naturally [φυσικῶς], as Theophylact says, for he no longer needed food, but economically [οἰκονομικῶς], that is, for the sake of confirming the resurrection and the reality of his true body. Nor should we omit, in this history of honey, what Eudoxus of Cnidus reports in Apollonius: that in Africa there is a certain people living beyond the Syrtes and Carthage,

units.la: NB.
units.tr: NB.

units.la: Melarti-ciale. nem incolat, gyzanteres vocatam, hancque exercere artem, vt flores in istis locis colligat, melque ex iis ea copia & qualitate conficiat, vt apum æquet mellificium. Mellis quoque boni vel mali indicia minime præ-tereunda sunt: iudicaturautem optimum, suaue, acre, flauum, odoratum, modiceque pingue & tenue, vernum & æstiuum. Plinius scriptor inter latinos grauissimus lib. 11.ca.14. sensisse videtur, optimum mel Sirio exoriente produci, & proculdubio ex Aristotelis sententia, nam, vt Mercurialis l.2. variarum lectionum notauit, in vetustissimo Scipionis Carteromachi codice scripta reperitur, mel maxime tunc ab aere cadere, cum inter astra Sirius exoritur: eo namque tempore ardere terram, siccitatesque maioresinstare, unde rotis mellei vbertas generetur, nemo ignorat: vt ita consequens sit mellis prouentum maxime præmonstrare summas siccitates, in quibus maior mellis copia super herbas, quas depascuntur apes, abundare deprehenditur. Idem Plin. maxime laudabile mel esse scribit quod per se fluit vt oleum. Galenus 7.de morb.curand. optimi mellis indicia esse ait, si colore flauo est, odore suaui, tum purum adeo, vt totum pelluceat, guflantique acutum, iucundissimumque, tamque sibi cohærens, vt si digito attollatur, continuum sibi nec intercisum ad humum defluat. Despumatum quoque minus excrementofum elfe, frigido ventriculo optimum nutrimentum, magifq; nutrire idem alserit lib.eodem. Crudum enim aluum inflare tuffimq; laceflere deprehensum est. Coquendum est autem supra prunas aut arida ligna fine fumo, ac probe despumandum. Vnde tutior etiam eius in medicinis est vsus, medicique ad occurrendum corruptionibus, putredinemq; compescendam in mellis vsu sunt audaciores.
units.tr: Of artificial honey. ... a people called Gyzanteres, who practise the art of gathering flowers in those places and make honey from them in such quantity and quality that it rivals the work of bees. The signs of good and bad honey must also not be passed over. The best is judged to be sweet, pungent, yellow, fragrant, moderately thick and thin, and spring or summer honey. Pliny, the most serious of the Latin writers (Nat. Hist. 11.14), seems to have held that the best honey is produced at the rising of Sirius, and doubtless this follows Aristotle's opinion. For, as Mercurialis noted in the second book of his Variae lectiones, it is found written in the most ancient codex of Scipio Carteromachus that honey falls most abundantly from the air when Sirius rises among the stars. At that time the earth burns and greater droughts threaten, and no one is unaware that this is why the abundance of honeydew is produced. So it follows that the yield of honey especially indicates the greatest droughts, since a greater quantity of honey is found over the herbs on which the bees feed. Pliny also writes that the most praiseworthy honey is that which flows of its own accord, like oil. Galen (On the Curing of Diseases, book 7) says the signs of the best honey are: a yellow colour, a sweet smell, and such purity that it is wholly transparent; sharp and most pleasant to the taste; and so cohesive that, if it is lifted with a finger, it falls to the ground in an unbroken, continuous thread. He also says that skimmed honey, having less excrement, is the best nourishment for a cold stomach, and in the same book he asserts that it nourishes better. For raw honey is found to inflate the belly and to irritate it greatly. It must be cooked over embers or dry wood without smoke, and skimmed thoroughly. Hence its use in medicines is also safer, and physicians are bolder in using honey to meet corruptions and to check putrefaction.

units.la: Ad extremum non ignorandum, esse adhuc alia duo mellis genera, vnam Saccharum vocatum Indi, quod India fert & f. lix Arabia, mel videlicet in arundinib. concretum gummi aut falis modo candidum ac friabile, vnde Megafthenes græcus Indiam mel,fine apum opificio gignere tradit: alterum ab aeris rore ἀερόμελι id est mel roscidum aut aerium, ab hebr.manna, latin. ros Syriacus dicitur, quoniam interdiu sublato æstiui solis vapore in aera, qui tandem serenæ nocti frigore concretus,in Syria & monte Libani, Neapolis,in Oenotria campo, ac Calabria, antelucano tempore supra saxa, aut laricis arboris,aut thymi,aliarumq; plantarum folia destillat, id collectum inq; massam globulosue effictum ad vsum seponitur. De hoc plura legantur apud Galenum, 3.de alim.& 4. de comp.med. secundum loca: Athen.l ii.
units.tr: Finally, it should not be forgotten that there are two other kinds of honey. One, which India and Arabia produce, the Indians call saccharum: honey found in reeds, white and friable, hardened like gum or salt. Hence the Greek Megasthenes reports that India produces honey without the work of bees. The other is from the dew of the air, called aerómeli, that is, honeydew or aerial honey; in Hebrew it is called manna, and in Latin ros. Because during the day, when the summer heat of the sun has drawn it up into the air, and then at night it condenses in the cold of the clear sky, it drips before dawn onto rocks, or onto the leaves of the larch, the thyme and other plants, in Syria and on Mount Lebanon, at Naples, in the plain of Oenotria, and in Calabria. It is collected, formed into a mass or into little globules, and set aside for use. More on this may be read in Galen, On Foods, book 3, and in his On the Composition of Medicines, book 4, according to places; and in Athenaeus, book 2.

units.la: Sardiniam, quod praeterire nefas est, ex apum ab sinthii pabulo mel amarum, Hera-cleam vero ponti ob herbas noxias virulentum proferre autores non protarii tradunt: mellis autem ita venenati indicia esse, si omnino non densatur, si color magis rutilus est, odor alienus, sternutamenta protinus movens, quod ponderosius innoxio, & qui ederunt si humi se abiiciunt quaerentes refrigerationem, Plin. li. 21. c. 13. scriptum reliquit, vbi quoq; remedium mellis venenati aic esse multum vetus e melle optimo & rutha, salsamenta etiam crebro sumta.
units.tr: It would be wrong to pass over that the authors, not unskilled, report that the bees in Sardinia, feeding on wormwood, produce bitter honey, and that at Heraclea on the Black Sea, on account of noxious herbs, they produce poisonous honey. The signs of such poisoned honey are: if it does not thicken at all; if its colour is more reddish; if its smell is foreign; if it at once provokes sneezing; and if it is heavier than harmless honey. Those who eat it throw themselves on the ground, seeking to cool down. Pliny left this written in book 21, chapter 13, where he also says that the remedy for poisonous honey is very old honey of the best quality, taken with rue, and salted foods taken often.

units.la: Hactenus de variis cibis & alimentis ad vitam prorogandam conseruandamque necessariis.
units.tr: So far concerning the various foods and nourishments necessary for prolonging and preserving life.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAP. XXI.

units.la: De Condimentis.
units.tr: On Condiments.

units.la: OPtimum cibi condimentum esse fa-mem, potionis sitim, Cicero l.1.de finibus scribit: Et certe melius habent, qui ita simpliciter cibos suos condiunt, quam qui saccharo, pipere vel garyophyllis, sine quibus millia gentium elegant ter & feliciter vixerunt ac etiamnunc degunt. Sunt enim Condimenta aliud nihil quam gulæ irritamenta, quæ ad condi‐enda obsonia fiunt, græcis ὀψωνήματα dicta & ἀρτύματα. Varia autem olim fuisse condimentorum genera in confesso est, vt garum, muriam, oxigarum, sinapidium, &c. Verum singula ea pertractare immensum foret, præcipua saltem, quæque in vita humana magis necessaria, quorumque vires compertæ habentur, attingam, qualia sunt sal, mel, saccharum, acetum.
units.tr: Cicero, in the first book of De finibus, writes that hunger is the best seasoning for food and thirst for drink. Certainly those fare better who season their food simply in this way than those who use sugar, pepper or cloves, without which thousands of nations have lived long and happily and still live. Condiments are nothing other than incitements to the palate, made to season dishes, and called in Greek opsōnēmata and artymata. It is agreed that there were once various kinds of condiments, such as garum, muria, oxygarum, sinapidium and others. To treat each of them individually would be endless, so I will touch only on the chief ones, those most necessary in human life and whose powers are known: salt, honey, sugar and vinegar.

units.la: De Sale notatu & lectu dignissima.
units.tr: On Salt, most worthy of notice and reading.

units.la: Principem inter condimenta locum merito obtinet Sal, vt, sine quo vita humanior degere non possit, adeoque, vt ait Plin. l. 30. c. 7. necessarium elementum sit, vt transierit intellectus ad voluptates animi quoque: nam ita salès appellantur, omnisque vitæ lepos & summa hilaritas laborumque requies non alio magis vocabulo constat, vnde etiam gratiarum nomen salibus à nonnullis impositum videtur, eo quod sales in suauitatem, cibi necessitatem conuertant.
units.tr: Salt rightly holds the first place among condiments. Without it life cannot be lived in a civilised way, and so, as Pliny says in book 30, chapter 7, it is a necessary element, so that the mind passes on to the pleasures of the spirit as well. For salt is called sales, and all the charm of life, the highest cheerfulness and the rest from labours are expressed by no other word. Whence some seem to have given the name of "graces" to salts, because salts turn the necessity of food into pleasantness.

units.la: Cum igitur Sale & Sole, eodem te fte, vtilius corporibus nihil fit, adq; excitandum sopitum ac deperditum cibariorum saposaporem, ac putredinem arcendā, ac diuturniorem carnium pisciumque inprimis conseruationem Sal præcipue conferat, & in vniuersum memorandos mortalibus præstet vsus, merito condimentum iucundissimum, atque adeo obsoniorum & condimentorum obsonium ac condimentum, quibus suauitatem conciliat, censebitur.
units.tr: Since nothing is more useful to bodies than salt and the sun, and since salt in particular helps to rouse the dulled and lost savour of food, to ward off putrefaction, and to preserve meat and fish for longer, and generally offers uses worth remembering for mortals, it is rightly reckoned the most pleasant condiment, and indeed the relish and seasoning of relishes and condiments, since it gives them their agreeableness.

units.la: Quare facti & intulsi plane sunt, qui à sale abstinent, insulsoque pane vtuntur & cibo, quod de sacerdotibus Ægyptiis Plutarchus s. sympos. probl. 10. prodidit, ii enim à salis vsu omnino abstinuerunt, forsan ob hanc causam, vt Lemnius quoque l. 2. ca. 36. de nat. miracul. notauit, quod Venerem irritare persuasum haberent: quapropter insipida potius sumenda existimabant, quam condimento omnium vulgatissimo vti & iucundissimo. Sed an satis valetudini consuluerint, (cum à corporibus hominum pu trilaginem sal arceat, humores alienos ex crementitiosque absorbeat, ac esculenta quæuis sapida reddat gustuiqe grata) dici non potest, sed potius nimis superstitiosè id eos obseruasse statuendum est. Adde quod fœcunditatem conferat, seu fœcunditatis progignendæque sobolis, atque sterilitatis expugnandæ vis sali insit, præter experien tiam eruditiores quosdam literis mandasse, certis enim rationibus persuasum habent,
units.tr: Hence there have been people who abstain from salt and eat unseasoned bread and food. Plutarch, in the Symposiacs, problem 10, reports this of the Egyptian priests, who abstained from the use of salt altogether, perhaps for this reason, which Lemnius also noted in book 2, chapter 36, De natura miraculorum: they were persuaded that it stirred up Venus. Therefore they thought unseasoned things should be taken rather than using the most common and most pleasant of condiments. But whether they consulted their health well enough cannot be said, since salt keeps putrid matter from bodies, absorbs foreign and excrementitious humours, and makes any food tasty and pleasing to the palate. It must rather be judged that they observed this too superstitiously. Add that salt has a power of fecundity, or of promoting fertility and bringing forth offspring, and of overcoming sterility. Besides experience, some more learned men have committed this to writing, for they are persuaded on certain grounds that

units.la: Pp multmulieres obesas, quae magna ex parte sunt steriles & effoetae moderato salis in cibis vsu fecundas fieri conceptuiq; idoneas, abstergere enim sic omnem vliginem, matricemque plus iusto vdam madidamque exiccare, efficereque vt genitale semen firmius vtero adhaerescat: Viris quoq; tentiginem moue-re lumbosq; excitare, testantur populi salitis tum carnibus tum piscibus marinis crebrius vtentes, idq; nullam aliam ob causam euenire affirmant quam mordacis caliditatis ratione. Accedit & illud fecunditatis inducendae argumentum, quod immensa vis murium in marinis nauibus soleat procreari, & quod mulieres salinariae continenter pruriant, multarumq; prolium sint feraces. Hinc quoque in nonnullis regionibus coloniiamentorum pabulo nonnihil inspergunt salis, quo sint ad cibum auidiores, gignenduq; magis alacres & erecti: agros deniq; steriles, vbi plus aequo palustres iunt & vliginosi, feraces effici illius confperfu experientia compertum habetur. Exiccandi autem, abstergendi, corporaque nimia humiditate luxuriantia à putredine conseruandi, in sale vis vel hoc vno quoq; illustrior euadit, quod cum Aegyptii plures haberent modos, quibus mortuos à putredine conseruarent immunes, primus tamen omnium atq; etiam frequentius vsurpatus fuit,
units.tr: obese women, who are for the most part sterile and worn out, become fertile and fit for conception through a moderate use of salt in their food. For it wipes away all moisture and dries the womb, which is too moist and wet, and makes the genital seed cling more firmly to the womb. Peoples who eat salted meats and sea fish more often testify that it also stirs lust in men and excites the loins, and they affirm that this happens for no other reason than the biting heat of salt. Add also this argument for inducing fertility: an immense number of mice is usually bred in sea-going ships, and women who work in salt-pans are continually lustful and fruitful in many offspring. Hence, too, in some regions they sprinkle a little salt on the fodder of livestock, so that they are keener on food and more lively and vigorous for breeding. Finally, experience has shown that barren fields, where there is too much marsh and wetness, are made fertile by sprinkling with it. But the power of salt to dry, wipe away and preserve bodies from putrefaction, when they abound with excess moisture, is made clearer still by this one thing: although the Egyptians had several methods by which they kept the dead free from putrefaction, the first and most frequently used of all

units.la: quifolo constabat sale, vnde etiam merito condire corpora dicebatur salire, & condita ⸗⸗⸗, vt notauit Merc. l. 3. variar. lect. c. 2. Idem Plutarchi sententiam iuste emendat in quest. nat. de carnib. salib. asserentis sal & salsa ad pinguefacienda corpora maxime valere, cum sal extenuandi potius quam crassefaciendi facultate præditum esse experientia comprobet, dulcia vero plus in corporibus crassefaciendis valere, salsorum autem vsum esse, sua siccitate aperiendique vialimentum ad partes nutriendas perferre. Caeterum non prætereundum, quod Lan-giusepist. 27. etiam ex Athen. l. 10. annotauit, apud veterum conuiuas non illaudata olim fuisse consuetudinem, vt qui gryphum propositum dissoluere non posset, is poculum salsuginis humore mixtum vno exhaurire spiritu cogeretur.
units.tr: consisted of salt alone. Whence bodies were rightly said to be "salted," and "preserved" (condita), as Mercerus noted in book 3, chapter 2 of his Variae lectiones. The same writer rightly corrects Plutarch's opinion in the Quaestiones naturales on salted meats, where Plutarch asserted that salt and salty things are very effective in fattening bodies. Experience proves that salt has the power of thinning rather than thickening, while sweet things are more effective in thickening bodies, and the use of salty things, by its dryness and opening power, carries the nourishment to the parts to be nourished. Moreover, it should not be passed over what Langius also noted in Epistle 27, following Athenaeus, book 10: among the ancient banqueters there was once a custom not without praise, that whoever could not untie a knot set before him was compelled to drain at one breath a cup mixed with salty brine.

units.la: Qui hodie salem poculis inspergunt (vtinam vero id fieret crebrius, minus enim tunc noxæ fœculenta vina bibentes contra-herent) ideo id factitare intelligo, vt, si vi-num sit fœculentum, saliddepuret, non modo enim vini fœculentiam ob grauitate suam trahit in fundum, & à corruptione niiaq; æstus ebullitione præseruat, sed etiam longe salubrius quàm sulphur efficit. Vnde torcularia marina aqua eluere & irrigare suadent: Græci quoq; & Romani, vt vinum
units.tr: Those who today sprinkle salt into their cups (would that they did so more often, for then those who drink turbid wines would incur less harm), I understand do this so that, if the wine is muddy, the salt may clear it. For salt not only draws the turbidity of the wine down to the bottom by its weight, and preserves it from corruption and the heat of fermentation, but also works far more healthily than sulphur. Hence sea-presses advise washing and soaking them with seawater. The Greeks and Romans too, to make their wine clearer and more refined, mixed must boiled down to a third with seawater or brine in a fixed measure, as Columella rightly says in book 3, where the method of boiling is also given.

units.la: Pp 2 desoc defæcatius ac delicatius redderent, mustum aquâ maris aut muria ad tertias vsque deco-ƈta certa mensura miscebant, reste Columel. l. 3. vbi quoque modus decoctionis traditur. Ob eam vero causam sale multum reddi defæcatius quidam existimant, quod salis liquor vini fæculentiam ei implicitam sua terrestri grauitate in fundum cadi velut hypostasin trahat, quam tamen rationem ab aliis improbari video, obiicientibus salis pinguedinem, ob quam enatare potius debebat quam subsidere. Verum plus terræ quam aeris sali inęsse paruulus eius grumus in vino vel aqua subsidens clare demonstrat cum vter oleo plenus emergat. Huc commode quoque referri potest, quare potatores sale frequentius vtantur inter bibendum, & an bene hoc ipso sibi prospiciant, vbi responderi potest ex salis natura, ideo, hoc ipsos facere, quia compererunt sal tor-pentem ventriculi excitare appetentiam, stomachique fastidium tollere, testante etiam Plin. l. 31. cap. 9. & Plutarch l. de causna-tur. 3. tum vt illa salsugo stimulet naturam ad celeriorem excretionem, ne videlicet vt ramque tres nimium distendantur. Ad extremum, quoniam salis natura est, vt exprædictis patet corporum, quibus inspergitur & adnoetur superfluos humores extenuare, ac dirigere, ipsa quoq; corpora in sese cogere, alliga. ligare & condensare, consequens est, ipsà et-iam experientia suffragante, arida sale asper-sa cibis inepta fieri, vt si quis lepores sale as-feruare tentet, edentibus admodum noxios reddet: sues contra bene saginatæ obesæq; summam à sale accipiunt commendatio-nem: pilces quoque mollis carnis, excre-mentisque vaccuos ad saliendum ineptos de-prehendes, cuiusmodi sunt saxatiles. Gran-diores vero humidioresque idonei sunt du-rantque sale conditi per secula. Quanto enim pituitosiores, humidiores, excremen-tosioresque carnes extiterint, tanto ad sali-endum sunt aptiores, id quod de cæteris o-mnibus cibariis intellexisse lectorem velim.
units.tr: For this reason some think that salt makes wine much clearer, because the liquid of salt draws the turbidity entangled in the wine down to the bottom of the cask, like a sediment, by its earthy weight. Others, I see, reject this reasoning, objecting to the fatness of salt, on account of which it ought rather to float than settle. But that salt contains more earth than air is clearly shown by its tiny grain sinking in wine or water, whereas a bladder full of air rises. Here it can also conveniently be considered why drinkers use salt more often while they drink, and whether they thereby take good care of themselves. To this it can be answered from salt's nature: they do it because they have found that salt rouses the sluggish stomach to appetite and removes its distaste, as Pliny (book 31, chapter 9) and Plutarch (De causis naturalibus 3) also testify; and also so that its saltiness stimulates nature to quicker excretion, lest both belly and veins be stretched too much. Finally, since it is the nature of salt, as shown above, to thin and carry off superfluous humours in the bodies it is sprinkled on and mixed with, and also to bind, compact and condense the bodies themselves, it follows, experience also supporting this, that food sprinkled with dry salt becomes unfit. If someone tries to keep hares with salt, he makes them very harmful to those who eat them. Pigs, on the other hand, when well fattened and obese, receive the highest commendation for salting. You will also find that fish of soft flesh and empty of excrement are unfit for salting, such as rock fish. The larger and moister ones are suitable, and they last preserved in salt for ages. For the more phlegmatic, moister and excrementitious the meats are, the more apt they are for salting, and I would have the reader understand this of all other foods as well.

units.la: Quapropter æstate modicum salis vsum prodesse experimentis quotidianis comper-tum est, sicut hieme, terris naturisque frigi-dioribus & pituitosioribus, obesioribus & crassioribus liberalior vsus haud noxius est: atrabiliarios vero, macros, graciles & calidi-ores præter modum sumtus lædit, adurit at-que resiccat. Vnde pessimus in corporibus ipsorum conducitur inquilinus Scorbutus, maritimis accolis, crebriusque ac quotidie ferè salsamentis salitisq; cum carnibus cum piscibus vescentibus peculiaris, gingiuas primo & pedes inficiens, pluribus latenter lethalis, præcipuè vero fœminarum choro.
units.tr: Therefore, in summer, daily experience has found that a moderate use of salt is beneficial, just as in winter a more liberal use is harmless for cold and phlegmatic lands and natures, and for the more obese and thick-set. But it harms, burns and dries those who are melancholic, lean, slender and of hotter temperament when taken beyond measure. Hence the worst lodger that settles in their bodies is scurvy, peculiar to seaside dwellers and to those who eat salted goods and salted meats and fish almost every day. It infects the gums first and then the feet, and it is latently lethal to many, especially to the female sex.

units.la: Nouiin Dania Nobiles vere fœminas eo extindtas, quæ sale maceratis piscibus carni-bufq; admodum delectabantur, ac crebrius vescebantur. Certissimum est exta & viscera vitiari ac tabescere, oraq; cum anima grave illius virus exhalare ex salsamentorum omnis generis immodico visu. Ergo sal, qui defunctorum corpora per secula a putrefactione vindicat, viuentia corrumpit ac enecat.
units.tr: Are you not aware that in Denmark noble women have been carried off by this very thing? They took great delight in fish and meat macerated in salt and ate them very often. It is most certain that the entrails and viscera are spoiled and decay, and that a foul poison exhales from the mouth and breath with the excessive consumption of every kind of salted food. So salt, which preserves the bodies of the dead from putrefaction for ages, corrupts and kills the living.

units.la: Viri quia in exercitamentis sunt impigriores, lentius scorbuto inficiuntur. Qui noui orbis res literis mandarunt, aiunt Nigritas sale valetudinem tueri, & pene cum auro æquare.
units.tr: Men, because they are more active in their exercises, are less quickly infected by scurvy. Those who have committed the affairs of the New World to writing say that the Negroes keep their health by means of salt, and almost value it equal to gold.

units.la: Et tantum de sale, quod salso Arist. putauit frigore & humore dissolui, calido ac sicco cogi, cu calido & humido quoq; eliquescat, nă raphano aspersus, aut si raphani, q natura calidus est & humidus, frusta salis aceruo indeteris, sal totus liquescet. Vide Langium in epist. 18 Plura de salis natura, conficiendi illius ratione singulari, visu ac differentiis, tu etiam herbis quibusdam maritimis salsugi-nofo succo imbutis, & ex quibus sal elicitur, inueniet lector apud Lemnium l. 3. de naturæ occult. mirac. c. 9. Plin. l. 31. c. 7. & 9. Plutarch. y. symposf. probl. 10. & 4. symp. probl. 4.
units.tr: And so much for salt. Aristotle thought that salt is dissolved by cold and moisture and hardened by heat, but it also melts with heat and moisture. For if salt is sprinkled on a radish, or if pieces of salt are thrown into a heap of radishes, which by nature are hot and moist, the whole of the salt will melt. See Langius, in epistle 18. The reader will find more on the nature of salt, its special method of preparation, its kinds and differences, and also on certain maritime herbs imbued with a salty juice from which salt is drawn, in Lemnius, book 3, On the Occult Miracles of Nature, chapter 9; Pliny, book 31, chapters 7 and 9; Plutarch, Symposiacs, book 9 problem 10, and book 4 problem 4.

units.la: De Melle & Saccharo.
units.tr: On Honey and Sugar.

units.la: De mellis natura & viribus dictum est c. praecedente inter ea quae ab animalibus proveniunt. Hodie vice eius vsurpari plurimum coepit saccharum, maximaque in tribu medicorum id excitavit lites, quas tandem Lusitanorum ac Hispanorum nauigationes ac negotiationes cum Alexandriae, nouaeque Indiae incolis videntur fedasse. Vix autem explicare est, quantum ad condimenta obsoniaque expetatur, adeo ventri gulaeq; exotica magis placent, domesticaque vero vbiq; sordent, vnde fit, vt mel, quia vbique fere prouenit, & vltro se porrigit, minoris nunc quam olim sit auctoritatis, licet viribus, facultateque tum cibariatum medica saccharo non cedat. Porro de saccharii natura variae fuerunt eruditorum opiniones, & praesertim Mauritanorum sententiae mire euariarunt. Constat tamen inter omnes, calidae, humectantis, abstergentisq; naturae esse, multaque praestare melle inualidius, idemque plurima posse validius. Et vno dicā verbo, omnium saporum videri potest dominitor, acria leniendo, acida retundendo, falsa suauiora reddendo, asperaque vincendo, acerba mitigando, fatuis & insipidis sensum tribuendo. Astate & in tempe ramentis calidioribus verti in bilem, obstructionibusq; nimiu ei vsum implicare
units.tr: The nature and powers of honey were discussed in the preceding chapter, among the things that come from animals. Nowadays sugar has begun to be used in its place to a great extent, and this has stirred up the greatest quarrels among the tribe of physicians, quarrels which the voyages and trade of the Portuguese and Spaniards with Alexandria and the inhabitants of the New India seem at last to have befouled. It is hard to explain how much is sought after for seasonings and delicacies, so greatly do exotic things please the belly and palate, while domestic ones are everywhere despised. Hence it comes that honey, because it is found almost everywhere and offers itself freely, is now of less esteem than formerly, although in power and efficacy, both as food and as medicine, it is not inferior to sugar. Moreover, the opinions of learned men about the nature of sugar have been various, and especially the views of the Moors vary wonderfully. Yet all agree that it is of a hot, moistening and cleansing nature, and that in many respects it surpasses honey, while in many things it is able to do more strongly. To say it in one word, it can be seen to be the master of all flavours: it softens sharp things, blunts sour ones, makes salty things sweeter, overcomes harshness, mitigates bitterness, and gives sense to dull and insipid things. In summer, and in hotter constitutions, it is turned into bile, and excessive use of it entangles one in obstructions.

units.la: Pp 4 vitaeviscera proditum reperio, pulmonibus tamen vesicæque, gutturi atque trachææ aiteriæ vtile ac salutare, sed dentibus inimicissimum, quibus nigredinem, rubiginem inducit ac mobilitatem, quare ab eius esu os colluendum quidam docuerunt. Vires porro pro coctura ratione atque differentia sortiri constat. Quo enim coctum exactius est, eo calere magis arbitrantur.
units.tr: I find it reported that it is good for the vital organs, and indeed useful and healthy for the lungs, bladder, throat, windpipe and arteries, but most hostile to the teeth, which it blackens, rusts and loosens. For this reason some have taught that the mouth should be rinsed after eating it. Moreover, it is agreed that its powers depend on the manner and degree of its cooking: the more thoroughly it is cooked, the more they think it heats.

units.la: Pistores dulciarios in varia panificiorum genera saccharum digerere, nec non Seplasiarios varias ei figuras effigiesque tribuere, totque eo incrustari ad delitias feminina, & vno verbo, nihil hodie pene sine saccharo condiri, inque eo monstrificum plane esse gulæ ingenium plusquam notum est. Panificiis additur, vinis miscetur, aqua eo suavior efficitur salubriorque, carnes eodem asperguntur & piscés, nec non oua crebrius quam sale. Eruditi palati homines præstantissimas eas escas putant, quæ suapte natura placent absque eiusmodi exoticis condimentis.
units.tr: Pastry-cooks work sugar into all kinds of bread, and sugar-workers give it various shapes and figures, and women are decked out with so many sweets for their delight. In a word, scarcely anything nowadays is seasoned without sugar, and it is more than known how monstrous the nature of gluttony is in this respect. It is added to bread, mixed with wines; water is made sweeter and more wholesome by it; meats and fish are sprinkled with it, and eggs more often than with salt. Men of refined palate think those the most excellent foods which please by their own nature, without such exotic seasonings.

units.la: De aceto, eiusdem vsu ac viribus in cibo & potu, sitiq; restinguenda.
units.tr: On vinegar, its use and powers in food and drink, and for quenching thirst.

units.la: Mirum certe, & vini cereuisiæque vitium transfire in alimentum. Est enim nihil aliud acetum quam vinum vel cereuisia vetustate corruptum, & in acidi liquoris saporem conuersum:
units.tr: Surely it is a remarkable thing that the fault of wine and beer passes over into food. For vinegar is nothing other than wine or beer spoiled by age and turned into the taste of a sour liquor.

units.la: Præclaré autem cibos & sapores quosdá commendabiles reddit atque sapidos, proximumq; à sale in conseruandis eduliis tenet locum, at non tam vi diuturna, nisi enim postaliquot menses priori effuso recens re- bus conditiis affundatur, mucore limoque obducuntur. Vires eius in medicorum scho- la excitauerunt controuersias. Omnes ta- men vel maior pars vim ei tribuit refrige- randi, repellendi, exiccandi, penetrandique.
units.tr: It makes foods and certain flavours agreeable and tasty, and it holds the next place to salt in preserving edibles; but not by lasting force, for unless it is poured off after some months and fresh vinegar is poured on the preserved things, they are covered with mould and slime. Its powers have aroused controversies in the schools of physicians. Yet all, or the greater part, ascribe to it the power of cooling, repelling, drying and penetrating.

units.la: Qui tamen absolute frigidum id cótendunt, hallucinantur. Plinius lib. 23. c. 1. summam ei vim esse in refrigerando, nec minoré difcu- tiendi affirmat, vnde terræ infusum spuma- re, medicosque nescium, quantum aspides contra polleret, ab aspide enim calcata per- cussum vtrem aceti ferentem, quoties depo- suffet, idem illæso aliâs similem.
units.tr: Those who maintain that it is absolutely cold are mistaken. Pliny, book 23, chapter 1, affirms that its chief power lies in cooling, and no less in dispersing; hence when it is poured on the ground it foams, and he says that physicians do not know how much it avails against asps. For when an asp has trampled on and pierced a skin carrying vinegar, whenever the vinegar has been poured out, the asp, otherwise unharmed, is similarly affected.

units.la: Sed mirabile & hoc in eo exemplum, quod idem addit. Nam M. Agrippa lupremis suis annis conflictatus graui pedum morbo, cum dolorem illum perpeti nequiret, vnius me- dicorum portentosa scientia, ignorante D. Augusto, tanti putauit vsu pedum sensuque omni carere, dummodo & doloreillo care- ret, demersis in acetum calidum cruribus in acerrimo impetu morbi. Galen. lib. 10. de morbis curand. acetum, omnium, quæ nota sunt, potestate refrigerantium tenuissimarum esse partium, admixtamque aliquam sibi caliditatem habere, propterea corpora, quae contingit, exiccare, scriptum reliquit, unde in iis affectibus, inquit, qui refrigerationem postulant & humectationem, non solo aceto vtendum, sed aquae frigidae tantum adminiscendum, vt bibi possit. Haec Galen. Quapropter immodicti aceti vsum cerebro nerui sque siccitatem inferre, semnumqueExcutere, pallorem inducere, exangues; reddere inficiari nemo potest, quia humorem omnem natiuum exiccando absorbet. Modicus contra eius vsus ad condimenta & intinctus stomacho vtilis est, fastidia enim discutit, singultus cohibet, & sternutamenta olfactu, testante Plin. Unde Seruius, & potu & fotu stomacho conducit acetum. Dioscorides quoque vini aceti dicit esse εὐστομαχὴν li. 5. c. 11. Hippocrates atram bilem parere inq; massam attollere, biliosis vero salubre affert lib. 3. de rat. victus acut. Et ibidem tamen Galenus quartanis ad incidendum & attenuandum dari meminit. Quod idem 14. de morb. curand. expresse his verbis significauit, siquidem, inquit, aceti vis modo eo quis modice & debito tempore vtatur, salutaris eiusmodi affectibus est, (loquitur autem de scirrhosis) ceu tenaces ac crassos humores dissecans ac resoluens, sin vel immoderatius vel in tempore non idoneo, tenuiores nuiores partes violenter absumens quod re- liquum est finit lapidescere. Sed fi quis eo diutius vtatur,ipsam neruorum substantiam delibauerit. Obid igitur nec sæpe,ac inter initia,nec longo tempore, medicamentis ex aceto ad ligamenta & tendines vtendum: at in liene & carnosis musculi partibus fcirrho affectis tutus eius vsus est. Hæc Galenus.
units.tr: But this too is a wonderful example, which he adds. Marcus Agrippa, struggling in his last years with a severe gout in the feet, could not bear that pain. So, at the height of the attack, and with the Emperor Augustus unaware, a physician of prodigious skill thought it worth losing the use and all sensation of his feet, provided he was also rid of that pain, and had his legs plunged into hot vinegar. Galen, in book 10 of On Curing Diseases, has left it written that vinegar, of all things known, has the greatest power of cooling, being made of the finest parts and having some heat mixed in with it; therefore it dries the bodies it touches. Hence in those affections, he says, which require cooling and moistening, one must use not vinegar alone but only cold water, so that it can be drunk. Thus Galen. Therefore no one can deny that immoderate use of vinegar brings dryness to the brain and nerves, induces drowsiness and paleness, and makes people bloodless, since by drying up all their natural moisture it absorbs it. A moderate use of it, on the other hand, in seasonings and dips, is useful to the stomach: it dispels loathing, checks hiccups, and provokes sneezing by its smell, as Pliny attests. Hence Servius says that vinegar benefits the stomach both as a drink and as a fomentation. Dioscorides too says that wine vinegar is good for the stomach [εὐστομαχὴν], book 5, chapter 11. Hippocrates says that it produces black bile and raises it up into the mass, but brings health to the bilious, in book 3 of On the Regimen in Acute Diseases. And yet Galen, in the same place, mentions that it is given to quartan patients for cutting and thinning. He signified the same expressly in book 14 of On Curing Diseases, in these words: "If indeed the power of vinegar is used moderately and at the proper time, it is healthful for affections of this kind" (he speaks of scirrhous tumours), "as dissecting and loosening thick and gross humours. But if it is used too immoderately or at an unsuitable time, violently consuming the thinner and finer parts, what remains ends by turning to stone. And if anyone uses it for longer, he will have impaired the very substance of the nerves. Therefore vinegar medicines should neither be applied often, nor at the start, nor for a long time, to ligaments and tendons; but in the spleen and in the fleshy parts of muscles affected with scirrhus its use is safe." Thus Galen.

units.la: Alii, quanto fuerit acrius,tanto minus frigi- dæ naturæ esse contendunt, acoremque il- lum & mordacitatem saccharo aut vuis paf- fis in eo decoctis corrigunt. Ruellius in Diofcoridem cap.11.lib. f. asserit, acetum crassis partibus,fæcibus,seu fæci proportio- ne respondentibus calidum esse, tenuibus vero partibus frigidum, idque magis quam calidum,aut forte frigidum per fe, calidum vero per accidens:& quo acrius est,minusq; vini naturam & qualitates repræsentat, tan- to tenuium magis esse partium idem affir- mat. Vide quoque Galenum lib.1. fimplic. lib.de compofit.medic. per gen. & lib.1.2.& 6.de comp.med. per part. Experientia quoq; vires aceti manifestat. Nam fi ouum in acerrimo aceto triduo maceretur, aut plus paulò,testa in eam teneritatem mollescit, vt veluttenuis membrana per annuli adiga- tur angustiam. Quin & coticula, aut silex aceto septem dierum spatio iniectus digiti attritu in puluerem redigitur. Hinc Hannibal Alpes sibi peruias faciens Italiaeque inhians feruenti aceto saxa dissoluere ac dissilire coegit. Vnde sanè penetrabilis aceti visconspicitur, quâ saxa etiam corrodit & comminuit, & margaritae resoluuntur in tabem. Sed & venenis resistit potenter, valeatque aduersus omnium aculeatorum animalium ictus, morsusque venenatos, necnon pruritus vlceraque manantia, testante etiam Plinio. Quare non inconsulto faciunt, qui, grassante morbo populari & pestilenti modicum aceti vsum sibi reddunt familiarem, dissipat enim ac discutit vitiosum aerem, & si quid in corpus est haustum, prohibet humores infici ac putrescere, astu quoq; in corpore vehementiorem infigniter arcet. Verum ne cerebro neruorum principio ipsisq; neruis sit nocumento, prudentiores aquam rosaceam admisceri iubent, pauxillumq; vini Rhenani, ac croci momentum, sic enim minus capiti incommodare experti sunt. Porro Romanos in expeditionibus suis eo vsos plurimum fuisse constat, vt mirum non sit (id quod nonnulli in admirationem trahunt) quod Suetonius scribat, Asiaticum Vitellii Imperatoris libertum, Puteolis poscam vendidisse, quoniam is potus non solum medicum in vsum, intus & extra adhiberetur, sed etiam, cum milites, vilisque plebecula illo in quotidiano victu in magnis praepræsertim caloribus vterentur,infignitere-nim refrigerat & humectar. Fit autem exa-ceto vel vinoacido & aqua. Secundum ve-teres concinnatur ex aquæ partibus ii,& vi-ni acidi part. 3. Ita hæc temperanda sunt, vt possint bibi. M. Catonem in militia fem-per aquam b b ffe ferunt, nisi quando fitie-bat ardentius, tunc enim acetum potasse le-gimus. Mirum itaque non est, milites Rom. Christo sitienti acetum porrexisse. Et hodie quoque milites acetum semper secum ferre consueuerunt.
units.tr: Others contend that the sharper it is, the less cold its nature is, and they correct its sourness and bite with sugar or raisins boiled in it. Ruellius, on Dioscorides, chapter 11 of book 5, asserts that vinegar is hot in its thick parts, that is, in its dregs or in proportion to the dregs, but cold in its thin parts, and cold rather than hot, or perhaps cold in itself and hot only by accident; and he affirms that the sharper it is, and the less it represents the nature and qualities of wine, the more it consists of thin parts. See also Galen, book 1 of the Simple Medicines, the book On the Composition of Medicines by Kind, and books 1, 2 and 6 of On the Composition of Medicines by Part. Experience too shows the powers of vinegar. For if an egg is steeped in very sharp vinegar for three days, or a little more, the shell softens to such tenderness that it can be drawn through the narrow opening of a ring like a thin membrane. Indeed a whetstone or flint, if put into vinegar for seven days, is reduced to powder by rubbing with the finger. Hence Hannibal, making the Alps passable for himself and longing for Italy, forced hot vinegar to dissolve and split rocks. From this the penetrating power of vinegar is seen, by which it even corrodes and crumbles stones, and pearls are dissolved into liquid. But it also resists poisons powerfully, and it avails against the stings of all stinging creatures, against venomous bites, against itching and running ulcers, as Pliny also attests. Therefore those do not act unwisely who, when a popular and pestilential disease is raging, make a moderate use of vinegar a familiar part of their diet: for it disperses and dissipates foul air, and if anything has been swallowed into the body, it prevents the humours from being infected and putrefying, and it remarkably keeps off more violent heat in the body. But lest it harm the brain, the origin of the nerves, and the nerves themselves, the more prudent order rose water to be mixed with it, along with a little Rhenish wine and a pinch of saffron; for they have found that in this way it does less harm to the head. Moreover, it is well established that the Romans used it greatly on their campaigns, so it is no wonder (which some draw into astonishment) that Suetonius writes that Asiaticus, a freedman of the Emperor Vitellius, sold vinegar at Puteoli. For this drink was used not only for medicinal purposes, internally and externally, but also, when soldiers and the common folk used it in their daily diet, especially in great heats, because it cools markedly and moistens. It is made of vinegar, or sour wine, and water. According to the ancients it is compounded of two parts of water and three parts of sour wine. These things must be so tempered that they can be drunk. They say that M. Cato always carried water with him in the field, unless he was thirsting more fiercely; then, we read, he drank vinegar. It is no wonder, therefore, that Roman soldiers offered vinegar to Christ when he thirsted. And even today soldiers are accustomed always to carry vinegar with them.

units.la: Sciendum enim & notandum diligen-ter est, nec vinum per se, quia calidum, nec a-cetum, quia siccum, nec aquam, quia tardius permeat & distribuitur, mistam autem aquā alterutri horum certa portione & quantitate sitim probe extinguere. Nam hæc vini caliditatem acetique siccitatem sua frigiditate & humiditate corrigit atque attemperat. Tam vinum autem quam acetum essentiæ suæ tenuitate ipsi aquæ celeritatem permeandique promptitudinem impertit. Quare pruden-ter quidam aquam insalubriorem admisto a-ceto corrigunt, præterquam enim quod, vt celerius hypochondria transeat, minusq; in-flet, præstat efficiqueque.
units.tr: It must be carefully noted and remembered that neither wine alone, because it is hot, nor vinegar alone, because it is dry, nor water alone, because it passes through and is distributed more slowly, quenches thirst well. But water mixed with either of these in a fixed proportion and quantity does so. For its coolness and moisture correct and temper the heat of the wine and the dryness of the vinegar. Both wine and vinegar, by the thinness of their substance, give the water speed and readiness in passing through the body. So some prudently correct more unwholesome water by adding vinegar, since this both lets it pass more quickly through the hypochondria, so that it swells them less, and is also effective.

units.la: Verum enimuero cum sitis sit humidæ substantiae appetentia, (fine qua animalium tota moles, quia in perpetuo fluore est, pro-tinus tinus collaberetur atque concideret, nisi si-mile quid, quod defluxit, restauraretur) eaq; duplex, vna quæ à feruore caloris q; abundantia, altera quæ ab humoris penuria ac in-opia concitatur, discrimen aperiendum est, aquaaceto diluta ac temperata quam litim restinguat? Certum est & in confetto, fer-uorem & ariditate. si concurrerint, vehemen-tem excitare sitim. Quod si vero humor ca-lori coniungatur, fiunt quidem homines si-ticulosi, sed moderatè, ideoque facilè illa si-tis sedatur. Vnde ex aceti quoque natura consequens est, sitim, quæ à feruore concipitur, posca salubriter leniri, eam vero, quæ ab humoris oritur penuria, nullum sentire auxilium. Acetum enim insigniter refrigerare ostensum est, sed leuius humectare, ideoque siti ab ariditate humorisque inopia manante, aut caliditate siccitateque coeuntibus, minimè proderit, si solum potetur, quin potius irritabit acriusque stimulabit. At si humiditas cum caliditate coiuncta est, (quod tamen raro visu venit, nisi in hydropisi & ventriculo salsa pituita scatente) generosum leuamen est, cuius rei experientia quoque testis est. Non omittam Plinii testimonium lib. 23. cap. 1. afferentis, æstus in balineis calorisque vim acetum arcere ore detentum, vel etiam aquâ potum, &c. Quid hic dicitur aliud, quam in vehementibus calo-
units.tr: But since thirst is a craving for moist substance (without which the whole mass of living creatures, being in constant flux, would immediately collapse and fall apart, unless what has flowed away were restored by something similar), and since it is of two kinds, one aroused by the heat and excess of warmth, the other by the lack and want of moisture, we must make clear which kind is quenched by water diluted and tempered with vinegar. It is certain that in a dried and roasted body, when heat and dryness come together, they provoke intense thirst. But when moisture is joined to heat, people indeed become somewhat thirsty, but only moderately, and so that thirst is easily allayed. Hence it follows from the nature of vinegar too that thirst which arises from heat is wholesomely relieved by posca, whereas the thirst that comes from a lack of moisture finds no help in it. For vinegar has been shown to cool markedly, but to moisten only slightly; therefore, in thirst arising from dryness and lack of moisture, or from heat and dryness combined, it will by no means help if it is drunk alone, but rather will irritate and sting the more sharply. But when moisture is joined with heat (which rarely happens, except in dropsy and in a stomach teeming with salty phlegm), it is a noble relief, and experience too bears witness to this. I shall not omit the testimony of Pliny, Book 23, chapter 1, who says that vinegar held in the mouth, or even drunk in water, wards off the heat of the baths and the force of warmth, etc. What else is this saying, than that people thirsty in great heats should drink that water diluted with vinegar most usefully?

units.la: Duplex sinu causarum ratione. Pofca, cui fitiregin-guenda communi-at, vita prorogan da cupido probè no-tandum. caloribus homines sitientes aquam illam aceto dilucam vtilissimè bibere.
units.tr: A twofold cause for posca, with which thirst is commonly quenched; the desire for prolonging life must be carefully noted.

units.la: Cæterum, quoniam plerosque noctu sitis fatigat, nonimmeritò & præter ordinem institutiqué rationem quæritur,an nocto sitientibus potus sit dandus? Æstate, aliane temporis conditione ferventi, terrisque æstuosis & calidioribus, quin & victu ciboque tali homines fieri siticulosiores, nemo, nisi omnium rerum iners, ibit insicias. Nihil hic fastidiosi dicetur & fabulosi. Ipsa veritas cum experientia aget. Me quod attinet, intra limites & metas consistam, nec extra Pomœria euagabor. De sitis nocturnæ origine & causis operæ pretium est aliquid hucapponere.
units.tr: But since thirst troubles most people at night, it is not unreasonably asked, and beyond the ordinary order and method of inquiry, whether drink should be given to those who are thirsty at night. Whether in summer or in another hot season, in fervent weather, in sultry and very warm lands, and indeed whether people become more thirsty from such a diet and food, no one, unless utterly dull, will deny. Nothing fastidious or fabulous will be said here; truth itself, with experience, will be our guide. As far as I am concerned, I shall keep within the boundaries and limits and not wander beyond the city walls. It is worth adding something here on the origin and causes of nocturnal thirst.

units.la: Qui ob inexplebilem illam & inex-haustam potandi cupiditatem vitam immaturè relinquunt, studioséque irritamenta exquirunt, quæ in siticulosam voraginem eos demergant, diligentiori, aiunt, potu potum prouocari, non aliter ac somno somnum, ideoque nocturnas potationes vespertinasque promtiores & parariores ad diurnas reddere persuasissimum habent. Bibendi enim consuetudo auiditatem auget, monstrificamque sitim comparat, adeò vt lecto se committentes dormituri cantharos vini plenos aut lagenas condormire & astare velint, dignissimi sane, qui mediis in vndis æquoris immensi, Tantali instar, perpetua siti excrucientur.
units.tr: Those who, through that insatiable and unexhausted desire for drinking, leave life before its time, and eagerly seek out stimulants that plunge them into the whirlpool of thirst, are firmly convinced (they say) that drink is provoked by more drink, just as sleep is by sleep; and so they believe that evening drinking-bouts make the daytime ones more ready and easier. For the habit of drinking increases the appetite and produces a monstrous thirst, so that those who commit themselves to bed wish to sleep and stand beside tankards or flagons full of wine, most fitting indeed to be tormented by perpetual thirst, like Tantalus, in the middle of the waves of the boundless sea.

units.la: Sitis verò noßurnæ irritamenta esse præcipua, liberaliorem vini potētis & meracioris potum, qui fit interdiu, vel etiam a cœna, piperis, zinziberis, & id genus Indica efcarū adulteria immodice sumpta, tum acriū quoque falsorumque saporum coacervationem vlumque immoderatum, quibus ventriculus visceraque intus omnia intolerabili feruore incenduntur, abunde testatum faciunt, qui crebrius iis ad vinarias & cereuisiarias cellas exhauriendas, vtuntur. Hinc tot magni sæpe in corpore tumultus immensique æstus non sine maxima valetudinis ruina & noxa, orisq; ac animæ exhalans virus. Constat namque ora vino nimio fœtere, eaque contactis etiam contagionem afferre. Quapropter detestanda illorum sententia est, vel potius nostra memoria vulgatissimum bibacium prouerbium, nihil æque sitim sedare, atque assiduos liberalioresque haustus. Ingens certè homine liberali sententia. Iam enim indicatum est intemperantiam illam a bibendi auiditate accendi.
units.tr: That the chief stimulants of nocturnal thirst are the more generous drinking of strong and undiluted wine, which is done by day or even after supper, and the immoderate eating of pepper, ginger and that kind of Indian foods, and also the piling up of sharp and salty flavours and immoderate use of salt, by which the stomach and all the inner organs are set on fire with unbearable heat, is amply shown by those who use these more often when draining the wine and beer cellars. Hence come so many great tumults and immense heats in the body, not without the greatest ruin and harm to health, and the noxious vapour of the mouth and breath. For it is well known that mouths smell of too much wine, and that this can even transmit infection to those who come into contact with them. Therefore the saying of those tipplers, or rather the most common proverb of our own time, that nothing quenches thirst so well as constant and more generous draughts, is to be detested. It is certainly a magnificent opinion for a generous man. For it has already been shown that this intemperance is kindled by the eagerness for drink.

units.la: Quin & errorem illorum deregere hic meracius, vitæ prorogandæ interest, qui volunt, vinū dilutius meraciorem potum magis quam dilutiorem sitim restinguere, cum vinum perpetuo suo magis fe- calore ac flamma sitim augeat magis atque det? proriproritet,consequenterque exiccando tabe-faciat,membraq; efficiat tremula, adq; mu-nia obeunda inepta. De aqua grauissimi autores prodiderunt,in hypochondriis diu-tius commorari atque hærere solam po-tam,nec adeo prompte sitim leuare, pene-trare,adq; partes permeare, nisi modico vi-no mixtam,quo tanquam deductore ac ve-hiculo opus habet,ad quod ipsum etiam a-cetum non parum momenti obtinere statu-endum est.
units.tr: Here it is also important for the prolonging of life to set right the error of those who hold that stronger, undiluted wine quenches thirst better than weaker drink, when wine, by its constant heat and flame, rather increases and inflames thirst, and consequently by drying out makes the body waste away, and renders the limbs trembling and unfit for their duties. The most weighty authors have taught that water alone, when drunk, lingers and stays a long time in the hypochondria, and does not so readily quench thirst, penetrate and pass into the parts, unless it is mixed with a little wine, which it needs as a carrier and vehicle; and that vinegar too must be counted as having no small importance in this.

units.la: Nunc ad quæstionem propositam.
units.tr: Now to the question proposed.

units.la: Qui noctu bibere appetunt, inquit do-ctiff. Hippoc.aph.27.l.5.iis admodum fitien-tibus,si superdormierint,bonum. Quema-phorifmum explicans Galenus censet omni-no dandum potum iis, qui vehementi siti torrentur,siue a penuria & defectu potus & humidi,siue ex vini meracioris vberiorisque hausta fuerit prouocata. Nam & defectui, in-quit,succurrere confert, illamque quæ facta est ex vino,caliditate,aquâ restinguere,theo-rema salubre est, & remedium certissimum, est enim aqua frigida maximeq; omnium humida. Quod si vero quis modice nec adeo vehementer sitiat, iis potum dandu non esse idem censet,sed considerandu, nunquid ex defectu humidi tale quid patiatur,an vero ex nimia vini potatione,satisq; auxilii somnum præstiturum,qui solet concoquere & propulsare quod sitim induxerit. Si vero a fo-mno excitato modica fitis permanserit, vi- gilia porrò medebitur. Verum qui paucum intus calorem habent, ab immodico frigidae potu abstinebunt. Galenus non proletarius autor affirmat aquae frigidae potu Æthiopes extingui, ob paucum, quem intus obtinent calorem. Vnde quae nitidioris vrbanioris-que vitae sunt omnibus modis aduersus fi-tim illam pugnant, sed inprimis aqua, in qua panem friatum macerant. Alii cautiores adhuc, fi vel interdiu vel noctu fitis obstre-pat, solent cibarium panem friatum in calice cem coniicere, deinde frigidam superadde-re, saepius tranfuafare, sicque potum efficere, quo liberaliffime falubriterq; vtuntur. Qui carius & pretiosius bibere concupiscunt, aq; saccharatam, vel iulepum, & cinnamomiten concinnant, cuius potu mirifice elegantio-res atque aulicas foeminas delectari norunt, qui extillandis eiusmodi liquoribus aulicam impendunt operam. Praestantissimus ad fi- tim quamuis feruoribus inprimis contra-ftam, potus est, qui in quibusdam celebrio-ribus vrbibus conficitur ex radice glycyrrhi-zae hordeo, caricis, vuis passis & prunis, ifq; in Seplasiariorum quorundam tabernis pro-stat venalis aiuntq; eius haustu somnos in-terturbatos mirè reuocari. Quare nocturna inquieinquietudine vexatis potus salutaris. Sed de calido frigidoq; potu, pauca, pfenti rei convenientia, attigisse, non displicebit sanitatis & vitæ prorogādæ studiosis. Non solum autem hominem, vt Ioh. Bruerinus l.15.de regimen potus cibaria vult, sed & alia animantia calidis potibus delectari, imo quadrupedum maxima partem iis pinguescere, inq; quibusdam regionibus obesari, mirum videbitur forsan ei, qui à patrio solo nusquam discesserit. Maiorem vero insaniam gulæ in frigidis potionibus prodigiosa ingenia commenta esse, diuerticulaq; omni studio quæsiuisse, quibus ludificetur vita, vel inde patet maximè, quidam potus suos æstate hiemant, niues iis addunt, alii glaciem, feruantq; algore æstib*, vt nix alienis mensibus algeat. Nerofua hic laude non fraudandus est, alioqui teterrim* toto principatu suo generis humani hostis, qui primus aqua decoquere instituit, vitroq; demissam in niues refrigerare, ita enim voluptatem sine vitiis niuis contingere. Verum Andromachi medici eius id inuentum fuisse quidam autumant. Galenus qui posteriori seculo vixit & scripsit, aquam calefactam eodem modo refrigerari imperatoribus indicauit. Quin & si nix defit in amnem profluentem, aut puteum demittere vascu- lum præcipit, id quod crebrius à se factitatū testatur, ægrotanti alicui frigida exhibiturus
units.tr: "Those who desire to drink at night," says the most learned Hippocrates, Aphorism 27, Book 5, "if they have slept on, it is good for those who are very thirsty." Explaining this aphorism, Galen thinks that drink should by all means be given to those who are tormented by a violent thirst, whether it is provoked by lack and want of drink and moisture, or arises from the drinking of stronger and more copious wine. For, he says, it is useful to remedy the want, and it is a wholesome principle, and a most certain remedy, to quench with water the thirst that comes from wine's heat, for cold water is the most moist of all. But if someone is thirsty only moderately and not very intensely, Galen thinks drink should not be given to him, but one should consider whether he is suffering something of this sort from a lack of moisture, or rather from excessive drinking of wine, and whether sleep, which usually digests and drives out what has caused the thirst, will give enough relief. But if a moderate thirst remains after he has been woken from sleep, then waking will be the remedy. Yet those who have little inner heat must abstain from an immoderate drink of cold water. Galen, no obscure author, affirms that the Ethiopians are quenched by drinking cold water, because of the little heat they keep within. Hence those who live a more refined and urbane life fight against that thirst in every way, but especially with water in which they steep crumbled bread. Others, even more cautious, when thirst troubles them by day or by night, are wont to put crumbled bread into a cup, then pour cold water on it, often strain it through, and so make a drink, which they use most freely and wholesomely. Those who desire to drink more dearly and luxuriously prepare sugared water, or julep, and cinnamon water; people know that more elegant and courtly ladies delight in its drinking, the ones who devote courtly effort to distilling such liquors. A most excellent drink for thirst, especially that which is caused by fevers, is that which is made in some busier towns from liquorice root, barley, figs, raisins and plums, and which is sold in the shops of certain sellers of such things; they say that by drinking it, interrupted sleep is wonderfully restored. So it is a wholesome drink for those troubled by nocturnal restlessness. But it will not displease those who study health and the prolonging of life to have touched briefly on hot and cold drink, things suited to the present matter. Not only does John Bruerinus, in Book 15 on the regimen of drink and food, hold that man, but also other animals delight in hot drinks, and indeed the greater part of four-footed beasts grow fat on them, and in some regions become obese; this will perhaps seem wonderful to one who has never left his native soil. That prodigious minds have devised a greater madness of gluttony in cold drinks, and have sought with all zeal diversions by which life is mocked, is shown most clearly by the fact that some people make their drinks into winter in summer, adding snow to them, others ice, and keep them cold in summer so that snow may be chilled in other months. Nero should not be denied praise here, though otherwise he was a most foul enemy of the human race throughout his whole reign; he was the first to make a practice of boiling water and cooling it in snow by lowering a glass vessel into it, for in this way he thought pleasure could be had from snow without its vices. But some think this invention was by Andromachus, his physician. Galen, who lived and wrote in a later age, showed the emperors that warmed water is cooled in the same way. Indeed, if there is no snow, he instructs that a small vessel be lowered into a flowing river or a well, which he often testifies he has done himself, when he was about to give cold things to some sick person.

units.la: Qq
units.tr: Qq

units.la: Qui in mari nauigant, vini lagenas noctu ad malos appendūt, vt a rolcido cœlo vina algorem assumerent, vbi verò dilucuit, eas multa veste obuelant, ita enim conceptam illam cœli frigiditatem durare in confcsso habent. Hic verò vinarii negotiatores ementes sæpe & facile deludunt, dum etiam infirmissima vina & vappida, quæ generosum pretiosumque in cellis vinariis algidis rigidisq; acquirunt saporem, vendunt, obstupescente scil. hebetatoq; palato algore vini. Quantum autem insidiarum potu eiusmodi frigido vitæ obtendatur, ii experiuntur, qui modum nullum adhibent gulamque in gelidissimis cellis algidi vini potu emori peneque obstupescere conqueruntur. Certissimum est, calido tepidoq; potu immodico vires stomachi elanguescere, cibi auiditatem minui, fastidia concitari, corporisque totius robur emolliri atq; effœminari. Frigido contra potu vitiari fauces & pectus, pulmones, stomachu, intestina & ipsa viscera, excitariq; non rato tusses, raucitates, colica tormenta quotidiana manifestat experientia. Constat epar aquæ frigidæ potione sæpius adeo corrumpi, vt morbus diuturnus insuperabilis atq; etiā mors sequatur. Felix certè qui aliena sapit insania, Galeno teste, qui frigidiore egere potu arbitratur eos, qui rerumpublicarum magistratus administrant, quiq; assiduis occupan-
units.tr: Those who sail on the sea hang flasks of wine at night from the masts, so that the wine may take in cold from the dewy sky. When day dawns, they wrap the flasks in thick cloth, for they hold that the chill the sky has imparted lasts in this way for a long time. Wine merchants often and easily deceive their buyers here: they sell even very weak and sour wines, which in cold, chilly wine cellars take on a fine and costly flavour, because the cold numbs and dulls the palate. How many traps are laid for life by drinking cold drinks of this kind is learned by those who use no restraint, and who drink icy wine in the coldest cellars and then complain that they nearly die of it or are almost numbed. It is most certain that immoderate drinking of warm or tepid liquids weakens the strength of the stomach, lessens the appetite for food, provokes distaste, and softens and enervates the strength of the whole body. On the other hand, everyday experience shows that cold drinks injure the throat, chest, lungs, stomach, intestines and the viscera themselves, and bring on, not infrequently, coughs, hoarseness and daily colic pains. It is established that the liver is so often damaged by drinking cold water that a lingering, incurable disease and even death follow. Happy indeed is the one who is wise through the madness of others, as Galen testifies, since he thinks that those who administer the magistracies of commonwealths, and who are constantly busy with affairs, need a colder drink.

units.la: {y} Potufrigido qui egeant? cupantur negotiis, qui castra sequuntur & bella, qui peregrinantur ac viatores agunt. Qui liberi sunt & soluti, suiq; iuris ac spontis raro frigida eiusmodi potione indigent. Feruida, inquit, æstate calore pressi, exercitiisq; non subiecti, bibant fontana, niuemq; omnino vitent. Plura de calido frigidoq; potu videat lector ap. Athen. l. 3.
units.tr: Who need cold drink? Those who follow the camps and wars, who travel abroad and live as wayfarers. Those who are free and unburdened, and their own masters, rarely need cold drinks of this kind. "In hot summer," he says, "when pressed by heat and not subject to exercise, let them drink from springs, and altogether avoid snow." The reader may see more on hot and cold drink in Athenaeus, book 3.

units.la: Porrò non omittenda in hoc discursu est quæstio, quæ inter epulas plerumq; moueri solet, de famis sitisq; tolerantia, famisne sc. an vero sitis facilior tolerantia sit. Tria gravissima tormenta esse, quæ hominem suis ædibus deturbent, famem, fumum & fœminam, communi apud quosdam iactatur probrio. Constat autem inter omnes grauissimos autores animalia propemodum cuncta diutius perdurare in siti quam fame, citiusq; contabescere ac gracilescere, corrumpiq; inedia quam potionis penuria. Et longum sane foret referre, qui fame mortem sibi conscivisse antiquorum monumentis reperiuntur. In exemplis est, grauesq; historiæ perhibent, quosdam annos totos sine cibo potuque vixisse, & quod inter ostenta magis & prodigia quam naturæ insignia reponendum est, puellam quandam natam plus minus annos 20. sine cibo permansisse salubriterq; vixisse. Notum est arces oppidaque munitissima validissimaque nec non vrbes inexinexpugnabiles fame potius quam siti oppugnatoribus sese dedidisse. Sitis enim inclementia frequentius minuitur atque sedatur patientia, neque ei certum attributum mortis diem invenire est, quemadmodum inediae, omnino enim famem inelementissimum tormentum esse notissimum est. Non contendum hydrope vexatos, cum potus abstinentia euasissent, postea non ita magnopere bibere appetiuisse, ut ita in totum dixisse licet cruciatus sit violentissimus, nihilominus tamen non aeque vitae aduersari atque famem, in qua citius contabescere animantia quam in siti dictum est. Unde mirum etiam videri et incredibile non debet, quod quidam sine cibo multos annos vixerint, soloque potu vitam traduxerint, ob celeriorem enim transitum ac exactiorem distributionem per corporis partes nutriendas celerius quoque ac facilius nutrire verisimile est.
units.tr: Further, in this discussion we must not pass over the question, which is usually raised at dinners, of endurance of hunger and thirst: whether hunger or thirst is easier to bear. Among some people it is a common reproach that there are three most grievous torments which drive a man from his own house: hunger, smoke and a quarrelsome wife. Yet all the most weighty authors agree that nearly all living creatures endure thirst longer than hunger, and waste away and grow thin more quickly, and are destroyed more quickly by lack of food than by lack of drink. It would be a long task to relate how many men are found in the records of the ancients to have killed themselves by hunger. Serious histories report examples of certain people who lived whole years without food or drink, and, what must be counted among portents and marvels rather than the remarkable works of nature, a certain girl, born about twenty years earlier, who remained without food and lived in good health. It is well known that strongholds, towns best fortified and strongest, and even cities that cannot be taken, have surrendered to their besiegers through hunger rather than thirst. For thirst is more often mitigated and calmed by endurance, and one cannot find a fixed day of death for it as for hunger; indeed it is most widely known that hunger is the most merciless torment. I do not argue that those afflicted with dropsy, who had escaped by abstaining from drink, afterwards did not much long to drink; so, although one may say in general that thirst is a most violent torment, nevertheless it does not threaten life as much as hunger, by which, as has been said, living creatures waste away more quickly than by thirst. Hence it should not seem strange or incredible that some have lived many years without food, and passed their lives on drink alone; for it is likely that, because of the quicker passage and more exact distribution through the parts of the body to be nourished, drink nourishes more quickly and more easily.

units.la: Hactenus de aceto eiusque viribus, ubi obiter et hoc meminisse lectorem velim, quoties aceti apud Medicos fit mentio, semper vini acetum intelligi oportere. In quibusdam etiam locis, praesertim Saxonia Brunsuicensi ex industria acetum sicut cereuisiam coquunt, quod tamen non fit cereuisia, sed musteum illud decoctum refrigeratum in acetu transit, quo finitimi etiam gentes plurimae in cibis utuntur. Fiunt quoque acetae salubres-
units.tr: So far concerning vinegar and its powers. Here I would also have the reader remember in passing that whenever vinegar is mentioned by physicians, wine vinegar must always be understood. In some places, especially in Brunswick in Saxony, they deliberately boil vinegar like beer, although this is not beer; that boiled must, once cooled, turns into vinegar, and many neighbouring peoples use it in their food. Wholesome vinegars are also made.

units.la: luberrima ex floribus siccatis rorismarini, saluiæ, lauendulę, lilii conuallium, sambuci, hyssopi, rosis siccis, & similibus, quæ vitam sanitatemq; prorogaturo, cumprimis verò politioris literaturæ studiosis, & vt vno dicam verbo, omnibus patribus familiàs tanquam pretiosissimum ad ingenii vires animiq; vigorem custodiendum thesaurum, vnicè commendo. Præstant autem id fotu, olfactu & illitu circa tempora, oculos, os, nares & carpum. Crocata autem omnia præstantiora. Ad extremum, vt tandem lucubrationibus hisce vigiliisq; meis finem imponam, in condimentorum quoq; vsum admitti, & aromata, vt gariophyllos, zinziber, piper, cinnamomū, corticè citri, cardamomū, crocū, macin, &c. non ignorandū est, quib. suauiter salutariterq; cibi potusq; codiri solent, iisq; innoxiè maximoq; valetudinis comodo vti possum, si moderatè & mediocriter adhibeantur. Immoderatū verò illorū, vsumq; frequentiore, ipsum stomachū viscerąq; int* omnia, præcipuè epar, intolerabili feruore incendere manifestū est, id cp sitis bibēdiq; auiditas indicat. Vbi peßimè sanitati vitæq; cōsulūt, q, dū ardore illū vini ingetib hauftib*, restinguere studēt, igneq; igni addētes, oleuq; flamis, ingētes in corpore cruciatus atq; tumult* excitat, feq; ipsos ad liberali* auidiusq; bibendū, inuitat, proritat, atq; inflammant.
units.tr: Most excellent ones are made from dried flowers of rosemary, sage, lavender, lily of the valley, elder, hyssop, dried roses and the like, which I especially commend to those who would prolong life and health, to students of more refined literature, and, to say it in one word, to all heads of households, as a most precious treasure for preserving the strength of the mind and the vigour of the spirit. They are effective when applied as a warm fomentation, by smell, and by rubbing on the temples, eyes, mouth, nostrils and wrists. Those made with saffron are the best of all. Finally, that I may at last bring these labours and my wakeful nights to an end, it should not be overlooked that spices may also be admitted into use: cloves, ginger, pepper, cinnamon, citron peel, cardamom, saffron, mace, and so on, with which food and drink are usually seasoned pleasantly and healthfully. These may be used without harm and to the great benefit of health, if they are taken moderately and in small amounts. But immoderate use of them, and more frequent use, plainly sets the stomach itself and all the viscera, especially the liver, aflame with intolerable heat, as the thirst and eagerness for drinking show. In this way those who most badly consult their health and life, while they try to quench that burning of wine by huge gulps, add fire to fire and oil to flames, stirring up huge torments and turmoil in the body, and invite, urge and inflame themselves to drink more greedily and freely.

units.la: Quare aromata cautè & modicè cibariis sunt inspergenda, habita ratione ætatis, temporis, temperamenti locique, in terris enim temporibus q; frigidioribus, naturis item pituitosioribus, liberaliorvsus concedi potest, &c, vt, facto fine, quiescam, aduersus stomachi infirmitates, ac cruditates, nec non viscerum temperaturam frigidam, cunctaq; ante alia ad Venerem concitandam aromata magnificant, ex quibus tamen piper, zinziberque nec suauitate, nec dulcedine, nec acido sapore placere, sed acrimonia tantum stimulante gulam, non immerito quis miretur, saltem quia exotici peregriniq; saporis sunt, &c ex India petuntur, illorum auiditas maior inter mortales existit, quibus suarum rerum alioqui satietas ingens est. Tantum de aromatis, quorum vires ac laudes, in potibus, si Deus voluerit, alibi vberius prosequar.
units.tr: Therefore spices must be sprinkled on food cautiously and sparingly, with regard to age, season, temperament and place. In colder lands and seasons, and in people of a more phlegmatic nature, a more generous use may be allowed, etc. So that I may bring this to an end and rest: against weaknesses and indigestion of the stomach, and against a cold temperature of the viscera, they praise spices above all others for arousing desire for Venus. Among these, one may not without reason be surprised that pepper and ginger please not by fragrance, sweetness or a sour taste, but only by a sharp sting that irritates the palate; and yet, because they are of foreign and strange flavour and are sought from India, the desire for them is greater among mortals, although they are generally sated with their own goods. So much on spices; if God wills, I shall treat their powers and praises more fully elsewhere, in the matter of drinks.

units.la: Ne verò plane arido palato & sine hypnofia extremam huic libro imposuisse manum videar, quaestionem Coronidis loco, an cœna potu fit finienda, subnectam. Discordes autè quorundam sententias hic esse animaduerti, praesertim inter coenandum, quo tempore potissimum exagitari videtur, de ea litigantium. Portentosis commessationibus dediti, si coenam potu non clauserint, crastinam lucem non aspicere nec iecoris pulmopulmonisque vitia ac tabitudines effugere posse, persuasum omnino habent. Quin & generosum hodie ducitur & praeclarum hodie bibendi strenue & quidem stando, potu coenam fini- tr repraesertim in Magnatum aulis in quibus, quo quis existit bibacior, eo censetur gene- rosior. Et nemo aestimatur pluris, quam qui egregie censum Domini sui mergit. Imo quod mirari haud immerito quis possit eius-modi de grege Epicureo porci, strenuiq; ca- licum gurgites non infimum obtinere locum cernuntur. Certe consque creuere immanes illae propinationes atque monstrificae potationes noctur-nae, ut cellae vinariae inde exhauriantur, corporis animique vires enervantur, asotique illi, qui in mensam vomentes de conuiuiis, ut cum Cicer. de finibus loquar, auferuntur, crudique postridie ferurfus ingurgitant, funeris ante diem mi-sere pereant. Iustae moderataeque propinationis legitimum censeri debere caritatem, amorem, amicitiamq; mutuam, cuius vel ineundae, vel fouendae atq; confirmandae causa olim ab honestis probisque viris eam fuisse adhibitam, passim apud autores videlicet. Immoderatarum vero istarum atq; cyclopicarum propinationum, quibus hodie plerique Christianorum quotidie fere vtuntur, finis non est caritas, amor, amicitia, honor, obseruantia, quam tamen helluones
units.tr: Lest I seem to have laid the final hand on this book with a quite dry palate and without a nap, I shall append, as a garland, the question whether dinner should be ended with drinking. I notice that the opinions of some are divided on this, and the quarrel of the disputants seems to be stirred up most of all during dinner. Those given to monstrous carousings are thoroughly persuaded that, if they do not close dinner with drink, they cannot see the next day's light, nor escape the diseases and wasting of the liver and lungs. Indeed, today it is thought a noble and distinguished thing to drink vigorously, and even standing, to finish dinner with drink, especially in the courts of the great, where the more a man is a heavy drinker, the more he is thought noble. And no one is valued more than the one who most splendidly drowns his lord's fortune. Indeed, which one might not without reason wonder at, such swine of the Epicurean herd and whirlpools of bold drinkers are seen to hold no low place. Certainly those monstrous toasts and portentous nightly drinking bouts have grown to such a degree that the wine cellars are emptied by them, the strength of body and mind is enervated, and those debauchees who, as Cicero says in the De Finibus, are carried from feasts vomiting onto the table, and, sick the next day, gorge again, perish wretchedly before their time for the funeral. A just and moderate toast ought to be regarded as a lawful pledge of charity, love and mutual friendship; it was used of old by honest and upright men, as is found everywhere in the authors, namely to make or foster and confirm such friendship. But the end of those immoderate and Cyclopean toasts, which most Christians today use almost every day, is not charity, love, friendship, honour or respect, which nevertheless the gluttons
