units.la: Propinationis lectio.
units.tr: On the reading of the drinking of healths.

units.la: isti verbis egregie simulant, sed ebrietas, &c quae illam necessario consequuntur, turpitudo, ignominia, sanitatis viriumque corporis labefactatio, tremor, grauedo, pallor, linguae titubatio, contentio extremitatum in neruis, torpor, vtplurimum vero resolutio. Et certe constat quotidiana experientia, plærosque acrium illorum potatorum hoc tantum spectare, vt illos, quos vel amicitiae, vel honoris specie, atq; simulatione ad immoderate bibendum inuitant, atq; cogunt, cunctis deridendos propinentatq; comedendos, vt metaphoricos Terentius in Eunucho dixit, vt ita in totum dixisse liceat, nihil esse tam vtile, laudabile atque honestum, quod non deformet abusus hominum; quis enim non videt quotidie, antiquam illam propinandi consuetudinem ac philothesian amoris per se amicitiaeque plenam, proindeque honestam, iam a multis seculis in turpissimum flagitiosissimumque abusum degenerasse, & ad Plutonis vsque Cancellos ipsos Christianos hodie sibi inuicem specioso amoris atque amicitiae obtentu propinare. Atq; hinc promanasse putatur vox crapula, quae pro ebrietate metonymicos vsurpatur, cum tamen proprie sit ebrietatis effectus capitis nimirum lucta, agitatioque, cum sc. ex temulentia caput aggrauatur & tremit.
units.tr: These men express it splendidly in words, but drunkenness and the things that necessarily follow it are shame, disgrace, the weakening of health and bodily strength, trembling, heaviness, pallor, stammering of the tongue, tension in the sinews of the limbs, torpor, and most often collapse. And it is certainly plain from daily experience that most of these fierce drinkers aim at nothing else than to make those whom they invite and compel to drink immoderately, under the appearance and pretence of friendship or honour, into objects of ridicule for everyone, to be "toasted and eaten up," as Terence says metaphorically in the Eunuch. So, to put it generally, there is nothing so useful, praiseworthy and honourable that the abuse of men does not deform it. For who does not see every day that the ancient custom of drinking healths, a display of goodwill full of love and friendship and therefore honourable, has for many centuries degenerated into the most shameful and disgraceful abuse, and that even within the very gates of Pluto's realm, Christians today drink to one another under the specious pretext of love and friendship? From this, it is thought, comes the word crapula, which is used metonymically for drunkenness, though properly it is the effect of drunkenness on the head, namely the reeling and agitation when, from intoxication, the head is weighed down and trembles.

units.la: Galenus in aphor.omnem noxam ex vino contractam κεφαλαλγίαν nominat, κεφαλή id est caput, & πάλλειν hoc est concuti, revera enim multis ex pridiana & hesterna temulentia tanta sentitur in capite grauedo, vt cyclopas sibi in cerebrum migrasse iurent, qui alternatis illud feriant ictibus, quos dolores Germani non inepte Trôscher oder Schmidtknecht appellant, q. τὰς πάλλοντας κεφαλάς. Sed ad rem. An expediat mensas claudere seu terminare potu, supra quaesitum fuit. Veterum autem morem poculo quodam certo siue propinatione coenam claudere seu terminare, idque partim religionis siue superstitionis potius, partim amicitiae ergo, passim apud autores traditur. Huiusmodi poculum appellarunt poculum ὑγείας forsan boni ominis ergo, quod illud sibi invicem bonae valetudinis ergo propinabant. Profanitate enim & olim propinationes fieri solitas & etiamnum hodie strenue hunc morem continuari maximo saepe corporis & valetudinis dispendio, plus quam notum est. Sunt in exemplis, quos pro ὑγείας poculo sorbendo principatum quaerentes & gloriam, truncorum siue stipitum instar & velut attonitos atque resolutos concidisse constat.
units.tr: Galen in the Aphorisms calls every ailment of the head contracted from wine kephalalgia [κεφαλαλγίαν], from kephale [κεφαλή], head, and pallein [πάλλειν], to be shaken, that is, to be struck. Indeed, after yesterday's or the day before's drinking, many people feel such heaviness in the head that they swear that Cyclopes have migrated into their brain and strike it with alternating blows. The Germans not unfittingly call these pains Trôscher oder Schmidtknecht, that is, "throbbing heads" [τὰς πάλλοντας κεφαλάς]. But to the point: whether it is advantageous to close a meal with drinking, was discussed above. That the ancients commonly ended or closed their dinner with a certain cup or toast, partly out of religious or superstitious feeling and partly for the sake of friendship, is handed down by writers everywhere. They called this cup the cup of health [ὑγείας], perhaps as a sign of good omen, because they drank it to one another for the sake of good health. For it is well known that toasts were customarily made even in profane matters in the past, and that this custom is still zealously kept up today, often at great cost to the body and health. There are examples of those who, seeking the first place and glory in swallowing the cup of health, have fallen like tree trunks or stumps, dazed and limp.

units.la: Præterea vltimum illud poculum maxi- me communi nomine appellatum quoque fuit boni dæmonis fiue boni genii, seu for- tunæ,de quo Theophraftus l.de ebriet.scri- bit in hunc modum. Vini meraci, quod in cœna datur, quod quidem boni dæmonis propinationem vocant,parum degustantes, in memoriam reuocant, quanta fit ipsius Dei vis, quantumque hoc sit illius donum. At postquam impleuerunt, dant quàm mi- nimum haustum,& tertio flexis genibus ad- orantes, ex mensa capiunt, tanquam Deo supplicantes, ne quid designent à decoro a- lienum, neue vehementi aliqua illius po- tus cupiditate accendantur, sed hauriant ab illo ea,quæ honesta sunt & vtilia. Philocho- rus similiter apud Athen.lib.15.de hoc potu sic scribit: more atque consuetudine fuit receptum, vt post cibos vinum meracum o- mnibus offerretur illud degustandi gratiâ ceu ad demonstrandam vim boni Dei: reli- quo autem omni conuiuii tempore vinum dilutius bibere consueuerunt, iccircoque ipsas etiam nymphas Bacchi nutrices appel- larunt. Ex quibus Theophrasti & Phi- lochori verbis colligitur, hunc vini puri ac meraci potum,quem boni dæmonis potum appellarunt,& ab initio cœnæ & in extremo conuiuio, antequam surgerent mensæue a- sportarentur, à conuiuis fuisse vsurpatum. Nec vero in deorum tantum honorem boni ominis auspiciique causâ vltima illa potatio fieri consueuit, verum etiam amicitiæ mutuæ testificandæ sanciendæque causâ, vnde Philotefia fuit appellata, propinatio sc. quædam post cœnam amicitiæ ergo fieri solita. Dicebatur quoque Tantali pocu-lum, cuius initiatorem & quasi pincernam fecerunt Tantalum, quod is incredibili inter homines beneuolentia liberalitateque præcelluiffe creditur.
units.tr: Moreover, that last cup was also commonly called by the general name the cup of the good daemon, or good genius, or fortune, of which Theophrastus, in his book On Drunkenness, writes in this manner: "Those who give the undiluted wine that is served at dinner, which they call the toast to the good daemon, taste it only a little, to recall how great the power of God himself is and how great a gift this is from him. But after they have filled the cups, they give only the smallest draught; and kneeling three times in worship, they take it from the table as if supplicating God, so that they may not do anything unbecoming, nor be inflamed by some violent desire for that drink, but may draw from it only what is honourable and useful." Philochorus likewise writes about this drink in Athenaeus, book 15: "By custom and usage it was the practice that after the food, undiluted wine was offered to all for tasting, as if to show the power of the good God; but for the rest of the feast they were accustomed to drink wine more diluted, and for this reason they even called the nymphs the nurses of Bacchus." From the words of Theophrastus and Philochorus it is gathered that this drink of pure and undiluted wine, which they called the drink of the good daemon, was taken by the guests both at the beginning of the dinner and at the end of the feast, before they rose and the tables were carried away. Nor was that final drinking customarily done only in honour of the gods, as a good omen and for good fortune; it was also done to bear witness to and seal mutual friendship. Hence it was called philotesia, namely a certain toast customarily drunk after dinner for the sake of friendship. It was also called the cup of Tantalus, whose inventor and, as it were, cupbearer they made Tantalus, because he is believed to have excelled among men in incredible goodwill and generosity.

units.la: Chriftophorus àVega l.2.de arte med. fect. 4. in hanc scribit sententiam de quæst. proposita. An,inquit,expediat mensas claudere potu, an vero cibo, scire oportet eum, cuius os ventris laxum est,aut cuius caput ex vini potu compatitur, egere cibo quopiam astringente postremo loco, quem non fe-quetur potus. Quorum autem venter siccus est,aut siti molestantur,non longe à cibo bibere debent,sed parum ad finem mensæ. Sic etiam iis,quibus nulla praua adest ventricu-li affectio, conuenit finito prandio aut cœ-na,parum vini, fi ita assueuerint, fumere, vt postremus ille cibus è gula descendat,liquetur, commisceaturque aliis cibi partibus: aliis vero æque similis potus conueniet: deinde os & dentes vino colluere omnibus ex vsu erit, diluatur, fi capitis malis tentantur, alias non. Celsus lib. i. vbi expletus est aliquis, inquit, facilius concoquit, si quicquid assumfit, potione aquæ frigidæ includit, tum paulisper inuigilat, deinde bene dormit. Quam sententiam Celsus videtur deprompsisse ex Hipp. l. 3. de victu acut. sic scribente, vbi timueris, ne vel caput vehementer vino, morboque grauetur, vel mens etiam tentetur, tum vel aquam, vel vinum aquosum & album, & neutiquam odorum exhibere, & deinde paululum aquæ superbibere conuenit. Sic enim vini potentia non tam facile caput mentemque attingit. Addit Pantimus interpres, perperam etiam non fecerint, qui pro aqua è Cidoniis malis conditi portiuncula, aut coriandri ex aceto præparati cochleari, aut citriorum succo, aut limonum, aut punicorum, aut istorum sirupis, aut denique astringentis alicuius maturique pomi esu ventriculi os occluserint, simul & vini exhalationem ac vim refrænauerint, præsertim, si quis etiam inter quiter ac somnum, & inter aquæ vinique fumtionem paulisper inuigilauerit. Et idem paulo post: Confert quoque neque cœnam, neque prandium potu vnquam finire, quin aliquid ex superioribus, aut quid escę superedatur, vnde tritum illud,
units.tr: Christophorus à Vega, in book 2 of his De arte medica, section 4, writes on the question proposed: "Whether it is advantageous to end meals with drink or with food. One must know that a person whose stomach is loose, or whose head suffers from wine-drinking, needs some astringent food last of all, which should not be followed by drink. Those whose stomach is dry, or who are troubled by thirst, ought to drink not far from their food, but a little towards the end of the meal. Likewise for those who have no bad affection of the stomach, it suits them, when the lunch or dinner is finished, to take a little wine, if they are accustomed to it, so that the last morsel of food goes down the throat, is dissolved, and mixes with the other parts of the food. Other people will be equally suited by a similar drink. Then rinsing the mouth and teeth with wine will be useful to everyone, but it should be diluted if they are troubled by headaches, and otherwise not." Celsus, book 1: "When someone has eaten his fill, he digests more easily if, after whatever he has taken, he takes a drink of cold water, then stays awake a little while, and then sleeps well." Celsus seems to have drawn this opinion from Hippocrates, book 3 of On Acute Diseases, who writes thus: "Where you fear that the head or even the mind may be seriously burdened by wine and disease, it is fitting to give either water, or watery and white wine, and by no means fragrant wine, and then to drink a little water afterwards. For in this way the power of the wine does not so easily reach the head and mind." The translator Pantimus adds: "Nor do they act wrongly who, instead of water, close the mouth of the stomach with a small portion of quince preserve, or a spoonful of coriander prepared in vinegar, or with juice of citrons, lemons or pomegranates, or with syrups of these, or finally by eating some astringent and ripe fruit, thereby also restraining the exhalation and force of the wine, especially if someone, between the drinking of the water and the wine, has stayed awake a little while between the quiet and the sleep." And again a little later: "It is also useful never to finish either dinner or lunch with drink, without some of the previous food, or some of the food, being left over; hence the well-worn saying,

units.la: Sit tibi postremum semper in ore cibus,
units.tr: Let food always be the last thing in your mouth.

units.la: Inna-
units.tr: Inna-

units.la: Conf. Hipp. ne vinum tentet meniem. Innatant siquidem cibi illico post coe-nam si quis largius biberit, ita vt eos ventri-culi corpus, propter interiectum humorem non contingat. Praeterea vtendum semper potu est ad desiderio satisfaciendum, & vt cibus nec sit in sicco, nec fluitet, sed moderato potu madescat.
units.tr: Compare Hippocrates, on whether wine should affect the mind. For food floats up at once after dinner if someone has drunk too freely, so that the body of the stomach does not touch it, because of the liquid lying between. Besides, one should always drink enough to satisfy the thirst, and so that the food is neither dry nor floating, but is moistened by a moderate drink.

units.la: Consultum quoque putatur inter e-dendum non confertim, nec auide, sed sen-sim ac paulatim bibere, quo commodius v-traque misceri queant, parique concoctione perfici. Qui vero ea edendi vtuntur consuetudine, vt ad prandii medium potu sibi temperent, affatim illis bibere expediet, vt potus penetret, ac per cibum vndique diffundatur. Optimus igitur ac securissimus bibendi modus statuendus est cuique pro sua aetate temporum ratione, inueterata consuetudine, ac pro vini natura ac viribus. Sanis quoque non posse certo aliquid aut determinate circa potum praescribi inde constat quod plaeriq; diuersae potandi consuetudini sint assueti, quam citra valetudinis iacturam mutare nemini sit facile.
units.tr: It is also thought advisable, while eating, not to drink in great gulps or greedily, but gradually and little by little, so that the two can be mixed more conveniently and be digested equally. But those who have the habit of eating so that they restrain their drinking until the middle of the lunch, it will be expedient for them to drink freely, so that the drink penetrates and is spread everywhere through the food. The best and safest manner of drinking, therefore, should be set for each person according to his age, the season, his established habit, and the nature and strength of the wine. That it is not possible to prescribe anything certain or fixed about drinking even for healthy people is clear from the fact that most people are accustomed to different habits of drinking, and it is not easy for anyone to change these without loss to his health.

units.la: Sic multo potui assueti pleniores possunt tolerari haustus, quam insueti. Cerebrum vero habentes imbecillum, vinum non tolerant. Signum enim fortitudinis cerebri ac bonitatis eius, teste Auicenna est, a vini generosi vaporibus non laedi, vinique potentiam sustinere. Certissimum est, medicaque grauitate ac experientia confirmatissimum, à cibo potasse concoctionem est uertere, flatusque multos ac cruditates gignere, ieiuno vero ventre vinum sumpsisse, neruos ac caput infigniter lædere. Dormiturıs vero & à cœna (nisi valida admodum sitis vrgeat) nocentissimus est omnium medicorum consensu potus, obidque recte docebat Hipp. 5. aphor. Qui noctu bibere appetunt, his admodum sitientibus si super-dormierint, bonum. Somnus enim eam sitim, quæ vtplurimum mendosa-est & falsa, sedare solet atque leuare. His ita obserua-tis, & caput minus offendetur, omneq; cor-pus somno fruetur iucundius. Non parumtamen emolumenti aliquem ex eo consecu-turum Auicenna putat, si quis semel in mé-sainebrietur, vt videl. per ebrietatem exci-tetur vomitus, quo chronicas diuturnasqueægritudines ait prohiberi. Verum Rabbi Moses tradtat. 4. ad Soltanum Babyloniæ, hanc illius sententiam ceu falsam conuellit, omnem ebrietatem & maxime assiduam nocere affirmans. Pestilentissimam assiduam ebrietatem esse dubium non est, quandam tamen vt quæ in mense semel contingit, vel ad summum bis, quibusdam vt quorum ventriculus crudis humoribus est re-sertus, non plane noxiam esse experientia testis est. Qui vero ex vini immodico hau- ftu temulenti euaserunt, omnium teftimo- nio consilium fuerit ciere vomitum,inedi- am imperare ac somnum, ac succum malo- rum punicorum, vel oxicratum exhibere potandum, aut caulium succum. Sybaritas ferunt olim crambén prius efitaffe, quo plus deinde bibere possent.
units.tr: Thus those accustomed to much wine can tolerate fuller draughts than those unaccustomed to it. Those who have a weak brain do not tolerate wine. For, as Avicenna testifies, it is a sign of the strength and good quality of the brain not to be harmed by the fumes of strong wine, and to bear the power of wine. It is most certain, and most firmly confirmed by medical authority and experience, that to drink after food is to disturb digestion and to produce many flatulences and crudities, while to take wine on an empty stomach notably injures the nerves and the head. And for those who are going to sleep, and for those who sleep after dinner (unless a very strong thirst presses), drinking is by the agreement of all physicians most harmful of all; and Hippocrates rightly taught this in the fifth book of the Aphorisms: "Those who desire to drink at night, if they are very thirsty and sleep on, it is well; for sleep usually allays and relieves that thirst, which is mostly deceptive and false." When these rules are observed, the head will be less troubled, and the whole body will enjoy sleep more pleasantly. Avicenna nevertheless thinks that someone who gets drunk once in a month will gain some benefit from it, namely that drunkenness brings on vomiting, by which, he says, chronic and long-lasting illnesses are prevented. But Rabbi Moses, in the fourth treatise to the Sultan of Babylon, refutes this opinion of his as false, asserting that every drunkenness, and especially constant drunkenness, is harmful. There is no doubt that constant drunkenness is most pestilential, but that drunkenness which occurs once a month, or at most twice, is not clearly harmful to some people, namely those whose stomach is full of crude humours, as experience bears witness. Those who have become drunk from an immoderate swallowing of wine, however, all agree that it is advisable to provoke vomiting, to prescribe fasting and sleep, and to give pomegranate juice or oxycrate to drink, or cabbage juice. They say the Sybarites formerly ate cramben before drinking, so that they could then drink more.

units.la: Diofcorides quoque ebrietatis & crapulæ incommoda tollere prodidit, fi cruda edatur ante cœnam ex aceto. Inesse autem peculiarem quandam vim vinô obsistendi incrambe, inde patet, quod in vineto fata, vinum proueniat dilutius. Proinde apud Ægyptios & Sybaritas folenne erat, ante omnia fúmere crambén coctam: quibusdam eius femen ante compotationem capere mos erat, quo citra ebrietatis periculum vi- nó possent indulgere. Ebrietatem quoque arcent amara potissimum, omniaq; ea quæ humores aquosos per vrinam expurgant, quibus præfumtis fit vt fumi alio quam ad caput deferantur, vinumque venas subire prohibeatur, exiccante etiam amarore hu- miditatem. Præcipuam vero inter ea ob- tinuerunt laudem amygdalæ amaræ ad fa- ftidium vsque nobilitatæ, (sed fallaci sæpe experimento) fi 6. vel 7. ante compotatio- nem comedantur. Huc pertinent antiquo- tum propomata, fiue propinamenta, intet
units.tr: Dioscorides also reported that drunkenness and the discomforts of a hangover are relieved if raw cabbage is eaten with vinegar before dinner. That cabbage has a particular power to resist wine is clear from the fact that wine which grows in a vineyard planted near cabbage comes out thinner. Accordingly, among the Egyptians and the Sybarites it was customary above all to take cooked cabbage first; some were in the habit of taking its seed before a drinking-bout, so that they could indulge in wine without danger of drunkenness. Bitter things in particular also ward off drunkenness, and all those things which purge watery humours through the urine, since when they are taken beforehand the fumes are carried anywhere but to the head, and the wine is prevented from entering the veins, the bitterness also drying up moisture. But the highest reputation among these has been won by bitter almonds, celebrated even to the point of nausea (though the experience is often deceptive), if six or seven are eaten before the drinking-bout. To this belong the ancients' preparatory drinks, or appetisers, among which

units.la: Rr
units.tr: Rr

units.la: quæ maxime commendantur, quæ ex absin-thio & aromatibus conficiuntur. In frequen-tissimo hodie vsu est propoma absinthites, quod vt Trallianus testatur vim habet sto-machum corroborandi, extenuandi, expel-lendiquè excrementa in eo contenta.
units.tr: those most highly recommended are made from wormwood and aromatic herbs. The preparation most widely used today is the wormwood drink, which, as Trallianus testifies, has the power to strengthen the stomach, to thin, and to expel the excrements contained in it.

units.la: Cinnamomites quoq; propoma vires insignes obtinet in corroborando cerebro & corde. Panis similiter buccella cum melle, cydoniaq; coꝯta ebrietati resistunt poten-ter. Plinius aduersus ebrietatem & temulen-tiam valere pecudum pulmonem assum præsumtum: inprimis vero apri, suis ac hœ-di : niriundinis rostri cinerem cum myrrha tritum, & in vinum bibendum inspersum l. 30. c. 15. testatur, huiusq; remedii inuentoré esse Horum Assyriorum Regem. Aduersus idem & iaspidem pollere affirmant, sed in-certo experimento. Ipsam vero ebrietatem discutere ne sentiatur, porrum sectiuum, aut crocum prius potum apud claros autores inuenio. Sed melilotus multorum etiam an-tiquissimorum consensu celebratur. Alii radiculam commendant elixam, quod testa-tur Alexis,
units.tr: The cinnamon drink also has remarkable powers in strengthening the brain and heart. Likewise bread-crumb with honey, and quince preserve, resist drunkenness powerfully. Pliny states that the roasted lung of cattle, taken as a remedy against drunkenness and intoxication, is effective, above all that of the boar, sow and kid; and that the ash of a swallow's beak, ground with myrrh and sprinkled into the wine to be drunk, is also effective, and he reports that the inventor of this remedy was a king of the Assyrians. They affirm that jasper also has power against the same thing, but by uncertain experiment. I find in famous authors that to dispel drunkenness itself, so that it is not felt, one should drink leek-juice or saffron beforehand. But melilot is celebrated by the agreement of many, even of the most ancient. Others recommend the boiled root of radish, as Alexis testifies:

units.la: Iam vero nonne omnium malorum est ebrietas Maximum hominibus & nocentissimum, Heri subbibisti, ideo nunc crapula vexaris, Obdormito, ac leuaberis, deinde tibi det Radiculam quis elixam. Sed satius esset ita bibere, ut medicamento opus non fit. Studium sobrietatis, ebrietatisq; odium optima temulentiae antipharmaca sunt. Non damnatur crater philotesius, qui amicitiae conciliandae causâ alteri praebibi ab antiquis solebat.
units.tr: Indeed, is not drunkenness the greatest and most harmful of all evils for men? You drank heavily yesterday, and so now you are tormented by a hangover. Sleep it off, and you will be relieved; then let someone give you a boiled radish. But it would be better to drink in such a way that no medicine is needed. Zeal for sobriety and hatred of drunkenness are the best antidotes to intoxication. The friendship cup, which the ancients used to drink on behalf of another in order to win friendship, is not condemned.

units.la: Permitiosissimum est sub amicitiae praetextu & specie ad bibendum inuitare, imo dirum propinandi hoc seculo certame apud quosdam Nobiles atque ignobiles. Unum meminisse hic lectorem velim, veteres vinum malum bibisse vomitus ciendi gratiâ, ut scil. euacuato exinanitoq; per vomitum stomacho tanto maior esset bibendi edendiq;orexis id est appetentia. Vinum pessimum vocarunt pedibus admotum, siue à pedib. quod ferruis apponi fuit solitum, quod ΣΚΥΦΟΠΙΑΝ id est versionem appellabant, quod stomachum subuerteret ac perturbaret. Huc facit illud Martialis, Nec cœnat prius aut recumbit Quam septem vomuit deunces.
units.tr: It is most pernicious to invite to drinking under the pretext and appearance of friendship, indeed the dreadful drinking-contest of this age among certain nobles and commoners is an abomination. I would have the reader remember one thing here: the ancients drank bad wine for the sake of inducing vomiting, namely so that, once the stomach had been emptied and drained by vomiting, their appetite for drinking and eating, that is, their appetency, would be so much greater. They called the poor wine brought to the feet, or from the feet, which was customarily set before servants, "skyphopia," that is, "turning-over," because it upset and disturbed the stomach. To this belongs that line of Martial: "He does not dine or recline before he has vomited seven times."

units.la: Qui sanitati vitaeq; prorogandae daturi sunt operam, ii, praesertim si intemperantius viuere cogantur, ut in aulis Magnatum quorundam visuenit, singulis mensibus ad summum bis vomitum sibi imperent, multorum namque morborum seminaria vna exturbari extra omnem est controuersiam. Quod enim ad sanitatem confert prorogandam&conseruandâ,prętermittere vel negligere homo mortalis non debet, nisi proprii sui corporis carnifex, tortor ac destructor perhiberi velit, quod ab homine Christiano debet esse quam longe alienum. Et certe nemo existimet, licet temperantissime etiam circa cibum & potum versetur, non posse in corpore superfluitates inutilesque sensim humores, hoc est, ad nutriendum ineptos, coaceruari, qui morborum tandem causam & fomentum sint præbituri: Et tantum de propositá quæst. dixisse sufficiat.
units.tr: Those who are going to take pains over health and the prolonging of life, especially if they are compelled to live more intemperately, as happens in the courts of certain great men, should impose on themselves vomiting at most twice a month; for that one removal drives out the seeds of many diseases is beyond all controversy. For a mortal man ought not to neglect or omit what contributes to prolonging and preserving health, unless he wishes to be regarded as the executioner, torturer and destroyer of his own body, which must be far removed from a Christian man. And certainly no one should think that, however temperately he lives in regard to food and drink, superfluous and useless humours, that is, those unfit for nourishment, cannot gradually collect in the body, and these will in the end provide the cause and fuel of diseases. Let it suffice to have said this much on the question proposed.
